Cinematic.cinematic.fallOfTungning.koxingaSon.beat:
In 1662, Koxinga died of illness in Tainan.
His eldest son, Zheng Jing, inherited the newly born kingdom.

In 1664, Zheng Jing renamed "Tungtu" to "Tungning" —
"Eastern Peace."
A Han kingdom on an island that had never belonged to the Han.

Chief minister Chen Yonghua built Taiwan's first Confucian temple in Tainan and founded its first official school.
Books from Fujian, seeds from the South Seas, took root in this new soil.

Tungning's merchant ships sailed between Nagasaki, Luzon, and Batavia.
Silk, sugar, and porcelain flowed in every direction.
Two decades of peace raised a generation on the island.
Cinematic.cinematic.fallOfTungning.palaceCoup.beat:
On his deathbed, Zheng Jing named his eldest son, Zheng Kezang, as successor.
Kezang had been groomed by Chen Yonghua —
composed, decisive, already capable of governing at nineteen.

But the chief of the imperial guard, Feng Xifan, did not trust him.
He spread rumors: "Kezang is no blood of the Zhengs — he is an adopted child."

Three days after Zheng Jing's death, Zheng Kezang was summoned to the palace.
In the great hall, he was strangled by trusted guards.
He was nineteen. He had reigned for three days.

Feng Xifan's son-in-law, the twelve-year-old Zheng Keshuang,
was raised up as the new lord of Tungning.

A child king, a manipulating minister, and a veteran soldier who trusted neither.
That night, the foundations of Tungning began to crack.
Cinematic.cinematic.fallOfTungning.penghuBattle.be:
In the summer of 1683, the Kangxi Emperor appointed Shi Lang as Admiral of the Fujian Naval Forces.
The Qing court had prepared for this moment for a decade —
three hundred warships, twenty thousand sailors.

Shi Lang had once served under Zheng Zhilong, and once been Koxinga's second-in-command.
His father and brother had died at Koxinga's hand.
This battle was not only state business —
it was a thirty-year private feud, finally being settled.

On June 22, the Qing fleet set sail from Tongshan, heading straight for Penghu.
Liu Guoxuan, commander of Tungning's navy, took Penghu as his natural stronghold and assembled two hundred warships to meet him.

Three days of battle. Cannon, boarding, fire-attacks, hand-to-hand.
Over the Penghu bay, smoke blotted out the sky.
Tungning's navy lost more than half its ships.

Liu Guoxuan led the survivors back to Taiwan.
From Penghu to Chengtien Prefecture was but one favorable wind away —
but he no longer had ships to fight with.
Cinematic.cinematic.fallOfTungning.penghuBattle.ti: Fire on the Sea at Penghu
Cinematic.cinematic.fallOfTungning.subtitle: 1683 · The Fall of Tungning
In Chengtien Prefecture, Zheng Keshuang heard the news from Penghu through the eunuchs.
He was thirteen. His ministers were silent.

Feng Xifan argued for terms.
Liu Guoxuan was silent for a long time, then nodded: "The army can fight no more."

I was thirteen.
They laid the paper before me and told me to write my name.
I wrote it.
They told me this was called "surrender."
I did not know what I was giving up —
and they did not tell me there was any other choice.

I served your grandfather.
I served your father.
Your grandfather killed my father and my brother.
Today, I stand before Chengtien Prefecture —
not for victory, but for thirty years of debt, finally laid to rest.

From the "Kingdom of Tungning" to the "Prefecture of Taiwan" — only one sheet of paper apart.
But that sheet changed the next three hundred years.
From then on, this island was no longer a refuge of the Han —
it was the frontier of an empire.

August 1683. Zheng Keshuang signed his name on the letter of surrender.
It was the first time he had not used the reign title "Yongli, Year 37."

Shi Lang entered Chengtien Prefecture, but did not first take his seat at court.
Instead, he walked to the Yanping Prince Shrine.
Before the spirit tablet of Koxinga, he knelt, and he wept.
Cinematic.cinematic.fallOfTungning.surrender.title: The Letter of Surrender
Cinematic.cinematic.fallOfTungning.taiwanPrefectur:
In 1684, the Qing court established the Prefecture of Taiwan under Fujian Province.
Taiwan was, for the first time, drawn onto the map of China.

Zheng Keshuang and his family were relocated to Beijing, granted the title "Duke of Haicheng," and confined to the capital for life.
He lived to thirty-seven, and never saw Taiwan again.

For the next 212 years, Taiwan was the Qing's frontier.
The Han came across the sea in endless waves.
The indigenous peoples retreated, inch by inch, toward the mountains.

Today, the Yanping Prince Shrine still stands in Tainan.
Koxinga's statue faces west —
toward the mainland he never reached in life.

A dynasty vanished.
An island stayed behind.
Cinematic.cinematic.fallOfTungning.title: The Fall of Tungning
Cinematic.cinematic.fallOfTungning.westwardCampaig:
In 1673, the Revolt of the Three Feudatories broke out in China.
Zheng Jing saw his chance to return —
to finish what his father, Koxinga, had not.

He landed in Fujian, took Quanzhou and Zhangzhou in succession, and pressed all the way toward Guangdong.
The banner of Tungning had returned to the mainland.

But the Three Feudatories did not trust one another, and the alliance fell apart quickly.
The Qing struck back. Zheng's armies retreated step by step.
In 1680, Zheng Jing returned to Tungning empty-handed, bringing back only broken troops and old wounds.

In 1681, Zheng Jing died of illness, aged thirty-nine.
He left behind an empty treasury, a battered army,
and a divided court.
Dream and Ash of the Western Campaign
Cinematic.cinematic.fortZeelandiaSiege.aftermath.b:
Today, the broken walls of Fort Zeelandia still stand in Anping, Tainan.
Tourists climb a surviving section of wall and take photos: "I'm at Anping Old Fort."

In Tainan, the Yanping Prince Shrine burns with incense; Koxinga has become a god.
In Amsterdam, the VOC archives carry only one line:
"Formosa, lost 1662."

In 1675, Coyett was pardoned and returned home; he published "Neglected Formosa" in the Netherlands.
He did not speak of victory or defeat. He said only:
"I hope future generations know — we were once here."

A war —
between the founder of an empire, and a company,
on a single island.
An island that never belonged to either of them.
Cinematic.cinematic.fortZeelandiaSiege.collapse.be:
Inside the fort, a Dutch soldier named Hans Radis climbed the wall and defected to Koxinga.
He brought a secret:
the greatest weakness of Fort Zeelandia was Fort Utrecht, on the hill behind it.

In January 1662, Koxinga's army pounded Fort Utrecht with twenty-eight cannons, day and night.
Three days later the bastion collapsed; the defenders all perished.

From the heights of Utrecht, Koxinga's guns could fire directly down into Fort Zeelandia.
Forty years of walls were walls no more.

Coyett proposed surrender to the council.
He had held the fort for 270 days.

I held the fort for 270 days.
The reinforcements Batavia promised never truly arrived.
I signed this treaty to save a thousand lives —
not to hand over this island.

This island never belonged to the Red-Haired Barbarians.
They built their walls, but they could not change the names of the land.
Today, we write the names back —
"Tungtu," "Chengtien," "land of the Han."

Thirty-four years later, Coyett wrote "Neglected Formosa" in Amsterdam.
He said: "I did not lose to Koxinga —
I lost to my own company."

February 1, 1662. The articles of surrender were signed at Koxinga's camp.
The Dutch departed in good order, carrying their arms, their banners, and the memory of a generation.
Inside, Governor Coyett commanded 1,100 defenders.
Outside, 25,000 of Koxinga's troops encircled the entire sandbar.

Day one: a full assault — cannon, scaling ladders, rockets.
The bastion's double walls held against everything.

The assault failed. Koxinga switched to a long siege.
Fort Provintia became his central command.

Inside: rice ran out, the wells turned foul, scurvy spread.
Outside: Han tenant farmers refused to sell a single grain of rice to the Red-Haired Barbarians.

Reinforcements from Batavia did reach the outer sea.
A typhoon scattered the fleet. They turned and left.
Coyett watched from the bastion for three days. He did not watch a fourth.
Cinematic.cinematic.fortZeelandiaSiege.retreat.bea:
February 9, 1662. Coyett led the remaining Dutch aboard their ships and sailed from Tayouan.
On the bastion, the company flag was slowly lowered.

Back in Batavia, Coyett was court-martialed.
The charge: signing surrender without authority, losing land and city.
The sentence: life exile, banished to the barren island of Rosengain.

Koxinga renamed Tayouan "Tungtu" and established the "Chengtien Prefecture."
He was already planning his next move — to attack Luzon, link up with what remained of the Southern Ming, and retake the mainland.

In June 1662, Koxinga died of illness in Tainan, aged thirty-eight.
It was only four months after his capture of Zeelandia.
In 1660, Koxinga was steadily losing ground in Xiamen.
With Qing armies at the gates, he needed a new rear base.

He Bin, the interpreter, crossed the sea from Tayouan.
He brought maps of Fort Zeelandia, tide charts, and a defector's promise:
"The Red-Haired Barbarians on that island will not stand a fight."

April 30, 1661. Twenty-five thousand troops of Koxinga's army and over four hundred warships
slipped through Luermen on the high tide.
From the city walls, the Dutch saw only sails on the sea.

Within days, Fort Provintia surrendered.
Only Zeelandia remained, standing on its sandbar —
from then on, alone in the sea.
Cinematic.cinematic.fortZeelandiaSiege.subtitle: 1661–1662 · Siege of Fort Zeelandia
Cinematic.cinematic.fortZeelandiaSiege.tayouanFlag:
In 1624, the Dutch East India Company raised its company flag on a sandbar off Tainan — Tayouan.
That year, the name "Taiwan" did not yet exist.

On that sandbar they built East Asia's strongest bastion fortress of the time — Fort Zeelandia.
Brick walls on four sides, bastions at four corners, double curtain walls.

Silk came from Fujian, silver from Manila, deerskins from the Siraya, sugar from the cane fields of Sinkan.
Tayouan became the busiest entrepôt on the Western Pacific.

Beyond the walls were Han tenant farmers and Siraya hunters.
Inside the walls: merchants, soldiers, missionaries, and a company flag fluttering in the sea wind.
Cinematic.cinematic.fortZeelandiaSiege.title: Siege of Fort Zeelandia
Cinematic.cinematic.linShuangwenUprising.changhuaF: On the night of November 27, 1786, Lin Shuangwen stormed Changhua's walled city. Magistrate Yu Jun did not live to see reinforcements. Within three days the entire Changhua basin had fallen.
Entering the city, Lin raised the Shuntien banner and declared a reign era. He did not call himself emperor, only "Allied Marshal" — a humble title in keeping with Tiandihui tradition.

To the south in Fengshan, the Quanzhou-born Zhuang Datian rose at the same hour. Lin and Zhuang owed each other nothing, yet between them they bled the Qing garrison from two directions. South of Changhua, almost the whole island lay between the two armies.

By early 1787, Lin's forces had pushed to the southern edge of Tamsui; Zhuang Datian was advancing on Taiwan Prefecture itself. The Qing had fewer than five thousand troops on the island — nowhere near enough. The whole island nearly changed hands.
Cinematic.cinematic.linShuangwenUprising.chiayiNam: Qianlong decreed that "Chu-luo" be permanently renamed "Chia-i." It was one of the rare cases in Chinese history of an emperor renaming a city by edict — a name forged in siege, still in use to this day.

In Tainan, Changhua and Chiayi, "Fukang'an's Pacification Stelae" rose — inscribed in Chinese, Manchu, Mongolian and Tibetan. For nineteenth-century Taiwan, this was the Qing empire's proudest frontier victory.
But in Dali-yi, in Changhua, in every Zhangzhou settlement, no one would speak Lin Shuangwen's name in public. He became a silent ancestor — traitor and hero at once, depending on where you stood.

What did the uprising burn? The Triad's red banners, twenty-six county yamen, thirty thousand lives, and the deepest layers of Taiwan's memory. Zhangzhou–Quanzhou feuds, settler–indigenous relations, the fragility of Qing rule — every question, after 446 days of civil war, was harder to answer than before.
Cinematic.cinematic.linShuangwenUprising.flight.be: Lin fled into the central mountains, hoping to find refuge among Atayal and Pazeh villages. But Fukang'an's men reached the indigenous headmen first, with silver, salt, and bolts of cloth. The frontier that should have sheltered him was bought, gap by gap.
At dawn on February 5, 1788, Lin Shuangwen was captured at Lao-qu-qi (in today's Miaoli County's Gongguan Township) by Qing troops guided by indigenous scouts. Only fifty men remained at his side.

Sent to Beijing in chains, Lin was executed by lingchi — death by a thousand cuts — on the tenth day of the third lunar month. He was thirty-two. He did not beg, nor did he betray a single fellow Triad leader. Zhuang Datian fell at the same hour in the south.

The 446-day civil war killed more than thirty thousand on both sides; half of all houses were destroyed. Fukang'an raised stone tablets across Taiwan listing thirty-eight loyal commanders — all Quanzhou, Hakka, or indigenous. The Zhangzhou were preserved in court archives only as rebels.
Cinematic.cinematic.linShuangwenUprising.fukanganC: Qianlong dismissed Chang-qing and named his nephew-by-blood — Fukang'an — to command reinforcements from nine provinces across the strait. Fukang'an was then the empire's most-favoured general, of the Bordered Yellow Banner. The emperor hosted his farewell feast in person.

In November 1787, Fukang'an led forty thousand troops from Xiamen and landed at Lugang. The local Quanzhou settlers met him with oxen and rice wine — their grudges against Lin's Zhangzhou faction were ancient. Ethnic division had become the Qing's instrument.

Fukang'an marched south along the western flank of Mount Bagua, smashing three Lin defensive lines in three days. By late November he had broken the siege of Chu-luo. When the gates opened, the defenders knelt in the streets, weeping. Many could no longer stand.
He pressed northward. In the first lunar month of 1788, he stormed Lin's stronghold at Dali-yi. The village burned through the night. Lin escaped on horseback, riding for the indigenous frontier.
Cinematic.cinematic.linShuangwenUprising.subtitle: 1786–1788 · The 446-day rebellion that renamed Chiayi
Cinematic.cinematic.linShuangwenUprising.tiandihui: At the eastern edge of the Changhua plain, the rice fields of Dali-yi had just been harvested. Before dawn, the young Lin Shuangwen was waiting by the ancestral hall — thirty-one years old, newly the head of the Triad's central Taiwan branch.

That year, the long-running feud between Zhangzhou and Quanzhou settlers had been smouldering for three years. Ethnicity, land, irrigation, religion — every reason was enough to spend a life. The Qing officials on Taiwan were too busy collecting taxes to care.

The Tiandihui wrote its oaths on red paper: "blood-sworn brothers, restore the Ming, overthrow the Qing." In Lin's family hall hung a small banner of two characters — "Shun-tien," Heaven's mandate — a Ming-loyalist emblem he had kept hidden for years.

In November 1786, the Changhua magistrate sent constables to Dali-yi to arrest Triad members. They burned a house as a warning. The whole village turned to rage. Lin's road forward had only one direction.
Cinematic.cinematic.linShuangwenUprising.title: The Lin Shuangwen Uprising
Cinematic.cinematic.linShuangwenUprising.zhuluoDef: The walls of Chu-luo (today's Chiayi) closed around two thousand defenders and ten thousand civilians, with grain for less than three months. Magistrate Zhang Zhi hanged himself in shame. Vice-General Chen Bangguang took up command.
Chu-luo held one month, then another. First the grain ran out, then the horses, then bark and grass. But the wall did not fall. Lin Shuangwen launched seventy attacks. Every one was thrown back.
Word reached Beijing. Qianlong was furious. He decreed that Chu-luo be temporarily renamed "Chia-i" — "praising loyalty." A decree to rally the besieged — and to save the court's face.

But the reinforcements never arrived. Min-Zhe Governor Chang-qing sent troops across the strait three times. Each crossing was turned back by typhoons, broken supply lines, and uncooperative islanders. Chu-luo held alone for two more months.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.crossing.beat.1.tex:
After the war, Mona Rudao's remains were long kept in a specimen room at National Taiwan University's medical college.
In 1973, they were finally returned to Wushe for burial.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.crossing.beat.2.tex:
In the 1980s, Taiwanese society began to re-examine this history.
Monuments, documentaries, and scholarship slowly restored their names.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.crossing.beat.3.tex:
April 23, 2008.
The Seediq were formally separated from the Atayal
and recognized as Taiwan's fourteenth officially acknowledged indigenous people.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.crossing.beat.4.tex:
"A true person must cross the Rainbow Bridge."
Eighty years on, they have finally crossed.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.crossing.beat.5.tex:
And we — we are still learning
how to remember their names.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.crossing.title: Crossing the Rainbow Bridge
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.kawanakajima.beat.1:
The surviving Seediq dwindled from over twelve hundred to five hundred.
They were forcibly interned at Lodofu and Sipo.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.kawanakajima.beat.2:
In April 1931, the Japanese incited the rival "loyal aborigines" to raid the camps.
The Second Wushe Incident broke out — another 216 dead.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.kawanakajima.beat.3:
The remaining 298 were forcibly relocated to "Kawanakajima" on the banks of the Beigang River —
today's Qingliu community in Ren'ai, Nantou.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.kawanakajima.beat.4:
From then on, the names of the six tribes vanished from the map.
The mountains fell silent for nearly half a century.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.kawanakajima.beat.5:
In 1934, a hunter discovered partially decomposed remains in the Mahebo mountains.
They were identified as Mona Rudao.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.kawanakajima.title: Echoes from Kawanakajima
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.mahebo.beat.1.text: The Governor-General's Office mobilized over three thousand troops and police — with mountain artillery, machine guns, and aircraft — to attack Wushe.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.mahebo.beat.2.text:
Mountain artillery thundered day and night.
The Seediq retreated into the Mahebo caves, defending with hunting rifles and machetes against a modern army.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.mahebo.beat.3.text:
The fighting reached a stalemate.
In violation of international convention, Japanese aircraft dropped vesicant poison gas.
The forests yellowed; the streams changed color.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.mahebo.beat.4.text:
To spare the warriors and avoid the shame of capture,
the Seediq women and children, beneath the great trees of the mountains, hanged themselves together.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.mahebo.beat.5.text:
Mona Rudao's wife, his sisters, his children —
one by one, they crossed the Rainbow Bridge.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.mahebo.beat.6.text:
December 1, 1930. The Mahebo caves fell.
Mona Rudao walked deep into the mountains. He was never seen again.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.mahebo.title: The Mahebo Caves
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.rage.beat.1.text:
Japan rolled out its "Aborigine Pacification Policy" across Taiwan.
Guard lines pushed deeper into the mountains; police stations were placed in every tribe.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.rage.beat.2.text:
The Seediq were forced into corvée labor — hauling timber, cutting mountain roads.
Their hunting grounds shrank, their guns were confiscated, headhunting forbidden.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.rage.beat.3.text:
Mona Rudao, chief of Mahebo, felt his people's dignity stripped away, inch by inch.
But he chose silence. He chose to wait.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.rage.beat.4.text:
Early October, 1930.
Mona Rudao's son, Tado Mona, was slapped by a Japanese officer for "unclean hands" while offering wine.
Thirty-five years of pent-up fury finally found its outlet.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.rage.title: Fire in the Mountains
"A true person must cross the Rainbow Bridge."
This is Gaya — the ancestral law of the Seediq.

Deep in the Central Mountain Range lies Wushe, where six Seediq tribes have lived for generations:
Mahebo, Boalum, Hogo, Lodofu, Talowan, and Suku.

A man must take a head in battle to earn the facial tattoos on his forehead and chin.
A woman must weave intricate cloth to earn the slanted lines on her cheeks.
Only then, in death, can they cross the Rainbow Bridge and meet their ancestors.

In 1895, the Qing Empire ceded Taiwan to Japan.
The world beyond the mountains was overturned.
But the people inside the mountains did not yet know.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.rainbowBridge.title: Children of the Rainbow Bridge
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.subtitle: 1930 · Seediq Bale
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.title: Seediq Bale
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.uprising.beat.1.tex:
October 27, 1930. Wushe, Nōkō District, Taichū Prefecture.
At six in the morning, before the mountain mist had cleared, the Rising Sun flag was slowly raised at Wushe Public School.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.uprising.beat.2.tex:
This was the day of the Taiwan Shrine Festival.
The regional joint schools' athletic meet had been scheduled for the same day.
Japanese officers, officials, teachers, and their families gathered before the school's main platform.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.uprising.beat.3.tex:
Mona Rudao was nearly fifty.
Deep in the mountains, he had waited years for this moment.
Behind him stood six tribes — some three hundred warriors with hunting rifles and machetes.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.uprising.beat.4.per:
I waited thirty-five years.
When the drums sounded, I finally pulled the trigger.
The bullet flew past the ceremonial flag and struck the face of the man who once slapped my son.
This is not revenge — this is Gaya.

The drums were still playing — I thought it was another drill.
Then I turned and saw Inspector Satsuka collapse.
Then the second shot, the third.
The principal ran toward the students, trying to push them into the classroom — but he himself never made it inside.

Eighty years on, we are still arguing:
should this be called the "Wushe Incident," the "Wushe Uprising," or the "Anti-Colonial War"?
To name a thing is to take a stand.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.uprising.beat.4.tex:
Around eight in the morning, the ceremony began.
The drums of the flag-raising had not yet died down when the first shot rang out from the forest.
The assembly ground became a battlefield in an instant.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.uprising.beat.5.tex:
That morning, 134 Japanese died in the Wushe region.
Among them: teachers, students, the wives and children of officials.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.uprising.beat.6.tex:
News traveled the telegraph lines and reached Taipei before noon.
The Governor-General's Office reeled. The whole island held its breath.
Cinematic.cinematic.seediqBale.uprising.title: The Morning of the School Athletic Meet

Figures.figure.andorikichi.bio:
Ando Rikichi, born in 1884 in Miyagi Prefecture, Japan, was an Imperial Japanese Army general who served as the nineteenth and last Governor-General of colonial Taiwan and led the formal Japanese transfer of the island to Chinese authority in October 1945.

He graduated from the Imperial Japanese Army Academy and rose through the army's general-staff and infantry tracks across a four-decade career in the late Meiji, Taisho, and Showa periods. He held senior commands across the empire, including military attaché posts in Europe, divisional command in China, and command of the Southern China Area Army during the early Sino-Japanese War.

In December 1944 he was appointed Governor-General of Taiwan and concurrently commander of the Tenth Area Army, the principal Japanese ground force on the island, consolidating civil and military authority on the eve of an expected Allied invasion.

Under his tenure the colony underwent its most intense wartime mobilization, including conscription of Taiwanese men into the imperial military, expanded volunteer auxiliary recruitment, and massive air-raid damage to major cities from sustained Allied bombing in 1944 and 1945.

He prepared elaborate beach and inland defenses against an Allied amphibious invasion that, in the event, never came — Allied strategists chose to bypass Taiwan and concentrate on Okinawa and the Japanese home islands.

Following the Showa Emperor's surrender broadcast on 15 August 1945, he prepared the orderly handover of the colony to Chinese forces under the directives of SCAP General Order No. 1. On 25 October 1945, in a public ceremony at the Taipei City Hall, he signed the formal instrument of surrender of Taiwan and the Pescadores to Chen Yi, representing the Republic of China and the Allied Powers. The ceremony, attended by representatives of the Allies and broadcast across the island, ended fifty years of Japanese colonial rule on Taiwan.

He oversaw the orderly withdrawal of more than four hundred thousand Japanese soldiers, administrators, and civilian colonists from Taiwan over the following year, while remaining nominally in command of the residual Japanese establishment on the island. He was extradited to Shanghai in 1946 to face war-crimes proceedings under Allied military authority, and was found dead in his cell of cyanide poisoning, an apparent suicide, in April 1946 at the age of 62.

Ando is remembered as the formal closer of the Japanese imperial chapter in Taiwan, the official whose signature ended five decades of colonial governance and inaugurated the bitter transition to mainland Chinese administration.
Figures.figure.andorikichi.event1: Last Governor-General of Taiwan; formally surrendered the colony to the ROC (1945)
Figures.figure.andorikichi.title: Last Governor-General of Taiwan
Figures.figure.anglee.bio: Ang Lee, born in 1954 in Chaozhou, Pingtung, is Taiwan's most representative film director on the world stage and the first Asian to win the Academy Award for Best Director. Raised in a family that valued education, he went to the United States as a young man to study film production at New York University, laying a solid creative foundation. He first drew notice with his "Father Knows Best" trilogy — "Pushing Hands," "The Wedding Banquet," and "Eat Drink Man Woman" — subtly depicting the tensions between Eastern and Western culture and family ethics. He then moved into English-language film, directing works such as "Sense and Sensibility" and showing a command of different cultural subjects. In 2000 his martial-arts film "Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon" swept the international scene and won the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film, bringing Chinese-language cinema into the global mainstream. In 2006, with "Brokeback Mountain," he became the first Asian to win the Academy Award for Best Director, and in 2013 he won it a second time for "Life of Pi." His works span art film, martial arts, epic, and fantasy, consistently attentive to themes of human nature, desire, and cultural identity. He is known for a gentle, restrained style and precise storytelling, combining artistic depth with commercial success. Lee is seen as a symbol of Taiwanese cinema and Chinese-language cultural export, his creative path across East and West long a key marker of Taiwan's soft power.
Figures.figure.anglee.event1: Won international acclaim and an Oscar with "Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon" (2001)
Figures.figure.anglee.event2: Twice won the Academy Award for Best Director (2006, 2013)
Figures.figure.anglee.title: Film Director & Two-Time Academy Award Winner
Figures.figure.arokus.bio: Arokus was the paramount chief of Mudan village (牡丹社), one of the most powerful Paiwan settlements in the mountainous Hengchun Peninsula of southern Taiwan, who led his people through escalating contact with the outside world before dying in battle against a Japanese expeditionary force in 1874. The Mudan people under Arokus occupied a strategically important interior position on the peninsula, and their territory neighbored coastlines where foreign ships frequently wrecked, placing them in recurring contact — sometimes violent — with shipwreck survivors from across the region. In November and December 1871, fifty-four crew members of a Ryukyuan vessel from Miyako Island were shipwrecked on the peninsula's southern shore; fifty of them were killed by Paiwan men, an event that set in motion the first modern Japanese overseas military expedition. Arokus, as chief of Mudan — the leading village among several implicated in the killings — bore the primary political responsibility for the incident in the eyes of Japanese planners, who used it to challenge the Qing court on the ambiguous status of the island's indigenous territories. When Japan launched its 1874 Taiwan Expedition under General Saigō Tsugumichi, landing several thousand troops on the Hengchun Peninsula in May of that year, Arokus organized the Mudan resistance and led his warriors in a series of engagements against Japanese forces. In the battle at Shimen (石門) in May 1874, Arokus was killed while commanding the defense of a narrow gorge, becoming the most prominent indigenous casualty of the campaign; his death broke the organized Paiwan resistance and allowed Japanese forces to advance toward the mountain villages. The engagement at Shimen became a defining moment in Japanese colonial historiography, portrayed as a military victory that demonstrated Japan's capacity to project force beyond its home islands. The diplomatic settlement that followed — in which China paid Japan an indemnity of five hundred thousand taels and implicitly acknowledged Japan's claim over the Ryukyus — transformed the geopolitics of the region and opened the door to Japan's formal annexation of Taiwan twenty years later. Arokus himself left no written record; his actions and death are reconstructed from Japanese military reports, Qing diplomatic correspondence, and oral tradition preserved by his Paiwan descendants. In the postwar era, his story underwent significant reinterpretation in Taiwan, shifting from a Japanese colonial narrative of conquest to a recognized act of indigenous resistance against imperial aggression. A monument to the fallen Paiwan warriors stands today at Shimen, near the site where Arokus died, and the Mudan Incident is now taught as the event that catalyzed the geopolitical transformation leading to Taiwan's colonial era. Arokus is generally regarded as a symbol of Paiwan resistance — a chief who faced the first armed incursion by a modern military power onto Taiwanese soil and chose to fight rather than submit, at the cost of his own life.
Figures.figure.arokus.event1: Organized Paiwan resistance against the Japanese 1874 Taiwan Expedition following the Mudan Incident
Figures.figure.arokus.event2: Died at the Battle of Shimen (1874), triggering the diplomatic settlement that reshaped East Asian geopolitics
Figures.figure.arokus.title: Chief of Mudan Village, Paiwan
Figures.figure.audreytang.bio: Audrey Tang, born in 1981 in Taipei, is a representative figure of contemporary Taiwan's civic technology and digital governance, and the first transgender member of the cabinet. Showing exceptional aptitude from childhood, she left conventional schooling early because it did not suit her, turning to self-study and taking up programming as a teenager. She was active in the free-software and open-source communities, contributing to many international open-source projects and building an international reputation in software engineering. Long attentive to combining technology with public participation, she was an important member of Taiwan's "g0v" civic-tech movement, promoting government transparency and citizen collaboration. In 2016 she was invited into the cabinet as a minister without portfolio responsible for open government, social innovation, and youth participation, advancing digital democracy through innovative collaborative methods. She promoted online deliberation platforms such as vTaiwan to let citizens take part in policy discussion, and during the COVID-19 pandemic she helped build digital tools such as the mask-availability map, drawing wide international attention. In 2022, when Taiwan established the Ministry of Digital Affairs, she became its first minister, overseeing digital governance, cybersecurity, and internet resilience. She advocates "radical transparency" and open collaboration and frequently shares Taiwan's experience of digital democracy at international forums. Tang is seen as a symbol of Taiwan's digital governance and inclusive diversity, her practice spanning the technical and public spheres embodying the innovative image of contemporary Taiwan.
Figures.figure.audreytang.event1: Became a cabinet minister without portfolio for open government (2016)
Figures.figure.audreytang.event2: Became the first Minister of Digital Affairs (2022)
Figures.figure.audreytang.title: First Digital Minister & Civic-Tech Advocate
Figures.figure.barclay.bio: Thomas Barclay, born in 1849 in Glasgow, Scotland, was a Free Church of Scotland-trained Presbyterian missionary whose nearly sixty-year ministry in southern Taiwan made him one of the architects of modern Taiwanese-language print culture and theological education. He took first-class honors at the University of Glasgow as a precocious student of mathematics and philosophy and entered service with the English Presbyterian Mission with the intention of joining its Taiwan field from the outset of his career. He arrived at Takow (打狗, modern Kaohsiung) in 1875 and the following year settled at Tainan, which would remain his permanent base for the rest of his life. In 1876 he founded Tainan Theological College (臺南神學院), the first institution of higher theological education in Taiwan, intended to train an indigenous Taiwanese pastorate. In 1881 he imported Taiwan's first modern printing press from England and personally trained local typesetters in romanized Taiwanese Hokkien (白話字, Pe̍h-ōe-jī), creating a publishing infrastructure that would survive every subsequent regime. In July 1885 he launched the Taiwan Church News (臺灣府城教會報, Tâi-oân Hú-siâⁿ Kàu-hōe-pò), the first newspaper printed in Taiwan and today the longest continuously published periodical produced on the island. He devoted decades of philological labor to revising the romanized Hokkien Bible, completing the New Testament in 1916 and the Old Testament in 1933, foundational works for the literary tradition of written Taiwanese. He also compiled a major supplement to Carstairs Douglas's Amoy dictionary, expanding the available scholarly resources for the study of southern Min Chinese. During the Japanese takeover in October 1895, when Tainan was on the brink of bombardment by approaching Japanese forces under General Nogi Maresuke, the city's gentry asked Barclay to lead a foreign-missionary delegation that negotiated a peaceful surrender. The intervention spared Tainan from the destruction visited on Hsinchu and other northern cities and won Barclay the lifelong gratitude of the city's residents and the eventual conferral of a Japanese imperial decoration. He continued his work through the early Japanese era, mentoring a generation of Taiwanese pastors, journalists, and educators, and died in Tainan on 5 October 1935 at the age of 86. Barclay is remembered alongside George Leslie Mackay as the most consequential foreign figure of late-Qing and early colonial Taiwan, his romanized Hokkien Bible and Tainan press still anchoring the institutional life of Taiwanese Christianity today.
Figures.figure.barclay.event1: Founded Tainan Theological College (1876) and the Taiwan Church News (1885)
Figures.figure.barclay.event2: Revised the romanized Taiwanese Hokkien Bible; negotiated Tainan's peaceful surrender in 1895
Figures.figure.barclay.title: Presbyterian Missionary
Figures.figure.boyang.bio: Bo Yang, born Kuo Yi-tung in 1920 in Henan, was one of the most influential and controversial writers and cultural critics of post-war Taiwan. He came to Taiwan with the government after the Chinese Civil War, working in teaching and journalism and becoming known for essays, fiction, and historical writing. His essays, sharp and satirical, boldly criticized current affairs and social ills and were widely popular. In 1968, for serializing a translation of the American "Popeye" comic that the authorities read as an allusion insulting the head of state, he was arrested on charges such as "insulting the president" — the so-called "Popeye Incident." He was consequently imprisoned on Green Island and elsewhere for nine years, a famous case of literary persecution during the White Terror. In prison he immersed himself in writing, beginning "Bo Yang's Edition of the Comprehensive Mirror," a retelling of Chinese history in accessible vernacular, turning his years behind bars into a long writing project. After his release he continued to write, publishing "The Ugly Chinaman" in 1985, a pointed critique of what he called "soy-paste vat culture" that sparked wide and heated debate across the Chinese-speaking world. In his later years he devoted himself to human-rights causes, attentive to wrongful imprisonment and freedom of speech and taking part in international human-rights work. He died in Taiwan in 2008, and part of his ashes were, by his wish, interred on Green Island. Bo Yang is seen as a representative writer who resisted authoritarianism and critiqued cultural malaise through words, his imprisonment and cultural criticism an important case for understanding the course of Taiwan's freedom of speech.
Figures.figure.boyang.event2: Wrote "The Ugly Chinaman," a cultural critique
Figures.figure.boyang.title: Writer & Political Prisoner
Figures.figure.caiaxin.bio: Tsai A-hsin was born in 1899 in Taipei and lost her father young, growing up in hardship that only sharpened her determination. Defying the expectations placed on women of her day, she travelled to Japan and graduated from the Tokyo Women's Medical College, then returned to Taiwan around 1921 to become the island's first female physician. She opened the Qingxin Hospital in Taichung, which grew into a substantial practice, and — keenly aware that most Taiwanese women still gave birth without trained help — she founded a school to train midwives, spreading modern maternal care across central Taiwan. Her life was marked by upheaval, including a difficult marriage and the turbulence of war and its aftermath. In later years she emigrated to Canada, where she continued to support Taiwanese causes from afar and endowed a foundation for widows. Her remarkable story later inspired a celebrated Taiwanese novel. Tsai A-hsin died in Canada in 1990, remembered as a pioneer who opened the medical profession to the women of Taiwan.
Figures.figure.caiaxin.event2: Founded a midwife-training school in Taichung
Figures.figure.caiaxin.title: Taiwan's First Female Physician
Figures.figure.caipeihuo.bio: Tsai Pei-huo (1889–1983) was born in Beigang in present-day Yunlin and became one of the core figures of cultural enlightenment and the modern Taiwanese national movement. After graduating from the Government-General's National Language School he studied at the Tokyo Higher Normal School in Japan, where he was deeply influenced by the climate of Taishō democracy and by Christian thought. In 1920 he joined fellow Taiwanese students in Tokyo to organize the Shin Min Hui society and launch the journal Taiwan Youth, becoming an early architect of the national movement. Returning to Taiwan in 1921 he joined Lin Hsien-tang in founding the Taiwanese Cultural Association and served as its managing director, running the day-to-day administration and propaganda work. From the same year he took part in the Petition Movement for the Establishment of a Taiwanese Parliament and was imprisoned in 1923 during the so-called Public Order Police Law Incident as one of the principal defendants. He was a long-time advocate of Pe̍h-ōe-jī, the church romanization of Taiwanese, arguing for mass literacy through a phonetic script, and compiled teaching materials and dictionaries to support it. He also composed nationalist songs such as the Taiwan Self-Government Song and 'Our Taiwan,' weaving the consciousness of the national movement into popular culture. After the 1927 split of the Cultural Association he remained with Lin Hsien-tang on the moderate right and helped to found the Taiwanese People's Party, sustaining a gradualist constitutional path. From the 1930s, as colonial repression intensified, his public activism receded, and during the Pacific War he undertook personal liaison and interpretation duties on the Chinese mainland. After 1945 he joined the Kuomintang and served as a minister without portfolio in the Executive Yuan, while continuing his church and social-reform work. He died in Taipei in 1983 at the age of 94, making him the longest-lived of the leading figures of the colonial-era national movement. He is widely credited with being the propaganda and organizational core of Taiwan's cultural enlightenment movement and a foundational figure of the Pe̍h-ōe-jī movement.
Figures.figure.caipeihuo.event1: 1921 Co-founded the Taiwanese Cultural Association, served as managing director
Figures.figure.caipeihuo.event2: 1923 Imprisoned in the Public Order Police Law Incident
Figures.figure.caipeihuo.title: Managing Director of the Cultural Association
Figures.figure.caiqian.bio: Cai Qian was the most renowned pirate king of the Qing maritime frontier during the Jiaqing era, born in 1761 to an impoverished fishing family on the coast of Tong'an in Fujian; orphaned as a child, he worked as a shoemaker's apprentice and a dock coolie in his youth. In the 1790s he turned to smuggling and piracy along the Fujian-Zhejiang coast, and through bold seamanship and a precise understanding of tides and monsoons he rapidly rose above his rivals, absorbing the other freebooter bands by the turn of the century to command a fleet of over a hundred ships and more than twenty thousand men. His flagship was enormous and equipped with bronze European cannon purchased from foreign smugglers, giving him firepower and range that outclassed the obsolete vessels of the imperial navy. He styled himself King of Zhenhai Weiwu, proclaimed the reign era Guangming, and instituted a protection-tax system that operated across the Fujian, Zhejiang, and Guangdong coasts. Every merchant ship crossing the strait was required to pay him a duty and receive his outbound tax certificate in order to pass the Black Ditch safely; those who refused were plundered or massacred, and in effect he operated a parallel maritime regime alongside the Qing. In 1804 the alarmed Qing court dispatched the Zhejiang admiral Li Changgeng to lead an elite naval force across the strait against him, and the two sides fought a years-long running campaign across the seas of Fujian, Zhejiang, and Taiwan with alternating victories. In 1807 Li Changgeng was killed in personal combat with him during a pursuit off the Zhejiang coast, sending shockwaves through the Qing coastal defenses and bringing his power to its peak. In 1806 he launched a large-scale raid against Lukang, the second-most prosperous commercial port of central Taiwan, hoping to seize grain and trade goods, but was driven off by a coordinated defense of Lukang's mercantile militia, the narrow alley-gate system of the town, and an imperial fire-ship counterattack. His wife, known to history simply as Madam Cai Qian, was a skilled warrior who fought beside him in many engagements, directing artillery and wielding a saber, an exceptionally rare female commander in his maritime kingdom. In 1809 the Qing court concentrated the combined naval forces of Fujian and Zhejiang under the new admiral Wang Delu, surrounding his remaining fleet in the open sea off Wenzhou in Zhejiang. With his ammunition exhausted and his ship overwhelmed he refused to surrender, personally setting fire to the powder magazine in the hold of his flagship and perishing in the blast with his wife at the age of forty-eight. Cai Qian is generally remembered as the gravest threat to Qing maritime security during the Jiaqing era, and his self-coronation, customs system, and raid on Lukang gave Taiwan a defining maritime dimension in the late imperial frontier narrative that complements its land-based history.
Figures.figure.caiqian.event1: Raided Lukang in 1806; self-immolated on his flagship off Zhejiang in 1809
Figures.figure.caiqian.title: Pirate King of the Black Ditch
Figures.figure.campbell.bio: William Campbell, born in 1841 in Glasgow, Scotland, arrived in southern Taiwan in 1871 as a missionary of the English Presbyterian Church and spent fifty years building educational, medical, and charitable institutions that fundamentally transformed southern Taiwanese society, most notably through his founding of Taiwan's first school for the blind in 1891. He was assigned to Tainan — the principal city of the island and the base of the southern Presbyterian mission established by his predecessor Hugh Ritchie — and immediately began the intensive study of Hokkien that would make him one of the most fluent foreign speakers of the language in the nineteenth century and equip him for a lifetime of preaching, translation, and literary work in the vernacular. In collaboration with Thomas Barclay, who arrived in 1875 and became his closest partner in the southern mission, Campbell helped establish the foundational institutions of what would become a major strand of Taiwanese Protestantism: congregations, schools, a medical clinic, and a printing press that produced religious and educational literature in romanized Hokkien (Peh-oe-ji). His most celebrated achievement was the establishment in 1891 of a school for blind students in Tainan, the first institution of its kind in Taiwan, which he founded after encountering the desperate situation of blind children in the city who had no access to education or employment and were condemned to begging; the school used embossed text and tactile learning methods adapted from Western models that Campbell had researched specifically for this purpose. Campbell was a prolific scholar and writer in addition to his pastoral work: he compiled the authoritative Dictionary of the Amoy Vernacular (1913), a bilingual reference work covering Hokkien vocabulary that remained a standard resource for missionaries and language learners for decades. He also wrote Sketches from Formosa (1915) and Missionary Success in the Island of Formosa (1889), which together constitute the most comprehensive English-language account of southern Taiwanese society, indigenous culture, and the progress of the Presbyterian mission in the late Qing period. Campbell documented the indigenous Siraya people of the Tainan plains — among whom earlier Dutch missionaries had worked two centuries before — in meticulous ethnographic detail, preserving records of their language and customs that later became invaluable to historians and indigenous rights advocates. He continued his work without interruption through the transition from Qing to Japanese rule in 1895, adapting the mission's activities to the new colonial framework while maintaining the school, the hospital, and the congregation networks that had been built over three decades. Campbell retired to Scotland in 1917 after forty-six years in Taiwan, and died in Edinburgh in 1921, having outlived nearly all of the colleagues with whom he had built the southern mission. His school for the blind continued to operate throughout the Japanese colonial period and still exists today as the Tainan Municipal Tainan Special Education School, one of the oldest continuously operating educational institutions in Taiwan. William Campbell is widely regarded as the founding figure of inclusive education in Taiwan and one of the most significant contributors to southern Taiwanese cultural and religious development in the nineteenth century.
Figures.figure.campbell.event1: Founded Taiwan's first school for blind students in Tainan (1891), introducing embossed-text education to the island
Figures.figure.campbell.event2: Compiled the Dictionary of the Amoy Vernacular (1913), the authoritative Hokkien bilingual reference work used by missionaries and scholars for decades
Figures.figure.campbell.title: Presbyterian Missionary and Pioneer of Blind Education
Figures.figure.candidius.bio: George Candidius was the first Protestant missionary dispatched by the Dutch East India Company to Formosa, born in the Palatinate region of Germany and later ordained in the Dutch Reformed Church. He arrived at Fort Zeelandia in 1627, becoming the founding figure of Dutch religious enterprise on the island. Immersing himself among the Siraya people, he mastered their language and became the first Westerner to document it systematically. In villages such as Mattau and Baccloangh, he established schools and taught indigenous people to write their mother tongue in Roman script — laying the foundation for what later became known as Sinkan manuscripts. His treatise Discourse on the Condition and Affairs of the Isle of Formosa provided the earliest systematic European account of Siraya religion and social customs, becoming a landmark document in Western knowledge of Taiwanese indigenous culture. Forced to leave in 1631 following a dispute with Governor Pieter Nuyts, he relocated to Batavia. In later years he undertook further missions across Southeast Asia before dying on the Coromandel Coast in 1647. Candidius's linguistic legacy endured: the Siraya language became the first indigenous language in Taiwan to be preserved in written form, and his educational model shaped how the Dutch administered the island's native peoples for decades.
Figures.figure.candidius.event1: Arrived in Formosa in 1627; established schools in Siraya villages and became the first Westerner to document the Siraya language systematically.
Figures.figure.candidius.event2: Authored the Discourse on Formosa, the earliest systematic European account of Siraya society; his Roman-script literacy programme gave rise to the Sinkan manuscript tradition.
Figures.figure.candidius.title: Dutch Reformed Missionary, First Sinologist of Formosa
Figures.figure.caojin.bio: Cao Jin, courtesy name Huaipu, was a Qing dynasty official from Huaiqing in Henan who earned his metropolitan degree during the Daoguang reign and came to be remembered as one of the most consequential administrators in southern Taiwan's history. Appointed magistrate of Fengshan County in 1838, he quickly diagnosed the root cause of the district's chronic agricultural instability: inadequate irrigation left farmland at the mercy of seasonal extremes. Over four years he mobilised local communities to construct a major canal network — the Cao Gong Canal system — stretching more than forty kilometres and irrigating thousands of jia of farmland across the Kaohsiung plain. The project transformed erratic, flood-prone lowlands into reliable agricultural land, triggering a surge in settlement and grain output across southern Taiwan. Beyond water management, Cao renovated the county seat's walls, pacified banditry, and promoted classical education, earning a reputation as a model official. Grateful residents enshrined him as Lord Cao, a title and temple that persist to this day; the canal bearing his name remains partially operational into the modern era. He returned to Taiwan in 1847 as Tamsui Sub-prefect, extending his agricultural development work northward. Cao Jin's hydraulic legacy stands as one of the most durable contributions any Qing administrator left on the island's landscape.
Figures.figure.caojin.event1: From 1838 to 1842, mobilised Fengshan communities to construct the Cao Gong Canal system — over forty kilometres of waterways irrigating thousands of jia of farmland across the Kaohsiung plain.
Figures.figure.caojin.event2: Venerated as Lord Cao by grateful residents; his canal remains partially operational today, and temples in his honour stand as testament to nearly two centuries of agricultural legacy.
Figures.figure.caojin.title: Qing County Magistrate, Builder of Cao Gong Canal
Figures.figure.changchunhung.bio: Chang Chun-hung, born in 1938 in Nantou, was one of the most important theorists and political-magazine editors of Taiwan's tangwai movement. He studied political science at National Taiwan University, earning a master's degree and a solid grounding in the discipline. In the early 1970s he took part in the reformist commentary of The Intellectual magazine, advocating political renewal and generational change, a representative of the young intellectuals engaging in public debate. He then joined the tangwai movement, helping found and edit Taiwan Political Review and lending theoretical depth to the opposition. With Hsu Hsin-liang and others he co-authored "An Analysis of Taiwan's Social Forces," dissecting Taiwan's political change through its social structure, with lasting influence. In 1979 he served as a core editor of Formosa Magazine, which became the tangwai's organizing platform across the island. When the Kaohsiung Incident erupted that year, he was listed among the key figures and sentenced to twelve years in a military trial. After the lifting of martial law he was released and continued with the Democratic Progressive Party, winning election as a legislator and serving as party secretary-general, long engaged in parliamentary and party affairs. He also kept writing, attending to Taiwan's political-economic system and cross-strait issues. Chang is seen as a pivotal figure in the tangwai movement's turn from the streets to discourse, his political writing and editing laying important intellectual and organizational foundations for Taiwan's opposition.
Figures.figure.changchunhung.event1: Editor of Formosa Magazine, imprisoned over the Kaohsiung Incident (1979)
Figures.figure.changchunhung.event2: Formulated tangwai political theory and analysis of social forces
Figures.figure.changchunhung.title: Tangwai Theorist & Kaohsiung Incident Prisoner
Figures.figure.chenbin.bio: Chen Bin was a Qing official from Guangdong who served as magistrate of Taiwan County from 1704, earning widespread admiration for his incorruptibility in an era when frontier corruption was endemic. He refused bribes, abolished extortionate customary levies, promoted agricultural settlement, and established charity schools. His administration of Taiwan's southern plains helped stabilize the early Qing colonial society. Promoted to the Taiwan-Xiamen Circuit intendant, he maintained his reformist standards. After his death in 1718, grateful Taiwanese residents built a temple in his honor — a rare tribute to a mainland-appointed official — cementing his legacy as the model of honest governance in early Qing Taiwan.
Figures.figure.chenbin.event1: Appointed Taiwan County magistrate in 1704, renowned for integrity and reform
Figures.figure.chenbin.event2: Honored with a temple by Taiwanese residents after his death
Figures.figure.chenbin.title: Incorruptible Magistrate
Figures.figure.chenchengpo.bio: Chen Cheng-po, born in 1895 in Chiayi to the family of a struggling Confucian scholar, became one of the most accomplished modern painters of colonial Taiwan and a victim of the post-war crackdown who has come to symbolize the violence of the February 28 Incident. He graduated from Taipei Normal School in 1917 and taught for several years in his hometown before entering the Tokyo Fine Arts School in 1924, where he trained under Japanese exponents of Western-style oil painting. In 1926 his work Outside Chiayi (嘉義街外) became the first painting by a Taiwanese artist to be selected for the prestigious Imperial Art Exhibition in Tokyo, and he went on to make multiple appearances at both the Teiten and the Taiwan Exhibition (Taiten). Between 1929 and 1933 he taught at the Xinhua College of Art in Shanghai, where he absorbed modernist currents while exhibiting alongside leading Republican-era Chinese painters. He returned to Taiwan in 1933 and co-founded the Tai-Yang Art Society (臺陽美術協會) in 1934, an influential salon that nurtured a generation of Taiwanese painters working outside the official exhibition system. His mature work fused Post-Impressionist palette and brushwork with attentive landscapes of Chiayi, Tamsui, Sun Moon Lake, and Yushan, creating a distinctive vocabulary of native Taiwanese subject matter. After the Japanese surrender in 1945 he served briefly as a Chiayi city councilman, embracing the new Republican administration with the optimism shared by many Taiwanese intellectuals of his generation. When the February 28 Incident erupted in early 1947 and unrest spread to Chiayi, he volunteered as one of six civilian negotiators to approach the besieged KMT garrison at Chiayi Airport in the hope of preventing further bloodshed. He and his fellow negotiators were detained on arrival, and on 25 March 1947 he was paraded through the streets of Chiayi and publicly executed by firing squad outside the railway station without trial. His family retrieved the body and his widow Chang Chieh quietly preserved his works, correspondence, and the bloodstained clothing through four decades of martial law. Beginning in the 1990s his paintings and personal effects re-emerged in major retrospectives, and his work has since commanded record-setting prices at international auctions. Chen is now widely commemorated as a pioneer of Taiwanese modern art and as one of the most evocative individual emblems of the cultural and human losses inflicted by the events of 1947.
Figures.figure.chenchengpo.title: Painter & Civic Leader
Figures.figure.chenchu.bio: Chen Chu, born in 1950 into a farming family in Yilan, is among the most representative women in Taiwan's democracy movement. In her youth she served as secretary to the tangwai elder Kuo Yu-hsin, whose influence drew her into the opposition movement and the work of aiding political prisoners. In the 1970s she actively connected tangwai figures and championed human-rights issues, one of the few women active on the front line at the time. When the Kaohsiung Incident broke out in 1979, she was the youngest woman among those indicted and was sentenced to twelve years in a military trial. She spent several years in prison, was released around 1986, and continued her work for democracy and human rights afterward. After the lifting of martial law she held senior posts in the Democratic Progressive Party and government, including labor-affairs chief in Taipei and at the central level, long attentive to labor and disadvantaged groups. From 2006 she was elected and re-elected mayor of Kaohsiung, serving twelve years and driving the city's modernization and transformation. She then became secretary-general to the president and, in 2020, president of the Control Yuan and first chair of the National Human Rights Commission, returning to the roots of her human-rights activism. Her life spans resistance under authoritarianism and governance after democratization, witnessing and shaping Taiwan's overall political transition. Chen is regarded as a symbolic figure of women's political participation and the human-rights movement, her path from political prisoner to local chief executive to head of a national human-rights body a telling microcosm of Taiwan's democratization.
Figures.figure.chenchu.event2: Long-serving mayor of Kaohsiung, later president of the Control Yuan
Figures.figure.chenchu.title: Kaohsiung Incident Prisoner & Human-Rights Advocate
Figures.figure.chengnanjung.bio: Cheng Nan-jung, born in 1947 in Yilan and raised in Taipei, was a publisher and activist who gave his life for the principle of "one hundred percent freedom of expression." Deeply steeped in liberal thought, he founded Freedom Era Weekly in 1984 and waged a relentless struggle against the regime's machinery of censorship: each time a publication was banned he revived another under one of the dozens of licenses he had applied for in advance. In late 1988 he published a Draft Constitution for a Republic of Taiwan, an act the authorities charged as sedition. Refusing to recognize the jurisdiction of a regime he deemed illegitimate, he declared, "The Kuomintang cannot arrest me; they can only seize my corpse," and locked himself in his editor's room for seventy-one days. On April 7, 1989, as police forced their way in, he set himself ablaze, fulfilling his vow in the flames. His self-immolation — followed by that of Chan Yi-hua at his funeral — seared the conscience of society and spurred the movement that led to the 1992 amendment of Article 100 of the Criminal Code, ending the criminalization of pure speech and thought. His scorched office is preserved today as the Cheng Nan-jung Memorial Museum, and April 7 was later designated Taiwan's Freedom of Speech Day.
Figures.figure.chengnanjung.event1: Founded Freedom Era Weekly in 1984, fighting for "one hundred percent freedom of expression"
Figures.figure.chengnanjung.event2: Self-immolated on April 7, 1989, resisting arrest for sedition; April 7 is now Freedom of Speech Day
Figures.figure.chengnanjung.title: Freedom of Speech Martyr
Figures.figure.chenjin.bio: Chen Chin was born in 1907 in Xiangshan, Hsinchu, into a well-to-do family that, unusually for the time, supported her artistic ambitions. She studied at the Women's Fine Arts School in Tokyo, mastering the meticulous gouache technique of Eastern-style painting. In 1927, at the very first Taiwan Fine Arts Exhibition, the twenty-year-old Chen Chin was selected alongside two other young Taiwanese while many established masters were rejected — and the press hailed the trio as 'the three youths of the Taiten.' She was the only woman among them. She went on to have works accepted at Japan's Imperial Exhibition and repeatedly at Taiwan's own shows, painting elegant portraits of women and serene Buddhist figures with exquisite refinement. Her celebrated Bereaved Mother Kannon and her graceful studies of Taiwanese women in traditional dress defined an era of Eastern-style painting on the island. As Taiwan's first professional female painter, she broke open a field long closed to women. Chen Chin painted into old age and died in 1998, her long career bridging the colonial and modern worlds.
Figures.figure.chenjin.event1: One of 'the three youths of the Taiten' (1927), its only woman
Figures.figure.chenjin.title: Painter
Figures.figure.chenshuchu.bio: Chen Shu-chu, born in 1950 in Taitung, is a figure known internationally for doing good through the strength of an ordinary person. Born into poverty, she lost her mother in her teens because the family could not afford medical care, after which she left school to shoulder the household, selling vegetables at a stall in Taitung's Central Market and raising many younger siblings. Frugal and hardworking all her life, rising early and living simply, she nonetheless gave away much of her hard-earned savings to charity. Over decades she donated to schools, orphanages, libraries, and medical institutions, amounts totaling millions and even tens of millions of NT dollars, far beyond what most would imagine. Her good works were long kept quiet, becoming widely known only after the media discovered them, moving countless Taiwanese. In 2010 she appeared on both Time magazine's list of the world's 100 most influential people and Forbes Asia's list of philanthropy heroes, letting the world see the goodness of Taiwan's grassroots. Amid the praise she remained humble, saying that doing good was simply "putting money to meaningful use," and continued to labor in the market. Her story became a symbol of Taiwan's civil society and the spirit of ordinary people's charity. Chen is seen as a model of extraordinary goodness achieved from an ordinary station, her long years of selfless giving revealing the resilient and warm side of the grassroots of Taiwanese society.
Figures.figure.chenshuchu.event1: Donated her savings over decades to help students and the poor
Figures.figure.chenshuchu.event2: Named one of Time magazine's 100 most influential people (2010)
Figures.figure.chenshuchu.title: Philanthropist Vegetable Vendor & Time 100 Honoree
Figures.figure.chenshuibian.bio: Chen Shui-bian, born in 1950 in Guantian, Tainan, to an impoverished tenant farming family, rose through Taiwan's elite legal profession to become the first Democratic Progressive Party president and the central political figure of the island's full democratic consolidation. He graduated at the top of his class from the law department of National Taiwan University and worked as a corporate lawyer specializing in shipping cases before entering politics in 1980 as a defense attorney for the Kaohsiung Incident defendants. He was elected to the Taipei City Council in 1981 and to the Legislative Yuan as a tangwai-affiliated member in 1986, becoming one of the founding generation of the Democratic Progressive Party that year. In 1985 his wife Wu Shu-jen was deliberately run over and rendered paraplegic by a small truck while campaigning for him in Tainan County, an unsolved attack widely attributed to political opponents. He served two terms as a legislator known for procedural innovation and aggressive oversight, then was elected Mayor of Taipei in 1994 — the first DPP mayor of the capital — and reorganized the city government before narrowly losing reelection in 1998. He won the 2000 presidential election with 39.3 percent of the vote in a three-way race split by the KMT, achieving Taiwan's first peaceful transfer of power between parties and ending more than half a century of KMT rule. He was re-elected in 2004 by a wafer-thin margin of 0.2 percent on the day after he and Vice President Annette Lu were shot and wounded in a still-unresolved campaign-day attack. His presidency oversaw cross-strait economic engagement alongside increasingly assertive language about Taiwanese sovereignty, including referenda on Taiwan's UN application and a constitutional rewrite project that drew strong opposition from both Beijing and Washington. From 2006 onward his administration was engulfed by a series of corruption investigations centered on his family, prompting the Red Shirt mass protests led by Shih Ming-teh and a sharp decline in his political support. He left office in 2008 and was indicted within months on charges of embezzlement, money laundering, and bribery, ultimately convicted and serving prison time before being released on medical parole in 2015. He has remained a polarizing presence in DPP politics in the years since, continuing to issue political commentary while remaining a contested symbol of both the democratic transition and the corruption that shadowed its first decade. Chen is generally remembered as the politician who completed Taiwan's peaceful transfer of power and broke the KMT's institutional monopoly, but also as the figure whose corruption convictions deeply damaged the DPP's moral authority for the better part of a decade.
Figures.figure.chenshuibian.event1: First peaceful party turnover in presidential election (2000)
Figures.figure.chenshuibian.title: President of the Republic of China
Figures.figure.chenweiying.bio: Chen Weiying was a northern Taiwan-born classical scholar and educator who became one of the most influential teachers in the Taipei area during the mid-to-late Qing period. Holding a juren degree, he spent much of his life directing academies in the Danshui Subprefecture, training generations of students in classical learning. Associated with the Mingzhi Academy and Xuehai Academy, he cultivated the local Confucian scholarly tradition in northern Taiwan. As a poet of note in his own right, Chen contributed to a local literary culture independent of mainland models. His students went on to pass examinations and shape the intellectual life of northern Taiwan, making him a foundational figure in the educational history of the region.
Figures.figure.chenweiying.event1: Directed classical academies in Taipei area, nurturing Confucian scholarship for decades
Figures.figure.chenweiying.event2: Wrote poetry and prose, representing 19th-century northern Taiwan literati
Figures.figure.chenweiying.title: Northern Taiwan Confucian Educator
Figures.figure.chenwencheng.bio: Chen Wen-cheng, born in Taipei in 1950, was a brilliant statistician whose death became one of the defining outrages of Taiwan's White Terror. After graduating from the Department of Mathematics at National Taiwan University, he pursued graduate study in the United States, earning his doctorate from the University of Michigan, and by the age of thirty-one had become an assistant professor of statistics at Carnegie Mellon University. Warm-hearted and devoted to his homeland, he joined Taiwanese hometown associations during his years abroad and donated to the Dangwai publication Formosa Magazine — acts that placed him on the watch list of the security services. In May 1981 he returned to Taiwan with his wife and child to visit relatives. On July 2, three agents of the Taiwan Garrison Command took him away for "questioning"; the following dawn his body was found on the lawn beside the NTU graduate library. The authorities declared it suicide, but the forensic pathologist Cyril Wecht, who came from the United States to examine the body, found the injuries inconsistent with a simple fall. His death stunned American academia and Congress, drawing intense international scrutiny to Taiwan's human rights record. Though the case was never solved, the lawn where he died now holds a memorial square within the NTU campus, and his name endures as a spiritual landmark in Taiwan's pursuit of academic freedom and freedom of speech.
Figures.figure.chenwencheng.event1: Detained and interrogated by the Taiwan Garrison Command, July 2, 1981
Figures.figure.chenwencheng.event2: Found dead on the NTU campus the next morning; the unsolved case drew international human-rights scrutiny
Figures.figure.chenwencheng.title: Mathematician & Democracy Martyr
Figures.figure.chenxin.bio: Chen Hsin, born in 1893 in Dajia, Taichung, was among the most prominent financiers and economists of the late-colonial and early post-war eras. He studied at Keio University in Japan and then pursued economics at Columbia University in the United States, earning a master's degree — one of the few Taiwanese of his time with full modern training in economics. Returning home, he devoted himself to finance, founding the Tai Tong Trust Company in 1926, one of the few Taiwanese-led financial institutions under Japanese rule. He argued that the Taiwanese should command their own capital and financial lifelines and raise their people's standing through economic power, and he actively joined social movements such as the Taiwan Cultural Association. Throughout the colonial period he worked, under the constraints of the colonial financial system, to win space for Taiwanese economic autonomy. After World War II he held hopes for the new order and organized the Ta Kung Enterprise Company, seeking to pool Taiwanese capital and take part in post-war reconstruction. Yet his social prestige and economic influence made him an object of the authorities' wariness. After the February 28 Incident broke out in 1947, security agents took him away in March under the pretext of negotiation; he was never seen again and is generally believed to have been killed. His death is a representative case of the purge of Taiwan's economic elite during the incident. Chen devoted his life to Taiwanese financial autonomy and economic modernization and is remembered as a pioneer of native Taiwanese finance, his tragic end symbolizing the grave setback to post-war Taiwanese private capital.
Figures.figure.chenxin.event1: Arrested and killed during the February 28 Incident (1947)
Figures.figure.chenxin.event2: Founded the Tai Tong Trust to advance Taiwanese financial autonomy
Figures.figure.chenxin.title: Financier & Economist
Figures.figure.chenyi.bio: Chen Yi, born in 1883 in Shaoxing, Zhejiang, was a Nationalist military officer and provincial administrator whose 1945–1947 governorship of Taiwan precipitated the February 28 Incident, the most violent event in modern Taiwanese history. He received early military training in Japan and entered the Beiyang army before joining Sun Yat-sen's Tongmenghui and shifting allegiance to the Nationalist movement. He served as Governor of Fujian Province from 1934 to 1941, where his administration of opium monopolies, currency reform, and wartime mobilization developed the harsh, monopolistic governance style he would later replicate on Taiwan. He headed the wartime Taiwan Investigation Committee from 1944, the body charged with planning the takeover of the colony from Japan, and was appointed Chief Executive of the Taiwan Provincial Administrative Office. On 25 October 1945 he accepted the formal Japanese surrender at the Taipei City Hall, an act marked by elaborate ceremony and high local expectations after fifty years of colonial rule. His administration imposed sweeping monopolies on tobacco, salt, alcohol, and camphor; permitted rampant corruption among mainlander officials; and engineered the hyperinflation that quickly destroyed the savings of the island's population. The new regime systematically excluded Taiwanese — including former colonial civil servants and professionals — from senior positions, replacing them with mainlander appointees whose conduct islanders frequently described as colonial behavior in a new uniform. On 27 February 1947 the beating of a Taipei cigarette seller by Monopoly Bureau officers ignited mass protests across the island, which Chen Yi initially negotiated with before secretly requesting military reinforcements from the mainland. From 8 March 1947 the arriving 21st Division and Garrison Command troops conducted a systematic crackdown that killed several thousand Taiwanese — including a deliberately targeted elite of professionals, intellectuals, and former local officials. He was removed from the Taiwan post in May 1947 in response to the scandal but was protected by Chiang Kai-shek and reassigned as Governor of Zhejiang Province in 1948. He attempted to defect to the Chinese Communist Party in early 1949, was discovered, arrested, and brought to Taiwan, where he was tried by court-martial. He was executed by firing squad in Taipei in June 1950 for treason, and remains one of the most reviled figures in Taiwanese historical memory, the official face of the post-war crackdown whose memory has been continually relitigated through the transitional-justice processes of the post-1987 era.
Figures.figure.chenyi.event1: Appointed Chief Executive of Taiwan (1945), overseeing the takeover from Japan
Figures.figure.chenyi.event2: His administration's failures led to the February 28 Incident (1947)
Figures.figure.chenyi.title: Chief Executive of Taiwan Province
Figures.figure.chenyonghua.bio: Chen Yong-hua, born in 1634 in Tong'an, Fujian, was the principal civilian architect of the Kingdom of Tungning and the most influential statesman of seventeenth-century Han Chinese Taiwan. His father Chen Ding was a Ming loyalist official who took his own life rather than serve the Qing after the fall of Fuzhou, an act that shaped the younger Chen's lifelong commitment to the Ming cause. Recommended to Koxinga as a young man, he impressed the warlord with his comprehensive policy proposals and was retained at the inner court as a trusted strategist. After the conquest of Taiwan he served Zheng Jing as Counsellor and Supervising Officer (諮議參軍), holding effective executive responsibility for the civilian government. He oversaw the systematic conversion of Han military colonies into permanent farms, introduced sugarcane cultivation and refined salt monopolies, and laid out the administrative grid of Chengtian Prefecture. In 1665 he founded the Tainan Confucian Temple, Taiwan's first such institution, and instituted civil examinations on the mainland model, opening pathways to scholarly status for islander Chinese for the first time. He expanded ceramic, sugar, and shipbuilding industries and cultivated trade routes to Japan and the Spanish Philippines, generating revenues that sustained the Zheng war effort. While Zheng Jing conducted the long mainland expedition from 1673 to 1680, Chen acted as effective regent in Taiwan alongside the young heir Zheng Kezang, whose education he also supervised. He married his daughter to Zheng Kezang, a union meant to bind the Tungning succession to civilian Confucian governance. Late tradition associates him with the founding of the secret Tiandihui (Heaven and Earth Society) brotherhoods, though the historical evidence for this connection is weak and contested. He died in 1680, shortly before Zheng Jing's defeated return from the mainland, sparing him the catastrophe of the palace coup that destroyed his family the following year. Chen is popularly known as Taiwan's Zhuge Liang for his role in turning a precarious military regime into a state with credible civilian institutions, an achievement that long outlasted the dynasty he served.
Figures.figure.chenyonghua.event1: Founded Taiwan's first Confucian Temple and civil examination system
Figures.figure.chenyonghua.title: Chief Administrator of Tungning
Figures.figure.chenzhonghe.bio: Chen Chung-ho was born in 1853 in Kaohsiung and made his start in the trading houses of the southern ports, dealing in sugar and rice during the late Qing when Taiwan's harbours were opening to the world. He built an extensive export business, shipping Taiwanese sugar and rice to markets across Asia, and sailed through the change of regime in 1895 with his commercial instincts intact. Under Japanese rule, as the colony poured investment into modern sugar manufacturing, he moved from trading into industry, founding the Shinko Sugar Company in the early 1900s and mechanising production on the Kaohsiung plain. His trading and manufacturing concerns grew into one of the leading enterprises of southern Taiwan, and he became the founding patriarch of the Chen family of Kaohsiung, counted among the island's 'five great families.' A bridge between the old world of the Qing merchant and the new world of colonial industry, Chen Chung-ho died in 1930, leaving a business and landholding legacy that shaped the development of the south for generations.
Figures.figure.chenzhonghe.event1: Built a sugar and rice export business across Asia
Figures.figure.chenzhonghe.event2: Founded the Shinko Sugar Company on the Kaohsiung plain
Figures.figure.chenzhonghe.title: Sugar and Trade Magnate
Figures.figure.chenzhouquan.bio: Chen Zhouquan led a rebellion in the Changhua area of central Taiwan in 1795, less than a decade after the major Lin Shuangwen Uprising. Exploiting reduced Qing military presence, he mobilized Tiandihui networks to attack and briefly capture the Changhua county seat.
