The uprising was suppressed within months when reinforcements arrived and Quanzhou-origin militia — who had long-standing ethnic rivalries with Chen's Zhangzhou followers — joined the counterattack. Chen was captured and executed. His rebellion illustrates the endemic instability of Qing Taiwan: the combination of Zhangzhou-Quanzhou ethnic conflict, opportunistic secret society organizing, and persistent administrative weakness repeatedly produced large-scale uprisings through the eighteenth century.
Figures.figure.chenzhouquan.event1: Led uprising in Changhua in 1795, briefly capturing the county seat
Figures.figure.chenzhouquan.event2: Captured and executed; event revealed deep social tensions in Qing Taiwan
Figures.figure.chenzhouquan.title: Leader of the 1795 Changhua Uprising
Figures.figure.chiangchingkuo.bio: Chiang Ching-kuo, born in 1910 in Xikou, Zhejiang, as the eldest son of Chiang Kai-shek, served as Premier and then as President of the Republic of China and is the figure most directly responsible for the political liberalization of Taiwan in the 1980s. He spent his formative years in the Soviet Union, where he had been sent in 1925 at the age of fifteen for ideological education and where he subsequently married a Belarusian woman, Faina Vakhreva, before returning to China in 1937 after twelve years in Soviet exile. After 1949 he followed his father to Taiwan and built his political base by running the security and intelligence apparatus, including the Investigation Bureau and the General Political Warfare Department of the armed forces. As Defense Minister from 1965 and Vice Premier from 1969 he gained operational control of the major government ministries, and from 1972 he served as Premier under his father's continuing presidency. He launched the Ten Major Construction Projects from 1974, a state-directed infrastructure and heavy-industry program that built the freeway, electrified the railway, expanded ports, and added the petrochemical and steel base of the island's export economy. Following his father's death in 1975 and the end of an interim presidency under Yen Chia-kan, he assumed the presidency in 1978 and was reelected for a second six-year term in 1984. He systematically recruited native Taiwanese elites into senior positions, including Lin Yang-kang, Hsieh Tung-min, and Lee Teng-hui, breaking with the previous reliance on the mainlander faction of the KMT. Externally, his presidency coincided with the most painful diplomatic period in ROC history, including derecognition by the United States in 1979 and the simultaneous shift of most other governments to recognition of Beijing. Domestically, the Kaohsiung Incident of December 1979 and the Lin family massacre of 1980 marked the high tide of state violence against the tangwai movement, all under his security apparatus. From 1986 onward he authorized a remarkable about-face: tolerating the founding of the Democratic Progressive Party in September 1986, lifting martial law on Taiwan in July 1987, legalizing newspapers and opposition parties, and opening cross-strait family visits later that year. He died in office in January 1988 of complications from diabetes at the age of 77, with the succession passing to his vice president Lee Teng-hui. Chiang's late-life turn from security strongman to architect of managed liberalization remains the most consequential and contested aspect of his legacy, framing all subsequent debate about whether Taiwan's democracy was bestowed from above or wrested from below.
Figures.figure.chiangchingkuo.event1: Lifted martial law (1987), ending 38 years of emergency rule
Figures.figure.chiangchingkuo.event2: Legalized opposition parties and opened cross-strait family visits
Figures.figure.chiangchingkuo.title: President of the Republic of China
Figures.figure.chiangkaishek.bio: Chiang Kai-shek, born in 1887 in Xikou, Zhejiang, to a salt merchant family, was the dominant Chinese Nationalist leader of the mid-twentieth century and the man whose 1949 retreat to Taiwan reshaped the island's twentieth-century history. He received early military training in China and then in Japan, where he attended preparatory schools and briefly served in the Imperial Japanese Army and joined Sun Yat-sen's Tongmenghui revolutionary organization. After returning to China at the outbreak of the 1911 Revolution, he rose under Sun Yat-sen and was sent to Moscow in 1923 to study Soviet military organization, helping found the Whampoa Military Academy as its commandant the following year. He launched the Northern Expedition in 1926, broke with the Communists in the violent 1927 Shanghai Massacre, and by 1928 had nominally reunified China under the Nationalist Government in Nanjing. He married Soong Mei-ling in 1927, converting to Methodism in 1930, an alliance that bound him to the Soong family and to substantial Anglo-American sympathy in the next two decades. From 1937 he led the Republic of China through the eight-year War of Resistance against Japan, securing recognition as one of the Big Four Allied leaders and obtaining at the 1943 Cairo Conference the formal commitment that Taiwan would be returned to Chinese sovereignty after Japan's defeat. Following Japan's surrender he resumed the civil war against the Chinese Communist Party but was decisively defeated by 1949, retreating with the remnants of his government, army, and over a million civilians to Taiwan. He declared martial law on Taiwan in May 1949 and used the security apparatus, the Garrison Command, and the Taiwan Provincial Government to consolidate authoritarian rule, while officially maintaining the claim to represent all of China. He oversaw the White Terror — the prolonged campaign of political repression that arrested, imprisoned, or executed tens of thousands of suspected dissidents, mainlanders and islanders alike, throughout the 1950s and 1960s. With substantial U.S. military and economic support after the outbreak of the Korean War in 1950, he stabilized the regime, presided over a land reform program, and laid the institutional foundations for the export-led industrialization of the following decades. He suffered the major diplomatic blow of the Republic of China's expulsion from the United Nations in 1971 and the U.S. opening to Beijing in 1972, signaling the international community's gradual shift away from the ROC. He died of heart failure in Taipei in April 1975 at the age of 87, and his legacy remains deeply contested — a leader of the Chinese resistance to Japan and architect of post-war Taiwan's economic foundations, but also the central figure in a state-violence regime whose victims and survivors continue to shape Taiwanese transitional-justice politics.
Figures.figure.chiangkaishek.event2: Oversaw the White Terror period of political repression
Figures.figure.chiangkaishek.title: President of the Republic of China
Figures.figure.chiangpengchien.bio: Chiang Peng-chien, born in 1940 in Taipei, was an important human-rights lawyer and political figure in Taiwan's democratization. He graduated in law from National Taiwan University and, after qualifying as a lawyer, practiced with a focus on judicial rights and the defense of the vulnerable. In the 1980 military trial of the Kaohsiung Incident he stepped forward as a defense lawyer, representing figures such as Shih Ming-teh — a highly risky act in the political climate of the time. The defense lawyers of that trial would largely go on to become the backbone of Taiwan's democracy movement and opposition party, and he was among the foremost. In 1986, when the Democratic Progressive Party was founded under the martial-law system, he was elected its first chairman, bearing the burden of the party's founding and survival. In the DPP's early days he worked to build its organization and advocated advancing democratic reform through reason and the rule of law. He later won election as a legislator, continuing to push human rights and democratic legal reform in parliament. In his later years he served as a member of the Control Yuan, extending his concern for judicial and human-rights issues. He died of illness in 2000 at the age of sixty. Chiang is seen as a model of the generation of human-rights lawyers who entered politics, and his dual role in defending the Kaohsiung Incident and founding the DPP is a key link in understanding the institutionalization of Taiwan's opposition movement.
Figures.figure.chiangpengchien.event1: Served as a defense lawyer in the Kaohsiung Incident trial (1980)
Figures.figure.chiangpengchien.event2: Became the first chairman of the DPP (1986)
Figures.figure.chiangpengchien.title: Kaohsiung Incident Defense Lawyer & First DPP Chairman
Figures.figure.chiangweishui.bio: Chiang Wei-shui, born in 1890 in Yilan to a fortune-teller's family, became the foremost civilian leader of the non-violent anti-colonial movement in Taiwan during the Japanese era. He entered the Taiwan Sōtokufu Medical School in Taipei, the colony's most prestigious institution open to islanders, graduating in 1915 and establishing the Dai-an Hospital in the bustling Daitōtei district of Taipei. Drawing on his medical training, in 1921 he published a satirical Clinical Diagnosis of the Patient Taiwan, diagnosing the island as suffering from ignorance of world culture and prescribing education as cure. That same year he co-founded the Taiwan Cultural Association with Lin Hsien-tang and others, sending lecture troupes, founding reading clubs, and screening educational films across the island to awaken islanders' cultural and political consciousness. He was a driving force behind the Taiwanese Home Rule Petition Movement, petitioning the Imperial Diet annually for a colonial parliament representing Taiwan residents. In 1923 he was arrested in the so-called Chih-an Police Law Incident, a wide crackdown on petitioners that became a watershed moment galvanizing Taiwanese political activism. As internal tensions split the Cultural Association along left–right lines in 1927, he led a moderate wing to found the Taiwan People's Party, the first modern political party organized by Taiwanese. Through the party he agitated for universal suffrage, labor protections, the abolition of forced labor, and the dismantling of opium-licensing schemes, and helped organize the Taiwan Workers' Alliance. He publicly denounced the colonial government's handling of the Wushe Incident in 1930 and the renewed issuance of opium permits, drawing repeated arrests and police harassment. The Taiwan People's Party was forcibly dissolved by the colonial authorities in February 1931, and within months his health, eroded by years of activism and detention, gave way to typhoid fever. He died in August 1931 in Taipei at the age of 40, with tens of thousands attending the funeral procession in what became the largest civic gathering in colonial Taiwan. Chiang is widely revered as a founding father of Taiwan's democratic and civic tradition, his integration of medical practice, journalism, and party politics seen as a model of public-spirited activism.
Figures.figure.chiangweishui.event1: Founded the Taiwan Cultural Association (1921) and Taiwan People's Party (1927)
Figures.figure.chiangweishui.title: Physician & Anti-Colonial Activist
Figures.figure.chipolin.bio: Chi Po-lin, born in 1964 in Taipei, was Taiwan's most representative aerial photographer and environmental documentary director. He worked early in his career in a government agency, where the need for engineering records first brought him to aerial photography, and he gradually became captivated by the view of the land from high above. For years he shot from helicopters, amassing a vast body of precious imagery recording Taiwan's mountains, rivers, coasts, and cities. He captured not only the island's magnificent beauty but also, with a keen eye, the scars left by deforestation, river pollution, and land development. To fully portray Taiwan, he resolutely quit his stable job and threw himself into high-risk, high-cost documentary filming. In 2013 his documentary "Beyond Beauty: Taiwan from Above" was released, its stunning aerial footage letting countless viewers see their homeland anew and stirring wide public concern for environmental issues, achieving rare box-office success for a Taiwanese documentary and winning recognition at the Golden Horse Awards. The work also pushed the government and society to take land conservation and environmental protection more seriously. In 2017, while scouting locations for a sequel, "Beyond Beauty: Taiwan from Above II," he died in a helicopter crash at fifty-three, shocking and grieving the whole island. Chi is seen as a pioneer who awakened environmental awareness through imagery, his aerial work and sacrifice long an important symbol of Taiwan's memory of its land and environment.
Figures.figure.chipolin.event1: Directed the documentary "Beyond Beauty: Taiwan from Above" (2013)
Figures.figure.chipolin.event2: Died in a helicopter crash while filming a sequel (2017)
Figures.figure.chipolin.title: Aerial Photographer & Director of "Beyond Beauty"
Figures.figure.coyett.bio: Frederick Coyett, born in 1615 in Stockholm to a Swedish noble family, was the last Dutch East India Company Governor of Formosa, whose 1662 surrender to Koxinga ended thirty-eight years of VOC rule over Taiwan and effectively closed the European chapter of seventeenth-century Taiwan. He entered VOC service as a young man, one of a handful of Scandinavian officers among the Dutch-led company's expanding Asian administration, and rose through postings in Japan and Batavia over two decades. He served as Opperhoofd of the VOC factory at Deshima in Nagasaki from 1647 to 1652, the only formal Dutch presence in Tokugawa Japan, and acquired the diplomatic experience that would later commend him for the Formosa appointment. He was appointed Governor of Formosa in 1656 and arrived in Tayouan with explicit instructions to defend the colony against the growing power of Koxinga's maritime empire across the strait. From 1659 he repeatedly warned the VOC headquarters at Batavia of intelligence indicating an imminent Zheng invasion, including the defection of the Hokkien interpreter He Bin and reports of fleet preparations at Xiamen. Batavia rejected his requests for substantial reinforcements, preferring to maintain garrisons in the more commercially valuable factories at Macassar, Malacca, and Java, and sent only minimal additional troops. When Koxinga's fleet landed at Lakjemuyse Bay in April 1661, his garrison of fewer than two thousand soldiers and civilians faced an invading army at least ten times their number, and the satellite Fort Provintia on the Tainan mainland fell within days. He concentrated his remaining forces inside Fort Zeelandia on the sandbar of Tayouan and conducted a determined nine-month siege defense, repulsing repeated assaults while petitioning Batavia for relief. A relief fleet from Batavia under Jacob Caeuw arrived in late 1661 but was driven off by Zheng warships and provided no effective assistance. Confronting starvation, dwindling munitions, and no prospect of further relief, he signed the formal capitulation in early February 1662, securing terms that allowed the Dutch population to evacuate with arms, personal property, and military honors. He was court-martialed at Batavia for the loss of Formosa, sentenced to death, and ultimately exiled to the Banda Islands for eight years, before securing his release in 1675 only through the personal intervention of Stadholder William III of Orange. He returned to the Netherlands and published the polemical anonymous defense of his governorship, 't Verwaerloosde Formosa (Neglected Formosa), before his death in Amsterdam in 1687, the book remaining the principal Dutch primary source on the fall of VOC Taiwan.
Figures.figure.coyett.event1: Surrendered Fort Zeelandia to Koxinga after a nine-month siege (1662)
Figures.figure.coyett.title: Last VOC Governor of Formosa
Figures.figure.daichaochun.bio: Dai Chaochun, a wealthy landlord from the Sishe district of Changhua County, was the leader of the third and last of the three major rebellions that punctuate the Qing imperial era in Taiwan, his birth year unrecorded. His family was prominent in the central Taiwan settler economy of the mid-nineteenth century, holding extensive sugarcane and rice land and patronizing a local mutual-defense and brotherhood association known as the Bagua Society (八卦會). The society, originally a network of armed retainers organized around family-based militias, gradually absorbed Tiandihui-style ritual and developed into an organized opposition to Qing magistrates accused of corruption. The opportunity for armed action came in early 1862, when Qing forces and military resources were heavily engaged in suppressing the Taiping civil war on the mainland and the colonial garrison on Taiwan was at its weakest. In March 1862 he led several thousand armed men into the walled city of Changhua, killed the magistrate, and proclaimed his own authority over the central plains. He adopted the reign title Yuantian (元天) and the royal style of Eastern King, issuing proclamations and reordering local government across the Changhua, Taichung, and Yunlin regions. The Wufeng Lin family, in particular Lin Wencha and Lin Wenming, raised loyalist Han militias from their estates, while Lugang merchants and Hakka villages of the Hsinchu region similarly armed themselves against the rebels. The Qing court, after considerable delay, sent the Taiwan Daotai (intendant) Ding Yuejian to coordinate military operations with the gentry militias from 1863 onward. Throughout 1863 the rebel positions on the central plains were ground down by combined gentry-militia and Qing forces, and Dai retreated into the hill country. He was captured at the end of 1863, transferred to Changhua for interrogation, and executed by slow slicing in early 1864; his immediate family was also extinguished. The rebellion's suppression confirmed the Wufeng Lin family as a dominant gentry house in central Taiwan and granted them official military rank and substantial estates. The Dai Chaochun affair exposed how thoroughly the Qing relied on Taiwanese Han gentry to maintain order on the frontier, and the gentry militia model it consolidated would shape the political ecology of Taiwan through to the Japanese annexation.
Figures.figure.daichaochun.event1: Led the Dai Chaochun Rebellion (1862–1865), one of the three great Qing-era uprisings
Figures.figure.daichaochun.title: Rebel Leader
Figures.figure.dika.bio: Dika was a chief (headman) of the Siraya village of Sinkan (新港社), located on the coastal plain near the new Dutch fort at Tayouan in the mid-1620s. The Siraya were the largest indigenous people of the southwestern Taiwan lowlands at the moment of Dutch arrival, organized in autonomous villages that traded, fought, and intermarried across the coastal plain. Sinkan had been one of the first villages to enter into a formal relationship with the new VOC administration, exchanging gifts and accepting protection in 1624 in return for political affiliation. By 1626 disputes between the Dutch governor at Tayouan, Pieter Nuyts, and the Japanese trader Hamada Yahyoe over silk monopolies and import duties had begun to strain relations between the VOC and the Tokugawa-aligned Hirado merchants. In 1627 Hamada brought Dika and approximately fifteen other Sinkan men to Edo on his return voyage to Japan, presenting them at the court of the Shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu as representatives of Formosa. The delegation, with Hamada acting as interpreter and political broker, was said to have offered Formosa to the Tokugawa shogunate as a tributary territory, in direct challenge to the VOC's claim over the island. The presentation was an embarrassment to the Dutch but had little immediate diplomatic effect, since the bakufu did not establish formal authority over the island and the Sinkan villagers held no recognized authority to dispose of Formosa. On their return to Tayouan in 1628 Dika and the other Sinkan envoys were detained by Pieter Nuyts, who treated their journey as an act of disloyalty and confiscated the prestigious gifts they had received from the Japanese court. The detention provoked the Hamada Incident of 1628, in which Hamada and his sailors seized Nuyts hostage in the governor's own residence at Tayouan and forced him to release the Sinkan envoys and pay compensation. The dispute escalated into a brief but consequential diplomatic crisis between the VOC and Tokugawa Japan, with the Tokugawa shogunate suspending Dutch trade until Nuyts himself was handed over for detention in Japan to satisfy Japanese honor. Dika's later life is not documented in either Dutch or Japanese sources and his date of death is unrecorded. He is remembered today not as an autonomous political actor but as the human face of one of the most striking moments in the seventeenth-century encounter of indigenous Taiwan with the rival imperial powers competing for the island, a brief moment when a Siraya chief's voyage placed Formosa within the political imagination of Edo.
Figures.figure.dika.event1: Led a Sinkan delegation to Edo in 1627, sparking the Hamada Incident
Figures.figure.dika.title: Chief of Sinkan (Siraya)
Figures.figure.dingrichang.bio: Ding Richang, born in 1823 in Fengshun County, Guangdong, was a leading official of the Qing Self-Strengthening Movement, a close associate of Li Hongzhang, and as Fujian Governor-General in the mid-1870s the most vigorous advocate for modernizing Taiwan in the decade before Liu Mingchuan formalized the island's transformation as its first governor. He rose through provincial administration in Jiangsu, where his management of the Shanghai arsenal and collaboration with Li Hongzhang in military reform established his reputation as one of China's foremost technocratic modernizers, committed to introducing Western industrial and military technology within the framework of Confucian governance. Appointed Fujian Governor-General in 1875 with responsibility over Taiwan, Ding immediately recognized the island's strategic importance in the context of Japan's 1874 Taiwan Expedition and the growing Western presence in East Asian waters, and he submitted a series of ambitious reform memorials to the emperor outlining a comprehensive program for Taiwan's military and economic modernization. Among his most important initiatives were proposals to lay submarine telegraph cables connecting Taiwan to the mainland and to other treaty ports, to develop the island's coal deposits at Jilong (Keelung) using foreign mining expertise, to construct new military fortifications along the coast, and to extend administrative presence into the indigenous highlands that remained outside Qing control. Several of these proposals were adopted in modified form, and Ding's tenure saw the first serious Qing investment in Taiwan's infrastructure since the Shen Baozhen mission of 1874, including the establishment of a coal mining operation at Keelung and preliminary work on coastal defenses. He also pushed for the reform of Taiwan's civil administration, arguing that the corrupt and understaffed county system was incapable of managing the island's complex multiethnic society, and that Taiwan deserved elevation to full provincial status rather than remaining a dependent prefecture of Fujian — a recommendation that was eventually implemented in 1885, a decade after he made it. Ding was a prodigious writer as well as an official, and he compiled an influential anthology of governance texts and published works on military technology, mathematics, and classical scholarship that were widely read among the reform-minded official class of the late Qing. His progressive program in Taiwan was cut short by illness: he was forced to leave his post in 1878 after chronic health problems that had troubled him throughout his career became incapacitating, and he spent his final years in retirement in Guangdong, dying in 1882. His successor as the driving force of Taiwan reform, Liu Mingchuan, implemented many of the specific proposals that Ding had first articulated, making Ding in retrospect the intellectual architect of the transformation Liu Mingchuan is credited with executing. Ding Richang is widely regarded as the most important Qing official for Taiwan between the Shen Baozhen mission and the Liu Mingchuan governorship — the man who first articulated a vision of Taiwan as a modern strategic province and laid the groundwork for the reforms that would define the island's final decade under Qing rule.
Figures.figure.dingrichang.event1: Submitted comprehensive reform memorials to modernize Taiwan's military, coal mining, telegraph infrastructure, and administration (1875–78)
Figures.figure.dingrichang.event2: First advocated elevating Taiwan to full provincial status, a recommendation eventually implemented by Liu Mingchuan in 1885
Figures.figure.dingrichang.title: Fujian Governor and Modernization Advocate for Taiwan
Figures.figure.dongwangfei.bio: Lady Dong was the principal consort of Koxinga, born to a prominent merchant family from Hui'an in Fujian, though her personal name is not preserved in the historical record. She married Koxinga in the 1640s and bore him a son, Zheng Jing, who would later succeed his father as ruler of the Tungning Kingdom. After the defection of Koxinga's father Zheng Zhilong to the Qing in 1646 and the death of Koxinga's mother of the Tagawa family, she accompanied the Zheng household through the long campaigns along the Fujian coast at the most precarious phase of the Ming loyalist resistance. When Koxinga crossed to Taiwan in 1661 she remained in the rear base at Xiamen, sustaining the political and logistical operations of the Zheng network alongside her daughter-in-law and grandchildren. In early 1662 Koxinga, enraged by reports from Xiamen that the heir apparent Zheng Jing had fathered a child by his younger brother's wet nurse Zhao Niang, issued an order from Fort Zeelandia for the execution of Lady Dong, Zheng Jing, the wet nurse, and the newborn infant. The Xiamen commanders collectively refused to obey, executing only the wet nurse and shielding Lady Dong and Zheng Jing, an act of insubordination that arguably saved the Zheng regime from self-destruction at its founding. After Koxinga's death in June 1662 and Zheng Jing's victory over his uncle Zheng Xi in the subsequent succession war, she crossed to Taiwan as Queen Dowager and became the senior authority of the Tungning inner court. Over the next two decades she mediated quietly behind the scenes among the leading commanders and clan members, playing a stabilizing role during Zheng Jing's prolonged westward campaign in support of the Revolt of the Three Feudatories. After Zheng Jing's death in 1681 she initially sought to install her eldest grandson Zheng Kezang, the heir designated by Zheng Jing and widely regarded as a competent prince. The minister Feng Xifan and allied courtiers persuaded her with the rumor that Kezang was not of Zheng blood but a child Zheng Jing had received from a Li merchant in Xiamen, and the exhausted dowager acquiesced to a deposition order under which Kezang was strangled in the palace by Feng's faction in what is known as the Coup of Eastern Ning. The murder of her favored grandson left her in inconsolable remorse, and she died of grief in the inner court of the Anping Palace only months later. Lady Dong is generally remembered as the dynastic pillar who bridged three generations of the Zheng family in Taiwan, and as the most direct witness to the internal collapse that drove the Tungning Kingdom to its end.
Figures.figure.dongwangfei.event1: Acquiesced to the deposition of her grandson Zheng Kezang in the Coup of Eastern Ning (1681)
Figures.figure.dongwangfei.title: Principal Consort of Koxinga
Figures.figure.douglas.bio: Carstairs Douglas was a Scottish Presbyterian missionary stationed primarily in Amoy who devoted decades to producing the Chinese-English Dictionary of the Vernacular or Spoken Language of Amoy (1873), one of the most comprehensive and scholarly dictionaries of Southern Min ever compiled. Drawing on fieldwork across the Amoy-Taiwanese speech community, Douglas documented tens of thousands of entries with phonological detail and contextual examples. The dictionary became an indispensable reference for missionaries working in Taiwan, facilitating Bible translation into romanized Taiwanese script and development of a literate tradition in the spoken language. His linguistic legacy shaped the infrastructure of Taiwanese-language writing and scholarship for generations, and remains cited by linguists working on Min Nan today.
Figures.figure.douglas.event1: Completed Amoy-English Dictionary in 1873, most comprehensive Min Nan linguistic reference
Figures.figure.douglas.event2: Laid foundation for Taiwanese-script Bible translation and literary tradition
Figures.figure.douglas.title: Compiler of the Amoy-English Dictionary
Figures.figure.ducongming.bio: Du Tsung-ming (1893–1986) was born in Sanzhi (then in Tamsui District), Taipei, and became the first Taiwanese to earn a doctorate in medicine, as well as the first locally born Taiwanese to obtain a doctorate in any discipline. He attended the Taiwan Government Medical School, a forerunner of National Taiwan University's College of Medicine, and after graduation pursued advanced study at Kyoto Imperial University, focusing on pharmacology and toxicology. In 1922 he received his doctorate in medicine, an unprecedented achievement for a Taiwanese under colonial rule. On his return he took up a teaching post at the Taipei Medical Specialty School and in time rose to full professor at Taihoku Imperial University's Faculty of Medicine. His research centered on opium addiction, snake venom, and the chemical analysis of traditional Chinese pharmacopoeia, drawing recognition from both the Japanese authorities and the international scientific community. From 1929 he led scientific treatment of opium addicts at the Gengshengyuan (Rehabilitation Institute) in Taipei, proposing a so-called gradual-withdrawal therapy that combined tapered dosing with psychological counseling. During the same period he developed a urinary morphine assay capable of objectively verifying abstinence, providing a crucial scientific basis for the era's opium-rehabilitation system. His work both responded to the Government-General's opium monopoly policy and made Taiwan an internationally significant site for opium-treatment research from the 1930s into the 1940s. After the Republic of China takeover, he served as the first dean of National Taiwan University's College of Medicine, helping to bridge the medical institutions of the colonial and postwar eras. In 1954 he founded Kaohsiung Medical College, today's Kaohsiung Medical University, opening a new chapter in medical education in southern Taiwan. He devoted decades to training local physicians and advancing public health, and his students went on to populate the upper ranks of Taiwan's medical profession. He died in Taipei in 1986 at the age of 93. He is widely credited with being a founding figure of modern medical education and of the scientific approach to opium rehabilitation in Taiwan.
Figures.figure.ducongming.event1: 1922 Earned doctorate in medicine, the first for a Taiwanese
Figures.figure.ducongming.event2: 1930s Led gradual-withdrawal opium therapy at Gengshengyuan
Figures.figure.ducongming.title: Taiwan's First Doctor of Medicine
Figures.figure.fengxifan.bio: Feng Xifan was a senior Tungning military officer and palace official whose 1681 coup catalyzed the rapid collapse of Han Chinese independent rule over Taiwan. He came from a Fujianese military family loyal to the Zheng house, served Koxinga in southern Fujian, and crossed to Taiwan with the main forces after 1661. Under Zheng Jing he rose to command the elite Personal Guards (侍衛), becoming one of the most powerful officials of the inner court and earning the trust of the ruler. He married his daughter to Zheng Keshuang, the younger son of Zheng Jing, a tie that placed him at the heart of the Tungning succession question. He came into open conflict with the heir apparent Zheng Kezang, whose strict supervision of officialdom threatened Feng's clients and patronage networks. When Zheng Jing died in January 1681 and Zheng Kezang assumed the throne, Feng allied with royal clansmen and Zheng Jing's brothers to engineer a coup in the name of dynastic legitimacy. They lured the young king to the Beiyuan Garden, strangled him, and installed his twelve-year-old brother — Feng's own son-in-law — in his place, in the event known as the Tungning Coup (東寧之變). Acting as effective regent alongside the general Liu Guoxuan, Feng pursued a hardline anti-Qing policy and continued to invest in coastal raids even as the kingdom's resources hemorrhaged. He resisted overtures from the Qing court for a negotiated settlement, betting on the strength of Liu Guoxuan's fleet at Penghu — a wager that ended in catastrophe in July 1683. After the surrender of Zheng Keshuang he accompanied the royal household to Beijing, where he was conferred an earl rank by the Qing court and a modest enfeoffment. He lived out the remainder of his life in the Qing capital and the precise date of his death is unrecorded. Feng is generally judged severely by Taiwanese historiography as the man whose ambition and clan jealousy destroyed the Tungning state from within, completing in months what the Qing had failed to achieve in two decades of warfare.
Figures.figure.fengxifan.event1: Led the palace coup of 1681 that murdered Zheng Kezang and installed Zheng Keshuang
Figures.figure.fengxifan.title: Minister & Architect of the Tungning Coup
Figures.figure.fukangan.bio: Fukang'an was the most celebrated Manchu general of the late Qianlong reign, born in Beijing in 1754 to the Fuca clan as the third son of the Grand Secretary Fuheng and nephew of the Empress Xiaoxianchun, and raised within the palace alongside the imperial princes. The Qianlong Emperor cherished him almost as an adopted son, and from his teenage years bestowed on him senior appointments such as Guard of the Imperial Presence, grooming him as the empire's most prized military reserve. From the 1770s he served successively as Governor-General of Sichuan, Shaan-Gan, and Yun-Gui, and on Qianlong's orders led campaigns to pacify the Jinchuan, the Muslim oases, and the Gurkha kingdom, accumulating deep experience in command, logistics, and frontier ethnic policy. After the Lin Shuangwen rebellion broke out on Taiwan in 1786 and several earlier expeditions across the strait had failed, the emperor appointed him in early 1787 as Grand General and Imperial Commissioner, with full authority over military and civil affairs on both sides of the strait. In the winter of that year he led a force of sixty thousand Manchu, Han, Muslim, and indigenous garrison troops, equipped with the finest imperial firearms, in a two-pronged landing at Lukang and Anping that rapidly reversed the war. He personally led cavalry through the rebel cordon at Changhua to relieve the besieged city of Chu-lo, which had been holding out for six months on the brink of collapse, and combined precise artillery tactics with a policy of dividing the Hoklo, Hakka, and indigenous coalition to crush the rebellion completely by early 1788. He memorialized the resolute defense of the Chu-lo townsmen to the court, prompting the emperor to bestow the imperial name Jiayi on the city, a name that has remained in use ever since. Returning to Beijing he was enfeoffed as Duke Jiayong of the First Class for his Taiwan campaign and rose to the pinnacle of Manchu military rank within the imperial court. In 1792, when the Gurkha kingdom invaded the western reaches of Tibet, he led another army across the Himalayas into the Kathmandu valley, compelling Nepal to send tribute to the Qing and consolidating the empire's suzerainty over Tibet. He died of exhaustion and malaria in his camp in Hunan in 1796 while supervising the suppression of the Miao uprisings, at the age of just forty-two. The Qianlong Emperor, deeply grieved, broke precedent by posthumously enfeoffing him as a junior prince and composed an imperial elegy in his honor, an unusual distinction for a Manchu general of the period. Fukang'an is generally regarded as the emblematic figure of late-Qianlong imperial military power, and his suppression of the Lin Shuangwen rebellion together with his role in the imperial naming of Jiayi left an indelible imprint on the early modern history of Taiwan.
Figures.figure.fukangan.event1: Led a 60,000-strong army to crush the Lin Shuangwen rebellion in 1787, prompting the imperial naming of Jiayi
Figures.figure.fukangan.title: Manchu General & Commander of the Lin Shuangwen Campaign
Figures.figure.fusinian.bio: Fu Ssu-nien, born in 1896 into a scholarly family in Liaocheng, Shandong, was a renowned modern Chinese historian and educator and a key figure in post-war Taiwanese higher education. He studied at Peking University, where his brilliance stood out, and in 1919 he served as a student leader in the May Fourth Movement while editing the journal Xinchao (New Tide) to champion the New Culture. He then studied in Britain and Germany, ranging widely across history, linguistics, and philosophy and building deep scholarly foundations. Returning to China, he founded and long directed the Institute of History and Philology at Academia Sinica, advancing the modernization and scientific rigor of Chinese historiography with his dictum that "history is the study of historical materials." Around the war years he served as acting president of Peking University, known for his outspokenness and rectitude and unafraid to criticize the ills of government and officialdom. In 1949 he came to Taiwan with the government and became president of National Taiwan University, a pivotal force in establishing the university's ethos. During his tenure he pushed educational reform, overhauled administration, and stressed academic freedom and university autonomy. In the early White Terror he sought to protect the university's faculty and students and to resist excessive political intrusion onto campus. In December 1950 he collapsed from a cerebral hemorrhage while answering questions before the Taiwan Provincial Assembly and died that day, aged just fifty-four. In his memory, NTU maintains the "Fu Bell" and "Fu Garden," and his stewardship is long remembered. Fu is regarded as a model intellectual uniting scholarly ideals with social conscience, and his brief presidency profoundly shaped National Taiwan University and the post-war academic climate.
Figures.figure.fusinian.event1: Served as president of National Taiwan University (1949–1950)
Figures.figure.fusinian.event2: Student leader of the May Fourth Movement
Figures.figure.fusinian.title: NTU President & Historian
Figures.figure.gaoyisheng.bio: Kao I-sheng, known by his Tsou name Uyongu Yatauyungana, was born in 1908 in the Tapangʉ community of Alishan and became one of the most prominent indigenous intellectual leaders of the late colonial and early post-war eras. Selected in youth into the Japanese education system, he graduated from the Tainan Normal School and served as both teacher and policeman, while displaying remarkable musical talent and composing many songs in the Tsou language. He worked to preserve his people's culture and modernize the tribe, promoting agriculture and education, and commanded great prestige within Tsou society. After the change of regime at the end of World War II, he became head of Wufeng Township (today's Alishan Township), an important local leader. During the February 28 Incident he helped maintain local order and sheltered people fleeing arrest. He went on to advocate "highland self-government," arguing that the indigenous peoples of the Alishan region should enjoy a substantial measure of autonomy — a stance that touched the authorities' nerves. During the White Terror of the 1950s he was accused of espionage and corruption and arrested in 1952. After prolonged detention and interrogation he was executed in 1954, together with fellow Tsou leaders such as Tang Shou-jen. His death dealt a devastating blow to a generation of Tsou leadership, gravely setting back the tribe's development and cultural transmission. Songs he wrote in prison, such as "Spring Goddess Saohime," later became emblems by which his people remembered him. Kao is remembered as a representative of the post-war indigenous elite persecuted under the authoritarian system, and his life is an important lens on the relationship between Taiwan's indigenous peoples and the state.
Figures.figure.gaoyisheng.title: Tsou Leader & Composer
Figures.figure.gechaozhi.bio: George H. Kerr, born in 1911 in the United States, was among the most important foreign witnesses and chroniclers of the February 28 Incident. He came to Taiwan in the late 1930s to teach English at the Taihoku High School, gaining firsthand contact with late-colonial Taiwanese society and its young intellectuals. During World War II he served in the US Navy, becoming one of the US government's few Taiwan-affairs specialists, involved in intelligence and post-war planning for the island. After the war he returned to Taiwan as vice-consul at the US consulate in Taipei, closely observing the Nationalist takeover and administration. When the February 28 Incident broke out in 1947 he was in Taiwan, witnessing the clashes between officials and the public and the bloody crackdown that followed, which he documented in detail and reported. Deeply sympathetic to the Taiwanese, he argued that Taiwan's future should be left to self-determination or international trusteeship, straining his relations with the Nationalist government. After leaving Taiwan he continued research and writing, publishing "Formosa Betrayed" in 1965, a systematic expose of the February 28 Incident and the problems of Nationalist rule. The book became an important text for post-war Taiwanese history and the independence movement, long circulated abroad. He also wrote a scholarly study of Taiwan's home-rule movement, a pioneer of Taiwan studies in Western academia. He died in the United States in 1992, and part of his ashes were, by his wish, interred in Taiwan. Kerr is regarded as a key international witness to February 28, and his writings preserve a valuable outside perspective for Taiwan's historical memory.
Figures.figure.gechaozhi.event1: Witnessed and documented the February 28 Incident (1947)
Figures.figure.gechaozhi.title: US Diplomat & Author of "Formosa Betrayed"
Figures.figure.gengjingzhong.bio: Geng Jingzhong was the third-generation Prince of Jingnan in early Qing service, born in 1644 into a Liaodong military family whose grandfather Geng Zhongming had defected from the late Ming to the rising Manchu state. Under the so-called Three Loyal Princes system that allowed defector families to garrison the southern frontier, his lineage held hereditary command over southern provinces, and in the late 1660s he succeeded to the Jingnan title and the perpetual governorship of Fujian. He established his princely seat at Fuzhou and controlled the coastal defenses of Fujian and Zhejiang as well as the southern Fujian frontier, sustaining a tense and ambivalent relationship — at once confrontational and quietly commercial — with the Zheng regime across the Taiwan Strait. The Jingnan fief in Fujian commanded its own armies and revenues and had become a semi-independent power that the Qing court found increasingly difficult to restrain. After Wu Sangui rose in revolt in Yunnan in 1673, he joined the rebellion in 1674, styling himself Grand Commander of the Armies and quickly seizing control of all of Fujian before sending troops into Zhejiang and Jiangxi. To strengthen the loyalist coalition he dispatched envoys across the strait to negotiate a joint operation with the Tungning ruler Zheng Jing at Xiamen, hoping to use the Zheng navy to tie down the Qing coastal forces in the southeast. The alliance rapidly fractured over disputes about jurisdiction in Quanzhou and Zhangzhou, the allocation of military grain, and command authority, and Zheng Jing's westward expeditionary forces ended up in open combat with his troops along the southern Fujian coast, depriving the rebellion of its decisive southeastern thrust. Hard pressed by Qing armies advancing south in 1676, he surrendered to the Qing and turned his troops against his former ally Zheng Jing. The Qing court nonetheless remained deeply suspicious of his repeated changes of allegiance. After the final suppression of the Three Feudatories Revolt in 1681, he and his brothers Geng Zhaozhong and Geng Juzhong were detained and brought to Beijing. In 1682 the Kangxi Emperor charged him with treason and ordered him executed by slow slicing in the marketplace at the age of thirty-eight, extinguishing the Jingnan princely line. Geng Jingzhong is generally regarded as the most politically opportunistic and strategically incoherent of the three feudatory princes, and his breakdown with Zheng Jing is widely cited as a principal cause of the Tungning Kingdom's failure to convert the rebellion into a lasting opening for the recovery of the mainland.
Figures.figure.gengjingzhong.event1: Joined the Three Feudatories Revolt in 1674; his alliance with Zheng Jing quickly broke down
Figures.figure.gengjingzhong.title: Prince of Jingnan & Fujian Leader of the Three Feudatories Revolt
Figures.figure.gotoshinpei.bio: Gotō Shinpei, born in 1857 in Mutsu Province (present-day Iwate Prefecture) to a former samurai family of the Date clan, served as Chief of Civil Affairs of Taiwan from 1898 to 1906 and is widely regarded as the principal architect of Japan's early colonial administration on the island. Trained as a physician, he studied medical hygiene in Germany and rose through Japan's home-affairs bureaucracy after organizing the celebrated quarantine of more than 230,000 returning soldiers at Hiroshima following the First Sino-Japanese War. Recommended to Taiwan by Governor-General Kodama Gentarō in 1898, Gotō wielded broad discretionary authority over civil governance while Kodama handled military and external affairs. He grounded his rule in what he called the biological principle, insisting that colonial policy be calibrated to existing local customs after rigorous empirical survey rather than imposed by abstract ideology. Under his direction the colony conducted comprehensive land surveys, established a household registration system, and built the police-and-headman (baojia) network that became the spine of social control in Taiwan for the next half century. He financed development through state monopolies on opium, camphor, salt, and tobacco, with the opium policy framed as gradual suppression rather than abrupt prohibition. His public works program built the north-south trunk railway, modernized the ports of Keelung and Kaohsiung, expanded irrigation, and introduced sanitary engineering that dramatically reduced bubonic plague and malaria mortality. He chartered the Bank of Taiwan, supported the modern sugar industry, and laid the institutional groundwork for the colony's transition from a security drain to a fiscal contributor of the Japanese empire. Pacification under his tenure combined the cooptation of local elites with harsh punitive expeditions against armed resisters, ending the chronic banditry of the 1890s but at a heavy human cost. After leaving Taiwan he served as the first president of the South Manchuria Railway Company, then as Communications Minister, Home Minister, and Mayor of Tokyo, leading the reconstruction of the capital after the Great Kantō Earthquake of 1923. He died in 1929 while on a speaking tour in Kyoto. Gotō is remembered as a controversial but transformative figure who built Taiwan's modern administrative, infrastructural, and public-health foundations while also entrenching colonial mechanisms of surveillance and exploitation.
Figures.figure.gotoshinpei.event1: Modernized Taiwan's public health and infrastructure as Chief of Home Affairs
Figures.figure.gotoshinpei.title: Chief of Home Affairs, Taiwan Governor-General's Office
Figures.figure.guohuaiyi.bio: Guo Huaiyi was a mid-seventeenth-century Hokkien settler leader in Dutch-ruled Taiwan who led the largest Han Chinese uprising against the Dutch East India Company in 1652. He came from coastal Fujian and migrated to Taiwan during the period when the VOC actively encouraged Chinese settlement on the southwestern plain, establishing himself as a sugar cane and rice cultivator on the outskirts of what is today Tainan. He was a man of standing within the immigrant farming community and is described in Dutch sources as a representative of the kapitan-class settler headmen, and at times cooperated with the colonial administration. From the late 1640s the VOC, seeking to offset its mounting fiscal deficits, raised the poll tax and the village-leasing (pacht) levies on Chinese settlers and tolerated abuses by the tax-farmers, sharply worsening relations between the immigrants and the Dutch officials. Compounded by successive crop failures and epidemics in the early 1650s, settler discontent reached a breaking point, and he covertly mobilized Hokkien migrants together with some indigenous allies in preparation for armed revolt. In September 1652 he led between four and five thousand Han Chinese, armed largely with agricultural tools and improvised weapons, in an attack near Saccam aimed at overrunning Fort Provintia and Fort Zeelandia under cover of darkness. The plan was betrayed in advance, and the VOC was able to mobilize its musketeers and indigenous allies in time to meet the rising on open ground with concentrated firepower. The fighting lasted some fifteen days, and he himself was killed early in the campaign, his body decapitated and displayed by the Dutch as a warning, while subsequent mop-up operations were carried out by VOC troops together with Siraya allies. Dutch records report that between four and five thousand Han Chinese were killed in combat and the executions that followed, making it the largest internal upheaval of the Dutch period. After the suppression the VOC tightened surveillance and taxation of the Chinese community and expanded the armed role of its indigenous allies to consolidate control of the plain. The uprising nonetheless signaled to the colonial administration that the island's Han Chinese population had grown large enough to threaten the regime, foreshadowing the defection of many settlers to Koxinga's invading forces nine years later. Guo Huaiyi is generally remembered as the leader of the first large-scale Han Chinese revolt against European colonial rule in Taiwan and as a symbolic figure of the conflict between an emerging immigrant society and the imperial powers that sought to rule it.
Figures.figure.guohuaiyi.event1: Led the 1652 Han Chinese uprising against the VOC at Tayouan
Figures.figure.guohuaiyi.title: Leader of the Han Chinese Uprising
Figures.figure.guoxiliu.bio: Guo Xiliu was a Fujianese immigrant who became the driving force behind the most important irrigation project in the Taipei Basin. Beginning around 1740, he spent thirty years and his personal fortune constructing the Liugong Canal, which diverted water from the Xindian River to irrigate more than a thousand jia of farmland on the eastern Taipei plains. The project required overcoming attacks from Atayal mountain communities and formidable engineering challenges. When completed in the 1760s, the canal transformed agricultural productivity and enabled rapid expansion of Han settler communities. Later generations named the canal after his courtesy title, and a temple was erected in his honor. Guo Xiliu's achievement stands as one of the greatest private hydraulic engineering feats of Qing-era Taiwan.
Figures.figure.guoxiliu.event1: Spent thirty years building Liugong Canal to irrigate the Taipei Basin
Figures.figure.guoxiliu.event2: Honored with canal bearing his name and a commemorative temple
Figures.figure.guoxiliu.title: Builder of the Liugong Irrigation Canal
Figures.figure.guxianrong.bio: Ku Hsien-jung was born in 1866 in Lukang, Changhua, into a merchant family. In 1895, as the Qing ceded Taiwan and the short-lived resistance collapsed, the gentry of a chaotic and leaderless Taipei were desperate to prevent looting — and it was Ku who went out to meet the advancing Japanese army and guided it into the city, an act that would define, and forever divide opinion on, his life. The colonial authorities rewarded him richly, granting him lucrative monopolies in salt, camphor and other trades on which he built one of Taiwan's great commercial fortunes. He became the leading Taiwanese collaborator-notable of his era, cultivated by the regime and appointed in 1934 to the House of Peers in Tokyo — the first Taiwanese to hold such a seat. To the colonial government he was a model loyal subject; to the activists of the parliament and cultural movements he was the embodiment of collaboration, and the two camps clashed bitterly. Ku Hsien-jung died in 1937, founder of the powerful Lukang Ku family and one of the most controversial figures of the colonial age.
Figures.figure.guxianrong.event1: Guided the Japanese army into Taipei (1895)
Figures.figure.guxianrong.event2: First Taiwanese appointed to Japan's House of Peers (1934)
Figures.figure.guxianrong.title: Merchant and Colonial Collaborator
Figures.figure.hamadayahyoe.bio: Hamada Yahyoe was a Nagasaki-based vermilion seal (shuinsen) merchant active in the maritime trade between Japan and East Asia during the early Edo period. He came from a Nagasaki commercial family and held shogunal trading licenses to conduct long-distance voyages dealing in silk, silver, and deerskins, the high-value commodities of the Japan-China-Southeast Asia circuit. Working in close partnership with the trading network of the Nagasaki deputy Suetsugu Heizo, by the 1620s he had become one of the largest Japanese traders operating on the Tayouan route. After the Dutch East India Company built Fort Zeelandia at Tayouan in 1624 and imposed import duties and restrictions on Japanese intermediary trade between Taiwan and China, his interests came into direct conflict with the VOC's emerging colonial monopoly. In 1627 he brought Dika and approximately fifteen other Sinkan (Siraya) villagers back to Edo with him, presenting them at the court of Shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu as representatives of Formosa and nominally offering the island in tribute to the bakufu in challenge to the VOC's territorial claim. He returned to Tayouan in 1628 with armed sailors and confronted the Dutch governor Pieter Nuyts over the seizure of his cargo and the detention of the Sinkan envoys. In June 1628 he and his men forced their way into the governor's residence and took Nuyts himself hostage, compelling the VOC to release the Sinkan envoys and to pay heavy compensation in what became known as the Hamada Incident. After returning to Japan with his hostages, he denounced the VOC before the Tokugawa shogunate, which suspended all Dutch trade with Japan from 1628 to 1632 in retaliation for the company's conduct in Taiwan. The four-year embargo forced VOC senior officials to capitulate, eventually surrendering Nuyts himself for detention in Japan as the price of restoring Dutch access to the Japanese market. The promulgation of the Tokugawa sakoku edicts from 1635 abolished the vermilion seal system altogether, ending his legal basis for long-distance trade and removing him from the East Asian commercial stage. His later life and date of death are not recorded in Japanese or Dutch sources. He is widely regarded as the protagonist of one of the rare successful confrontations between a private Japanese trader and a European colonial power in the seventeenth century, and as the figure who triggered the first major international crisis to arise from Taiwan's emerging role as a contested node of East Asian empire.
Figures.figure.hamadayahyoe.event1: Seized Dutch Governor Pieter Nuyts in 1628, triggering the Hamada Incident
Figures.figure.hamadayahyoe.title: Vermilion Seal Ship Merchant
Figures.figure.hamanoyashiro.bio: Hamano Yashiro (1869–1932) was a Japanese sanitary engineer honoured as the 'Father of Taiwan's Waterworks.' He was a student and able assistant of the British engineer William K. Burton, who had been hired to come to Taiwan, and from the early years of Japanese rule he accompanied his teacher to the island to survey and plan modern water-supply and sewerage systems. At the time epidemics raged across Taiwan and public sanitation was wretched, and the supply of clean water was regarded as fundamental to colonial modernization and to safeguarding the health of the population. After Burton died young of malaria, Hamano carried on his teacher's mission, single-handedly undertaking waterworks for Taiwan's major cities for more than twenty years. He successively planned and built the water-supply and sewerage systems of Taipei, Keelung, Tainan, Chiayi and other cities, introducing modern techniques such as sedimentation, filtration and pressurized supply, thereby laying the foundation of modern sanitary water supply for Taiwan's cities and greatly improving urban drinking water and disease prevention. His engineering ideals and his cultivation of talent were passed down across generations; his student Hatta Yoichi later completed the unprecedented Chianan Canal, allowing the lineage of Taiwan's modern hydraulic engineering to continue. Though Hamano's contributions were less conspicuous than those of battlefield heroes, they profoundly changed the daily life and health of countless Taiwanese.
Figures.figure.hamanoyashiro.event1: 1896+ Planned water-supply and sewerage systems for Taiwan's cities
Figures.figure.hamanoyashiro.event2: 1900s–10s Established modern sanitary water supply in Taipei, Tainan and elsewhere
Figures.figure.hamanoyashiro.title: Father of Taiwan's Waterworks
Figures.figure.hambroek.bio: Antonius Hambroek was a Dutch Reformed missionary born in Delft, dispatched by the East India Company to Formosa in 1648, where he served in the Siraya village of Mattau. Over more than a decade on the island, he learned the Siraya language, built schools, and cultivated a community of indigenous Christians. In April 1661, Koxinga's forces besieged Fort Zeelandia; Hambroek and his two daughters were among those taken captive. Governor Frederick Coyett, facing dwindling supplies, chose Hambroek as an emissary — sending him through enemy lines to persuade the Dutch garrison to surrender and spare further bloodshed. Instead, Hambroek delivered the opposite message: he exhorted the defenders to hold fast and fight for their freedom in God's name. Returning to Koxinga's camp as honour demanded, he was swiftly executed on the warlord's orders. His daughters were absorbed into Koxinga's household. The story of Hambroek's defiant sacrifice spread widely across Europe, inspiring plays, poems, and paintings for generations. He came to embody the tragic intertwining of faith and colonial fate at the close of the Dutch era — a martyr who chose death over dishonour at the edge of empire.
Figures.figure.hambroek.event1: Served as a Dutch Reformed missionary in Mattau for over a decade, learning the Siraya language and building one of the island's most established indigenous Christian communities.
Figures.figure.hambroek.event2: Sent as emissary by Governor Coyett during Koxinga's 1661 siege; instead of urging surrender, he rallied the garrison to resist, then returned to enemy lines and was executed.
Figures.figure.hambroek.title: Dutch Reformed Missionary, Martyr of Fort Zeelandia
Figures.figure.hanaokaichiro.bio: Hanaoka Ichiro, whose original name was Dakis Nomin (1908–1930), was a Seediq of the Hogo community and a model figure deliberately cultivated by the Japanese colonial policy of 'savage management' and assimilation. Selected into the Japanese education system as a child, he excelled, graduated from a normal school and obtained a post as an assistant policeman, and the colonial authorities held him up as an exemplar of a 'successfully civilized savage,' even changing his name to the Japanese 'Hanaoka Ichiro.' Yet this assimilated identity left him caught between his own people and the colonizers, bearing a profound rupture of identity. When the Wushe Incident broke out in 1930 and his people rose in revolt under Mona Rudao, as a policeman raised by the Japanese he could neither betray the people who had reared him nor stand against the colonial system he served, and was trapped in an impossible dilemma. In the chaos and despair of the uprising he finally hanged himself in the mountains together with his wife and kin in the traditional Japanese manner, leaving a sorrowful suicide note bearing the words 'it could not be helped.' His death became a tragic symbol of how colonial assimilationist education forcibly tore apart indigenous identity, and it remains an important window into the complexity of the Wushe Incident.
Figures.figure.hanaokaichiro.event1: 1920s Educated in the Japanese system and served as a policeman
Figures.figure.hanaokaichiro.event2: 1930 Hanged himself during the Wushe Incident
Figures.figure.hanaokaichiro.title: Seediq Policeman Educated in the Japanese System
Figures.figure.hanaokajiro.bio: Hanaoka Jiro, whose original name was Dakis Nawi (1908–1930), was a Seediq of the Hogo community and, like Hanaoka Ichiro, a representative figure cultivated by Japanese colonial assimilation policy. Though the two shared the surname 'Hanaoka' and bore linked given names, they were in fact unrelated by blood, having been deliberately arranged by the colonial authorities as 'model brothers' to symbolize the achievements of 'savage education.' He too was educated in the Japanese system from childhood, took up a police post after graduating, and played the role of an intermediary between his people and the colonial system, living the life of one expected to become 'civilized.' When the Wushe Incident broke out in 1930 he, like Ichiro, was caught in the dilemma of loyalty to his people and loyalty to the colonial government, unable to choose and in deep anguish. As the uprising reached its hopeless end, he hanged himself in the mountains together with Ichiro's household and his kin, ending his torn life in the most resolute way. The deaths of both Hanaoka Jiro and Ichiro stand as another witness to the tragedy of indigenous identity wrought by colonial assimilation policy, laying bare the cruel cost behind the apparent success of the 'savage management' program.
Figures.figure.hanaokajiro.event1: 1920s Educated in the Japanese system and served as a policeman
Figures.figure.hanaokajiro.event2: 1930 Hanged himself during the Wushe Incident
Figures.figure.hanaokajiro.title: Seediq Policeman Educated in the Japanese System
Figures.figure.hasegawakinsuke.bio: Hasegawa Kinsuke (1855–1921) was a Japanese railway engineer and official honoured as the 'Father of Taiwan's Railways.' Trained in Japan's railway world in his early years, he accumulated rich experience in line construction, and in 1899 he came to Taiwan, where under the regime led by Kodama Gentaro and Goto Shinpei he served as chief engineer of the Taiwan Railway Bureau and directed the building of the trunk line. At the time north–south travel in Taiwan depended on walking and boats, often taking several days, severely constraining economic development and administrative control. With decisive engineering skill and a pragmatic construction strategy—advancing section by section, seeking through service first and refinement later—Hasegawa overcame the many difficulties of the numerous rivers and complex terrain along the route. In 1908 the trunk railway from Keelung to Kaohsiung opened along its entire length, shortening a north–south journey from several days to within a single day and knitting western Taiwan into a tightly linked 'one-day living circle.' This railway not only transformed the movement of people, goods and information within the island but also reshaped Taiwan's urban development and economic map, and it stands as one of the most representative infrastructural achievements of the Japanese period. Through the trunk line Hasegawa Kinsuke laid the backbone of Taiwan's modern transport, and his contribution endures to this day.
Figures.figure.hasegawakinsuke.event1: 1899+ Directed the construction of the trunk railway
Figures.figure.hasegawakinsuke.event2: 1908 The Keelung–Kaohsiung trunk railway opened end to end
Figures.figure.hasegawakinsuke.title: Father of Taiwan's Railways
Figures.figure.hasegawakiyoshi.bio: Hasegawa Kiyoshi (1883–1970), a Japanese navy admiral by background, served as the eighteenth Governor-General of Taiwan from 1940 to 1944, in the crucial years when the Pacific War broke out in full and Taiwan was pushed onto a wartime footing. Inheriting his predecessor Kobayashi Seizo's governing line of 'imperialization, industrialization and use as a southward base,' he steered Taiwan fully toward war mobilization: he promoted the establishment of the Kominhokokai (Imperial Subjects Public Service Association), enrolling the whole island's population in a top-down service organization that mobilized manpower, materiel and spiritual energy in support of the front. During his tenure he introduced a volunteer-soldier system for Taiwanese, recruiting army and then navy volunteers and sending Taiwanese youth to the battlefields of the South Seas, and he conscripted large numbers of indigenous people into the 'Takasago Volunteer Units' for jungle warfare. Compared with his predecessor he took a somewhat more conciliatory cultural stance, easing some of the harsher measures of imperialization and courting the Taiwanese gentry, seeking through the slogan of 'Japan and Taiwan as one' to win Taiwanese cooperation with the war. The famous 'Bell of Sayun' was presented by the Governor-General's Office during his tenure to honour a so-called 'patriotic maiden,' becoming a representative case of wartime mobilization propaganda. Hasegawa Kiyoshi's governorship coincided exactly with the period when Taiwanese society was wholly swept into the war machine and its people and resources were devoted on a massive scale to the Japanese empire's war, profoundly reflecting the plight of a colony under a wartime regime.
Figures.figure.hasegawakiyoshi.event1: 1940 Became the eighteenth Governor-General of Taiwan
Figures.figure.hasegawakiyoshi.event2: 1941 Founded the Imperial Subjects Public Service Association and drove wartime mobilization
Figures.figure.hasegawakiyoshi.title: Wartime Mobilization Governor-General
Figures.figure.hattatoyoki.bio: Hatta Toyoki (1900–1945) was the wife of Hatta Yoichi, the engineer of the Chianan Canal. She married Hatta at the age of sixteen, binding her life thereafter closely to her husband's mission. After marriage she left the comforts of city life to follow him, living for years at the remote and desolate construction site of the Wushantou Reservoir alongside the families of the engineering staff, accompanying her husband through the decade of hard labour that built the Chianan Canal and raising eight children in those rough conditions, a steadfast pillar behind him. In 1930 the canal was completed and water flowed, turning a hundred and fifty thousand jia of rain-dependent fields on the Chianan plain into fertile farmland—an achievement that also embodied her quiet sacrifice and devotion. In 1942 Hatta Yoichi died when the ship carrying him to the Philippines was torpedoed, and she bore her grief alone to support the whole family. In 1945, as Japan was defeated and she saw that her family was about to be repatriated and that the Wushantou Reservoir, the work of her husband's life, would pass into other hands, she threw herself into the reservoir's outlet at dawn on September 1, dying at only forty-five, following her late husband in the most resolute way and coming to rest on the land to which they had together devoted themselves. Her ashes are buried beside Hatta Yoichi by the reservoir, and their story is the most humanly poignant and tragic chapter in the legend of the Chianan Canal.
Figures.figure.hattatoyoki.event1: 1916 Married Hatta Yoichi and lived with him at the Wushantou site
Figures.figure.hattatoyoki.event2: 1945 Drowned herself at the Wushantou Reservoir outlet
Figures.figure.hattatoyoki.title: Wife of Hatta Yoichi
Figures.figure.hattayoichi.bio: Hatta Yoichi (1886–1942) was a hydraulic engineer from Ishikawa Prefecture in Japan and a graduate of the Imperial University of Tokyo. He came to Taiwan in 1910 as a civil engineer for the Government-General and was first involved in waterworks and power surveys before turning to large-scale irrigation. From 1920 he directed the construction of the Wushantou Reservoir and the Chianan Irrigation System (Chianan Tatsun), then the largest water project in Asia, designed to transform the chronically dry Chianan Plain. To build the dam he adopted the unusual semi-hydraulic fill method, then rarely used in the world, and personally championed mechanized construction by importing large American excavators. Equally important was his 'three-year crop rotation water-distribution system,' which rationed scarce water across rice, sugarcane, and other crops so that some 150,000 hectares of rain-dependent land could be cultivated. The works were completed and water began flowing in 1930, multiplying agricultural output across the plain. Hatta was known for treating Japanese and Taiwanese workers equally, for prioritizing labor welfare and safety, and for building schools and housing for the families at the construction site, which earned him lasting respect among local people. In 1942, during the Pacific War, he was ordered to the Philippines; the transport ship Daiyo Maru was torpedoed and sank, and he died at sea at the age of 56. His wife Toyoki later took her own life at the reservoir's outlet in 1945. After the war local residents continued to hold annual memorial rites for him, and a bronze statue of him seated in contemplation still stands beside the Wushantou Reservoir, where he is honored as the 'Father of the Chianan Irrigation System.'
Figures.figure.hattayoichi.event1: 1910 Came to Taiwan as a civil engineer for the Government-General
Figures.figure.hattayoichi.event2: 1920 Began construction of the Wushantou Reservoir and Chianan Irrigation System
Figures.figure.hattayoichi.event3: 1930 The Chianan Irrigation System was completed and began supplying water
Figures.figure.hattayoichi.event4: 1942 Died at sea when his transport ship was sunk en route to the Philippines
Figures.figure.hattayoichi.title: Father of the Chianan Irrigation System
Figures.figure.hebin.bio: He Bin was a Hokkien Chinese merchant and interpreter who served both the Dutch East India Company and the Zheng commercial network in the mid-seventeenth century, and whose 1659 defection helped enable Koxinga's eventual conquest of Dutch Taiwan. He came from a southern Fujian merchant family with established commercial ties to the Penghu and Tayouan trade circuit, and arrived in Dutch Formosa as a young man during the period of consolidated VOC rule in the 1640s. He prospered as a Hokkien interpreter and tax farmer for the VOC, taking advantage of his cultural and linguistic bridging role between the Dutch administration and the rapidly growing Hokkien settler and trader community. He simultaneously maintained covert commercial relations with the Zheng family's maritime network across the strait, exploiting the licit and illicit channels of the Sino-Japanese trade that flowed through Dutch Tayouan. By the late 1650s his finances had collapsed under the weight of borrowing from the VOC tax authorities and competing creditors, and warrants for his arrest were issued by the Dutch administration. In 1659 he fled Tayouan by sea and made his way to Xiamen, where he sought refuge in the court of Koxinga, who was at the time considering a fallback base on Taiwan after his failed mainland campaign against the Qing. He presented Koxinga with detailed sketches and maps of the Tayouan harbor and Fort Zeelandia, including descriptions of the channels through the sandbars, the placement of artillery, and the disposition of the small VOC garrison. He argued forcefully that Taiwan was a rich, lightly defended prize whose loyal Hokkien settlers would welcome Zheng forces, encouraging the warlord to redirect his strategic ambitions from the mainland coast to the island. His intelligence was central to the operational planning of Koxinga's 1661 amphibious crossing, including the decision to land at Lakjemuyse Bay through a channel often considered unnavigable by the Dutch. He accompanied the Zheng fleet on the crossing and served as a senior advisor and Hokkien-Dutch interpreter during the nine-month siege of Fort Zeelandia. His role in the post-conquest Tungning regime is poorly documented, and contemporary Dutch sources record only that he survived the campaign and continued in some capacity in the new administration. He Bin is generally remembered as the indispensable insider whose firsthand knowledge of Dutch defenses provided the operational basis for Koxinga's gamble on Taiwan and thereby the end of the VOC's thirty-eight-year rule.
Figures.figure.hebin.event1: Defected from the VOC to Koxinga (1659), providing the maps that enabled the invasion of Taiwan
Figures.figure.hebin.title: VOC Interpreter & Defector
Figures.figure.hongtengyun.bio: Hong Tengyun, born in 1819 in Anxi County, Fujian, and arriving in Taiwan in his youth, became the wealthiest and most philanthropically active Hokkien merchant in northern Taiwan during the second half of the nineteenth century, best known for his decisive financial contribution to the construction of Taipei City (臺北府城) and his patronage of the Taipei City God Temple (臺北府城隍廟), institutions that remain central to the city's identity today. He built his fortune through tea and rice trade in the Tamsui and Danshui regions, benefiting from the rapid expansion of northern Taiwan's export economy following the opening of the treaty ports, and used his wealth to establish a commercial and philanthropic network that made him the preeminent patron of public life in what would become the Taipei basin. When Liu Mingchuan was appointed Taiwan's first governor and began the project of constructing Taipei City as the island's new capital in 1879, Hong Tengyun was among the handful of local merchants whose financial contributions made the enterprise possible, donating substantial sums and land that were essential to the construction of the city's walls, gates, and administrative buildings. He was also the founding patron of the Taipei City God Temple, established in 1881 on land he donated in what is today the Zhongzheng District of Taipei, which became the most important ceremonial center for the Hokkien settler communities of the Taipei basin and remains an active religious site today. Hong invested in a wide range of public goods: he contributed to the repair of roads and bridges, donated to charitable granaries during famines, sponsored the construction of public baths and market infrastructure, and funded the maintenance of schools and examination halls, embodying the Confucian ideal of the benevolent merchant using private wealth for collective benefit. He also navigated with skill the complex patronage networks linking Hokkien merchant communities, Qing officials, and indigenous peoples in the Tamsui basin, serving as a broker whose connections across these different worlds gave him access to both official favor and commercial opportunity. His social prominence was formalized through the purchase of official titles and the accumulation of honorific recognition from Qing authorities, who valued his ability to mobilize local resources for state projects without drawing on imperial funds. Hong Tengyun died in 1899, having witnessed the transition from Qing to Japanese rule in 1895; his business empire was absorbed by his descendants, who continued to operate in the new colonial economy. His most visible legacy is the Taipei City God Temple, which stands today in the old city center as a direct physical embodiment of his patronage and is visited by hundreds of thousands of worshippers annually. Hong Tengyun is widely regarded as the model of the nineteenth-century Taiwanese civic merchant — a man who accumulated wealth through trade and invested it in the institutions that gave a new city its communal identity, social cohesion, and spiritual center.
Figures.figure.hongtengyun.event1: Donated land and funds essential to the construction of Taipei City's walls, gates, and administrative buildings (1879–84)
Figures.figure.hongtengyun.event2: Founded the Taipei City God Temple (臺北府城隍廟, 1881), which remains the spiritual center of Taipei's Hokkien communities
Figures.figure.hongtengyun.title: Merchant and Patron of Taipei City
Figures.figure.hsiehtsungmin.bio: Hsieh Tsung-min, born in 1934 in Changhua, was an important witness to and participant in Taiwan's post-war human-rights and democracy movements. He studied at National Taiwan University and National Chengchi University, receiving a full training in the social sciences and attending to Taiwan's political future. In 1964, together with NTU professor Peng Ming-min and the young Wei Ting-chao, he co-drafted the "Declaration of Taiwanese Self-Salvation," calling for a new constitution and for Taiwan to join the international community as its own entity — an exceptionally early and weighty document of political dissent in the post-war period. The declaration was seized before it could be widely distributed, and the three were arrested; he was sentenced to prison, becoming a political prisoner of the White Terror. After his release he remained under close surveillance, and in the 1970s he was arrested again over accusations involving bombing cases, imprisoned for years in total and tortured during interrogation. He later went into exile, continuing to advocate for Taiwan's human rights and democracy in the United States and exposing political persecution in Taiwan to the world. After the lifting of martial law and democratization he returned, won election as a legislator, and continued to push human-rights legislation and the clarification of authoritarian-era history. In his later years he devoted himself to organizing political archives and to transitional-justice work, giving voice to victims. He died in Taiwan in 2019. Hsieh is seen as a pivotal figure bridging generations of Taiwan's post-war human-rights movement, his drafting of the self-salvation declaration and long imprisonment an important testimony linking the White Terror to the democratic transition.
Figures.figure.hsiehtsungmin.event1: Co-drafted the Declaration of Taiwanese Self-Salvation (1964)
Figures.figure.hsiehtsungmin.event2: Repeatedly imprisoned and tortured in political cases
Figures.figure.hsiehtsungmin.title: Co-author of the Taiwan Self-Salvation Manifesto
Figures.figure.hsuhsinliang.bio: Hsu Hsin-liang, born in 1941 in Zhongli, Taoyuan, is one of the key figures in Taiwan's tangwai electoral movement and democratization. He studied at National Chengchi University and pursued further study in Britain, returning as a young elite once cultivated by the Kuomintang.
