Clashing with the party over his convictions, he left the KMT and defied party discipline to run for Taoyuan county magistrate in 1977. Amid disputes over vote-rigging during the count, crowds surrounded the Zhongli police station in a mass protest known as the "Chungli Incident" — the first large-scale street demonstration of the post-war era — and he ultimately won by a wide margin. In 1979 he was suspended from office for supporting cases such as that of Yu Teng-fa, then went abroad, taking part in the Formosa Magazine movement and overseas opposition, long blacklisted and barred from returning. From the late 1980s into the 1990s he repeatedly attempted to "break through" and return to Taiwan, becoming a symbolic case of exiled dissidents seeking to come home. After the lifting of martial law he formally joined the Democratic Progressive Party and twice served as its chairman, advocating an assertive mass-mobilization and electoral strategy. He also put forward controversial lines such as "boldly going west," sparking debate within the party. He gradually parted ways with the DPP mainstream and ran for president as an independent in 2000. Hsu is seen as one of the trailblazers of Taiwan's tangwai electoral movement, his turn from KMT elite to street protester to opposition leader an important case for understanding the path of Taiwan's democratization.
Figures.figure.hsuhsinliang.event1: Sparked the Chungli Incident and won the Taoyuan magistracy (1977)
Figures.figure.hsuhsinliang.event2: Twice served as chairman of the DPP
Figures.figure.hsuhsinliang.title: Central to the Chungli Incident & DPP Chairman
Figures.figure.hsuwenlung.bio: Hsu Wen-lung, born in 1928 in Tainan, was a representative entrepreneur of post-war Taiwan who combined industrial achievement with cultural ideals. Growing up in Tainan in the late colonial period, he held a deep interest in art and natural history from childhood, a passion that shaped his whole life. Rising from nothing, he founded Chi Mei Corporation around 1960, entering the production of plastics and petrochemical materials. He built Chi Mei into one of the world's largest suppliers of ABS resin and expanded into the optoelectronics industry, making it a major Taiwanese conglomerate. His management style emphasized humane treatment and employee well-being, championing the idea of the "happy enterprise," distinctive in the business world. Once successful, he poured great resources into culture and philanthropy, realizing the dreams of his youth. He founded the Chimei Museum, collecting Western art, musical instruments, arms, and natural-history specimens, and became renowned for a rich collection of fine violins, long lent free of charge to musicians to nurture Taiwanese musical talent. He was himself a well-known amateur violinist, devoted throughout his life to popularizing art and the education of beauty. In politics he leaned toward supporting Taiwanese identity and served as a senior adviser to the president. He died in Tainan in 2023. Hsu is seen as a model among Taiwanese entrepreneurs of turning wealth into a cultural public good, his Chimei Museum and violin collection long enriching Taiwan's artistic and humanistic soil.
Figures.figure.hsuwenlung.event2: Founded the Chimei Museum, promoting art and a violin collection
Figures.figure.hsuwenlung.title: Founder of Chi Mei Corporation & the Chimei Museum
Figures.figure.huanghsinchieh.bio: Huang Hsin-chieh, born in 1928 in Taipei to a Hokkien family, was the most senior tangwai elder statesman of his generation and one of the founding architects of organized opposition politics in martial-law Taiwan. He graduated from National Taiwan University and entered local Taipei politics as an independent in the late 1950s, winning seats on the Taipei municipal council during the era when the KMT monopolized national-level office. He was elected as a supplementary member of the Legislative Yuan in 1969, becoming a leading voice for the small tangwai (outside the party) opposition through the 1970s. He cultivated a generation of younger tangwai activists across local elections and intellectual circles, mentoring figures who would later define the Democratic Progressive Party. In 1979 he co-founded Formosa Magazine (《美麗島》雜誌), the most ambitious tangwai publication of the era, which served as a de facto opposition organization with chapters across the island. As publisher of Formosa, he was a principal target of the Kaohsiung Incident crackdown of December 1979 and was sentenced by a military court to fourteen years in prison. He was released on medical parole in 1987 amid the lifting of martial law, immediately resumed political work, and helped consolidate the newly founded Democratic Progressive Party, founded in 1986 while he was still imprisoned. He served as chairman of the DPP from 1988 to 1991, presiding over the party's first electoral breakthroughs in the post-martial-law era. He led the party through the constitutional reform negotiations of the early 1990s and helped articulate the case for direct presidential elections, which were finally held in 1996. He ran for the presidency in the 1996 election in a four-way race against Lee Teng-hui, finishing third behind Lee and Peng Ming-min but giving the DPP its first competitive national platform. He died of stroke in 1999 in Taipei at the age of 71, before he could see Chen Shui-bian's victory in the following year's presidential race that would complete Taiwan's first peaceful party turnover. Huang is widely commemorated in Taiwan as one of the foundational elders of the democracy movement, the bridge between an older generation of local-politics tangwai and the post-1987 party-political opposition.
Figures.figure.huanghsinchieh.title: Democracy Activist & DPP Chairman
Figures.figure.huangjindao.bio: Huang Chin-tao, born in 1926 in Dajia, Taichung, was one of the few surviving frontline commanders of the armed resistance during the February 28 Incident. As a young man he was conscripted as a Taiwanese soldier in the Japanese army and sent to fight in the South Seas during the Second World War, where he acquired real combat experience. Returning home after the war, he was drawn into the uprising that swept Taichung in March 1947. When Hsieh Hsueh-hung organized the 27 Brigade, Huang joined as a squad leader, and after the brigade withdrew from the city to the mountain town of Puli he was placed in command of the defensive line at Wuniulan. On March 16, drawing on the high ground of the Ailan plateau and the narrow bridgehead, he led a force of young students and demobilized veterans that briefly inflicted heavy losses on the advancing 21st Division, in what became the last and fiercest engagement of organized Taiwanese armed resistance in the entire February 28 period. After the brigade disbanded he went into hiding, but was eventually arrested, sentenced, and imprisoned for more than twenty years, much of it on Green Island. Released only in his later years, he devoted the rest of his life to testifying to what had happened, becoming a living witness to the Wuniulan battle until his death in 2014. His account preserved for later generations the concrete texture of a battle that the authorities had long tried to erase.
Figures.figure.huangjindao.event1: Commanded the frontline at the Battle of Wuniulan (1947)
Figures.figure.huangjindao.event2: Imprisoned for over twenty years as a February 28 political prisoner
Figures.figure.huangjindao.title: 27 Brigade Frontline Commander at Wuniulan
Figures.figure.huangshujing.bio: Huang Shujing was appointed in 1722 as one of Taiwan's first two imperial inspectors-general, tasked with conducting a systematic survey of the recently pacified frontier territory. He traveled extensively across western Taiwan, visiting indigenous communities, Han settler villages, and coastal ports. His observations were compiled into the Taihai Shichailu (Record of a Mission to the Taiwan Sea), completed in 1724, covering indigenous customs in three detailed sections. This remains the most comprehensive official account of early Qing Taiwan and the primary reference for historians studying indigenous societies of the period. Huang's meticulous documentation of languages, agricultural practices, and ceremonies gave the Qing bureaucracy its first detailed empirical knowledge of the island's diverse peoples.
Figures.figure.huangshujing.event1: Appointed first imperial inspector-general of Taiwan in 1722
Figures.figure.huangshujing.event2: Compiled Taihai Shichailu, most comprehensive early Qing Taiwan survey
Figures.figure.huangshujing.title: First Inspector-General of Taiwan
Figures.figure.huangtushui.bio: Huang Tu-shui was born in 1895 in Bangka, Taipei, the son of a rickshaw repairman, and grew up among the woodcarvers of the temple district whose craft first drew him to sculpture. His talent won him a place at the Tokyo Fine Arts School, making him the first Taiwanese ever to study there. In 1920 he became the first Taiwanese artist selected for Japan's prestigious Imperial Art Exhibition, with a work depicting an Indigenous boy — a breakthrough that made him a source of pride across the island. His marble figure Sweet Dew and other works fused Western academic technique with the subjects of his homeland, and he dreamed of creating a truly Taiwanese art. He poured his final years into the great relief Buffaloes, a serene vision of the island's rural life. But he drove himself relentlessly, and in 1930, at only thirty-five, he died suddenly of peritonitis, leaving that masterpiece as his testament. Huang Tu-shui remains revered as the pioneer of modern Taiwanese sculpture, an artist who proved a colonial subject could reach the summit of the art world.
Figures.figure.huangtushui.event1: First Taiwanese selected for Japan's Imperial Art Exhibition (1920)
Figures.figure.huangtushui.title: Sculptor
Figures.figure.inokanori.bio: Ino Kanori was born in 1867 in Iwate in northern Japan and came to Taiwan in 1895, in the very first year of colonial rule, driven by a scholar's hunger to understand the island's peoples. At a time when little was known of Taiwan's Indigenous societies, he undertook arduous field surveys across plains and mountains, recording languages, customs and migration histories at first hand. From this work he produced the first systematic classification of Taiwan's Indigenous peoples, distinguishing the plains-dwelling groups from those of the high mountains — a framework that shaped Indigenous studies for generations. He also turned his attention to the island's documented past, compiling an encyclopaedic history of Taiwanese culture that drew together records from the Dutch, Zheng, Qing and Japanese eras. The malaria he contracted during his years of fieldwork undermined his health, and he died in 1925; his monumental cultural history was published only after his death. Ino Kanori is remembered as a founding figure of Taiwan studies, whose meticulous records remain an indispensable source even as later scholars have questioned his colonial-era assumptions.
Figures.figure.inokanori.event1: Made the first systematic classification of Taiwan's Indigenous peoples
Figures.figure.inokanori.event2: Compiled a monumental history of Taiwanese culture
Figures.figure.inokanori.title: Anthropologist and Historian
Figures.figure.isoeikichi.bio: Iso Eikichi (1886–1972) was an agricultural scientist from Hiroshima Prefecture in Japan and is honored as the 'Father of Ponlai Rice.' After graduating from the Agriculture Department of Tohoku Imperial University he came to Taiwan in 1912 to work at the Government-General's agricultural experiment station, devoting himself to the improvement of rice cultivation. At the time Taiwan grew mainly native indica rice, whose long, loose grains were not favored in the Japanese market. Iso and his collaborator Suehiro Yotaro set out to acclimatize and breed Japanese japonica varieties to Taiwan's subtropical climate, overcoming difficulties such as premature flowering and disease. Through years of trials at the Tatun (Yangmingshan) experiment fields and elsewhere, they succeeded in developing high-quality japonica strains suited to Taiwan's land and weather. In 1926 Governor-General Izawa Takio formally named the new rice 'Ponlai Rice' at a meeting in Taipei, and it was rapidly promoted across the island. Ponlai rice greatly raised both the yield and the quality of Taiwanese rice, made large-scale export to Japan possible, and reshaped the agricultural economy of the colony, though it also tied Taiwan more tightly into the imperial food-supply system. Iso continued his research and teaching, training a generation of agronomists, and was made a professor at Taihoku Imperial University. Unusually among Japanese officials, after the war he was specially retained by the Republic of China government to keep advising on agriculture, and he remained in Taiwan until 1957. In recognition of his contributions he was granted a lifetime supply of Ponlai rice. He returned to Japan in his later years and died there in 1972, leaving a lasting mark on Taiwan's modern agriculture.
Figures.figure.isoeikichi.event1: 1912 Came to Taiwan to work at the Government-General's agricultural experiment station
Figures.figure.isoeikichi.event2: 1920s Bred the Ponlai rice japonica varieties
Figures.figure.isoeikichi.event3: 1926 Ponlai Rice was formally named and promoted across Taiwan
Figures.figure.isoeikichi.event4: 1945–57 Retained after the war to keep advising on Taiwan's agriculture
Figures.figure.isoeikichi.title: Father of Ponlai Rice
Figures.figure.jiandashi.bio: Jian Dashi, born in 1870 in what is today greater Taipei, was the foremost armed anti-Japanese guerrilla leader of the northern mountains in the early Japanese colonial period and was grouped with Ke Tiehu and Lin Xiaomao as one of the so-called 'Three Fierce Anti-Japanese Leaders.' In his earlier years he operated as a local militia figure across the Datun Mountains, Shilin, and Tamsui, taking part in informal local security affairs. After the Yiwei War, members of his family were killed during the Japanese army's advance, prompting him to swear lifelong resistance and to organize a guerrilla force in the Datun range. From 1896 he repeatedly attacked Japanese garrisons, police substations, and communication lines, frustrating the Government-General's efforts to consolidate control across the Taipei periphery. His tactics relied on rapid raids and orderly withdrawals through the mountain forests, and on several occasions his forces approached the outskirts of Shilin and Yuanshan. From 1898 the Japanese intensified sweep operations and promulgated the so-called 'Bandit Surrender Regulations,' but he refused all amnesty offers and continued to fight. Eventually, under combined pressure from Japanese troops and police, his network was worn down, and he fled to Xiamen in 1899. In 1900 Qing authorities, responding to Japanese diplomatic pressure, arrested him and extradited him to Taiwan under treaty obligations. He was executed by the Japanese in Taipei in March of the same year, leaving a final statement that condemned the colonizers' conduct and reaffirmed his commitment to resistance. The statement was later widely circulated in popular memory and became one of the most symbolic pieces of writing in Taiwan's anti-Japanese tradition. His execution effectively dismantled the largest organized armed resistance network in the north. He is widely regarded as the figure whose death marked the close of large-scale northern Taiwanese armed resistance to Japanese rule.
Figures.figure.jiandashi.event1: 1896 Took up arms in the Datun Mountains
Figures.figure.jiandashi.title: Leader of Anti-Japanese Resistance in Northern Taiwan
Figures.figure.jiangding.bio: Jiang Ding, born in 1866 in Zhutouqi in the Nanxi area of Tainan, was a locally powerful figure who became one of the two principal leaders of the Tapani Incident (the Xilai Temple Incident or Jiaobani Incident) during the mid-colonial period, on a par with Yu Qingfang. He had served earlier as a district headman and was already an influential figure in the Nanxi mountains in the early years of Japanese rule, maintaining sustained contact with local Indigenous communities and possessing detailed knowledge of mountain geography and methods of mobilization. Around 1914 he came into contact with the religiously framed anti-Japanese organization led by Yu Qingfang, embraced its anti-colonial stance, and brought his local networks and mountain contacts into the conspiracy. During the planning phase he was chiefly responsible for mobilizing supporters and concentrating arms across Nanxi, Yujing, and Nanhua in Tainan. When the uprising broke out he led raids on Japanese police substations as the most important field commander in the Jiaobani sector. When Japanese forces launched their major encirclement in July and August 1915, he withdrew with Yu Qingfang and the remaining fighters into the Houjuezi mountains and continued a guerrilla campaign. After Yu Qingfang was captured, he held out in the deep mountains for several more months, leading the last cohesive remnant of the uprising. In April 1916 the colonial authorities adopted an inducement policy, promising leniency to draw him out of the hills, and he led his remaining followers down in surrender. He was, however, arrested immediately afterward, tried, and sentenced to death the same month, with the sentence carried out at Tainan. His prolonged resistance in the deep mountains was the final operational chapter of the Tapani Incident. His surrender and execution closed out the southern guerrilla phase that followed Yu Qingfang's capture. He is widely regarded, together with Yu Qingfang, as a figure whose fall marked the end of Han armed resistance built on religiously framed mass mobilization.
Figures.figure.jiangding.title: Southern Field Commander of the Tapani Incident
Figures.figure.jiangshaozu.bio: Chiang Shao-tsu, born in 1876 in Beipu, Hsinchu, into the powerful Hakka Chiang clan descended from the Beipu pioneer Chiang Hsiu-luan, grew up within the cultural and economic orbit of the family's Jinguangfu pioneer settlement enterprise. He received a classical education and martial training in his youth and at eighteen took over family affairs and local responsibilities. When news of the cession of Taiwan reached him in 1895 he was only twenty, yet he immediately expended his personal fortune, sold family land, and raised a volunteer unit drawn from his home villages. Operating from Beipu and the Hsinchu uplands, his force fought alongside the Hakka volunteers of Wu Tangxing and Hsu Hsiang and contested Japanese advances around Hsinchu. In July 1895 his unit was surrounded in fighting north of Hsinchu, and after attempting to break out he was captured in close combat. Brought into custody at Hsinchu, he refused to surrender or collaborate and took his own life in his cell by swallowing opium, at the age of twenty. His death made him the youngest and most poetically tragic martyr of the 1895 resistance, and news of it spread rapidly through the Hakka communities of the north. Traditional accounts and later literature have cast him as the archetypal 'young man of family and country,' and he is grouped with Wu Tangxing and Hsu Hsiang as one of the 'Three Heroes of the Yi-Wei War.' The Chiang clan compound at Beipu — the Jinguangfu Public House — preserves relics and memorial spaces dedicated to him and remains a central site in Hakka memory of the 1895 war. Chiang is widely commemorated in modern Taiwanese history as the emblem of Hakka youth gentry who gave themselves wholly to the defense of their homeland.
Figures.figure.jiangshaozu.event1: 1895 Spent his family fortune to raise a volunteer army
Figures.figure.jiangshaozu.event2: 1895 Took his own life in custody after capture
Figures.figure.jiangshaozu.title: Young Hakka Volunteer Leader of Beipu, Hsinchu
Figures.figure.jiangwenye.bio: Jiang Wenye was born in 1910 near Tamsui in northern Taiwan and educated in Japan, where he first trained in engineering before his overwhelming gift for music took over his life. He studied composition under leading teachers in Tokyo and began as a singer before emerging as one of the most original composers of his generation in the Japanese music world. In 1936 his orchestral Formosan Dance won an honourable mention in the art competitions of the Berlin Olympics, carrying the name of Taiwan onto a world stage. Drawn to explore his Chinese roots, he moved to Beijing in the late 1930s to teach and compose, immersing himself in Confucian ritual music and Chinese themes. That choice left him stranded by history: cut off from Taiwan and Japan, he endured decades of political hardship in China and was persecuted during the Cultural Revolution. He died in Beijing in 1983, his music long forgotten on the island of his birth. Only later was Jiang Wenye rediscovered and celebrated as one of the first Taiwanese composers to win genuine international acclaim.
Figures.figure.jiangwenye.event1: Formosan Dance honoured at the 1936 Berlin Olympics art competition
Figures.figure.jiangwenye.event2: Moved to Beijing to teach and compose in the late 1930s
Figures.figure.jiangwenye.title: Composer
Figures.figure.jianji.bio: Chien Chi was born in 1903 in Fengshan, near Kaohsiung, and began his career as a public-school teacher. Confronted daily by pupils too hungry and overworked in the fields to learn, he came to believe that no amount of teaching could help them until their families were freed from exploitation — so he laid down the chalk and took up organising. Inspired by the Erhlin farmers, in 1926 he founded the Taiwan Farmers' Union, welding scattered local disputes into the largest mass movement of the colonial era, with tens of thousands of members across the island. He crisscrossed Taiwan by bicycle rallying tenant farmers against landlords and sugar companies, and was jailed repeatedly for his activism. After the war his convictions led him into the underground Communist organisation on the island, and in the White Terror he was arrested and executed in 1951. Chien Chi is remembered as the tireless organiser who gave Taiwan's farmers a collective voice.
Figures.figure.jianji.event1: Founded the island-wide Taiwan Farmers' Union (1926)
Figures.figure.jianji.title: Founder of the Taiwan Farmers' Union
Figures.figure.johndodd.bio: John Dodd was the British merchant who pioneered the export of Taiwanese oolong tea to New York in the nineteenth century, born in 1838 in Scotland and drawn to the Far East as a young man through his family's textile trade connections. In the late 1850s he served at successive European trading houses in Hong Kong, Canton, and Amoy, building up a deep familiarity with the southern Chinese commercial world and the compradore partnership system. After the Second Opium War the Treaty of Beijing in 1860 forced the Qing court to open the Taiwanese ports of Tamsui, Keelung, Anping, and Takao to international trade, exposing the island to Western capital and goods for the first time. He arrived in Tamsui in 1865 as the resident representative of the British firm Dent and Co. At that time the tea industry of northern Taiwan was rudimentary and lacked any international market, but after surveying the Tamsui basin and the hills further inland he became convinced that the climate, terrain, and soils were exceptionally well suited to high-grade oolong tea cultivation. In 1866 he imported tea seedlings from Anxi in Fujian and promoted their planting in what are today the Sanxia and Wenshan districts of Taipei, providing interest-free loans and technical training to farmers and transforming the agricultural fabric of the northern hills. After Dent and Co. went into liquidation in 1867 he established his own firm, Dodd and Co., set up refining plants in Dadaocheng, and partnered with the Hokkien merchant Li Chunsheng to build a complete picking, sorting, firing, and packaging system for high-quality oolong. In 1869 he shipped approximately two hundred and twenty thousand pounds of Formosa Oolong directly to New York, triggering a global craze for premium tea, establishing Formosa Oolong as a luxury commodity among Western elites, and placing Taiwan on the world commercial map through a single export industry for the first time. Over the next three decades Dadaocheng's Dihua Street became the most prosperous and cosmopolitan quarter on the island, with foreign trading houses, Western-style buildings, telegraph offices, and piped water concentrated there, laying the foundations of northern Taiwan's enduring economic leadership through the Japanese colonial period and beyond. From the 1880s he shifted the center of his business activity back to Britain and Southeast Asia but continued to underwrite the marketing of Taiwanese tea at international expositions in London and New York. He retired in England in the 1890s and died in 1907 at the age of sixty-nine. John Dodd is generally regarded as the key figure who transformed the Taiwanese economy from a frontier agricultural backwater into an internationally oriented export economy, and the tea industry he pioneered was the first Taiwanese product to establish a truly global brand.
Figures.figure.johndodd.event1: Shipped Formosa Oolong directly to New York for the first time in 1869, triggering a global craze
Figures.figure.johndodd.title: British Tea Pioneer of Northern Taiwan
Figures.figure.johnthomson.bio: John Thomson, born in 1837 in Edinburgh, Scotland, was a pioneering documentary photographer who visited Taiwan (Formosa) in 1871 and produced the earliest photographic record of the island's people, landscapes, and communities, images that remain among the most important visual documents of pre-colonial Taiwan. He had trained as an optician and lens maker in Edinburgh before turning to photography in the early 1860s and establishing himself in Asia, first in Singapore and then in Bangkok, Hong Kong, and Cambodia, where he documented the ruins of Angkor Wat and became recognized as one of the foremost photographers working in Asia. His Taiwan visit in 1871 was part of an extended journey through China and Formosa that would eventually produce his landmark multi-volume work Illustrations of China and Its People (1873–1874), one of the most significant photographic documents of nineteenth-century Asia. In Taiwan, Thomson traveled from Tamsui south to Anping and Tainan, photographing the treaty port communities, Qing administrative buildings, Han settler villages, and most significantly the indigenous Siraya and other Pingpu communities of the southern plains, whose way of life he documented with a sympathetic eye rare among Western visitors of his era. His portraits of Siraya men and women, the streetscapes of Tainan's commercial districts, the fortified walls of the Anping Dutch-era fort, and the faces of merchants, officials, and ordinary people represent the only photographic record of Taiwanese society from before the final decades of Qing rule, making them invaluable primary sources for historians and a touchstone for Taiwanese cultural identity. Thomson used the wet collodion process, which required him to prepare and develop glass-plate negatives in the field under conditions of intense heat and humidity, a technically demanding achievement that required skill and patience in equal measure. He was accompanied on some of his Taiwan travels by James Richardson, a British merchant based at Tamsui who served as guide and interpreter, and the two men ventured inland from the coastal plains to document indigenous communities that were rarely if ever visited by outside observers. His written account of Taiwan, published as part of the Illustrations of China volumes and in separate magazine articles for the Geographical Magazine, complemented his photographs with precise observations on geography, social customs, trade, and the political situation of the island, making Thomson a dual-medium witness of exceptional quality. Thomson returned to London in 1872 and eventually became one of the most celebrated documentary photographers of the Victorian era, known particularly for his work Street Life in London (1877–1878), which pioneered the use of photography as social documentary in the metropolitan context. His Taiwan photographs are held in the Wellcome Collection in London, where they have been digitized and made publicly accessible, and they have been widely reproduced in Taiwan through exhibitions, publications, and educational materials that use his images to anchor the island's visual historical memory. Thomson was appointed photographer to the British Foreign Office in 1881, in recognition of his unparalleled contribution to documenting the peoples and societies of Asia. John Thomson is widely regarded as the founder of Taiwan's photographic heritage — the man who, in a brief visit to a remote treaty port, produced the visual archive that allows people today to see the faces of the Taiwanese world that existed before the colonial transformation of 1895.
Figures.figure.johnthomson.event1: Photographed Taiwan in 1871, producing the earliest photographic record of the island's people, landscapes, and indigenous communities
Figures.figure.johnthomson.event2: Published Illustrations of China and Its People (1873–74), including his Taiwan photographs, establishing the island's visual presence in the Western historical record
Figures.figure.johnthomson.title: Pioneer Photographer of Taiwan
Figures.figure.kabayamasukenori.bio: Kabayama Sukenori, born in 1837 in Kagoshima as a lower-ranking samurai of Satsuma Domain, took part in the Anglo-Satsuma War and the Boshin War in his youth and was one of the Satsuma-faction officers groomed for senior office under the new Meiji government. He served in the army before transferring to the navy, and in 1874 he joined the Japanese expedition to Taiwan during the Mudan Incident, conducting reconnaissance and combat operations on the Hengchun Peninsula and acquiring first-hand knowledge of the island and its indigenous societies. He subsequently held senior posts including Navy Vice-Minister, Chief of the Naval General Staff, and Superintendent-General of the Metropolitan Police, was promoted to full admiral in 1893, and was serving as Chief of the Naval General Staff when the First Sino-Japanese War broke out in 1894. After the Treaty of Shimonoseki in 1895 he was appointed the first Governor-General of Taiwan and in May presided over the formal transfer of the island from Qing representative Li Jingfang aboard the steamer Yokohama-maru off the coast of Keelung. He then directed the military takeover during the 1895 war, coordinating the Imperial Guards and the Second Division as they advanced southward and suppressed the so-called Republic of Formosa and local volunteer forces. On November 18, 1895 he issued a report to Tokyo declaring the island 'pacified,' formally inaugurating colonial rule. During his tenure he established the foundational military-administrative apparatus of the Government-General of Taiwan and put in place transitional policies that anchored the absolute power of the Governor-General. He left office in June 1896 to return to Japan and later served as Navy Minister and Privy Councillor, being elevated to the rank of viscount in the new peerage. He died in Tokyo in 1922. Kabayama is widely regarded as the founding figure of Japanese colonial Taiwan, whose appointment and 'pacification report' marked the end of Qing rule and the beginning of fifty years of Japanese governance, embedding the Government-General as the central institution of Taiwanese politics throughout the colonial era.
Figures.figure.kabayamasukenori.event2: 1895 Oversaw the takeover and 'pacification' of Taiwan
Figures.figure.kabayamasukenori.title: First Governor-General of Taiwan
Figures.figure.kamadayahiko.bio: Kamada Yahiko (1879–1948) was a general of the Japanese army who served as commander of the Taiwan Army when the Wushe Incident broke out in 1930, making him the supreme commander of the Japanese military suppression. In the Wushe Incident the Seediq peoples, led by Mona Rudao, rose against colonial rule and attacked an athletic meet, shaking both Taiwan and the Japanese home islands. After the uprising he was ordered to direct the punitive campaign, mobilizing large numbers of regular troops, police and units equipped with mountain guns and machine guns to encircle the rebel communities deep in the mountains. Yet the Seediq warriors, relying on their knowledge of the terrain and their tenacity, waged a stubborn guerrilla resistance among the steep ranges, so that the Japanese forces could not subdue them quickly and suffered considerable casualties. In the deadlock he ordered aircraft to drop bombs containing blister gas on the communities holding out in the mountains; this means, in violation of the international norms of the time, caused heavy indigenous casualties and made him one of the most controversial figures of the incident. The Wushe Incident ended with the near annihilation of the rebel communities, followed by the so-called Second Wushe Incident and forced relocation. His decisions to use poison gas and large-scale military repression remain a major focus in examining the violent nature of Japanese colonial rule.
Figures.figure.kamadayahiko.event1: 1930 Directed the suppression of the Wushe Incident as Taiwan Army commander
Figures.figure.kamadayahiko.event2: 1930 Ordered aircraft to drop poison-gas bombs on the rebel communities
Figures.figure.kamadayahiko.title: Taiwan Army Commander Who Suppressed the Wushe Incident
Figures.figure.kangninghsiang.bio: Kang Ning-hsiang, born in 1938 in Taipei, was a representative figure of the parliamentary line within Taiwan's tangwai movement. Of humble origins, he worked in his early years at jobs such as a gas-station attendant before entering local politics, rising on a grassroots image and a talent for oratory. From 1969 he was elected to the Taipei City Council and later entered the Legislative Yuan, becoming one of the few tangwai legislators to openly challenge the authorities from within the system during martial law. He advocated advancing democratic reform through peaceful means — parliamentary debate and the scrutiny of speech — complementing the street-protest line. In 1975 he helped found Taiwan Political Review and later ran magazines such as The Eighties, an important promoter of tangwai expression. In his legislative interpellations he touched on sensitive issues such as full re-election of parliament, lifting martial law, and freedom of speech, repeatedly breaking through the political taboos of the time. Compared with the more radical line of the Kaohsiung generation, he was regarded as a tangwai "moderate" and a bridge between generations, and the line dispute sparked debate within the camp. After the lifting of martial law and democratization he served as legislator, deputy defense minister, member of the Control Yuan, and senior presidential adviser. Kang is seen as one of the founders of the tangwai parliamentary-democracy line, his long career of legislative work and publishing building crucial momentum for Taiwan's freedom of speech and parliamentary reform.
Figures.figure.kangninghsiang.event1: Founded tangwai magazines such as Taiwan Political Review and The Eighties
Figures.figure.kangninghsiang.event2: Long used the Legislative Yuan as a platform for democratic reform
Figures.figure.kangninghsiang.title: Parliamentary Tangwai Leader & Political-Magazine Founder
Figures.figure.kangxi.bio: The Kangxi Emperor, personal name Xuanye, was the second emperor of the Qing dynasty after its conquest of China proper, and his sixty-one-year reign from 1662 to 1722 is the longest of any Chinese emperor. Born in 1654 in Beijing as the third son of the Shunzhi Emperor, he ascended the throne at the age of seven under a regency dominated by the Manchu noble Oboi. In 1669 he removed Oboi in a palace coup and assumed personal rule, beginning the active phase of his reign at the age of fifteen. He consolidated Qing power by suppressing the Revolt of the Three Feudatories between 1673 and 1681, in which the southern warlords Wu Sangui, Shang Zhixin, and Geng Jingzhong, supported externally by the Kingdom of Tungning, contested Qing rule for nearly a decade. With the mainland secured, he turned his attention to the surviving Zheng base in Taiwan, supporting Shi Lang's appointment as Fujian Naval Commander and authorizing the 1683 invasion that ended the Kingdom of Tungning. Initial Qing court opinion favored abandoning Taiwan after the victory, with senior officials arguing that the island was a remote burden, but Shi Lang's memorial persuaded the emperor to incorporate it as Taiwan Prefecture under Fujian Province in 1684. His Taiwan policy combined economic restriction — limiting immigration from the mainland and barring most coastal residents from settling — with a light administrative footprint that nonetheless integrated the island into the Qing tax and tributary system. Beyond Taiwan, his reign saw the Treaty of Nerchinsk with Russia in 1689 (the first treaty between China and a European power), the submission of the Khalkha Mongols, and the establishment of Qing protection over Tibet. He cultivated an image of a model Confucian ruler, lectured on the classics, sponsored the great Kangxi Dictionary, and maintained close personal relationships with Jesuit advisors at court. His twilight years were marred by an unresolved succession dispute among his many sons that would dominate court politics for a decade and shape the bloody accession of his fourth son as the Yongzheng Emperor. He died in December 1722 at the age of 68 at the Garden of Joyful Spring outside Beijing. For Taiwan, the Kangxi Emperor's decisions in 1683–1684 are foundational: his ratification of Shi Lang's case for retention is the moment that anchored the island to the East Asian mainland imperial system for the next two centuries.
Figures.figure.kangxi.event1: Ordered Shi Lang's expedition that ended the Kingdom of Tungning (1683)
Figures.figure.kangxi.title: Emperor of the Qing Dynasty
Figures.figure.ketiehu.bio: Ke Tiehu, born in 1876 in Dapingding (later renamed Iron Kingdom Mountain) in Yunlin, was one of the most prominent armed anti-Japanese guerrilla leaders in central Taiwan in the early years of Japanese rule. His given name was Ke Tie, and he acquired the nickname 'Iron Tiger' because of his powerful build and combat prowess. After the Yiwei War of 1895 scattered Han Chinese resistance across central and southern Taiwan, he gathered followers in the Yunlin highlands and turned the rugged terrain into a stronghold. In June 1896 the so-called Yunlin Massacre, in which Japanese forces burned numerous villages along the foothills under the pretext of bandit suppression, fueled widespread popular outrage and prompted him to rise in revolt later that year, styling himself 'President' and establishing a base on Iron Kingdom Mountain. At its peak his network reached into the mountain districts of Chiayi, Changhua, and Nantou, and he was grouped together with Jian Dashi and Lin Xiaomao as the so-called 'Three Fierce Anti-Japanese Leaders.' Between 1896 and 1899 he repeatedly engaged Japanese troops, frustrating several sweep operations and waging a war of attrition that relied on the difficult mountain terrain. Japanese policy at first emphasized military sweeps with limited success. After 1898 the new administration under Governor-General Kodama Gentaro and civilian chief Goto Shimpei shifted to a so-called pacification-by-amnesty policy intended to divide the resistance from within. The Iron Kingdom Mountain camp gradually wavered, and a portion of his followers accepted surrender terms. Ke Tiehu himself died of illness on the mountain in 1900 at the age of only twenty-four, after which the Iron Kingdom Mountain force collapsed. His campaign is regarded as one of the final high-water marks of Han Chinese armed resistance in central Taiwan during the late-Qing-to-early-Japanese transition. He is widely credited with being the most enduring figure among the so-called 'Three Fierce Anti-Japanese Leaders' of the early colonial period.
Figures.figure.ketiehu.event1: 1896 Raised the banner of resistance on Iron Kingdom Mountain
Figures.figure.ketiehu.event2: 1900 Died of illness on Iron Kingdom Mountain
Figures.figure.ketiehu.title: Guerrilla Leader of Iron Kingdom Mountain
Figures.figure.kitashirakawayoshihisa.bio: Prince Kitashirakawa Yoshihisa, born in Kyoto in 1847 as the ninth son of Prince Fushimi-no-miya Kuniie and an uncle of Emperor Meiji, was a senior member of the Japanese imperial family. In early life he was named abbot of Rinnō-ji and during the Boshin War was briefly proclaimed by the Ōuetsu Reppan Domei coalition as the so-called Eastern Emperor in opposition to the new Meiji government before submitting to its terms. He was then sent to Prussia, where he received several years of training in the Royal Prussian Army; on returning to Japan he advanced through the new Imperial Japanese Army, rising to lieutenant general and commander of the Imperial Guards Division. After the signing of the Treaty of Shimonoseki in 1895 he was ordered to lead the Imperial Guards in the takeover of Taiwan and landed at Aodi on the northeast coast in late May. His division advanced southward, fighting the troops of the so-called Republic of Formosa and Taiwanese volunteer forces at Keelung, Taipei, Hsinchu, Miaoli, Changhua, Yunlin, Chiayi, and Tainan, and constituted the main Japanese force in the 1895 war. Prolonged marching and combat in subtropical conditions caused widespread malaria and dysentery among his troops, and he himself fell ill in the south — some accounts attribute his decline to an infected combat wound — and his condition deteriorated steadily. He died at Tainan in late October 1895, the first member of the Japanese imperial family to die on overseas service and the highest-ranking Japanese casualty of the 1895 war. His body was returned to Japan with state honors, he was posthumously promoted to full general, and after deification he was enshrined and commemorated at numerous sites in Japan and Taiwan, including the Taiwan Grand Shrine in Taipei. Throughout the period of Japanese rule colonial authorities promoted his memory as the heroic spirit of the conquest of Taiwan, making him one of the most symbolically charged Japanese figures in the historiography of colonial Taiwan.
Figures.figure.kitashirakawayoshihisa.event1: 1895 Led the Imperial Guards Division to take over Taiwan
Figures.figure.kitashirakawayoshihisa.title: Commander of the Imperial Guards Division
Figures.figure.kobayashiseizo.bio: Kobayashi Seizo (1877–1962), a Japanese navy admiral by background, served as Governor-General of Taiwan from 1936 to 1940 and was the first military governor restored after the era of civilian governors, symbolizing the renewed hardening of Japanese rule under the shadow of war. He took office at the height of Japanese militarism, with war between Japan and China imminent, and put forward three guiding principles for governing Taiwan—'Kominka (imperialization), industrialization, and use as a base for the southward advance'—positioning Taiwan as a forward base for Japan's expansion to the south and pushing assimilation across the board. Under the Kominka movement he vigorously enforced the use of Japanese, abolished the Chinese-language columns of newspapers, rewarded 'national-language households,' promoted the campaign to adopt Japanese surnames, and required people to worship at Shinto shrines and venerate the sun goddess Amaterasu, seeking to remake the Taiwanese—from language, names and faith to ways of life—into 'imperial subjects' loyal to the emperor. The movement profoundly shook Taiwan's traditional culture and identity, suppressing the mother tongues, rituals and customs of many Han and indigenous people. At the same time he advanced industrialization and military production to meet wartime needs. As the foremost promoter of the Kominka policy, the measures of his tenure had a profound and complex impact on Taiwanese society and culture.
Figures.figure.kobayashiseizo.event2: 1937 Launched the Kominka movement in full
Figures.figure.kobayashiseizo.title: Governor-General Who Drove Kominka
Figures.figure.kodamagentaro.bio: Kodama Gentaro (1852–1906) was a Japanese army general and statesman who became the fourth Governor-General of Taiwan in 1898. Before him, the early years of Japanese rule had been mired in difficulty by continual armed resistance and huge fiscal deficits, to the point that some even proposed selling Taiwan. Kodama's most crucial step on taking office was to recruit the physician Goto Shinpei as head of civil affairs, granting him real power and full trust; together they formed the famous 'Kodama–Goto system' that laid the foundation of Japanese colonial rule and modernization in Taiwan. Governing on what Goto called 'biological principles,' they first carried out large-scale surveys of land, population and old customs and then pushed institutional reform on that basis: they established the baojia system to strengthen public order, reorganized the monopolies on opium, camphor and salt to enrich revenues, and developed sanitation, railways, harbours and urban construction, turning Taiwan's long-deficit finances into self-sufficiency. Though authoritarian in method and merciless in suppressing resistance, this system did set colonial governance on a stable course. Because Kodama concurrently held high posts at home for years and took part in the Russo-Japanese War as chief of staff of the Manchurian Army, the practical administration of Taiwan was largely entrusted to Goto. He left the post of Governor-General in 1906 and died that same year. The framework of rule and construction he established profoundly shaped Taiwan for the following decades.
Figures.figure.kodamagentaro.event1: 1898 Became the fourth Governor-General of Taiwan
Figures.figure.kodamagentaro.event2: 1898 Recruited Goto Shinpei to drive modernization
Figures.figure.kodamagentaro.title: Fourth Governor-General of Taiwan
Figures.figure.kondohyotaro.bio: Kondo Hyotaro (1888–1966) was a baseball coach from Ehime Prefecture in Japan. He had played for the powerful Matsuyama Commercial School team in his youth and came to Taiwan to teach, eventually taking charge of the baseball team at the Chiayi Agriculture and Forestry School (Kano) from 1928. When he arrived the team was weak and undisciplined, but Kondo rebuilt it through a famously strict, Spartan training regime and an ethic captured in his maxim, 'Do not think about winning; think about not losing.' What made his Kano team historic was its makeup: it brought together Japanese, Han Chinese, and indigenous Taiwanese players in what was celebrated as a 'harmony of three peoples,' with Kondo assigning roles according to each group's strengths. Under his leadership the team was transformed, and in 1931 Kano won the right to represent Taiwan and traveled to the National High School Baseball Championship at Koshien in Japan. There the unheralded team stunned the nation by advancing all the way to the final, finishing as runner-up (jun-yusho) and winning admiration across Japan with their fighting spirit, even as their ace pitcher played on with an injured hand. The achievement made Kano a legend and later inspired the 2014 film KANO, in which Kondo is the central figure. Kondo continued to coach in Taiwan for years afterward, shaping the island's early baseball culture, before returning to Japan. He is remembered as the demanding mentor who forged a multi-ethnic team into one of the most celebrated stories in the history of Taiwanese baseball.

Figures.figure.kondohyotaro.event2: 1931 Led Kano to the right to represent Taiwan at Koshien

Figures.figure.koxinga.bio: Zheng Cheng-gong, better known by his honorific name Koxinga (Kok-seng-iâ, Lord of the Imperial Surname), was born in 1624 in Hirado, Japan, to the powerful Fujianese merchant-pirate Zheng Zhilong and a Japanese mother of the Tagawa family. Brought to his father's homeland in southern Fujian at the age of seven, he received a classical Confucian education and was studying at the Imperial University in Nanjing when the Ming dynasty collapsed in 1644. The Southern Ming court of the Longwu Emperor bestowed upon him the imperial Zhu surname, the source of his lifelong honorific, marking him out as one of the rising hopes of the loyalist resistance. In 1646, when his father Zheng Zhilong defected to the Qing and his mother died during the ensuing Qing raid on the family home, Koxinga refused to follow his father and raised an independent army committed to restoring the Ming. Operating from a maritime base centered on Xiamen and Kinmen, he built one of the largest privately commanded fleets in the seventeenth century and conducted prolonged campaigns along the Fujian and Zhejiang coasts. His attempt in 1659 to break Qing power by besieging Nanjing ended in disastrous defeat, forcing him to seek a more secure rear base for the resistance. In April 1661 he launched a massive amphibious operation across the Taiwan Strait, landing his fleet of some four hundred ships at Lakjemuyse Bay and beginning a nine-month siege of the Dutch East India Company's Fort Zeelandia. After repeated naval clashes, supply blockades, and the storming of Fort Provintia, the Dutch Governor Frederick Coyett capitulated in February 1662 under treaty terms that allowed the Company to withdraw with honor. Koxinga reorganized the former Dutch colony as the Kingdom of Tungning, founding Chengtian Prefecture in Tainan with the counties of Tianxing and Wannian and inaugurating Han Chinese settler administration of the island. He encouraged systematic land reclamation by military garrisons, imposed Confucian administrative norms, and laid the foundations of an immigrant agrarian society that displaced the prior indigenous and Dutch order. He died in Tainan in June 1662, only months after his triumph, almost certainly of malaria, at the age of 38. Koxinga is venerated across Taiwan and southern Fujian as the Sage King who Opened Taiwan (開臺聖王), and his role has been variously reframed by Qing, Japanese, and post-1945 regimes as Ming loyalist hero, founder of overseas Chinese rule, and symbol of cross-strait struggle.
Figures.figure.koxinga.event1: Siege and capture of Fort Zeelandia from the Dutch (1661–1662)
Figures.figure.koxinga.event2: Established the Tungning Kingdom in Taiwan
Figures.figure.koxinga.title: Ming Loyalist General & Founder of Tungning
Figures.figure.laihe.bio: Lai He was born in 1894 in Changhua into a modest family and trained as a physician at the Medical School of the Taiwan Governor-General's Office. After a spell practising in Xiamen, he returned home to run a clinic in Changhua, where he treated the poor with such generosity that people called him a living Buddha. Deeply stirred by the political awakening of the 1920s, he joined the Taiwan Cultural Association and was imprisoned during the Chih-ching Incident of 1923. Turning to writing, he pioneered a plain vernacular literature rooted in Taiwanese life; his stories A Steelyard and The Festival exposed the everyday injustices of colonial rule with unflinching sympathy. As editor of the literary pages of the Taiwan Minpao, he mentored and published a whole generation of younger writers, earning the title 'father of Taiwanese new literature.' He was jailed a second time in 1941, and his health broke under the strain. Lai He died in early 1943 at the age of forty-eight, remembered as both a healer of bodies and a conscience of his people.
Figures.figure.laihe.event1: Wrote A Steelyard and pioneered Taiwanese vernacular fiction
Figures.figure.laihe.event2: Edited the literary pages of the Taiwan Minpao
Figures.figure.laihe.title: Father of Taiwanese New Literature
Figures.figure.landingyuan.bio: Lan Dingyuan, born in 1680 in Zhangpu County, Fujian, was a Qing military adviser, local official, and prolific writer who played a decisive role in suppressing the Zhu Yigui rebellion of 1721 and then produced the most comprehensive body of early eighteenth-century Chinese scholarship on the governance and society of Taiwan. He came from a scholarly family but took no formal examination degree, instead building his reputation through writing and service to powerful patrons, most notably his cousin Lan Tingzhen, the Qing commander dispatched to crush the Zhu Yigui uprising that had briefly expelled Qing authority from the entire island in 1721. Lan Dingyuan crossed to Taiwan in 1721 as an unofficial adviser attached to his cousin's expedition, observing the campaign at close range and documenting its operations in detail — an experience that gave him direct knowledge of Taiwan's geography, population, and social tensions that few mainland scholars possessed. After the rebellion was suppressed within months, he remained in Taiwan briefly and conducted a systematic survey of the island's settlement patterns, indigenous territories, administrative weaknesses, and economic conditions, which he compiled into two landmark works: the Record of the Eastern Expedition (東征集, 1721) and the Brief Account of the Pacification of Taiwan (平臺紀略, 1722). These texts constitute the most detailed first-hand account of early eighteenth-century Taiwan in Chinese, covering not only military events but also agriculture, indigenous customs, Han settler communities, administrative abuses, and strategic recommendations for long-term Qing governance. Lan's central argument — that Taiwan required more aggressive settlement promotion, stronger county-level administration, and a coherent indigenous policy rather than containment — anticipated the policy debates that would recur throughout the Qing period and beyond. He was particularly critical of the exploitative conduct of local officials and middlemen toward indigenous Taiwanese, documenting cases of land fraud and labor coercion that he argued were the structural causes of frontier unrest. On his return to the mainland, Lan Dingyuan served in several local official posts, eventually becoming prefectural magistrate of Chaoyang in Guangdong Province, where he applied similar reformist ideas to local administration before dying in 1733. His advocacy for Taiwan was taken seriously enough that the Yongzheng Emperor reviewed and partially implemented some of his governance recommendations, making him one of the few non-official commentators of his era to influence imperial Taiwan policy. He is regarded today as the founding figure of systematic Chinese scholarship on Taiwan — the first writer to treat the island as a subject worthy of comprehensive empirical study rather than a distant administrative problem. Lan Dingyuan's work remains an indispensable primary source for historians of Qing Taiwan, and his insight that Taiwan's social stability depended on integrating rather than isolating its diverse population proved to be one of the most prescient analyses of the island's colonial condition.
Figures.figure.landingyuan.event1: Served as military adviser in the suppression of the Zhu Yigui rebellion (1721) and compiled its first systematic account
Figures.figure.landingyuan.event2: Wrote Record of the Eastern Expedition (東征集) and Brief Account of the Pacification of Taiwan (平臺紀略), the most comprehensive Chinese scholarship on early eighteenth-century Taiwan
Figures.figure.landingyuan.title: Qing Military Adviser and Taiwan Governance Scholar
Figures.figure.leetenghui.bio: Lee Teng-hui, born in 1923 in Sanzhi, Taipei Prefecture, to a Hoklo-Hakka mixed family during the Japanese colonial period, served from 1988 to 2000 as the first native Taiwanese president of the Republic of China and is widely credited as the principal architect of Taiwan's democratic transition. Educated under the Japanese colonial system, he attended Kyoto Imperial University before wartime evacuation and then completed his undergraduate studies in agricultural economics at the post-war National Taiwan University. He briefly joined the Chinese Communist Party in 1946–47 before quitting in disillusionment and later went to the United States, earning a master's degree at Iowa State University and a doctorate in agricultural economics at Cornell University in 1968. He returned to Taiwan as a leading agricultural policy specialist and was recruited into the KMT in 1971 by Chiang Ching-kuo, who saw native Taiwanese technocrats as essential to the regime's long-term legitimacy. He rose rapidly under Chiang's patronage as Minister without Portfolio, Taipei mayor, Governor of Taiwan Province, and Vice President from 1984, succeeding to the presidency on Chiang's death in January 1988. He moved cautiously but decisively to consolidate his power within the KMT, sidelining the mainlander old guard and securing his election as both KMT Chairman and full-term President by the early 1990s. Between 1991 and 1992 he ended the Period of Mobilization Against Communist Rebellion, retired the elderly mainland-era legislators of the Legislative Yuan and National Assembly, and supervised the first fully direct elections to both bodies. His unprecedented 1995 alumni visit to Cornell University provoked the Third Taiwan Strait Crisis, during which the People's Liberation Army fired missiles into waters near Taiwan in an attempt to intimidate voters before the upcoming election. In March 1996 he won Taiwan's first direct presidential election with 54 percent of the vote against three other candidates, decisively legitimizing the new constitutional order. In 1999 he characterized cross-strait relations as a special state-to-state relationship, a formulation that infuriated Beijing and that became a foundational reference point for subsequent Taiwanese diplomatic positioning. He left office in 2000 after the DPP's Chen Shui-bian won the presidency, was expelled from the KMT in 2001 after openly supporting the new Taiwan Solidarity Union, and remained a vocal advocate of Taiwanese identity until his death. He died in 2020 at the age of 97 and is now widely regarded as Mr. Democracy, the most consequential single architect of Taiwan's transformation from one-party authoritarianism to a consolidated competitive democracy.
Figures.figure.leetenghui.event1: Led Taiwan's first direct presidential election (1996)
Figures.figure.leetenghui.event2: Abolished the Temporary Provisions and ended the Period of National Mobilization
Figures.figure.leetenghui.title: President of the Republic of China
Figures.figure.leeyuantseh.bio: Lee Yuan-tseh, born in 1936 in Hsinchu, is the first Nobel laureate of Taiwanese origin and an important guide of post-war Taiwan's science and education. Showing a keen interest in science from childhood, he studied at National Taiwan University and National Tsing Hua University before going to the United States, earning a doctorate from the University of California, Berkeley. He devoted himself to chemical reaction dynamics, developing experimental methods such as the crossed molecular beam to probe the microscopic processes of chemical reactions. In 1986, for his pioneering contributions to reaction dynamics, he shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry with two other scholars, becoming a landmark figure in the ethnic-Chinese scientific world. He taught at several leading American universities and built a distinguished research team at Berkeley, enjoying high standing in the international academic community. In 1994 he returned to Taiwan to become president of Academia Sinica, devoting himself to building the country's research system and cultivating talent over twelve years. In office he attended to higher education and science policy and led the push for education reform, whose proposals sparked wide public debate and controversy. After stepping down he continued to take part in international scientific organizations, serving as president of the International Council for Science and engaging with global issues such as sustainable development and climate change. Lee is seen as a symbol of Taiwanese science reaching the world, his scholarly achievement and public engagement long a key benchmark for Taiwan's scientific and educational circles.
Figures.figure.leeyuantseh.event1: Awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry (1986)
Figures.figure.leeyuantseh.event2: Served as president of Academia Sinica and led education reform
Figures.figure.leeyuantseh.title: Nobel Chemistry Laureate & President of Academia Sinica
Figures.figure.legendre.bio: Charles William Le Gendre was born in France in 1830, emigrated to the United States, and fought as a Union officer in the American Civil War, losing an eye and suffering wounds that marked him for life. In 1866 he was posted as the American consul at Amoy, whose jurisdiction reached across the strait to Taiwan. When the merchant bark Rover was wrecked off Taiwan's southern cape in 1867 and its crew killed by the Paiwan, Le Gendre took up the case with relentless energy. Rebuffed by Qing officials who disclaimed authority over the 'savage territory,' he did what no diplomat had dared: he journeyed into the south and negotiated face to face with the paramount chief Tokitok, securing a direct pact for the protection of shipwrecked sailors. His travels convinced him that much of Taiwan lay beyond any effective Qing control — a conclusion with far-reaching consequences. In the early 1870s he entered the service of the Japanese government and became a key adviser to its 1874 expedition against the same region, lending it maps, arguments and legitimacy. He later advised Korea and died in Seoul in 1899. Le Gendre remains a pivotal and controversial figure, the foreign go-between whose knowledge helped open Taiwan to the ambitions of a rising Japan.
Figures.figure.legendre.event1: Negotiated the South Cape pact with chief Tokitok (1867)
Figures.figure.legendre.event2: Advised Japan's 1874 expedition against southern Taiwan
Figures.figure.legendre.title: American Consul and Foreign Adviser
Figures.figure.leichen.bio: Lei Chen, born in 1897 in Changxing, Zhejiang, was a Republican-era liberal intellectual who became, through his Free China Journal and his abortive 1960 effort to found an opposition party, the most prominent victim of KMT political repression on Taiwan in the early 1960s. He studied law and economics at Kyoto Imperial University in the 1920s and returned to China to join the Nationalist movement, serving in central party and government positions through the Republican era. He held senior policy posts under Chiang Kai-shek in the 1940s, including secretary-general of the People's Political Council and member of the National Government Council, and was an intimate of the party's reformist wing. He moved to Taiwan with the Nationalist government in 1949 and continued in advisory positions while founding the bilingual liberal journal Free China (自由中國半月刊) in November 1949 with the philosopher Hu Shih as honorary publisher. Through the 1950s Free China became the most influential platform for constitutionalist criticism of the KMT regime, publishing articles on civil liberties, judicial independence, and the abuses of the security apparatus. The magazine's coverage of the abuse of constitutional norms and Chiang's evasion of the two-term presidential limit by amending the Temporary Provisions in 1960 made it a target of the security agencies. In mid-1960 Lei attempted to organize a new opposition party, the China Democratic Party (中國民主黨), in coalition with Taiwanese tangwai politicians including Kuo Kuo-chi and Wu San-lien. He was arrested with three associates on 4 September 1960, charged with sedition and 'knowingly harboring a communist spy' (referring to his colleague Liu Tzu-ying), and tried by military court in proceedings widely regarded as a political show trial. He was convicted and sentenced to ten years' imprisonment, sentences that effectively destroyed both Free China — whose publication was immediately suspended — and the nascent opposition party. He served the full ten-year sentence and was released in 1970, after which the security services closely monitored his remaining activities and continued to harass his family. He devoted his remaining years to writing his memoirs and remained in correspondence with younger democracy activists until his death in Taipei in 1979 at the age of 82. Lei is widely commemorated as the principal mainlander liberal martyr of the early authoritarian era, the man whose abortive 1960 cross-strait coalition with Taiwanese tangwai figures prefigured by twenty-six years the founding of the Democratic Progressive Party.
Figures.figure.leichen.event1: Arrested for attempting to form an opposition party (1960)
Figures.figure.leichen.title: Publisher of Free China Journal
Figures.figure.lianheng.bio: Lian Heng (1878–1936), courtesy name Yatang and sobriquet Jianhua, was born in the Mabingying neighborhood of Tainan and became one of the most important historians of modern Taiwan. Of scholarly family background, he was trained in classical learning and poetry from boyhood and traveled extensively in China during his early adulthood. He briefly served on the staff of the Fujian Daily News in Fuzhou, and his exposure to mainland intellectual life shaped his later historiographical ambitions. After returning to Taiwan he devoted himself to preserving and organizing the island's history, observing that despite Taiwan's many changes of regime — from the Dutch period through Koxinga, the Qing, and Japanese rule — no systematic chronicle of the island had ever been written. He resolved to compile one single-handedly and, beginning in 1908, set out to write the General History of Taiwan, a project of more than a decade. The work was published in successive volumes between 1920 and 1921 in thirty-six chapters modeled on Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian and divided into annals, biographies, treatises, and tables — the first general history of Taiwan written by a Taiwanese. After its completion, he also compiled the Taiwan Poetry Anthology and the Jianhua Studio Poems, securing a high standing in Taiwan's literary world and joining classical-poetry societies such as the Liushe. His historiographical contributions were widely recognized; however, in 1930 his essay 'On the Question of the Opium License in Taiwan' argued that opium was 'beneficial and not harmful' and defended the Government-General's renewed issuance of opium licenses, in sharp conflict with the prevailing anti-opium stance of Taiwan's cultural circles. The essay led to his expulsion from the Liushe and a break with many colleagues at the Taiwan Cultural Association, marking the gravest controversy of his career. In 1933 he relocated his family to Shanghai, in part to distance himself from the controversies surrounding him. He died of illness in Shanghai in 1936 at the age of 58, and his grandson Lien Chan would later become a senior figure in Republic of China politics in the postwar era. He is widely credited with founding the systematic historiography of Taiwan, though the opium controversy left a lasting blemish on his later reputation.
Figures.figure.lianheng.event1: 1920 Completed the General History of Taiwan
Figures.figure.lianheng.event2: 1930 Published pro-opium essay; expelled from the Liushe
Figures.figure.lianheng.title: Author of the General History of Taiwan
Figures.figure.lianwenqing.bio: Lien Wen-ching (1894–1957), born in Taipei, was an important driving force of Taiwan's early socialist movement and a pioneer of the Esperanto movement on the island. Of humble origins, he absorbed socialist and internationalist ideas largely through self-study, and he energetically promoted Esperanto in the hope that a common language might foster solidarity among oppressed peoples. In the 1920s he devoted himself to the enlightenment and mass work of the Taiwanese Cultural Association, arguing that the movement should shift from the petition-based path of the gentry toward the class struggle of workers and peasants. When the Cultural Association split in 1927 over differences of line, he and other leftists such as Wang Min-chuan seized the leadership, transforming the association into a socialist-leaning mass organization and promoting labour activism, peasant unions and youth movements; he was a key figure in moving Taiwan's left-wing movement from ideas to organization. He was gradually pushed from the centre of the movement amid factional struggles within the left and the increasingly severe repression of the colonial authorities. After the war he was not active in politics, turning instead to the compilation of documents and the writing of memoirs, leaving important records of the social movements of the Japanese period. He died in Taiwan in 1957 and is regarded as one of the most representative native thinkers of Taiwan's early socialist thought.
Figures.figure.lianwenqing.event1: 1920s Promoted Esperanto and the socialist movement
Figures.figure.lianwenqing.event2: 1927 Led the left wing in taking over the Cultural Association
Figures.figure.lianwenqing.title: Left-Wing Leader of the Cultural Association
Figures.figure.liaotianding.bio: Liao Tianding (1883–1909) was born in Xiushui Village, Taichung (today's Qingshui District), and became the most iconic folk bandit of the early Japanese colonial period in Taiwan. Coming from an impoverished family, he drifted through the streets from childhood and clashed repeatedly with Japanese police over petty theft as a youth. Under the tight surveillance of the colonial police apparatus he chose theft as his livelihood, operating with audacity and a remarkable skill at disguise. His targets were concentrated among Japanese officials, wealthy merchants, and local police officers, all of whom belonged to the beneficiaries of the colonial system. In oral tradition he was reshaped into a so-called 'rob the rich, aid the poor' righteous bandit, although the historical reality was likely embellished. His repeated escapes from Japanese police dragnets spread his fame across Taiwanese society and made him a celebrated figure in popular storytelling. Against a backdrop of widespread Taiwanese resentment of colonial rule, he came to be regarded as a symbol of defiance against the colonial order, with some accounts even linking him loosely to anti-Japanese movements. In 1909 he was pursued by Japanese police and died at the Houdong cave on Bali's Guanyin Mountain, though the precise cause of his death remains disputed. After his death, local residents pooled funds to build a temple in his memory, giving rise to a distinctive folk cult around the so-called righteous bandit, and the Liao Tianding Temple in Bali still draws devoted worshippers today. From the late colonial period onward, his story became popular material for vernacular fiction, budaixi puppet theatre, Taiwanese opera, and radio drama. After the war, it was repeatedly adapted into films and television series, ensuring his presence in modern Taiwanese popular culture. He is widely credited with being one of the most emblematic folk-legend figures of colonial-era Taiwan.
Figures.figure.liaotianding.event1: 1900s Robbed Japanese officials and wealthy merchants
Figures.figure.liaotianding.event2: 1909 Tracked down by Japanese police, died at Bali
Figures.figure.liaotianding.title: Legendary Folk Bandit
Figures.figure.liaowenyi.bio: Liao Wen-yi, born in 1910 into a prominent family in Xiluo, Yunlin, was a founding figure of the overseas Taiwan independence movement after the war. He studied in China and the United States, earning a doctorate in chemical engineering from Ohio State University, a classic Western-trained high intellectual. After World War II he initially hoped to take part in the new order, engaging in public affairs and standing for election. The suppression of the February 28 Incident in 1947 shattered his hopes, and he came to argue that Taiwan's future should be decided by its own people, even under United Nations trusteeship. He then went into exile, organizing the League for the Re-liberation of Taiwan in Hong Kong in 1948 and bringing the independence cause onto the international stage. In the 1950s he moved to Tokyo, continuing to rally overseas Taiwanese. In 1956 he proclaimed in Tokyo the Provisional Government of the Republic of Taiwan and took office as its president — the first overseas independence organization in governmental form after the war. Through publications and diplomatic activity he promoted Taiwanese independence to the international community, becoming the Nationalist government's foremost overseas dissident. Yet under the authorities' pressure on and arrest of his relatives in Taiwan, and amid internal divisions in the movement, he returned to Taiwan in 1965 and publicly renounced independence — a move that made his later reputation deeply contested. He withdrew from politics after his return and died in Taipei in 1986. Liao is seen as the founder of the post-war overseas independence movement, and his winding path from Western-trained elite to exiled leader to returning compromiser is an important case for understanding post-war Taiwanese identity and the history of overseas dissent.
Figures.figure.liaowenyi.event1: Founded the Provisional Government of the Republic of Taiwan as its president (1956)
Figures.figure.liaowenyi.event2: Returned to Taiwan and renounced independence under pressure (1965)
Figures.figure.liaowenyi.title: Pioneer of the Overseas Taiwan Independence Movement
Figures.figure.lichunsheng.bio: Li Chunsheng was one of the most influential Taiwanese-Chinese industrialists of the late nineteenth century, whose career spanned the closing decades of Qing rule and the opening years of Japanese colonization, born in 1838 in Xiamen in Fujian. Baptized as a Christian in his youth, he served for more than a decade with the British firm Elles and Co. in Xiamen, acquiring a deep familiarity with international trade and Western commercial institutions. Around 1865 he was recruited by the British merchant John Dodd of Dent and Co. to cross to Taiwan, initially based at Tamsui to assist in the experimental cultivation and export of oolong tea from the northern hills. After Dodd introduced Anxi tea seedlings to Sanxia and Wenshan in 1866, he assumed the role of compradore — purchasing leaf from Chinese farmers, extending interest-free loans, and organizing the sorting and firing operations — and quickly built a working partnership that bridged Han Chinese settlers and Western capital. After the first direct shipment of Formosa Oolong to New York in 1869 transformed Dadaocheng into the richest commercial quarter on the island, he co-founded several tea firms with Dodd, acquired property along Dihua Street, built Western-style mansions and refining plants, and rose to become the foremost native merchant leader of Dadaocheng. As tea profits grew he diversified into real estate, coal mining, and shipping, and underwrote Liu Mingchuan's modernization projects in railways, telegraphy, and waterworks, becoming after Taiwan's elevation to a province in 1885 the most important native economic pillar of the new administration. Culturally, in 1875 he assisted George Leslie Mackay in establishing a church in Dadaocheng and funded Presbyterian missionary work, hospitals, and Western-style schools across northern Taiwan. Under his patronage northern Taiwan acquired by the late nineteenth century an urban infrastructure of a modernity exceptional anywhere in East Asia at the time. After the cession of Taiwan to Japan under the Treaty of Shimonoseki in 1895, when many leading merchants chose to return to the mainland, he remained out of a sense of responsibility to the local population and personally negotiated the peaceful transfer of Taipei to advancing Japanese forces, sparing the city from a destructive entry. In the early colonial period he was invited by the Government-General to visit Japan, where he met Goto Shinpei and the Meiji Emperor; on his return he wrote his sixty-four-day travel journal and several volumes of Christian theology. He was respectfully referred to by Japanese contemporaries as the philosopher of Taiwan, and died at his Dadaocheng residence in 1924 at the age of eighty-six, buried in Sanzhi. Li Chunsheng is generally regarded as the most important Taiwanese-Chinese figure bridging the agricultural society of late Qing Taiwan and the modern capitalist society that followed, whose contributions in tea, urban development, and cultural transition made Dadaocheng one of the principal cradles of Taiwanese modernization.
Figures.figure.lichunsheng.era: Late Qing to Early Japanese Colonial Era
Figures.figure.lichunsheng.event1: Built the Dadaocheng tea empire with John Dodd; brokered the peaceful transfer of Taipei in 1895
Figures.figure.lichunsheng.title: Tea Magnate of Dadaocheng & Modernization Patron of Northern Taiwan
Figures.figure.lienchan.bio: Lien Chan, born in 1936 in Xi'an to Taiwanese mainlander parents during the Sino-Japanese War, is a senior KMT statesman who served as Vice President under Lee Teng-hui and as the first KMT chairman to meet a Chinese Communist Party leader in nearly six decades. He is the grandson of the historian Lien Heng (連橫), author of the classical General History of Taiwan (臺灣通史), and his father Lien Chen-tung was an early Taiwanese member of the KMT central leadership. The family returned to Taiwan after Japan's surrender, and Lien received his early education on the island before earning his bachelor's at National Taiwan University and his doctorate in political science at the University of Chicago. He returned to Taiwan as a professor at NTU and was recruited into the foreign-service track of the KMT in the 1970s, serving as ambassador to El Salvador in 1975 and then in successive ministerial positions. He served as Foreign Minister, Governor of Taiwan Province, and Premier through the early 1990s, building a record as a competent technocrat with deep KMT institutional roots. He was elected Vice President in 1996 as Lee Teng-hui's running mate in Taiwan's first direct presidential election and held the position through Lee's second term until 2000. He ran for president as the KMT nominee in 2000 but finished a humiliating third behind Chen Shui-bian and James Soong, with the pan-Blue vote fatally split. As KMT chairman from 2000, he ran again in 2004 with Soong as his vice-presidential candidate, losing in the closest presidential race in Taiwanese history after the still-disputed shooting of Chen Shui-bian the day before the vote. In April 2005 he led a KMT delegation to Beijing in the first formal visit by a KMT chairman to mainland China and held a high-profile meeting with CCP General Secretary Hu Jintao, opening regularized KMT-CCP party-to-party contacts. The Lien-Hu framework established the political foundation for Ma Ying-jeou's later cross-strait normalization and entrenched a pattern of party-to-party cross-strait diplomacy that would persist into the 2020s. He stepped down as KMT chairman in 2005 and has since served in various honorary capacities, attending PLA military parades and meeting subsequent PRC leaders into his eighties.
