Lien is generally remembered as the bridge between the late-Chiang KMT and the post-millennial cross-strait engagement framework, a figure whose 2005 Beijing visit redefined the institutional limits of cross-strait political contact.
Figures.figure.lienchan.event1: Historic visit to mainland China as KMT chairman (2005)
Figures.figure.lienchan.title: Vice President & KMT Chairman
Figures.figure.linchaodong.bio: Lin Chaodong, born in 1851 in Wufeng (霧峰), Taichung, to the prominent Wufeng Lin military family, commanded the private Dongying militia (棟軍) and led Taiwan's most effective indigenous military force during the island's last two major crises under Qing rule: the Sino-French War of 1884–1885 and the Japanese invasion of 1895. He was the son of Lin Wencha — the Qing general who had pacified the Dai Chaochun rebellion and died fighting Taiping forces on the mainland — and inherited both his father's military reputation and his command of the formidable Lin family militia, which by the 1880s numbered in the thousands and was better equipped and disciplined than most regular Qing forces in Taiwan. When French naval forces blockaded Taiwan's ports and landed troops at Keelung in 1884, Lin Chaodong moved his Dongying units north from Taichung and conducted sustained guerrilla operations in the jungle terrain around Keelung and Danshui that proved far more effective against the French than the regular Qing garrisons. His operations at Keelung, which resulted in significant French casualties and denied the French a decisive land victory despite their naval superiority, established his reputation as Taiwan's most capable military commander and contributed to the stalemate that eventually led to the French withdrawal after the Treaty of Tientsin. In the aftermath of the war, Governor Liu Mingchuan — who had worked closely with Lin during the French campaign — relied heavily on the Dongying militia to extend Qing administrative control into the mountainous interior of Taiwan, where regular forces had never penetrated, in a series of campaigns that subjugated a number of indigenous highland communities. Lin Chaodong prospered in the 1880s through official patronage: he received land grants in the camphor-producing mountain regions as compensation for his military service, transforming the Dongying militia into an economic as well as military enterprise and making him one of the wealthiest men in late Qing Taiwan. When Japan invaded Taiwan following the Treaty of Shimonoseki in 1895, Lin Chaodong initially pledged to defend the island under the banner of the short-lived Taiwan Republic (臺灣民主國), and his Dongying forces fought a series of engagements against the advancing Japanese columns in central Taiwan. However, as the Taiwan Republic collapsed within weeks and Japanese military superiority became overwhelming, Lin made the pragmatic decision to withdraw to the mainland in mid-1895 rather than face certain defeat, taking his family and remaining troops with him. He lived out his remaining years in Fujian and Guangdong, dying in 1904 without returning to the island his family had dominated for three generations. Lin Chaodong is commemorated in Wufeng today through the preserved Lin family compound (霧峰林家), a UNESCO-recognized heritage site that embodies the rise, military service, and eventual departure of one of Taiwan's most consequential nineteenth-century dynasties. He is widely regarded as the last great commander of Taiwan's private military tradition — the man who led the island's final indigenous defense against two foreign invasions before that tradition was extinguished by the total transformation of 1895.
Figures.figure.linchaodong.event1: Led the Dongying militia against French forces at Keelung (1884–85), inflicting significant casualties and contributing to the French withdrawal
Figures.figure.linchaodong.event2: Commanded the defense of central Taiwan during the Japanese invasion of 1895, ultimately withdrawing to the mainland as the Taiwan Republic collapsed
Figures.figure.linchaodong.title: Commander of the Dongying Militia
Figures.figure.linchengzu.bio: Lin Chengzu was a Fujianese land developer who became one of the most significant private colonizers of northern Taiwan during the Qianlong reign. He acquired extensive land concessions in modern Taoyuan and New Taipei City, organized settler labor gangs, and sponsored construction of multiple irrigation channels that substantially expanded cultivable farmland. His enterprise exemplifies the large-scale, capital-intensive land development model used by well-resourced Fujianese migrants to systematically push the Han agricultural frontier northward. The Lin family became a major landowning gentry lineage in northern Taiwan. Lin Chengzu represents the typical trajectory of the successful Qing-era settler capitalist: from immigrant to entrenched landlord and local power broker.
Figures.figure.linchengzu.event1: Developed farmland in Taoyuan and New Taipei during the Qianlong period
Figures.figure.linchengzu.event2: Lin family became major gentry landlords of northern Taiwan
Figures.figure.linchengzu.title: Major Land Developer of Northern Taiwan
Figures.figure.linkungang.bio: Lin Kungang, born in 1832 in present-day Jiangjun District, Tainan, in a rural community known as Chu-tsu-kha, was a village schoolmaster and military examination graduate who taught the Confucian classics and military texts and organized local militia. By the time news of the cession of Taiwan reached southern Taiwan in 1895 he was already sixty-three, but he answered the call to arms and raised a volunteer force from the villages of Jiangjun and Jiali. His unit took up defensive positions along the Zengwen River, blocking the Japanese line of advance and operating in support of Liu Yongfu's Black Flag Army and other southern volunteers in the Tainan defenses. In September 1895 the Japanese Imperial Guards and Second Division advanced south of Chiayi toward the Zengwen River, and Lin deployed his men along the riverbank to prevent a crossing. In early October the climactic battle was fought along the river, in which his volunteers engaged Japanese regular troops in close combat; overwhelmed in numbers and firepower, most of his family and a majority of his men were killed, and Lin himself fell in action. After his death organized grassroots resistance in the south effectively collapsed, the Japanese pressed on to Tainan, and Liu Yongfu fled across the strait later in the month. His story long remained primarily a local tradition, with a memorial and shrine later established in Jiangjun. Lin embodies the southern rural counterpart to the better-known northern Hakka resistance: village schoolmasters and martial examination graduates who mobilized their kin and neighbors to fight. The annihilation of his family in battle remains the central image of his legacy in local historical memory. He is widely regarded as the representative figure of grassroots southern resistance in the 1895 war, complementing the 'Three Heroes' of the north.
Figures.figure.linkungang.event1: 1895 Raised village volunteers to defend the Zengwen River line
Figures.figure.linkungang.event2: 1895 Killed in action at the Battle of the Zengwen River
Figures.figure.linkungang.title: Tainan Volunteer Leader
Figures.figure.linmaosheng.bio: Lin Mao-sheng, born in 1887 in Tainan into a Presbyterian family, was among the most prominent Taiwanese intellectuals bridging the Japanese colonial and early post-war eras. He studied at the Presbyterian school in Tainan before pursuing higher education in Japan, and in 1916 he graduated in philosophy from Tokyo Imperial University, becoming the first Taiwanese to earn a bachelor of letters there. Returning home, he devoted himself to education, teaching at institutions such as the Tainan Commercial College while actively joining the cultural enlightenment movement. In 1927 he traveled to Columbia University in the United States, where he studied under the education philosopher John Dewey, earning a doctorate in philosophy in 1929 — the first Taiwanese ever to hold such a degree. After returning to Taiwan he continued to work for education and for the cultural standing of the Taiwanese people, enjoying great prestige even under colonial rule. When the Nationalist government took over Taiwan at the end of World War II, he initially held hopes for the new order and founded and edited the Minbao (People's Journal) to scrutinize public affairs. He was also appointed to National Taiwan University, serving as director of its preparatory division and acting dean of the College of Liberal Arts, a key founder of early post-war higher education on the island. Yet his frequent criticism of the incoming administration's failings marked him out as a target of the authorities. After the February 28 Incident erupted in 1947, security agents took him from his Taipei home on March 11; he was never seen again and is generally believed to have been killed. His disappearance became a symbolic case of the mass loss of the Taiwanese elite during the incident. Spanning both Japanese and American scholarly training and fusing Eastern and Western thought, Lin is remembered as a model of the modern Taiwanese intellectual, and his tragic end remains central to the memory of February 28.
Figures.figure.linmaosheng.event1: Abducted and vanished during the February 28 Incident (1947)
Figures.figure.linmaosheng.event2: Earned a Ph.D. in philosophy from Columbia University (1929)
Figures.figure.linmaosheng.title: Taiwan's First Doctor of Philosophy
Figures.figure.linpinhou.bio: Lin Pinhou, born in 1766 in Zhangzhou Prefecture, Fujian, arrived in Taiwan as a destitute youth and through shrewd commerce and timely alliance-building rose to become the founder of the wealthiest Han Chinese family in nineteenth-century Taiwan, the Banciao Lin family (板橋林家). He began his career as a laborer and shop assistant in the rice trade, gradually accumulating capital before establishing his own grain brokerage in the Tamsui River region, where he built connections with incoming settlers and Qing officials that proved decisive for his later ambitions. By purchasing the title of Imperial Student (監生) and later a military rank through contributions to the Qing treasury, Lin Pinhou secured the legal standing that enabled him to acquire large tracts of land across the Tamsui basin and the Keelung River plain in what is today the greater Taipei area. His business empire expanded from rice into landlordship, moneylending, and the management of reclamation projects, and he became one of the most important brokers between Qing authorities and the Han settler communities of northern Taiwan. In the turbulent 1810s and 1820s, Lin used his private militia to suppress local banditry and to mediate the fierce armed conflicts between settlers of Zhangzhou and Quanzhou origin that periodically devastated northern Taiwan, a role that reinforced his position as the dominant patron of the region. He relocated his household to Banciao around 1820, drawn by its strategic position between the Tamsui and Xinzhuang lowlands, and began constructing the fortified compound that would grow over the following decades into the celebrated Lin Family Mansion and Garden (林家花園). Lin Pinhou fathered five sons, among whom he distributed his landholdings and commercial interests, and he systematically invested in their education and official careers, laying the institutional foundation for the family's multigenerational influence. His son Lin Guohua and later his grandson Lin Weiyuan — already a figure in this archive — would expand the family's reach to include extensive philanthropic activity, public infrastructure, and service to successive colonial administrations. Lin Pinhou himself was known for generous donations to local temples, charitable granaries during famines, and the sponsorship of civil examinations in northern Taiwan, activities that embedded the family's name in the community fabric of Banciao and Taipei. He died in 1844 at the age of seventy-eight, having transformed the family from Fujian immigrants into the paramount landholding dynasty of northern Taiwan in the space of a single lifetime. The Lin family compound he established endured through the Japanese colonial period and is today preserved as a national historic site in New Taipei City, one of the finest examples of Qing-dynasty garden architecture surviving in Taiwan. Lin Pinhou is widely regarded as the exemplary figure of the self-made Qing immigrant who parlayed commercial acumen, political patronage, and strategic marriage into enduring dynastic power on the Taiwan frontier.
Figures.figure.linpinhou.event1: Established the Banciao Lin family fortune through land reclamation and grain trade in the Tamsui basin
Figures.figure.linpinhou.event2: Founded the Lin Family compound in Banciao (c. 1820), later expanded into the celebrated Lin Family Mansion and Garden
Figures.figure.linpinhou.title: Founder of the Banciao Lin Family
Figures.figure.linshuangwen.bio: Lin Shuang-wen, born in 1756 in Pinghe County, Fujian, migrated with his family to Taiwan in 1773 and settled in Dali (大里杙) on the central Taichung plain. The family farmed and engaged in petty commerce in a frontier zone marked by intense competition for land, water, and labor among recent immigrants from Fujian and Guangdong. He joined the Heaven and Earth Society (天地會), a secret brotherhood network linking Han migrant communities across the southeastern coast, and rose to become a regional leader of its Taiwan branches. A Qing crackdown on the Tiandihui in late 1786, which followed the arrest and execution of several brothers near Changhua, prompted Lin and his allies to take preemptive armed action. In November 1786 he raised the standard of Ming restoration, took the reign title Shun-tien (順天), and within weeks captured Changhua, the new Tanshui sub-prefecture, and the fortified town of Zhuluo (modern Chiayi). He coordinated with Zhuang Datian, who led a parallel uprising in the southern plains, briefly bringing most of the western Taiwan lowlands under rebel control. The Qing local administration collapsed under the pressure, while Hakka villages around Zhuluo refused to join the Hokkien-led rising and organized their own loyalist militias known as Yimin (義民). The Qing court eventually dispatched the senior Manchu general Fukang'an in December 1787 with a large expeditionary force including Manchu bannermen drawn from the capital region and Sichuanese auxiliaries. After months of hard fighting through the central Taiwan hills, Lin was captured in Laochiqi near present-day Miaoli in March 1788. He was transported to Beijing and executed by slow slicing in September 1788, his rebellion counted by the Qianlong Emperor among his celebrated Ten Great Campaigns. The emperor renamed Zhuluo as Jiayi (嘉義, honoring the righteous) to commemorate the loyalist Hakka and Pingpu villagers who had defended it through the uprising. Lin Shuang-wen's rebellion was the largest and most disruptive of Qing-era Taiwan revolts, exposing the limitations of mainland garrisons and accelerating the consolidation of Han gentry militia networks that would dominate the next century of Taiwanese politics.
Figures.figure.linshuangwen.title: Rebel Leader
Figures.figure.linweiyuan.bio: Lin Wei-yuan, born in 1838, was the leading figure of the Banqiao Lin family, which by his lifetime had grown into the wealthiest house in all of Taiwan. Built on land reclamation, rice, and above all the trade in tea and camphor, the family's fortune gave it influence to match its riches. Lin cultivated close ties with the Qing state, contributing vast sums to the treasury for coastal defence and disaster relief, and was rewarded with rank and official standing. When Liu Ming-chuan set about modernising Taiwan in the 1880s, he made Lin his partner: as deputy commissioner for land reclamation and pacification, Lin helped finance and organise the opening of the mountains, the reform of the land tax, and new commercial ventures, becoming the indispensable bridge between the reforming governor and Taiwanese wealth. His family's Banqiao garden and mansion stand today as a monument to the height of Qing-era Taiwanese gentry culture. When Taiwan was ceded to Japan in 1895, Lin refused to live under the new rulers and withdrew across the strait to Xiamen, where he died in 1905. He is remembered as the richest man of Qing Taiwan and a patron whose money underwrote the island's first age of modernisation.
Figures.figure.linweiyuan.event1: Partnered Liu Ming-chuan as deputy reclamation commissioner
Figures.figure.linweiyuan.event2: Refused Japanese rule and withdrew to Xiamen (1895)
Figures.figure.linweiyuan.title: Magnate of the Banqiao Lin Family
Figures.figure.linwencha.bio: Lin Wen-cha was born in 1828 into the Wufeng Lin family of central Taiwan, a clan that would rise through his exploits from local strongmen to one of the island's great gentry houses. In an age of feuds and disorder he built a formidable private militia, and when he led his Taiwanese braves across the strait to fight the Taiping rebels who were convulsing the Qing empire, his talent as a commander won swift promotion. Recalled to Taiwan, he played a decisive part in crushing the Dai Chao-chun rebellion of the early 1860s, the last of the great mid-century revolts, cementing both the empire's control and his family's dominance in the central plains. His service carried him to the rank of provincial military commander for Fujian, an extraordinary height for a Taiwanese of his day. But the wars that made him also claimed him: sent back to the mainland to fight, Lin Wen-cha was killed in battle against Taiping forces near Zhangzhou in 1864, still in his thirties. His death in imperial service earned the Wufeng Lin family lasting honours and vast landholdings, laying the foundation for its later prominence — a dynasty built on the battlefield.
Figures.figure.linwencha.event1: Led Taiwanese braves against the Taiping rebels in China
Figures.figure.linwencha.event2: Crushed the Dai Chao-chun rebellion in Taiwan (1860s)
Figures.figure.linwencha.title: Provincial Military Commander
Figures.figure.linxiantang.bio: Lin Hsien-tang (1881–1956) was the leader of the prominent Lin family of Wufeng and is honored as the 'Father of the Taiwanese Parliament.' Born into one of Taiwan's wealthiest and most influential gentry families, he chose, after the island was ceded to Japan in 1895, to pursue political rights for Taiwanese people through moderate, gradual, and legal means rather than armed resistance. A famous meeting with the Chinese reformer Liang Qichao in Nara in 1907 reinforced his belief that Taiwan's path lay in lawful self-strengthening and alliance with sympathetic Japanese liberals. In 1921 he served as the managing director (sōri) of the newly founded Taiwanese Cultural Association, which became the central engine of cultural enlightenment and the national movement, organizing lectures, reading rooms, and cultural activities across the island. From 1921 to 1934 he led the Petition Movement for the Establishment of a Taiwanese Parliament, repeatedly petitioning the Japanese Diet for an elected representative assembly for Taiwan, a campaign that, though never fully successful, became the longest-running and most symbolic political movement of the colonial era. He also financed and supported the influential newspaper Taiwan Min Pao, providing a vital platform for Taiwanese voices. As a moderate he kept the movement on a constitutional, non-violent course even after the Cultural Association split along left-right lines in 1927, and he later helped sustain the Taiwanese People's Party and local self-government leagues. After the war, disillusioned by the February 28 Incident of 1947 and the political climate under the Kuomintang, he went into self-imposed exile in Tokyo, where he died in 1956. He is remembered as the foremost moderate leader of the Taiwanese national movement and the man who laid its political groundwork.
Figures.figure.linxiantang.event1: 1907 Met the reformer Liang Qichao in Nara
Figures.figure.linxiantang.event2: 1921 Became managing director of the Taiwanese Cultural Association
Figures.figure.linxiantang.event3: 1921–34 Led the Petition Movement for the Establishment of a Taiwanese Parliament
Figures.figure.linxiantang.event4: 1949 Went into self-imposed exile in Tokyo, where he died in 1956
Figures.figure.linxiantang.title: Father of the Taiwanese Parliament
Figures.figure.linxiaomao.bio: Lin Xiaomao, born in 1865 in the Fengshan area, was the most prominent armed anti-Japanese leader in southern Taiwan during the early Japanese colonial period and was counted with Ke Tiehu and Jian Dashi as one of the so-called 'Three Fierce Anti-Japanese Leaders.' A locally powerful figure from the start, he commanded substantial personal networks and landholdings across Fengshan, Pingtung, and Donggang, and refused to accept the Japanese takeover after the Yiwei War, taking up arms instead. By around 1898 his influence extended along the lower Tamsui River basin and into Akō (Pingtung) and northern Hengchun, making his force the largest single armed resistance in the south during the early colonial years. He clashed repeatedly with Japanese troops and police and at one point attacked the administrative outposts at Chaozhou and Donggang, prompting the Government-General to dispatch reinforcements south. In 1899 the colonial government shifted to the so-called pacification-by-amnesty policy promoted by Goto Shimpei, mediated by local gentry, and Lin Xiaomao accepted Japanese terms that allowed him to manage farmland and local security around what is today Houbilin in Kaohsiung. Outwardly disarmed, he in practice retained a private armed retinue and an autonomous sphere of influence that the Japanese came to regard as a latent threat to southern stability. In 1902 the colonial authorities ruled that he had violated the terms of his surrender and launched a surprise assault on Houbilin that May. Lin Xiaomao was shot dead in the ensuing battle, much of his family and retinue were killed, and the largest armed resistance force in southern Taiwan was thus destroyed. His campaign closed the chapter of large-scale armed resistance organized around landed strongmen in the southern lowlands. Later opposition to Japanese rule would persist mainly as scattered actions or, eventually, as nationally inflected revolutionary movements. He is widely regarded as the figure whose downfall marked the end of large-scale armed resistance in lowland Taiwan.
Figures.figure.linxiaomao.event1: 1898 Led the largest armed resistance in the south
Figures.figure.linxiaomao.title: Leader of Anti-Japanese Resistance in Southern Taiwan
Figures.figure.linyihsiung.bio: Lin Yi-hsiung, born in 1941 in Yilan to a Hokkien family, was a defense lawyer turned tangwai politician who became one of the moral centers of Taiwan's democracy movement following the tragedy of the 1980 Lin Family Massacre. He graduated from the law department of National Taiwan University and built a successful Yilan practice in the 1970s, defending tangwai candidates and labor disputes in the late martial-law era. He was elected to the Yilan provincial assembly in 1977 and quickly emerged as one of the most articulate younger members of the tangwai opposition. As one of the principal defendants in the 1979 Kaohsiung Incident, he was tried by military court and sentenced to twelve years' imprisonment for sedition. On 28 February 1980 — while he was being interrogated in detention — his mother and seven-year-old twin daughters were murdered at his home in Taipei, and his elder daughter was gravely wounded, in a case that remains officially unsolved and has never been credibly attributed to anyone other than the security apparatus that controlled access to the property. The Lin Family Massacre became one of the defining moral atrocities of the late martial-law period and a permanent indictment of the regime's apparatus of fear. Released in 1984, he travelled abroad for several years and earned graduate degrees at Harvard and Cambridge before returning to Taiwan to resume political work. He served as chairman of the Democratic Progressive Party from 1998 to 2000, helping lay the foundations for Chen Shui-bian's election to the presidency in 2000. After leaving party leadership he devoted himself to constitutional reform causes, especially the campaign for direct democracy through referendum, and to the anti-nuclear movement. He undertook multiple high-profile fasts, including a 2014 hunger strike that helped force the indefinite suspension of construction at the Fourth Nuclear Power Plant in Gongliao. He converted his Taipei family home where the murders had taken place into a foundation and church, refusing to be drawn back into electoral politics in his later decades. Lin is widely regarded as one of the moral consciences of Taiwan's democratic transition, a figure whose suffering, principled withdrawal from power, and long advocacy of direct citizen participation continue to influence Taiwanese civic culture.
Figures.figure.linyihsiung.event1: Kaohsiung Incident defendant; family murdered in 1980 Lin Family Massacre
Figures.figure.linyihsiung.event2: Served as DPP chairman and led anti-nuclear and constitutional reform movements
Figures.figure.linyihsiung.title: Democracy Movement Leader
Figures.figure.linyouchun.bio: Lin Yu-chun (1880–1939), a member of the Lin family of Wufeng and a nephew of Lin Hsien-tang, was a celebrated classical poet and a key figure of the national movement under Japanese rule. Steeped in the classics from childhood and precocious in literary talent, he joined the Lo She, the leading poetry society of central Taiwan, where his vigorous and brooding verse gave voice to thoughts of country and to national integrity, making him a representative of the traditional literati who took up the modern national movement. From 1921 he helped his uncle Lin Hsien-tang found and run the Taiwanese Cultural Association and threw himself into the Petition Movement for the Establishment of a Taiwanese Parliament, travelling to build alliances and writing to rally support, becoming an important spiritual and propaganda pillar of the petition campaign. When the Public Order Police Law Incident broke out in 1923, he was arrested and imprisoned by the colonial authorities for his role in the league supporting a Taiwanese parliament, standing as a defendant alongside Chiang Wei-shui and Tsai Pei-huo; he kept his integrity unbroken in prison and recorded the spirit of the struggle in verse to encourage his comrades. After his release he continued to support the national movement through his writing and took an interest in the rise of Taiwan's new literature, earning a reputation as a pivotal literary figure bridging the early phase of the new-literature movement. He died in 1939, leaving a large body of classical poetry imbued with national feeling and standing as a model of intellectuals resisting colonial rule through literature.
Figures.figure.linyouchun.event1: 1921 Took part in founding the Cultural Association and the parliamentary petition
Figures.figure.linyouchun.event2: 1923 Imprisoned in the Public Order Police Law Incident
Figures.figure.linyouchun.title: Poet of the Lo She and Parliamentary Petition Leader
Figures.figure.linzhanmei.bio: Lin Zhanmei was the foremost cultural patron of northern Taiwan in the mid-nineteenth century. Born into a wealthy Hakka merchant-gentry family in Hsinchu, he used the family fortune to build the Qianyuan (Hidden Garden) estate, which became a gathering place for poets, calligraphers, and scholars, transforming Hsinchu into the cultural capital of Qing northern Taiwan. Lin was himself a prolific classical poet who left a substantial body of verse. When the Dai Chaochun Rebellion erupted, Lin organized and personally funded local militia forces to defend Hsinchu, demonstrating the dual role of the Qing gentry as cultural arbiter and military organizer. The garden was eventually destroyed in fighting, but Lin Zhanmei's legacy as northern Taiwan's great literary patron endures.
Figures.figure.linzhanmei.event1: Built Qianyuan Garden, making Hsinchu northern Taiwan's cultural hub
Figures.figure.linzhanmei.event2: Organized militia to defend Hsinchu during the Dai Chaochun Rebellion
Figures.figure.linzhanmei.title: Cultural Patron of Qianyuan Garden
Figures.figure.liuao.bio: Liu Ao, courtesy name Yizhai, was a Qing military official from Linxiang in Hunan who rose through the ranks during the suppression of the Taiping Rebellion before entering the Taiwan administration in the late Tongzhi reign. Known for his assertive style, he prioritised coastal defence and frontier policy, pushing to extend Qing administrative reach into indigenous territories. When France went to war with China in 1884 and launched naval attacks on Formosa, Liu Ao took charge of defensive deployments in southern Taiwan and the Penghu Islands. His strategic approach, however, diverged sharply from that of Liu Mingchuan, who commanded northern Taiwan — both were seasoned commanders valued by the court, yet they clashed persistently over resource allocation and tactical priorities. After the war, when Taiwan was elevated to a province and Liu Mingchuan was appointed its first governor, Liu Ao found himself outmanoeuvred in the ensuing political reckoning; he was impeached and sent into exile. He died in banishment, his later years consumed by frustration and obscurity. His military efforts in southern Taiwan were not without effect, but his combative temperament and factional positioning cast him as a tragic figure in the province's founding moment — a capable warrior marginalised by the institutional transition he could not adapt to.
Figures.figure.liuao.event1: During the Sino-French War of 1884, commanded the defence of southern Taiwan and Penghu; clashed with Liu Mingchuan over strategy, reflecting a deep factional rift within Qing command.
Figures.figure.liuao.event2: After Taiwan became a province in 1885 and Liu Mingchuan was appointed governor, Liu Ao was impeached and exiled — a capable commander undone by factional politics at the moment of institutional transformation.
Figures.figure.liuao.title: Qing Military Commander, Defender of Southern Taiwan
Figures.figure.liuguoxuan.bio: Liu Guoxuan, born in 1629 in Tingzhou, Fujian, was the most accomplished general of the Kingdom of Tungning and the commander whose 1683 defeat at Penghu effectively ended Zheng family rule over Taiwan. Originally a junior officer in a Ming garrison at Zhangzhou, he defected to Koxinga's resistance in 1654, bringing the strategically vital coastal town with him and gaining the warlord's confidence overnight. Throughout the late 1650s he commanded land forces in Koxinga's mainland operations, including the rear-guard actions that protected the retreat from the failed siege of Nanjing in 1659. He participated in the 1661–1662 conquest of Taiwan and the early consolidation of Tungning, rising rapidly through the new regime's military hierarchy. Under Zheng Jing he held both land and naval commands and became, after the death of older generals, the kingdom's senior strategist. During the Revolt of the Three Feudatories from 1673 to 1680, he led Tungning's expeditionary forces on the mainland and conducted the difficult fighting retreat back to Taiwan as the coalition unraveled. After 1680 he was effectively co-regent for the boy king Zheng Keshuang alongside Feng Xifan, although his orientation was more pragmatic and his counsel often favored seeking terms with the Qing. In 1683 he was placed in personal command of the defense of Penghu, fortifying the islands with batteries and concentrated naval forces in expectation of the long-anticipated Qing assault. The Battle of Penghu in late June 1683, fought in three engagements over a week, ended in the destruction of most of his fleet by the Qing admiral Shi Lang. He returned to Taiwan with a small remnant and counselled Zheng Keshuang to surrender, judging that further resistance would mean the annihilation of the regime and its people. After Tungning's submission he was incorporated into the Qing military hierarchy, ennobled as an earl, and served as Brigade Commander of Tianjin until his death in 1693. Liu is remembered as a soldier of unusual range — a defector who became a loyal pillar of his adopted house, a general who lost his decisive battle but counselled the surrender that spared his sovereign's life and people.
Figures.figure.liuguoxuan.event1: Defeated by Shi Lang at the Battle of Penghu (1683)
Figures.figure.liuguoxuan.title: Admiral of the Tungning Navy
Figures.figure.liumingchuan.bio: Liu Ming-chuan, born in 1836 to a poor farming family in Hefei, Anhui, was a self-made military officer of the Huai Army who later served as the first Governor of Taiwan Province and the foremost architect of late-Qing modernization on the island. He joined a local militia as a teenager and rose through the Huai Army under Li Hongzhang, distinguishing himself in major battles against the Taiping rebels in the lower Yangzi region in the 1860s. After the Taiping War he led campaigns in the north against the Nian rebels and was eventually ennobled as an earl of the first rank, before retiring to his estates in the late 1870s as factional politics turned against him. The Sino-French War of 1884 returned him to active service: appointed to defend Taiwan against the French Far East Squadron, he arrived in July 1884 with broad authority over military and civil affairs. He withdrew from indefensible Keelung after heavy French bombardment but held Tamsui in October 1884, beating off a French landing in the famous Battle of Hobe (滬尾大捷) — the only significant Chinese land victory of the war. After the truce of 1885, the Qing court upgraded Taiwan from a prefecture under Fujian to a full province, with Liu as its inaugural governor and a sweeping mandate for self-strengthening reform. Between 1885 and 1891 he built Taiwan's first railway from Keelung toward Hsinchu, strung telegraph lines across the western corridor and to Penghu, and inaugurated a postal service that issued the island's earliest stamps. He oversaw the comprehensive land survey known as the Qingfu (清賦), modernized customs administration, opened coal mines at Keelung, and installed gas street lighting in Dadaocheng. He attempted ambitious institutional reforms, including a Western-style academy in Taipei, integration of indigenous polities into the tax system, and the development of Taipei as a new administrative center. Many of these programs ran into stiff opposition from elite landowners disliking the new survey and tax burdens, as well as from court conservatives reluctant to underwrite their expense. He resigned in 1891 amid these political pressures and a tax revolt in Changhua, and his successor Shao Youlian let several of his initiatives lapse before Taiwan's cession to Japan in 1895. Liu died in 1896 in Hefei at the age of 60, his legacy mixed — a visionary modernizer who in six years gave Taiwan its first modern infrastructure but whose programs were incomplete and unevenly absorbed by the time of the Qing exit from the island.
Figures.figure.liumingchuan.event1: Established Taiwan as a province and modernized its infrastructure (1885–1891)
Figures.figure.liumingchuan.title: First Governor of Taiwan Province
Figures.figure.liuyongfu.bio: Liu Yongfu, born in 1837 in Qinzhou, Guangxi (today part of Guangdong), into an impoverished Han family, trained in martial arts from youth and joined the secret society networks of the late Taiping era. After the Taiping rebellion he led his followers across the border into Tonkin in northern Vietnam, where he organized the Black Flag Army around their distinctive black banners and gained de facto control of the upper Red River region. During the Sino-French War he led the Black Flags against French forces at the request of both the Qing court and the Vietnamese Nguyễn dynasty, winning international notoriety at the 1883 Battle of Paper Bridge near Hanoi, where his troops killed the French commander Henri Rivière. After the war his army was partially absorbed into the Qing military, and he was reassigned to garrison duty along the southwestern frontier. With the outbreak of the First Sino-Japanese War in 1894, the Qing court ordered him to Taiwan, where he commanded the southern defenses from Tainan. Following the cession of Taiwan in 1895 and Tang Jingsong's flight from Taipei, Liu was acclaimed second President of the Republic of Formosa over its southern remnant and continued the resistance with combined Black Flag and Taiwanese volunteer units against the Japanese advance. Southern resistance lasted until October 1895, when, his supplies exhausted and external aid impossible, he disguised himself as an elderly woman and escaped aboard a British merchant ship to Xiamen on the eve of the fall of Tainan, ending organized resistance in the south. After returning to China he resumed service as Commander-in-Chief of land forces in Guangdong and was briefly named head of the Guangdong militia after the 1911 Revolution. He died at his home in Qinzhou in 1917. Liu is remembered across Vietnam, China, and Taiwan as one of the most colorful frontline commanders of the late Qing era, whose campaigns ranged from the anti-French struggle in Tonkin to the closing chapter of Han resistance to Japanese rule in Taiwan.
Figures.figure.liuyongfu.event1: 1895 Led the southern resistance and held Tainan
Figures.figure.liuyongfu.event2: 1895 Escaped to Xiamen on the eve of the fall of Tainan
Figures.figure.liuyongfu.title: Black Flag General and Leader of the Southern Resistance
Figures.figure.lixianglan.bio: Li Xianglan, whose real name was Yamaguchi Yoshiko (1920–2014), was born into a Japanese family in northeastern China and became a wartime film superstar spanning China, Japan and Manchukuo, as well as an important instrument of the Japanese empire's cultural propaganda. Raised in China from childhood and fluent in Chinese, she was recruited by the Manchukuo Film Association (Man'ei) and was built up under the name 'Li Xianglan' into a hugely popular singing-and-acting star who appeared to be Chinese, starring in many state-policy films that beautified Japanese aggression and promoted 'Japan–Manchukuo friendship,' becoming famous across East Asia. In 1943 she starred in The Bell of Sayun, a Man'ei–Shochiku co-production based on the story of the Atayal girl Sayun of Taiwan, which embellished what had been a simple mountain accident into a moving legend of a 'patriotic maiden' devoting herself to the nation, making the film a representative work of Taiwan's wartime mobilization and imperialization propaganda, while her sweet image and singing made the propaganda all the more affecting. After the war, because of her Chinese persona as 'Li Xianglan' she was for a time tried as a collaborator, but was finally released and repatriated to Japan upon proof of her Japanese citizenship, resuming her real name, Yamaguchi Yoshiko. She later remade herself as an actress and presenter and went on to enter politics, winning election to the Japanese House of Councillors and devoting many years to questions of war responsibility and peace. The life of Li Xianglan and The Bell of Sayun vividly bear witness to how film and stars were swept into wartime mobilization and made part of the empire's propaganda machine.
Figures.figure.lixianglan.event1: 1943 Starred in the propaganda film The Bell of Sayun
Figures.figure.lixianglan.event2: 1945 Tried after the war, then repatriated to Japan and resumed her real name
Figures.figure.lixianglan.title: Star of Wartime Propaganda Films
Figures.figure.liyingzhang.bio: Li Ying-chang was born in 1897 in Erhlin, Changhua, and trained as a doctor at the Medical School of the Taiwan Governor-General's Office, where he was among the students who founded the Taiwan Cultural Association. Returning to practise medicine in his home town, he saw at first hand how the sugar company cheated local cane farmers on weight and price, and he resolved to organise them. In 1925 he helped found Taiwan's first cane growers' union in Erhlin and led its demands against the Lin Pen-yuan Sugar Company. That autumn the confrontation exploded into the Erhlin Incident, the colonial era's first large-scale farmers' protest; Li was arrested and imprisoned as a ringleader. Blacklisted and harried after his release, he eventually left for China, where he practised medicine in Shanghai under the name Li Weiguang and drew close to the communist movement. He remained in China after 1949 and died there in 1954. Li Ying-chang is remembered as a doctor who turned his stethoscope aside to fight for the dignity of Taiwan's farmers.
Figures.figure.liyingzhang.event1: Founded Taiwan's first cane growers' union in Erhlin (1925)
Figures.figure.liyingzhang.event2: Led the Erhlin Incident and was imprisoned
Figures.figure.liyingzhang.title: Physician and Farmers' Movement Leader
Figures.figure.luheruo.bio: Lu Heruo was born Lu Shih-tui in 1914 in Tanzi, Taichung, into a landowning family, and grew into one of the most dazzling talents of his generation — so gifted that admirers called him 'Taiwan's finest genius.' Trained as a teacher, he made his literary debut in 1935 when his story The Oxcart was published in a leading Tokyo magazine, a searing portrait of a peasant family crushed by modernisation. Not content with the pen alone, he travelled to Japan to train as a baritone and performed on the operatic stage, moving between literature and music with rare ease. His fiction, including the celebrated Clear Autumn, probed the tensions of family, tradition and colonial modernity. After the war his idealism drew him leftward, and amid the gathering White Terror he went underground, joining an armed base in the hills of Luku. It was there, around 1951, that he died — by most accounts from a venomous snakebite while in hiding — his brilliant life cut short at thirty-six. His grave was never found, and his finest works were long suppressed before Taiwan reclaimed him as a master of colonial-era fiction.
Figures.figure.luheruo.event1: Debuted with The Oxcart in a Tokyo literary magazine (1935)
Figures.figure.luheruo.event2: Died around 1951 while hiding at the Luku armed base
Figures.figure.luheruo.title: Writer and Baritone
Figures.figure.luhsiulien.bio: Lu Hsiu-lien, born in 1944 in Taoyuan, is a leading figure in Taiwan's post-war women's and democracy movements. A high achiever in her youth, she graduated in law from National Taiwan University and later pursued studies in the United States, earning master's degrees in law from the University of Illinois and Harvard University. In the 1970s she was the first to champion "new feminism" in Taiwan, advancing gender equality through her writings and the Pioneer Press, a forerunner of the local women's movement. She then joined the tangwai (non-party) movement, concerned with human rights, democracy, and Taiwan's future. When the Kaohsiung Incident erupted in 1979, she was arrested for taking part and speaking at the demonstration and sentenced to twelve years in a military trial. After serving about five years, she was released on medical parole in 1985. With the lifting of martial law and democratization she returned to politics, winning election as a National Assembly delegate, legislator, and Taoyuan county magistrate, with a distinctive governing style. In 2000, running alongside Chen Shui-bian, she was elected Vice President of the Republic of China — the first woman to hold the office — and was re-elected through 2008. In office she promoted human-rights diplomacy, gender equality, and Taiwanese identity, fostering related international exchange. After leaving office she continued to engage with environmental, peace, and women's issues and repeatedly returned to public affairs. Lu is regarded as a key symbol of Taiwan's women's movement and democratic transition, her path from feminist advocate to the highest office held by a woman embodying the breakthrough of women's political participation in post-war Taiwan.
Figures.figure.luhsiulien.event2: Elected the first female Vice President of the ROC (2000)
Figures.figure.luhsiulien.title: New-Feminism Pioneer & Kaohsiung Incident Prisoner
Figures.figure.luofuxing.bio: Luo Fuxing, born in 1886 in Zhenping (modern Jiaoling) in Guangdong, was a Hakka revolutionary whose career represented the shift of Taiwan's armed resistance toward modern nationalist revolutionary ideology in the mid-colonial period. In his youth he followed his family to Southeast Asia and Taiwan, was drawn to the revolutionary ideas of Sun Yat-sen, and joined the Tongmenghui in Southeast Asia, where he engaged in fundraising and propaganda work. After the founding of the Republic of China in 1912 he traveled from Guangdong to Taiwan under instructions from the Tongmenghui (later reorganized as the Kuomintang) and, using a coolie association and a sundry-goods shop in the Miaoli area as cover, began recruiting members and organizing an underground revolutionary network. The movement framed itself as anti-colonial and oriented toward returning Taiwan to the mainland, and it planned a coordinated island-wide uprising — the events later known as the Miaoli Incident. He extended his contacts to Keelung, Hsinchu, and Taichung, and his network coordinated loosely with smaller resistance cells around the Guandi Temple in Taitung and the Dongshijiao area, making it the most organized revolutionary network operating inside Taiwan at the time. The plan called for several risings to break out together, drawing on the symbolic prestige of the 1911 Revolution to attract recruits across class and ethnic lines. From mid-1913, after related cells in the east and north were exposed prematurely, the Government-General launched extensive investigations and mass arrests, and Luo Fuxing himself was captured in Tamsui while attempting to escape back to China. In March 1914 he and his fellow defendants were sentenced to death by a special tribunal in Miaoli, and he was executed in Taipei the same month, leaving behind a farewell poem affirming his commitment to resistance. The wider sweep of arrests dismantled the connecting network across central and northern Taiwan in a matter of months. The Miaoli Incident is regarded as a key turning point in which Taiwan's armed resistance shifted from locally rooted strongman warfare toward modern nationalist revolutionary thought. He is widely credited as one of the principal figures through whom the influence of the 1911 Revolution reached the island.
Figures.figure.luofuxing.event1: 1912 Arrived in Taiwan to organize a revolutionary network
Figures.figure.luofuxing.event2: 1913 Captured after the Miaoli plot was exposed
Figures.figure.luofuxing.title: Leader of the Miaoli Uprising
Figures.figure.luojun.bio: Luo Jun, born in 1854 in what is today Douliu in Yunlin, was one of the core leaders of the Tapani Incident (the Xilai Temple Incident or Jiaobani Incident) and was chiefly responsible for organizing and mobilizing the central and northern regions of Taiwan. A generation older than Yu Qingfang, he was a widely traveled figure who had moved through Fujian, Guangdong, and the islands of Southeast Asia in the course of religious work and small-scale trade. He had a fuller understanding of the anti-colonial currents then circulating in the wider ethnic-Chinese world than either of his fellow leaders. Returning to Taiwan around 1914, he joined the Xilai Temple resistance organization led by Yu Qingfang and used his religious and commercial networks to recruit members and circulate anti-Japanese messages quietly across Chiayi, Yunlin, Changhua, and Hsinchu. The network he assembled in the central and northern regions was what allowed the uprising to be conceived as an island-wide action, and many of those later arrested in Chiayi, Linqipu, and Erlin were connected to his lines of contact. In early 1915 he traveled repeatedly between Tainan and Chiayi to coordinate the timing of the uprising and to organize logistics and synchronization across the north and center. In May of that year, before the uprising could be set in motion in full, an informant exposed the plot, and he was captured by Japanese investigators in the Chiayi area. He was transferred to Tainan for trial and sentenced to death together with Yu Qingfang in September of the same year, with the sentence carried out at Tainan. His arrest before the rising could be triggered island-wide left the eventual Jiaobani battle without the northern and central support originally expected. The Tapani Incident accordingly unfolded as an isolated southern uprising rather than the coordinated island-wide action it had been planned to be. He is widely regarded as the figure whose early capture critically disrupted the network's strategic design.
Figures.figure.luojun.event1: 1915 Organized resistance networks in central and northern Taiwan
Figures.figure.luojun.title: Central-Northern Coordinator of the Tapani Incident
Figures.figure.macarthur.bio: Douglas MacArthur, born in 1880 in Little Rock, Arkansas, into a distinguished American military family, was one of only five U.S. five-star Generals of the Army and the senior American military figure whose post-1945 directives directly shaped the trajectory of Taiwan in the aftermath of the Second World War. He graduated first in the West Point class of 1903 and served with distinction in the Philippine pacification campaigns, in Mexico, and in France during the First World War, where he commanded the Rainbow Division. He served as Superintendent of West Point from 1919 to 1922 and as Army Chief of Staff from 1930 to 1935 before accepting an appointment as Field Marshal of the Commonwealth of the Philippines. After the Japanese invasion of the Philippines in 1941 he led the doomed defense of Bataan and Corregidor before being ordered by President Roosevelt to evacuate to Australia, where he famously pledged 'I shall return.' He commanded Allied forces in the Southwest Pacific Area for the remainder of the war, conducting the island-hopping campaign that closed in on the Japanese home islands by 1945. He accepted the formal Japanese surrender aboard the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay on 2 September 1945 in his capacity as Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP). On the same day, in his SCAP General Order No. 1, he directed which Allied forces would receive the surrender of Japanese troops in each theater, specifying that the Republic of China would accept the surrender of Japanese forces in China proper north of Indochina, including Formosa and the Pescadores. This directive made the Republic of China the receiver of the Japanese administration in Taiwan in October 1945, an instruction whose legal interpretation continues to shape debates over Taiwan's international status into the twenty-first century. From late 1945 through 1951 he served as the de facto American proconsul of occupied Japan, overseeing demilitarization, the drafting of the post-war Japanese constitution, land reform, and the rebuilding of the Japanese economy. He returned to active field command during the Korean War from 1950, executing the strategically brilliant Inchon landings before being relieved by President Truman in April 1951 for publicly disputing the president's strategy of limited war against the People's Republic of China. He returned to the United States to a hero's welcome and delivered the famous Old Soldiers Never Die farewell address to a joint session of Congress before retiring from public life. He died in 1964 at the age of 84, and his General Order No. 1 remains one of the foundational legal acts shaping Taiwan's modern history, although his personal involvement with the island during his lifetime was limited.
Figures.figure.macarthur.event1: Issued General Order No. 1 (1945), directing the ROC to accept Japan's surrender in Taiwan
Figures.figure.macarthur.title: Supreme Commander of the Allied Powers
Figures.figure.mackay.bio: George Leslie Mackay, born in 1844 in Zorra township, Ontario, to Scottish Highland immigrant parents, became the founding figure of the Canadian Presbyterian Church's Taiwan mission and the most celebrated foreign resident in nineteenth-century northern Taiwan. After studying at Knox College in Toronto, Princeton Theological Seminary, and the University of Edinburgh under Alexander Duff, he volunteered for foreign mission service and was assigned to Formosa as the Canadian Church's first overseas missionary. He landed at Tamsui on 9 March 1872 and made it his lifelong base, immediately beginning the rigorous self-study of Taiwanese Hokkien that would soon make him one of the most fluent foreign speakers of the language. He travelled itinerantly through the Tamsui, Keelung, Yilan, and Hsinchu basins on foot for decades, founding more than sixty congregations among Hokkien, Hakka, and Kavalan indigenous communities. A self-trained dentist, he carried portable instruments on his preaching tours and personally extracted, by his own meticulous count, more than twenty-one thousand teeth, an outreach that won him acceptance in villages otherwise wary of foreign missionaries. He established the first Western-style hospital in northern Taiwan in 1880, the forerunner of today's Mackay Memorial Hospital, with funding raised from a Detroit benefactor of the same surname. In 1880 he married Tiunn Chhang-miâ (張聰明), a young Taiwanese woman from a Christian household near Wuku, who became an indispensable partner in his work and a respected teacher of converts in her own right. He founded Oxford College (理學堂大書院) at Tamsui in 1882 with funds raised in Oxford County, Ontario — the predecessor of today's Aletheia University — and opened Tamsui Girls' School (淡水女學堂) in 1884, the first formal school for girls in Taiwan. He continued mission work through the violence of the Sino-French War in 1884–1885, when several of his northern chapels were burned by anti-foreign mobs and Tamsui itself was bombarded by French ships. His memoir From Far Formosa, published in 1895, remains one of the most detailed and sympathetic late-Qing portraits of northern Taiwanese society in any Western language. He died of throat cancer at Tamsui on 2 June 1901 at the age of 57 and was buried in the Mackay family plot inside the walled grounds of Oxford College. Mackay's adopted Taiwanese name (偕叡理) and his motto 「寧願燒盡，不願銹壞」 (Rather burn out than rust out) remain widely cited touchstones of foreign engagement with Taiwan, and his lineage continues through descendants and institutions that bear his name across the island.
Figures.figure.mackay.event1: Founded Oxford College (1882) and Tamsui Girls' School (1884)
Figures.figure.mackay.event2: Established northern Taiwan's first Western-style hospital and dental clinic
Figures.figure.mackay.title: Presbyterian Missionary
Figures.figure.mahungmona.bio: Mahung Mona (1908–1973), a daughter of Mona Rudao, the chieftain of the Mahebu community of the Seediq, was one of the few survivors directly involved in the Wushe Incident of 1930. After the uprising broke out her father Mona Rudao led the people in revolt against the Japanese and finally took his own life in defeat, while her elder brother Tado Mona and the other men of the clan died in battle or hanged themselves under the overwhelming Japanese forces and gas attacks, so that the entire family and community were all but wiped out. As a woman she survived the catastrophe, yet had to bear the heavy trauma of losing her father, brothers and most of her people. In the aftermath the surviving Seediq suffered the retaliatory 'Second Wushe Incident' and were forcibly relocated by the colonial authorities to Kawanakajima (today's Qingliu community) for concentrated control, and she too was driven from her ancestral land. Over the long years that followed she lived on as a survivor into the postwar period, preserving the memories she had witnessed through oral testimony and becoming an important witness for later generations seeking to understand the truth of the Wushe Incident and the suffering of the Seediq people. She died in 1973, her life embodying the collective trauma and resilience of a people torn apart by colonial violence.
Figures.figure.mahungmona.event1: 1930 Lost her family in the Wushe Incident
Figures.figure.mahungmona.event2: 1931+ Survived and was relocated to Kawanakajima
Figures.figure.mahungmona.title: Survivor of the Wushe Incident
Figures.figure.maxwell.bio: James Laidlaw Maxwell was a Scottish physician and English Presbyterian missionary who arrived in Taiwan in 1865, establishing the island's first Western-style clinic in Tainan. Initially expelled by hostile local residents, he relocated to Cihou before returning permanently to Tainan. Maxwell's skills in surgery and ophthalmology gradually won the trust of Han and Pingpu indigenous communities who had never encountered Western medicine. He trained local assistants, built up a network of clinics, and created institutional foundations that developed into the present Xinlou (New Building) Hospital in Tainan, still operational today. Maxwell is revered as the founder of modern medicine in southern Taiwan and a key figure in the early history of Christianity on the island.
Figures.figure.maxwell.event1: Established Taiwan's first Western-style hospital in Tainan in 1865
Figures.figure.maxwell.event2: Founded institutional predecessor of today's Xinlou Hospital in Tainan
Figures.figure.maxwell.title: First Western Medical Missionary in Taiwan
Figures.figure.mayingjeou.bio: Ma Ying-jeou, born in 1950 in Hong Kong to KMT-aligned mainlander parents who had recently fled the civil war, was brought to Taiwan as a small child and rose through the ROC bureaucratic and party hierarchy to serve two terms as President of the Republic of China from 2008 to 2016. He graduated from the law department of National Taiwan University and pursued advanced legal studies at New York University and at Harvard Law School, where he received his doctoral degree in 1981. Returning to Taiwan he served as English-language secretary to President Chiang Ching-kuo and as deputy secretary-general of the KMT, establishing himself as a rising mainlander star within the post-Chiang reform generation. He served as Justice Minister from 1993 to 1996, winning a reputation as an anti-corruption advocate during his prosecution-led campaign against vote-buying in local elections. He was twice elected mayor of Taipei from 1998 and 2002, ousting Chen Shui-bian in the first contest and establishing the foundation for his national-level career. As KMT chairman from 2005, he repositioned the party as a credible governing alternative after years of identity crisis under Lien Chan, and won the 2008 presidential election in a landslide against the DPP's Frank Hsieh. His first term emphasized cross-strait rapprochement: direct passenger and cargo flights between Taiwan and mainland China were opened in 2008–2009, mainland tourist arrivals were liberalized, and the Economic Cooperation Framework Agreement (ECFA) was signed in 2010. He was reelected in 2012 with 51.6 percent against the DPP's Tsai Ing-wen and continued an unprecedented expansion of cross-strait economic ties, ultimately concluding twenty-three formal cross-strait agreements. His proposed Cross-Strait Service Trade Agreement triggered the March 2014 Sunflower Movement, in which student protesters occupied the Legislative Yuan for twenty-four days and forced the suspension of the pact. In November 2015 he met with PRC President Xi Jinping in Singapore in the first direct face-to-face encounter between the heads of the ROC and PRC governments since 1945, an event celebrated in some quarters and criticized in others. He left office in 2016 after the DPP's landslide return to power and has pursued an active post-presidency, including several high-profile visits to mainland China in 2023 and 2024. Ma is widely credited with completing the institutional infrastructure of cross-strait economic engagement, though the political backlash to that engagement reshaped Taiwanese identity politics and contributed to the DPP's subsequent decade of national dominance.
Figures.figure.mayingjeou.title: President of the Republic of China
Figures.figure.monarudao.bio: Mona Rudao, born around 1882 in Mehebu village in the highlands of central Taiwan, was the hereditary chief of the Mehebu community within the Tgdaya subgroup of the Seediq people and the most renowned indigenous leader of armed resistance during the Japanese colonial era. As a young man he was brought to Japan in 1911 on a colonial tour designed to impress indigenous leaders with imperial power, an experience that gave him an unusually clear-eyed view of the empire he would eventually challenge. The colonial government in the 1920s extracted ever more forced labor from the Wushe (Musha) highlands for timber felling, dormitory construction, and road work, often without pay and under brutal supervision. Cultural suppression compounded the grievances, including bans on facial tattooing, restrictions on traditional hunting, and the imposition of political marriages between Japanese policemen and indigenous women that frequently ended in abandonment. The immediate trigger came in October 1930, when his son Tado Mona scuffled with a Japanese constable named Yoshimura at a wedding feast, an incident that left the family fearing severe reprisal. On 27 October 1930, during the annual sports day at Wushe Public School, Mona Rudao led an alliance of six Tgdaya villages, totaling roughly three hundred fighters, in a coordinated attack that killed 134 Japanese, an event known as the Wushe Incident. The colonial response mobilized over three thousand troops and police backed by aircraft, artillery, and aerial drops of poison gas, in one of the few documented uses of chemical weapons against a civilian-allied population in the inter-war period. The authorities also armed rival Seediq factions, particularly the Toda group, as friendly aborigines to track down survivors in the Second Wushe Incident of April 1931, which all but annihilated the rebelling communities. Refusing surrender, Mona Rudao retreated into the mountains with a remnant of his fighters and is believed to have shot himself in a cave near Mount Maxibu in early December 1930. His remains were discovered by hunters four years later and eventually returned to Wushe for burial after the Second World War. Following the war the surviving Tgdaya populations were forcibly resettled in Qingliu (Chuanzhongdao), and indigenous communities continue to commemorate the uprising annually. Mona Rudao is today widely honored as a symbol of indigenous resistance and Taiwanese collective memory, depicted on the NT$20 coin and lionized in the film Warriors of the Rainbow: Seediq Bale.
Figures.figure.monarudao.title: Seediq Chief & Resistance Leader
Figures.figure.moriyamamatsunosuke.bio: Moriyama Matsunosuke (1869–1949) was a Japanese architect who graduated from the architecture department of Tokyo Imperial University as a pupil of the renowned Tatsuno Kingo. During the Japanese period he was employed in the construction section of the Taiwan Governor-General's Office, becoming one of the most important official architects of his day in Taiwan and leading the design of a great many representative government and public buildings. He excelled at shaping the authority of the colonial government through ornate European historicist styles—drawing on Baroque, Renaissance and other elements—and his works include the Monopoly Bureau of the Governor-General's Office, the Taipei, Tainan and Taichung prefectural halls, and the Taipei waterworks pump house, many of which remain landmark monuments in their cities today. With symmetrical and dignified façades, elaborate ornament, domes and towers, these buildings conveyed the grandeur and order of colonial modernization and profoundly shaped the official architecture and streetscapes of Taiwan's cities under Japanese rule. Moriyama's designs not only displayed the most advanced building techniques and aesthetics of the time but also became important models for the development of Taiwan's modern architecture. He continued to practise after returning to Japan, but the many works he left in Taiwan make him an indispensable figure for understanding the island's modern architectural history.
Figures.figure.moriyamamatsunosuke.event1: 1900s–20s Designed many of Taiwan's government buildings
Figures.figure.moriyamamatsunosuke.event2: 1910s Completed the Tainan and Taichung prefectural halls and other major works
Figures.figure.moriyamamatsunosuke.title: Architect of Government Buildings
Figures.figure.morrischang.bio: Morris Chang, born in 1931 in Ningbo, Zhejiang, China, is the key figure behind Taiwan's semiconductor industry and the global chip supply chain. He pursued his education through wartime upheaval before studying in the United States, earning a master's degree from MIT and a doctorate in electrical engineering from Stanford University. He spent many years at Texas Instruments, rising to senior vice president, one of the few ethnic Chinese to reach the upper ranks of a major American technology company. In 1985 he was invited to Taiwan to head the Industrial Technology Research Institute, taking up the planning and upgrading of Taiwan's technology industry. In 1987 he founded the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), pioneering the entirely new "dedicated foundry" business model — neither designing nor selling branded chips but focusing on manufacturing for clients worldwide. This model transformed the division of labor in the semiconductor industry, enabling the rise of fabless design firms and making TSMC the sector's central hub. Under his leadership TSMC long held the lead in advanced process technology, becoming the world's largest contract chipmaker. Semiconductors thus came to be seen as Taiwan's "sacred mountain of national protection," bearing on global technology and geopolitics. He retired and returned before finally handing over leadership in 2018, and had represented Taiwan at international forums such as APEC. Chang is regarded as the pivotal force in Taiwan's transformation from a contract-manufacturing island into a technology powerhouse, his entrepreneurship and management philosophy profoundly shaping the industrial landscape of Taiwan and the world.
Figures.figure.morrischang.title: TSMC Founder & Semiconductor Pioneer
Figures.figure.nuyts.bio: Pieter Nuyts was a Dutch East India Company official born in Zeeland, who served at the Hirado trading post in Japan before being appointed Governor of Formosa in 1627. During his tenure he sought to tighten company control over indigenous villages on the island, and clashed repeatedly with missionary George Candidius over the boundaries between ecclesiastical and administrative authority. In 1628, the Japanese merchant Hamada Yahyoe arrived in Taiwan with armed men and took Nuyts hostage, demanding compensation for grievances against the company — an incident that threw Dutch-Japanese relations into crisis. The East India Company, unwilling to let a single governor's miscalculations endanger its lucrative Japan trade, arrested Nuyts and handed him over to Japanese authorities in 1632 as a diplomatic hostage. He remained imprisoned in Japan for several years before finally being released and returning to the Netherlands. In his later years he served as a member of the Zeeland provincial assembly. Nuyts's diplomatic failures inflicted lasting damage on Dutch commercial ambitions in East Asia, exposing the inherent tension between colonial governance and trade pragmatism that would shadow the VOC throughout its engagement with the region.
Figures.figure.nuyts.event1: Appointed Governor of Formosa in 1627; clashed with missionary George Candidius over the limits of ecclesiastical authority on the island.
Figures.figure.nuyts.event2: Taken hostage by Japanese merchant Hamada Yahyoe in 1628; handed to Japan as a diplomatic pawn in 1632 to salvage Dutch trade relations.
Figures.figure.nuyts.title: Governor of Formosa, VOC
Figures.figure.panshengqing.bio: Pan Shengqing was a Pingpu (assimilated indigenous) official who served in Qing administrative roles including as interpreter in southern Taiwan during the Tongzhi and Guangxu periods, making him one of the most prominent Pingpu individuals in nineteenth-century Qing Taiwan's political landscape. Using his bilingual ability in Hokkien and Pingpu languages, he acted as a broker between Qing authorities and indigenous communities, facilitating administration and occasionally representing indigenous interests to officials. He was particularly active around the Hengchun Peninsula in southern Taiwan. Pan's career exemplifies the pathway available to 'cooked savages' under Qing colonialism — sinicization through education and official collaboration — while illustrating the constraints inherent in being an indigenous person serving a Han-dominated bureaucracy.
Figures.figure.panshengqing.event1: Served as Qing interpreter-official, one of most prominent Pingpu figures in governance
Figures.figure.panshengqing.event2: Used bilingual ability to broker indigenous-Han relations and protect community interests
Figures.figure.panshengqing.title: Pingpu Official and Cultural Intermediary
Figures.figure.panxianwen.bio: Pan Xianwen was an eighteenth-century Kavalan Pingpu indigenous figure who occupied the frontier role of cultural and political intermediary between Han settlers and the Kavalan communities of the Yilan plain. As Han migration began penetrating the Yilan basin during the Qianlong period, individuals like Pan who possessed knowledge of both Han and indigenous languages became essential brokers for negotiating land use and administrative compliance. Pan facilitated communications between Kavalan communities and incoming settlers as well as Qing officials, helping manage the complex ethnic frontier in northeastern Taiwan. His career exemplifies the go-between who navigated shifting ethnic boundaries of Qing Taiwan — simultaneously protecting indigenous interests and serving as a colonial collaborator.
Figures.figure.panxianwen.event1: Active during the Qianlong period as intermediary between Kavalan and Han settlers
Figures.figure.panxianwen.event2: Facilitated negotiations between Kavalan, Han settlers, and officials
Figures.figure.panxianwen.title: Kavalan-Han Cultural Intermediary
Figures.figure.pelosi.bio: Nancy Pelosi, born in 1940 in Baltimore, Maryland, to the prominent Italian-American D'Alesandro political family, served as Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives from 2007 to 2011 and again from 2019 to 2023, and is the highest-ranking U.S. official to have visited Taiwan in the modern era. The daughter of a Baltimore mayor and congressman, she entered electoral politics later in life and was first elected to the House of Representatives from San Francisco in 1987. She became the first female Speaker of the House in 2007 and has been one of the most influential and longest-serving Democratic congressional leaders in U.S. history. She is also one of the most consistently pro-Taiwan members of the U.S. Congress: she made her first protest visit to Taiwan in 1991, and during the same trip famously unfurled a banner mourning the victims of the Tiananmen massacre on Beijing's Tiananmen Square. As Speaker she opposed the granting of permanent normal trade relations to the PRC in 2000 and supported the Taiwan Travel Act signed into law in 2018, which removed remaining U.S. self-imposed limits on high-level visits to Taiwan. Her August 2022 visit to Taiwan as part of an Indo-Pacific congressional tour was the highest-level U.S. congressional visit to the island in twenty-five years, since Speaker Newt Gingrich's 1997 visit. The Biden administration unsuccessfully sought to dissuade her from the visit on national-security grounds, citing risks of provoking a PRC military response during a period of high tensions. Her visit took place over 2–3 August 2022 and included a meeting with President Tsai Ing-wen, a speech to the Legislative Yuan, and visits to human-rights sites; she described Taiwan as one of the freest democracies in the world. The PRC responded with the largest military exercises around Taiwan in modern history, conducting four days of live-fire drills in six zones encircling the island and firing ballistic missiles that overflew Taiwanese territory. The post-Pelosi exercises permanently shifted the operational baseline of PLA activity around Taiwan and were widely understood as a rehearsal for blockade and encirclement scenarios. She stepped down from the Democratic House leadership in late 2022 but remained a member of Congress, and she remains a high-profile public figure on Taiwan-related issues into her eighties. Pelosi's 2022 visit is now widely regarded as a turning point in U.S.-Taiwan-PRC relations, reshaping how successive U.S. officials weigh the symbolic value of in-person engagement against the now-elevated PRC retaliatory baseline.
Figures.figure.pelosi.event1: Visit to Taiwan triggered PRC military exercises (August 2022)
Figures.figure.pelosi.title: Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives
Figures.figure.pengmengji.bio: Peng Meng-chi, born in 1908 in Wuchang, Hubei, was the most controversial military commander of the February 28 Incident and later a trusted senior general under the Chiang father and son. He studied at the Whampoa Military Academy and pursued advanced training at the Japanese Army Artillery School, one of the few Nationalist officers with modern artillery training. He held artillery commands during the war against Japan and, after the war, was posted to Taiwan as commander of the Kaohsiung Fortress. When the February 28 Incident broke out in 1947 and clashes between officials and the public spread across the island, local Kaohsiung leaders went to the fortress to negotiate with him. He refused to compromise and on March 6 ordered his troops to attack, striking the city hall, the railway station, and the urban area with machine guns and artillery, causing heavy casualties. This made Kaohsiung one of the most brutally suppressed areas on the island and earned him the epithet "Butcher of Kaohsiung." After February 28 he faced no accountability but was instead promoted for "quelling the rebellion." His career then soared: he served successively as Taiwan garrison commander-in-chief, commander-in-chief of the army, and chief of the general staff, rose to full general, and served as envoy to Japan and Thailand. Long at the core of military-political power, he was a key pillar of the authoritarian system, dying in Taipei in 1997. Peng's life epitomizes the perpetrator's perspective in February 28, and his decisions and subsequent rise remain focal points in debates over transitional justice and historical responsibility.
Figures.figure.pengmengji.event1: Ordered the armed suppression of Kaohsiung during February 28 (1947)
Figures.figure.pengmengji.event2: Later served as garrison commander-in-chief and chief of the general staff
Figures.figure.pengmengji.title: Kaohsiung Fortress Commander & Army General
Figures.figure.pengmingmin.bio: Peng Ming-min, born in 1923 in Taichung, was a distinguished scholar of international law whose life traced the long arc of Taiwan's struggle for self-determination. A graduate of National Taiwan University who studied in Canada and France, he became the youngest professor and chair of NTU's political science department and served as an adviser to the Republic of China at the United Nations. In 1964, together with his students Hsieh Tsung-min and Wei Ting-chao, he drafted the Declaration of Formosan Self-Salvation, calling for a new constitution and a Taiwan determined by its own people. Arrested and imprisoned for the act, he was later placed under surveillance and in 1970 escaped Taiwan in disguise, beginning twenty-three years of exile in Sweden and the United States, where he became a leading voice of the overseas independence movement. He returned home in 1992 as democratization advanced, and in 1996 stood as the Democratic Progressive Party's candidate in Taiwan's first direct presidential election — his very candidacy a moving testament to how far the island had traveled. Though he did not win, his lifelong advocacy made him an enduring symbol of Taiwanese self-determination and democratic ideals.
Figures.figure.pengmingmin.event1: Co-drafted the Declaration of Formosan Self-Salvation in 1964; imprisoned, then fled into 23-year exile
Figures.figure.pengmingmin.event2: Ran as the DPP candidate in Taiwan's first direct presidential election, 1996
Figures.figure.pengmingmin.title: Scholar & First Direct-Election Candidate
Figures.figure.pickering.bio: William Alexander Pickering, born in 1840 in England, served as an officer of the Imperial Chinese Maritime Customs in Taiwan from 1863 to 1872 and became one of the most intrepid foreign travelers of the island in the nineteenth century, acquiring a command of Hokkien and several indigenous languages that enabled him to venture into regions where no Westerner had previously gone, and later documenting his experiences in the vivid memoir Pioneering in Formosa (1898). He arrived at Tamsui as a young customs officer and immediately threw himself into the study of the local language with unusual intensity, becoming fluent in Taiwanese Hokkien within months and using this fluency to move freely through communities that were wary or hostile to foreign visitors. Pickering traveled extensively along the western plains, the eastern coast, and the mountainous interior of Taiwan, visiting indigenous settlements of Atayal, Amis, and Siraya peoples, trading with local communities, and gathering detailed observations on geography, agriculture, natural resources, and social customs that he recorded in diaries and letters. He was involved in several dramatic incidents during his years in Taiwan, including an encounter with indigenous warriors in which he survived an attempted ambush, and a period when he was employed by local merchants to suppress the camphor trade disputes that frequently erupted into violent conflict between Han settlers and the mountain communities who controlled camphor-producing territories. Pickering also played a role in some of the diplomatic incidents of the period, serving as an interpreter in negotiations involving shipwreck cases and indigenous land rights, and providing firsthand testimony to British consular officials on the state of indigenous communities in the interior. He left Taiwan around 1872 and went on to a distinguished career in the Straits Settlements, eventually becoming the first Protector of Chinese in Singapore and Penang, where he applied the language skills and cross-cultural experience he had developed in Taiwan to the protection of Chinese immigrant laborers from exploitation by employers and secret societies.
