His memoir Pioneering in Formosa, published in 1898 after his retirement, compiled his Taiwan observations into a vivid narrative that remains one of the most readable and detailed firsthand accounts of the island's interior in the mid-nineteenth century, covering topics ranging from headhunting practices and camphor production to the workings of the Qing customs service and the character of the Tamsui port community. Pickering died in 1907, having lived long enough to see Taiwan pass from Qing to Japanese rule and to reflect on the dramatic changes that had transformed the island he had known in its most turbulent frontier years. His Hokkien fluency, physical courage, and genuine curiosity about the communities he encountered set him apart from most foreign officials of his era, and his writings provide a perspective on mid-nineteenth-century Taiwan — simultaneously administrative, adventurous, and ethnographic — that no other source of the period can fully replicate. Pickering is generally regarded as one of the most significant foreign witnesses to Taiwan's final decades under Qing rule, a man whose firsthand knowledge of the island's interior was unmatched among Western visitors of his time.
Figures.figure.pickering.event1: Traveled Taiwan's interior in the 1860s, reaching indigenous settlements no Westerner had previously visited and recording detailed observations on society and geography
Figures.figure.pickering.event2: Published Pioneering in Formosa (1898), one of the most detailed English firsthand accounts of mid-nineteenth-century Taiwan
Figures.figure.pickering.title: British Explorer and Customs Officer in Taiwan
Figures.figure.qianlong.bio: The Qianlong Emperor, personal name Aisin Gioro Hongli, was born in Beijing in 1711 as the fourth son of the Yongzheng Emperor and was personally selected by his grandfather the Kangxi Emperor as the dynasty's eventual heir. After Yongzheng's death in 1735, he formally ascended the throne the following year as Emperor Gaozong of the Qing. His reign of sixty years and a further three years as retired emperor amounted to roughly sixty-three years of effective rule, the longest period of personal authority of any Chinese monarch in recorded history. From the outset of his reign he pursued a policy of personal autocracy that built upon the centralized administration of his father and grandfather, expanding the role of the Grand Council and refining the balance between Manchu and Han Chinese officials. He waged the so-called Ten Great Campaigns — including expeditions against the Dzungar Khanate, the Tarim oases, the Jinchuan tribes, Burma, Annam, and Nepal, along with the suppression of the Lin Shuangwen rebellion on Taiwan and the early White Lotus uprisings in Fujian — pushing the Qing empire to its greatest territorial extent. In his governance of Taiwan he maintained the strict savage-boundary policy of his predecessors and remained extremely conservative regarding migration permits and frontier expenditure. When the Lin Shuangwen rebellion broke out in 1786, he personally ordered his favored general Fukang'an to lead a sixty-thousand-strong army across the strait to suppress it. In 1787, to honor the residents of the city of Chu-lo for their resolute defense against the rebels, he bestowed the new name Jiayi — meaning praiseworthy righteousness — on the city, a name that survives to this day. Culturally he sponsored the compilation of the Siku Quanshu, the largest officially commissioned anthology in Chinese history at over three thousand four hundred titles and nearly eighty thousand fascicles, while simultaneously pursuing more than a hundred literary inquisitions that brought thought control to its Qing-era peak. In his later years he came under the influence of the corrupt favorite Heshen, and the costs of his seven southern tours and the construction of the imperial gardens at Chengde and Yuanmingyuan drained a once-flush treasury, setting the stage for the decline of the early nineteenth century. In 1796 he formally abdicated in deference to his vow not to exceed his grandfather's sixty-one-year reign, but he continued to govern from behind the throne until his death at the age of eighty-eight in 1799. The Qianlong Emperor is generally regarded as the last symbol of the High Qing era, and his military suppression of Taiwan together with his imperial naming of Jiayi constituted the most emblematic act of the Qing transition from defensive containment to active management of the Taiwanese frontier.
Figures.figure.qianlong.event1: Imperially named Jiayi County in 1787 after the suppression of the Lin Shuangwen rebellion
Figures.figure.qianlong.title: Sixth Emperor of the Qing Dynasty
Figures.figure.qiufengjia.bio: Qiu Fengjia, born in 1864 into a Hakka family in Tongluo, Miaoli, and later resettled in Taichung, was a late-Qing scholar-official, poet, and educator who became a central figure of the 1895 Taiwanese resistance to Japan. He earned the highest imperial examination degree in 1889 and was appointed a junior compiler at the Hanlin Academy but soon returned to Taiwan, citing filial duty, where he founded schools to educate local youth. Influenced by reformist thinkers such as Liang Qichao, he advocated self-strengthening on the island. When news of the Qing defeat in the First Sino-Japanese War and the cession of Taiwan reached him in 1895, he joined Tang Jingsong and other gentry in calling for the establishment of the so-called Republic of Formosa, personally drafting its proclamations. He was appointed Commander of the Righteous Army and Inspector-General of the militia and exhausted his personal fortune raising volunteer units in Taichung, Hsinchu, and other parts of central Taiwan. After Japanese forces broke the northern defenses and pushed south, he withdrew with his troops into the Hsinchu–Miaoli hills before defeat and exhaustion forced him to flee across the strait to Guangdong. In retirement at his ancestral home in Zhenping (modern Jiaoling), Guangdong, he wrote the famous couplet — 'The minister has power to cede land; the loyal subject lacks strength to redeem heaven' — which became one of the most enduring poetic expressions of the loss of Taiwan. He later joined late-Qing educational reform efforts, founded modern schools, and served as Vice-Speaker of the Guangdong Provincial Assembly. After the 1911 Revolution he supported the new republic and was appointed Education Commissioner of the Guangdong military government. He died in 1912 at the age of forty-eight from overwork and illness. Qiu is widely commemorated on both sides of the Taiwan Strait as a leading literati voice of the 1895 resistance and a transitional figure linking late-Qing reform to early Republican-era education and politics.
Figures.figure.qiufengjia.event1: 1895 Co-founded the Republic of Formosa and raised volunteer armies
Figures.figure.qiufengjia.event2: 1895 Withdrew to Guangdong after the collapse of resistance
Figures.figure.qiufengjia.title: Hakka Gentry and Volunteer Army Leader
Figures.figure.qiulianggong.bio: Qiu Lianggong was a Qing naval commander from Kinmen who became the hero of the final campaign against Cai Qian, Taiwan's most formidable pirate-rebel of the Jiaqing period. After years of failed attempts to suppress Cai Qian's fleet, Qiu led a decisive naval engagement in waters northeast of Taiwan in 1809, routing the pirate forces and killing Cai Qian himself. The victory ended more than a decade of disruption to Taiwan Strait commerce and coastal security. Qiu was ennobled for his achievement and rose to command the Fujian Land Forces. Back in his native Kinmen, his mother's memorial arch still stands as a monument combining family piety and military glory.
Figures.figure.qiulianggong.event1: Defeated and killed Cai Qian in naval battle in 1809, ending years of piracy
Figures.figure.qiulianggong.event2: Ennobled and rose to command Fujian Land Forces
Figures.figure.qiulianggong.title: Naval Commander Who Defeated Cai Qian
Figures.figure.quataong.bio: Camachat Aslamie was the paramount chief of the Kingdom of Middag in central Taiwan during the mid-seventeenth century; his dates of birth and death are not recorded, and the sources preserve Aslamie as a personal name in the Babuza language and Camachat as the lineage and political title of his ruling house. The Kingdom of Middag was not a kingdom in the Chinese imperial sense but a cross-ethnic political confederation of more than a dozen Babuza, Babusaga, Hoanya, and Pazeh villages spread across what are today the Taichung, Changhua, and Nantou plains. In Dutch sources the confederation was referred to as Middag or as the land of Quataong, and it remained throughout the Dutch period the principal indigenous power in central Taiwan that the VOC was never able to fully incorporate into its village-leasing system. Inheriting the title of King of Dadu around the 1640s, he governed the populous settlements from the basin of the Dadu and Dadu rivers north to the Dajia and south to the Zhuoshui. In his external relations he negotiated commerce with Dutch officials when convenient and mobilized the confederate villages by force when required to defend his people's hunting grounds and farmlands. Between 1644 and 1645 the VOC dispatched punitive expeditions to Sarcam and the Dadu region, after which he accepted the symbolic transfer of a staff of office at the annual landdag assembly held by the Dutch governor. He nominally acknowledged VOC suzerainty but in practice his autonomous authority over the confederation remained largely intact. After Koxinga's invasion of Taiwan and the Dutch withdrawal in 1661, his confederation faced a new adversary in the form of a Han Chinese settler regime whose project was no longer commercial colonization but systematic military colonization of the land. The Zheng policy of garrison-farming pushed tens of thousands of soldier-settlers into central Taiwan and provoked repeated clashes with confederate villages over land seizures and grain levies at Sarcam, Goema, and Taikia. In the 1670s the Zheng general Liu Guoxuan, on orders from Zheng Jing, led a campaign of suppression in central Taiwan in which the village of Sarcam was destroyed in a near-total massacre that broke the military strength of the Kingdom of Middag. Whether he was still in power during these events, and when he died, is not recorded in Dutch, Zheng, or later sources; only the rapid disintegration of the confederation's political structure during the 1680s and its complete collapse in the early Qing period is documented. Camachat Aslamie is generally remembered as one of the very few indigenous confederation leaders in early Taiwanese history capable of simultaneously holding off both European colonial power and Han Chinese settler-state expansion, and as a representative figure of how the lowland indigenous peoples of central Taiwan passed from relative autonomy into historical eclipse under the dual pressure of successive foreign regimes.
Figures.figure.quataong.event1: Led the Kingdom of Middag in resistance to both VOC and Zheng territorial expansion
Figures.figure.quataong.title: Paramount Chief of the Kingdom of Middag
Figures.figure.ritchie.bio: Hugh Ritchie was a Scottish Presbyterian missionary who arrived in Taiwan in 1867 and spent over a decade building up the Church of Christ in Taiwan in the southern regions. Working alongside James Maxwell and other early missionaries, Ritchie established congregations across southern Taiwan and trained indigenous evangelists. He was a dedicated language learner who mastered Taiwanese Southern Min and contributed to Bible translation in romanized Amoy script, supporting mother-tongue evangelism that became a hallmark of the Presbyterian mission. Ritchie and his wife also worked with Pingpu indigenous communities in the Tainan area. He died in 1879 at only 39, but his decade of foundational work helped establish the organizational and linguistic infrastructure on which the Presbyterian Church in Taiwan would grow.
Figures.figure.ritchie.event1: Arrived 1867, established churches and trained local evangelists across southern Taiwan
Figures.figure.ritchie.event2: Contributed to Amoy-script Bible translation, advancing mother-tongue evangelism
Figures.figure.ritchie.title: Presbyterian Missionary
Figures.figure.sakumasamata.bio: Sakuma Samata was born in 1844 in the Choshu domain and rose through the Imperial Japanese Army as a career soldier who had fought in Japan's earliest overseas expedition to Taiwan back in 1874. In 1906 he was appointed the fifth Governor-General of Taiwan, an office he would hold for nine years — longer than any other. Where his predecessors had concentrated on the lowlands, Sakuma set his sights on the mountains and the Indigenous peoples who still lived beyond colonial control. In 1910 he launched the Five-Year Plan to Subjugate the Aborigines, driving armed guard-lines deep into the highlands to seize the camphor forests. Its climax was the Taroko War of 1914, in which the seventy-year-old governor personally led a force of over twenty thousand against the Truku people. He was gravely injured in the campaign, resigned the following year, and died in 1915. Sakuma is remembered as the iron-fisted architect of the colonial state's conquest of the mountains — a legacy of roads and administration built atop immense Indigenous suffering.
Figures.figure.sakumasamata.event1: Launched the Five-Year Plan to Subjugate the Aborigines (1910)
Figures.figure.sakumasamata.title: Fifth Governor-General of Taiwan
Figures.figure.sayun.bio: Sayun, in full Sayun Hayung (1921–1938), was an Atayal girl from the South'ao area of Yilan. In 1938 the Japanese teacher stationed there, Tabei Masaki, was called up for military service amid wartime mobilization, and Sayun joined other villagers in helping to carry his luggage and see him off down the mountain. On the way the weather suddenly turned and a storm struck; while fording a stream she lost her footing, fell into the water and disappeared, only seventeen years old. This was in itself an ordinary mountain accident, yet in the atmosphere of wartime imperialization and mobilization propaganda the colonial authorities greatly embellished the event, casting her as a model 'patriotic maiden' who had devoted herself to the nation and helped a teacher off to war. In 1941 Governor-General Hasegawa Kiyoshi presented a bronze bell inscribed with the words 'Bell of the patriotic maiden Sayun' in her honour, known as the 'Bell of Sayun.' Her story was thereafter adapted into songs and paintings and made into the film The Bell of Sayun, a Man'ei–Shochiku co-production starring the popular actress Li Xianglan, becoming a propaganda model to rouse indigenous people and Taiwanese to loyalty and devoted service to Japan in wartime. Sayun's brief life, an innocent accident, was swept into the flood of colonial propaganda, and it stands as an important case for understanding how late-colonial imperialization and wartime mobilization manipulated personal stories.
Figures.figure.sayun.event1: 1938 Carried luggage for a teacher going to war and was lost in a stream
Figures.figure.sayun.event2: 1941 The Governor-General's Office presented the 'Bell of Sayun,' promoting a patriotic image
Figures.figure.sayun.title: The Girl Behind the 'Bell of Sayun'
Figures.figure.shenbaozhen.bio: Shen Baozhen, born in 1820 in Fuzhou, Fujian, was a senior Qing official and naval modernizer whose 1874–1875 mission as Imperial Commissioner to Taiwan inaugurated the late-Qing transformation of the island. He passed the metropolitan examination in 1847 and rose through the bureaucracy with a reputation for incorruptibility and administrative skill, serving in Jiangxi as a major provincial governor during the Taiping Civil War. He married a daughter of the famed anti-opium statesman Lin Zexu, a family connection that placed him at the heart of the reformist gentry network associated with the Self-Strengthening Movement. From 1867 he served for nearly a decade as the founding head of the Fuzhou Navy Yard at Mawei, building the Qing's first modern shipyard and naval academy and producing the early generation of Chinese steam warships. The 1874 Japanese punitive expedition against the Paiwan villages of Mudan, in southern Taiwan, prompted the Qing court to send him as Imperial Commissioner with full authority over military and civil affairs. Arriving at Tainan in June 1874, he combined firm diplomatic posture with battlefield buildup, eventually persuading Japan to withdraw under a Beijing-mediated settlement that October. He launched the long-planned Open the Mountains, Pacify the Indigenes (開山撫番) campaign, cutting three trans-island military roads — northern, central, and southern — across the central range to integrate indigenous territories with the Qing administrative system. He lifted the centuries-old restriction on family migration from the mainland, abolished the ban on settler-indigenous intermarriage, and authorized large-scale Han settlement in formerly off-limits regions. He reorganized Taiwan's administrative geography, creating Taipei Prefecture, Beinan and Puli sub-prefectures, and elevating the status of eastern and inland districts. He commissioned the construction of the Eternal Golden Castle (億載金城) modern artillery fort at Anping to anchor coastal defense, and modernized the harbors at Anping and Tamsui. He returned to the mainland in mid-1875 to take up senior posts as Governor-General of Liang-Jiang and continued to oversee naval modernization until his death from illness in 1879. Shen's brief but intensive Taiwan mission marked the decisive shift in Qing frontier policy and laid the groundwork for the elevation of Taiwan to provincial status in 1885 under the reformist program of his successor Liu Mingchuan.
Figures.figure.shenbaozhen.event1: Launched the 'open the mountains, pacify the aborigines' (開山撫番) policy
Figures.figure.shenbaozhen.event2: Lifted the migration and family ban; reorganized Taiwan's administrative divisions
Figures.figure.shenbaozhen.title: Imperial Commissioner
Figures.figure.shihmingteh.bio: Shih Ming-teh, born in 1941 in Kaohsiung to an enlightenment-minded medical family, spent twenty-five and a half years as a political prisoner under the KMT regime — the longest term served by any prominent tangwai dissident — and remained a central, often divisive figure in Taiwanese politics until his death in 2024. He attended the ROC Military Academy as a teenager but was arrested in 1962 for organizing a secret independence-minded cell within the army and was sentenced to fifteen years for sedition under the martial-law statutes. Released in 1977, he immediately re-engaged with the tangwai movement and became a leading organizer of Formosa Magazine, advocating an open, non-violent, mass-mobilization strategy against the KMT. He was the principal field organizer of the Human Rights Day demonstration in Kaohsiung on 10 December 1979 that became known as the Kaohsiung Incident, and was the most senior defendant condemned to life imprisonment in the ensuing military trial. He embarked on multiple hunger strikes during this second imprisonment and reportedly went on his longest at over four years, becoming an international cause for groups such as Amnesty International. Released in 1990 under Lee Teng-hui's amnesty, he served three terms in the Legislative Yuan, was elected DPP chairman from 1993 to 1996, and was widely seen as one of the party's principal national-stature figures. He resigned from the DPP in 2000 after disagreements over party direction, advocating cross-strait Great Reconciliation (大和解) rather than confrontation and increasingly criticizing what he viewed as the new democratic establishment's hypocrisy. In 2006 he founded and led the Million Voices Against Corruption Red Shirt movement, a months-long mass protest in Taipei calling for the resignation of President Chen Shui-bian over corruption scandals. His later years were marked by repeated unsuccessful runs for the presidency, advocacy for constitutional reform, and a steady stream of provocative interventions across the political spectrum. He maintained a public position that Taiwan's identity and dignity required confronting both the KMT's authoritarian inheritance and the DPP's electoral compromises, and refused political party affiliation in his last decade. He died of cancer in Taipei in January 2024 at the age of 82. Shih is widely regarded as one of the most prominent embodiments of Taiwan's democracy struggle and one of its most provocative public consciences, his combination of long imprisonment, principled non-violence, and willingness to break with allies making him one of the most singular figures of the post-war era.
Figures.figure.shihmingteh.event1: Chief organizer of the 1979 Kaohsiung Incident
Figures.figure.shihmingteh.event2: Served as DPP chairman; led the 2006 Red Shirt anti-corruption movement
Figures.figure.shihmingteh.title: Democracy Movement Leader
Figures.figure.shilang.bio: Shi Lang, born in 1621 in Jinjiang, Quanzhou, was the Qing admiral whose 1683 victory at Penghu ended the Kingdom of Tungning and incorporated Taiwan into a Chinese imperial polity for the first time. He came from a Fujianese maritime family and entered service under Zheng Zhilong, accompanying that branch of the Zheng house into Koxinga's resistance after 1646. He rose rapidly under Koxinga as a senior naval commander, but the two men quarreled bitterly in 1651–1652, and after Shi Lang protected a fugitive officer Koxinga had ordered killed, Koxinga retaliated by executing Shi's father, brother, and son. Shi Lang escaped by sea to Qing-controlled territory and submitted to the new dynasty, carrying with him both detailed knowledge of Zheng naval doctrine and an irreparable personal feud. Over the next thirty years he served the Qing in successive naval commands, including two earlier expeditions against Taiwan in 1664 and 1665 that were aborted by storms. Court factions opposed to active maritime engagement repeatedly sidelined him; he spent long years at the inner court arguing for a decisive campaign against the surviving Zheng base. In 1681, after the Tungning succession crisis, the Kangxi Emperor returned him to the southeastern coast as Fujian Naval Commander with a renewed mandate to invade. After two years of preparation, he attacked the Tungning fleet at Penghu in late June 1683, defeating the kingdom's senior commander Liu Guoxuan in three engagements over roughly a week. Upon Tungning's surrender he conspicuously did not exact private vengeance, visiting the shrine of Koxinga to declare publicly that the Qing campaign had been a matter of state rather than personal blood debt. He argued forcefully against the Kangxi court's initial inclination to abandon Taiwan after victory, contending in a famous memorial that the island's defense was essential to securing Fujian and the maritime southeast. His advocacy prevailed: Taiwan was retained as a prefecture under Fujian Province, and Shi Lang was rewarded with the hereditary title of Marquis of Jinghai (靖海侯) and large land grants on the island. He died in 1696, remaining a divisive figure in Taiwanese memory ever since — the Qing hero who shaped Taiwan's two-century imperial chapter, but also the apostate who turned his weapons against the house that had once raised him.
Figures.figure.shilang.event1: Victory at the Battle of Penghu, leading to Qing annexation of Taiwan (1683)
Figures.figure.shilang.title: Qing Admiral
Figures.figure.shishibang.bio: Shi Shi-bang was born in 1671 into a well-to-do family with roots in Jinjiang, Fujian, and became one of the great landowning developers of early Qing Taiwan. Holding minor official rank, he acquired extensive land rights on the Changhua plain — fertile ground that suffered from a chronic want of water. Resolving to unlock its potential, he financed and organised one of the most ambitious irrigation works the island had yet seen: a great canal to divert the powerful Zhuoshui River across the plain. Begun in 1709, the project was beset by years of difficulty in taming the river at its intake, and tradition holds that a mysterious old man remembered only as Mr. Lin appeared to teach the builders the technique of the woven-bamboo weir that finally succeeded, then departed without reward. Completed around 1719, the canal watered eight districts — the 'eight bao' that gave it its name — and transformed Changhua into one of Taiwan's richest granaries, drawing waves of settlers to its newly productive fields. Shi Shi-bang died in 1743. He is remembered as the patron and builder of the Babao Canal, a work of private enterprise and collective labour whose waters still cross the Changhua plain nearly three centuries later.
Figures.figure.shishibang.event1: Financed and built the Babao Canal on the Changhua plain
Figures.figure.shishibang.event2: Turned Changhua into one of Taiwan's richest granaries
Figures.figure.shishibang.title: Builder of the Babao Canal
Figures.figure.shishijie.bio: Shi Shijie was one of the last Taiwanese-born individuals to achieve the jinshi degree under the Qing imperial examination system, passing in 1883. When Taiwan was ceded to Japan in 1895, Shi chose to remain rather than relocate to the mainland as many officials did. In the early Japanese colonial period he became a leading voice among the remnant-subject (yimin) literati, writing classical poetry and prose that expressed grief over Taiwan's lost sovereignty and resistance to cultural assimilation. He was active in poetry societies across Taiwan, which served as refuges for classical Chinese literary culture under Japanese rule. His work bridges the late Qing literary tradition and early colonial-period resistance culture, a testimony to Taiwan's classical scholars maintaining cultural identity in the face of political rupture.
Figures.figure.shishijie.event1: Passed the jinshi examination in 1883, one of Taiwan's last native imperial graduates
Figures.figure.shishijie.event2: Remained in Taiwan after 1895, writing as a yimin poet in the early colonial period
Figures.figure.shishijie.title: One of Taiwan's Last Imperial Jinshi · Remnant Poet
Figures.figure.sonck.bio: Martinus Sonck, born in 1590 in the Dutch Republic, was a Dutch East India Company official who became the first formal Governor of Dutch Formosa during the brief year between the VOC's withdrawal from Penghu and his own death in office. He studied law at the University of Leiden and entered VOC service as one of a small generation of university-trained administrators who would shape the company's expansion into East Asia in the early seventeenth century. He rose through the VOC's Batavia administration and became a member of the Council of the Indies, the central executive body of the company's Asian empire. The VOC had seized the Penghu Islands in 1622 and built a fortress at Makung in defiance of Ming claims, provoking a prolonged military standoff with Fujian provincial authorities and the imperial court at Beijing. He was sent north in 1624 with explicit authority to negotiate an end to the standoff, arriving at Penghu in August to face a substantial Ming fleet and ground force commanded by the Fujian regional commander. Through a tense series of negotiations and diplomatic gestures he agreed in late August 1624 to evacuate Penghu in exchange for Ming acquiescence to a Dutch settlement on Taiwan, which was nominally outside Ming jurisdiction. He directed the relocation of the garrison and stores from Makung to Tayouan, a sandy island flanking the harbor of present-day Anping in Tainan, and initiated the construction of Fort Zeelandia on that site in October 1624. He laid the basis for an integrated VOC colonial administration on Formosa, including diplomatic outreach to the Siraya villages of the surrounding mainland and the regulation of Hokkien Chinese merchants and settlers around the new fort. He established the early framework for the VOC's relations with the indigenous polities of the southwest Taiwan plain, encouraging missionary contacts and beginning the exchange of gifts and acknowledgments that would later form the basis of the colonial Landdag assemblies. He died of illness in office in 1625, less than a year after the founding of the new colony, before the rudimentary fortifications at Tayouan had been fully completed. He was succeeded by a series of governors who would consolidate Fort Zeelandia, build Fort Provintia at modern Tainan, and expand Dutch control over much of the southwestern coastal plain over the next four decades. Sonck is remembered as the diplomat who negotiated the founding act of Dutch Taiwan, transforming a confrontation with the Ming empire into a permanent VOC presence that would shape the southwestern lowlands of the island for two generations.
Figures.figure.sonck.event1: Established Fort Zeelandia at Tayouan (1624), inaugurating VOC rule over Taiwan
Figures.figure.sonck.title: First VOC Governor of Formosa
Figures.figure.soongchuyu.bio: James Soong Chu-yu, born in 1942 in Xiangtan, Hunan, was brought to Taiwan as a young child with his KMT-officer father and rose through the party's elite as one of the most capable mainlander administrators of his generation. He earned a master's degree at the Catholic University of America and a doctorate from Georgetown University before returning to Taiwan to serve as English-language secretary to President Chiang Ching-kuo from 1974. He directed the Government Information Office during the politically critical years of 1979–1984, controlling media policy through the Kaohsiung Incident, the lead-up to the lifting of martial law, and the Lin Family Massacre. He served as Secretary-General of the KMT from 1989 to 1993, helping Lee Teng-hui consolidate his hold over the party during the most delicate transitional years. Appointed Governor of Taiwan Province in 1993, he won the office in the first direct provincial election in 1994 with 56 percent of the vote, building an effective province-wide patronage and constituency network through frequent grassroots travel. The 1998 constitutional freeze of the provincial government — engineered with Lee Teng-hui's support to consolidate administrative authority at the central level — ended his post and ruptured his relationship with Lee. He ran for the presidency in 2000 as an independent after the KMT nominated Lien Chan, finishing a close second with 36.84 percent to Chen Shui-bian's 39.3 percent and ahead of the official KMT nominee. He founded the People First Party (親民黨) shortly after the election, drawing many former KMT voters and legislators and establishing himself as the head of a third force on the pan-Blue side of Taiwanese politics. He ran as Lien Chan's vice-presidential candidate in 2004, narrowly losing to the re-elected Chen Shui-bian and Annette Lu, and made unsuccessful presidential bids again in 2012, 2016, and 2020. He led a People First Party delegation to mainland China in 2005, a controversial trip that paralleled Lien Chan's earlier KMT visit and brought him into direct dialogue with the CCP leadership. He served as a special envoy to APEC summits under both the Ma Ying-jeou and Tsai Ing-wen administrations, an unusual cross-party diplomatic role reflecting his broad international network. Soong remains the most enduring example of an elite mainlander politician who shaped Taiwan's transition both as an authoritarian-era functionary and as a competitive electoral figure, his career a barometer of how the post-1990 KMT-PFP split reconfigured pan-Blue politics.
Figures.figure.soongchuyu.event1: Independent presidential candidacy split the pan-Blue vote (2000)
Figures.figure.soongchuyu.title: Governor of Taiwan Province & PFP Chairman
Figures.figure.stanshih.bio: Stan Shih, born in 1944 in Lukang, Changhua, was one of the founders of Taiwan's information-technology industry and a key advocate of branding among ethnic-Chinese enterprises. Having lost his father in early childhood and been raised by his mother, he studied electronic engineering at National Chiao Tung University, earning a master's degree and a solid technical foundation. In 1976 he co-founded Acer with partners, entering the then-emerging fields of microprocessors and personal computers. He led Acer from contract manufacturing toward its own brand, one of the few entrepreneurs to challenge major international firms and bring a Taiwanese brand to the global market. He formulated the famous "Smiling Curve" theory, holding that industrial value concentrates at the two ends of research and branding rather than in the middle of manufacturing, profoundly shaping the strategic thinking of Taiwan's industry. He argued for raising added value through branding and innovation and drove the restructuring and internationalization of enterprises. In his later years he championed a "kingly way" management philosophy stressing value creation and balanced interests, and actively engaged in cultural-creative industries and philanthropy. He also long took part in industrial policy and talent cultivation, attentive to Taiwan's long-term competitiveness. Shih is seen as a pivotal force in Taiwan's technology industry moving from contract manufacturing toward branding, his management theory and practice long an important reference for Taiwan's industrial upgrading.
Figures.figure.stanshih.event1: Founded Acer, pioneering Taiwanese IT branding (1976)
Figures.figure.stanshih.event2: Formulated the "Smiling Curve" theory of industrial value
Figures.figure.stanshih.title: Founder of Acer & Branding Theorist
Figures.figure.steere.bio: Joseph Beal Steere was an American naturalist from the University of Michigan who conducted a major fieldwork expedition across Taiwan from 1873 to 1874, making him one of the most significant American scientific visitors to the island before the Japanese period. Over nearly a year he collected thousands of specimens of animals, birds, insects, and plants, many previously unknown to Western science. He also spent extensive time with various indigenous communities — Paiwan, Rukai, Amis, and others — documenting their material culture and languages. His collections, housed at the University of Michigan, remain research resources today. Steere's published accounts provided English-language readers with a vivid picture of late Qing Taiwan, and his ethnographic observations are still cited by researchers of nineteenth-century Taiwanese indigenous studies. He lived to the extraordinary age of 97.
Figures.figure.steere.event1: Conducted year-long natural history fieldwork in Taiwan 1873–74
Figures.figure.steere.event2: Specimens and reports are major primary sources for 19th-century Taiwan natural history
Figures.figure.steere.title: American Naturalist · Taiwan Explorer
Figures.figure.suniyuwu.bio: Suniuo (1919–1979), an Amis man from Taitung, known by the Japanese name 'Nakamura Teruo' and the postwar Chinese name 'Li Kuang-hui,' is the most representative symbol of the tragic fate of Taiwanese soldiers in the Japanese army. During the Second World War, swept up in the tide of imperialization and wartime mobilization, he was enrolled in the Japanese army's 'Takasago Volunteer Units' and in 1943 was sent to fight on the island of Morotai in the Indonesian South Seas. When Japan was defeated and the war ended in 1945 he became separated from his unit and never received word of the surrender, and so he fled alone deep into the jungle to survive. There he lived off the land in the most primitive way, building a crude shelter, planting crops and setting traps to hunt, passing nearly thirty years in solitude, wholly unaware that the war had long since ended and the world had been turned upside down. Only in 1974 was he discovered and recovered in Indonesia, stunning the world and becoming, after the Japanese soldiers Yokoi Shoichi and Onoda Hiroo, another legend of a 'holdout soldier.' When he returned to Taiwan his homeland, family and the whole of society had utterly changed, and even his language and sense of identity faced a vast rupture—he was neither simply Japanese nor able to reintegrate into postwar Taiwan. Only four years after returning, he died of illness in 1979. The life of Suniuo distils the collective tragedy of the Taiwanese, mobilized, forgotten and cast adrift by the tides of history in the crevice between colonialism and war.
Figures.figure.suniyuwu.event1: 1943 Enrolled in the Takasago Volunteer Units and sent to fight in the South Seas
Figures.figure.suniyuwu.event2: 1974 Found in the Indonesian jungle, ending nearly thirty years in hiding
Figures.figure.suniyuwu.title: The Last Taiwanese Japanese Soldier to Return
Figures.figure.sunliren.bio: Sun Li-jen, born in 1900 in Lujiang, Anhui, was a decorated World War II general who was nonetheless kept under house arrest for decades after the war — a deeply controversial figure. He graduated from Tsinghua College before studying in the United States, first in civil engineering and then at the Virginia Military Institute, making him one of the few Chinese generals with a Western education. During the war against Japan he led newly formed units in major battles such as the Battle of Shanghai, known for strict discipline and flexible tactics. In 1942 he led troops on the Burma expedition, and at the Battle of Yenangyaung he drove back Japanese forces and rescued encircled British troops, winning international acclaim. In the later war years he commanded the New First Army in northern Burma, repeatedly distinguishing himself and being hailed as one of China's finest field commanders. Toward the end of the Chinese Civil War he came to Taiwan with the government, charged with retraining the army, establishing a training base at Fengshan and serving successively as commander-in-chief of the army and chief aide to the president. Yet his close ties to the Americans and his prestige within the military gradually made him an object of the authorities' suspicion. In 1955 the "Sun Li-jen Case" erupted, in which he was accused of involvement in a mutiny plot by his subordinates and was dismissed and investigated. He was thereafter kept under house arrest at his Taichung residence, cut off from the outside world for thirty-three years, until his freedom was restored only in 1988. He died in Taichung in 1990, having maintained his innocence to the end. Sun's fate is seen as a classic case of military purges and leadership suspicion during the authoritarian era, and both his achievements and his injustice remain focal points in the study of modern Taiwanese history.
Figures.figure.sunliren.event1: Placed under house arrest for over three decades in the "Sun Li-jen Case" (1955–1988)
Figures.figure.sunliren.event2: Relief of Yenangyaung on the Burma front in WWII
Figures.figure.sunliren.title: Army General
Figures.figure.sunyuanheng.bio: Sun Yuanheng was a Qing official and poet from Anhui who served as Taiwan Sea-Defense Sub-Prefect around 1706, stationed in the Tainan area. He compiled his verse and prose observations into the Chikan Ji (Chikan Collection), one of the earliest and most literarily accomplished Chinese-language works composed on Taiwan. The collection's poems describe the tropical climate, Siraya indigenous customs, the perilous sea crossing, and the rough life of Han frontier settlers, blending literary artistry with historical documentation. Sun Yuanheng's double identity as official and poet positioned him as an early voice in Taiwan's distinct literary tradition, offering a cultured mainland perspective on the alien frontier that he recorded with care.
Figures.figure.sunyuanheng.event1: Served as Taiwan Sea-Defense Sub-Prefect around 1706
Figures.figure.sunyuanheng.event2: Compiled Chikan Ji, landmark early work of Taiwan Chinese literature
Figures.figure.sunyuanheng.title: Poet-Official · Author of Chikan Ji
Figures.figure.swinhoe.bio: Robert Swinhoe, born in 1836 in Calcutta to a British family, served as British vice-consul and then consul in Taiwan from 1861 to 1866 and conducted during those years the most systematic natural history survey the island had ever received, naming and describing over a hundred new species of birds, mammals, and reptiles and establishing Taiwan's place in the global scientific record of the natural world. He had developed his interest in natural history during earlier postings in Hong Kong and Amoy and brought to Taiwan a rigorous scientific method, collecting specimens, drawing detailed illustrations, and dispatching them to the Zoological Society of London, where his descriptions were formally described and published in the Society's Proceedings throughout the 1860s. Among the species Swinhoe named and described from Taiwan were the Taiwan blue magpie (臺灣藍鵲, Urocissa caerulea), now one of the most beloved national symbols of the island; the Mikado pheasant (帝雉, Syrmaticus mikado), which was later depicted on Taiwan's thousand-dollar banknote; Swinhoe's pheasant (藍腹鷴, Lophura swinhoii), named in his honor by later taxonomists; and dozens of other birds, along with mammals including the Formosan rock macaque, the Formosan serow, and several bat species unique to the island. Swinhoe also collected ethnographic information on the indigenous peoples of Taiwan, producing some of the earliest systematic accounts in any Western language of Siraya, Pazeh, and other Pingpu groups as well as highland Atayal communities, and he documented the physical geography of the island, including the routes through the central mountain range, with a precision that no previous Western observer had achieved. His consular duties required him to manage the complex relations between British merchants, Qing officials, and local communities in the treaty ports of Tamsui and Takao, which he handled with diplomatic skill while continuing his scientific observations in every spare moment. He also made important observations on the island's agriculture, natural resources, and the state of indigenous land rights, which he communicated to both scientific and governmental audiences in London. Swinhoe left Taiwan in 1866 due to deteriorating health and spent the remainder of his career at consular posts in Amoy and Ningbo, continuing to publish on Chinese and Taiwanese fauna and contributing to the broader European scientific understanding of East Asian biodiversity. He was elected a fellow of the Royal Society in 1876 for his contributions to natural history, one of the highest scientific honors of the Victorian era, but died in 1877 at the age of forty before he could fully exploit the recognition his work had earned. His Taiwan specimens, held in the collections of the Natural History Museum in London and the Zoological Society, continue to serve as type specimens for the species he described, meaning that his collections remain scientifically authoritative documents one hundred and fifty years after they were made. Robert Swinhoe is widely regarded as the founding figure of Taiwanese ornithology and zoology — the man who first systematically documented the island's extraordinary biodiversity and placed it within the framework of global natural science.
Figures.figure.swinhoe.event1: Named and described over one hundred new species during his Taiwan posting (1861–66), including the Taiwan blue magpie and Mikado pheasant
Figures.figure.swinhoe.event2: Elected Fellow of the Royal Society (1876) for his contributions to natural history, cementing Taiwan's place in global scientific literature
Figures.figure.swinhoe.title: British Consul and Naturalist
Figures.figure.tadomona.bio: Tado Mona (1901–1930) was the eldest son of Mona Rudao, the chief of the Mahebu community of the Seediq people, and one of the principal warriors of the Wushe (Musha) Incident of 1930. Growing up under the tightening control of the Japanese colonial 'savage-管理' policy, he witnessed the forced labor, humiliations, and disruption of traditional life that fueled deep resentment among the Seediq. When the uprising broke out on 27 October 1930 during a school athletic meet at Wushe, Tado Mona, as a warrior in his prime, became a leading figure on the battlefield, helping to coordinate the attack and the subsequent resistance. As the Japanese mobilized overwhelming military force, including artillery, aircraft, and ultimately poison gas, against the rebel communities, Tado Mona led fighters in a desperate defense, withdrawing to the cliffs and caves around Mahebu to wage guerrilla resistance in the mountains. Knowing that defeat and capture were inevitable and that surrender would bring dishonor, many Seediq warriors and their families chose death over submission; numerous women hanged themselves so that the men could fight without the burden of protecting them. In the end, with resistance crushed, Tado Mona himself died in the mountains, hanging himself rather than surrender. He is remembered as a representative warrior of the Seediq armed resistance and one of the tragic central figures of the Wushe Incident, embodying both the courage and the catastrophic cost of the uprising against colonial rule.
Figures.figure.tadomona.event1: 1930 Joined the Wushe Uprising as a leading warrior
Figures.figure.tadomona.event2: 1930 Led guerrilla resistance in the mountains around Mahebu
Figures.figure.tadomona.event3: 1930 Faced overwhelming Japanese force, including poison gas
Figures.figure.tadomona.event4: 1930 Hanged himself in the mountains rather than surrender
Figures.figure.tadomona.title: Lead Warrior of the Mahebu Community
Figures.figure.tangdezhang.bio: Tang Te-chang, born in 1907 in Tainan to a Japanese police-officer father and a Taiwanese mother, carried the distinctive background of mixed Japanese-Taiwanese heritage. He served for a time as a policeman before resolving to study law, going to Japan where he passed both the judicial and administrative divisions of the notoriously difficult higher civil-service examination, a mark of exceptional ability. Returning to Taiwan, he practiced as a lawyer in Tainan, known for his integrity, outspokenness, and defense of the vulnerable, one of the few Taiwanese legal professionals in the south at the time. After World War II he actively engaged in local public affairs, concerned with post-war order and the rights of the Taiwanese. When the February 28 Incident broke out in 1947, a settlement committee was formed in the Tainan area and he was chosen as a leading member, mediating and seeking to maintain order. As Nationalist troops launched their armed crackdown, he stepped forward to take responsibility and tried to shield the youths and students who had joined the protests. He was arrested and severely tortured, yet steadfastly refused to hand over the students' names, bearing the consequences alone. In March 1947 he was publicly executed at Tainan's Minsheng Green Park (today's Tang Te-chang Memorial Park), reportedly calm to the end and refusing to kneel. His sacrifice embodied a jurist's resolve to defend justice and human rights, and he has long been mourned locally. Tainan today observes a memorial day in his honor and renamed the execution-site park after him. Tang is remembered as a representative of grassroots professionals who stood up to protect the people during February 28, a deeply symbolic figure in Taiwan's memory of human rights.
Figures.figure.tangdezhang.event1: Died protecting students during the February 28 Incident (1947)
Figures.figure.tangdezhang.event2: Passed both the judicial and administrative higher civil-service exams in Japan
Figures.figure.tangdezhang.title: Lawyer & Martyr of the 228 Incident
Figures.figure.tangjingsong.bio: Tang Jingsong, born in 1841 in Guanyang, Guangxi, was a late-Qing Chinese scholar-official who served as the last governor of Taiwan under Qing rule. He passed the highest imperial examination in 1865 and entered the Hanlin Academy as a junior compiler, building his early career on classical scholarship. During the Sino-French War he volunteered for service in Vietnam, where he persuaded the Black Flag Army under Liu Yongfu to fight alongside Qing forces against the French in Tonkin, earning rapid promotion. He was appointed Provincial Administration Commissioner of Taiwan in 1891 and acting Governor of Taiwan Province in 1894, becoming the final Qing civil official to head the island. After the Qing defeat in the First Sino-Japanese War in 1895 the Treaty of Shimonoseki ceded Taiwan to Japan, and Taiwanese gentry proclaimed the so-called Republic of Formosa, electing Tang its first President under the reign title Yongqing in a bid to invite foreign intervention. The new regime sought diplomatic recognition and military support from European powers — particularly Britain and France — but received no substantive backing and remained internationally unrecognized. When the Japanese Imperial Guards Division landed at Aodi and the northern defenses collapsed, Tang abandoned his post on the eve of the fall of Taipei and fled by German merchant steamer from Tamsui to Xiamen. His departure precipitated the immediate collapse of northern resistance, while in the south Liu Yongfu sustained the war effort for several more months. After returning to mainland China he retired to his home in Guilin and died there in 1903. His career arched from late-Qing literati prestige and decorated service against the French to the contested final act of his flight from Taipei, an episode widely regarded in Taiwanese historiography as one of the most controversial moments of the 1895 transition.
Figures.figure.tangjingsong.event1: 1895 Proclaimed President of the Republic of Formosa
Figures.figure.tangjingsong.event2: 1895 Fled to Xiamen on the eve of the fall of Taipei
Figures.figure.tangjingsong.title: First President of the Republic of Formosa
Figures.figure.tauketok.bio: Tauketok, known in contemporary Western sources as Tokitok, was the paramount chief of the Seqalu (斯卡羅) confederation, a political alliance of Paiwan-speaking groups that controlled the Hengchun Peninsula at the southern tip of Taiwan during the mid-nineteenth century. The Seqalu occupied a strategically critical stretch of coastline where foreign vessels frequently ran aground on the rocky shores near South Cape, and Tauketok's authority over the fate of shipwreck survivors made him the most consequential indigenous political figure on the island in dealings with Western powers. In March 1867, the American merchant brig Rover was wrecked on the South Cape shore and its captain and wife were killed by men under Seqalu jurisdiction, setting off a diplomatic crisis that would define Tauketok's historical legacy. United States Consul Charles Le Gendre traveled to the Hengchun Peninsula that autumn to negotiate directly with Tauketok, bypassing Qing authorities who openly admitted they had no effective control over the indigenous south. After weeks of deliberation, Tauketok and Le Gendre concluded the South Cape Agreement (南岬之盟) in October 1867 — an informal but landmark compact in which Tauketok agreed not to harm the crews of foreign vessels that flew their flags to identify themselves, in exchange for recognition of Seqalu sovereignty over the peninsula. This agreement was the first recorded treaty negotiated between a Taiwanese indigenous polity and a Western power, and it operated effectively for nearly a decade without a single violation. Le Gendre wrote admiringly of Tauketok as a sovereign ruler whose word was law across a territory the Qing state could not enter, a portrayal that shaped how foreign observers understood indigenous governance in Taiwan. The arrangement also exposed the limits of Qing jurisdiction over the island's interior and southern coast, a structural reality that Le Gendre documented in his influential 1871 memoir and that later informed Japanese strategic thinking about Taiwan. In 1874, Japan launched a punitive expedition against the Mudan villages following the massacre of Ryukyuan castaways in 1871, an incident in a neighboring territory where Seqalu authority was disputed; Tauketok did not lead forces against the Japanese but was drawn into the diplomatic aftermath. The Japanese expedition resulted in China paying an indemnity and implicitly acknowledging Japan's claim over the Ryukyus — a geopolitical shift made possible in part by the precedent of indigenous autonomy the South Cape Agreement had established. Tauketok died around 1874, leaving his confederation to face accelerating Qing military expansion into the peninsula that followed the Mudan Incident, when China finally moved to assert formal control over southern Taiwan. His story was dramatized in the 2021 Taiwanese television series Seqalu: Formosa 1867, which brought his negotiation with Le Gendre to a broad contemporary audience. Tauketok is widely recognized as the most diplomatically significant indigenous leader in nineteenth-century Taiwan, the man who negotiated the island's first international agreement and defined the boundaries of indigenous sovereignty on the eve of colonial transformation.
Figures.figure.tauketok.event1: Concluded the South Cape Agreement with US Consul Le Gendre (1867), the first treaty between a Taiwanese indigenous polity and a Western power
Figures.figure.tauketok.event2: His established sovereignty over the Hengchun Peninsula formed the diplomatic backdrop to Japan's 1874 punitive expedition
Figures.figure.tauketok.title: Chief of the Seqalu Confederation
Figures.figure.tengyuhsien.bio: Teng Yu-hsien, born in 1906 in Longtan, Hsinchu Prefecture, into a Hakka family of scholar-teachers, became the most celebrated composer of Taiwanese popular songs in the colonial period and is remembered as the Father of Taiwanese folk song. His family moved to Taipei in his early childhood, where his father taught classical Chinese in the colonial school system, giving Teng an unusually bilingual cultural grounding. He graduated from Taipei Normal School in 1925 and briefly taught at Daitōtei Public School, where he absorbed both the Hokkien-speaking urban culture of the city and Western and Japanese musical training. In 1929 he travelled to Tokyo to study composition formally, returning to a Taiwan in which the new gramophone industry was just beginning to create a Hokkien-language popular music market. He joined the Columbia Records Taiwan branch as a staff composer in 1933, where he collaborated with lyricists such as Lee Lin-chiu and Chou Tien-wang to produce a series of defining songs. Within a few years he had composed the four works later canonized as the Four Months — Hope, Rain, Spring, Sorrow (四月望雨) — namely Moonlit Sorrow (月夜愁), Bāng Chhun-hong / Longing for the Spring Breeze (望春風), Rain Night Flower (雨夜花), and Four Seasons Red (四季紅). These songs, sung most famously by Chun Chun, fused pentatonic Hokkien melody, jazz-age instrumentation, and lyrics depicting working-class courtship and sorrow, and quickly became the soundtrack of urban Taiwan. After the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War in 1937, the colonial authorities increasingly pressured popular music into wartime mobilization, forcibly rewriting his works into Japanese-language military songs such as Honourable Soldiers Going to the Front (誉れの軍夫). Disenchanted with the imposed conversion, he resigned from Columbia in 1940 and retreated to teach music at a small public school in Chuhuangkeng (now part of Zhudong, Hsinchu). Weakened by chronic heart and lung disease and the austerity of the late war years, he died there in 1944 at the age of 38, before his songs were freed from wartime Japanese substitutions. After the war his original Hokkien lyrics were restored and his compositions resumed a central place in Taiwanese popular memory, performed across regimes and generations. Teng is now honored not only as Taiwan's pre-eminent pre-war composer but as a cultural figure whose melodies have outlasted every political reorganization of the island they emerged from.
Figures.figure.tengyuhsien.title: Composer
Figures.figure.teresateng.bio: Teresa Teng, born in 1953 in Yunlin, was the most representative legendary singer of twentieth-century Chinese-language popular music. Born into a military family, she showed a gift for singing from childhood and debuted as a young girl, quickly rising to fame on a clear, sweet voice. Her repertoire spanned Mandarin, Taiwanese, Cantonese, and Japanese, blending Chinese folk tunes, ballads, and modern pop into a distinctive gentle style. Songs such as "The Moon Represents My Heart," "Sweet as Honey," and "I Only Care About You" have been sung continuously, becoming cross-generational Chinese-language classics. In the 1970s and 1980s her influence reached across Taiwan, Hong Kong, Southeast Asia, and Japan, where she repeatedly won major awards, one of the few Chinese-language singers to gain international fame. Her voice also slipped quietly into a still-closed mainland China, where a folk saying held that "by day it's Deng Xiaoping, by night it's Teresa Teng" — a unique symbol of cross-strait cultural exchange. She never married, lived abroad in her later years, and engaged with charitable and social causes. In 1995 she died suddenly of an asthma attack in Chiang Mai, Thailand, at just forty-two, shocking the entire Chinese-speaking world. Her songs are still widely sung today and are carried on in various forms through technology. Teng is seen as a symbolic figure of Taiwan's cultural soft power, her voice crossing regions and generations to become a shared memory of the Chinese-speaking world.
Figures.figure.teresateng.event1: Beloved across the Chinese-speaking world for songs such as "The Moon Represents My Heart"
Figures.figure.teresateng.event2: An icon across Greater China and Asia, she died suddenly in 1995
Figures.figure.teresateng.title: Legendary Mandopop Singer
Figures.figure.tsaiingwen.bio: Tsai Ing-wen, born in 1956 in Taipei with Hakka and Paiwan indigenous heritage on her father's side traceable to Pingtung, served as President of the Republic of China (Taiwan) from 2016 to 2024 and is the first woman to hold the office. Trained as a legal scholar, she earned a law degree from National Taiwan University, a master of laws from Cornell University, and a doctorate in law from the London School of Economics, before returning home to teach trade law at Soochow University and National Chengchi University. She entered public service in the 1990s as a key negotiator for Taiwan's accession to the World Trade Organization, drawing on her expertise in international trade law. Under President Chen Shui-bian, she chaired the Mainland Affairs Council from 2000 to 2004 and later served as Vice Premier, becoming a central architect of cross-strait policy. She joined the Democratic Progressive Party in 2004 and rose rapidly, taking the party chair in 2008 to rebuild it after the corruption scandals of the late Chen era. After narrowly losing the 2012 presidential election to Ma Ying-jeou, she won a landslide victory in 2016 against the backdrop of the Sunflower Movement, becoming the first president in Taiwanese history elected without having previously held an elected office. Her presidency advanced a series of landmark domestic reforms, including pension restructuring, transitional justice legislation, a formal apology to the indigenous peoples, and — in May 2019 — the legalization of same-sex marriage, the first such law in Asia. She pursued a New Southbound Policy to diversify economic ties beyond China and presided over Taiwan's globally lauded response to the COVID-19 pandemic. In cross-strait relations, her refusal to accept the so-called 1992 Consensus led Beijing to suspend official communications and to escalate military and economic pressure, culminating in large-scale PLA exercises around Taiwan after U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's visit in August 2022. She strengthened defense capabilities by extending compulsory military service, accelerating investment in asymmetric warfare, and deepening security cooperation with the United States, Japan, and European partners. Re-elected in 2020 with a record 8.17 million votes, she completed her second term in May 2024 and handed power to her vice president Lai Ching-te in a peaceful democratic transition. Tsai is widely credited with consolidating Taiwan's democratic identity, raising the island's international profile, and reshaping global perceptions of Taiwan as a frontline democracy in the contest between democratic and authoritarian systems.
Figures.figure.tsaiingwen.event1: Third party turnover — elected as Taiwan's first female president (2016)
Figures.figure.tsaiingwen.event2: Legalization of same-sex marriage, first in Asia (2019)
Figures.figure.tsaiingwen.event3: Chaired the Mainland Affairs Council, a central architect of cross-strait policy (2000)
Figures.figure.tsaiingwen.event4: Took the DPP chair, rebuilding the party (2008)
Figures.figure.tsaiingwen.event5: Re-elected with a record 8.17 million votes (2020)
Figures.figure.tsaiingwen.event7: Completed her term, peaceful transfer of power to Lai Ching-te (2024)
Figures.figure.tsaiingwen.title: President of the Republic of China
Figures.figure.wangdelu.bio: Wang Te-lu was born in 1770 in Zhuluo, near present-day Chiayi, and rose to become the highest-ranking official Taiwan produced under Qing rule. As a young man he raised local militia to help the imperial army suppress the great Lin Shuang-wen rebellion of the 1780s, and the merit he won there launched a military career that carried him from Taiwan into the wider empire's service. His defining struggle was against the pirate king Cai Qian, whose fleets terrorised the Taiwan Strait for years; Wang pursued him across the seas and, in a decisive engagement off the Zhejiang coast in 1809, finally destroyed the pirate armada. For this he was showered with honours, rising to admiral of the navy and grand guardian of the heir apparent — heights no other Taiwanese reached in the dynasty. He continued to serve as an elder statesman of coastal defence, and when war with Britain loomed, the aged admiral took up a command in the Pescadores, dying there on duty in 1842. Wang Te-lu is remembered as Taiwan's foremost military son of the Qing era; his grand tomb in Chiayi survives as one of the island's most important historic monuments.
Figures.figure.wangdelu.event1: Destroyed the fleet of the pirate king Cai Qian (1809)
Figures.figure.wangdelu.event2: Rose to admiral and grand guardian of the heir apparent
Figures.figure.wangdelu.title: Admiral of the Qing Navy
Figures.figure.wangminchuan.bio: Wang Min-chuan (1889–1942), born in Changhua, was a leading figure of the Taiwanese Cultural Association, the chief editor of the Taiwan Minpao, and one of the foremost representatives of the left-wing national movement under Japanese rule. As a young man he studied in Tokyo, where he was deeply influenced by the currents of Taishō democracy and socialism, and on returning to Taiwan he threw himself into enlightenment and political work. For years he directed the editorial affairs of the Taiwan Minpao, using his pen to advance anti-colonial thought and popular awakening, and he took an active part in the Petition Movement for the Establishment of a Taiwanese Parliament and in lecture tours across the island, becoming a core figure in the association's propaganda and journalistic work. When the Cultural Association split in 1927 over questions of strategy, he joined Lien Wen-ching and others in advocating a more radical path of class and national liberation, becoming a leader of the association after its turn to the left and steering it toward a mass movement of workers, peasants and youth. He was thereafter repeatedly placed under surveillance, arrested and imprisoned by the colonial authorities for his ideas and political activity, and his health was gravely broken in prison. He died of illness in 1942 amid the harsh wartime regime, without living to see Taiwan's liberation, yet he left a deep mark on Taiwan's early socialist and left-wing national movement and is remembered as one of the most representative thinkers and activists of the association's leftist line.
Figures.figure.wangminchuan.event1: 1920s Edited the Taiwan Minpao and promoted enlightenment journalism
Figures.figure.wangminchuan.event2: 1927 Led the left-wing line after the split of the Cultural Association
Figures.figure.wangminchuan.title: Left-Wing Leader of the Cultural Association
Figures.figure.wangshijie.bio: Wang Shijie was one of the earliest Han Chinese pioneers to settle the Hsinchu area of northern Taiwan. Around 1704 he led settlers from Guangdong to clear land, build irrigation channels, and establish villages in what had been Taokas indigenous territory on Taiwan's northwestern coastal plain. His enterprise formed the nucleus of the Han community that grew into the city of Hsinchu. The Wang family became one of the foundational gentry lineages of the Hsinchu area, with descendants active in local politics and commerce through the late Qing period. Wang Shijie represents the vanguard of the northward Han migration wave that transformed the demographic landscape of northern Taiwan during the early eighteenth century.
Figures.figure.wangshijie.event1: Led settlement of Hsinchu area around 1704, founding its Han community
Figures.figure.wangshijie.event2: Wang family became leading gentry lineage of the Hsinchu region
Figures.figure.wangshijie.title: Founding Pioneer of Hsinchu
Figures.figure.wangtiandeng.bio: Wang Tien-teng, born in 1901 in Ankeng, Xindian, near Taipei, into a farming family, was among the most prominent political and public voices of early post-war Taiwan. Rising through hardship as a working student, he later grew wealthy running the Wenshan Tea Company in Taipei, a self-made tea merchant. Devoted to public affairs, he joined social movements in the late colonial period, concerned with livelihoods and the rights of the Taiwanese. After World War II he was elected to the Taiwan Provincial Consultative Assembly and successively ran newspapers such as the People's Herald and the Liberty News, known for outspoken criticism of the authorities and for his motto that he would "serve the people as an ox and horse." When the February 28 Incident erupted in 1947, he was made a central figure of its Settlement Committee, serving as head of propaganda and broadcasting the unfolding events across the island by radio. He led the drafting of the "32 Demands" (later expanded to 42) submitted to the Administrative Executive Office, calling for political reform and local self-government — the fullest statement of Taiwanese demands during the incident. Yet the authorities treated the document as evidence of rebellion, making him a prime target of the crackdown. After Nationalist troops landed, he was arrested by security agents in March. He is said to have been tortured in custody and then killed, and his body was never recovered. His death became a symbolic case of the purge of the political elite during February 28. Wang is remembered as the spokesman for Taiwanese political aspirations during the incident, and his drafted demands and tragic end remain central texts for understanding the post-war conflict between the state and society.
Figures.figure.wangtiandeng.event1: Drafted the "32 Demands" of the February 28 Incident (1947)
Figures.figure.wangtiandeng.event2: Killed during the February 28 Incident, his body never found (1947)
Figures.figure.wangtiandeng.title: Key Leader of the 228 Settlement Committee
Figures.figure.wangyude.bio: Wang Yu-te, also known by his romanized Taiwanese name Ong Iok-tek, born in 1924 in Tainan, was a pioneering linguist of Taiwanese Hokkien and one of the founding figures of the overseas Taiwan independence movement. He came from a prominent Tainan family and was educated under the Japanese colonial system at the elite Tainan Second Higher School and then at Taipei Imperial University, where he studied Japanese literature. After Japan's surrender in 1945 he returned to teach Japanese and English at Tainan First High School and witnessed firsthand the deteriorating relationship between the mainlander administration and the local population. His elder brother Wang Yu-lin (王育霖), a Hsinchu prosecutor, was abducted and murdered by KMT security forces in the aftermath of the February 28 Incident of 1947, a personal tragedy that radicalized him politically. Threatened by ongoing arrests in the southern Taiwan crackdown, he fled the island in 1949 and made his way to Tokyo, where he would spend the remainder of his life. He resumed academic study at the University of Tokyo and earned a doctorate in linguistics with a pioneering dissertation on the phonological systems of southern Min Chinese. He held appointments at Meiji University and other Tokyo institutions and produced a series of foundational scholarly works, including his Studies on the Southern Min Phonological System (閩音系研究) and the influential primer Introduction to Taiwanese (臺灣語入門). His scholarship was politically significant as well as academically pathbreaking, establishing Taiwanese Hokkien as a fully-fledged language with its own historical phonology rather than a mere dialect of standard Chinese. In 1960 he founded the journal Taiwanese Youth (臺灣青年), the most influential periodical of the overseas independence movement, which sustained debate and organization across the Japanese, North American, and European diaspora communities for decades. He was a co-founder of the World United Formosans for Independence (WUFI), launched in 1970, and remained one of its principal intellectual figures. He was placed on the KMT regime's blacklist for decades and was unable to return to Taiwan during his lifetime, conducting his entire career in exile in Japan. He died of heart failure in Tokyo in September 1985, and his scholarly and political legacies have since converged in the post-democratization Taiwanese language movement, where his Hokkien linguistics remain canonical and his political vision has been widely reassessed.
Figures.figure.wangyude.event1: Fled to Japan after the 228 Incident; became a pioneer of the overseas Taiwan independence movement and Taiwanese linguistics
Figures.figure.wangyude.title: Linguist & Taiwan Independence Pioneer
Figures.figure.wangyungching.bio: Wang Yung-ching, born in 1917 into a poor tea-farming family in Xindian, Taipei, was among the most representative entrepreneurs of post-war Taiwan, hailed as the "God of Management." With only a primary-school education, he left home to make a living as a youth, starting with a rice shop and accumulating his first capital through diligence and care. In 1954, seizing the opportunities of US aid and industrialization, he founded the Formosa Plastics Company, entering the then-emerging production of plastic raw materials. With a management philosophy of "getting to the root of things and striving for perfection," he built Formosa Plastics step by step into a vast conglomerate spanning petrochemicals, plastics, fibers, and electronics. He drove major investments such as large petrochemical complexes and the Sixth Naphtha Cracker, profoundly shaping Taiwan's industrial structure and economic growth. Known for rigorous cost management and efficiency, his methods and sayings were long treated as gospel in the business world. Beyond industry he engaged in philanthropy, founding the Chang Gung Memorial Hospital and establishing educational institutions such as Chang Gung University and Ming Chi University of Technology to give back to society. He prized diligence and simplicity all his life, keeping a frugal lifestyle even in great wealth, a model of the self-made man. He died in 2008 while inspecting operations in the United States. Wang is seen as an emblematic entrepreneur of the Taiwan economic miracle, his path and philosophy a lasting footnote to the spirit of Taiwanese industry.
Figures.figure.wangyungching.event2: Built Chang Gung Memorial Hospital and invested in education and healthcare
Figures.figure.wangyungching.title: Founder of Formosa Plastics & "God of Management"
Figures.figure.wufeng.bio: Wu Feng, born around 1699 in Pinghe County, Fujian, came to Taiwan as a young man and served for decades as the official interpreter (通事) mediating between Qing authorities and the Tsou indigenous communities of the Alishan mountain region, accumulating significant personal landholdings and commercial influence before dying under violent circumstances in 1769 in a conflict whose details remain disputed. He learned the Tsou language and became the essential intermediary through whom Qing officials communicated with and taxed the Alishan communities, a role that gave him extraordinary personal influence and access to the camphor, deer hide, and trade goods that flowed through the mountain communities, and which he leveraged to build substantial personal wealth. The historical facts of Wu Feng's life and death are relatively sparse — what is known is that he served as interpreter for the Tsou for approximately forty years, that he accumulated land and commercial interests in the Alishan foothills, and that he was killed around 1769 in circumstances that appear to have involved disputes over trade goods or tribute payments. However, Wu Feng's real historical significance lies not in his life but in his legend: in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, a story circulated — and was widely propagated — in which Wu Feng voluntarily sacrificed himself to persuade the Tsou people to abandon the practice of headhunting, appearing dressed in red and telling them he was a criminal who deserved to be killed, thereby triggering a killing that then caused the Tsou to swear off headhunting out of remorse. This legend was adopted and amplified by Japanese colonial authorities, who erected a shrine to Wu Feng at Alishan and incorporated his story into the colonial education curriculum as an example of Han civilization's civilizing influence on indigenous peoples — a narrative that served Japanese colonial ideology by presenting indigenous headhunting as backward and in need of external correction. After the Second World War, the story was preserved by the Republic of China government and taught in Taiwanese schools as a patriotic legend until 1989, when indigenous rights activists successfully campaigned to have it removed from the curriculum on the grounds that it was a fabrication that demeaned Tsou culture and justified their dispossession. The Alishan Wu Feng Shrine was demolished by Tsou activists in 1989 in a symbolic assertion of indigenous dignity, and historians have since confirmed that the self-sacrifice narrative is a colonial-era invention with no basis in contemporary historical sources. Wu Feng himself — the real interpreter who lived, traded, and died at Alishan — remains an intriguing figure whose actual role in the complex economy of the Qing frontier deserves scholarly attention independent of the mythological overlay that obscured him for two centuries. He is recognized today as an example of how colonial powers constructed ideological narratives around historical individuals, and his story — both the fiction and its dismantling — is taught in Taiwan as a lesson in critical historical thinking about indigenous peoples' representation.
Figures.figure.wufeng.event1: Served as interpreter for the Tsou indigenous people of Alishan for approximately forty years under Qing rule
Figures.figure.wufeng.event2: His colonial-era legend — used for two centuries to justify indigenous assimilation — was dismantled in 1989 when Tsou activists demolished the Alishan shrine and had the story removed from Taiwan's school curriculum
Figures.figure.wufeng.title: Interpreter Between Han and Tsou Indigenous Peoples
Figures.figure.wuguangliang.bio: Wu Guangliang was a Guangdong-born military commander who led the construction of the central cross-island trail (the Baguashan Trail) in 1875, as part of Shen Baozhen's 'Open the Mountains, Pacify the Savages' campaign. Beginning from Zhushān in Nantou County, his forces cut a 265-kilometer road through some of Taiwan's most rugged mountain terrain, crossing the Central Mountain Range to reach Beinan on the east coast. Completed after months of brutal construction through hostile indigenous territory, the central trail was the most difficult of the three Qing cross-island routes. Its completion connected Taiwan's east and west coasts for the first time by overland path, facilitating expansion of Qing administration into eastern Taiwan and accelerating Han colonization of indigenous territories.
Figures.figure.wuguangliang.event1: Led construction of the central cross-island Baguashan Trail in 1875
Figures.figure.wuguangliang.event2: Promoted agricultural settlement and governance of eastern Taiwan
Figures.figure.wuguangliang.title: General Who Opened the Central Mountain Trail
Figures.figure.wuluanqi.bio: Wu Luanqi was a major gentry figure in central Taiwan whose family rose to prominence in the aftermath of the Dai Chaochun Rebellion of the 1860s. The Wu family became one of the dominant gentry lineages of the Taichung area, controlling extensive landholdings and wielding considerable social authority. When Japanese forces advanced into central Taiwan following the Treaty of Shimonoseki in 1895, Wu Luanqi organized resistance fighters and engaged Japanese troops, becoming the central Taiwan counterpart to the better-known resistance leaders of the north and south. Although ultimately defeated, his military resistance made him a symbol of Taiwan's gentry determination to contest the colonial handover. He died in 1898, his post-surrender years marked by the frustration of defeat and occupation.
Figures.figure.wuluanqi.event1: Led armed resistance against Japanese forces entering Taichung in 1895
Figures.figure.wuluanqi.event2: Wu family was the dominant gentry lineage of Qing-era Taichung
Figures.figure.wuluanqi.title: Taichung Magnate · 1895 Resistance Leader
Figures.figure.wumingjie.bio: Wu Ming-chieh (1911–1987), born in Miaoli and of Hakka descent, was a baseball player who served as the ace pitcher and cleanup hitter of the Chiayi Agriculture and Forestry School (Kano) team and the very soul of the Kano legend. Under the strict Spartan training of coach Kondo Hyotaro, the Kano team—made up of a 'three-ethnic harmony' of Japanese, Han Chinese and indigenous players—was utterly transformed, winning the right to represent Taiwan in 1931 and travelling to Japan's Koshien tournament. In that contest, which stunned all of Japan, Wu became the focus of attention with his astonishing pitching and hitting: fierce in velocity, steady in control, and able to carry the team at the plate, he was hailed by the Japanese press as the 'Kirin child' (a prodigy). Kano fought its way through to the final, and although Wu injured and bled from a finger in a crucial game, he gritted his teeth and kept taking the mound to pitch, displaying remarkable will and sportsmanship. Kano finished as runner-up, glorious in defeat, and the name 'Kano of the realm' rang throughout Japan, writing an immortal page in the history of Taiwanese baseball. Afterward Wu went on to play for Waseda University in Japan, setting several batting records. His story with Kano later became an important subject of the film KANO and remains a symbol of the Taiwanese baseball spirit.
Figures.figure.wumingjie.event1: 1931 Pitched as Kano's ace at the Koshien tournament
