Figures.figure.wumingjie.event2: 1931 Pitched on with an injured finger in the Koshien final, glorious in defeat
Figures.figure.wumingjie.title: Ace Pitcher of Kano
Figures.figure.wusangui.bio: Wu Sangui was a pivotal military figure of the late Ming and early Qing transition, born in 1612 into a Liaodong military lineage and trained from boyhood by his father Wu Xiang to become one of the most renowned cavalry commanders of the northern Ming frontier army. When the rebel leader Li Zicheng captured Beijing in 1644 and the Chongzhen Emperor hanged himself, he was the regional commander of Shanhai Pass and found himself caught between three competing powers: Li Zicheng's Shun forces, the Manchu armies under Dorgon, and the remnants of the Southern Ming. In April 1644 he opened the pass to Dorgon's Qing armies and led them through Shanhai Pass to crush Li Zicheng's rebels at Beijing, an act that earned him an enduring reputation as the man who let the Qing into China. He subsequently led the Qing pursuit of the Southern Ming southwards, conquering Yunnan in the 1660s and personally executing the last Southern Ming emperor, the Yongli Emperor, at Kunming, thereby extinguishing Ming loyalist resistance on the mainland. For these services the Qing court enfeoffed him as Prince of Pingxi and assigned him perpetual rule over Yunnan, including the right to raise his own armies, collect his own taxes, and appoint his own officials, effectively making his fief an independent kingdom within the Qing empire. When the young Kangxi Emperor came of age and moved to abolish the feudatories in 1673, he raised the banner of revolt in Yunnan and quickly drew the Jingnan Prince Geng Jingzhong of Fujian and the Pingnan Prince Shang Zhixin of Guangdong into a coordinated rebellion known as the Revolt of the Three Feudatories. The early phase of the rebellion proved devastatingly successful, sweeping across Hunan and Sichuan and reaching the middle Yangtze, throwing the southern half of the Qing empire into crisis. From Taiwan the Tungning ruler Zheng Jing seized the opportunity to launch his own seaborne westward campaign in concert with Geng Jingzhong, making the Three Feudatories Revolt the last historical opening for a Ming-loyalist counterattack on the mainland. In 1678 he proclaimed himself emperor at Hengzhou in Hunan, declaring a new dynasty styled the Great Zhou with the reign title Zhaowu, in open repudiation of the Qing. He died of illness at Hengzhou only five months after his coronation, at the age of sixty-six. His grandson Wu Shifan inherited the throne but quickly lost momentum, and the Great Zhou regime was crushed by Qing armies in 1681, ending the Three Feudatories Revolt. Wu Sangui is generally regarded as a deeply ambivalent figure who united in himself both the man who let the Qing into China and the man who later sought to break it apart, and whose revolt provided the historical opening for Zheng Jing's westward expedition and decisively shaped the final decade of the Tungning Kingdom.
Figures.figure.wusangui.event1: Launched the Revolt of the Three Feudatories in 1673, the historical opening for Zheng Jing's westward campaign
Figures.figure.wusangui.title: Prince of Pingxi & Leader of the Three Feudatories Revolt
Figures.figure.wusha.bio: Wu Sha was born in 1731 in Zhangpu, Zhangzhou, on the Fujian coast, and crossed to Taiwan as a young man to seek his fortune on the northern frontier. Settling near the mountain pass at Sandiao, he made his living trading with the Kavalan people of the plain beyond the ranges, learning their ways and earning a reputation for fair dealing. Where others saw only forbidden and dangerous country, Wu saw the last great expanse of unclaimed farmland in Taiwan. In 1796 he gathered a band of Han and Hakka settlers, armed and provisioned, and led them over the pass to build a fortified camp at Toucheng — the first Han foothold on the Kavalan plain. The Kavalan resisted the intrusion fiercely, and the early years were bloody; the turning point came when a smallpox epidemic struck the villages and Wu used his knowledge of variolation to treat the sick, winning a trust his weapons could not. He laid out the pattern of communal, walled settlements that would define the plain's development, but died in 1798, only two years into the enterprise. His kinsmen carried the work southward until the Qing, confronted with the accomplished fact, annexed the region as Kavalan Sub-prefecture. Wu Sha is remembered as the man who opened Yilan — a pioneer whose achievement, like all on the frontier, came at the cost of the people who were there first.
Figures.figure.wusha.event1: Led Han settlers over the pass to found Toucheng (1796)
Figures.figure.wusha.event2: Used variolation to win the trust of the Kavalan people
Figures.figure.wusha.title: Pioneer of the Kavalan Plain
Figures.figure.wutangxing.bio: Wu Tangxing, born in 1860 in Tongluo, Miaoli, into a Hakka farming family, earned the lowest imperial examination degree as a young man and combined teaching in his home village with martial training and local self-defense. When the Treaty of Shimonoseki ceded Taiwan to Japan in 1895, he was among the first in the Miaoli region to answer the call of the so-called Republic of Formosa, expending his family's resources to recruit a Hakka volunteer force. Using the hill country of Hsinchu and Miaoli as a base, he fought alongside other Hakka leaders such as Hsu Hsiang and Chiang Shao-tsu, engaging the advancing Japanese Imperial Guards Division in skirmishes and pitched battles at Niu-pu, Ta-ko-ham, and Hsinchu. Japanese firepower and discipline were overwhelming, but Hakka villages organized by lineage supplied food and intelligence that enabled the volunteers to delay the advance for months. In August 1895 his forces joined the climactic Battle of Baguashan near Changhua, the largest and bloodiest engagement of the 1895 war, in which casualties on both sides were severe. He is recorded as having directed his troops at the front and was killed in action at the age of thirty-five. His death marked the high point and effective end of organized central-Taiwan resistance, while surviving volunteers retreated south under Hsu Hsiang to continue the struggle. After the war his story was preserved in the Hakka communities of Miaoli and Hsinchu, and a memorial was later erected at Tongluo. Wu is remembered as one of the foremost martyrs of Hakka volunteer resistance in 1895 and is grouped with Hsu Hsiang and Chiang Shao-tsu as one of the 'Three Heroes of the Yi-Wei War.'
Figures.figure.wutangxing.event1: 1895 Raised Hakka volunteer forces in Miaoli
Figures.figure.wutangxing.event2: 1895 Killed in action at the Battle of Baguashan
Figures.figure.wutangxing.title: Hakka Volunteer Leader of Miaoli
Figures.figure.wuzhuoliu.bio: Wu Zhuoliu, born Wu Chien-tien in 1900 in Hsinpu, Hsinchu (present-day Hsinchu County) into a Hakka family, was steeped in classical Chinese learning from childhood. He trained at the normal division of the Governor-General's National Language School in Taipei, and after graduating in 1920 returned home to teach at public elementary schools, a profession he pursued for nearly two decades. During his teaching years he grew resentful of the discriminatory treatment that Japanese inspectors meted out to Taiwanese teachers, and in 1940 he resigned from his post in protest. In 1941 he traveled briefly to Nanjing in China as a reporter for the Continental Daily News (大陸新報), witnessing conditions in wartime China before returning to Taiwan. Back home he moved into journalism, working over the years for the Taiwan Daily News and, after the war, papers such as the Taiwan Shin Sheng Daily News and the Min Pao, making reporting his long-term livelihood. Between 1943 and 1945, under the close surveillance of the Japanese colonial authorities, he secretly wrote the novel Orphan of Asia (亞細亞的孤兒). Through its protagonist Hu Tai-ming, the work depicts the plight of Taiwanese caught between Japan and China, belonging fully to neither and left in a state of orphaned identity. After the war he lived through the February 28 Incident and the White Terror, and his disillusionment led him to write the autobiographical works The Fig Tree (無花果) and Taiwan Lianqiao (臺灣連翹), both of which were banned for a time for touching on political taboos. In 1964 he founded the magazine Taiwan Literature (臺灣文藝), which gave post-war nativist writing a lasting platform and nurtured many younger authors. In 1969 he donated his personal savings to establish the Wu Zhuoliu Literary Award, encouraging literature centered on Taiwan itself. Wu died in Taiwan in 1976 at the age of seventy-six. He is widely regarded as a pioneer of Taiwanese nativist literature, and Orphan of Asia is seen as the most representative literary emblem of the identity dilemma of colonial Taiwan.
Figures.figure.wuzhuoliu.event1: Secretly wrote the novel Orphan of Asia (1943–1945)
Figures.figure.wuzhuoliu.event2: Founded Taiwan Literature magazine and endowed the Wu Zhuoliu Literary Award
Figures.figure.wuzhuoliu.title: Novelist & Journalist
Figures.figure.xiaxianlun.bio: Xia Xianlun was a Hunanese official who served as Taiwan circuit intendant during the Tongzhi and early Guangxu periods and became an early advocate for systematic development of eastern Taiwan. He personally surveyed eastern Taiwan's terrain and resources, recognized the region's agricultural and strategic potential, and submitted repeated memorials urging active colonization of the east coast, strengthened coastal defenses, and construction of north-south mountain trails. His recommendations directly influenced the Qing court's subsequent 'Open the Mountains' policy accelerated by the 1874 Mudan Incident. Though his tenure was brief, Xia's surveys and memorials were foundational in shifting Qing strategic thinking toward eastern Taiwan at a critical moment before Japanese encroachment made the question urgent.
Figures.figure.xiaxianlun.event1: Surveyed eastern Taiwan and memorialized court to develop the 'back mountain'
Figures.figure.xiaxianlun.event2: Advocacy shaped Qing eastern Taiwan policy, laying groundwork for opening the mountains
Figures.figure.xiaxianlun.title: Advocate for Opening Eastern Taiwan
Figures.figure.xiexuehong.bio: Hsieh Hsueh-hung, born in 1901 into a poor family in Changhua, was sold in childhood as a child-bride and servant, making her the most humbly born yet far-reaching woman revolutionary in modern Taiwanese history. Breaking past the limits of her status through self-education, she encountered socialist ideas in her youth and threw herself into the leftist movement. She studied in Shanghai and Moscow, receiving training from the Communist International and becoming one of the few Taiwanese women of her time with an international outlook. In 1928 she took part in founding the Taiwanese Communist Party in Shanghai, advocating national liberation and class revolution as one of its core leaders. Under Japanese rule she was repeatedly arrested and imprisoned for her political activity, yet held fast to her convictions. After World War II she organized popular forces in Taichung, attentive to the injustices of post-war society. When the February 28 Incident broke out in 1947, she led the "27 Brigade" in Taichung — one of the largest armed resistances on the island — and for a time controlled the Taichung area. After the resistance failed she fled by stages to Hong Kong and then to mainland China. There she founded the Taiwan Democratic Self-Government League, a leading organization for Taiwanese on the mainland. Yet in China's successive political campaigns she was branded a rightist and subjected to struggle sessions, ending her life in bleak circumstances and dying in Beijing in 1970. Hsieh's life was full of controversy, but her overlapping identities as a woman leader, leftist revolutionary, and commander of February 28 armed resistance make her a weighty and complex figure in modern Taiwanese history.
Figures.figure.xiexuehong.event1: Led the 27 Brigade in armed resistance during February 28 (1947)
Figures.figure.xiexuehong.title: Communist Leader & 27 Brigade Commander
Figures.figure.xuxiang.bio: Hsu Hsiang, born in 1860 in Toufen, Miaoli, into a Hakka family in the same year as his comrade Wu Tangxing, earned a low imperial degree and ran a private academy in Toufen while taking part in local militia organization. After the cession of Taiwan in 1895 he joined the call of the so-called Republic of Formosa and organized a Hakka volunteer force together with Wu Tangxing, Chiang Shao-tsu, and other Miaoli gentry. His unit, raised in Hsinchu and Miaoli, became one of the most tenacious volunteer formations of the 1895 war. After the northern front collapsed he withdrew with other commanders along the western corridor, continuing to fight in Hsinchu, Miaoli, and at the Battle of Baguashan in Changhua. With Wu killed and Chiang captured and dead, Hsu emerged as the principal surviving commander of the Hakka volunteers and pressed south into Yunlin and Chiayi. In October 1895 he was killed in action near Toulu (some accounts place the battle in the Chiayi area) at the age of thirty-five. Tradition records his last words — 'It is no regret for a true man to die for his country' — as among the most-quoted martyr's testaments of the 1895 resistance. After his death organized Hakka resistance in central and southern Taiwan effectively dissolved, although scattered guerrilla activity continued into 1896. His story was preserved in Toufen and across the Yunlin–Chiayi region, and a memorial was later erected in his home town. Hsu is grouped with Wu Tangxing and Chiang Shao-tsu as one of the 'Three Heroes of the Yi-Wei War' and is widely commemorated as a leading representative of Hakka militia and lower gentry resistance to Japanese rule.
Figures.figure.xuxiang.event1: 1895 Fought through central Taiwan against the Japanese advance
Figures.figure.xuxiang.event2: 1895 Killed in action at the Battle of Toulu
Figures.figure.xuxiang.title: Hakka Volunteer Leader
Figures.figure.xuzonggan.bio: Xu Zonggan was a Jiangsu scholar-official who served in senior positions in Taiwan during the Daoguang and Xianfeng periods, including as circuit intendant. His collected writings, Siweixinzhai Wenbian, compiled essays, administrative documents, and poetry composed during his Taiwan postings, providing a rich source for understanding Taiwan's political climate in the mid-nineteenth century. Xu embodied the ideal of the Confucian literati official — governing by moral example, prioritizing education, and seeking to pacify a fractious settler society through cultural refinement. He also wrote thoughtfully about the island's natural environment and indigenous peoples. His writings are cited by historians studying the administrative and cultural history of mid-Qing Taiwan.
Figures.figure.xuzonggan.event1: Served as circuit intendant, compiled Siweixinzhai Wenbian on Taiwan governance
Figures.figure.xuzonggan.event2: Governed as a scholar-official, promoting culture and clean administration
Figures.figure.xuzonggan.title: Scholar-Official and Circuit Intendant
Figures.figure.yangkui.bio: Yang Kui was born Yang Kuei in 1906 in Xinhua, Tainan, and as a boy witnessed the aftermath of the Tapani uprising, an experience that shaped his lifelong sympathy for the oppressed. He studied in Tokyo, where he steeped himself in socialist thought and threw himself into labour and farmers' movements after returning to Taiwan, being arrested again and again for his activism. In 1934 his story The Newspaper Carrier was selected by a central literary magazine in Tokyo — the first work by a Taiwanese writer to break into Japan's mainstream literary press. With his wife he ran the Shouyang Farm, scraping a living from the soil while continuing to write. After the war his hopes for a new era were crushed, and in 1949 his brief Peace Declaration calling for reconciliation led to a twelve-year sentence on Green Island. There he wrote the allegory The Indomitable Rose, its title an image of the spirit he embodied. Released in the early 1960s, Yang Kui lived to see a younger generation rediscover him, and died in 1985, honoured as a writer who never stopped resisting.
Figures.figure.yangkui.event1: The Newspaper Carrier entered Tokyo's central literary press (1934)
Figures.figure.yangkui.event2: Jailed twelve years on Green Island for the Peace Declaration
Figures.figure.yangkui.title: Writer and Social Activist
Figures.figure.yangtingli.bio: Yang Tingli, courtesy name Youxi, was a Qing dynasty official from Guangxi who passed the imperial examinations during the Qianlong reign and went on to serve multiple terms in Taiwan — developing an unusually intimate knowledge of the island across seven separate postings, earning the sobriquet seven crossings to Taiwan. During successive missions he ventured into the mountainous interior and amassed detailed intelligence on the Kavalan people of the Lanyang Plain, recognising the urgency of bringing the region under formal administration. As Han settlers poured into the valley during the Jiaqing era, friction between migrants and indigenous communities escalated, yet the court remained indecisive. Yang repeatedly memorialized the throne, arguing that only official governance could arbitrate competing claims and maintain order. In 1809, serving as Circuit Intendant, he led the formal establishment of Kavalan Sub-prefecture — the administrative foundation of modern Yilan County. He personally surveyed the terrain, negotiated with the descendants of pioneer settler Wu Sha, and designed the governance framework that mediated Han-indigenous relations. Beyond administrative construction, he promoted Confucian education in frontier communities. Venerated by later generations in Yilan as the patron of the region's civilisation, he exemplifies the Qing official who shaped northern Taiwan not by conquest but by persistent institutional perseverance.
Figures.figure.yangtingli.event1: Served seven separate postings in Taiwan across three reigns, conducting surveys deep into the Kavalan territory and persistently memorialising the court to establish formal governance in Yilan.
Figures.figure.yangtingli.event2: In 1809, as Circuit Intendant, led the establishment of Kavalan Sub-prefecture — the administrative foundation of modern Yilan County; venerated in local temples as the patron of the region's civilisation.
Figures.figure.yangtingli.title: Qing Circuit Intendant, Founder of Kavalan Administration
Figures.figure.yansiqi.bio: Yan Siqi, born in 1589 in Haicheng, Zhangzhou Prefecture, Fujian, was a Fujianese maritime trader and corsair traditionally honored in Taiwan as the Pioneer King who Opened Taiwan (開臺王) for his role in leading one of the earliest organized Han Chinese settlements on Formosa. According to traditional accounts, he killed a local official in a dispute as a young man and fled across the sea to Hirado, Japan, where a large community of overseas Hokkien merchants operated under the toleration of the Tokugawa bakufu. He prospered as a textile and rice merchant in Hirado, joined the regional Hokkien-Japanese trading network, and became a prominent figure among the émigré Chinese commercial community on the southern Japanese coast. Tradition records that he and twenty-seven sworn brothers — including a young Zheng Zhilong — plotted in 1624 to seize power in Japan, an undertaking that failed and forced their flight from the archipelago. He led the fleet across the Taiwan Strait and made landfall at Penkang (笨港), in the lowlands of modern Beigang in Yunlin County, where he established a coastal base from which to organize Han settlement. He built ten stockades along the coastal plain and dispatched recruiters back to Zhangzhou and Quanzhou to draw landless Hokkien farmers across the strait, accelerating Han immigration well before the formal Dutch and Spanish arrivals. He maintained an independent trading and raiding operation across the South China and East China Seas, operating outside Ming jurisdiction and competing with the rising Dutch East India Company. His settlement at Penkang antedated the formal Dutch occupation at Tayouan in 1624 and the Spanish settlement at Keelung in 1626, making it one of the earliest mass Han colonization efforts on Taiwan. He died unexpectedly in 1625, traditionally said to have succumbed to illness contracted on a hunting expedition in the lowland forests, at the age of 36. His following — fleet, settlement networks, and trading partners — passed to his lieutenant Zheng Zhilong, who within a few years built the larger maritime power that defined East Asian seas in the mid-seventeenth century. He is commemorated by shrines at Beigang and elsewhere in Yunlin and remains an officially recognized historical figure in Taiwanese local memory, though academic scholarship debates the documentary basis and the precise dates of his career. Yan is widely remembered as the principal organizer of the first large-scale Han settlement on Taiwan and the prologue to the maritime empire that his successor Zheng Zhilong, and ultimately Koxinga, would forge across the strait.
Figures.figure.yansiqi.event1: Led the first major Hokkien settlement at Penkang, becoming known as the 'Pioneer of Taiwan'
Figures.figure.yansiqi.title: Pioneer of Taiwan
Figures.figure.yanyunnian.bio: Yen Yun-nien was born in 1874 in Ruifang, in the gold-bearing hills of Taiwan's northeast, into a family of modest means. Sharp-witted and fluent in dealing with the new Japanese authorities, he began by leasing and subcontracting mining rights in the Jiufen and Jinguashi goldfields, steadily building his position until he controlled much of the region's gold and coal production. Through shrewd partnerships with Japanese capital he expanded into a mining empire that would become the basis of the Taiyang Mining Company, one of the largest Taiwanese-run enterprises of the colonial era. His wealth transformed Ruifang and Jiufen into booming towns and made the Yen family of Keelung one of Taiwan's celebrated 'five great families.' A patron of poetry and traditional letters as well as a businessman, he embodied the new class of Taiwanese entrepreneurs who prospered by working within the colonial economy. Yen Yun-nien died in 1923, still in his prime, having built a commercial and industrial legacy that his family would carry forward for decades.
Figures.figure.yanyunnian.event1: Built a gold- and coal-mining empire at Jiufen and Jinguashi
Figures.figure.yanyunnian.event2: Founded the Yen family, one of Taiwan's 'five great families'
Figures.figure.yanyunnian.title: Mining Magnate
Figures.figure.yaochiawen.bio: Yao Chia-wen, born in 1938 in Changhua, is a representative figure in Taiwan's democracy movement who combined the roles of lawyer, writer, and statesman. He graduated in law from National Taiwan University and, after qualifying, practiced with a long-standing concern for judicial reform and human rights. In the 1970s he joined the tangwai movement and contributed to publications such as Taiwan Political Review, becoming one of the camp's important writers. With Lin Yi-hsiung he co-authored works such as "The Tiger Falls to the Plain," documenting election lawsuits and judicial injustice and drawing public attention. When the Kaohsiung Incident broke out in 1979 he was among the principal participants and was sentenced to twelve years in a military trial. In prison he devoted himself to writing, completing "The Seven-Color Chronicles of Taiwan," a long novel set against Taiwanese history, turning his years behind bars into literary creation. After the lifting of martial law and democratization he was released and returned to politics, joining the Democratic Progressive Party and serving as its chairman. Following the change of ruling party in 2000, he was appointed president of the Examination Yuan for eight years, advancing reform of the civil-service examination system. His life spanned law, literature, and politics, a microcosm of the diverse talents of the tangwai generation. Yao is seen as a model of the intellectual who joined the democracy movement with pen and law, his prison literature and later public career embodying the resilience and transformation of dissidents in Taiwan's democratic transition.
Figures.figure.yaochiawen.event2: Later served as DPP chairman and president of the Examination Yuan
Figures.figure.yaochiawen.title: Kaohsiung Incident Prisoner & Writer
Figures.figure.yinhaiguang.bio: Yin Hai-guang, born in 1919 in Huanggang, Hubei province, was the most influential Chinese liberal philosopher to operate in 1950s and 1960s Taiwan, whose work on logic, analytic philosophy, and political thought provided much of the intellectual scaffolding for the constitutionalist opposition of the early authoritarian era. He came of age during the Sino-Japanese War, studying at Southwest Associated University (the wartime amalgamation of Peking, Tsinghua, and Nankai universities) in Yunnan, where he was deeply marked by exposure to Anglo-American analytic philosophy. He completed his graduate study at Tsinghua University and entered the Republican-era public intellectual world as a younger associate of the philosopher Chin Yueh-lin (金岳霖) and the liberal reformer Zhang Foquan. He moved to Taiwan with the Nationalist government in 1949 and joined the philosophy department of National Taiwan University, where for two decades he became one of the most influential teachers of his generation. He was the foremost essayist of the Free China Journal during its years of liberal criticism in the 1950s, writing extensively on logic, scientific method, civil liberties, and the limits of authoritarian governance. His thinking drew openly on Bertrand Russell, Karl Popper, F.A. Hayek, and contemporary analytic philosophy, importing into Chinese liberal discourse a set of categories distinct from older Confucian or Marxist frameworks. He published widely throughout the 1950s and 1960s, with major works including Logic and Method (思想與方法) and a sustained critique of authoritarian politics under the rubric of Chinese Cultural Prospects (中國文化的展望). The crackdown on Lei Chen in 1960 and the suspension of Free China deprived him of his principal publication venue and marked the beginning of his sustained marginalization by the security state. He was placed under constant police surveillance, his lectures monitored, his graduate students harassed, and his publications increasingly banned or rewritten. The Ministry of Education stripped him of his teaching duties at National Taiwan University in 1966, a humiliation that intensified the stress that medical historians have linked to his rapidly deteriorating health. He died of stomach cancer in Taipei in September 1969 at the age of 50, his death widely viewed by his students and colleagues as the result of slow political destruction. Yin is now widely revered as one of the foundational figures of post-war Chinese liberalism, his students and writings shaping a generation of post-1987 Taiwanese democratic intellectuals and his treatment by the KMT state standing as one of the most representative cases of late-authoritarian intellectual persecution.
Figures.figure.yinhaiguang.event1: Dismissed from NTU for criticizing the KMT regime
Figures.figure.yinhaiguang.title: Philosopher & Liberal Intellectual
Figures.figure.yuqingfang.bio: Yu Qingfang, born in 1879 in what is today Luzhu in Kaohsiung, was the principal leader of the Tapani Incident, also known as the Xilai Temple Incident or the Jiaobani Incident, the largest armed anti-Japanese uprising of the mid-colonial period. In his early years he served as a junior police assistant, gaining first-hand familiarity with the workings of the colonial system. He later resigned in dissatisfaction with Japanese policy and gravitated toward popular religious circles. Combining Zhaijiao Buddhism with folk beliefs, he used the Xilai Temple in Tainan as his base and proclaimed a divine mandate to establish a so-called Great Ming Compassionate Kingdom on Taiwanese soil, drawing on religious appeal to mobilize anti-Japanese followers. In early 1915 he, together with Jiang Ding and Luo Jun, planned a coordinated island-wide uprising and distributed talismans through the religious network with the claim that believers would be impervious to blades and bullets. The uprising broke out in haste in June and July of that year, attacking Japanese police substations and stations in the Jiaobani area (modern Yujing in Tainan) and inflicting Japanese casualties. The Government-General quickly transferred troops from across the island to the south and launched a major military operation in the mountains of Yujing and Nanxi. In addition to battlefield deaths, Japanese forces carried out large-scale executions in several settlements, causing heavy civilian losses among the people of Jiaobani — one of the most controversial repressive episodes of the colonial era. Yu Qingfang withdrew into the mountains with the remnants of his force, was captured at Nanxi in August, and was sentenced to death in September and executed at Tainan. The Tapani Incident was the last large-scale armed uprising launched by the Han Chinese population of Taiwan. It was also the largest and most costly in human terms, and is widely regarded as the closing chapter of the Han armed resistance tradition. He is widely credited as the figure after whom Taiwanese opposition shifted into modern political channels such as the Taiwanese Cultural Association.
Figures.figure.yuqingfang.event2: 1915 Defeated at Jiaobani, captured and executed
Figures.figure.yuqingfang.title: Leader of the Tapani Incident
Figures.figure.yutengfa.bio: Yu Teng-fa, born in 1904 in Qiaotou, Kaohsiung, was a pioneer of the post-war tangwai movement in southern Taiwan and an important local political leader. Of local origin, he engaged in public affairs early and steadily built grassroots networks and prestige, becoming a core figure of the Kaohsiung local faction. After the war he long took part in local elections and self-government affairs and served as Kaohsiung county magistrate, wielding deep influence in southern politics. Unlike most local powers of the time who attached themselves to the system, he was known for daring to challenge the authorities and for supporting the tangwai movement, a key bridge linking local factions to the democracy movement. In January 1979 he and his son Yu Jui-yen were arrested on charges of involvement with "communist spies" and sedition, shocking the tangwai camp. Tangwai figures led by Hsu Hsin-liang promptly staged a demonstration in Qiaotou in support of the Yu family — the "Bridgehead Incident," the first openly political street demonstration under the martial-law system and regarded as a prelude to that year's Kaohsiung Incident. His arrest and trial shifted the tangwai movement's forms of resistance from parliament to the streets, a landmark development. In 1989 he was found dead under mysterious circumstances at his home, the cause still disputed and one of the unsolved cases in the history of the democracy movement. Yu is seen as a pivotal figure bridging generations of the southern tangwai movement, and his family and the Bridgehead Incident remain important cases for understanding Taiwan's grassroots democratic mobilization.
Figures.figure.yutengfa.event1: His arrest sparked the Bridgehead Incident (1979)
Figures.figure.yutengfa.event2: Served as Kaohsiung county magistrate, a leader of the southern tangwai
Figures.figure.yutengfa.title: Southern Tangwai Pioneer & Catalyst of the Bridgehead Incident
Figures.figure.yuwenyi.bio: Yu Wenyi was a Qing official who served as Taiwan Prefect and directed the compilation of the Continued Revised Taiwan Prefecture Gazetteer, completed in 1764. This comprehensive administrative and geographical survey covered the full range of Taiwan's counties, indigenous communities, agricultural products, population registers, and customs. As one of the definitive official gazetteers of the Qianlong period, it synthesized earlier surveys and added fresh fieldwork observations, providing the Qing bureaucracy with the most thorough portrait of mid-Qing Taiwan society. His administrative career also encompassed efforts to improve agricultural productivity and clean up official corruption. The gazetteer remains an indispensable primary source for Qing Taiwan history.
Figures.figure.yuwenyi.event1: Directed compilation of Continued Revised Taiwan Prefecture Gazetteer in 1764
Figures.figure.yuwenyi.event2: Served as Taiwan Prefect, promoting agriculture and clean governance
Figures.figure.yuwenyi.title: Chief Compiler of the Taiwan Prefecture Gazetteer
Figures.figure.yuyonghe.bio: Yu Yonghe was a Qing official from Zhejiang who traveled to Taiwan in 1697 on an imperial commission to collect sulfur from the northern hot springs. Over three months he journeyed from Tainan north to the sulfur fields near modern Danshui, recording his observations in a diary. On his return he compiled these notes into Bihai Jiyou (Travels to the Marginal Sea), the earliest and most comprehensive firsthand Chinese-language account of Taiwan. The work describes indigenous communities of the western plains, Kavalan peoples of the northeast, and the nascent Han settler society. Yu's writing blends scholarly observation with literary sensitivity, capturing the alien terrain and unfamiliar customs with curiosity and candor. Bihai Jiyou remains an indispensable primary source for historians of early Qing Taiwan and indigenous Taiwan studies.
Figures.figure.yuyonghe.event1: 1697 sulfur mission to Danshui hot-spring fields
Figures.figure.yuyonghe.event2: Wrote Bihai Jiyou, earliest firsthand account of Taiwan
Figures.figure.yuyonghe.title: Sulfur Collector · Travel Writer
Figures.figure.zhangdajing.bio: Zhang Dajing, born around 1690 in Guangdong Province, came to Taiwan in the early eighteenth century and rose to become the most powerful interpreter (通事) mediating between Han Chinese settlers and the Pazeh indigenous group of the Anli Society (岸裡社) in the Taichung basin, accumulating in the process one of the largest landholdings in central Taiwan. He first established himself as a trader and broker in the settlements along the edge of indigenous territory, learning the Pazeh language and gaining the trust of Anli Society leaders at a time when Qing authorities relied heavily on such intermediaries to manage the volatile frontier between Han immigration and indigenous land. Zhang's decisive rise came through his promotion of the so-called 'land-for-water' arrangements (割地換水), in which he organized Han settler capital to fund the construction of irrigation channels on land controlled by the Anli Society, with indigenous communities granting long-term land rights to the investors in exchange for access to the new water infrastructure. Over several decades of such transactions, Zhang Dajing accumulated vast tracts of the fertile Taichung plain, transforming what had been the core territory of the Anli Society into Han farmland while the Pazeh people were progressively confined to smaller and more marginal areas. He simultaneously cultivated his position as the essential broker for the Anli Society in its dealings with Qing officials, helping the group obtain military commissions, land patents, and legal recognition that gave them a degree of formal protection — though critics have noted that this protection came at the cost of their land base. By the middle of the eighteenth century, Zhang Dajing and his associates had brought under cultivation a large portion of present-day Taichung and Changhua counties, a transformation of the landscape that made central Taiwan one of the most productive agricultural regions in the island. He accumulated official rank through donations to the Qing treasury and became a recognized patron of local temples and community institutions, embedding his family name in the social fabric of the Taichung region. Zhang died in 1773, leaving behind a legacy that has been interpreted in sharply divergent ways: celebrated by later Han settler communities as a visionary developer who opened central Taiwan to agriculture, and condemned by indigenous rights scholars as the architect of a systematic dispossession that destroyed the land base of the Pazeh people within a century. His story is now recognized as the archetypal case study of how Qing frontier land relations produced wealth for Han intermediaries while structurally impoverishing the indigenous societies with whom they nominally cooperated. Zhang Dajing is generally regarded as the foundational figure in the settlement history of the Taichung basin — a man whose commercial genius and political skill reshaped central Taiwan's human geography, at an irreversible cost to those who had lived there first.
Figures.figure.zhangdajing.event1: Organized the 'land-for-water' (割地換水) arrangements with the Anli Society, trading irrigation infrastructure for indigenous land rights
Figures.figure.zhangdajing.event2: Accumulated vast landholdings across the Taichung basin, transforming Anli Society territory into the most productive agricultural region in central Taiwan
Figures.figure.zhangdajing.title: Interpreter Between Han Settlers and the Anli Indigenous Society
Figures.figure.zhengchonghe.bio: Zheng Chonghe was the patriarch of the most influential gentry family in the Hsinchu area during the mid-Qing period. An immigrant from Chaozhou in Guangdong, he built the family's fortune through land reclamation and commerce. His most lasting achievement was the education of his son Zheng Yongxi (1788–1858), who in 1823 became the first native-born Taiwanese to pass the imperial jinshi examination, earning the honorific 'Pioneer Jinshi of Taiwan.' The elder Zheng's investment in his son's classical education reflects the broader ambition of first-generation settler families to transition from frontier landowners to recognized Confucian elite. The Zheng family thus embodies the transformation of Qing Taiwan's gentry from pioneering settlers to culturally accomplished literati.
Figures.figure.zhengchonghe.event1: Founded Hsinchu Zheng family through land reclamation and commerce
Figures.figure.zhengchonghe.event2: Raised son Zheng Yongxi to become Taiwan's first native-born jinshi
Figures.figure.zhengchonghe.title: Pioneering Gentry Patriarch of Hsinchu
Figures.figure.zhengjing.bio: Zheng Jing, born in 1642 in Quanzhou as the eldest son of Koxinga, ruled the Kingdom of Tungning for nearly two decades and is the central figure of independent Han Chinese rule over Taiwan in the seventeenth century. Educated in the classical tradition and trained in the military arts of his father's house, he served as the trusted garrison commander of Xiamen and Kinmen while Koxinga conducted the conquest of Taiwan. His affair with the wet nurse of his younger brother — which produced his eldest son Zheng Kezang — provoked his father's fury and an ultimately unenforced order for his execution. When Koxinga died suddenly in June 1662, a Tainan faction tried to install Koxinga's kinsman Zheng Xi in his place, but Zheng Jing crossed the strait, defeated the rival party in a short campaign, and consolidated the succession by 1663. Over the next several years the surviving Zheng coastal positions in Fujian collapsed under combined Qing-Dutch pressure, forcing him to withdraw fully to Taiwan and to make Tainan the seat of an island-based state. With the able administrator Chen Yong-hua as his chief minister, he expanded military colonies, built schools and a Confucian temple, and developed monopolies on salt and sugar that financed the regime. He cultivated commercial ties with Japan, the Spanish Philippines, and English East India Company traders, who briefly maintained a factory at Anping, embedding Taiwan deeply in the East Asian maritime economy. He maintained a defiant stance toward the Qing, repeatedly rejecting compromise proposals that would have granted him quasi-tributary status in exchange for cutting hair and adopting Qing dress. In 1673 he seized the opportunity of the Revolt of the Three Feudatories to launch a major mainland expedition, occupying portions of coastal Fujian and Guangdong for nearly seven years. Tungning's mainland gains were lost by 1680 after Qing counterattacks and the strategic isolation of his alliance, forcing him to retreat to Taiwan with a depleted military and a damaged treasury. Demoralized by the failure of the western campaign, he largely withdrew from administration in his final months and died in January 1681 at the age of 39. He is generally credited with transforming Taiwan from his father's military foothold into a functioning state with sustained agricultural, fiscal, and educational institutions, while his failed mainland gambit set the stage for the dynastic crisis that destroyed Tungning two years later.
Figures.figure.zhengjing.event1: Consolidated Tungning governance with Confucian institutions and maritime trade
Figures.figure.zhengjing.title: King of Tungning
Figures.figure.zhengkeshuang.bio: Zheng Keshuang, born in 1670 as the second son of Zheng Jing, was the third and final ruler of the Kingdom of Tungning and the last representative of the Zheng family's independent rule over Taiwan. His mother was Lady Huang, a formally recognized consort of Zheng Jing, in contrast to the irregular parentage of his elder brother Zheng Kezang. He was married while still a child to a daughter of the influential officer Feng Xifan, a bond that would prove decisive in the dynastic crisis of 1681. When his father Zheng Jing died in January 1681 and his elder brother Kezang assumed the throne, Feng Xifan and the royal clansmen quickly orchestrated a coup against Kezang and installed the twelve-year-old Keshuang in his place. He reigned as a figurehead under the regency of his father-in-law Feng Xifan and the senior commander Liu Guoxuan, with no independent authority over major policy. The court was fatally divided: Feng's faction insisted on continued resistance, while pragmatic officials began to weigh accommodation with the Qing. The Qing dynasty had meanwhile completed its consolidation of the mainland and, under the Kangxi Emperor, decided to settle the Tungning question by force. In July 1683 Liu Guoxuan's navy was destroyed by the Qing admiral Shi Lang at the Battle of Penghu, and most of the Tungning fleet was lost. With no military option remaining, Zheng Keshuang accepted the advice of his advisors and offered formal surrender to the Qing court in August 1683. The Qing court treated him generously, awarding him the hereditary noble title Duke of Haicheng and resettling him together with his family and senior officials in Beijing. He lived out the rest of his life in the Qing capital under court patronage and died there in 1707 at the age of 37. Zheng Keshuang is generally remembered not as an independent actor but as the boy-king whose surrender closed twenty-two years of Zheng family rule and inaugurated Taiwan's first incorporation into a Chinese imperial polity.
Figures.figure.zhengkeshuang.event1: Surrendered Taiwan to the Qing dynasty (1683), ending the Kingdom of Tungning
Figures.figure.zhengkeshuang.title: Last Prince of Yanping
Figures.figure.zhengkezang.bio: Zheng Kezang, born in 1664, was the eldest son of Zheng Jing and the recognized heir apparent of the Kingdom of Tungning, despite a controversial birth that initially provoked the rage of his grandfather Koxinga. His mother was the wet nurse of Zheng Jing's younger brother, and the affair that produced him was the cause of Koxinga's near-execution order against his own son, an order ultimately never carried out. Brought up at the Tungning court, he received a thorough classical education under the personal supervision of the chief minister Chen Yong-hua, who later betrothed his own daughter to the young prince. He was praised in contemporary records as resolute, demanding of his officials, and intolerant of corruption — traits that earned the loyalty of the civilian bureaucracy but the resentment of his father's brothers and the royal kinsmen. From 1673 onward, while Zheng Jing was campaigning on the mainland in alliance with the Three Feudatories revolt, the teenage Kezang served as Regent (監國), assisted by Chen Yong-hua, and effectively ran the civilian government of Taiwan for seven years. His firm management included punishment of corrupt clansmen, creating powerful enemies within the royal family, including his own uncles and the senior officer Feng Xifan. When the western campaign collapsed in 1680, Chen Yong-hua's death later that year removed his most experienced protector and weakened his political base. Zheng Jing died in January 1681 after a prolonged illness, and Zheng Kezang formally assumed the throne as heir at the age of seventeen. Within days, Feng Xifan and a coalition of royal clansmen, including Zheng Jing's brothers, denounced his legitimacy by reviving the old scandal of his parentage. They lured him into the Beiyuan Garden, where he was strangled to death, and installed his younger brother Zheng Keshuang in his place — an event later remembered as the Tungning Coup (東寧之變). His wife, denied permission to retrieve his body, refused food and committed suicide rather than survive him, a story that became a celebrated tale of marital loyalty. The coup that killed Zheng Kezang shattered the Tungning court's political cohesion and is widely regarded as the proximate cause of the kingdom's surrender to the Qing two years later.
Figures.figure.zhengkezang.event1: Murdered in the palace coup of 1681 led by Feng Xifan
Figures.figure.zhengkezang.title: Regent & Designated Heir of Tungning
Figures.figure.zhengxi.bio: Zheng Xi was a kinsman and younger contemporary of Koxinga who became the figurehead of the brief succession dispute that followed the warlord's death in 1662. He grew up within the Zheng commercial-military house and held subordinate commands during the years when Koxinga's forces operated out of southern Fujian. He accompanied the great crossing to Taiwan in 1661–1662, settling in the new Tungning territory with the bulk of the senior generals. When Koxinga died suddenly in Tainan in June 1662, the heir presumptive — Koxinga's eldest son Zheng Jing — was still stationed at Xiamen and was viewed by some on Taiwan as compromised by a notorious sexual scandal. A faction of senior officers led by Huang Zhao and Xiao Gongchen sought to circumvent Zheng Jing's accession and to install Zheng Xi as ruler of the new island domain. The party physically secured Zheng Xi in Tainan and issued proclamations in his name, presenting him as the legitimate continuation of Koxinga's mission. Zheng Jing responded by crossing the strait with his Xiamen garrison in late 1662 and routing the rival faction in a short, decisive campaign. Huang Zhao was killed and Xiao Gongchen executed, while Zheng Xi himself, having been a largely passive participant, was placed under house arrest. In the years that followed he was effectively sidelined from political life and reportedly sent back to Fujian, where he ultimately submitted to the Qing court. His later years are sparsely documented and his date of death is not reliably recorded. The episode established Zheng Jing's undisputed succession and shaped the Tungning court's lasting wariness of intra-clan rivals. Zheng Xi is remembered chiefly as the unwitting focal point of Taiwan's first dynastic crisis rather than as a ruler in his own right.
Figures.figure.zhengxi.event1: Briefly contested the succession against Zheng Jing in 1662
Figures.figure.zhengxi.title: Contender in the Succession of 1662
Figures.figure.zhengyongxi.bio: Zheng Yongxi, born in 1788 in Zhubei (竹北) in what is today Hsinchu County, became the first person born and raised on Taiwan to pass the highest level of the imperial civil service examination, earning the degree of jinshi (進士) in 1823 and winning the honorific title 'First Graduate of Taiwan' (開臺黃甲). He was of Hakka descent, raised in a family that had been in Taiwan for several generations, and his success in the notoriously competitive metropolitan examinations in Beijing — which required mastery of classical literature, history, and statecraft composition — demonstrated that the island's scholarly community had matured to a level comparable with the mainland heartland. After receiving his jinshi degree, Zheng was appointed to a series of positions in northern China, serving as a county magistrate in Hebei, where he gained practical experience in the daily administration of a heavily populated agricultural region far removed from the frontier conditions of his homeland. He returned to Taiwan after completing his mainland service and became the leading literati figure in northern Taiwan during the mid-nineteenth century, hosting examination preparation gatherings, sponsoring the construction of academies, and acting as a patron of local Confucian culture. In 1853, during the severe Zhangzhou-Quanzhou settler violence that swept northern Taiwan, Zheng composed the influential essay Persuasion to Harmony (勸和論), urging rival communities to lay down arms and restore order through Confucian moral suasion rather than continued bloodshed — a text widely circulated and credited with contributing to the eventual pacification. He also participated actively in public infrastructure projects, including the repair of irrigation channels and the maintenance of educational facilities in the Hsinchu and Zhubei region, applying the administrative skills he had acquired on the mainland to the problems of a still-developing colonial frontier. Zheng's scholarly residence in Zhubei, known as the North Gate House (北門屋), became a center of literary and intellectual life in northern Taiwan and attracted students and officials throughout the region. His poetry and prose compositions were collected and circulated, establishing him as a recognized literary figure whose work engaged themes of frontier life, Confucian ethics, and the hopes and hardships of immigrant society. He died in 1858 at the age of seventy, having spent the latter part of his life in retirement devoted to scholarship, community service, and the cultivation of a new generation of educated Taiwanese men. His jinshi examination success in 1823 is commemorated on a stone stele that still stands in Zhubei, marking the spot where news of his achievement was announced to the community. Zheng Yongxi is widely regarded as the founding figure of Taiwanese literati culture — the man whose examination success proved that Taiwan-born scholars could compete at the highest levels of the imperial system and demonstrated that the island had developed an indigenous educated class worthy of the mainland's intellectual traditions.
Figures.figure.zhengyongxi.event1: Passed the metropolitan jinshi examination in Beijing (1823), becoming the first Taiwan-born holder of the degree — honored as 'First Graduate of Taiwan' (開臺黃甲)
Figures.figure.zhengyongxi.event2: Composed Persuasion to Harmony (勸和論, 1853) during the Zhangzhou-Quanzhou settler conflicts, credited with helping restore peace in northern Taiwan
Figures.figure.zhengyongxi.title: First Native-Born Taiwanese Jinshi
Figures.figure.zhengzhilong.bio: Zheng Zhilong, born in 1604 in Nan'an County, Fujian, baptized as Nicholas Iquan and known to the Dutch as such, was the dominant Fujianese sea lord of the early seventeenth century and the father of Koxinga. As a teenager he was sent to Macao to live with relatives, where he learned Portuguese, was baptized as a Roman Catholic, and acquired the linguistic and commercial skills that would shape his later career. In the early 1620s he moved to Hirado, Japan, the principal Chinese émigré port on Kyushu, and married a Japanese woman of the Tagawa family who in 1624 gave birth to their son Zheng Sen — later Koxinga. The Dutch East India Company hired him as a Hokkien-Portuguese interpreter for their factory at Penghu and then Tayouan, giving him direct experience of European commercial and naval methods. After the death of his patron Yan Siqi in 1625, he inherited the latter's fleet and trading network and over the next three years built it into the most powerful privately commanded armed force in the East China and South China Seas. He accepted a Ming amnesty in 1628 and was appointed a senior naval commander, giving the Ming court its only effective fleet along the Fujian coast in exchange for a license to monopolize maritime commerce. In October 1633 he commanded the Ming forces that destroyed a combined Dutch and Chinese pirate fleet at the Battle of Liaoluo Bay off Quemoy, breaking the VOC's challenge to his trade hegemony and establishing his fleet as the unrivaled power of regional waters. He used his quasi-state monopoly to amass an enormous fortune from silk, sugar, copper, and silver flows between China, Japan, Manila, and the Indonesian archipelago, becoming one of the wealthiest individuals in East Asia. After the Ming dynasty's collapse in 1644 he supported the Longwu Emperor of the Southern Ming in Fuzhou and was promoted to senior generalship, while his son Koxinga rose to prominence at the same court. In 1646 he abruptly accepted a Qing offer of surrender against the strong objections of his son and was taken to Beijing under nominal ennoblement but effective detention. He was held in the Qing capital for fifteen years and was executed by the Shunzhi court in 1661, partly in retaliation for his son's continuing armed resistance. Zheng Zhilong is generally remembered as the architect of the maritime power that his son would later use to conquer Dutch Taiwan, a figure whose biography uniquely fuses Hokkien trade, Japanese marriage, Catholic conversion, Dutch service, Ming office, and Qing detention.
Figures.figure.zhengzhilong.event1: Defeated the VOC fleet at the Battle of Liaoluo Bay (1633)
Figures.figure.zhengzhilong.title: Sea Lord of the South China Sea
Figures.figure.zhimuliu.bio: Zhimuliu was an eighteenth-century chieftain of the Saisiyat indigenous people of the Hsinchu-Miaoli mountain borderlands. During a period when Han settler expansion was pressing into the foothills of northwestern Taiwan and Qing officials were seeking to regulate the 'savage boundary,' Zhimuliu navigated the complex ethnic frontier as a tribal leader — defending Saisiyat territory from encroachment while engaging in pragmatic diplomacy with Qing authorities. The Saisiyat occupy an ecologically and politically squeezed position between the larger Atayal to the north and the advancing Han frontier to the west, and Zhimuliu's leadership represented the delicate balancing act required for a smaller mountain group to survive in this competitive environment.
Figures.figure.zhimuliu.event1: Served as Saisiyat chief in Hsinchu-Miaoli mountains, navigating the aboriginal-Han frontier
Figures.figure.zhimuliu.event2: Represented Saisiyat survival strategy between Atayal and Han pressures
Figures.figure.zhimuliu.title: Saisiyat Chief
Figures.figure.zhouzhongxuan.bio: Zhou Zhongxuan served as magistrate of Zhuluó County (modern Chiayi) during the early Qing period and oversaw the compilation of the Zhuluó County Gazetteer, completed in 1717 — one of the earliest county-level gazetteers of Taiwan. The work provides irreplaceable primary source data on the geography, indigenous communities, Han settlements, agricultural production, and social customs of southern and central Taiwan. Zhou also promoted agricultural settlement, established charity schools, and worked to maintain order between Han settlers and Siraya communities. His gazetteer became a foundational reference for subsequent administrators and historians studying early Qing colonization of central Taiwan.
Figures.figure.zhouzhongxuan.event1: Compiled Zhuluó County Gazetteer in 1717, one of Taiwan's earliest county gazetteers
Figures.figure.zhouzhongxuan.event2: Promoted agriculture and schools, stabilizing the Chiayi region
Figures.figure.zhouzhongxuan.title: Zhuluó Magistrate · Gazetteer Compiler
Figures.figure.zhuangdatian.bio: Zhuang Datian was a Zhangzhou-origin settler who commanded the southern front of the Lin Shuangwen Rebellion, one of the largest uprisings in Qing-era Taiwan. When Lin Shuangwen launched his rebellion in central Taiwan in late 1786, Zhuang mobilized Tiandihui networks in the Fengshan area, captured the Fengshan county seat, and coordinated north-south pressure on the Qing administration. The court dispatched General Fu Kangan with a large expeditionary force in 1787; Zhuang Datian was cornered in the Hengchun peninsula and killed in 1788. The rebellion they co-led left a lasting mark on Qing Taiwan policy, prompting reforms in troop deployment and tighter regulation of secret societies.
Figures.figure.zhuangdatian.event1: Led southern uprising in 1786, capturing Fengshan county seat
Figures.figure.zhuangdatian.event2: Cornered and killed by Qing forces in 1788
Figures.figure.zhuangdatian.title: Southern Commander of the Lin Shuangwen Rebellion
Figures.figure.zhushugui.bio: Zhu Shugui was a late-Ming imperial prince enfeoffed as Prince of Ningjing, born in 1617 into a branch of the Liao royal line that traced its descent from the founding emperor of the Ming, Zhu Yuanzhang. After the fall of Beijing to Qing forces, he followed the Southern Ming court into exile across southern China, attaching himself to a succession of loyalist regimes and accepting an honorary military supervisorship at the Fuzhou court. In 1648 he joined Koxinga's maritime forces during the southern Ming retreat and from then on lived under the protection of the Zheng resistance along the southeast China coast. He crossed to Taiwan with Koxinga's expedition in the 1660s and was provided with royal fields, tenant farmers, and a princely household by the Zheng administration, becoming the highest-ranking Ming nobleman within the Tungning Kingdom. He established the Ningjing Princely Mansion in the Xiding ward of Tainan and represented Ming ritual and cultural legitimacy in the ceremonies and ancestral sacrifices of the Zheng regime. Koxinga and his son Zheng Jing both treated him with the deference due to a senior Ming relative, making him the living embodiment of the Tungning Kingdom's claim to Ming legitimacy. After Zheng Jing's death in 1681 he witnessed the Tungning coup that installed the boy king Zheng Keshuang and watched the loyalist banner grow increasingly hollow as the court fell under factional rule. Following the catastrophic defeat at the Battle of Penghu in July 1683 and the Tungning court's decision to surrender to the Qing, he refused to shave his head and adopt Manchu dress, regarding such an act as a betrayal of his Ming ancestors. On the eve of the surrender he summoned his five consorts — Lady Yuan, Lady Wang, Xiujie, Meijie, and Hejie — and informed them of his decision to die for the dynasty; the five women hanged themselves before him. He then distributed his lands to the local peasantry, burned the deeds to his property, dressed in full Ming court attire, and hanged himself at the Ningjing Mansion at the age of sixty-six. After taking the city, the Qing admiral Shi Lang respectfully preserved the mansion by converting it into the Grand Mazu Temple, and the burial site of the five consorts came to be venerated as the Temple of the Five Concubines, which remains an active place of worship in Tainan today. Zhu Shugui is generally remembered as the last representative of the Ming imperial house to die in exile for the dynasty, and as an emblematic figure in early Taiwanese history through whom the personal honor of dying with the fallen state was given visible form.
Figures.figure.zhushugui.event1: Hanged himself on the eve of Tungning's surrender in 1683, accompanied in death by his five consorts
Figures.figure.zhushugui.title: Ming Imperial Prince of Ningjing
Figures.figure.zhuyigui.bio: Zhu Yigui, born in 1690 in Changtai County, Fujian, migrated to Taiwan around 1713 and settled in the rural Luohanmen area near present-day Neimen, Kaohsiung. He earned his living raising ducks on the lowland marshes and acquired local fame for his skill in herding the flocks with simple gestures, a reputation that gave rise to his later popular nickname, the Duck Emperor (鴨母王). In 1720 the acting prefect Wang Zhen and his sons imposed harsh new levies and arbitrary punishments on settlers, igniting widespread grievance among Hokkien immigrants in southern Taiwan. In April 1721 Zhu rallied a band of followers in Luohanmen, raised the banner of Ming restoration, and within two weeks routed Qing garrisons across the southern plains. He was joined by a separate Hakka force under Du Junying from the Pingtung plain, and the combined armies entered the prefectural city of Tainan with little resistance. Acclaimed by his followers as the rightful descendant of the Ming imperial Zhu line, he assumed the title King of Central Restoration (中興王) and issued proclamations from a hastily organized court at Tainan. The alliance quickly fractured along ethnic lines, with the Hokkien and Hakka contingents fighting each other over titles, share of plunder, and political precedence. The Qing court dispatched the naval commander Shi Shibiao — son of the conqueror of Tungning — and the general Lan Tingzhen with reinforcements from Fujian and Penghu within weeks of the news reaching Beijing. The internally divided rebels were defeated in a series of clashes through May and June 1721, and Zhu was captured at Goutou village near present-day Jiayi. He was transported in a cage to Beijing, paraded before the Kangxi court, and executed in 1722, his head subsequently displayed in the southern provinces as a warning. The Qing tightened administration of Taiwan in the wake of the revolt, building walled cities and adding new sub-prefectures while still maintaining strict bans on family migration from the mainland. Zhu Yigui's uprising — the first major Han Chinese rebellion in Qing Taiwan — established the long-running characterization of the island as a chronically unruly frontier and prefigured the more catastrophic revolts of the Lin Shuangwen and Dai Chaochun generations.
Figures.figure.zhuyigui.event1: Led the Zhu Yigui Rebellion of 1721 ('Duck Emperor' uprising)
Figures.figure.zhuyigui.title: Rebel Leader

Images.image.americanLiaisonGroup.description: Members of the American military liaison group photographed in Taiwan. The group was responsible for observing and reporting on post-war Taiwan's political and social conditions. Their reports became essential American archives for understanding this period.
Images.image.andoRikichiSigning.description: The historic moment of Ando Rikichi, Japan's last Governor-General of Taiwan, signing the instrument of surrender, marking the formal end of Japan's fifty-year colonial rule over Taiwan.
Images.image.antiSecessionLawProtest.descriptio: 26 March 2005: the "Democracy, Peace, Protect Taiwan" rally in Taipei drew an estimated one million demonstrators against the Anti-Secession Law passed days earlier by the People's Republic of China's National People's Congress.
Images.image.cairoConference.description: November 1943: Chiang Kai-shek, Roosevelt, and Churchill photographed during the Cairo Conference. The Cairo Declaration issued afterward stated that Japan should return Taiwan to the Republic of China.
Images.image.chenShuiBianInauguration.descripti: 20 May 2000: Chen Shui-bian of the Democratic Progressive Party takes the oath of office as the tenth-term President of the Republic of China, marking the first peaceful transfer of executive power between parties in Taiwan's history.
Images.image.chenShuiBianInauguration.source: Office of the President, Republic of China (Taiwan)
Images.image.defenseLawyersGroupPhoto.descripti: Group photograph of the Formosa defense attorneys including Chen Shui-bian, Frank Hsieh, and Su Tseng-chang, whose courtroom careers launched Taiwan's next generation of democratic leadership.
Images.image.dominicanMissionNorth.description: A Dominican missionary manuscript recording vocabulary and baptismal notes among the Basay and Kavalan peoples of northern Formosa in the 1630s.
Images.image.dominicanMissionNorth.source: Archivo de la Provincia del Santísimo Rosario, Ávila
Images.image.dppFoundingGrandHotel.description: Founding meeting of the Democratic Progressive Party at Taipei's Grand Hotel, September 28, 1986, where 135 Dangwai activists announced the new party in defiance of the party ban.
Images.image.dutchLandingFormosa.description: 1624: Dutch East India Company vessels arriving at the Taiwan Strait, depicted in a seventeenth-century engraving. After withdrawing from the Pescadores, the VOC fleet made landfall on the sandy peninsula of Tayouan.
Images.image.ecfaSigningCeremony.description: 29 June 2010: representatives of Taiwan's Straits Exchange Foundation and Beijing's Association for Relations Across the Taiwan Straits sign the Economic Cooperation Framework Agreement in Chongqing, the most comprehensive cross-strait trade pact to date.
Images.image.ecfaSigningCeremony.source: Mainland Affairs Council, Republic of China (Taiwan)
Images.image.februaryIncidentMemorial.descripti: The 228 Peace Memorial Monument in Taipei's 228 Peace Park, dedicated in 1995 alongside President Lee Teng-hui's formal apology — the first state acknowledgment of the 1947 massacre and a foundational gesture of Taiwan's transitional-justice work.
Images.image.formosaMagazineCover.description: Cover of Formosa Magazine's inaugural issue, August 1979, the flagship publication of the Dangwai movement whose nationwide branches coordinated pre-Kaohsiung Incident democratic advocacy.
Images.image.formosaMilitaryTribunal.descriptio: Military tribunal hearing of the Formosa defendants, March 1980 — the first sedition trial opened to domestic press, where defendants turned the dock into a democratic pulpit.
Images.image.fortSanSalvador.description: A seventeenth-century Spanish plan of Fort San Salvador on Heping Island in Keelung Harbor, the northernmost stronghold of the Spanish empire in East Asia.
Images.image.fortSantoDomingo.description: Fort Santo Domingo overlooking the Tamsui River, built by the Spanish in 1628 and later rebuilt by the Dutch after 1642 as the \"Red Hair Fort\".
Images.image.fortSantoDomingo.source: New Taipei City Government, Tamsui Historical Museum
Images.image.fortZeelandiaMap.description: A mid-seventeenth-century Dutch survey map of Fort Zeelandia and the surrounding Tayouan bay, showing the fortress layout, outer redoubts, and Han settlements along the inner lagoon.
Images.image.greenIslandPoliticalPrisonYard.des: Aerial view of the Green Island Reform-through-Labor Prison, where thousands of White Terror political prisoners were held in stone barracks ringed by barbed wire, 1960s.
Images.image.hakkaReturnMotherTongueMarch.descr: The Hakka "Return My Mother Tongue" march of December 1988, demanding the end of Mandarin-only broadcasting and the restoration of Hakka in schools and public media.
Images.image.homareNoGumpu1938.description: Record sleeve of Homare no Gumpu (1938), the Japanese-language military-song rewriting of Hō-iā-hoe (Rainy Night Flower).
Images.image.huangHsinchiehRally.description: Formosa Magazine publisher Huang Hsin-chieh addressing a Dangwai campaign rally in southern Taiwan, autumn 1979, weeks before the Kaohsiung Incident.
Images.image.indigenousRecognitionCeremony.desc: A formal recognition ceremony for one of Taiwan's sixteen officially acknowledged indigenous nations, a milestone of the post-democratization reclassification that replaced the single "mountain compatriots" category with pluralistic ethnic standing.
Images.image.indigenousRecognitionCeremony.sour: Council of Indigenous Peoples, Republic of China (Taiwan)
Images.image.julyFifteenthNewspaperFrontPage.de: Front pages of major Taiwanese newspapers on July 15, 1987, announcing the lifting of martial law and the impending end of newspaper and party bans.
Images.image.june1950ExecutionNotice.descriptio: Public execution notice from June 1950 posted outside the Ma-chang-ting execution ground at Liuzhangli, Taipei, during the single largest execution wave of the White Terror.
Images.image.kaohsiungIncidentRallyNight.descri: Torch-lit crowd at the Kaohsiung Human Rights Day rally, December 10, 1979, moments before riot police encircled the marchers with tear gas and armored vehicles.
Images.image.kominkaPropagandaPoster.descriptio: Government-General propaganda poster for cultural control during the Kōminka campaign.
Images.image.koxingaPortrait.description: A formal portrait of Zheng Chenggong (Koxinga), the Ming loyalist commander who in 1661 led the expedition across the Taiwan Strait and established the first Han Chinese regime on the island.
Images.image.koxingaShrineTainan.description: The Koxinga Shrine in Tainan, originally built in 1663 as a family ancestral hall and later elevated to an official state shrine — the oldest continuously venerated memorial to the founder of the Kingdom of Tungning.
Images.image.landdagAssembly.description: A Dutch illustration of the annual landdag assembly at Sakam, where indigenous village elders received rattan staffs of office from the VOC governor in a public ritual of submission.
Images.image.macArthurMemorandum.description: General Order No. 1 issued by MacArthur designated Chiang Kai-shek to accept the surrender of Japanese forces in Taiwan on behalf of the Allies. This memorandum became one of the core documents in the dispute over Taiwan's post-war political status.
Images.image.mattauPunitiveExpedition.descripti: A depiction of the 1636 VOC punitive expedition against Mattau and allied villages, following the armed resistance of 1635–1636 against Dutch taxation policies.
Images.image.nationalityRestorationOrder.descri: The nationality restoration order issued by the Nationalist government in January 1946, collectively conferring ROC nationality on all Taiwanese. The legal validity of this order under international law remains disputed to this day.
Images.image.ongIoktek.description: Ong Iok-tek's Republic of China Resident Identity Card (June 1947). Photographed at the Ong Iok-tek Memorial Museum, where it is on display
Images.image.peacefulTransferCeremony.descripti: Outgoing President Lee Teng-hui hands the seal of state to President-elect Chen Shui-bian at the Presidential Office Building — a symbolic gesture that formalized Taiwan's first democratic transfer of power between rival parties.
Images.image.presidentialElection2000Ballot.des: The official ballot for the 2000 Republic of China presidential election, listing the five candidate pairings including Chen Shui-bian, James Soong, and Lien Chan — the three-way race that ended more than half a century of Kuomintang rule.
Images.image.presidentialElection2000Ballot.sou: Central Election Commission, Republic of China
Images.image.shiLangPortrait.description: A formal portrait of Admiral Shi Lang, the former Zheng lieutenant who defected to the Qing and, twenty years later, led the naval campaign that conquered Taiwan for the Kangxi Emperor in 1683.
Images.image.sinckanManuscript.description: A Sinckan Manuscript — a land contract written in the romanized script devised by Dutch missionaries to record the Siraya language, preserving the earliest written voice of Formosa's indigenous communities.
Images.image.sirayaSinckanContract.description: A bilingual Sinckan-script land contract between a Siraya villager and a Han settler, bearing both the romanized Siraya text and Chinese characters — a rare document of indigenous literacy.
Images.image.sirayaSinckanContract.source: Institute of Taiwan History, Academia Sinica
Images.image.sunflowerMovementOccupation.descri: March 2014: students and activists occupy the Legislative Yuan chamber for twenty-four days in protest against the Cross-Strait Service Trade Agreement, in what became known as the Sunflower Movement — the largest civic occupation in Taiwan's democratic history.
Images.image.surrenderCeremony.description: October 25, 1945: The surrender ceremony held at Taipei Public Hall (now Zhongshan Hall). Chen Yi, representing the ROC government, accepted the surrender of Japanese Governor-General Ando Rikichi.
Images.image.taiwaneseIdentitySurveyChart.descr: Longitudinal chart of Taiwanese/Chinese identity published by the Election Study Center at National Chengchi University, tracking responses from 1992 to the present and documenting the decisive shift toward an exclusively Taiwanese self-identification.
Images.image.taiwaneseIdentitySurveyChart.sourc: Election Study Center, National Chengchi University
Images.image.taiyuRevivalClassroom.description: A primary school mother-tongue class offering instruction in Taiwanese Hokkien (Taiyu), part of the post-2001 native-language curriculum that reversed decades of Mandarin-only schooling and reopened space for the island's local languages.
Images.image.taiyuRevivalClassroom.source: Ministry of Education, Republic of China (Taiwan)
Images.image.tengYuhsienLateYears.description: Photograph of Teng Yu-hsien during his time as a training officer at Chiung-lin Public School in Hsinchu (circa 1942).
Images.image.tengYuhsienLateYears.source: Teng Yu-hsien Cultural and Educational Foundation
Images.image.transitionalJusticeCommissionInaug: May 2018: commissioners of the newly established Transitional Justice Commission are sworn in at the Executive Yuan, taking on the mandate to open political archives, remove authoritarian symbols, and redress wrongful convictions from the martial-law era.
Images.image.tuntianMilitaryColonyMap.descripti: A reconstructed map of the tuntian military-colony allotments across the southwestern plains under Koxinga's administration, marking regimental garrisons whose names — Zuozhen, Xinying, Youwu — endure in the landscape today.
Images.image.wangChungHuiCairoDiary.description: Wang Chung-hui's diary manuscript from the Cairo Conference, documenting the Chinese delegation's internal discussions and diplomatic negotiations regarding Taiwan's disposition.
Images.image.wartimeGramophoneParlor.descriptio: A scene of gramophone listening at a café in Dadaocheng during the late war years.
Images.image.whiteTerrorRehabilitationCertifica: A certificate of rehabilitation issued to a White Terror survivor under the compensation and redress statutes of the 2000s, formally voiding a martial-law-era conviction and restoring the bearer's civic record.
Images.image.yinHaiguangSeditionVerdict.descrip: Military tribunal verdict in the Lei Chen case, 1960, sentencing the Free China Journal publisher and philosopher Yin Haiguang's associates under the Statute for the Punishment of Sedition.
Images.image.zeelandiaBastionView.description: A seventeenth-century perspective view of Fort Zeelandia, showing the masonry bastions, inner citadel, and the merchant town of Tayouan extending along the sandbar.
Images.image.zeelandiaBastionView.source: Atlas of Mutual Heritage, The Netherlands
Images.image.zeelandiaSiegeMap.description: A Dutch military map of the 1661–1662 siege of Fort Zeelandia, showing Zheng fleet positions, siege batteries, and the outlying fortifications of Tayouan during the nine-month campaign.
Images.image.zeelandiaSurrenderTreaty.descripti: The articles of surrender signed on 1 February 1662 by Governor Frederick Coyett and Koxinga's envoys, ending thirty-eight years of Dutch rule on Formosa.
Images.image.zeelandiaSurrenderTreaty.source: Dutch East India Company Archives (VOC), Nationaal Archief

Volumes.perspective.228.chiang.label: Chiang Kai-shek
Volumes.perspective.228.chiang.narrative:
Chiang Kai-shek's diary entries during the 228 Incident reveal a leader preoccupied with the Chinese Civil War on the mainland, viewing Taiwan's unrest through the lens of communist agitation and threats to national stability. In his March 2 entry, he noted the disturbance with concern but framed it as a matter requiring firm restoration of order.

By March 5, Chiang had decided to dispatch troops from the mainland. His diary entries suggest he believed the situation was being exploited by communist infiltrators and local opportunists. The military crackdown that followed — resulting in thousands of civilian deaths — was recorded in his diary with clinical detachment. For Chiang, Taiwan was a strategic rear base that could not be allowed to fall into chaos while the existential battle against the Communists raged on the mainland. The human cost of pacification barely registered against the calculus of national survival.
Volumes.perspective.228.civilians.label: Taiwanese Civilians
Volumes.perspective.228.civilians.narrative:
For ordinary Taiwanese, the 228 Incident began as a spontaneous protest against a corrupt tobacco monopoly agent's assault on a widow, but quickly became the eruption of months of accumulated grievances. The uprising that spread across the island was not a communist plot — it was the desperate voice of a people who had watched their hopes for a better future under Chinese rule dissolve into corruption, inflation, and discrimination.

The military crackdown that arrived on March 8 was indiscriminate and devastating. Soldiers rounded up intellectuals, local leaders, lawyers, and doctors — anyone who might organize resistance or represent the Taiwanese voice. Entire families were destroyed. The elite diaries of this period record the terror in agonizing detail: neighbors disappearing in the night, bodies floating in Keelung Harbor, the silence that descended over communities gripped by fear. The 228 Incident became the founding trauma of modern Taiwanese identity — a wound that would remain unspoken for decades under martial law.
Volumes.perspective.228.us.label: American Observers
Volumes.perspective.228.us.narrative:
American diplomats stationed in Taiwan provided some of the earliest outside documentation of the 228 Incident. Vice Consul George Kerr, who had deep knowledge of Taiwan from his wartime intelligence work, sent alarming cables to Washington describing the systematic targeting of Taiwanese elites and the scale of military violence.

The US perspective was shaped by Cold War calculations. While American officials were disturbed by the brutality, Taiwan's strategic importance as an anti-communist bulwark limited Washington's willingness to intervene. Kerr's detailed reports — later published in his book 'Formosa Betrayed' — documented the gap between Chiang's government rhetoric and the reality on the ground. The American diplomatic record reveals a pattern of concern tempered by realpolitik: human rights weighed against geopolitical necessity, with the latter consistently prevailing.
Volumes.perspective.assembly1946.banshan.label: The Broker in the Speaker's Chair
Volumes.perspective.assembly1946.banshan.narrati:
When the provincial assembly convened, the man the localities expected was Lin Hsien-tang — leader of the petition movement for a Taiwanese parliament under Japanese rule and the summit of the island's civic prestige. The speaker elected was Huang Chao-chin: born in Tainan, educated in Japan and the United States, a wartime officer of China's diplomatic service, a "half-mountain" man who spoke Mandarin and understood how Nanking worked. Deputy speaker Li Wan-chu had mainland credentials of his own.
