To many people the outcome explained something: the new order was willing to use Taiwanese, provided they were Taiwanese it could trust.

From inside that broker's position, matters were less simple. They had to keep the chamber's questioning within what the Executive Office could tolerate while translating public grievance into documents officials would read; every successful mediation looked like weakness to islanders, and every principled stand looked like provincial self-interest to their superiors. After 1947 the role became both more important and more humiliating. As for the man passed over, Lin Hsien-tang left for Tokyo in 1949 on the stated grounds of medical treatment, never returned, and died there in 1956. The first fork in postwar Taiwanese politics lies in the distance between where those two men ended up.
Volumes.perspective.assembly1946.councilors.narr:
In 1946 more than eleven hundred candidates ran for thirty seats in the provincial assembly — the first time Taiwanese chose by ballot who would speak for them. Once the chamber opened on May 1, it quickly became the most watched room on the island: Kuo Kuo-chi interrogated officials so ferociously that he was nicknamed "Kuo the Cannon," and Wang Tien-teng, who took as his motto the greatest happiness of the greatest number, pressed session after session on the Monopoly Bureau's books, the Trade Bureau's sugar and rice, police discipline, and the proportion of mainlanders in official appointments. Newspapers printed the questions and answers verbatim, and readers saw officials publicly contradicted for the first time.

Then they discovered how much institutional distance lay between the questions they could ask and the things they could change. The assembly's powers were to resolve and to recommend; the Administrative Executive Office was free not to adopt. Budget, personnel, monopoly, and trade all stayed in the Office's hands. By the end of 1946 the tone of interrogation had shifted from inquiry to warning, and the words Wang Tien-teng spoke in that chamber became, a year later, the text of the demands issued by the February 28 Settlement Committee. He was killed in March 1947 and Kuo Kuo-chi was arrested; most of the boldest speakers in that room paid for it during the incident. The first provincial assembly thus left a contradictory record: the freest place for speech in postwar Taiwan was also the place with the least power.
Volumes.perspective.assembly1946.executive.label: The Administrative Executive Office
Volumes.perspective.assembly1946.executive.narra:
The Executive Office had its own consistent account of this arrangement, and did not regard it as a fig leaf. Under the central legal framework of the day the country was still in the period of political tutelage; provincial assemblies everywhere were consultative and supervisory bodies, and Taiwan had not been singled out for a lesser grade. If anything Taiwan had completed a three-tier indirect election in 1946, ahead of many mainland provinces. Chen Yi said repeatedly in public that what he was building was the preparation for self-government: spread Mandarin and civic training first, transfer real authority in stages, and do not rush it.

The question of appointments had an official answer too. The Office's position was that trained personnel were lacking — Taiwanese officials had mostly held junior posts under the colonial system, and statutes, official documents, and the entire judicial apparatus were being converted to Chinese practice, which islanders could not take up overnight; senior posts therefore went mainly to mainlanders as a transitional measure. On paper each of these reasons holds. Together they yielded a single conclusion: Taiwanese could not yet govern themselves. What the chamber of 1946 kept asking, underneath every question, was how much longer. The Office never produced a timetable, and that absence was the political precondition of what happened in 1947.
Volumes.perspective.assembly1946.voters.label: Voters and the Localities
Volumes.perspective.assembly1946.voters.narrativ:
At the township level, the elections of 1946 were a noisy and very concrete affair. The system was three-tier and indirect: township and municipal representatives were elected first, those representatives chose the county and city councilors, and the councilors in turn chose the provincial assembly. Turnout at the first tier was high, and villagers gathered in temple courtyards to argue over candidates for the first time; the consultative councils of the Japanese period had been only partly elective and thinly empowered, and this time, at least nominally, people were choosing their own.

Indirect election also taught everyone something else, quickly: what decided the outcome were the few dozen votes at the tier above. Influential families, the brokers of irrigation associations and farmers' associations, the men who could host a banquet and settle a dispute — these carried the most weight in such a structure. Nineteen forty-six is therefore both the starting point of electoral politics in Taiwan and the starting point of local factions, which are two faces of one thing. For the next half century that structure would be used again and again: elections held from the bottom up, gathered at each tier into a few hands, and producing exactly the sort of figures the level above found easiest to deal with.
Volumes.perspective.cairo.allies.label: The Allies and the State Department
Volumes.perspective.cairo.allies.narrative:
In Washington's files, what came out of Cairo was a press communiqué: unsigned, never submitted for ratification, carrying the force of a statement of intent. General Order No. 1 of September 2, 1945 likewise dealt only with the arrangements for surrender — who would disarm Japanese forces in which zone — and transferred no sovereignty of its own. By the wartime practice of the Allied powers, final title to territory waited on the peace treaty with Japan; until then an occupying power administers, it does not own.

That technical distinction turned intensely political four years later. The Nationalist government fell back to Taiwan in 1949; the Korean War broke out on June 25, 1950, and two days later Truman ordered the Seventh Fleet into the Taiwan Strait and declared that the determination of the island's future status must await the restoration of security in the Pacific, a peace settlement with Japan, or consideration by the United Nations. In the San Francisco Peace Treaty signed on September 8, 1951, Japan renounced all right, title, and claim to Formosa and the Pescadores — without naming a recipient; the Treaty of Taipei of 1952 used the same formula. The sentence written at Cairo has stayed where it was ever since: a promise, and one that no treaty ever countersigned.
Volumes.perspective.cairo.islanders.label: The People on the Island
Volumes.perspective.cairo.islanders.narrative:
When the Cairo Declaration was published in December 1943, almost no one in Taiwan had a chance to read it. The wartime press was censored by the Government-General, the island was in the middle of imperialization campaigns and conscription drives, and for most people the first certain news of their situation came at noon on August 15, 1945, with the Emperor's broadcast. Once word spread, welcome committees appeared everywhere: in Taipei, local gentry formed a preparatory committee to greet the Nationalist government, and Lin Hsien-tang and others travelled north to take part; slogans went up rewritten in Chinese characters, and people learned, at short notice, to sing an unfamiliar anthem. When the 70th Army came ashore at Keelung on October 17, the crowds filled the road.

The diaries of those same people, however, hold another register as well. No one had ever asked them when their nationality would change, or who would decide it. From the Treaty of Shimonoseki in 1895 to Cairo in 1943 and Taipei in 1945, the island changed hands twice, and both times the transfer was completed at a conference table somewhere else. In 1945 that feeling was drowned out by expectation; it surfaced only a year or so later — and by then people were talking less about sovereignty than about the price of rice, about work, and about whether they could speak in their own language.
Volumes.perspective.cairo.japan.label: Tokyo and the Government-General
Volumes.perspective.cairo.japan.narrative:
Japan's position in 1945 and its position in 1952 were two different things. When the imperial government accepted the Potsdam Proclamation in August 1945 and signed the instrument of surrender on September 2, what it understood itself to be conceding was disarmament and the surrender of administration. On October 25, Ando Rikichi — the nineteenth governor-general of Taiwan and commander of the Tenth Area Army — signed the receipt at the Taipei Public Hall, the Government-General was reorganized into the Taiwan Provincial Administrative Executive Office, and Japanese technical officials stayed at their desks until the handover was complete. Ando himself died in a detention cell in Shanghai in April 1946.

The formal renunciation of rights did not come until the San Francisco Peace Treaty of September 8, 1951, in force from April 28, 1952. As the Foreign Ministry read it then, Japan gave up Formosa and the Pescadores but had no standing to name a recipient and offered no view on where title went. Through 1946 more than four hundred thousand Japanese soldiers and civilians were repatriated in batches from Keelung and Kaohsiung, each allowed a fixed limit of baggage and cash; families born on the island who had never seen the home country left the place they had always called "the main island." For them, fifty years of rule ended before the documents, not after them.
Volumes.perspective.cairo.roc.label: The Chinese Delegation
Volumes.perspective.cairo.roc.narrative:
For the Chinese delegation that flew into Cairo in November 1943, Taiwan was one of the things the trip was meant to bring home. Chiang Kai-shek attended with Soong Mei-ling and Wang Chung-hui, secretary-general of the Supreme National Defense Council, and the diaries kept by that party record a process of drafting word by word: the Chinese side insisted that "Taiwan and the Pescadores" be named in the document rather than folded into vague talk of a postwar settlement. The Cairo Declaration, released on December 1, stated that the territories Japan had stolen from China, "such as Manchuria, Formosa, and the Pescadores, shall be restored to the Republic of China"; Article 8 of the Potsdam Proclamation of July 26, 1945 confirmed that the Cairo terms would be carried out. As Chungking and then Nanking understood it, the legal question was settled there.

What remained was the mechanics of the handover. General Order No. 1, issued by the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers on September 2, 1945, designated Chiang Kai-shek to receive the surrender of Japanese forces in Taiwan, the Pescadores, and the China theater; on October 25 Chen Yi presided over the surrender ceremony at the Taipei Public Hall, and that same day the Administrative Executive Office proclaimed Taiwan's retrocession, a date kept as a holiday every year thereafter. For this government, October 25 was not the beginning of an occupation but the completion of a return — which is why every later claim that Taiwan's status was "undetermined" would sound to it not merely like a legal argument but like a denial of its standing as a victor.
Volumes.perspective.chengnanjung.after.label: Those Who Came After
Volumes.perspective.chengnanjung.after.narrative:
On May 19, 1989, Cheng Nan-jung was buried. As the funeral procession reached Chieh-shou Road in front of the Presidential Office, Chan Yi-hua set himself alight at the barricades and died. He was thirty-two. Two fires in two months turned freedom of expression from an abstract principle into something concrete, and lethal.

What followed moved slowly. In 1991 the Independent Taiwan Association case brought fresh arrests of students and researchers under Article 100, triggering class boycotts across the island; academics from Academia Sinica and activists formed the Alliance of 100 Action and demanded the clause's repeal through sit-ins and hunger strikes. The amendment passed on May 15, 1992. In 2012 the Tainan city government was the first to designate April 7 as Freedom of Expression Day, and in 2016 the Executive Yuan made it a national commemoration. From one man striking a light in an editor's room to a country marking that day on its calendar took twenty-seven years.
Volumes.perspective.chengnanjung.cheng.label: Cheng Nan-jung Himself
Volumes.perspective.chengnanjung.cheng.narrative:
Cheng Nan-jung was the son of a mainlander from Fuzhou, born in Yilan and raised in Taipei. In 1984 he founded Freedom Era Weekly under the masthead "We fight for one hundred percent freedom of expression". To defeat suspension orders he applied in advance for a stack of publishing licences and rotated through them — ban one title and the next week the same magazine appeared under another name. It was banned repeatedly and never actually stopped.

In December 1988 he printed the Draft Constitution of the Republic of Taiwan, written by Hsu Shih-kai. In January 1989 the High Prosecutors Office issued a summons on suspicion of sedition. He refused to appear, and said publicly: the Kuomintang cannot arrest me, it can only take my corpse. He then shut himself inside the editor-in-chief's room at the magazine, and stayed there seventy-one days with petrol on hand. On April 7 the police came to take him by force; as they broke through the door he set the petrol alight and burned to death. He was forty-one. What he meant to prove was quite simple: he did not recognize this government's jurisdiction over speech.
Volumes.perspective.chengnanjung.police.label: The Officers at the Door
Volumes.perspective.chengnanjung.police.narrativ:
From the enforcement side this was a procedurally complete case: the High Prosecutors Office held that printing a draft constitution for a new state constituted preparation to overthrow the government under Article 100 of the Criminal Code; the summons went unanswered, a warrant was issued, and the police executed it as the law provided. The precinct running the operation had arranged fire and ambulance cover in advance and knew there was petrol inside. Their assessment was that it was a posture meant to deter.

The assessment was wrong, and the cost of being wrong exposed the whole legal construction. Article 100 criminalized intent and expression, so that a draft constitution was enough to make a man a preparatory offender in sedition. Under a clause like that, an officer can be lawful at every step and the result is still the power of the state deployed against an article in a magazine. In May 1992 the Legislative Yuan amended Article 100 and removed peaceful expression from its reach. After that, what Cheng Nan-jung had been prosecuted for was no longer a crime.
Volumes.perspective.chengnanjung.staff.label: The People at the Magazine
Volumes.perspective.chengnanjung.staff.narrative:
Through the seventy-one days of the self-confinement, the magazine kept publishing. Staff took shifts at the stairwell to turn back anyone who might come up; some went out on stories, some handled distribution, and the editor-in-chief went on writing copy and setting headlines from inside. They knew there was petrol in that room. They had argued with him about it. None of them really believed the day would come.

On the morning of April 7 a large police detail came up the stairs. From outside the door his colleagues heard him lock it, and then the fire. His wife, Yeh Chu-lan, was downstairs at the time. She left her work afterwards and went into politics, serving as a legislator, then as minister of transportation and head of the Hakka Affairs Council, and in one setting after another she has said the same thing: she does not want her husband's death romanticized. The scorched editor's room was preserved exactly as it was, and is now the Nylon Cheng Memorial Museum.
Volumes.perspective.chenwencheng.america.label: American Academia and Congress
Volumes.perspective.chenwencheng.america.narrati:
The scale of the American reaction exceeded anything Taipei had anticipated. Carnegie Mellon publicly demanded an investigation, scholars at universities across the country signed open letters, Congress held hearings, and for years afterwards returned to Taiwan's human-rights record — it was in this period that the Kuomintang's practice of placing "professional students" on American campuses to monitor Taiwanese students was brought into the open.

The case also redefined what it meant to be a Taiwanese student abroad. People realized that a sentence spoken in Pittsburgh could be recorded, reported, and turn up years later in Taipei as a summons. The fear crossed the Pacific — and in crossing it pushed scattered hometown associations and student societies into organizing. Most of the congressional hearings on Taiwan's human rights held through the 1980s trace back to that summer of 1981.
Volumes.perspective.chenwencheng.family.label: The Chen Family
Volumes.perspective.chenwencheng.family.narrativ:
In May 1981 Chen Wen-cheng brought his wife, Chen Su-chen, and their one-year-old son home to visit family. He was thirty-one, an assistant professor of statistics at Carnegie Mellon, and had been away for seven years. On the morning of July 2 three men from the Garrison Command came to the door for what they called a conversation; he was returned near his residence late that night. At dawn on July 3 his body was found on the lawn beside the graduate library at National Taiwan University.

The first explanation the family was given was suicide out of guilt. They refused it: a man with a return ticket booked, who the day before had been planning where to take his son, does not end his life after being questioned. Chen Su-chen left Taiwan with the child. More than three decades later the university named the spot where he was found the Chen Wen-cheng Memorial Plaza — and the years of argument on campus over that name say a great deal about how long this could not be spoken of plainly in Taiwan.
Volumes.perspective.chenwencheng.forensics.label: The Second Autopsy
Volumes.perspective.chenwencheng.forensics.narra:
At the request of the family and the American side, Cyril Wecht, the forensic pathologist from Carnegie Mellon, came to Taiwan to take part in the examination. His conclusion differed from the official one: the distribution of injuries was inconsistent with an unassisted fall, some wounds could have been inflicted before it, and he inclined to the view that Chen Wen-cheng was already unconscious, or dead, when he struck the ground.

Two findings stood side by side, neither able to persuade the other, and the only party with authority to decide between them was the party under suspicion. This is the shared structure of every politically charged death of the authoritarian period: the evidence, the scene, the choice of examiners and the custody of the file all rested in the same pair of hands. Four decades later the Transitional Justice Commission reopened the case; it could not identify who was responsible, but it held that the account of suicide could not stand.
Volumes.perspective.chenwencheng.garrison.label: The Garrison Command's Account
Volumes.perspective.chenwencheng.garrison.narrat:
The Garrison Command's account ran as follows: Chen Wen-cheng had been called in over suspected funding of Formosa Magazine and statements made in the United States; the conversation ended late on July 2, he was returned, and nothing thereafter concerned the Command; the cause of death was suicide or an accidental fall. Internally the account was complete — the session was logged, the return had witnesses, and the position of the body and the marks at the scene were cited in support.

The difficulty was that no one outside accepted the frame. Being called in was itself an exercise of power: the person summoned could not decline, no lawyer was present, there was no limit on how long it lasted, and nothing obtained was subject to review. When a man dies within ten hours of being processed by that procedure, "nothing to do with us" may hold technically and persuade no one politically. No one was ever charged in the case. What it did was change, permanently, what the word "summons" meant in Taiwan.
Volumes.perspective.chiangdiary.archive.label: The Archive and Its Door
Volumes.perspective.chiangdiary.archive.narrativ:
The reading history of these diaries is itself a piece of political history. Chiang wrote from 1917 to 1972, bound year by year; after 1975 the family held them, in 2005 they were deposited at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, opened to readers in batches from 2006, and fully available by 2009. The terms of access mattered: readers could copy by hand in the reading room but not photograph or photocopy, so for more than a decade the passages transcribed by the first scholars through the door were the only version anyone outside could quote — who copied what, and where they placed the punctuation, shaped the public impression of the source.

A lawsuit over ownership ran alongside. Claims by Chiang's descendants, by Academia Historica, and by others tangled together for more than ten years, until in 2023 the original diaries of both Chiangs were shipped back to Taiwan, to be held and opened by Academia Historica. With that, a ruler's private record became a public archive, and anyone may now sit down and turn to any day he wrote. For Taiwan the significance is not merely one more body of sources: a name that once had to be quoted with care can now be checked page by page — a political change accomplished by the act of opening an archive.
Volumes.perspective.chiangdiary.chiang.label: The Man Writing
Volumes.perspective.chiangdiary.chiang.narrative:
In March 1947 Chiang Kai-shek was handling three things at once: civil war in north China, the aftermath of the constitution in Nanking, and an island acquired barely eighteen months earlier that had suddenly gone out of control. Taiwan therefore appears in the diary always as a square on a national board. On March 5 he decided to send the 21st Division; on the 7th, receiving Chen Yi's alarm, he wrote that mobs had seized the moment when the garrison was transferred away to gather and make demands; at the memorial-week address on the 10th he attributed the affair to Communist incitement and to gentry kept by the Japanese. From where he sat these judgments were coherent: what a regime at civil war fears is not protest but the loss of its rear.

The same diary carries another hand as well. On March 13 he wired Chen Yi to forbid reprisals by military and civil personnel on pain of being charged with disobeying orders; on the 17th he sent Defense Minister Pai Chung-hsi to Taiwan to pacify and console; of Chen Yi himself he wrote that the man had misjudged his people and mishandled the affair, and never gave him Taiwan again. Sympathy and troop dispatch coexist without contradiction — in his logic, sending troops restored order and forbidding reprisals preserved legitimacy, two hands of a single statecraft. That is where the diary's value lies: it lets you watch a decision-maker hold local officials responsible and put an army on ships within four days, and see no inconsistency in himself.
Volumes.perspective.chiangdiary.historians.label: The Limits of a Source
Volumes.perspective.chiangdiary.historians.narra:
Historians treat these diaries as invaluable and insufficient on their own. Chiang wrote consciously for posterity — weekly, monthly, and annual reflections, in a register close to giving an account of himself to history — and his appraisals of others and his attributions of cause tend to carry a self-justifying structure. Beyond that, a diary records what its author knew at the time rather than what happened: the Taiwan he read about in Nanking was Taiwan after Chen Yi and the intelligence services had filtered it.

So the method is to read across. Set the March entries beside the telegrams in the Ta-hsi archives, the Garrison Command's reports, Pai Chung-hsi's dispatches during his pacification mission, and the oral accounts gathered in the localities, and you can see at which layer information was filtered, on what day a decision was actually taken, and how far execution diverged from the order. Conclusions reached that way rarely match anyone's propaganda: they establish both that the center did order reprisals to stop and that reprisals continued and no one was punished for them. The value of a source is not that it convicts or acquits, but that it forces every account back to a particular document on a particular day.
Volumes.perspective.chiangdiary.readers.label: Readers in Taiwan
Volumes.perspective.chiangdiary.readers.narrativ:
For the families of the victims, reading this diary is hard work. Someone who lost a father in March 1947 and for sixty years was told nothing about why can now turn to those days and find what the decision-maker was writing at the same hour: unit designations, sailing dates, and an appraisal of a provincial official. Her father's name is not in the diary, and that is the part hardest to bear — not being recorded as an enemy, but not being recorded at all.

It also changed how Taiwanese society argues. Before the 1990s, most accounts of February 28 hovered between two kinds of rumor; as the diary and the Ta-hsi archives came out, the argument acquired a base that could be checked day by day — when the order was given, when the troops landed, when the telegram forbidding reprisals was sent, and on what days reprisals nevertheless took place. Lee Teng-hui's apology as president in 1995, the compensation and rehabilitation statutes that followed, and the transitional justice program begun in 2017 all rest on the premise that the records can be cited. The diary offers readers no comfort. It offers something more basic: the ability to point at a line and say what happened on that day.
Volumes.perspective.constitution.afterlife.label: The Constitution's Afterlife
Volumes.perspective.constitution.afterlife.narra:
The only place this constitution ever really took effect was Taiwan, and it did so in a way its authors had not imagined. It came into force on December 25, 1947; the Temporary Provisions were promulgated in May 1948; martial law was declared on the island on May 20, 1949. Those three documents stacked together suspended the constitutional guarantees of speech, assembly, and personal liberty for thirty-eight years. The National Assembly delegates, legislators, and control members elected across the mainland provinces in 1948 could not stand for re-election once the government moved to Taiwan, and a single term ran until the end of 1991 — the assembly people came to call eternal.

The paradox is that because this constitution stayed in Taiwan, later political change had a common text to cite. Dangwai defendants invoked the freedom of assembly and association in Article 14 from the dock; students in 1990 demanded the dissolution of the National Assembly; 1991 brought the end of the period of Communist rebellion and the retirement of every senior member, 1992 the full re-election of the Legislative Yuan, 1996 the direct election of the president. Each step thawed, item by item, what had been frozen in the document of December 25, 1946. The delegates who argued in Nanking for provincial self-government and died in 1947 never saw that process; but the text they signed became the ground on which others finished their argument for them.
Volumes.perspective.constitution.delegates.label: The Delegates from Taiwan
Volumes.perspective.constitution.delegates.narra:
On November 15, 1946, the National Constituent Assembly opened in Nanking, and seventeen delegates elected from Taiwan sat for the first time in a Chinese national chamber. Their backgrounds say a good deal about the island: Lin Hsien-tang had spent more than twenty years petitioning for a Taiwanese parliament; Nan Chih-hsin, a Puyuma, was Taiwan's first indigenous physician trained in Western medicine and attended as a representative of indigenous people; Lin Lien-tsung of Changhua was a lawyer and also a provincial councilor; Chang Chi-lang, a doctor from Fenglin in Hualien, paid his own way north after raising an arch in his home town inscribed with words of welcome to the motherland. Most had been educated in Japanese, and parliamentary procedure, legal vocabulary, and the official speech of the hall all had to be learned on the spot.

The demand they carried came down to one thing: provincial and county self-government. The Taiwanese delegates argued for writing local autonomy into the text concretely and irreversibly, so the island could elect its own governor and manage its own finances; that left a framework for local government in Chapter XI of the Constitution — and also left one clause requiring a general statute on provincial and county self-government. Without the statute, no autonomy. The Constitution passed its third reading on December 25 and the delegates went home with a basic law they had helped write. Three months later Lin Lien-tsung was taken away in Taipei and never seen again; on April 4, Chang Chi-lang and two of his sons were taken and shot at Fenglin. Part of the roll of the constitution-makers and part of the roll of the dead of February 28 are the same names.
Volumes.perspective.constitution.government.narr:
Seen from Nanking, the significance of that assembly at the end of 1946 had nothing to do with Taiwan. The political consultation that followed the war against Japan had collapsed, the Communists and the Democratic League refused to attend, and civil war was already open in north China; the Nationalist government needed a constitution to prove that tutelage could end, that its authority was legitimate, and to trade for support in its dealings with Washington. The draft came largely from Carsun Chang of the Democratic Socialist Party, fusing the earlier draft of 1936 with the resolutions of the political consultation, setting a responsible cabinet alongside the five-power structure — a text designed so that several parties could sign it.

On that agenda Taiwan was a newly recovered province, and seventeen seats were close to symbolic. What occupied the conveners were the powers of the president and the Executive Yuan, the competence of the National Assembly, and the hole in legitimacy left by those who had stayed away — not whether a province recovered barely a year ago should elect its own governor. The Constitution was promulgated on January 1, 1947 and came into force on December 25 of that year. Four months later the National Assembly of 1948 passed the Temporary Provisions Effective During the Period of Communist Rebellion, freeing the president to act by emergency decree outside constitutional limits. To the conveners this was a necessary wartime exception. In effect, the chapter the Taiwanese delegates had fought for was frozen in the Constitution's first year.
Volumes.perspective.constitution.press.label: The Island's Press
Volumes.perspective.constitution.press.narrative:
While the delegates sat in Nanking, the island's newspapers were keeping a different set of accounts. The Min Pao, the People's Herald, and the Taiwan Shin Sheng Daily News printed the assembly's progress day by day, and their editorials kept returning to one question: would this constitution let Taiwanese govern Taiwan. The concrete demands were the abolition of the Administrative Executive Office in favor of an ordinary provincial government, the implementation of provincial and county self-government under the Constitution, and the appointment of Taiwanese to the principal posts. By the end of 1946, opinion on the island had stopped accepting "when conditions are ripe."

That expectation had a clear reference point. Taiwanese had just run a three-tier election in 1946 and had just watched a year of unanswered questioning in the provincial assembly; the Constitution gave them a higher ground from which to raise their demands from petition to entitlement. When the February 28 Incident came in 1947, the sections of the Settlement Committee's thirty-two demands dealing with provincial autonomy, elected county and city chiefs, and the localization of courts and police were very nearly a continuation of those editorials. The difference was that at the end of 1946 such words in print were public opinion, and in March 1947 the same words spoken aloud became evidence of rebellion.
Volumes.perspective.dangwai.candidate.label: A Dangwai Candidate
Volumes.perspective.dangwai.candidate.narrative:
The Dangwai had no party headquarters, no party assets, and no access to television. They had three things: the microphone at a campaign rally, magazines printed on coarse paper, and one election after another. In the five-office local elections of 1977 they took an unprecedented number of county magistracies and provincial assembly seats; that November, a suspected ballot-rigging incident in Chungli brought a crowd around the local police station — the Chungli Incident. After that night, a good many people came to believe that "the crowd" actually existed.

Losing a race did not disband anything. Cassette tapes of the rally speeches circulated in markets and taxis, the volunteer rosters became the next campaign's organization, and the same people turned up three years later at a podium in another county. They knew exactly what they were doing: in a place where a party could not be founded, they were using elections to build the shape of one first. By the day the party was actually founded in 1986, the rosters, the donors, the speeches and the crowds were already in place.
Volumes.perspective.dangwai.censor.label: The Censors
Volumes.perspective.dangwai.censor.narrative:
Seen from the regulating side, the problem was never the elections; it was the printed matter. Publications under martial law fell under the Taiwan Provincial Regulations on the Control of Newspapers, Magazines and Books, and the Garrison Command and the Government Information Office could seize an issue at the press, the newsstand or the post office on the day it appeared. Suspend a magazine for a year and its publisher would reappear the next day under another licence, applied for well in advance. The longer the banned list, the higher the price on the black market.

They held a second set of tools as well: administrative resources during campaigns, the mobilization of local factions, and the summoning and surveillance of candidates and their volunteers. On the files, the system worked — the Dangwai never took a meaningful share of seats in the national legislature. What the files could not measure was that every confiscation served as an endorsement of the words confiscated, and every summons added a measure of standing to the person summoned, in the town where he lived.
Volumes.perspective.dangwai.kmt.label: The Party's Local Machine
Volumes.perspective.dangwai.kmt.narrative:
The Kuomintang's dominance in the localities did not rest on ideology but on a dense web: farmers' associations, irrigation and fishermen's associations, credit cooperatives, township and borough chiefs, and a system of nominations and patronage organized around factions. Local elections could be opened precisely because that web all but guaranteed the outcome. An election was not a threat; it was the channel through which local elites were absorbed into the system.

From the late 1970s the arithmetic began to fail. Economic growth produced a middle class and an urban electorate attached to no faction; expulsion from the United Nations and the severing of relations with Washington eroded the regime's claim to represent all of China; and the Dangwai rewrote the subject of an election from local personalities into institutional questions. Two positions emerged inside the party: tighten the screws, or accept that an opposition visible above ground is easier to manage than one gathering below it. The lifting of martial law, and the tolerance shown to a new party, were extensions of the second view.
Volumes.perspective.dangwai.reader.label: A Reader of the Banned Magazines
Volumes.perspective.dangwai.reader.narrative:
Buying a Dangwai magazine took a little technique. The newsstand kept it under the other titles, and the owner would look you over first; sometimes it came as a photocopy passed along by a classmate, the type crooked and the pages out of order, so far down the chain that no one could say how many hands it had been through. Inside was what the newspapers did not carry: February 28, the names of political prisoners, the Lin family and Chen Wen-cheng, and why the National Assembly had gone decades without facing an election.

What changed a person, though, was usually not the magazine but the campaign rally. The improvised stage at the temple square would be packed, the speaker would say the sentence you had assumed could only be thought, and the several thousand people around you would not walk away. In that moment you knew you were not the only one. Most political awakenings in 1980s Taiwan happened on nights like that: one microphone, a stack of magazines, and a crowd that would not disperse.
Volumes.perspective.dejapanization.government.na:
In Chen Yi's plan, the hardest part of taking over Taiwan was not administration but what he called psychological reconstruction. After fifty years of colonial schooling the island's educated class thought in Japanese and wrote in Japanese, and the authorities held that unless the change of language and culture was completed quickly, the new rule would have a form and no content. The Taiwan Provincial Mandarin Promotion Committee, established on April 2, 1946 under Wei Chien-kung with Ho Jung as his deputy, took a surprisingly careful approach: it argued for working through the correspondences between Taiwanese and Mandarin — reviving the vernacular first and reaching Mandarin through it, rather than drilling phonetic symbols.

The real break came from a different order. On October 25, 1946, the first anniversary of the retrocession, the Administrative Executive Office abolished the Japanese-language editions and sections of newspapers and magazines. Administratively this was a clear, enforceable, symbolic date. In its effects it abolished overnight the publishing outlet of every fully educated person on the island. The official reasoning never varied: Japanese was an instrument of colonization, and to keep it was to keep the enslavement. There was no malice in that judgment, but neither was there a thought for one thing — what had been abolished was not only a script but the expressive capacity a whole generation had spent twenty years acquiring.
Volumes.perspective.dejapanization.schools.label: Inside the Classroom
Volumes.perspective.dejapanization.schools.narra:
The most thorough conversion happened in primary-school classrooms. Between the autumn of 1945 and the spring of 1946, textbooks, morning assemblies, the language of instruction, and the names of subjects were all replaced across the island; the portraits on the wall changed faces and the maps changed centers. Taiwanese teachers who had taught in Japanese had to become students first, learning phonetic symbols and Mandarin at summer training sessions before going back to teach children. Qualified Mandarin teachers were badly short, so the common arrangement was this: the teacher had started learning the language three months before the class had.

For a child this was a dynastic change of language — Taiwanese or Hakka at home, Mandarin at school, and not one book on the father's shelf still readable. For teachers the cost was more concrete: seniority turned overnight into unfitness, and pay grade, position, and standing went together, while mainland-born teachers and administrators filled the upper ranks quickly. From 1946 two things went on in the same classroom: a new state teaching its next generation, and an older generation losing its voice in the room where it worked. The fissure would later be called the provincial divide, but it appeared first on roll sheets and in composition books.
Volumes.perspective.dejapanization.translators.l: The Scholars of the Compilation Office
Volumes.perspective.dejapanization.translators.n:
Not everyone who came from the mainland believed in the word "enslavement." The Taiwan Provincial Compilation and Translation Office, founded in August 1946, was headed by Hsu Shou-shang — Lu Xun's close friend from their student years in Japan and an educator of the May Fourth generation. He accepted Chen Yi's invitation with a different kind of re-Sinicization in mind: not stripping out what was Japanese and calling it done, but bringing in the vernacular literature, thought, and translation of the May Fourth era while organizing research into Taiwan's own history and folklore, so that the two could meet on one desk. He introduced Lu Xun in the pages of the Taiwan Shin Sheng Daily News and let the office's Taiwanese researchers carry on surveys left unfinished under Japanese rule.

That road lasted nine months. Politics tightened after February 1947, the office was abolished in May, and Hsu Shou-shang moved to chair the Chinese department at National Taiwan University; on February 18, 1948 he was killed in his residence in Taipei, in a case still disputed today. The bibliographies and translations he left behind are among the few attempts at a cultural handover made without hostility. Set beside the administrative orders of the same months, they show that re-Sinicization never had only one version — only that the version remembered afterward was the one issued as an order.
Volumes.perspective.dejapanization.writers.label: The Writers Struck Dumb
Volumes.perspective.dejapanization.writers.narra:
After October 25, 1946, Lung Ying-tsung lost the Japanese-language literary section he edited at the Chung Hwa Daily News and published no fiction for years afterward. Wu Cho-liu had just finished Orphan of Asia in Japanese and spent the next decade wrestling with Chinese; Lu Ho-jo shut himself in to relearn the classical script, moved into the underground after 1947, and died in the hills of Luku in 1951. Yang Kui was one of the few who converted quickly, at the price of setting aside twenty years of his own work and starting again with short commentary and translation.

What they objected to was not learning Chinese but an inference: that not speaking Mandarin meant having been enslaved. In January 1946, Wang Pai-yuan pushed back directly in the Political and Economic Review, writing that many mainlanders began by pronouncing that their Taiwanese compatriots had been enslaved by the Japanese for fifty years and had crooked minds — and that his own observation was precisely the reverse, that it was under colonial rule that Taiwanese had learned what the rule of law and modern life meant. The exchange ran for a full year before February 1947, the first public argument in postwar Taiwan over who was entitled to define the island's people. It reached no conclusion; it was simply buried by a larger event.
Volumes.perspective.diaries.huang.label: Sixty Years of a Reporter
Volumes.perspective.diaries.huang.narrative:
Huang Wang-cheng's diary runs from 1912 to 1973, across Japanese rule, war, takeover, and martial law — one of the longest private records surviving in Taiwan. He had been a public-school teacher, a tutor in a gentry household, and a reporter for the Taiwan Min Pao, writing political commentary under the pen name Chen Wang-cheng; after the war he wrote for the press and entered a local assembly in the elections of 1946. The same pair of eyes watched the Government-General's censorship system and then the new regime's press controls, so the diary preserves an unusually direct comparison.

His record points to something easily missed: the disappointment of the early postwar years was not an ideal measured against a reality, but one concrete experience measured against another. These men knew how a newspaper could be censored, and that censorship could follow rules; they knew what an administrative procedure looked like, and under what conditions corruption got investigated. After 1947 none of those comparisons could be written down. The prose accordingly retreats into the everyday — weather, visitors, household matters, politics appearing only in the shortest of sentences. A man who wrote for sixty years choosing to write less is, in itself, the clearest record that era produced.
Volumes.perspective.diaries.lin.label: The Ledger of Lin Hsien-tang
Volumes.perspective.diaries.lin.narrative:
Lin Hsien-tang wrote from 1927 to 1955 almost without a break, in the diaries later published as the journals of the Kuan-yuan studio. His register is close to bookkeeping: who called today, what was discussed, which meeting he attended, what the household spent. Feeling is rarely stated outright. That is precisely why the change across 1945 to 1947 shows so clearly in his pages — not through adjectives but through the density of names and appointments. In the autumn of 1945 he travels north constantly for welcomes and preparatory committees; through 1946 his days fill with petitions and mediation; after March 1947 the list of callers abruptly shortens.

What says most about his position are the intercessions he records: so-and-so has been arrested, the family has come to ask, he goes to see whom, and this is what came of it. A man who had once led delegations petitioning the imperial parliament now spent his working days pleading with a new government on behalf of his neighbors, with a success rate that kept falling. In 1949 he left for Tokyo for medical treatment and went on writing, the entries shifting from meetings in Taiwan to the weather, the visitors, and the letters from home; envoys came repeatedly to urge his return, and he never went back. He died in Tokyo in 1956. The ledger he had kept for twenty-eight years ends on a foreign page.
Volumes.perspective.diaries.silence.label: The Blanks in the Page
Volumes.perspective.diaries.silence.narrative:
Under martial law a private diary was not private. Mail was inspected, homes could be searched, and the notebooks, reading-group minutes, and diaries turned up in those searches served directly as evidence for prosecution in many White Terror cases — writing a thought down was itself a risk. This was never announced, but every literate person learned it: no small number of people burned their diaries after 1947, and those who kept writing changed how they wrote.

So the sources carry a distinctive kind of mark. Volumes for certain years are missing; the paper for certain dates has been cut out cleanly; some writers replaced sensitive names with code or bare surnames; some, after switching from Japanese to Chinese, suddenly write in flat, featureless sentences. Researchers today read these diaries for what is set down and also for what is not — where the blanks fall, which category of person goes unmentioned, at what point the author begins to record only the weather. This is the shape a state apparatus leaves on a private text. It never had to search every house; it only had to make everyone who picked up a pen think of the possibility first.
Volumes.perspective.diaries.wu.label: The Doctor of Chiali
Volumes.perspective.diaries.wu.narrative:
Wu Hsin-jung practised medicine in Chiali, Tainan, and stood at the center of the literary circle of the salt-flat district; his diary runs from 1933 to 1967 and is among the fullest records of local life in postwar Taiwan. He writes down his consultations, the price of rice, the weddings and funerals of neighbors, the books he has read. Because it is so granular, you can watch a market town being passed through by a national event. The 1946 entries are shortages of medicine, of grain, and of money. The entries of March 1947 are news, rumor, closed roads, and names disappearing from the village one by one.

He was himself put on a wanted list, hid for a time, then decided to turn himself in, and was released after several months in prison. Afterward the diary's center of gravity visibly shifts: he put his energy into documentary fieldwork across Tainan county, travelling the townships to record temples, steles, place names, and the testimony of the old, and editing the local historical journal. In an era when politics could not be discussed, his chosen method was to store up local memory one entry at a time. It was a common turn for that generation — when public speech is closed, they take up whatever looks most harmless, and those notebooks became the most solid foundation postwar Taiwanese local history has.
Volumes.perspective.dpp.chiang.label: Chiang Ching-kuo's Calculation
Volumes.perspective.dpp.chiang.narrative:
The news reached the Seven Seas residence that afternoon. Plenty of voices inside the Kuomintang argued for shutting the new party down; the Emergency Period Civic Organizations Act and the martial-law decree both offered ample grounds. Chiang Ching-kuo's reply has been quoted ever since: the times are changing, the environment is changing, the tide is changing too. He chose not to make arrests.

This was not magnanimity but arithmetic. By 1986 his health was failing badly and he was arranging the succession; abroad he faced pressure from the US Congress and international opinion, and at home he had the recent examples of South Korea and the Philippines in view. Banning a party would hand the initiative on reform to the street. Tolerating it would draw the opposition into an arena where the regime still set the rules. The lifting of martial law in 1987 and the 1989 amendment of the Civic Organizations Act, which finally legalized party registration, followed the same logic: rather than prohibit, legislate and manage.
Volumes.perspective.dpp.exiles.label: The Exiles' Route
Volumes.perspective.dpp.exiles.narrative:
In the same year the party was founded at home, Hsu Hsin-liang and others in exile in the United States were pushing a parallel project abroad — found the party overseas and move it back to Taiwan — and repeatedly tried to force their way home. At Taoyuan airport on November 30, 1986, tens of thousands came to meet his flight and spent the day facing water cannon and riot vehicles. He never left the aircraft. That people on the blacklist could not go home became one of the sharpest demands the new party carried.

Relations between the diaspora and the island were not always easy. Overseas organizations had more resources and took harder positions; those at home carried the actual political risk and had elections to win. Whether independence should be written into the platform, and how strongly, was argued between them for years. That argument runs all the way to the DPP's adoption of the independence clause in 1991, and to the gradual lifting of the blacklist through the 1990s, as the exiles came home one by one.
Volumes.perspective.dpp.founders.label: In the Room at the Grand Hotel
Volumes.perspective.dpp.founders.narrative:
On the morning of September 28, 1986, one hundred and thirty-five Dangwai figures gathered in the Min Hall on the second floor of the Grand Hotel in Taipei, under the name of the Dangwai Election Support Association. The announced agenda was coordinating nominations for the year-end supplementary elections. Midway through, someone moved that a party be founded then and there; the motion carried, and the name Frank Hsieh proposed — the Democratic Progressive Party — was adopted.

The ban on new parties had not been lifted and martial law was still in force, so founding a party was simply illegal. A number of those present had come with a toothbrush and washing kit, expecting to be arrested as a group before the meeting broke up; some had left instructions with their families that morning. In hindsight, what mattered most that morning was not courage but judgement. They had calculated that Chiang Ching-kuo would not overturn his own reform and succession plans over a single party registration. It was a gamble, and they were right.
Volumes.perspective.dpp.prisoners.label: Still Inside
Volumes.perspective.dpp.prisoners.narrative:
When the party was founded, most of the principal defendants of the Kaohsiung Incident were still in prison. Shih Ming-teh was serving a life sentence; Huang Hsin-chieh, Yao Chia-wen and Chang Chun-hung had not been released. The new party's first cadre included their defence lawyers, their wives and their assistants: Hsu Jung-shu, Chou Ching-yu and Fang Su-min had all won office in those years standing in their husbands' place, and Chiang Peng-chien, elected first party chairman in November 1986, was Shih Ming-teh's defence counsel.

Those inside took part in their own way. Shih Ming-teh's long hunger strike in prison, and the force-feeding that went on for more than four years, leaked out in fragments and became the single most effective cause for supporters abroad. For this group, the founding of 1986 was not a beginning but the continuation of the trial seven years earlier: the arguments that had been charged as sedition were now the platform of a political party.
Volumes.perspective.economy1946.households.label: Households Under the Price of Rice
Volumes.perspective.economy1946.households.narra:
Ordinary households judge a government by the price of a peck of rice. From the takeover in October 1945 to the beginning of 1947, that price rose several dozenfold; Taiwan grew rice, and yet in 1946 there were shortages across the island and panic buying in the markets. There was more than one cause: wartime requisitioning had emptied village stores, the 1946 harvest was poor, fertilizer and transport had not been repaired, and at the same time large quantities of rice and sugar were moving to the mainland through the Trade Bureau's channels. To a housewife none of these reasons mattered. What mattered was that what she could afford yesterday she could not afford today.

The evaporation of savings was just as concrete. On May 20, 1946 the Bank of Taiwan issued new Taiwan dollar notes in exchange for the old colonial currency, and the gap between the conversion rate and actual prices wiped out lifetimes of saving; wartime bonds, insurance policies, and postal deposits from the late Japanese period were mostly waste paper. Pawnshops filled up in the cities and land began to be sold in the countryside. From the winter of 1946 into early 1947, rice grabs, crowds, and petitions appeared in the local pages of the newspapers week after week, and the authorities handled them as matters of public order. The February 28 Incident is often traced to a single cigarette seizure; more precisely, it was a year of prices no one would answer for that pushed people into the street that night.
Volumes.perspective.economy1946.monopoly.label: The Monopoly and Trade Bureaus
Volumes.perspective.economy1946.monopoly.narrati:
What Chen Yi brought to Taiwan was the whole apparatus of controlled economy he had run in Fujian. The Taiwan Provincial Monopoly Bureau, established in November 1945, took over the Japanese monopoly system — tobacco, liquor, camphor, matches, weights and measures — while the Trade Bureau centralized the purchase and export of rice, sugar, and other staples. The official reasoning was not unusual for the time: goods were desperately short after the war, and a free market would let hoarding and speculation starve the poor first; only unified state allocation could hold prices and supply. Industries and plant left by the Japanese were likewise taken into state ownership, on the same ground that they must not fall into a few private hands.

The difficulty was in the execution. Monopoly and centralized purchasing concentrated both profit and discretion in a handful of agencies, the seizure of untaxed tobacco, liquor, and sugar became routine police work, and the conduct of the enforcement agents instantly became the face of the entire system. On the evening of February 27, 1947, Monopoly Bureau agents confiscated contraband cigarettes outside the Tianma Tea House in Taipei and struck the vendor Lin Chiang-mai, then fired a shot that killed a bystander, Chen Wen-hsi. The shot that set the island alight was fired from the far end of this economic system. What the authorities reviewed afterward was enforcement discipline. What the public saw was a system that held their livelihoods in its hands and enforced them at gunpoint.
Volumes.perspective.economy1946.nanjing.label: The Ledger in Nanking
Volumes.perspective.economy1946.nanjing.narrativ:
Shipping Taiwan's rice and sugar to the mainland was, in Nanking's ledger, a reasonable allocation. Full-scale civil war opened in 1946, military spending swallowed most of the treasury, inflation of the national currency was already out of control, and the price of grain in Shanghai bore directly on the regime's support in the cities. Taiwan was a province relatively lightly damaged by the war and able to produce at once: sugar in store, rice in the fields, industrial plant intact. When the Administrative Executive Office sent 150,000 tons of the sugar corporation's stock to Shanghai to be sold, the center saw a necessary move on a single national board.

On the Taiwanese side of the ledger the entry did not balance at all. They had not fought that war and were being asked to finance it; harder still was the accounting — goods went out one way, and what came back was mostly inflation. The center's logic was the internal transfer of resources within one country; the island's experience was of having exchanged one metropole for another. After 1949, when that same government fell back onto the island and could no longer draw supplies from an interior, it began in earnest to build Taiwan's industry and countryside. The same island was treated as the rear depot in 1946 and, after 1950, as the only property left.
Volumes.perspective.economy1946.unemployed.label: The Jobless Generation
Volumes.perspective.economy1946.unemployed.narra:
Taiwan in 1946 met two inflows of people and one shutdown at the same time. Two hundred thousand Taiwanese who had served in the Japanese forces came home in batches, and Taiwanese abroad were being repatriated; meanwhile the factories, sugar mills, mines, and trading houses left by the Japanese largely stopped work during the takeover, cut off at once from raw materials, technical staff, and markets, with no date for restarting. The state enterprises formed out of them reorganized their personnel, and Taiwanese who had held posts in colonial-era firms and offices were mostly demoted or dismissed, while the middle and upper ranks that fell vacant were filled by mainlanders.

What resulted was a distinctive class of unemployed men: fully educated, trained under arms, able to run machinery, in their twenties, with no work and no prospects. They read the takeover's achievements in the newspapers, saw the prices on the street, and faced their elders at home. In March 1947 the first units to organize anywhere — the 27th Brigade in Taichung, the militias in Chiayi — were built around exactly these men. Postwar Taiwan assembled, by 1946, the set of statistics that ought to worry any government: high education, high unemployment, military training, and no channel upward.
Volumes.perspective.election1996.beijing.label: Beijing's Calculation
Volumes.perspective.election1996.beijing.narrati:
From Beijing's vantage point the election was itself the problem. A president chosen directly by twenty-one million people on Taiwan would, in practice, establish a political entity independent of China; and Lee Teng-hui's visit to Cornell in June 1995, where he spoke as an alumnus, read in Beijing as Washington acquiescing in Taiwan's rising international standing.

Hence the sequence of exercises beginning in July 1995 and the missile tests and joint service manoeuvres of March 1996. The object was not attack but the ballot: to convince Taiwanese voters that a vote for Lee Teng-hui was a vote for war. It produced the opposite. Lee's share ran ahead of every pre-election poll, and the United States moved two carrier battle groups into waters near Taiwan. After that year Beijing's approach shifted its weight from military intimidation toward economic and diplomatic instruments, while Taiwan's defence procurement and its military relationship with the United States took a different road.
Volumes.perspective.election1996.exile.label: The Returning Exile
Volumes.perspective.election1996.exile.narrative:
The Democratic Progressive Party's candidate in 1996, Peng Ming-min, had been chairman of the political science department at National Taiwan University thirty-two years earlier. In 1964 he drafted, with Hsieh Tsung-min and Wei Ting-chao, the Declaration of Formosan Self-Salvation, calling for a new constitution and for joining the international community under Taiwan's own name. The declaration was seized before it could be distributed and all three were arrested; he was sentenced to eight years, placed under house arrest after a pardon, and in 1970 slipped out of the country in disguise under an assumed name. He spent twenty-two years in exile.

The blacklist released him in 1992 and he came home. In 1996 he held campaign rallies as a presidential candidate in the city where he had once been a wanted man. He lost, with twenty-one percent. But the central claim of the declaration that had served as evidence of sedition in 1964 — that the future of Taiwan is for the people of Taiwan to decide — had by 1996 become the shared premise of the campaign, no longer disputed even by his opponents. And the provision under which he had been convicted had been struck out in 1992.
Volumes.perspective.election1996.voter.label: A Voter in the Queue
Volumes.perspective.election1996.voter.narrative:
On March 23, 1996, turnout was seventy-six percent. It was the first time Taiwanese had elected a president directly, and in the three months before the vote the People's Liberation Army conducted missile tests and joint exercises in the Taiwan Strait, with impact zones set off Keelung and Kaohsiung. The stock market fell; people bought dollars, people filed emigration papers. On the day itself the queues formed as usual outside the assembly halls of primary schools.

For most voters the ballot carried two meanings. One was the choice of a candidate: Lee Teng-hui with Lien Chan, Peng Ming-min with Frank Hsieh, Lin Yang-kang with Hau Pei-tsun, Chen Li-an with Wang Ching-feng — four tickets spanning unification and independence, reform, and money politics. The other meaning was the act itself, casting a vote inside the range of the missiles. Lee Teng-hui won with fifty-four percent. The message from across the strait was perfectly clear, and so was the reply.
Volumes.perspective.election1996.washington.narr:
In March 1996 the United States sent two carrier battle groups, built around the Independence and the Nimitz, into waters near Taiwan — the largest American military response to a strait crisis since the Taiwan Relations Act. The Clinton administration's reading was that staying out would be taken as acquiescence in changing the status quo by force, while going too far in risked escalation. It settled on sending the ships, but not through the strait itself.

The crisis redefined the triangle. For Washington, Taiwan was no longer merely an inherited commitment but a variable bearing on the whole of the relationship with Beijing. For Taipei, it confirmed that American support was real, and also that it had limits and could not substitute for a defence of one's own. For Beijing, it became the most direct spur to two decades of military modernization. The balance of forces in the strait after 1996, the American arms-sales list, and the shape of Taiwan's own force structure all trace back to that March.
Volumes.perspective.elites.critics.label: The Critics with Pens
Volumes.perspective.elites.critics.narrative:
Another group chose to say it in the newspapers. Lin Mao-sheng ran the Min Pao — Taiwan's first doctor of philosophy and a student of John Dewey — and its editorials itemized the disorder of the takeover; Sung Fei-ju founded the People's Herald, a Peking University graduate who had served as deputy chief of the education department and used his own paper to expose the government he worked for; Wang Tien-teng took over the Herald while sitting in the provincial assembly, so that questioning in the chamber and editorials in print relayed each other. Their positions were not radical. The demands concentrated on official appointments, economic controls, and judicial independence — still the vocabulary of the system.

In March 1947 this group was emptied out almost at a stroke. Lin Mao-sheng was taken from his Taipei home on March 11 and never seen again; Sung Fei-ju was killed; Wang Tien-teng, having served as head of publicity for the Settlement Committee and read out its demands, was arrested and killed. The papers were shut and their manuscripts and subscriber lists carried off. The official account afterward was that these newspapers had incited a riot; open the 1946 issues, however, and what is printed there is the price of rice, corruption cases, and transcripts of parliamentary questions. The fate of Taiwan's first postwar generation of liberal newspapermen determined what kind of sentence would not appear in print for the next forty years.
Volumes.perspective.elites.reformers.label: The Reformers Inside
Volumes.perspective.elites.reformers.narrative:
In the autumn of 1945, choosing to cooperate hardly required thought. Lin Hsien-tang had led the petition movement for a Taiwanese parliament for more than twenty years under Japanese rule; now he chaired welcome committees, sat in the provincial assembly, and was put forward as a representative on every kind of board. Tu Tsung-ming in medicine, Chen Hsin in finance, and Lin Mao-sheng in the university took posts in the new order as well. Their reasoning was the same: the Japanese were gone, Taiwanese could at last serve in their own government, and even an incomplete system should be pried open from within.

Within two years that road narrowed section by section. Questioning in the assembly changed nothing, the important posts in the Executive Office still went to mainlanders, and economic control left Taiwanese capital nowhere to go. When Chen Hsin organized the Ta Kung enterprise company to pool local capital for reconstruction, it made him an object of official wariness instead; in March 1947 he was taken away on the pretext of negotiations and never seen again. Lin Hsien-tang left for Tokyo in 1949 on the grounds of medical treatment, refused every request to return, and died there in 1956. The lesson the cooperative road finally left was not that cooperation had been wrong, but that cooperation requires the other side to treat it as such.
Volumes.perspective.elites.security.label: The Lists Held by the Security Services
Volumes.perspective.elites.security.narrative:
In the files of the security services, "native elite" was not a compliment but a list requiring constant updating. After the takeover of 1945, operatives of the military and party intelligence systems were established on the island at once; the Fourth Regiment of the military police was stationed under Chang Mu-tao, and the Taiwan station of the Bureau of Investigation and Statistics was run by Lin Ting-li, an islander who also raised his own special detachment. County and city reports recorded, by category, the movements of local gentry, newspapermen, physicians, lawyers, graduates of Japanese universities, and local factions. Within the system of the day this was routine work: a newly acquired province where the language was strange and Japanese influence not yet undone had first to know who could summon a crowd.

In March 1947 those lists became operational orders directly. The membership of the February 28 Settlement Committee, the staff registers of the newspapers, the assembly rolls, and the signatures on local petitions were all ready-made target lists. After the 21st Division landed on March 8, the sequence of arrests was strikingly precise: those taken away were overwhelmingly the people who could write, speak, and organize. Ko Yuan-fen, chief of staff of the Garrison Command, was recorded afterward as saying it was better to kill in error than to let one go. By the system's own logic this was a successful preventive clearance — what it cleared away was precisely the group most capable of leading, which was exactly the point.
Volumes.perspective.elites.silence.label: Silence and Withdrawal
Volumes.perspective.elites.silence.narrative:
The third road had no name, and the most people took it. After March 1947 some burned their diaries and address books, some moved their Japanese libraries into storage, some resigned from public office and went home to practise medicine, to teach, to manage family land. Wu Hsin-jung, a doctor in Chiali, turned himself in after the incident and served time, then redirected his energy into local documents and folklore surveys; Tu Tsung-ming, dean of the medical college, kept out of sight for a period once his name began to circulate, and on his return did nothing but research and teaching. This was not cowardice but arithmetic: there were people at home to feed, children to put through school, and the price of speaking had just been posted very plainly.

The cost of that road showed only much later. The generation of Taiwanese best equipped to organize and to articulate withdrew from public life together after 1947; they poured themselves into hospitals, schools, families, and land, and left politics to those willing to enter the party-state. The White Terror of the 1950s removed another portion of whoever remained. By the time the Dangwai movement rose in the 1970s, the people picking it up were an entirely different generation, and the blank stretch between them is the time bought by that silence. They kept their families, and they kept alive the people Taiwanese society would need when it opened its mouth again.
Volumes.perspective.erqi.brigade.label: The Brigade
Volumes.perspective.erqi.brigade.narrative: We did not choose the gun; the gun was forced into our hands. When the soldiers fired on unarmed crowds in Taipei, we in Taichung understood that petitions would no longer save us. Commander Hsieh told us plainly: hold the city, protect the people, and if we must fall back, fall back fighting. We were teachers and students, not soldiers — yet for ten days we governed ourselves, and for one march to Puli we were an army.
Volumes.perspective.erqi.government.label: The Government
Volumes.perspective.erqi.government.narrative: From Nanjing the rising in Taichung looked like nothing less than armed rebellion — arsenals looted, garrisons overrun, a Communist agitator at the head of an organized force. The 21st Division was dispatched to restore order by whatever means required. To the authorities, the disbanding of the brigade at Puli was not an ending but a beginning: the roster of names it left behind would guide the arrests, tribunals, and executions of the cleansing that followed.
Volumes.perspective.erqi.students.label: The Students
Volumes.perspective.erqi.students.narrative: We were nineteen, twenty years old, raised under one empire and handed to another. We believed, for a few luminous days, that we could build something clean out of the chaos — that the island might finally belong to those who lived on it. Then the transports came, and the mountains swallowed our retreat, and the friends who marched beside us to Puli did not all come home. What we lost at Puli was not only the brigade. It was the last time we believed idealism alone could win.
Volumes.perspective.formosa.dangwai.label: The Dangwai Movement
Volumes.perspective.formosa.dangwai.narrative:
For the people of Formosa Magazine, the Kaohsiung gathering of December 10, 1979 was not a riot but a speech that should long since have been made in public. The magazine had launched in August and within four months had opened more than a dozen service offices across the island — a party in everything but name. The denial of their assembly permit, the repeated ransacking of those offices, and the detention and beating of two volunteers at the Gushan police station on December 9 all read, to them, as notice of what was coming. The march went ahead as planned, and the torches were lit on Chungshan Road.

The order they remember is this: the encirclement came first, the violence second. Riot vehicles and tear gas sealed the procession into the traffic circle, and only once there was no way out did the pushing turn into a brawl. The island-wide arrests over the following three weeks confirmed their reading — the authorities did not want a rally dispersed, they wanted the Dangwai organization pulled up by the roots. Yet in the military courtroom the dock became the largest platform any of them would ever have: they rebutted the indictment point by point, named the torture inflicted during interrogation, and invoked the constitutional freedom of assembly. The photograph of Shih Ming-teh smiling at his own trial became the most reproduced image of the proceedings. The sentences were heavy; the words got out.
Volumes.perspective.formosa.garrison.label: The Garrison Command
Volumes.perspective.formosa.garrison.narrative:
In the Garrison Command's files the affair is called the Kaohsiung Violence Sedition Case. The United States had severed relations with the Republic of China that January, and Beijing had issued its Message to Compatriots in Taiwan the same month; under martial-law logic, any street mobilization at such a moment was not a policing matter but an opening the enemy could use. The authorities stated that more than a hundred and eighty military police and officers were injured that night, and on that basis held that the crowd had attacked law enforcement first and been dispersed second. The simultaneous arrests across the island were carried out from lists of Dangwai figures compiled long before.

What was genuinely unusual was the decision that followed: an open trial. The government let the domestic press into the courtroom and allowed the newspapers to print the defendants' statements — partly to display due process to Washington and the wider world, partly out of confidence that the case would speak for itself. In March 1980 the military tribunal handed down severe sentences: life imprisonment for Shih Ming-teh, fourteen years for Huang Hsin-chieh, twelve years each for the remaining principal defendants. As a matter of case closure it was a complete victory. As a matter of public opinion, the trial put the Dangwai argument, in its own words, on the front pages of every newspaper in the country for the first time.
Volumes.perspective.formosa.international.label: International Observers
Volumes.perspective.formosa.international.narrat:
To observers abroad, the trial was never only about its verdicts. The Taiwan Relations Act, passed by the US Congress in 1979, named the human rights of the people on Taiwan as an objective of American policy — making Taipei's internal affairs, for the first time, something Washington could formally raise. After the arrests, members of Congress, State Department officials and Amnesty International pressed continuously for open proceedings and humane treatment, and Amnesty adopted the Kaohsiung defendants as prisoners of conscience. Admitting foreign correspondents and congressional staff to the courtroom was the compromise Taipei found between preserving a substantive relationship and absorbing that pressure.

The compromise produced a result Taipei may not have anticipated: the statements made in court traveled out through the wire services, giving overseas Taiwanese communities a common cause — one of the starting points for the Formosan Association for Public Affairs, founded in 1982. Throughout the 1980s, congressional hearings returned again and again to these names. Seen from outside, the Kaohsiung Incident was not an isolated act of repression but a public stress test — the moment Taiwan's democratization acquired international witnesses, and the reason the lifting of martial law seven years later looked less like a gift.
Volumes.perspective.formosa.lawyers.label: The Defense Lawyers
Volumes.perspective.formosa.lawyers.narrative:
Fifteen lawyers took these cases, and at the time taking them was itself a declaration. Chiang Peng-chien handled the most sensitive brief of all, Shih Ming-teh's; Chen Shui-bian defended Annette Lu, Frank Hsieh defended Yao Chia-wen, Su Tseng-chang defended Lin Yi-hsiung, and You Ching, Chang Chun-hsiung and others took the remaining defendants. Many were warned off by their families and their colleagues, for a practical reason: a lawyer who defends sedition defendants may not have a practice left. Their strategy was not to deny that the rally had happened but to break the equals sign between assembly and sedition — challenging confessions obtained under torture and quoting Article 14 of the Constitution back at a military court.

Around the trial, on February 28, 1980, while Lin Yi-hsiung was still in custody, his mother and twin daughters were murdered at the family home in Taipei; his eldest daughter survived with severe wounds. The house was under surveillance at the time, and the case remains unsolved. For the defense team, that day defined what kind of case this was: they were not merely arguing against an indictment. After the verdicts, most of them went into politics — Chiang Peng-chien became the first chairman of the Democratic Progressive Party, and Chen Shui-bian, Frank Hsieh, Su Tseng-chang and Chang Chun-hsiung would all reach the center of Taiwanese political life. The Kaohsiung Incident thus produced two generations at once: the one in the dock, and the one at the defense table.
Volumes.perspective.kinmen.beijing.label: The Calculation in Beijing
Volumes.perspective.kinmen.beijing.narrative:
Outside observers have always assumed the objective was to take Kinmen. Given the firepower and manpower committed, if capture had been the aim, these islands would not have held out long. The real question was what would happen afterward.

Kinmen and Matsu were the last physical umbilical cord between Taiwan and the mainland. So long as Chiang Kai-shek held islands two kilometers off the coast, he was still claiming to fight an unfinished Chinese civil war, and the two sides of the strait remained one country whose conflict had not yet concluded. But if the Nationalist forces withdrew from the offshore islands and consolidated on Taiwan and Penghu, the line would become clean — clean enough for the international community to read as a border between two states. Washington was pressing Chiang to abandon Kinmen and Matsu at that very moment, and for precisely that reason.

So the shelling functioned not as seizure but as tether: put the noose on, tighten it when useful, never pull it closed. Firing on odd days and holding fire on even ones looks absurd until you see how exact it is — it keeps the line permanently at war without ever having to finish the war.
