That the shelling finally stopped on January 1, 1979, the day Washington recognized Beijing, was likewise no coincidence. From beginning to end, this rope was a language rather than a weapon.
Volumes.perspective.kinmen.islanders.label: The People of Kinmen
Volumes.perspective.kinmen.islanders.narrative:
When the shells came down, we had no rear to fall back to. People on the main island read about heroism at the front; we learned about this war from the sound of our own roofs coming off. Over forty-four days, more than a dozen shells fell for every person on these islands. For twenty years afterward, life ran on odd and even days — take cover on the odd, work the fields on the even. Children could recite which days they were allowed to walk to school.

The Wartime Administration turned the whole island into a garrison. Curfew, blackout, permits to leave or return, every household enrolled in a civil defense unit. The men cut tunnels into the granite, and so did the women. We had no elections and no freedom of movement. What was called martial law on Taiwan proper was, on Kinmen, something a layer deeper than that.

Later the shell casings were forged into kitchen knives and sold as souvenirs, and the tunnels became ticketed attractions. This is not a complaint; we live off it now. But whenever someone praises this island for having witnessed the price of freedom, we understand one thing very clearly: the people who paid the price were never the people who decided it would be paid. We did not live here in order to become a symbol. We simply lived here.
Volumes.perspective.kinmen.washington.label: Washington
Volumes.perspective.kinmen.washington.narrative:
From Washington the problem was one of proportion: a granite island of sixty thousand people that could drag the United States into a nuclear war with China. The Joint Chiefs did in fact study the use of tactical nuclear weapons against coastal targets, and the mere existence of that option was enough to make the Eisenhower administration determined not to let the crisis climb.

So policy ran on two levels. In public: the Seventh Fleet escorting convoys to the three-mile limit, eight-inch howitzers and Sidewinder missiles delivered to the island, so that Beijing would understand this line was not to be tested. In private: continuous pressure on Chiang Kai-shek to pull his forces off Kinmen and Matsu. The State Department's reasoning was blunt — stationing a hundred thousand of his best troops in a position that could not be held, and that lay outside the explicit language of the Mutual Defense Treaty, handed the decision for American war-making to someone else.

Chiang refused to withdraw, because leaving the offshore islands would have been an admission that he governed Taiwan and nothing more. In the end each side gave ground. In the joint communiqué of October 23, the Republic of China declared that recovery of the mainland would not rest principally on force. It was a successful piece of crisis management, and a trade with a clear price: we bought a guarantee against fighting a nuclear war over Kinmen, Chiang bought the right to remain, and what was spent was the entire story on which his regime depended for its existence.
Volumes.perspective.linfamily.family.label: The Family That Survived
Volumes.perspective.linfamily.family.narrative:
On February 28, 1980, Fang Su-min went as usual to the Chingmei detention centre to visit her husband. When she left the house it held her sixty-year-old mother-in-law, Lin Yu A-mei, and three daughters: nine-year-old Lin Huan-chun and the seven-year-old twins, Lin Liang-chun and Lin Ting-chun. When she returned to the flat on Hsinyi Road, her mother-in-law and the twins had been killed and her eldest daughter, stabbed six times, survived only after emergency surgery. The day was the thirty-third anniversary of the February 28 Incident.

Lin Yi-hsiung learned of it in custody. After his release he did not pursue retribution. The house was given up and later bought back, and rebuilt as the I-Kuang Presbyterian Church; the surviving daughter spoke publicly about that day only many years later. What the family went on to devote itself to was the referendum against the fourth nuclear plant, referendum legislation, and nonviolent protest — not revenge. That choice became one of the most quoted passages in Taiwan's democratic movement: a family that absorbed the most extreme violence the shadow of the state could produce, and still answered through institutions.
Volumes.perspective.linfamily.overseas.label: Abroad
Volumes.perspective.linfamily.overseas.narrative:
Word reached the diaspora within days. Taiwanese hometown associations and human-rights groups carried the details into the US Congress and the American press, less than a year after the passage of the Taiwan Relations Act — the law that wrote the human rights of the people on Taiwan into American policy objectives, making Taipei's internal affairs something Washington could formally raise.

For Taiwanese abroad, the killings changed how risk was calculated. They had believed that a family which stayed out of politics stayed safe; the Lin case cancelled that assumption. Overseas Taiwanese organizations grew markedly more active through the 1980s: hearings, newspaper advertisements, lists of political prisoners handed to one legislator after another. They could not investigate a crime in Taiwan. What they could do was make it impossible to close the file internationally.
Volumes.perspective.linfamily.public.label: Those Who Had Stayed Out of It
Volumes.perspective.linfamily.public.narrative:
The deepest effect of the killings landed on people who never went to a campaign rally and never read a Dangwai magazine. Official propaganda described dissent as a source of disorder threatening stability, and most people chose to believe it — stability had, after all, delivered factories, export orders and school fees.

Then the mother and the seven-year-old daughters of a political prisoner were murdered in their own home, under the eyes of the security services. That could not be explained as disorder. For many people, 1980 was the first time they genuinely asked what claim to obedience a system could have when it could not protect women and children, and might itself have harmed them. The shift left no statistics behind, but it showed up in every election of the following decade.
Volumes.perspective.linfamily.watchers.label: The Watchers
Volumes.perspective.linfamily.watchers.narrative:
At the time of the killings the Lin residence was a priority case for the Garrison Command. Lin Yi-hsiung was in custody on a sedition charge, the surroundings were under watch, the telephone was tapped, and everyone entering or leaving was logged. This is the part of the case that cannot be walked around: inside an airtight net of surveillance, the killer went in, killed, and left — and the records that should have existed came back blank.

The official line was always that the investigation continued. Bruce Jacobs, a foreign scholar then in Taiwan who was named as a subject of inquiry, was never charged, and the case remains open. After martial law ended, the security agencies' files were declassified in batches, yet the wiretap logs and duty records were missing exactly the stretch that mattered. Every transitional-justice inquiry has returned to the same question: even granting that the apparatus was not involved, it still owes an explanation of why, for those few hours, it saw nothing at all.
Volumes.perspective.martiallaw.blacklist.label: A Name on the Blacklist
Volumes.perspective.martiallaw.blacklist.narrati:
On the day martial law ended, thousands of Taiwanese were not in Taiwan and could not return. They had been placed on a list barred from entry for joining overseas Taiwanese organizations, for what they had said, or for funding the Dangwai. Some had not seen their parents in more than twenty years; some spent the day of a father's funeral beside a telephone. Lifting martial law did not lift the blacklist — control over entry and exit had been written into the National Security Act.

So the late 1980s produced the practice of "running the gate": buy a ticket, fly into Taoyuan, be stopped at the airport and deported — or come home hidden in a shipping container or a fishing boat. Every attempt was a public political act, and every one left images in the press. The list was dismantled only gradually in the early 1990s. When the last of them finally set foot in Taiwan, it was thirty years after they had left.
Volumes.perspective.martiallaw.chiang.label: The Man Who Signed It
Volumes.perspective.martiallaw.chiang.narrative:
On July 14, 1987, Chiang Ching-kuo issued the presidential order lifting martial law in Taiwan from midnight on July 15, ending thirty-eight years of emergency rule dating from 1949. The National Security Act took effect alongside it — the lifting was not a release of control but an exchange of legal instruments: verdicts handed down by military courts under martial law could not be appealed, and entry and exit remained regulated.

He made the decision gravely ill, his eyesight badly degraded by diabetes, needing support to walk. In October 1986 he had disclosed his intention to Katharine Graham, the visiting publisher of the Washington Post — announcing it internationally first, then turning back to handle the opposition inside his own party. He was pursuing something else at the same time: Taiwanization, replacing the ageing mainland-born elders with Taiwan-born technocrats, and choosing Lee Teng-hui as vice president in 1984. He died on January 13, 1988, and Lee succeeded him under the constitution. The road he laid was only walked to its end after he was gone.
Volumes.perspective.martiallaw.everyday.label: An Ordinary Household
Volumes.perspective.martiallaw.everyday.narrativ:
For most people the end of martial law arrived not as a decree but as a run of small things. Newspapers got thicker — on New Year's Day 1988 the press restrictions went, lifting both the cap on pages and the ban on registering new titles. Radio discovered the call-in, and listeners could ring up late at night to complain about the government. Banned songs were recorded and released again, with their lyrics intact. Taiwanese, Hakka and Indigenous languages began drifting back into television and popular music.

In November 1987 visits to the mainland were permitted, and veterans who had not been home in forty years began queuing for paperwork; some came back with a photograph of their parents' gravestone. None of this was written in the order lifting martial law, yet this is the version most people remember: not the moment freedom was granted, but the months afterwards, when one thing at a time people discovered what they were already allowed to do.
Volumes.perspective.martiallaw.garrison.label: The Agency That Gave Power Back
Volumes.perspective.martiallaw.garrison.narrativ:
For the Garrison Command, the end of martial law meant a real stripping of power. Under martial law it could control publications, inspect mail, regulate entry and exit, and try civilians before military courts. Afterwards, civilians were no longer under military jurisdiction, and what the Command had handled reverted to the ordinary courts and civil agencies. In 1992 the Garrison Command was dissolved and reorganized as the Coastal Patrol Command.

The transition was not a cliff edge, though. Three statutes — the National Security Act, the Assembly and Parade Act and the Civic Organizations Act — took over the functions the martial-law decree had carried. People were still prosecuted for street protest, and Article 100 of the Criminal Code, which made speech itself a form of sedition, was not amended until 1992. Taiwan at the end of the 1980s occupied a peculiar interval: martial law was gone, but the legal instruments of the authoritarian period were still on the shelf, and reaching for one now simply required a different reason.
Volumes.perspective.movements.farmers.label: A Farmer on May 20
Volumes.perspective.movements.farmers.narrative:
On May 20, 1988, tens of thousands of farmers came north by coach from Yunlin, Chiayi and Changhua. Their demands included opposition to opening the market to American agricultural imports, universal farmers' health insurance, the free purchase of fertilizer, and direct election of farmers' association general managers. The column was blocked outside the Legislative Yuan; fighting broke out in the evening and the two sides faced each other in the streets of central Taipei until dawn, through tear gas, batons and stones. More than a hundred people were arrested and dozens charged — the largest single-day round-up since the Kaohsiung Incident.

On the farmers' side the cause was not politics but prices. Trade negotiations with the United States in the mid-1980s had put agricultural market access on the table, and imports of turkey, fruit and grain pressed directly on rice and orchard farmers; meanwhile the farmers' and irrigation associations that were supposed to represent them had long been controlled through factions and the ruling party's nomination system. After May 20 the movement's demands entered policy one by one: farmers' health insurance began in 1989, and the elderly farmers' welfare allowance was legislated in 1995. The street had not been stood on for nothing.
Volumes.perspective.movements.labour.label: The Independent Unions
Volumes.perspective.movements.labour.narrative:
Unions under martial law were not organized by workers. The Labour Union Act mandated one union per plant with compulsory membership, all of it under the umbrella of the Chinese Federation of Labour, and chairmanships were generally arranged by management or the party branch. After 1987 that changed: bus drivers in Taoyuan took collective leave over Lunar New Year and extracted overtime pay, and independent unions and strikes appeared at Far Eastern Textile, the state railway, the state oil company and the textile mills, outside the official structure. 1988 was called Taiwan's year of labour.

The cost came at once. In the 1989 Far Eastern Textile strike, union officers were dismissed and prosecuted; independent union leaders at several bus companies were convicted of coercion and unlawful assembly. The thresholds the Labour Dispute Act set for a lawful strike made striking all but impossible. Most of that generation of organizers did not survive at their own plants, but they left two things behind: organizations such as the Taiwan Labour Legal Aid Association founded in 1984 — the forerunner of the Taiwan Labour Front — and the Labour Party of 1987, and a question still unanswered: where do workers' collective rights rank on the list of things democratization is for.
Volumes.perspective.movements.language.label: Mother Tongue and the Right to a Name
Volumes.perspective.movements.language.narrative:
On December 28, 1988, Hakka people marched through Taipei. The Return My Mother Tongue movement carried a portrait of Sun Yat-sen at its head and made three demands: open broadcasting and television to Hakka, amend Article 20 of the Broadcasting Act restricting the use of dialects, and adopt a plural and open language policy. Until then, Taiwanese-language programming was capped at one hour a day on television, Hakka was almost entirely absent, and children caught speaking a dialect at school were fined or made to wear a placard.

The Indigenous movement took a different road. The Alliance of Taiwan Aborigines was founded in 1984, and there followed three Return Our Land marches and a long campaign over names: changing the official term from "mountain compatriots" to "Indigenous people", the right to use one's own name on an identity card, and the return of traditional territory enclosed by the forestry agencies and the national parks. The 1994 constitutional amendments wrote "Indigenous people" into the additional articles; in 1997 the wording became "Indigenous peoples". The difference between the two phrasings is the difference between a group of persons and a nation — which was precisely what the movement was for.
Volumes.perspective.movements.state.label: The State Facing the Street
Volumes.perspective.movements.state.narrative:
For the agencies responsible, 1987 to 1990 was one unbroken stretch of overtime. In the first year after martial law ended, street protests ran into the thousands, and the police had to handle farmers, workers, environmental self-help groups, students and demobilized soldiers at once. The newly passed Assembly and Parade Act required advance permits, designated routes and restricted zones — and was immediately proved unenforceable by the sheer volume of unpermitted gatherings.

Opinion inside the government was divided. One view held that disorder in the streets would frighten off investment and shake social stability, and argued for strict enforcement. The other held that most of these demands had nothing to do with the survival of the regime and everything to do with distribution, and should be answered with policy rather than police. The second view gradually prevailed: the expansion of farmers' and labour insurance, the creation of environmental impact assessment, the Indigenous clauses in the constitution — all were legislative answers to the street. This is the least-discussed and most substantial lesson of the passage from authoritarian rule to democracy: the state discovered it did not have to win every confrontation.
Volumes.perspective.nineYearEducation.planners.n:
It is often said that nine-year education was the product of a single sentence — the leader gave an instruction at a memorial assembly and the system complied. The instruction was indeed given that way, but to understand why it could be implemented in fifteen months, you have to see that it satisfied several unrelated needs at once.

The economic planning agencies had the clearest arithmetic. Export-oriented industry was taking off, and what the processing zones lacked was not cheap labor but literate labor — workers who could read a work instruction and be retrained. Stopping half the population's education at twelve was a waste the economy could not afford. That argument appears far more often in internal documents than in public proclamations.

The second need was political. Extending compulsory schooling by three years meant three more years of every citizen inside a state-specified curriculum: Chinese history and geography, the Three Principles of the People, military training, Mandarin. No instrument of propaganda has the penetration of a classroom.

The third was legitimacy. A regime steadily losing international recognition needed an achievement it could display to its own people, and universal education is the hardest kind to dispute.

Three separate arguments pointed at the same policy, which is why it moved. As for what sort of people it would eventually produce, that fell outside the scope of every assessment written at the time.
Volumes.perspective.nineYearEducation.students.n:
We were the first cohort to enter middle school without an examination. The students a year ahead of us were still staying up for the junior high entrance exam; what we received was an assignment notice. That year my class included farmers' children and the son of a blacksmith. Under the old system, their schooling would have ended with primary school.

The new buildings were often unfinished. On the first day the classroom was a shell smelling of wet cement, with no glass in the windows, so on rainy days we moved the desks. There were more than seventy of us in a room, and many teachers had come straight from a short training course. But that leaking classroom was something we would not otherwise have had.

We learned the price soon enough. The pressure had not disappeared; it had moved back three years, and the senior high entrance exam became the new bottleneck. Schools streamed us by score. The top classes had extra lessons until dark, the bottom ones were called the cattle-herding classes, and the teachers spoke to them differently. At thirteen we were told plainly which side we belonged to. Speaking Taiwanese in the corridor still cost you a fine, the portrait of the head of state hung at the front of the room, and the civics textbook told us which country we came from.

It took many years to see it clearly: that door was opened for us by them, and what we learned behind it was later used to question the people who opened it.
Volumes.perspective.nineYearEducation.teachers.n:
The directive came down in June, and the term began in the autumn. In an education system, that is not called reform; it is called firefighting. Several hundred middle schools, several thousand classrooms, and tens of thousands of teachers had to exist across Taiwan within a single semester, and not one of those three things can be manufactured quickly.

Where buildings were not ready we borrowed primary school rooms, temple courtyards, community halls, and ran double shifts. The teaching shortage was harder still: the normal colleges produced nowhere near enough graduates in a year, so the gap was filled with short training courses, substitutes, and cross-subject assignments. I taught Chinese, and was also timetabled for history, geography, and music. The homeroom teacher next door had been working at the farmers' association twelve months earlier. We all knew we were underqualified, and we all knew that if we did not stand up in front of those rooms, the rooms would be empty.

The hardest part was not the exhaustion. It was knowing you were doing something right and could only do it in the wrong way. Some children were genuinely failed — streamed into a bottom class and taught for three years by someone learning the material a week ahead of them. And yet among that same intake were children who sat in a middle school classroom for the first time only because of this scramble.

We had no time in those years to weigh any of it. We finished the day's lessons and went home to prepare tomorrow's three subjects.
Volumes.perspective.redLeaf.players.label: The Boys on the Field
Volumes.perspective.redLeaf.players.narrative:
We knew what we were playing. We were less sure what the adults were watching. To us it was just a game — except that this time the Taipei stadium was full, and there were lights. Normally we practiced on the gravel of a riverbed, with bats whittled from bamboo and balls made of stones wrapped in cloth, running the bases barefoot, our soles by then thick enough that broken glass barely registered.

The day after the seven-to-nothing, we were heroes in the newspapers. People sent equipment. People came to take photographs. People asked us to shout slogans at the camera. Those months felt unreal, like something borrowed.

Then at the end of the year it all turned over. Some of us had played under other boys' names and other boys' ages. That was not a scheme we invented; it was what the adults worked out so that we could take the field at all. Our teacher was convicted, and we went back up the mountain. After that, nobody sent equipment and nobody came to take photographs. Most of us did not finish school, and there was no more baseball. Most went down to the plains for manual work, and several of us died young.

That game still gets mentioned, and we are still glad we played it. It was only later that we understood: what was lifted up that day was not us but something else. We just happened to be standing underneath it.
Volumes.perspective.redLeaf.state.label: The State's Use of a Game
Volumes.perspective.redLeaf.state.narrative:
For the propaganda apparatus, the game of August 1968 arrived with timing almost too good to be true. Over the following decade the regime lost internationally again and again: expulsion from the United Nations, the break with Japan, the break with the United States. Every defeat created a domestic need for an occasion where the flag could be raised, the anthem sung, and the fact that we still existed confirmed. The stands at Williamsport supplied exactly one such occasion per year.

So youth baseball was amplified deliberately. The government coordinated broadcasts, encouraged the whole country to stay up, and turned the image of a village gathered around a black-and-white set at three in the morning into a patriotic rite in itself. Slogans of dignity and self-reliance were printed beside the team photographs. Layer by layer, the outcome of a children's game came to carry far more than a game: to lose was no longer merely to lose.

Emotionally the operation worked. The costs landed elsewhere. Youth baseball became a national project, and the resulting problems — punishing practice loads, falsified ages, adolescent pitchers used far past what their arms could bear — were tolerated for years, because the political cost of stopping was too high. And the children who actually played were caught by no institution once the cameras turned away. What the state needed was the second in which the flag went up, not the forty years that followed for the people who raised it.
Volumes.perspective.redLeaf.village.label: The Village
Volumes.perspective.redLeaf.village.narrative:
When outsiders tell this story, they always begin with the poverty — no bats, no shoes, bare feet. All of that is true, but it gets told as a kind of virtue, as though scarcity itself were inspiring. In the village, scarcity was not a rhetorical device. It was the accumulated result of policy: restrictions on reserved mountain land, the low wages of forestry work, the penalties for speaking our own language at school. That the children were good at baseball cannot be separated from any of this, because it was one of the very few things up here that cost nothing and required no Mandarin to prove.

That winter, the whole mountain lit up for a moment. For the first time our people saw their own children on television and on the front page, and heard the word Bunun spoken aloud, and spoken with praise. Only those who have spent decades being written down as "mountain compatriots" can measure what that weighed.

Then the fever left. When the business of the borrowed names came out, the blame settled on the village, as though we had been the ones cutting corners rather than a system that had never offered these children a legitimate road in the first place. In the decades since, the visiting reporters have grown fewer, and when they come the question is usually what became of them afterward. Each time, we have to say the names again, and say again when each of them died.
Volumes.perspective.repatriation.authorities.nar:
On the desks of the Administrative Executive Office, repatriation was a set of numbers that contradicted one another. Berths were limited, and in 1946 alone more than four hundred thousand Japanese soldiers and civilians had to be shipped out; the same holds were needed to bring back Taiwanese scattered through Japan, China, and Southeast Asia. Quarantine capacity at the ports was inadequate, and cholera spread along the Keelung and Kaohsiung docks in the summer of 1946; food was already tight after the takeover, and every shipload of returnees meant another gap in the ration. The administratively rational choice was slower and fewer, and that is what happened.

More delicate still was the screening. The day before the war ended these people had been Japanese nationals; once it ended, the government had to decide whether Taiwanese who had served the Japanese side counted as traitors to China. Through 1946, procedures and denunciations proceeded side by side on the island while lawyers argued over whether a Taiwanese could even commit such an offense, and most cases were settled somewhere between the file and the favor. From the authorities' side this was the unavoidable housekeeping of a change of regime. From the returnee's side it was the first checkpoint he met in the motherland — where he had to prove he was not an enemy, and the evidence was the whole of the previous fifty years of his life.
Volumes.perspective.repatriation.exiles.label: Those Who Stayed Away
Volumes.perspective.repatriation.exiles.narrativ:
Not everyone wanted a place on those boats. Wang Yu-teh, born in Tainan in 1924, was studying at Tokyo Imperial University, returned to Taiwan late in the war, and taught at a Tainan high school; his elder brother Wang Yu-lin had been the first Taiwanese to serve as a prosecutor in Japan and came home after the war to the district prosecutors' office in Hsinchu, resigning when his pursuit of a corruption case against a local chief was blocked. On March 14, 1947, Wang Yu-lin was taken away in Taipei and never seen again. Two years later his younger brother left Taiwan, slipped through Hong Kong to Japan, and did not return for more than thirty years.

In Tokyo he finished a doctorate and taught the study of Hokkien and Taiwanese, and in 1960 he founded the journal Taiwan Youth, turning his brother's death into a periodical that kept appearing and an organization that kept growing — the early backbone of the overseas independence movement came largely from people like him, who had left to study or to escape and then found they had emigrated. For them home was not unreachable so much as fatal: to return was to disappear. So they deferred the homecoming into a political project, speaking from other people's cities and in other people's languages for the part of the island that could not speak. Wang Yu-teh died in Tokyo in 1985, two years before martial law was lifted.
Volumes.perspective.repatriation.mainland.label: Those Who Came Back from China
Volumes.perspective.repatriation.mainland.narrat:
There was also a road that ran west. Taiwanese who had gone to China during the colonial period had formed another kind of identity in wartime: they worked for the Chinese government, spoke Mandarin, and were called "half-mountain people." Li Yu-pang assembled the Taiwan Volunteer Corps at Jinhua in Zhejiang in 1939, the largest Taiwanese anti-Japanese organization of the war; Huang Chao-chin, Lien Chen-tung, Yu Mi-chien, and Liu Chi-kuang built seniority and connections inside the offices of Chungking. After 1945 they came back with the takeover columns and were quickly installed as speakers, mayors, county chiefs, and party officials.

They saw themselves as the only bridge that could actually be crossed: fluent in how Taiwan worked and in what Nanking expected. But a bridge is the worst place to stand. To islanders they were the men who spoke for the new regime; to mainland officials they were, in the end, Taiwanese. That in-between position did not grow safer after 1947 — Li Yu-pang was executed in April 1952 and his wife Yen Hsiu-feng served fifteen years in prison. When he raised his corps at Jinhua in 1939, his reason had been that Taiwanese, too, should take part in this war.
Volumes.perspective.repatriation.soldiers.label: Taiwanese in the Japanese Forces
Volumes.perspective.repatriation.soldiers.narrat:
The war sent more than 207,000 Taiwanese off the island: over 80,000 as soldiers and more than 126,000 as military employees and laborers, scattered across Hainan, the Philippines, Borneo, New Guinea, and the China theater, and more than 30,300 of them never came back. After August 1945 the survivors were gathered into holding camps to wait — for a ship, for a ruling on their status, for a queue whose order no one could explain. They wore Japanese uniforms and spoke Japanese, and they would board the boats home as Chinese.

For some of them the wait ended not in a ship but in a courtroom. Taiwanese who had served as guards in prisoner-of-war camps were prosecuted in the British, Australian, and Dutch Class B and C war crimes trials; more than 170 were convicted and 26 were executed — men who had carried out the orders of the Japanese army and stood trial holding a different nationality. Those who reached the Keelung docks did not necessarily fare better: their years of service and their injuries were not recognized by the new government, Japanese pensions were unthinkable before a peace treaty, work had to be found again and a language learned again. In the February 28 Incident of 1947, a good number of the people on the streets who knew how to handle a rifle and organize a unit were veterans only recently off those boats.
Volumes.perspective.retrocession.japan.label: Japanese Administration
Volumes.perspective.retrocession.japan.narrative:
For Japan's colonial administration, the surrender marked the end of fifty years of empire-building in Taiwan. Governor-General Ando Rikichi oversaw the orderly transfer of power, dismantling an extensive colonial apparatus that had built railways, hospitals, universities, and a modern legal system — all primarily serving imperial interests, but leaving an indelible mark on the island.

The handover was conducted with characteristic Japanese administrative precision. Colonial officials catalogued assets, transferred records, and prepared for repatriation. For many Japanese residents who had spent their entire lives in Taiwan, the departure was tinged with personal loss. The colonial government's final act was to ensure a smooth transition — not out of generosity toward the incoming Chinese administration, but as a matter of institutional pride and the desire to preserve the legacy of what they considered a model colony.
Volumes.perspective.retrocession.roc.label: ROC Government
Volumes.perspective.retrocession.roc.narrative:
For the Republic of China, the retrocession of Taiwan on October 25, 1945, represented the rightful recovery of national territory lost fifty years earlier. Governor-General Chen Yi presided over the surrender ceremony in Taipei, formally accepting Japanese capitulation and declaring Taiwan restored to Chinese sovereignty.

The ROC government viewed Taiwan through the lens of national reunification and anti-colonial triumph. However, the administration that arrived was shaped by years of continental warfare and corruption. Chen Yi's government imposed a state monopoly system, appointed mainland officials to key positions, and showed little understanding of a society that had undergone half a century of Japanese modernization. The gap between the government's rhetoric of liberation and the reality of its governance would soon become a source of deep Taiwanese disillusionment.
Volumes.perspective.retrocession.taiwanese.label: Taiwanese Elites
Volumes.perspective.retrocession.taiwanese.narra:
Taiwanese elites initially greeted the end of Japanese rule with genuine euphoria. Intellectuals, doctors, and local leaders who had long chafed under colonial discrimination saw the retrocession as a chance to finally participate as equal citizens in their own nation. Streets filled with celebrations, and many eagerly studied Mandarin and prepared to serve in the new government.

But disillusionment came swiftly. The incoming administration's corruption, economic mismanagement, and cultural arrogance shattered expectations. Monopolies replaced Japanese-era industries, inflation spiraled, and Taiwanese professionals found themselves shut out of leadership positions in favor of mainland appointees. The contrast between the orderly, if oppressive, Japanese system and the chaotic new administration was stark. Within months, the joy of liberation had curdled into a bitter realization: they had exchanged one form of colonial subjugation for another.
Volumes.perspective.shibuya.formosans.label: Formosans in Japan
Volumes.perspective.shibuya.formosans.narrative:
After the autumn of 1945, the thirty-odd thousand Taiwanese still in Japan found themselves standing in a position with no name: no longer Japanese in law, not yet Chinese in fact. Food rations were issued by nationality, work and residence permits were granted by nationality, and their nationality was waiting on a peace treaty that had not been signed. Black markets grew in the burned-out districts of Tokyo and Osaka, where Taiwanese and Koreans kept stalls to survive, and the Japanese press began calling them "third-country people" — a term for those who were neither victors nor vanquished.

On July 19, 1946, a group of Taiwanese on their way to the Shibuya police station to negotiate over stall crackdowns was ambushed en route; when the shooting stopped, several Taiwanese and one Japanese policeman were dead. That December a US Eighth Army military court closed the case: more than thirty Taiwanese were convicted, sentenced to prison and deportation, while the Japanese participants faced no comparable reckoning. For Taiwanese in Japan, the verdict answered the question that had hung over the whole year — in the occupation's classification scheme, they did not, in the end, count as nationals of a victorious power. When the news reached the island, the Min Pao and members of the provincial assembly spoke out one after another; it was the first time postwar Taiwanese society got angry, collectively, on behalf of its people abroad.
Volumes.perspective.shibuya.ghq.label: The Occupation Authorities
Volumes.perspective.shibuya.ghq.narrative:
General Headquarters was handling an administrative problem on the scale of millions: Japan held Koreans, Taiwanese, Chinese, and prisoners of war of many nationalities, and the occupation had to decide, before any peace treaty, who fell under which set of rules. The basic occupation directive of November 1945 gave a compromise answer — Koreans and Formosans were to be treated as liberated peoples, but, having been Japanese subjects, might be treated as enemy nationals where necessary. On paper that sentence was flexibility. On the street it was discretion.

By that logic, those who registered as Chinese could apply for repatriation and the treatment that came with it, while those who did not remained under Japanese law; and when violence was involved, occupation courts took the case directly, on the ground that public order was the occupation's responsibility. The Shibuya verdict was a product of that framework: the court found the defendants had engaged in an armed affray inside occupied territory, sentenced them, and deported them, without ruling on which country they belonged to. For headquarters this was a public-order case closed under existing rules. For the men sentenced, it was the moment they learned for certain that until a treaty was signed, no country's law quite covered them.
Volumes.perspective.shibuya.japan.label: Japanese Police and the Street
Volumes.perspective.shibuya.japan.narrative:
The police force of 1946 Tokyo was an institution stripped of most of its power. The Special Higher Police had been dissolved, weapons were restricted, the ration system had broken down, and the burned districts were held at every intersection by the stallholders' syndicates; to shut down a single stall was to face an entire street. In that condition the police folded the problem of black-market order together with the problem of "third-country people": those who were not bound by Japanese law and not clearly under anyone else's became the visible proof that policing had failed. The formulation spread quickly through the newspapers, and it was convenient.

After the shooting of July 19, most of Japanese memory settled on one side of the day — an officer killed in the line of duty. On the other side of the same day, several Taiwanese died on a road they never finished walking to the police station. Postwar Japan's account of that year has long been one of ruins and reconstruction, with little room for the people who had been imperial subjects and were now drawn outside the line. The Shibuya Incident thus has two shapes in two societies: in Japan an episode in the history of public order, in Taiwan the first bloodshed to prove that a nationality left pending is not an abstraction.
Volumes.perspective.shibuya.roc.label: The Chinese Mission in Tokyo
Volumes.perspective.shibuya.roc.narrative:
Nanking's position was consistent and simple: Taiwanese were already nationals of the Republic of China. On January 12, 1946, the Executive Yuan issued an order restoring their Chinese nationality retroactive to October 25, 1945 — Taiwan having been recovered, Taiwanese at home and abroad were covered alike. On that basis Chu Shih-ming, head of the Chinese mission in Tokyo, pressed the Supreme Command to list Taiwanese in Japan among United Nations nationals, with the rations and the legal standing that went with it.

The Shibuya trial forced that claim up against reality. The mission protested the American court's jurisdiction and its sentences, and reported back to opinion in Taiwan that it had done what it could; but under the occupation the Republic of China was one Allied power among several, able to argue for treatment and unable to decide status. More awkward still was the dilemma at home: the government insisted these people were its nationals while lacking the ships, the funds, and the capacity to bring them all back. For years afterward, then, the answer to "what nationality are you" for a Taiwanese in Tokyo depended on the registration card in his pocket rather than on any declaration.
Volumes.perspective.shimonoseki.japan.label: Japanese Government
Volumes.perspective.shimonoseki.japan.narrative:
For Meiji Japan, the Treaty of Shimonoseki represented a triumphant validation of three decades of modernization. Prime Minister Itō Hirobumi and Foreign Minister Mutsu Munemitsu pressed for maximum concessions, viewing Taiwan as Japan's first colonial acquisition and a gateway to Southeast Asia.

The acquisition of Taiwan served multiple strategic purposes: it demonstrated Japan's arrival as an imperial power on the world stage, provided a laboratory for colonial governance, and secured a vital link in Japan's southern maritime defense chain. The Japanese government immediately began planning the island's integration into its empire, dispatching Governor-General Kabayama Sukenori with military forces to establish control — fully aware that resistance would need to be crushed before colonial modernization could begin.
Volumes.perspective.shimonoseki.qing.label: Qing Court
Volumes.perspective.shimonoseki.qing.narrative:
Li Hongzhang arrived at Shimonoseki bearing the weight of a dynasty in decline. The First Sino-Japanese War had exposed the Qing military's fatal weaknesses, and the court in Beijing was desperate to end hostilities. Taiwan, a peripheral frontier province only recently modernized under Liu Mingchuan, became a bargaining chip on the negotiation table.

For the Qing court, ceding Taiwan was a painful but calculated sacrifice — preserving the Liaodong Peninsula and containing further Japanese advances on the mainland took priority. The court reasoned that Taiwan was distant, difficult to defend, and less strategically vital than Manchuria. Li Hongzhang reportedly wept as he signed the treaty, but the decision reflected cold imperial calculus: the dynasty's survival demanded the sacrifice of its margins.
Volumes.perspective.shimonoseki.taiwan.label: Taiwanese Residents
Volumes.perspective.shimonoseki.taiwan.narrative:
When news of the treaty reached Taiwan, shock and fury swept the island. The residents had not been consulted, and many felt betrayed by a distant court that had traded away their homeland. Local elites, led by Tang Jingsong and Qiu Fengjia, hastily declared the Republic of Formosa on May 25, 1895 — Asia's first republic — in a desperate attempt to maintain international sympathy and resist Japanese takeover.

But the republic crumbled within days as its leaders fled to the mainland. What remained was the raw courage of ordinary Taiwanese — farmers, militia members, and local gentry — who mounted fierce guerrilla resistance as Japanese forces advanced southward. For the people of Taiwan, the treaty was not a diplomatic abstraction but an existential rupture: they had been abandoned by one empire and claimed by another, with no voice in their own fate.
Volumes.perspective.taiyuan.authorities.label: The Authorities
Volumes.perspective.taiyuan.authorities.narrativ:
From a security standpoint, the most serious feature of the Taiyuan Incident was not that it nearly succeeded. It did not nearly succeed: the armory never opened and the action was over within hours. The real warning lay in the structure itself.

Several hundred political prisoners were concentrated in a single prison on the main island, and a substantial proportion of the guards were Taiwanese — sharing a language with the inmates, sharing home districts, in some cases sharing relatives. This was not a discipline problem but a design problem: two groups liable to sympathize with each other, held for years on opposite sides of the same wall. That the same year saw shots fired at the vice premier on a street in New York sharpened the assessment. This was not an isolated case but a spreading willingness to act.

The response operated on two levels. Externally: no publicity, no announcement, no show trial. A public trial would have put the words "Taiwanese independence" on the front page, and the last thing required of us was to complete, on their behalf, the broadcast they had failed to make. The five were executed in May and the matter stopped inside the files.

Internally: in 1972 a new reformatory was built on Green Island and the political prisoners were moved offshore, with a strait between them and everything else — language, kinship, and terrain support all severed. That was the one conclusion drawn from Taiyuan that was carried out in full.
Volumes.perspective.taiyuan.five.label: The Five
Volumes.perspective.taiyuan.five.narrative:
We were all serving long sentences — fifteen years for some, life for others. After enough time inside you understand one thing very clearly: this system will not loosen its own grip, and no one outside knows you are still here. Waiting is not a strategy. Waiting is only returning your life in installments.

So what we wanted was not escape. Escape would have saved a handful of us, which would have meant nothing. What we wanted was the radio station. Just once, let this island hear someone say in Taiwanese that Taiwan should be independent, and the thing could never be taken back. The third day of the Lunar New Year was when the watch was thinnest, and there were Taiwanese guards willing to help. On paper the plan was complete.

The armory did not open. From that moment everything after it was hollow — without weapons there was no station, without the station there was no broadcast, and all that remained to us were the mountains.

We know we failed. But we do not accept that the action amounted to nothing. One thing was always clear to us: if everyone judges that now is not the time, then there will never be a time. Someone has to move first, even if no one ever learns that they did.
Volumes.perspective.taiyuan.guards.label: The Taiwanese Guards
Volumes.perspective.taiyuan.guards.narrative:
We stood in the middle, which is a position with no correct answer. The uniform came from the state, but we spoke the same language as the men behind that wall, we came from the same villages, and some of them were the same age as my younger brother. Roll call, meals, escorting them out for exercise — do that long enough and it becomes impossible not to know why they were in there.

So when they came to us, we did not report it immediately. Some genuinely agreed to help. Others simply chose not to see, and in those years choosing not to see was already taking a side.

Then Sergeant Lung was killed. He was a mainlander, sent across an entire strait to this island, with no more choice in the matter than we had. Inside the wall he supervised us; outside it he smoked with us. After that day, nothing about this could be contained by a word like allegiance. Some of us grieved for him and grieved for the five men in the mountains, and both of those things were true at the same time.

When the reckoning came, several of us were prosecuted too. The political prisoners' names were later carved into memorials. Our names appear on neither side — we do not count as victims and we do not count as loyal. This island has become good at commemorating heroes, but it has never quite known where to put people like us.
Volumes.perspective.takasagoVolunteers.command.n:
From headquarters it was a logistics problem. What was defeating the Imperial Army was not the Allies but the rainforest — trucks could not enter, horses died, supply lines dissolved in mud, and men went down in numbers to fever. And in the mountains of Taiwan there were people who could move where there was no road, orient where there was no map, and find water where there was no supply.

The praise was genuine, but it was praise for an instrument. They were sent to cut trails, carry ammunition and stretcher the wounded, and pushed to the front when lines gave way — because they could endure it, and because their losses were easier to absorb. They served another purpose too: their loyalty could be held up as proof that assimilation had worked, that the empire could turn the conquered into its own. It was proof the empire only ever demanded of them, and never of conscripts from the home islands.
"Takasago" was a name given by others. The men who boarded the transports were Atayal, Bunun, Paiwan, Amis — distinct peoples with their own languages, hunting grounds and ancestors, compressed into a single column on an imperial form. Only one generation earlier, their grandfathers had lost those mountains to the same army.

Why go anyway? Colonial rule had closed every old road by which a young man proved himself — the hunt, the raid, the earning of a name within the village. The army opened one, and the hand that opened it was the hand that had closed the others. School had taught loyalty, teachers and police urged them on, the village had a quota, and refusing marked a man. Some also simply wanted to go, wanted to be seen. In the jungles of the south they were praised for precisely the skills the government had spent decades trying to school out of them: reading ground, tracking, staying alive in dense forest. Officers said supplies would never have reached the front without them. It was the first time the empire admitted they were irreplaceable — and the price was carrying the heaviest loads and walking in front.
The call-up fell on the village, not the individual. Quotas came down, the village had to produce men, and a village that produced none was remembered for it. Those who saw them off were mothers, wives and children too small to walk far. For many it was the last time.

Most did not come back. Often there were no remains, only a notice — and sometimes not even that. After the war it became harder still to speak of. The empire they had served dissolved; Japan's compensation excluded former colonial subjects for decades, offering only token condolence payments in the 1990s; and the government that took over Taiwan saw only men who had fought for the enemy. Memorials were removed, and the whole experience became something not said aloud. In 1974 one soldier walked out of the jungle on Morotai to discover that the nation he had served, the home he had left and the language he knew had all ceased to exist — living out, alone, what had happened to all of them. Two states forgot them. The villages did not.
Volumes.perspective.unWithdrawal.delegation.narr:
The moment the important-question motion failed fifty-five to fifty-nine, our side of the hall went quiet. Four votes. Twenty-two years of representation, short by four votes.

Years later people would ask whether accepting dual representation earlier might have preserved the seat. In the Taipei of that time, the question could not be asked. The refusal to sit alongside Beijing was not a slogan; it was where the regime's legitimacy lived. If Beijing could also represent China, then what was this government on Taiwan? Our instructions were unambiguous throughout: the seat may be lost, the title may not be conceded.

So the minister rose before the vote was completed to announce our withdrawal, and the delegation walked out of the chamber. In a situation where nothing else remained within our control, this was the one act still in our hands: not expelled, but departing. We all understood that the distinction meant nothing to the outside world. It meant something to us.

Nobody could speak that evening. A colleague wept in the corridor. We knew what we had just left behind in that hall, and we knew that from the next morning this country would have to learn to exist in some other way — without a seat, without a title, with nothing but an island and the fifteen million people on it.
Volumes.perspective.unWithdrawal.washington.narr:
We did argue for Taipei on the floor, and we were negotiating in Beijing at the same time. The two look contradictory; in fact they were the two ends of a single policy. Strategically the door to China had to be opened, and morally and domestically we could not be seen abandoning an ally.

So we promoted dual representation — preserve the Republic of China's General Assembly seat, concede the Security Council seat to Beijing. Technically workable; politically it required two things at once: that other states be willing to vote for it, and that Taipei be willing to accept it. The second never happened. We pressed the point for years, and Chiang Kai-shek rejected any arrangement resembling two Chinas on the grounds that it amounted to self-negation. From Washington's side, that converted a negotiable position into one where the only available outcome was total loss.

We should also concede that our own effort fell short. During the very days of the vote, Kissinger was in Beijing. Any wavering member state could read that signal. We were asking others to vote for Taipei while personally demonstrating which way the wind blew.

The outcome did not surprise us. What was underestimated was what it produced inside Taiwan. This was not merely a diplomatic defeat; it was the first time the story by which a regime explained itself stopped working in front of its own people.
Volumes.perspective.unWithdrawal.youth.label: The Students
Volumes.perspective.unWithdrawal.youth.narrative:
We were the generation raised inside the textbooks: how many provinces China had, how many rivers, where the capital lay — all of it memorized cold, while the name of the creek outside our own door was not taught. We were told repeatedly that this government represented all of China, and that the world recognized it as such.

Then in 1971 the world withdrew the recognition.

What collapsed first was not trust in the government but trust in the story. If we were not the representatives of all China, then what were we? Once that question is asked aloud it cannot be put back. In the Diaoyutai protests that same year we took to the street for the first time and discovered that patriotism did not have to be defined by the authorities — and discovered, also for the first time, who was standing on the other side once our slogans went past the permitted range.

Some of us went from there to the street and to the dangwai opposition. Others went into literature. The Nativist Literature debate of 1977 appeared to be an argument about how to write; underneath, it was an argument about the same question: whether the people and things of this island were worth making the protagonists.

Our parents' generation read the diplomatic defeats as national humiliation. Ours gradually read them as something else. When a regime can no longer prove itself through the world's recognition, sooner or later it has to turn around and seek legitimacy from the people standing on the ground beneath it. That road was long, but it started in that year.
Volumes.perspective.usview.consulate.label: The Consulate in Taipei
Volumes.perspective.usview.consulate.narrative:
After 1945 the American consulate in Taipei was one of the few channels through which news could leave the island. Vice-consul George Kerr had taught in Taipei before the war and served as a Taiwan specialist for the Navy during it, and knew both the terrain and the people; Consul Ralph Blake handled dealings with the Administrative Executive Office. Their reporting was already blunt in 1946: the corruption of takeover officials, monopoly and trade controls, prices, unemployment, judicial abuse, and the speed with which Taiwanese feeling toward the new government turned hostile, itemized for Washington.

In March 1947 the event was outside the consulate's windows. Taiwanese brought in a petition asking for American intervention or for United Nations trusteeship; the consulate recorded gunfire and bodies while explaining that it could offer no refuge. Kerr's subsequent report became one of the fullest accounts from outside, and made him, in the eyes of the Republic of China's government, a man promoting Taiwanese independence; he left the island that year. In 1965 he published Formosa Betrayed, turning what he had seen into an indictment. For overseas Taiwanese that book was the most important narrative source for decades afterward. For Taipei it confirmed that the diplomat had been on the wrong side from the start.
Volumes.perspective.usview.military.label: The Map in the War Room
Volumes.perspective.usview.military.narrative:
On American military maps Taiwan was first a target and then a springboard. In 1944 the Pacific theater planned an amphibious assault on Formosa under the code name Causeway; after weighing the costs, the effort went to Okinawa and the Philippines instead, and the island was spared a ground war. But from late 1944 through 1945 American air raids continued: military installations at Kaohsiung and Hsinchu and the district around the Government-General in Taipei were bombed, and the great Taipei raid of May 31, 1945 caused heavy civilian casualties. For the people on the island, the most immediate shape of the war was an American aircraft.

The postwar assessment ran the other way. Taiwan holds the middle of the first island chain, touching the Ryukyus to the north and commanding the Bashi Channel to the south, with harbors and airfields already built out under Japanese rule; in hostile hands it would cut the American line in the western Pacific in two — MacArthur called it an unsinkable aircraft carrier. After 1950 military aid and an advisory group followed, and the island was written into the American defense system. That reasoning has not changed since, and it explains something else: for the war planners, who lived on the island and what had happened to them was for a long time a secondary note on the map.
Volumes.perspective.usview.roc.label: Taipei's Reply
Volumes.perspective.usview.roc.narrative:
The Republic of China's government had one consistent reply to American reporting: internal affairs are not open to interference. As Nanking saw it, a consulate that went beyond its remit to meet local figures, record troop movements, and accept petitions was itself intervening; after 1947 officials traced the trusteeship argument and the case for Taiwanese independence directly to those American diplomats and missionaries, and George Kerr was named for years afterward. The charge was not wholly invented — Taiwanese had indeed sought a way out through foreigners — but it also supplied a convenient frame: explain discontent as foreign incitement, and you need not answer where the discontent came from.

Harder was that this government desperately needed the United States at the same time. Military aid, economic aid, diplomatic recognition, and the seat at the United Nations all ran through Washington; it therefore had to protest the contents of the reports while making sure the aid kept coming, and after 1949 that dependence became absolute. When the Seventh Fleet entered the strait in June 1950, Taipei accepted the protection and swallowed, in the same statement, the sentence about Taiwan's undetermined status. From then on its posture toward the United States stayed fixed in one place: unable to do without it in security, unable to agree with it in argument.
Volumes.perspective.usview.statedept.label: Washington's Calculus
Volumes.perspective.usview.statedept.narrative:
The reports on Taiwan that reached Washington were never single documents but chapters inside the whole Chinese situation. Between July and September 1947, General Wedemeyer was sent to survey China and stopped in Taiwan for several days; his report used severe language about the Nationalist government's corruption and incompetence and noted that Taiwanese would rather be placed under trusteeship. The Truman administration chose to classify it rather than publish — publishing would have meant publicly disowning the regime it was backing in the middle of a civil war. The China White Paper of August 1949 continued the same predicament: assign the blame to the Nationalist government, and go on looking within the Cold War frame for a usable position.

On January 5, 1950, Truman declared that the United States would not intervene in the Chinese civil war and would provide no military aid to Formosa. Six months later the Korean War broke out, and on June 27 the Seventh Fleet entered the Taiwan Strait, the same statement holding that the island's future status must await a peace settlement or the United Nations. The move from letting go to defending took half a year, and the reason was not any change inside Taiwan but gunfire on the Korean peninsula. Thirty years of relations rested on that structure: strategic need set the level of support and remarks on human rights went in the footnotes — until the Taiwan Relations Act of 1979 put the human rights of the people on Taiwan into the body of a law for the first time.
Volumes.perspective.wildlily.city.label: Outside the Square
Volumes.perspective.wildlily.city.narrative:
The square was not only students. Teachers from National Taiwan, Tsinghua and Chengchi universities came in shifts, and figures such as Ho Te-fen, Chu Hai-yuan and Chang Chung-tung acted as intermediaries — vouching for the students and absorbing part of the political pressure aimed at them. Residents brought lunchboxes, raincoats, sleeping bags and hot soup; nearby shops opened their toilets; taxi drivers ferried students back and forth for free.

That support came with conditions. Polling at the time showed a majority agreeing that the legislature had to face election, and an equally large majority hoping the movement would not turn into street violence. The students' strict nonviolence, the tidiness of the square, the transparency of their decisions — these apparently formal commitments were how they kept the public with them. After 1990 Taiwan's social movements largely adopted the same grammar: win sympathy first, then negotiate. The other face of it is that a demand which cannot win sympathy struggles to be heard at all.
Volumes.perspective.wildlily.deputies.label: The Perpetual Deputies
Volumes.perspective.wildlily.deputies.narrative:
The men called the perpetual deputies did not think of themselves as usurpers. They were the first-term members of the National Assembly, the Legislative Yuan and the Control Yuan, elected across the provinces of mainland China in 1947 and 1948, who under the Temporary Provisions continued exercising office for more than forty years because no election could be held. As they understood it, they embodied the legal continuity of all China; hold a full election and the Republic would consist of Taiwan alone — the very conclusion they had spent their lives refusing.

The reality was otherwise. Many were past eighty, wheeled into the chamber by carers, needing help to raise a hand for a vote. The self-serving amendments they passed in 1990 were the last straw for public tolerance. That June the Council of Grand Justices issued Interpretation No. 261, requiring all first-term national representatives to cease exercising office by December 31, 1991. In the end they were shown out by a written interpretation, and left with retirement payments under a voluntary retirement statute. The question of legal continuity was never answered; it was simply walked around.
Volumes.perspective.wildlily.lee.label: Lee Teng-hui's Problem
Volumes.perspective.wildlily.lee.narrative:
Lee Teng-hui's hold on power in March 1990 was not secure. He had succeeded to the presidency in 1988 and the party's non-mainstream faction still questioned his legitimacy; while the students sat in the square, the National Assembly was conducting a presidential election in which Lin Yang-kang and Chiang Wei-kuo were briefly advanced against him. And the same assembly had just passed measures extending its own terms and enlarging its own powers, turning the public's anger squarely on itself.

Lee chose not to clear the square but to talk. On March 21 he received the student delegates at the Presidential Office and promised a national affairs conference and a reform timetable. The decision solved two problems at once — the pressure in the square, and the resistance inside his own party — by turning the students' demands into the popular mandate for his own constitutional revisions. The conference convened in June 1990; the Temporary Provisions were abolished in May 1991; at the end of that year the entire first-term national legislature retired and the whole body faced election. Everything the students had asked for arrived within about a year.
Volumes.perspective.wildlily.students.label: A Student in the Square
Volumes.perspective.wildlily.students.narrative:
On March 16, 1990, nine students from National Taiwan University sat down in the plaza of Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall beneath a banner reading: how can we go on tolerating the rule of seven hundred emperors. Within three days there were thousands, from campuses across the island. In the square they built a structure: a decision-making committee of delegates from each university, with separate marshalling, catering, medical and press teams, every action put to a vote, and any involvement by a political party publicly refused.

The four demands were: dissolve the National Assembly, abolish the Temporary Provisions Effective During the Period of Communist Rebellion, convene a national affairs conference, and publish a timetable for political and economic reform. On March 21 some fifty student delegates entered the Presidential Office to meet Lee Teng-hui; on March 22 the square voted to withdraw. The movement lasted six days. No one was arrested and no one was hurt. They came to be called the student movement generation, and many entered politics, the academy and the press; the methods of deliberation and organization they learned in that square surfaced again twenty-four years later in the Sunflower movement.
Volumes.perspective.wuniulan.army.label: A Soldier of the Advancing Army
Volumes.perspective.wuniulan.army.narrative: Our orders were to sweep out the rebels in Puli; we assumed it was nothing more than clearing a rabble. At first light our vanguard stepped onto that narrow bridge, and halfway across, the heights on both sides opened up with a sky full of bullets — we were prey trapped in a sack, unable to advance or retreat, comrades pitching one after another into the ravine. All morning we simply could not get across that bridge. Who could have guessed that the ones holding the far side were a band of seventeen- and eighteen-year-old students? Only later did we bring up mortars and work around the flank onto the plateau, and only then did the tide turn. By the time we finally took Ailan, the far side was empty — they had scattered in the night. That was the most humiliating fight of my whole time in the army. Years later I slowly came to understand that what we faced that day was not a rebellion, but a pack of children who would not let their island be trampled.
Volumes.perspective.wuniulan.frontline.label: A Frontline Fighter
Volumes.perspective.wuniulan.frontline.narrative: The commander told us to keep calm, to let them come close before we fired. I lay on the red-earth slope at the bridgehead, my palms soaked with sweat, counting the enemy as they stepped onto the suspension bridge one by one. They surely never imagined that the far side was held by a pack of students who hadn't even grown proper beards. When the whole bridge was packed with them, the commander gave the word, and I squeezed the trigger — the first time in my life I ever fired at a man. The instant the shots burst out, the bridge dissolved into chaos; men fell into the river, their screams mixing with the roar of the water. We really did hold them off, a whole morning long. But our rounds grew fewer and fewer, and by afternoon shells began falling from the flank, and one by one the classmates beside me stopped moving. When darkness came, the order reached us: disband. I buried my rifle in a gully, took one last look at that bridge, and turned to slip into the pitch-black mountain path. I lived. But many did not.
Volumes.perspective.wuniulan.locals.label: A Resident of Puli
Volumes.perspective.wuniulan.locals.narrative: For those few days the mountain town was full of unfamiliar faces — young students, youths shouldering rifles, and hard men back from the South Seas. They lodged in the Butoku-den and under the eaves of our houses, courteous, never troubling anyone. We all knew in our hearts that these children had come to take the blade for us. At dawn on March 16, gunfire carried from the direction of Wuniulan and went on past noon; we hid indoors, hardly daring to breathe, listening as those shots counted out the hours for us. Only when the gunfire stopped after nightfall did we learn they had scattered. The next day a few boys, covered in mud and blood, came quietly to beg for water and a change of clothes; we asked nothing, gave what we could, and let them go. Later the purge troops entered Puli and searched house by house, and none of us dared admit to knowing those children. But I will remember all my life who it was that stood in front of us, for a whole morning of gunfire at that suspension bridge.
Volumes.perspective.wushaOpensKavalan.kavalan.na:
To the Kavalan, the plain was never wilderness awaiting cultivation. Thirty-six villages were spread across it, the paddy fields long since cleared, the streams running down to fishing grounds, deerskin and mountain goods moving north to Tamsui along trade routes that already existed. They had dealt with Han merchants for decades — Wu Sha among them, a familiar face. The word "opening" carries someone else's vantage point: by any measure that mattered to the people living there, the land was already open.

The earthen wall raised in 1796 changed that. Resistance lasted years and cost lives. What broke the villages, though, was not weapons but the smallpox that arrived alongside the traffic — and when whole settlements fell ill, the remedy lay in the newcomers' hands. What followed was slower and more complete: contracts written in a script they could not read, debts that never closed, a boundary giving way inch by inch. By the middle of the nineteenth century many Kavalan had moved south along the coast to the Qilai plain to build again elsewhere. The plain kept their place names. It did not keep them.
Volumes.perspective.wushaOpensKavalan.qing.label: Qing Court
Volumes.perspective.wushaOpensKavalan.qing.narra:
In the official record, what Wu Sha did was illegal. Kamalan lay beyond the boundary, and Han settlers were forbidden to cross it. The prohibition was not there to protect the indigenous inhabitants; it was there to save trouble. Unrest on the frontier meant troops, troops meant expense, and the court collected not a single tael from land it did not administer. Forbidding it was simply the cheapest form of government.

The ban did not hold. By the time officials looked again, Han settlements ran the length of the plain, the rice harvest came in year after year, and the population was too large to ignore. In 1812 the court reversed itself, established Kamalan prefecture, and sent officials to survey fields and levy taxes — folding an accomplished fact into imperial order. It was a rhythm the Qing repeated across Taiwan: draw a line, fail to hold it, then recognise and tax what had happened regardless. Less an expansion of the realm than an acknowledgement. The court never led this settlement; it walked in once the dust had settled and collected what was there.
Volumes.perspective.wushaOpensKavalan.settlers.n:
For the men who followed Wu Sha over the pass, this was not conquest but the end of the road. By the close of the eighteenth century the western plains had no land left to parcel out, and the luohanjiao who had crossed the strait held no fields, no households, no lineage to fall back on. Behind them was the sea; staying meant hunger. The fertile ground beyond the mountains was the only opening left.

Wu Sha's capital was not force but standing — decades of trade had made him known on both sides of the boundary. He knew the paths, knew the headmen, knew when to pull back. The settlers organised themselves under the jieshou system: shared costs, shared clearing, shared defence. It was at once a method of cultivation and the only way a group of unattached men could stay alive on unfamiliar ground. Many died in those first years, and Wu Sha himself was gone within two of entering the plain. They channelled water into the fields and pushed their settlements southward, ring by ring — in their own telling, people who built a home out of nothing. That home stood on someone else's.
Volumes.perspective.zhongli.crowd.label: The Crowd
Volumes.perspective.zhongli.crowd.narrative:
At first we only went to look. Word was that someone had been caught spoiling a ballot at polling station 213 — the kind of thing we had heard about for decades and never seen proved, and this time there was a witness and there was evidence. The police took the principal away, and we assumed he was being taken in. When nothing happened for hours, we understood he was being protected.

More and more people came. The strange part is that past a certain size of crowd, the fear you are taught from childhood simply thins out. Walking alone you lower your eyes when you see a policeman; that afternoon tens of thousands of us stood on the same street and nobody lowered their eyes. Beside me were laborers, students, a woman with a child on her hip. Nobody was shouting about any ideology. It was one sentence: count the votes properly.

After dark it went out of control. Vehicles burned, glass broke, then there were gunshots and someone went down. That was not the ending any of us had imagined when we set out.

But the sun came up the next day, no troops entered the town, and there was no knock at the door in the night. That fact weighed more with us than the election result did. It turned out we were not the only ones who were afraid, and it turned out that going into the street did not necessarily mean dying. Once that thought exists, it never goes away.
Volumes.perspective.zhongli.party.label: The Party's Calculation
Volumes.perspective.zhongli.party.narrative:
Not deploying the army was the most important decision of that day, and it was a calculation rather than an act of mercy.

First, the election was still in progress. Voting was taking place island-wide on the same day, and using troops at Zhongli would have amounted to declaring the election void — and the regular holding of local elections was this system's principal evidence to the outside world that it was not a dictatorship. Smashing the whole display case over one county magistracy was a poor trade. Second, the international position in 1977 was already thin: the United States was negotiating normalization with Beijing, and a photograph of troops clearing a street would surface at the worst possible moment. Third, the intelligence assessment held that these people wanted an honest count, not the overthrow of the government; if the ballots were tallied truthfully, the crowd would disperse of its own accord.

All three assessments were correct. The crowd did disperse that night, Hsu Hsin-liang won, and the system passed through the evening untouched.

What was wrong was longer-term. We treated restraint as a technical matter of crisis management and failed to reckon that tens of thousands of people present would remember it, and would draw a conclusion from it: that going into the street might carry no price. Two years later in Kaohsiung we corrected that impression by force, and succeeded only in moving the opposition from the street onto the front pages of the world and into the memory of the next generation. Taken together, the two decisions are the actual lesson: a system that runs on fear has already begun to lose once people have measured where the fear ends.
Volumes.perspective.zhongli.police.label: Inside the Precinct
Volumes.perspective.zhongli.police.narrative:
Counting everyone on duty, there were fewer than two hundred of us inside the station and tens of thousands outside. By the afternoon we were no longer maintaining order; we were waiting for instructions. The instructions never came. What our superiors were weighing was bigger than us. We were weighing how long the windows would hold.

When the supervising officer was brought in, we handled it by procedure. What the crowd saw was not procedure but protection, and there was no way to explain the difference in that moment. Many of us lived in Zhongli ourselves. Some of the faces outside were neighbors, and one was a classmate's father.

After dark the vehicles were pushed over and set alight, and the glass came in pane by pane. In the seconds when the shots were fired, nobody was acting on an order. I do not defend it — those two lives were real, and one of them was a student. Nor was anyone clearly held to account afterward, which means the matter was never settled inside the force either.

Years later this day is written up as a turning point for democracy, with the people outside on the right side of it. I will not argue with that. I only want to say that the people inside were also ordinary people, put in a position that should never have been ours to hold: an accusation of ballot tampering, ending with junior officers paying for it with their lives.
Volumes.record.chiangDiary.entry.1.content: The surrender ceremony in Taiwan was held successfully. Taiwan has been under foreign rule for over fifty years since the First Sino-Japanese War. Its retrocession today is truly a great national celebration. However, the takeover work is immensely complex and must be handled with utmost care.
Volumes.record.chiangDiary.entry.10.content: The pain of the Taiwan incident must not be easily forgotten. Henceforth, governing Taiwan should be based on benevolence and respect for the feelings and interests of the local people. However, with the nation facing both internal and external crises, whether this intention can be carried through remains uncertain.
Volumes.record.chiangDiary.entry.2.content: There are many shortcomings in Taiwan's administration. Chen Yi's personnel appointments are inappropriate, and economic controls have provoked public resentment. This should be reviewed and improved, but given the current focus on the mainland military situation, Taiwan affairs are difficult to attend to for now.
