Volumes.record.chiangDiary.entry.3.content: Severe unrest has erupted in Taipei. The cigarette monopoly crackdown bloodshed has triggered large-scale conflict. The severity of the situation exceeds expectations. Ordered Chen Yi to restore order immediately, but must not use excessive force.
Volumes.record.chiangDiary.entry.4.content: The situation in Taiwan continues to deteriorate, with riots spreading to major cities. Taiwanese compatriots were deeply influenced by Japanese enslaving education, combined with Chen Yi's poor governance, leading to an explosion of public anger. Deeply pained by this.
Volumes.record.chiangDiary.entry.5.content: The Taiwan incident grows increasingly complex. Local gentry have formed the "228 Incident Settlement Committee" demanding political reform. Some demands are reasonable, but ambitious agitators are exploiting the situation to attempt to overthrow the government.
Volumes.record.chiangDiary.entry.6.content: Reinforcement troops have arrived in Keelung. Military action was unavoidable to restore social order. However, after suppression, we must show magnanimity and soothe the people's hearts, otherwise irreparable wounds will remain.
Volumes.record.chiangDiary.entry.7.content: Order in Taiwan is gradually being restored, but reports of excessive killing by the military are deeply disturbing. Ordered strict investigation of military discipline and punishment of offending soldiers. The lesson of this incident is that governance must put the people first.
Volumes.record.chiangDiary.entry.8.content: Decided to replace Chen Yi and appoint Wei Tao-ming as Chairman of the Taiwan Provincial Government. Chen Yi's maladministration caused this tragedy, and his responsibility is undeniable. Taiwan's administrative system should undergo comprehensive reform to demonstrate sincerity.
Volumes.record.chiangDiary.entry.9.content: Post-incident relief work in Taiwan is urgent. Dispatching Bai Chongxi to Taiwan on a pacification mission, hoping to calm the people. Must deeply reflect on the root causes of this incident and improve governance policies toward Taiwan.
Volumes.record.chiangDiary.title: Selected Entries from Chiang Kai-shek's Diary
Volumes.record.eliteDiaries.entry.1.content: The motherland's troops have finally arrived. Welcome banners are everywhere on the streets, and everyone greets the new era with anticipation. However, seeing the arriving soldiers with their shabby equipment and loose discipline, I cannot help but feel somewhat disappointed. But I believe this is only temporary — the motherland will ultimately bring progress and prosperity.
Volumes.record.eliteDiaries.entry.2.content: Prices rise three times a day, and the people are suffering beyond endurance. Rice prices at the market have multiplied several times over the past year, making it nearly impossible for ordinary families to make ends meet. The government's monopoly policies only add insult to injury. The 'retrocession' we once anticipated now appears to have been the beginning of a nightmare.
Volumes.record.eliteDiaries.entry.3.content: After the troops entered the city, the killing began. Many innocent people were dragged from their homes and never returned. My friends — those who had fought for Taiwan's future — disappeared one after another. The entire city is shrouded in terror. The ideals and justice we once believed in seem so fragile before the barrel of a gun.
Volumes.record.eliteDiaries.title: Selected Entries from Taiwanese Elite Diaries
Volumes.volume.breakingTheSilence.chenWenchengIn:
At dawn on July 3, 1981, the cicadas had not yet begun their song on the campus of National Taiwan University, and the morning mist had not yet lifted. A janitor discovered a cold male corpse on the lawn beside the graduate library. The body lay face down, limbs twisted — it was Chen Wen-cheng, the U.S.-based scholar who had been taken away for questioning by the Taiwan Garrison Command only the day before. This body, appearing suddenly within the nation's highest seat of learning, struck like a thunderclap that split open the seemingly tranquil halls of academia under martial law and sent shockwaves through communities at home and abroad.

Chen Wen-cheng, a native of Taipei, had graduated from NTU's Department of Mathematics before pursuing study in the United States, earning a doctorate from the University of Michigan. At just thirty-one he had become an assistant professor of statistics at Carnegie Mellon University, his future bright. Warm-hearted and devoted to his homeland, he had actively joined Taiwanese hometown associations during his years abroad and had donated to the Dangwai publication Formosa Magazine. In May 1981 he returned to Taiwan with his wife and child to visit relatives — an ordinary homecoming — not knowing that he had long since been placed on the watch list of the security services.

On the morning of July 2, three agents of the Garrison Command came to his door and took him away for "questioning." The authorities claimed they had merely inquired about his statements in the United States and his support for the Dangwai, and that they had returned him home late that night. Yet by the next morning he lay dead on the NTU campus. The Garrison Command publicly declared that Chen had committed "suicide out of guilt" or had "fallen accidentally," but this account was riddled with holes from the very start and convinced no one. How could a young scholar, only moments earlier reunited with his family and at the height of his career, end his own life immediately after being interrogated?

At the request of the Chen family and the American side, Dr. Cyril Wecht, an authority in forensic pathology, traveled to Taiwan to examine the body. After a detailed inspection he stated that the injuries were inconsistent with a simple fall, and that the evidence suggested Chen may have suffered external violence before the fall — perhaps even that he was already dead before he struck the ground. This assessment from an international expert was a bombshell against the official suicide narrative, deepening the mystery.

The death of Chen Wen-cheng stunned the entire American academic and congressional community. The case exposed the long arm of Taiwan's surveillance over overseas dissidents and outraged an American society that prized human rights and academic freedom. Members of Congress demanded a full investigation; the pressure of public opinion mounted like a tidal wave, ultimately drawing intense attention to Taiwan's human rights situation within the framework of the Taiwan Relations Act and indirectly hastening the later loosening of Taiwan's politics. The fall of one young scholar shook the political order on both sides of the Pacific in the most tragic of ways.

On the island, however, the truth was buried beneath layer upon layer of concealment. The authorities clung to the verdict of suicide and closed the case hastily. Who the killer was, and what truly happened that night, all sank into the abyss of the martial-law system. Chen's widow and young child carried their heavy grief into exile abroad. Like the Lin family massacre, this unsolved case became ironclad evidence of how the state apparatus silently terrorized intellectuals in the age of the White Terror.

Chen Wen-cheng's death also laid bare the most chilling face of the authoritarian system — that its terror was not confined within the borders of the island. Whether you were in Taipei or far away in Pittsburgh across the ocean, if you had ever lent a hand to the Dangwai movement or voiced any "improper" opinion, your every word and deed might be recorded by the all-pervasive informants and professional students. Many Taiwanese studying abroad realized only after this incident that even in a free country, they too lived under the invisible shadow of surveillance. This cross-border fear drew the overseas Taiwanese associations and student organizations into tighter solidarity; no longer silent, they turned grief and indignation into strength, working actively within the international community to expose Taiwan's human rights conditions.

Within academia, Chen's colleagues and mentors were filled with righteous anger. Carnegie Mellon University and scholars from dozens of leading American institutions signed joint protests demanding that the U.S. government confront the human rights atrocities within an ally's borders. This moral pressure from the halls of learning resonated with the congressional investigations, pushing the human rights dialogue between the United States and Taiwan into the open. A young man who had wanted only to pursue his scholarship quietly and care for his homeland — his sudden death became, unexpectedly, a fissure that moved international politics and shook the foundations of authoritarian rule.

With the passing of years, the lawn where the body was found now holds the Chen Wen-cheng Memorial Square, standing quietly within the NTU campus, keeping company day and night with generations of students. The full truth may still not have surfaced, but the name has long since become a spiritual landmark in Taiwan's pursuit of academic freedom and freedom of speech. That we can today speak freely of politics on campus, criticize the powerful, and debate our convictions is because a young scholar once paid with his life to illuminate the truth that thought must never be imprisoned by fear. His silent sacrifice still echoes in every heart that seeks the truth, reminding future generations that the air of freedom never comes from nowhere — it is a grace purchased with the blood and tears of countless forerunners.
Volumes.volume.breakingTheSilence.chengNanjungSe:
At dawn on April 7, 1989, in the offices of Freedom Era Weekly on Minquan East Road in Taipei, a fire offered as a sacrifice of life suddenly engulfed the editor-in-chief's room. When riot police broke down the door, they were met not by a suspect surrendering, but by raging flames and a body that had immolated itself to affirm a conviction. That year, Cheng Nan-jung was forty-one. In the most resolute way imaginable, he proclaimed to an island still bound by the shackles of speech his belief in "one hundred percent freedom of expression."

Cheng Nan-jung, a second-generation mainlander born in Yilan and raised in Taipei, was deeply steeped in liberal thought. After Taiwan lifted martial law, the forbidden zones of speech seemed to loosen, yet hidden reefs lay everywhere. In 1984 he founded Freedom Era Weekly under the creed of "fighting for one hundred percent freedom of expression." Amid the regime's bans and suspension orders, he pressed on relentlessly: he applied in advance for dozens of magazine licenses, and each time one publication was banned he immediately revived another under a new license — waging a near-tragic, ceaseless struggle against the vast machinery of censorship.

In late 1988, Cheng published in his magazine a Draft Constitution for a Republic of Taiwan — an act that, at the time, trampled upon the most sensitive red line of the authoritarian order. The authorities promptly issued a summons charging him with suspected "sedition." But Cheng refused to recognize the jurisdiction of what he regarded as an illegitimate regime, declaring publicly: "The Kuomintang cannot arrest me; they can only seize my corpse." From that moment he locked himself inside the editor's room, beginning a self-imposed confinement that lasted seventy-one days. He prepared gasoline within the room and, in the most uncompromising posture, awaited the inevitable hour of confrontation.

On April 7, the police at last launched their forced arrest. The instant the officers tried to break through the door, Cheng ignited the gasoline he had long prepared, fulfilling in the flames his vow to "fight for one hundred percent freedom of expression." He made a torch of his own flesh, illuminating the dark corners of an age without free speech. This self-immolation, which shook the entire island, allowed countless once-silent people to feel for the first time, with such piercing clarity, just how heavy the price of freedom could be.

Cheng's sacrifice did not end there. On the day of his funeral, another democratic fighter, Chan Yi-hua, set himself ablaze before the procession of mourners, answering the unfinished ideal with his own life. Two pillars of fire seared the conscience of an entire society and branded the words "freedom of expression" indelibly into the history of Taiwan's democratization. The rulers might ban a magazine or arrest an editor, but they could never extinguish the longing for freedom in the human heart.

To understand why Cheng Nan-jung was willing to go to his death in so resolute a manner, one must recall the real predicament of speech in that era. Although the lifting of martial law ended thirty-eight years of military rule, Article 100 of the Criminal Code — the crime of "sedition by speech" — still hung overhead, and anyone who advocated Taiwanese independence or criticized the national system could at any moment be thrown into prison. The towering legal wall the authorities had built in the name of "sedition" made the very words "freedom of expression" a luxury and a danger. Cheng saw through it clearly: he knew that if he surrendered and entered that judicial process, it would be tantamount to acknowledging the authoritarian system's right to sit in judgment over thought. And so he chose the destruction of his own body to utterly repudiate this unjust order, posing to all of society in the most extreme way the question: do human beings have the right to speak the truth free from the rule of fear?

His death was like a blade tempered in flame, cutting through the numbness and silence that Taiwanese society had long maintained toward political taboo. After his self-immolation, the calls to abolish Article 100 of the Criminal Code grew ever louder, and people from all walks of life began to confront the fundamental value of freedom of speech and thought. After several years of advocacy and struggle, Article 100 was finally amended in 1992, so that pure speech and thought would no longer constitute the crime of sedition. The difficult question Cheng had posed with his life at last received an institutional answer through the efforts of those who came after him.

With the passing of years, the scorched editor's room has been preserved intact as the Cheng Nan-jung Memorial Museum. The burn marks on its walls and the twisted iron window grilles speak silently of that morning of martyrdom. April 7, the day he died, was later designated as Taiwan's Freedom of Speech Day, reminding every generation that our power today to speak our minds, to criticize freely, and to debate openly without fear of prison is no gift fallen from the sky. When we raise our voices today online, in the streets, and in the chambers of government, that undying flame still seems to burn in the depths of history, reminding future generations that Taiwan's freedom of speech is an eternal lamp that men like Cheng Nan-jung and Chan Yi-hua were willing to fuel with their own flesh and blood — lit and guarded for the generations to come.
Volumes.volume.breakingTheSilence.dangwaiMovemen:
Under one-party authoritarian rule, a group of courageous Taiwanese chose to seek political participation outside the KMT system. "Dangwai" (literally "outside the party") — originally a neutral administrative term describing non-KMT candidates permitted to contest limited local offices — gradually evolved into a sweeping democratic movement that coordinated lawyers, professors, journalists, shopkeepers, and former political prisoners into something approaching a shadow opposition without the legal right to call itself one.

Beginning with supplementary elections in the 1970s, Dangwai candidates used street speeches at temple squares, mimeographed underground publications passed from hand to hand, and boisterous campaign rallies as weapons to challenge the authoritarian system. Each election cycle produced new martyrs, new slogans, and new networks: candidates who lost on election day often spent the next three years building the next campaign, traveling between townships to distribute sermon-like addresses on constitutional reform, lifting martial law, and the right of Taiwanese to elect their own president.

The founding of Formosa Magazine in 1979 marked the Dangwai movement's transformation from scattered individual actions into an organized political force with bureau offices across the island, an editorial line that linked human rights to economic justice, and a rally calendar that rivaled the state's own ceremonial life. Kang Ning-hsiang represented the moderate parliamentary wing, Huang Hsin-chieh bridged factions as publisher and strategist, and Shih Ming-teh — veteran of the White Terror prisons — carried the movement's uncompromising moral charge; together they formed a leadership that the regime could neither co-opt nor cleanly destroy.

This volume chronicles the Dangwai movement's journey from inception to maturity, presenting how a group of people who refused to stay silent carved a path for democracy within the confines of authoritarianism, and how the rehearsal years of speeches, magazines, and street rallies supplied the organizational muscle memory that would later make a party, an election victory, and a peaceful transfer of power thinkable at all.
Volumes.volume.breakingTheSilence.firstPresident:
On March 23, 1996, the skies over Taiwan were charged with an unprecedented tension and exhilaration. On this day, twenty-one million Taiwanese would, for the first time, directly elect the head of their own nation with the ballots in their hands. Yet on the eve of this historic moment, missiles from across the strait were streaking across the heavens one after another, falling into the waters off Keelung and Kaohsiung. A test launch meant to intimidate by force, and a democracy realized through the ballot, formed upon this land the sharpest and most stirring of contrasts.

Since 1947, Taiwan's president had long been chosen indirectly by the representatives of the National Assembly, with the people having no say whatsoever. After decades of authoritarian rule, the sacrifice of countless martyrs, and a series of constitutional amendments under Lee Teng-hui's leadership, direct popular election of the president was finally settled in the constitutional revision of 1994. It meant that the highest power of the nation would, for the first time, be truly returned to the hands of every citizen. This was the ideal the Dangwai movement had dreamed of for decades, the distant shore toward which Formosa, Cheng Nan-jung, and the Wild Lily Movement had all pointed.

This first direct presidential election featured a vigorous contest among four pairs of candidates: the incumbent Lee Teng-hui with Lien Chan; the DPP's Peng Ming-min with Hsieh Tsung-min; and Lin Yang-kang with Chen Li-an, who ran after breaking with the Kuomintang. Among them, Peng Ming-min was none other than the legal scholar who had spent twenty-three years in exile for drafting the Declaration of Formosan Self-Salvation; that he now returned to his homeland as a presidential candidate was itself a moving footnote to Taiwan's democratic journey. The four tickets waged fierce policy debates and rallies across the island, and the whole nation was immersed in the passion and clamor of democracy.

And yet this feast of democracy was held under the shadow of war. Viewing the direct election as a dangerous signal of a move toward independence, the authorities in Beijing conducted massive military exercises around the strait in the months before the vote and launched missiles into the waters off Taiwan — an episode known as the Taiwan Strait Missile Crisis. The stock market plunged, public anxiety surged, and some people even rushed to stockpile goods and move their assets. The United States promptly dispatched two aircraft carrier battle groups to the strait, demonstrating through action its resolve to preserve regional peace. Amid the howl of missiles, the people of Taiwan faced a severe test of courage and conviction.

At last the day of voting arrived. Far from shrinking before the military threats from across the strait, the people of Taiwan responded with the firmest and most dignified answer of all — a turnout as high as seventy-six percent. With calm and solemn ballots, they proclaimed to the whole world that the future of the Taiwanese people could be decided only by the Taiwanese people themselves, and that they would never submit to intimidation from without. In the end Lee Teng-hui and Lien Chan were elected with a majority of the vote, becoming the first president and vice president in Taiwan's history chosen directly by the people.

The significance of this election, completed amid raging storms, long ago surpassed the matter of victory or defeat. It marked Taiwan's formal transformation from an authoritarian system into a democratic nation with sovereignty vested in the people, completing the most crucial final step of its democratic transition. From the street cries of the Dangwai movement, to the blood and tears of the Lin family and Chen Wen-cheng, to the flames of Cheng Nan-jung and the sit-in of the wild lilies, the ideal that countless forerunners had pursued for decades finally crystallized, on this day, into the thin yet immeasurably weighty ballot held in the hands of every citizen.

The historic significance of this election lay also in how it utterly overturned the source and legitimacy of state power. Through the long authoritarian years, the ruler's power had come from the gun, from the party machine, from indirect elections monopolized by a few; the people were merely the governed, not the masters of the nation. Yet when twenty-one million people cast that ballot with their own hands for the first time, the wellspring of power returned, irreversibly, to every citizen. From then on, anyone who wished to lead this nation had to walk among the people, listen to their will, and submit to the test of the ballot, never again able to issue orders from behind the high walls of authoritarianism. This fundamental reversal in the very conception of power was the deepest inner marker of Taiwan's farewell to authoritarianism and its march toward mature democracy. More precious still, Taiwan accomplished this feat under the intimidation of missiles from across the strait — making the election not merely an internal exercise of democracy but a solemn declaration to the whole world of the Taiwanese people's pursuit of autonomy and their refusal to be swayed by any outside force.

That we can today, every four years, calmly walk into a polling station and decide with our ballots who shall lead this nation — behind that seemingly self-evident right lies a road paved by an entire generation with blood and tears, fire, and youth. The figures who stood up to vote under the shadow of missiles that year seem to echo still through history, reminding future generations that the dignity of democracy is an eternal lamp that the people of Taiwan, with unyielding courage, lit with their own hands — for themselves and for the generations to come.
Volumes.volume.breakingTheSilence.kaohsiungIncid:
On December 10, 1979 — International Human Rights Day — Formosa Magazine organized a massive public rally in Kaohsiung demanding democracy, an end to martial law, and the release of political prisoners. What began as a procession of torches down Chungshan Road escalated when authorities encircled the marchers with armored vehicles and tear gas, deploying riot police to forcefully disperse the crowd before launching mass arrests across the island over the following three weeks.

Core Dangwai figures including Shih Ming-teh, Huang Hsin-chieh, Annette Lu, Chen Chu, Lin Yi-hsiung, Yao Chia-wen, Chang Chun-hung, and Lin Hung-hsuan were indicted for "sedition" — a capital offense — and hauled before a military tribunal whose verdicts had historically been foregone conclusions. The trial proceeded under intense international scrutiny, however, with American congressional staff, Amnesty International observers, and foreign correspondents forcing the regime to open the courtroom to domestic press for the first time in a sedition case.

The defendants used that unprecedented opening to transform the dock into a pulpit: they delivered impassioned statements defending the legitimacy of peaceful assembly, cross-examined prosecution witnesses about torture during detention, and quoted the Republic of China Constitution back at their judges. Although the principal defendants received heavy sentences — from twelve years to life imprisonment — the Kaohsiung Incident instead sparked broader social sympathy and political awakening, deepened by the chilling February 1980 murder of Lin Yi-hsiung's mother and twin daughters while he was still in custody. The defendants' defense attorneys — including Chen Shui-bian, Frank Hsieh, Su Tseng-chang, You Ching, and Chang Chun-hsiung — later became key drivers of Taiwan's democratization, in many cases converting their courtroom experience directly into political careers.

This volume recreates the complete course of the Kaohsiung Incident, from the torchlit rally and the midnight arrests to the courtroom confrontations and the second-generation trauma that shaped an entire democratic cohort, presenting this pivotal event that changed Taiwan's destiny by turning a planned show of state strength into the opposition's most galvanizing public platform.
Volumes.volume.breakingTheSilence.liftingMartial:
On July 15, 1987, President Chiang Ching-kuo announced the lifting of Taiwan's thirty-eight-year martial law — one of the longest continuous periods of military-backed emergency rule in world history. In a single stroke the Taiwan Garrison Command lost its jurisdiction over civilian courts, tens of thousands of blacklisted overseas Taiwanese could begin the long process of returning home, and the restraints that had governed every public gathering since 1949 were formally rolled back, replaced by a new Assembly and Parade Act whose loopholes the courts and the opposition would spend the next decade testing.

The end of martial law meant the lifting of bans on new newspapers and political parties, the opening of mainland visits for veterans separated from their families for four decades, and the legalization of labor unions outside the official federation, as Taiwanese society began experiencing a sweeping wave of liberalization that touched everything from late-night radio call-in shows to university campus magazines. Banned songs were recorded openly, publishers who had operated under pseudonyms reissued their back catalogues, and Hokkien, Hakka, and indigenous languages — suppressed for decades in schools — began to reappear in television programming and popular music.

The decision to lift martial law was not made overnight. From the mid-1980s, the global wave of democratization sweeping South Korea, the Philippines, and Eastern Europe, mounting internal pressures from Dangwai victories in elections and the DPP's de facto founding, and Chiang Ching-kuo's own political judgment — shaped by his declining health, diabetes-induced blindness, and a clear-eyed reading that the regime's long-term survival required controlled opening — collectively led to this historic decision. In the final stage of his life, Chiang promoted localization policies, replaced mainlander elders with Taiwanese technocrats, and elevated Lee Teng-hui to the vice presidency, laying crucial groundwork for Taiwan's democratic transition.

This volume focuses on the political maneuvering and social transformation surrounding the lifting of martial law, exploring how authoritarian rule came to an end through a combination of external pressure, internal reform, and pragmatic succession planning, and how the tremendous energy released by Taiwanese society during the initial phase of liberalization — messy, exuberant, and at times disorienting — set the baseline conditions for every democratic institution Taiwan would build thereafter.
Volumes.volume.breakingTheSilence.linFamilyMassa:
On February 28, 1980 — the thirty-third anniversary of the 228 Incident — the late-winter chill still cut through the streets of Taipei. While the entire city remained shrouded in the grim atmosphere of the Kaohsiung Incident military trials, an ordinary residence on Hsinyi Road became the site of a massacre that would shake the whole island and remain unsolved to this day. The victims were the family of Lin Yi-hsiung, the gentle Dangwai leader who at that very moment sat in a military detention center awaiting trial.

Lin Yi-hsiung, a lawyer from Yilan known for his moderation and reason, had been indicted for sedition following the previous year's Kaohsiung Incident. As he defended the legitimacy of peaceful assembly before the military tribunal, his wife Fang Su-min shouldered alone the burden of caring for their family and traveling to the prison to visit him. On that February day she went to the detention center as usual, leaving behind her aged mother-in-law, Lin Yu A-mei, and three young daughters. When she returned home, she was met not by warm lamplight or her children's laughter, but by a scene of horror that no words could ever fully contain.

In broad daylight, under the constant watch of security agents, an assailant entered the Lin residence and brutally stabbed to death Lin Yi-hsiung's sixty-year-old mother along with his seven-year-old twin daughters, Lin Liang-chun and Lin Ting-chun. The eldest daughter, Lin Huan-chun, was stabbed six times and left clinging to life; she survived only through emergency surgery and what many called a miracle. In a single instant, a whole family was shattered. The news stunned the nation and sent shockwaves across overseas communities.

What made the crime most chilling was its setting. As a major political prisoner under surveillance by the Taiwan Garrison Command, Lin's home was monitored around the clock, surrounded by informants and listening devices. Yet under such airtight watch, the killer somehow entered, committed the murders, and escaped without a trace — while the surveillance records inexplicably went blank. This string of impossible coincidences turned public suspicion, almost unanimously, toward the very state apparatus that was supposed to "protect" its citizens. Was the regime merely negligent, or had it turned a blind eye — or worse, orchestrated the act? The question lodged itself like a splinter that still pierces Taiwan's collective memory.

Although authorities claimed to investigate fully, they produced nothing. The American scholar Bruce Jacobs was briefly named a suspect, but the inquiry led nowhere. With the passing years, the case became one of the darkest and most painful unsolved mysteries of Taiwan's White Terror era. It silently proclaimed that in those days, even unarmed elders and children could not escape the shadow of state violence.

Yet the bloodshed did not extinguish the flame of the Dangwai movement; instead it kindled a deeper grief and a firmer resolve. Countless people who had once watched from the sidelines resolved, after this tragedy, to throw themselves into the democratic cause. After his release, Lin Yi-hsiung was not consumed by hatred but chose to respond to this land with a far broader heart. He sold the house of sorrow and had it rebuilt as the Yikuang Presbyterian Church, transforming a place of grief into a sanctuary of prayer and forgiveness. For decades he devoted himself to the anti-nuclear referendum and social reform, quietly practicing his belief in nonviolence through fast after fast and pilgrimage after pilgrimage.

The massacre also tore apart the facade of "harmony" the authorities sought to maintain. In that era, the official propaganda machine tirelessly extolled stability and prosperity, painting all dissent as a source of disorder. Yet the Lin family massacre exposed this veneer in the cruelest possible way: when the family of a political prisoner could be slaughtered under heavy surveillance, the so-called "stability" was revealed to be nothing more than a sandcastle built upon fear. Many intellectuals and ordinary citizens who had once been indifferent to politics, content to keep their heads down, awakened after this tragedy. They began to ask: what legitimacy could remain for a regime that could not even protect women and children — and might even have harmed them? Such awakening spread like underground fire through the lower strata of society, quietly transforming countless people's attitudes toward the authoritarian system.

At the same time, the case became an important measure by which the international community judged Taiwan's human rights. Overseas Taiwanese communities and human rights groups made the details of the massacre known to the world, and the U.S. Congress and media once again turned their attention to the island. Under pressure from within and without, the rulers could still control the appearance of the judiciary and public opinion, but they could no longer conceal the violent nature at the heart of the system. The suffering the Lin family endured in their own flesh became, unexpectedly, a sorrowful force that moved international opinion and hastened Taiwan's democratization.

To this day, the truth of the Lin family massacre remains buried in the mist of history; the identity of the killer and of whoever may have directed him is still unknown. But the tragedy long ago transcended the bounds of a single crime, becoming a touchstone for measuring whether an era has truly bidden farewell to authoritarianism. When we walk today along the bustling length of Hsinyi Road, the innocent smiles of those twin girls and the image of the grandmother guarding her home seem to remind future generations that Taiwan's hard-won democracy and human rights were purchased with the blood and tears of countless innocents — and that only by refusing to forget, refusing to look away, and continuing to seek truth and justice can the lamp lit for freedom be kept from ever going dark again.
Volumes.volume.breakingTheSilence.oppositionPart:
On the morning of September 28, 1986, one hundred and thirty-five Dangwai activists gathered under the banner of a "campaign assistance committee" in the second-floor Ming Room of the Yuanshan Grand Hotel in Taipei. The announced agenda was to coordinate candidate nominations for the year-end supplementary elections to the central legislature; midway through, however, the participants overturned the planned program, moved and voted on the spot, and announced the founding of the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) — a direct challenge to more than three decades of KMT one-party rule. With the ban on new parties still in force and martial law still in effect, it was a decision of enormous political risk: many in the room had steeled themselves for the possibility that everyone present would be arrested before the session adjourned, and some had brought a toothbrush and toiletries with them.

The danger was no abstraction. Just seven years earlier, during the Kaohsiung Incident, core Dangwai figures — Huang Hsin-chieh, Yao Chia-wen, Chang Chun-hung, and Lin Yi-hsiung — had been convicted of sedition and handed heavy sentences, and remained behind bars at that very moment; Shih Ming-teh had been sentenced to life imprisonment. To found a party was, in effect, to publicly take up their unfinished political cause while they were still imprisoned. It was precisely for this reason that the organizers designed the meeting as a decoy: a small inner circle — Hsieh Chang-ting, You Ching, Yu Shyi-kun, and others — had secretly drafted the party platform and charter in the preceding weeks, hedged by a careful calculation that Chiang Ching-kuo, already turning toward reform and arranging his own succession, would not order a sweeping sedition prosecution over a single party registration and destroy his reformist image in the process. The gamble held.

Two months after its founding, in November of the same year, the party convened its first national congress to elect a chairman. Chiang Peng-chien, who had served as a defense lawyer in the Kaohsiung Incident trials, narrowly defeated the veteran politician Fei Hsi-ping to become the DPP's first chairman. A lawyer who had spent years working on behalf of political prisoners and human rights cases, he took the post fully aware that he could be indicted and imprisoned at any time; on assuming office he openly acknowledged that he had long regarded a prison term as part of the job. Though his one-year tenure was brief, he steadied the party's organization and operations through its most fragile founding phase, laying the groundwork for Yao Chia-wen to take over as chairman after his release the following year, and for the party competition that followed.

The newborn DPP was no monolith but a coalition of political forces spanning a wide spectrum. Abroad, Hsu Hsin-liang, exiled in the United States, had long promoted an overseas party-building movement and repeatedly attempted to force his way back into Taiwan, echoing the founding effort on the island. On the island itself there were moderates, represented by Kang Ning-hsiang, who favored steady reform through parliamentary channels; the social-democratic New Tide line that fused democratic goals with labor and environmental movements; and radical Taiwan independence advocates who insisted the charter must ultimately embrace a plebiscite on the island's national future. How to address questions of national identity while pursuing democratization became a core issue the new party had to face from its very first day, and the debates over direction that followed would shape the DPP's development for the next three decades.

Confronted with this sudden act of party-building, the KMT protested loudly and briefly threatened to suppress it under the law, but ultimately chose to tolerate it, allowing this "illegal" party to operate in a legal grey zone until the lifting of martial law in 1987 and the amendment of the Civic Organizations Act in 1989 formally opened the door to party politics. This volume traces the DPP's path from secret preparations in law offices and magazine editorial rooms to its public founding at the Grand Hotel, and to its first chairman stepping into the breach amid the storm — showing how a single risk-laden weekend afternoon pried open the authoritarian framework and made multi-party democracy in Taiwan not only imaginable but institutionally irreversible.
Volumes.volume.breakingTheSilence.socialMovement:
Around the time of martial law's lifting, long-suppressed social energy erupted like a volcano. Labor movements pushed back against the state-controlled Chinese Federation of Labor and founded autonomous unions in shipyards, railways, and electronics plants; farmers' movements organized island-wide road blockades against agricultural liberalization; environmental protection movements stopped the construction of petrochemical complexes and documented industrial pollution with amateur cameras; women's movements built the first rape crisis hotlines and campaigned for equal inheritance; and indigenous rights movements demanded the rewriting of textbooks and the return of ancestral lands — various social movements blossomed across the island within just a few years, fundamentally transforming Taiwan's social landscape.

The 520 Farmers' Movement of May 20, 1988 brought tens of thousands of farmers to Taipei to protest import liberalization under U.S. pressure, leading to a violent nighttime clash outside the Legislative Yuan and the largest single-day mass arrest since the Kaohsiung Incident. The Hakka "Return My Mother Tongue" movement of 1988, marching beneath banners of Sun Yat-sen remade in Hakka script, demanded an end to the Mandarin-only broadcasting policy and the restoration of Hakka in schools and media; the indigenous peoples' name rectification movement fought through three waves of demonstrations for the right to use their own names on ID cards and for the legal renaming of the official category from "mountain compatriots" to "indigenous peoples." Each of these campaigns demonstrated the pursuit of justice and rights by different social groups.

These movements not only challenged unjust systems left over from the authoritarian era — a state-run single union federation, Mandarin-only classrooms, the casual seizure of indigenous land for national parks and timber concessions, a household registration system that denied women their birth names — but redefined Taiwan's public agenda around citizenship, cultural pluralism, and accountability. Their intellectual scaffolding was built in the new independent magazines and NGOs of the late 1980s; their activists would populate the legislative staff, university faculties, and city governments of the democratic era.

This volume presents the vibrant panorama of social movements during Taiwan's democratization period, documenting how various social forces — farmers, workers, women, Hakka, indigenous peoples, environmentalists, student activists — fought for their rights and dignity amid the wave of democratic transformation, and how their overlapping campaigns wove the dense civil-society fabric that still distinguishes Taiwan's democracy in the twenty-first century.
Volumes.volume.breakingTheSilence.wildLilyMoveme:
In March 1990, the chill of early spring had not yet fully faded from Taipei, yet on the broad plaza before the Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall a tide of youth gathered — powerful enough to shake the entire national order. Thousands of university students from across Taiwan sat in protest on the cold stone ground, taking as their emblem the wild lily, a flower symbolizing autonomy, purity, and resilience, and raising a deafening cry against a political structure long since ossified.

The spark of this movement lay in the absurd political reality of the time. Although Taiwan had lifted martial law three years earlier, the nation's highest organ of power — the National Assembly — was still occupied by a group of "ten-thousand-year representatives" elected on the Chinese mainland in 1947 and never re-elected since. These aging delegates not only never had to face voters, but that very year sought through legal amendments to expand their own power and terms of office — an act that utterly enraged a society hungry for democratic reform. On March 16, a handful of NTU students were the first to begin a sit-in at the memorial plaza; the single spark swiftly set the prairie ablaze.

Within just a few days the sitting students swelled from a mere handful to several thousand, gradually developing a rigorous self-governing organization. On the plaza they established a decision-making committee, discussing and voting on every action through democratic procedure, displaying remarkable self-discipline and reason. They put forward four great demands: dissolve the National Assembly, abolish the Temporary Provisions Effective During the Period of National Mobilization for Suppression of the Communist Rebellion, convene a National Affairs Conference, and set a timetable for political and economic reform. Each of these demands struck at the very heart of the authoritarian system, calling for sovereignty to be truly returned to the people. Through cold nights the students sustained one another with song, speeches, and hunger strikes; the wild lily on the plaza only grew more steadfast amid the wind and rain.

Facing this irresistible student force, President Lee Teng-hui, newly inaugurated that same year, displayed a political wisdom utterly different from the past. Rather than deploying the state apparatus to crush the protest, on March 21 he personally received more than fifty student representatives at the Presidential Office, listened to their demands, and promised face-to-face to convene a National Affairs Conference and advance constitutional reform. This historic dialogue between students and the highest power brought the movement to a peaceful and fulfilling close. Having achieved their immediate goals, the students rationally announced their withdrawal from the plaza and departed unharmed.

The impact of the Wild Lily Movement reached far beyond those six days of sitting. Upon the powerful mandate of public opinion the movement created, Lee Teng-hui was able to press forward with his blueprint for reform. The following year, the ten-thousand-year representatives who had clung to power for decades finally retired en masse, and the legislature achieved comprehensive re-election; the Temporary Provisions, too, passed into history. From that point Taiwan's constitutional order took its single most crucial step toward democratization. A peaceful protest launched by students had pried loose the heavy wheel of history in a manner so rational and graceful.

That this movement could gather such tremendous force within just a few days was inseparable from the society-wide yearning for change at the time. After the lifting of martial law, the energy of Taiwanese society surged like spring waters breaking through the thaw; social movements of every kind rose one after another, and the people's imagination of democracy grew ever clearer. Yet the pace of reform in the political system lagged far behind society's expectations — and the existence of the ten-thousand-year legislature was the most glaring symbol of that gap. That the students chose the plaza of the Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall as the site of their sit-in carried a profound symbolism in itself: before this monument built for an authoritarian leader, they would proclaim, in the most peaceful and rational posture, that a new era belonging to the people was about to dawn.

What was especially precious was the rare maturity and self-restraint this movement displayed in the history of Taiwanese social activism. The students strictly upheld the principle of nonviolence, maintaining astonishing order and cleanliness on the plaza; they made every decision through open and transparent procedure, refusing the intervention or co-optation of any political party and insisting on the autonomy and purity of the movement. This rational and restrained style of protest not only won the broad sympathy and support of the public but also set a model for the citizen movements of Taiwan's later years. While the democratic transitions of many nations were accompanied by bloodshed and turmoil, Taiwan was able to advance its reforms in so graceful a manner — and for this the Wild Lily Movement deserves no small credit.

With the passing of years, many of the once-callow students who sat on that plaza became pillars of Taiwan's political, academic, and social-movement worlds, and the years they shared became an indelible democratic awakening for an entire generation. That we can today enjoy a regularly re-elected legislature and decide our nation's direction with our ballots is because a group of young people, on that slightly cold spring more than three decades ago, guarded the seed of democracy on the plaza with the innocence and resilience of a wild lily — quietly, yet with unshakable resolve. That lily standing firm in the wind seems to bloom still on the plaza of history, reminding future generations that Taiwan's democracy never descended from nowhere, but is a lamp watered and guarded by the hands of generation after generation of people unwilling to remain silent, with reason and with courage.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.aboriginalFronti:
Throughout the Qing period, the relationship between Han settlers and Taiwan's indigenous peoples was defined by an official boundary — the 'savage boundary' (番界) — a line of earthen mounds, ditches, and guard posts stretching across the island's western foothills. East of this line lay the territories of indigenous communities whom the Qing classified as 'raw savages' (生番), largely beyond imperial control; to the west spread the Han-settled plains, where 'cooked savages' (熟番) — indigenous groups that had adopted Han customs and paid taxes — occupied an increasingly precarious middle ground.

This frontier was never stable. Generation after generation, Han settlers pushed eastward in search of arable land and the island's lucrative camphor forests, encroaching on indigenous hunting grounds and provoking violent confrontations. The Qing authorities alternated between enforcing the boundary to maintain order and quietly tolerating its violation to collect land taxes from newly cleared fields. For plains-dwelling indigenous peoples, the result was a slow dispossession: their communal lands were absorbed through lease agreements, intermarriage, and outright seizure, gradually eroding their cultural and economic autonomy.

The Mudan Incident of 1874 — when Japan launched a punitive expedition into southern Taiwan after Paiwan warriors killed shipwrecked Ryukyuan sailors — exposed the consequences of Qing neglect. Japan's intervention demonstrated that territories the Qing claimed but did not effectively govern could become pretexts for foreign aggression. The crisis prompted Shen Baozhen's 'open the mountains, pacify the savages' (開山撫番) campaign, a belated and often brutal effort to extend roads, military posts, and administrative control into the island's mountainous interior.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.babaoCanal.descr:
The broad Changhua plain had deep, rich soil that should by rights have yielded abundant harvests, yet it suffered from one great want: water. Flat and low-lying, the plain saw its rivers flood in the rainy season and run dry in the drought, leaving farmers at the mercy of an unreliable sky. A single dry year could ruin a crop. Until the land could be steadily irrigated it remained a country of parched fields and uncertain harvests, where settlers came and went and villages struggled to take root. In the early eighteenth century, seeing such fertile ground lying idle for lack of water, the wealthy landowner Shi Shi-bang resolved to change all of this, undertaking one of the most ambitious engineering feats of Qing Taiwan: a great canal to draw the waters of the Zhuoshui, the island's mightiest river, out across the plain.

It was a nearly defiant ambition. The Zhuoshui ran fierce and heavy with silt, its wide bed shifting and unruly, and to dam and divert such an untamed river was no small task. Shi poured a vast fortune and great labour into the work, engaging craftsmen and mobilising tenant farmers to cut the channels inch by inch along the planned course. Begun in 1709 and completed around 1719 after years of struggle, the canal took the better part of a decade to finish — a work of a scale and duration then unmatched on the island.

What nearly undid the whole enterprise was the intake. However the builders raised their weir, the racing current tore it away again and again, silt choked the mouth, and the river simply would not be led into the channel. With years of effort on the verge of coming to nothing, legend tells that in the darkest hour a mysterious old man known only as Mr. Lin appeared, and taught the builders how to fashion a weir of bamboo and stone that worked with the river's force rather than against it, at last coaxing the water into the canal. His task done, Mr. Lin vanished without taking any reward, leaving behind only a near-legendary memory that is honoured to this day.

Once complete, the canal and its branching web of channels watered eight of the plain's districts — the 'eight bao' from which it took its name. The bao were the basic administrative units of Qing local government, and these eight, joined together, covered the broad heartland of the Changhua plain. Clear and steady water flowed down the channels and split across the fields, turning cracked and parched earth into some of the most productive rice land in all of Taiwan.

Wherever the water reached, the countryside was transformed. Fields that had once depended on the whims of the weather could now yield two rice crops a year, and yields multiplied. The Babao Canal made Changhua one of the foremost granaries in all of Taiwan, its rice not only feeding the region but shipped through the ports to Fujian and the mainland beyond, a vital link in sustaining the empire's southeast. Plenty brought wealth, wealth drew people, and waves of new settlers came to farm wherever the canal's water ran. Market towns rose and villages lined the channels, and the whole human landscape of the plain was rewritten.

The Babao Canal did not stand alone. It belongs with the other great waterworks of the age, together sketching the central story of Qing Taiwan's frontier settlement: that the wealth of the island was built not only by the plough but by the patient, collective labour of moving water. Such canals were costly undertakings, often financed by the wealthy and dug by the combined effort of many tenants, and when they succeeded they enriched generations — the fruit of countless nameless craftsmen and farmers. The making of waterworks reshaped the value of the land and the distribution of its people, and left a deep mark on the society of Taiwan's western plains.

Three centuries on, the Babao Canal still carries the waters of the Zhuoshui quietly across the plain, nourishing the same fields. It is a hydraulic inheritance that shaped the island's agriculture for centuries, and a witness to the long struggle — and final reconciliation — between the settlers, the land, and the great river. Mr. Lin who vanished may be only a legend, but the people of Changhua, who have depended on the canal's water for generation upon generation, long ago wove that gratitude and reverence deep into the memory of the plain.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.babaoCanal.title: The Babao Canal
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.birthOfChiayiNam:
In mid-eighteenth-century central Taiwan, the migrants who had braved the deadly Black Ditch crossing and survived the Qing's restrictive isolation policies found themselves in a society far more chaotic than the one they had left behind. The Qing Empire still treated the island with wary suspicion rather than genuine governance. Local officials grew rich through corruption, and rank-and-file Green Standard soldiers were little better than roaming thugs. Worse still, as arable land grew scarce, migrants from Zhangzhou, Quanzhou, and the Hakka regions of Guangdong fought endless ethnic feuds over water rights and farmland. In a land where law offered no justice and officials offered only extortion, the lower classes turned to extralegal networks for survival. This twisted pressure cooker eventually birthed a vast underground mutual-aid society in Dali, Taichung — the Tiandihui, or "Heaven and Earth Society."

At the heart of the storm that would sweep across Taiwan stood a Zhangzhou migrant named Lin Shuangwen. In his thirties, broad-shouldered and stoic, Lin had settled in Dali as a farmer and cart driver. In secret, however, he served as the lodge master of the central Taiwan Tiandihui. The Tiandihui of that era was essentially the immigrant society's mutual-aid network fused with an underworld brotherhood. Members swore blood oaths, called Heaven their father and Earth their mother, and stood by one another in ethnic clashes and against official extortion. With his easy charisma and remarkable organizational skill, Lin drew thousands of homeless Luohanjiao and desperate tenant farmers to his side. While this force quietly gathered strength underground, the Qing authorities played with fire atop the powder keg.

In 1786 (the fifty-first year of the Qianlong reign), the magistrate of Zhanghua and the Taiwan military authorities recognized the Tiandihui's expansion and ordered a sweeping crackdown. But Qing "crackdowns" were often nothing more than plunder dressed in official robes. Soldiers stormed villages near Zhanghua and Dali, unable to distinguish criminals from civilians — burning homes, extorting wealth, and abusing women. Some commanders openly threatened to exterminate the families of any suspected society members. This tyranny, leaving no path forward, finally ignited the rage that had simmered for years. Tiandihui leaders gathered at Lin Shuangwen's home in fury. Watching the smoke from his burning village, Lin shed his peasant linens, donned battle robes, and raised the banner of "Obeying Heaven" — the rebellion's standard against the Qing.

Lin's rebel army struck like a bolt of black lightning, tearing apart the Qing's grip on Taiwan. These men, hardened by years of frontier feuding, unleashed astonishing destructive power. Within days they had taken Zhanghua and beheaded the magistrate. Luohanjiao and oppressed peasants across the island rushed to join the cause; in the south, Zhuang Datian raised his own army in echo. In a matter of weeks, the rebels swept across most of Taiwan, surrounded the Tainan prefectural city, and routed the regular Qing garrisons stationed on the island. When news of the uprising crossed the strait to Beijing, the Qianlong Emperor flew into a rage. He could not tolerate that during his self-proclaimed "Ten Great Campaigns" era of imperial glory, a remote island had erupted in a rebellion that shook the empire. He dispatched general after general to suppress the revolt — each one defeated in turn.

At last, he played his trump card. He sent his most trusted Manchu commander, Fukang'an, Governor-General of Shaanxi-Gansu, leading sixty thousand elite Manchu, Han, and Hui troops armed with the empire's finest weaponry, bearing down on the Taiwan Strait.

But before that thunderous clash of steel could unfold, the rebellion's fate took a strange turn at a place called Zhuluo. The walled city of Zhuluo (today's Chiayi City) was the choke point on the rebels' path to Tainan. Lin's forces besieged it for months, but Zhuluo held like a nail driven into their throat. The defense was not the work of the Qing army; it was the result of a brutal ethnic survival contest within the walls. Zhuluo's residents were mostly Quanzhou migrants and local "cooked savages" (the Pingpu people), while the rebels outside were largely Zhangzhou Luohanjiao. The long-festering hatred of the Zhangzhou-Quanzhou feuds bred terror among Zhuluo's Quanzhou residents: they believed that if the Zhangzhou rebels broke through, the slaughter would be unimaginable.

Driven by sheer survival instinct, Zhuluo became the stage for one of the era's most harrowing scenes. The city's Quanzhou merchants, gentry, and common people — men, women, and children — climbed the walls together, allied with Pingpu militia and the remnants of the Qing garrison. For months under siege, with food and arms exhausted, residents boiled bark, roots, and even the leather of their mules and horses to survive. Not one opened the gates. Lin's army hammered the walls day and night while the defenders hurled logs, stones, and crude cannon fire in return. Corpses piled high outside; blood reddened the moat. This unity, forged from ethnic hatred and existential fear, pinned down Lin Shuangwen's elite forces and bought Fukang'an the critical time he needed to land his sixty-thousand-strong army.

In the depths of winter 1787, Fukang'an's massive fleet landed at Lugang and Anping. The renowned Qing commander combined relentless artillery advance with masterful political manipulation, exploiting the Zhangzhou-Quanzhou and Hokkien-Hakka rifts to woo one side while crushing the other. Fukang'an personally led the Manchu cavalry that broke the siege of Zhuluo. When this general in the imperial yellow jacket stepped into the scarred, skeletal city, the surviving residents knelt across the streets. Fukang'an's report on Zhuluo's loyal defense reached the Qianlong Emperor — then basking in the joy of the "Pacification of Taiwan." Reading how the city had withstood the "rebels" for months without imperial relief, sustained only by its civilian militias, Qianlong was deeply moved. To honor the residents' loyalty — "the righteous people of all mountains, united as one heart" — he personally issued an edict renaming Zhuluo County to "Chiayi County" (literally "Praising Righteousness"). This is the origin of the place name "Chiayi" that Taiwan carries to this day.

But the renaming came with a historical reckoning. Lin Shuangwen's forces, encircled by Fukang'an's regulars, collapsed step by step. Fierce as the rebels were, they could not withstand the discipline, heavy artillery, and divide-and-rule tactics of imperial troops. Lin retreated with his remnants into the Nantou mountains along the old aboriginal boundary. Starving and freezing, betrayed and informed upon by former comrades, he was captured by Qing soldiers in a valley between Hsinchu and Miaoli. In 1788, Lin was hauled to Beijing. Under torture in the imperial clan court, he refused to yield. He was sentenced to lingchi — death by a thousand cuts — and his entire family was brutally executed.

The end of the Lin Shuangwen rebellion was yet another historic hangover of Qing policy in Taiwan. In this bloody storm that swept across the island, there were no true winners. The Qing court used treasury silver and sixty thousand troops to crush the revolt, but it never resolved the deeper contradictions of institutional exploitation and resource scarcity that drove the immigrant society to violence. The name "Chiayi" — sounding so noble and righteous — was in truth painted onto history with the blood of ethnic feuds, the survival gambits of the powerless, and the political calculations of an emperor.

The story of how Chiayi got its name is, in miniature, the story of Qing-era Taiwan itself — a land where "small revolts every three years and great upheavals every five" became proverbial. Bureaucratic corruption forced the Tiandihui into armed resistance, while the deeply rooted ancestral feuds within immigrant society became the empire's most effective weapon against rebellion.

Lin Shuangwen lost his life on history's chessboard. But he and the men of Dali, through a rebellion that shook the Forbidden City, carved into the mountains and plains of central Taiwan the eternal mark of the powerless yearning for survival and refusing to bow.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.caogongCanal.des:
The Fengshan plain south of present-day Kaohsiung had been under continuous Han Chinese cultivation since the early eighteenth century, yet its agricultural productivity remained hostage to the region's unpredictable hydrology. The summer typhoon season brought brief floods that sometimes drowned standing crops; the long dry season left the soil cracked and unworkable. Farmers had developed local workarounds — small weirs, seasonal channels, water-sharing arrangements — but no systematic infrastructure capable of irrigating the plain at scale.

Cao Jin arrived as magistrate of Fengshan county in 1837 and encountered a community whose relationship with the authorities was marked by deep suspicion. His predecessors had generally treated the magistracy as a license to extract rather than to administer. Cao's response was to stake his tenure on solving the water problem at source. He conducted a personal survey of the terrain, consulted local farmers and gentry, and developed a plan to divert water from the Donggang River's upper reaches through a series of channels that would reach across the Fengshan plain from north to south.

Construction began in 1838 and proceeded with a speed that surprised observers accustomed to the glacial pace of official projects. Cao managed the work personally, controlled costs without recourse to the customary unofficial surcharges, and maintained quality standards throughout. Within two years the main trunk line was functional, and the canal network ultimately irrigated more than ten thousand jia of farmland — roughly a third of the county's arable area.

The farmers who had watched the canal come to life named it the Caogong Canal — the Canal of Magistrate Cao — and built a temple in his honor when he departed. He was transferred to Fujian and never returned to Taiwan, but his canal continued to water the Fengshan plain for more than a century, eventually becoming part of the modern irrigation system that still operates in the region today. His name survives in place names across southern Kaohsiung as a memorial to the principle that government, when it chose to, could serve the people rather than extract from them.
Before the tide of Han migration swept across central Taiwan, this fertile plain was already the homeland of the plains peoples — the Taokas, the Papora, the Pazeh and their neighbours — who for generations had fished, hunted, farmed and multiplied here. But as the Qing brought Taiwan into its realm, these "acculturated aborigines" were enrolled into the system of rule, becoming subjects burdened with corvée labour and tribute.

For the plains communities, no burden was heavier than the endless corvée. They were conscripted at the officials' whim to haul documents and military supplies, to build walls and roads, and to furnish whatever the runners demanded, often missing their own planting season and left without food or clothing. The interpreter-brokers wedged between the government and the Han settlers frequently worked both ends, exploiting the people layer upon layer and wringing them dry. Resentment accumulated, drop by drop, in this daily round of conscription and abuse.

In the winter of 1731 the burden finally broke them. Provoked by an especially cruel demand for labour, the Taokas of Dajiaxi, near present-day Dajia in Taichung, could bear no more, and under a leader remembered as Lin Wu-li they rose in revolt. They burned government offices and attacked garrison posts, hurling a cry of rage at the colonial order that oppressed them.

What began as one community's defiance spread swiftly across the central plain. Neighbouring communities suffering the same oppression answered the call one after another, until more than a dozen Indigenous communities were drawn in, forming the largest plains-aborigine uprising the Qing ever faced. For a time this prairie fire paralysed the officials of the centre and shook Qing rule in central Taiwan.

The alarmed court swiftly mustered heavy forces in reply. The provincial military commander of Fujian led a great army across the strait, and joining the local garrisons, unleashed overwhelming and merciless force to encircle and crush the communities in revolt. After months of bloody suppression, this desperately unequal resistance was at last put down.

The reprisals that followed were devastating. Villages were burned to the ground, and the people were slaughtered, captured and scattered; the Shalu community suffered most grievously, all but annihilated, its population dwindling to a mere handful of households. And Dajiaxi, the heart of the uprising, was pointedly renamed by the Qing as "Transformed by Virtue" — in the sense of "having submitted and been civilised" — a permanent brand upon its subjugation and humiliation.

The failure of the Dajiaxi Uprising became a turning point in the fate of the central plains peoples. With the road of armed resistance now closed, they could only, beneath the flood of Han settlement and the government's policies of assimilation, gradually lose the autonomy of their land, language and culture. Over the century and more that followed, many of the plains communities either migrated elsewhere or dissolved into Han society, their once-distinct identity fading year by year.

After the uprising was put down, the Qing added garrison posts and tightened its guard in the centre, yet never truly addressed the roots of the oppression — the heavy corvée and the layered exploitation of the interpreter-brokers went on as before. With the road of armed resistance now utterly closed, the plains peoples could only bear in silence a fate of land lost inch by inch and livelihoods growing ever harder.

Into the nineteenth century, as the pressure of Han settlement mounted, the Pazeh, Taokas and other central groups even undertook large-scale collective migrations, crossing mountains to the distant Puli basin, and on to Yilan and Hualien in the east, in search of new ground on which to make a life. The plains settlements that had once spread across the central plain withered in these successive dispersals, and the languages and customs of many groups drifted, with them, toward the edge of extinction.

This uprising was the desperate last stand of the central plains peoples against a state that both extracted their labour and eroded their land and dignity. Its terrible outcome not only hastened the long decline of the very societies it crushed, but also wrote an unforgettable chapter in this island's heavy history of how Indigenous peoples lost their homelands under foreign powers.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.dazhongyeAndWans:
In mid-Qing Taiwan, whether walking the winding alleys of Tainan prefecture or the dusty plains of Zhanghua and Chiayi, one often comes across small, unassuming shrines tucked beneath banyan trees or beside abandoned burial grounds far from any village. They lack the grand swallowtail roof ridges or ornate carved beams of major temples; their red-brick walls bear only a stone tablet inscribed with "Dazhongye" (Lord of the Multitude) or "Wanshan Tonggui" (Ten Thousand Souls Returning Together).

These are not the temples of well-known deities, but the "yin temples" that shelter unclaimed wandering spirits. Pull back the veil of history, however, and the spiritual roots of these constantly-tended shrines trace back more than a century — to the apocalyptic tragedy at the end of the Dutch period, the Guo Huaiyi Incident, and the century of echoes and reflection it left in mid-Qing immigrant society.

The story's hidden origin lies in 1652. Taiwan then was ruled by the Dutch East India Company, and Han migrants — crushed by harsh exploitation, oppressive head taxes, and extreme class hierarchy — were a powder keg of accumulated rage. Han leader Guo Huaiyi could no longer bear seeing his countrymen treated as slaves, and raised the banner of rebellion near Chikan in Tainan, vowing to overthrow the "red-haired barbarians." But the peasant uprising met an extraordinarily cruel end. The Dutch allied with thousands of indigenous (Pingpu) warriors and unleashed a campaign of extermination.
It was a one-sided slaughter. Han farmers wielding hoes and machetes faced Dutch flintlocks and indigenous spears. Within days the uprising was crushed in blood, Guo Huaiyi was killed, and of the roughly twenty thousand Han migrants in Taiwan at the time, between four and five thousand were massacred. Corpses piled high, the streams near Chikan ran red, and the stench lingered for months. These migrants who had come seeking survival in a foreign land never saw a harvest — they became the unclaimed bones in the wilderness, picked apart by wild dogs.

After Zheng Chenggong drove out the Dutch and Shi Lang's 1683 conquest formally brought Taiwan into the Qing Empire, the island entered more than two centuries of Qing rule. But history was not made gentler by changing regimes. The early Qing court imposed the strict "crossing prohibition" that barred migrants from bringing families, leaving Taiwan's society overwhelmed with wifeless, childless, propertyless single men — the famous "Luohanjiao," or "Arhat-feet."

By the mid-Qing, the western plains were saturated, and competition for survival turned vicious. These men, unmoored from family and consumed by frustration, channeled their fury into extreme violence under the catalyst of official corruption. Taiwan descended into chronic chaos — endless Zhangzhou-Quanzhou feuds (Zhangzhou and Quanzhou Han slaughtering each other), Hokkien-Hakka feuds (Hokkien Han battling Hakka), and Han-indigenous clashes over hunting grounds.

In that mid-Qing era of "small revolts every three years and great upheavals every five," Taiwan became a vast grinder. One day Zhangzhou men burned a Quanzhou village; the next, Hakka men took Hokkien heads. Each feud left fields and ditches strewn with broken corpses. Like the victims of the Guo Huaiyi Incident, many of the dead had no kin in the world — no descendants to bury or mourn them.

In traditional Han belief, the souls of those without descendants to make offerings became starving, vengeful "wandering ghosts" (ligui) who would bring plague, famine, and misfortune to a region. Faced with countless unsolved deaths and unnamed bones, the survivors carried a vast collective trauma and fear. They began to ask: from the Guo Huaiyi Incident in the Dutch era to the ancestral feuds of their own day, was this island doomed to sink eternally into seas of blood?

To pacify these violently dead spirits, and to ease the guilt and dread of the living, mid-Qing immigrant society developed a uniquely inclusive culture of yin worship.

In Tainan, Zhanghua, and Taipei alike, local people and merchants began to organize on their own. Carrying baskets and hoes, they walked across the wildernesses and dry creek beds where feuds had been fought, gathering the white bones bleached in the sun. While collecting these remains, they could not tell whether each bone had belonged to a Zhangzhou man, a Quanzhou man, a Hakka, or an indigenous person. Before death, all ethnic hatreds dissolved. They were simply souls who had fallen on this island in the struggle to survive.

People cleansed the commingled bones and buried them together in great collective tombs. Before each tomb they built a small shrine, inscribing on its stone tablet the four characters "Wanshan Tonggui" (Ten Thousand Souls Returning Together). These four characters held the deepest insight Taiwan's migrants drew from their history: no matter how viciously we hacked at each other in life for ancestral loyalties and selfish gain, in death our ashes mix together inseparably — returning to nothingness, and to this earth, as one.

As for the nameless heroes who died in uprisings, in resistance against officials, or defending their homes, local people honored them as "Dazhongye" (Lord of the Multitude) or "Shenggongma." Communities held grand pudu rituals on a regular schedule, offering rich food and wine to these wandering souls. In psychological terms, this was a subtle defensive mechanism — by ritually transforming "vengeful ghosts" into "deities," the living no longer feared retaliation, and instead, through collective worship, forged communal identity. In a frontier society without order, a moral and emotional order was built outside of institutions.

Today, when we walk the streets and alleys of Taiwan and see the small shrines of Wanshan Tonggui, Youyinggong, or Dazhongye, the curling incense smoke is a historical umbilical cord stretching back centuries.

It records the tragic resistance of Guo Huaiyi and his four thousand countrymen in the Dutch era; it records the bloody struggles of countless Luohanjiao caught in ancestral feuds during the mid-Qing. These yin temples are Taiwan's own "monuments to collective trauma."

They tell later generations that Taiwan's prosperity today was built, inch by inch, by countless lives that lost in history's cracks — lives whose names were never even recorded. The flesh and bones of those nameless people leveled the ground beneath us. After blood and conflict, the ancestors finally chose the compassion of "Ten Thousand Souls Returning Together" to find reconciliation and peace for this turbulent island.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.earlyQingRecords:
By the final years of the Kangxi Emperor's reign, the Qing court was confronting an awkward truth: more than three decades after annexing Taiwan, it still knew almost nothing about the island. Officials rotated in and out on brief appointments, completing their terms and departing for more comfortable postings on the mainland, leaving behind few records of what they had seen. The vast interior remained unmapped. Taiwan, for the purposes of imperial governance, was administered rather than known.

This began to change in 1722, when a small cohort of serious officials arrived with an unusual ambition — to understand the island they had been sent to govern.

Huang Shujing arrived as a censor with a mandate to inspect conditions across the island. He took his mandate seriously. Over two years he traveled the length of the western plains, crossed into frontier zones that most officials avoided, and observed ceremonies of indigenous villages. The result was the Taihai Shicha Lu — the most detailed and systematic account of Taiwan produced during the Qing era. What distinguished his work was genuine curiosity: he wrote about indigenous communities not as threats to be suppressed, but as peoples with their own coherent social structures and ways of life. His ethnographic notes on the tribes he observed remain among the earliest first-hand accounts of Taiwanese indigenous cultures.

Chen Bin served as circuit magistrate during roughly the same period and became Taiwan's first official celebrated specifically for incorruptibility. In a posting notorious for the enrichment of officials at the expense of the population, Chen refused all customary gifts, used his personal savings to repair public buildings, and funded schools out of his own pocket. Residents erected a living shrine to him while he was still in office — an honor normally reserved for the deceased — and continued to honor it for decades after his departure.

Sun Yuanheng was a poet-official who transformed his Taiwan observations into verse. Hundreds of his poems recorded the textures of frontier life — the flooded paddies of the plains, the morning mist at the mountain boundary, the terror of crossing the Black Ditch. He wrote with the detachment of a classical scholar but with an eye sharp enough to catch what the administrative records missed.

Zhou Zhongxuan, magistrate of Zhuluoshire, oversaw the first systematic compilation of a local gazetteer for the western plains — a comprehensive record of land, population, and history that gave the region a formal written identity within the imperial record-keeping system.

Together, these officials produced Taiwan's first layer of written documentation. Their work was not entirely free of imperial assumptions, but within those limits they looked, listened, and wrote with a seriousness that distinguishes their accounts from the bureaucratic placeholders that came before.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.ethnicFeuds.desc:
For much of the Qing era, Taiwan was a young society of migrants from every quarter packed in together. They had crossed the treacherous Black Ditch to get there, and on unfamiliar ground they contended fiercely over fields, water and livelihood. Such a society was restless and unsettled, and it earned a grim reputation: "a small revolt every three years, a great upheaval every five."

Beneath the periodic rebellions against the state ran a violence more constant, and closer to daily life — the subgroup feuds. "Subgroup" meant that people formed sharply divided camps along the lines of their ancestral origins: Zhangzhou against Quanzhou, Hokkien against Hakka, and even, among fellow Quanzhou folk of different counties, the Tongan people against the people of the Three Districts, who could turn their weapons on one another.
