The sparks that set off a feud were often trivial: a disputed field boundary, a fight over water for the paddies, control of a market or a harbour, a clash at a temple festival, even an unpaid debt. But in a land where the imperial magistrate was far away and his soldiers few, such ordinary quarrels could, once clans and fellow-villagers were mobilised, escalate swiftly into pitched battles.

Once a feud broke out, hundreds or even thousands would gather, armed with blades, spears and staves, to burn homes, destroy fields and plunder villages, leaving dozens or hundreds dead or wounded. The losers, at best, lost their property and were scattered; at worst, whole villages were burned to ash and entire lineages forced to migrate. The Qing-era local gazetteers of Taiwan are full of records of such bloody clashes, mirroring a frontier of weak order where everyone lived in peril.

The most famous erupted in 1853 in Bangka — the Dingxiajiao feud. The Three Districts people of the "upper guild" and the Tongan people of the "lower guild," both from Quanzhou, turned on one another over wharves and commercial interests. The defeated Tongan were forced to abandon Bangka and move north to make a fresh start at Dadaocheng — a move that, unexpectedly, made Dadaocheng's later prosperity and forever redrew the commercial map of the Taipei basin.

In Yilan there was the curious spectacle of the "Xipi" and "Fulu" factions, whose young men feuded for years over rival schools of music and turf. On the surface these conflicts were struggles of pride and profit, but deeper down they reflected a society without any public authority to arbitrate, in which people could seek security and belonging only through blood, native place and the worship of their gods.

The frequency of the feuds was branded deep into Taiwan's landscape and folk custom. Many settlements raised high walls and set up defensive gates because of them; and the local deities each group revered — the Sage King of Zhang for the Zhangzhou people, the Great Emperor Baosheng for the Quanzhou, the Three Mountain Kings for the Hakka — became spiritual banners that bound one's own kind together and marked off outsiders, still scattered through the temples of Taiwan to this day.

Fuel was added, too, by the peculiar demography of the early crossings. The Qing long enforced bans on migration to Taiwan and restrictions on bringing families, so that the early migrants teemed with able-bodied young men who had come alone, unencumbered by household ties — the so-called "rootless wanderers." Drifting from place to place with no fixed home, they became, whenever trouble flared in a village, the fiercest and most reckless fighters in a feud, making conflicts all the easier to spin out of control.

Faced with feud after feud, the Qing officials were often unequal to the task, and at times were secretly content to see the different groups hold one another in check, standing aside in a spirit of "divide and rule" and intervening only reluctantly, with troops, once matters had grown large enough to threaten order. This passive and calculating manner of governing only drove the cycle of private violence and inter-group enmity deeper, and made it harder to undo.

Only in the later Qing, as local administration gradually strengthened, as the opening of the ports brought a new order, and as the different groups, living intermingled over generations, slowly let the lines of ancestral origin fade and grew a shared consciousness of being "all Taiwanese," did this century-long fire of feuding at last die down. The subgroup feuds were a painful scar in the maturing of a frontier society — and a testament to how the people of Taiwan moved, step by step, from enmity toward a shared fate.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.firstSteamLocomo:
At the close of the nineteenth century, the Qing Empire stood in the bleak autumn of its decline. Yet on this side of the strait, in Taipei, an unfolding modernization experiment would prove the most radical and forward-looking the empire had ever attempted. Shaken by the Sino-French War, the Qing court in 1885 resolved to elevate Taiwan to provincial status, appointing the open-minded Huai Army general Liu Mingchuan — celebrated for his battlefield exploits — as its first governor.

Liu Mingchuan was an eagle-eyed, iron-willed statesman of remarkable boldness. Standing on the newly built Taipei city wall, looking out across the basin's rice paddies and screwpine groves, he was not planning the cautious routine of a typical Qing official. He envisioned turning Taiwan into the most advanced modernization model province in all of China. He would light the streets with electric lamps, string telegraph lines across the island, and found schools of Western learning. At the very heart of his ambitions — the project most condemned as "heretical" by the conservative bureaucracy — was the construction of Taiwan's first passenger railway.

In the Qing Empire of that era, many conservative ministers regarded the steam train as a demonic apparition. They believed the locomotive's thundering roar would disturb the dragon veins of the empire, its black smoke would offend the gods, and even the iron rails might ruin the geomancy of the land. Liu Mingchuan stood his ground against the court's opposition, facing endless impeachments and constant threats of having his funding cut off. Yet through extraordinary political skill, and with the wholehearted backing of local merchants and gentry — among them the Dadaocheng tycoon Li Chunsheng — he managed to establish the "Taiwan Railway Commerce Bureau" and formally opened the project to international bids.

The difficulty of the engineering surpassed anyone's imagination. Liu's planned first stage ran from Keelung Harbor, over a tangle of mountain ridges, to Taipei, then extended onward to Hsinchu. Between Keelung and Taipei the mountains were steep, the rivers swift, and the terrain treacherous. Taiwan's chronic plagues of malaria and miasma added to the toll. Thousands of Taiwanese laborers and Green Standard soldiers — hoes in hand one day, iron shovels the next — chipped their way inch by inch through rock under blazing sun and pouring rain. The excavation of the "Shiqiuling Tunnel" near Keelung was particularly brutal: poor rock conditions and endless seepage caused repeated collapses, and countless laborers perished from accidents and fever. But Liu Mingchuan did not retreat. He personally inspected the works on site, and after thirty months of grinding labor, the first railway tunnel in Taiwan was finally bored through.

The climax of history arrived in the autumn of 1891.

On that day, Taipei's Dadaocheng railway station (roughly today's Zhengzhou Road in Taipei) was a sea of people, drums and gongs ringing through the air. Tens of thousands of Taipei residents in long robes and skullcaps, joined by curious folk who had traveled all the way from central and southern Taiwan, packed the station grounds shoulder to shoulder. Necks craned, eyes wide with curiosity, tension, and even a flicker of fear.

Suddenly, from far down the rails, came a piercing, brilliant whistle that cut across the entire Taipei Basin skyline. Then the ground began to tremble. Through clouds of steam and black smoke, a passenger steam locomotive — manufactured by Germany's Hohenzollern Locomotive Works, its body gleaming with cold steel — pulled slowly into the platform. Named "Tengyun" ("Cloud-Soaring") by Liu Mingchuan himself, the engine breathed white steam in heavy, beast-like exhalations.

When "Tengyun" came to a perfect halt with its wooden passenger carriages trailing behind, the crowd erupted in thunderous cheers and gasps of amazement. Local officials and gentry boarded, and at the conductor's signal, "Tengyun" sounded its whistle once more. The wheels struck dazzling sparks against the rails, and Taiwan's first official railway passengers were carried at the breathtaking speed of twenty or thirty kilometers per hour across the rolling rice fields of the Taipei plain. Farmers and water buffaloes in the paddies, watching this iron beast tear across the earth trailing smoke, stood frozen with disbelief. On that day — October 20, 1891 — the Keelung-to-Taipei railway officially opened, marking Taiwan's entry into the age of modern industrial civilization.

Liu Mingchuan's "Tengyun" was not merely a locomotive; it was a time machine, hauling at full throttle this island — once dismissed and nearly abandoned by the Kangxi Emperor two centuries earlier — into the future of modernity. Thanks to this railway, the coal of Keelung Harbor and the "tea gold" of Dadaocheng could flow in perfect commercial circulation. Thanks to this railway, Taiwan's political and economic axis was permanently riveted to the north of the island.

Sadly, the modernization miracle Liu Mingchuan had single-handedly engineered soon met its historical dusk. In 1891, weakened by factional struggles within the court and by his own failing health, Liu resigned and left Taiwan in disgrace. Just four years later, in 1895, the Qing Empire suffered devastating defeat in the First Sino-Japanese War and signed the Treaty of Shimonoseki, ceding Taiwan to Japan. When Japanese troops marched into Taipei across the very railway Liu had built with his own hands, more than two centuries of Qing rule over Taiwan formally came to an end.

Yet the legacy that Liu Mingchuan and the laborers who shed their sweat and blood at Shiqiuling Tunnel left behind has never vanished. Today, when we sit in sleek, comfortable high-speed or TRA trains and glide effortlessly between Taipei, Keelung, and Hsinchu in mere minutes, every inch of rail beneath us traces its origin back to that locomotive a century ago — to "Tengyun," whistling into the world through clouds of black smoke and tears.

It was the final scene of Taiwan's two-hundred-year Qing chapter — and at the same time, the first proudest cry that Taiwan, armed with technology and an unbending spirit, sent forth to the modern world.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.foreignNaturalis:
The opening of Taiwan to foreign residence following the Treaty of Tientsin in 1858 coincided with the high period of the Victorian collecting expedition, when natural history museums across Europe and North America were actively soliciting specimens and observations from the frontiers of empire. Taiwan's combination of geographic accessibility, biological diversity, and indigenous communities largely untouched by Western contact made it unusually attractive to the naturalists, adventurers, and cultural observers who began arriving in the port towns of Danshui and Dagou in the 1860s and 1870s.

Robert Swinhoe, a British consular officer who first arrived in Taiwan in 1856 — before the formal opening of the treaty ports — was the pioneer of this wave of observation. A trained ornithologist with wide-ranging interests in natural history, Swinhoe documented Taiwan's fauna with methodical thoroughness, describing more than fifty species previously unknown to Western science. The species he described continue to bear his name in their scientific taxonomy: Swinhoe's buttonquail, Swinhoe's pheasant, Swinhoe's tree lizard. He also produced some of the earliest Western accounts of Taiwanese indigenous peoples, writing with genuine anthropological interest about social structures and ceremonies that most consular colleagues preferred to avoid.

Joseph Steere, an American zoologist from the University of Michigan who visited Taiwan in the 1870s, pushed deeper into indigenous territory than most Western visitors of his era. His fieldwork brought him into contact with communities that had seen few outsiders, and his field notes filled gaps in Western understanding of both the island's natural history and its human populations.

William Pickering arrived in Taiwan in 1863 and, thanks to his fluency in Hokkien, gained access to communities and conversations closed to most contemporaries. His later memoir, Pioneering in Formosa, remains one of the most readable first-hand accounts of frontier Taiwan in the English language.

John Thomson, a Scottish photographer who visited Taiwan in 1871, contributed something qualitatively different: photographs. He moved through Taiwan's treaty-port settlements and selected indigenous villages with a large-format camera, producing a series of images that constitute the earliest systematic visual record of the island. His photographs of Tainan's streets, the harbor at Dagou, and the faces of indigenous men and women he encountered captured details of material culture and everyday life that no written account could fully convey. Distributed in published albums in Europe, they shaped Western visual understanding of Taiwan for decades.
Observers at the Edge of Empire
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.indigenousLandCo:
The expansion of Han Chinese settlement across Taiwan's plains during the Qing era operated through a distinctive set of legal instruments — known collectively as indigenous land contracts, or fan qi — that served as the formal mechanism through which frontier agricultural land moved from indigenous to Han Chinese ownership and control. These contracts existed at the intersection of Qing legal norms, indigenous customary practices, and the raw economics of land hunger, and they produced outcomes that were systematically disadvantageous to the indigenous communities who entered into them.

Zhang Dajing operated within this system with exceptional effectiveness. Arriving in the central Taiwan frontier zone in the early eighteenth century with the official designation of interpreter — a position that gave him formal authorization to interact with indigenous communities — he leveraged his language skills and personal relationships with Taokas and Papora tribal leaders to accumulate land-use rights across a wide area. His signature technique was the exchange of irrigation infrastructure for land access: he financed the construction of canals and weirs that brought water to previously uncultivable land, and accepted rights over the newly irrigated acreage as payment. The arrangement was beneficial to both parties in the short term — the tribe gained water, Zhang gained land — but the long-term effect was to transfer the productive base of indigenous territories into Han Chinese hands. He became one of the largest landholders in central Taiwan, his fortune built on contracts that had seemed, at the time of signing, to offer fair value.

Pan Xianwen's position was different and in some ways more tragic. A Kavalan intermediary on the northeastern frontier around present-day Yilan, he navigated the impossible role of advocate and facilitator simultaneously — helping Han settlers access Kavalan land and resources while attempting to negotiate terms that would leave his community with enough of a material base to survive the transition. His efforts produced contracts that were somewhat more explicit about terms than the norm, but could not ultimately reverse the structural disadvantage of a non-literate indigenous community negotiating with parties who controlled the writing, the courts, and the administrative apparatus. In his later years, Pan led a group of Kavalan families southward along the eastern coast, resettling in the Hualien area in an attempt to find land beyond the reach of Han expansion — a journey that prefigured the forced relocations and dispersals that would characterize Taiwan's indigenous experience in the centuries that followed.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.indigenousResist:
The encounter between Taiwan's indigenous peoples and Qing Chinese expansion did not have a single form or a single outcome. It was not simply a story of conquest followed by resistance followed by defeat, though all three were certainly present. It was a more complicated set of negotiations, adaptations, and confrontations spread across more than two centuries, involving dozens of distinct peoples facing a colonial pressure that arrived with different intensities in different places and at different times.

Zhi Muliu was a Saisiyat chief whose career fell in the early eighteenth century, when the frontier between Han settlement and indigenous territory was still being established and both sides were still testing what was possible. Zhi Muliu pursued a strategy of selective engagement — trading with Han merchants for goods the Saisiyat wanted, resisting by force when settlement pushed too close to vital resources, and maintaining enough ambiguity in his commitments to avoid being bound by any agreement that would have foreclosed future options. His flexibility gave the Saisiyat a degree of autonomy that lasted longer than it might have under more rigidly confrontational leadership.

Arokus was a leader in the Mudan community, the Paiwan village at the center of the 1874 incident that changed the trajectory of Taiwanese history. When Ryukyuan sailors shipwrecked on the southern coast in 1871 were killed following indigenous customary law, the incident became the pretext for Japan's first military expedition to Taiwan. Arokus fought in the Japanese engagement and was killed. His resistance made the incident internationally significant, forced the Qing court to confront its claims about eastern Taiwan, and triggered the 'opening the mountains' program that would reshape the island's geography and demographics.

Pan Shengqing chose the path of integration. A man of mixed Kavalan and Pingpu descent who obtained official appointments within the Qing administrative system, he became one of the very few indigenous people in the Qing era to hold formal bureaucratic authority. The price of this strategy was visible: integration required adopting the cultural markers of Han Chinese respectability and accepting the premises of a system that classified his own people as backward. Whether his career achieved net benefit for the communities he represented is a question that cannot be answered simply — it illustrates, at minimum, the impossible trade-offs that indigenous survival in Qing Taiwan required.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.kavalanOpening.d:
The Kavalan plain — known in the Qing records as Jiazinanlai, today as Yilan — lay on the other side of the Snow Mountains from the rest of Qing Taiwan's administrative world. The Kavalan people had farmed, fished, and traded there for centuries. The Qing court had long classified the plain as 'savage territory' and issued formal prohibitions against Han Chinese settlement, a policy designed more to avoid the administrative complications of a new frontier zone than to protect the Kavalan from encroachment.

The prohibitions were not enforced. From the late eighteenth century onward, illegal migrants crossed the mountain passes in increasing numbers, establishing farming hamlets in the plain's river deltas and occupying land in the informal but persistent way that characterized frontier expansion throughout Qing Taiwan. The court knew this was happening and chose not to intervene.

Yu Wenyi, serving as circuit intendant of Taiwan in the 1760s, was among the first officials to argue in writing that this ambiguity was unsustainable. His memorial laid out the case for bringing the Kavalan plain into the formal administrative system: the alternative was a growing population of unregistered settlers outside imperial jurisdiction, a situation that would eventually produce the unrest and violence the court most wanted to avoid. The argument was sound, but the court filed and ignored it for three decades.

What finally forced the issue was Wu Sha's large-scale migration campaign beginning in 1796. Within a decade, the plain held a substantial Han Chinese population with no formal legal status, no court system, and no mechanism for resolving disputes. Yang Tingli was the official sent to assess the situation — three times over more than a decade he crossed the mountain paths, conducted surveys, recorded population figures, interviewed settlers and indigenous leaders, and submitted detailed reports to the court. His persistence was the decisive factor in the eventual decision to act. In 1812 the Kavalan Sub-Prefecture was formally inaugurated. The plain that had been off the map for a century was now part of the empire. For the Kavalan people, it was the beginning of the end of their autonomy over the land their ancestors had cultivated for generations.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.kingOfTheBlackFl:
While the Luohanjiao on land battled the Qing with broadswords and blood, the Black Ditch — the strait separating Taiwan from the mainland — entered its most chaotic and dramatic golden age. In the early nineteenth century, the Taiwan Strait was at once a golden corridor of merchant ships and rolling wealth, and a lawless blue wasteland beyond the reach of any government. Out of these storm-tossed seas rose a pirate king whose very name made the Qing Empire, Western powers, and merchant houses tremble: Cai Qian.

Cai Qian was born into desperate poverty in Tong'an, Fujian. Orphaned young, he survived as a cobbler, then as a dock laborer, witnessing the worst of human cruelty. With no path forward, he plunged into the Black Ditch and joined the pirates. With astonishing nerve, a precise mastery of winds and tides, and a leader's mix of generosity and ruthlessness, Cai Qian rapidly absorbed the strait's smaller pirate bands. By around 1800 he had built a vast maritime empire — over a hundred massive refitted warships and more than twenty thousand followers.
His flagship was magnificent, even mounted with state-of-the-art Western bronze cannons bought from European smugglers, with firepower and range far exceeding the antiquated ships of the Qing navy. Unlike common bandits, Cai harbored grand political ambitions. He proclaimed himself "King of Subduing the Seas" and established his own reign title, official ranks, and laws. His fleet flew a great banner of black emblazoned with a golden phoenix tail. Any vessel crossing the Black Ditch had to pay heavy tribute to his bases in exchange for a personally signed "voyage tax certificate" — without it, ships were boarded, plundered, and their crews slaughtered.

At that time, Taiwan, rich from exports of tea, sugar, and rice, was in its "money up to the ankles" boom. The fertile western plains looked to Cai Qian like a perfect supply base and an inexhaustible source of plunder. To eliminate this threat to the empire's maritime defense, the Qing court in 1804 dispatched the most formidable naval commander in all of China — Li Changgeng, Admiral of the Zhejiang Navy — to wage a relentless cross-sea pursuit.

The climax of this duel between titans erupted off the Penghu Islands, a maze of treacherous reefs. It was a wooden-hulled showdown worthy of any modern Asian naval history. Using the monsoon winds, Li Changgeng led dozens of elite naval vessels into a narrow Penghu channel and surrounded Cai Qian's main fleet and flagship. At dawn the battle began; a furious northeast monsoon whipped up massive waves, the wooden hulls groaning and splintering. Both fleets pitched in the storm, cannon fire deafening, thick black smoke turning day into night across the strait.

In this carnage Cai Qian faced the gravest crisis of his life. His flagship, pinned by three Qing warships, lost its mast as blood ran on the decks. But he did not fight alone. His wife — known as "Mother Cai Qian" — was a legend in her own right, fearless and skilled in arms. Bloodied head to toe, she swung her broadsword at the bow and directed gunners through the rain of shot. Just as Li Changgeng's flagship, riding the wind, slammed into Cai's vessel and Qing marines prepared to board and seize him, Cai Qian showed his iron-cold composure as a pirate king. He pushed aside a wounded gunner, personally lit a Western cannon, and aimed it at Li's nearby ship. With a thunderous explosion, the shot struck Li Changgeng squarely in the throat. One of the Qing Empire's greatest naval commanders fell dead on his own deck. With Li gone, the Qing navy panicked; Cai seized the moment, broke through the encirclement, and vanished once more into the vast Black Ditch.

After killing Li Changgeng, Cai Qian's confidence reached its peak. In 1806 he set his sights on the commercial heart of central Taiwan — Lugang, then the second-greatest trading port on the island after Tainan.

Lugang was at that time the hub of Taiwan's bulk trade, packed with wealthy merchant houses. Cai Qian led over a hundred warships into Lugang's waters, the masts blanketing the coastline. His pirates landed in small sampans, intent on seizing the prosperous city. But Cai had underestimated his foe — not weak Qing soldiers, but Lugang's wealthy merchants and townspeople, ready to die defending their homes and fortunes.

Lugang's great merchants quickly funded a formidable civilian militia and recruited strong dock laborers. The city's layout suddenly proved decisive: the famous "Nine Turns Lane" was winding enough to block sea winds and disorient invading pirates, while the city's gated lanes served as natural fortresses. When pirates burst into the streets, militia and residents rained bricks and torches from rooftops, fighting brutal hand-to-hand battles in the narrow alleys.

Meanwhile, Qing reinforcements raced up from Tainan, and a naval relief fleet arrived offshore. Under cover of darkness, the Qing launched dozens of "fire ships" packed with straw and oil, riding the wind into Cai's fleet anchored in the shallows. Soon the Lugang waters became a sea of flame, the sky red with inferno. Seeing the city unyielding and his fleet under fire attack, Cai Qian read the shifting wind and made his iron decision. Abandoning his landing force, he took the helm himself, drove his remaining ships through a desperate breakout before the encirclement closed, and disappeared once more into the fog and waves of the Black Ditch.

Cai Qian's saga ended in 1809. After repeated failures, the Qing court finally assembled the combined naval might of Fujian and Zhejiang under the new Admiral Wang Delu and cornered Cai's remaining fleet off Wenzhou in eastern Zhejiang. The outcome was a foregone conclusion: Cai's ammunition and supplies were exhausted, his flagship riddled with holes. In the final moment, Wang Delu shouted for surrender, but the man who had ruled the Black Ditch for a decade displayed his last defiance. Refusing to be paraded to Beijing in chains like Zhu Yigui, Cai Qian fired one last cannon round at the Qing fleet, then walked into his ship's powder magazine. He lit the fuse and gave his wife a final, tragic smile.

A thunderous explosion shattered the sky. The flagship dissolved into countless splinters. The pirate king and his wife — along with a decade's worth of legendary treasure — sank together to the depths of the Black Ditch. With this final, absolute gesture, he closed the curtain on a life of extraordinary tumult.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.lastQingElites.d:
The final two decades of Qing rule in Taiwan — the period between the inauguration of Liu Mingchuan's modernization program in the mid-1880s and the island's transfer to Japan in 1895 — were in some respects the most active period in the history of the Taiwanese gentry class. The construction projects of the late Qing era — the first railway, the telegraph system, the new stone walls of Taipei, the government schools — required capital and social organization that the state could not supply entirely from its own resources. What filled the gap was the wealth, the local networks, and the organizational capacity of the island's established merchant-gentry families.

Hong Tengyun exemplified the merchant-gentry who made this moment possible. He had built his fortune in the tea trade — northern Taiwan's most important export industry in the late nineteenth century — and used that wealth to ascend from merchant to recognized gentry status through large donations to official purposes. His most consequential contribution was financial: he provided substantial private funding for the construction of Taipei's stone city walls and the official buildings of the new provincial capital. His name was inscribed on commemorative monuments, and the city whose physical form his money had helped create became the center of the briefly existing Republic of Formosa in 1895 — a republic that lasted eleven days before Japanese forces arrived.

Xu Zonggan was the Qing official who did most to nurture the literary and scholarly culture of mid-nineteenth-century Taiwan. Serving as circuit intendant during a period when the island's examination culture was beginning to produce a locally-rooted intelligentsia, he invested in the quality of existing academies and made deliberate efforts to identify and support talented individuals who might otherwise have lacked the access to instruction needed to advance. His patronage of Chen Weiying — who became one of the most significant poet-teachers of the late Qing period — was typical of his approach: finding people whose potential was visible but whose circumstances were limiting, and removing the limitation.

Wu Luanqi's story brings this history to its close. In the summer of 1895, when news of the Treaty of Shimonoseki reached the central plains, Wu — serving in a middle-ranking administrative position in Taichung — became one of the organizers of the armed resistance that the central Taiwan gentry attempted to mount against the Japanese advance. He helped recruit local militia, coordinated supply lines, and maintained communications during the weeks when the outcome was still theoretically uncertain. The resistance failed — as it was always going to fail against a modern military force with better weapons and unlimited political backing. But the gentry who led it left behind a record of choice: when the empire abandoned the island, they decided, however briefly and however hopelessly, to stay and fight for it themselves.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.liugongCanal.des:
The Taipei Basin had rich soil, but for most of the Qing era it could not realize its agricultural potential. The basin's geography was frustrating: the central lowlands accumulated standing water and flooded regularly, while the terraced hillsides were chronically dry, too far above the nearest river to be irrigated by gravity. Farmers who settled here found themselves fighting on two fronts — against inundation in the wet season, against drought in the dry.

Guo Xiliu, a Fujianese settler who arrived in the Taipei area in the 1740s, took on this challenge with the particular combination of vision and stubbornness that characterizes the great private infrastructure builders of history. He had no official backing, no government funding, and no formal engineering training. What he had was a clear analysis of the problem — the Xindian River upstream carried ample water year-round, and the terrain between its gorge and the Taipei plain could, with sufficient effort, be shaped to carry that water across the hills — and a willingness to stake everything on his plan.

The project consumed more than two decades of his life. Working without the resources of the state, Guo mobilized capital through partnerships with other settlers, sold shares in the future canal's water rights to finance excavation, and managed the complex challenge of organizing hundreds of laborers on a construction site that periodically came under attack from indigenous communities displaced by the works. Floods destroyed completed sections; funding dried up; partners withdrew. Several times the project seemed finished.

Guo did not live to see the canal completed. It was his son, Guo Yuanfen, who finally closed the circuit, connecting the upstream intake to the distribution network across the basin. The finished canal — named the Liugong Canal in honor of Guo Xiliu, 'Liugong' being a respectful title meaning 'Master Liu' — stretched more than forty kilometers and irrigated the entire eastern half of the Taipei Basin. The paddy fields it fed supplied the rice that underpinned the commercial growth of Wanhua and Dadaocheng in the nineteenth century. Guo spent a fortune, mortgaged his family's future, and is remembered today in street names across Taipei as the man who gave the city its agricultural foundation.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.luohanjiaoCrossi:
In the late seventeenth century along the Fujian and Guangdong coast, deciding whether to cross to Taiwan was a deadly gamble with one’s life as the stake.

The Qing Empire had just defeated the Kingdom of Tungning ruled by the Zheng family. Although Shi Lang persuaded the Kangxi Emperor to incorporate Taiwan into the empire, he soon drafted strict migration restrictions known as the “Taiwan Crossing Ban.” The government’s logic was simple: Taiwan was too distant and too chaotic. The safest approach was to isolate it through rigid population controls. Migrants were forbidden from bringing families, many Hakka from Guangdong were barred entirely, and anyone wishing to cross the sea needed an official travel permit issued by the authorities.

But frontier isolation policies could not overpower hunger. Inland Fujian and Guangdong were overcrowded, farmland was scarce, and famine struck repeatedly. For many poor villagers, staying home meant starvation anyway, while rumors painted Taiwan as a fertile land where hard work could buy survival. The economic pull was far stronger than fear of the law. As the scholar Lan Dingyuan observed, the harsher the prohibition became, the greater the profits hidden beneath it. Since legal permits were difficult to obtain, a vast underground smuggling network emerged instead. Naval patrol officers, corrupt officials, and ruthless traffickers formed a system built on shared interests, transporting fugitives and desperate unmarried laborers — later commonly called “Luohanjiao” — onto illegal boats bound for Taiwan.

The journey usually began in darkness. Under the shouts of traffickers, men climbed silently onto fragile wooden sampans in the middle of the night. To evade Qing naval patrols, captains often forced everyone into the cargo hold before departure, sealing the hatch shut with planks and iron locks.

Once the vessel began violently rocking, the suffocating hold quickly filled with the stench of sweat and vomit. Everyone understood they had entered the “Black Ditch” — the dangerous waters now known as the Taiwan Strait. The traveler Yu Yonghe described the region in Notes from a Journey Across the Sea as waters so dark and deep they terrified even experienced sailors. Under such extreme maritime conditions, illegal migrant ships were dangerously overcrowded and poorly equipped. Death by suffocation or disease was common. Worse still, if Qing patrols appeared during the voyage, traffickers sometimes threw entire groups of migrants into the sea to destroy evidence of illegal transport. This horrifying practice became known as “releasing the pigeons” or “water burial.”

In the midst of this collective trauma — where death could come at any moment — the migrants’ only comfort was the protection of the gods. In the darkness below deck, men clutched incense ashes and charms dedicated to Mazu or local Wangye deities, praying and crying together. Out of this intense fear of death, the Mazu faith, once centered mainly along the Fujian coast, became deeply rooted in Taiwan. Over time, she transformed from a regional sea goddess into one of Taiwan’s island-wide spiritual centers that transcended ancestral divisions.

After days trapped in a floating hell, survival itself felt miraculous. If the hatch was finally broken open and sunlight poured into the hold, it meant they had lived. One of the fortunate survivors was Lin Xiujun, who later helped develop areas around present-day Banqiao and Tucheng in northern Taiwan. After landing on Taiwan’s muddy shores, he leased land from Indigenous communities, organized reclamation enterprises, built irrigation systems such as the Daan Canal, and eventually rose to become a powerful local landholder.

Stories of successful settlers like Lin Xiujun spread back to the mainland, drawing wave after wave of young men willing to risk crossing the Black Ditch. As for those who lost the gamble — drowned at sea or left to die anonymously by the roadside — surviving migrants often buried them collectively out of mutual solidarity. Over time, these graves evolved into the countless shrines dedicated to wandering spirits found throughout Taiwan, such as temples honoring the “Youying Gong” or “Wan Shan Tong Gui.” Sociologically, these spirit cults functioned as psychological mechanisms that helped stabilize early immigrant society by comforting restless souls and easing communal fear.

This chapter of Taiwan’s migration history emerged from the tension between Qing isolation policies, the profits of smuggling networks, and the desperate survival instincts of ordinary people. The Taiwan Strait and the migration bans acted like a brutal filter. Cruel as they were, they also selected for settlers with extraordinary resilience and adaptability. These survivors, rooted in an unfamiliar land through blood, labor, and tightly bound local faith communities, gradually transformed the remote island once dismissed by the Kangxi Emperor into the prosperous and commercially vibrant society that Taiwan would later become.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.openingOfPorts.d:
Following the Second Opium War, the Treaty of Tianjin (1858) and the Convention of Peking (1860) compelled the Qing to open Taiwan's ports to international trade — a turning point that would transform the island from an imperial backwater into a node of global commerce. Tamsui, Keelung, Anping, and Takao (present-day Kaohsiung) were designated as treaty ports, and by the 1860s foreign merchants, missionaries, and consular officials had established a permanent presence on Taiwan's shores.

The economic impact was swift and profound. Taiwan's tea — cultivated in the misty hills north of Taipei — became a prized export to the United States and Europe, rivaling the famous teas of Fujian. Camphor, essential for celluloid manufacturing and pharmaceutical production, made Taiwan one of the world's leading suppliers. Sugar continued its centuries-old role as a staple export to Japan and China. British trading houses such as Jardine, Matheson & Co. and Dent & Co. established operations, while John Dodd's pioneering direct export of Formosa Oolong to New York in 1869 opened an entirely new market. Alongside commerce, Presbyterian missionaries — notably George Leslie Mackay in the north and Thomas Barclay in the south — introduced modern hospitals, schools, and romanized writing systems for local languages.

This volume traces how the forced opening of Taiwan's ports drew the island into global networks of trade, religion, and diplomacy, fundamentally altering its economy, society, and relationship with the outside world in the decades before Japanese colonization.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.openingTheMounta:
The Mudan Incident of 1874 — in which Japanese forces landed in southern Taiwan on the pretext of punishing an indigenous village for the killing of Ryukyuan sailors — delivered a shock to the Qing court that transcended its immediate military dimension. The real blow was conceptual: when Qing officials attempted to protest the Japanese landing, they found their position undermined by their own previous statements classifying eastern Taiwan as territory beyond effective imperial administration. They had, in effect, conceded their own sovereignty over the areas they now sought to defend. The resulting settlement required the Qing to pay an indemnity to Japan, making clear that the island's internal geography had become an external vulnerability.

The response was the program known as 'opening the mountains and pacifying the savages' — a phrase encoding within its bureaucratic language the twin agenda of infrastructure development and indigenous displacement. Three mountain crossing routes were to be constructed simultaneously, with army units serving as both construction crews and combat forces against indigenous communities that resisted their advance.

Wu Guangliang was given command of the central route, the most ambitious of the three. Starting from Linqipu (today's Jiji in Nantou) in 1875, his force cut a path through the Central Mountain Range to the Hualien coast — more than two hundred li through terrain previously accessible only to those who knew it well. His soldiers felled forest, blasted rock, bridged gorges, and fought repeated engagements with Atayal and Bunun communities who understood that the road was not merely a road but the advance guard of a colonization they had no power to prevent.

Ding Richang approached Taiwan's modernization from a bureaucratic angle. As governor of Fujian with responsibility for Taiwan, he oversaw the extension of the island's first telegraph lines, connecting Tainan and Taipei and making Taiwan one of the earliest parts of China to have electrical communication infrastructure. Xia Xianlun's systematic surveys produced the most accurate maps of Taiwan's terrain that the Qing period generated, giving the administration an actual understanding of the mountain topography that made the road-building campaigns possible to plan and execute.

Lin Chaodong was the warrior face of this late Qing period — a member of one of Taiwan's prominent military families who rose through campaigns against indigenous resistance and the Sino-French War to become the island's most effective native military commander. When the Japanese arrived in 1895, Lin organized one of the more sustained military resistances the situation permitted before eventually withdrawing to mainland China — embodying the contradiction of the late Qing moment: a man of real talent serving an empire that had run out of the will to commit the resources his talent required.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.presbyterianMiss:
On a summer day in 1865, James Laidlaw Maxwell — known in Taiwan as Ma Yage — stepped ashore at the port of Dagou with a medicine chest and the New Testament in Chinese. He was the first Western physician to establish a permanent medical presence in Taiwan, and his arrival initiated a mission that would, over the following three decades, transform the social landscape of southern Taiwan in ways that went far beyond the conversion of souls.

Maxwell's early months were difficult. He attempted to set up a practice in Tainan city, only to find himself at the center of a rumor campaign accusing foreign doctors of removing the eyes and organs of their patients. A crowd surrounded his clinic and the hostility made continued operation impossible. He withdrew to Dagou, established a small hospital, and used effective treatment of conditions that local practitioners could not manage to build a reputation that slowly extended his credibility. Within a few years he was able to return to Tainan and establish the permanent presence that became the foundation of Western medicine in Taiwan.

Hugh Ritchie arrived in 1867 to take on the evangelical side of the mission. Where Maxwell built hospitals, Ritchie built churches — not just in the coastal port towns but in the agricultural interior, among farming communities that had had almost no contact with Western culture. He trained local preachers who could continue the work in places he could not personally reach, and invested heavily in producing Taiwanese-language materials, including translations of scripture into the vernacular Hokkien spoken across the region.

William Campbell directed his energies primarily toward the education of the blind, establishing what was almost certainly the first school for blind students in Taiwan's history. He also produced a comprehensive Hokkien-English dictionary that documented the spoken language of southern Taiwan with a linguistic precision that made it an invaluable resource for subsequent generations of scholars. Carstairs Douglas had preceded him in the linguistic documentation project, completing his Amoy Chinese-English Dictionary before his death in 1877 and providing the lexical foundation for the Romanized writing system — called 白話字, 'vernacular script' — that made the Bible and educational materials accessible to readers without classical education.

The medical missions established by Maxwell and his colleagues were the direct ancestors of several of Taiwan's most important hospitals. The linguistic documentation they produced preserved a detailed record of southern Taiwanese vernacular speech at a time when the classical Chinese educated class had little interest in recording it.
The Medical Mission in Southern Taiwan
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.qingIncorporatio:
In 1683, Qing admiral Shi Lang defeated the remnants of the Zheng dynasty at the Battle of Penghu, bringing Taiwan under Qing sovereignty for the first time. The annexation was far from inevitable — a fierce debate erupted at the imperial court over whether to retain or abandon this distant island. Minister Shi Lang argued that Taiwan's strategic position made it essential for coastal defense, while others viewed it as a lawless frontier not worth the administrative burden. Emperor Kangxi ultimately sided with retention, incorporating Taiwan as a prefecture of Fujian Province.

The early Qing administration treated Taiwan with cautious neglect. A garrison of rotating soldiers was stationed on the island, and a civil bureaucracy of magistrates and prefects was installed, but the court imposed strict limits on migration. A permit system required prospective settlers to obtain official approval before crossing the Taiwan Strait, and families were initially forbidden from accompanying male migrants — a policy designed to prevent permanent settlement but widely circumvented in practice. Illegal migration from Fujian and Guangdong surged throughout the eighteenth century, transforming the island's western plains into a patchwork of Hokkien and Hakka farming communities.

This volume examines how a reluctant empire absorbed a peripheral island, tracing the policies that shaped Taiwan's early Qing identity: the quarantine line (番界) separating Han settlements from indigenous mountain territories, the rotating garrison system that prevented military entrenchment, and the informal networks of kinship and commerce that bound Taiwan to the mainland despite official restrictions. These administrative choices — born of imperial ambivalence — would define Taiwan's ethnic geography and frontier character for the next two centuries.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.rebellionsAndUnr:
Qing-era Taiwan earned a reputation as one of the empire's most turbulent frontiers. The folk saying 'every three years a minor revolt, every five years a major rebellion' (三年一小反、五年一大亂) was no exaggeration — over two hundred recorded uprisings occurred during two centuries of Qing rule. The roots of this instability lay in the island's unique social fabric: a rapidly growing settler population, weak imperial oversight, ethnic rivalries between Hokkien and Hakka communities, exploitative local officials, and the absence of a deeply rooted gentry class to mediate disputes.

The most consequential revolts each revealed different fault lines in Taiwanese society. The Zhu Yigui Rebellion of 1721 began as a protest against corrupt magistrates and briefly seized control of the entire island before Qing reinforcements arrived from the mainland. The Lin Shuangwen Rebellion (1786–1788), the largest uprising of the Qing period, mobilized tens of thousands of fighters across ethnic lines and required imperial troops dispatched by Emperor Qianlong himself to suppress. The Dai Chaochun Rebellion (1862–1865) engulfed central Taiwan for three years and exposed the frailty of Qing garrison forces. In each case, the court responded with a familiar pattern: military suppression followed by limited administrative reform — adjusting jurisdictional boundaries, rotating officials more frequently, or briefly relaxing migration restrictions.

This volume charts the cycle of revolt and response that defined Qing Taiwan's political life, examining how chronic instability shaped both the imperial administration's view of the island as an ungovernable periphery and the local population's growing sense of self-reliance and distinct identity.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.riseAndFallOfGol:
In mid-eighteenth-century Taiwan, as the gunpowder smoke of rebellions and ancestral feuds slowly settled on land, a golden artery — woven from wealth, sails, and the currents of the Black Ditch — began to pulse violently along the western coast. It was an age called "Taiwan's money up to the ankles." As the Kangxi Emperor's once-strict crossing prohibition collapsed before the sheer pressure of survival, waves of Han migrants who had gambled their lives to reach Taiwan cut irrigation channels across the western plains, turning wilderness into endless seas of rice paddies and sugarcane fields.

This island, once dismissed by the Kangxi Emperor as a useless overseas waste, unleashed astonishing productive power. But under the Qing's restrictive "designated port crossing" policy, Taiwan's own market could not absorb such vast quantities of rice, sugar, and tea. Meanwhile, the densely populated coastal regions of Fujian and Guangdong across the strait hungered for grain. This massive supply-and-demand pull pried open a sweeping age of maritime commerce in the Taiwan Strait. The folk saying "first Fu, second Lu, third Bangka" — 「一府、二鹿、三艋舺」 — captures not only the rise of Taiwan's three great trading ports, but a historical movement of the island's center of gravity from south to north between the eighteenth century and the Tongzhi era.

The throne of this port saga belongs without question to "Fu" — Tainan prefectural city. As Taiwan's earliest political and cultural center, Tainan's Wutiaogang (Five-Channel Harbor) district entered its golden era in the eighteenth century. The Tainan coast then was an immense lagoon called the Taijiang Inland Sea, and five hand-like channels extended from outside the city's western gate into its waters: Fotou Harbor, Nanshi Harbor, Nanhe Harbor, Xingangqian Harbor, and Anhai Harbor.

Each dawn, when the tides rose into the five harbors, hundreds of "ganmou" sailboats and "big-eye chicken" junks that had crossed the Black Ditch from Xiamen glided up the channels, their patched canvas sails creaking in the morning light. On the wharves, shirtless dock coolies — the Luohanjiao, their skin burned dark by the sun — hauled heavy sacks of Taiwanese sugar and rice across oily, swaying wooden planks. The air mingled sweat, seawater, and the resin of Fuzhou cedar with the dry-grass scent of imported silks, fabrics, and herbal medicines.

In the alleys of Wutiaogang, the merchant princes who held the city's economic life sat in the tea-scented back chambers of their trading houses, turning the pages of thick ledgers. They were called the "jiaoshang" — Taiwan's cross-strait trade monopolists. Those trading with Xiamen formed the "Xiajiao"; those dealing with Quanzhou, the "Quanjiao." These tycoons were richer than nations, and on this frontier they organized their own guilds, the "jiaohang" — funding temples, paving roads, dredging rivers, and even raising militias to defend the region. At their peak, Tainan's "Three Jiao" (the North Jiao, South Jiao, and Sugar Jiao) were so powerful that even local prefects greeted their heads with deference. Wine houses and song halls rang day and night with merchant gatherings, embodying the most opulent chapter of Qing Taiwan: the "splendor of Fucheng."

But as time passed and southern arable land grew scarce, migrants' footprints extended northward along the coast — giving rise to the second golden port: "second Lu," Lugang in Zhanghua.

Mid-eighteenth-century Lugang was a wild reed-grown coast where herds of deer still roamed. Yet it held one unmatched geographic advantage: it was the closest port on Taiwan to Hanjiang Port in Quanzhou, Fujian. In 1784 (the forty-ninth year of the Qianlong reign), the Qing court formally opened Lugang and Hanjiang for "designated crossing." Overnight, this unremarkable fishing village was swept up in a storm of wealth.

Lugang's rise was an all-out "Quanzhou migrant carnival." Countless merchants from Quanzhou's "Three Counties" (Jinjiang, Nan'an, and Hui'an) flooded in, and along the narrow streets they built the unique "Sky-Hidden Street" — to shield against ocean winds and burning sun, shopkeepers roofed over the entire street, lining both sides with long Xiajiao trading houses, shop in front, warehouse behind. Lugang's jiaoshang shipped the finest rice and timber from the Zhanghua plains and the Nantou mountains to Quanzhou, returning with porcelain and Fuzhou cedar.

"Lugang's Flying Sails" became a famed sight of the age. At dusk, looking out from Lugang's river mouth, one saw countless white sails veiling the sea against the sinking sun in a magnificent tableau. Lugang's commercial might began to rival Tainan. Yet its prosperity carried an inborn fragility. The Zhuoshui River and surrounding streams carried enormous sediment loads year after year, silting up Lugang's harbor at frightening speed. By the mid-nineteenth century, the harbor that had once moored massive merchant ships had become a mudflat. Large vessels could only anchor far offshore and transfer cargo by sampans. The once-bustling "second Lu," swallowed by silt, slowly relinquished its golden port crown and passed the historical baton to a darker horse further north.

That dark horse was "third Bangka" — today's Wanhua in Taipei.

While southern and central Taiwan languished in long cycles of development and infighting through the mid-Qing, the Taipei Basin in the north remained a wild frontier where Pingpu Ketagalan indigenous peoples still paddled their "mangka" dugout canoes. Han migrants pushed up the Tamsui River into the basin, finding fertile soil and a deep river channel running directly to the sea — a magnificent natural harbor. At the wharf where the Dahan and Xindian rivers converged, a riverside settlement named for the gathering of indigenous canoes was quietly born: Bangka.

In the early nineteenth century, large numbers of Tong'an migrants from Quanzhou settled in Bangka. They built wharves along the river, raised the Longshan Temple, and developed northern trade routes to ports like Yantai and Tianjin in China's north — forming the powerful "Beijiao." Bangka stood at the peak of its golden port age. The Tamsui River was thick with merchant masts; camphor, tea, and sugar from local mills piled high on its banks.

But Bangka's prosperity came hand-in-hand with the fiercest dark violence of Qing-era Taiwan. In 1853, Bangka erupted in the cruelest ancestral feud in its history — the "Dingxia Jiaopin." The Quanzhou Three-County faction (the Dingjiao), long monopolizing Bangka's port, feared losing their entrenched interests and launched a coordinated attack on their Quanzhou Tong'an neighbors (the Xiajiao) living in Xiakan. In the bloodbath, the Tong'an village was burned, and a great mass of refugees, led by Lin Youzao, fled north along the Tamsui carrying the image of their patron deity, Xiahai Chenghuang.

Yet this brutal expulsion accidentally opened a more brilliant era. Driven from Bangka, the Tong'an migrants settled a few kilometers north on what was then a barren riverbank — a place called Dadaocheng. Lin Youzao and the Tong'an merchants regrouped there, built broader wharves, and seized their chance. After the Second Opium War of 1860 forced Taiwan's ports open to international trade, foreign trading houses established themselves in Tamsui. The British merchant John Dodd discovered that northern Taiwan's hills were ideally suited for tea cultivation. He partnered with the Dadaocheng tycoon Li Chunsheng, brought in Anxi tea cuttings, processed "Formosa Oolong" in Dadaocheng, and shipped it directly to New York.

Overnight, Dadaocheng's "tea gold" legend exploded onto the global market. As Dadaocheng made astronomical sums in foreign silver from tea exports and became Taiwan's richest, most cosmopolitan modern city, once-proud Bangka withered. Silt choked the Tamsui, and the conservative refusal to admit foreign trading houses finally shut down its port economy entirely.

The rise and fall of "first Fu, second Lu, third Bangka" looks on the surface like a story of wealth and harbors, but beneath it is a fate-script woven from natural forces and the ancestral rivalries of human society. Wutiaogang's Taijiang Inland Sea was always destined to silt into land; Lugang's Hanjiang crossing always destined to be swallowed by sediment; and Bangka's Tong'an exiles destined to find in Dadaocheng their stage for revenge. The rise and fall of these three golden ports was an invisible hand that pushed Taiwan's economic and political center of gravity, in just over a century, from Tainan in the south to the Taipei Basin in the north — laying the foundation of Taiwan's modern urban geography.

Today, when we walk the old Wutiaogang district's Heping Street in Tainan, look at the red brick of Lugang's Nine Turns Lane, or stroll beneath the Baroque facades of Dadaocheng's Dihua Street, the lingering tea and herb scents in the air are the warmest historical afterglow that "first Fu, second Lu, third Bangka" left to this island.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.roverIncident.de:
In the early spring of 1867, the monsoon winds and ocean currents of the Pacific converged upon the southernmost tip of Taiwan. This was a stretch of water that sailors spoke of with dread, thick with hidden reefs and vaguely charted, its coast ringed by ranges of forested mountains upon which the Qing empire had never truly set foot. It was here, in the wild seas off the southern cape near present-day Kenting, that the American merchant bark Rover struck the reefs and was wrecked. As the vessel broke apart in the surf, the surviving crew rowed desperately for shore and struggled onto unfamiliar ground, believing they had escaped death, unaware that they had entered a far more perilous realm.

That shore belonged to the Koalut, a Paiwan community that regarded all intruders on their coast as enemies. To them, the strangers washed up from the sea were not shipwrecked men in need of rescue but invaders to be driven off, and if necessary destroyed. Such hostility was not wholly unprovoked; for years the landing of foreign ships had brought plunder and conflict, and the coastal peoples had learned to guard their homeland by the most uncompromising means. Nearly the entire crew of the Rover was killed there, and only a handful escaped to carry word of the tragedy to the outside world.

When the news spread, the seafaring powers of the world saw it as an intolerable outrage: crewmen of the civilised world slaughtered in what seemed a lawless no man's land. To the Qing, however, it was an embarrassment beyond easy remedy. Officials in Beijing and Taiwan insisted repeatedly that the mountainous south lay beyond the court's 'civilising jurisdiction,' that its communities paid no grain tax and answered to no magistrate, and that the court was therefore unwilling, and by its own account unable, to bear responsibility for what happened there. This evasion laid bare the hollowness of the empire's grip upon the island.

Confronted by the blood of the dead and by international pressure, a United States punitive expedition landed to take revenge. Armed sailors pushed into the unfamiliar jungle, only to be fought off, step by step, by Paiwan warriors who knew the dense and impassable terrain intimately, and at last withdrew having achieved nothing. Where gunboats and firepower proved helpless amid these mountains and shores, the outcome made one truth plain to all: force alone could not solve the problem of the southern cape.

What the gunboats could not do, one determined diplomat accomplished. Charles Le Gendre, the American consul at Amoy, travelled repeatedly to the south, venturing into country from which imperial troops had recoiled, and did what no Qing official was willing to do. Bypassing the equivocating local yamen, he sought dialogue directly with the leaders of the land. After considerable effort he met face to face with Tokitok, the paramount chief of the confederation to which the Koalut belonged, and negotiated a direct agreement as between equals, the so-called Treaty of the South Cape, under which sailors wrecked on that coast would thereafter be spared and aided rather than killed.

Though the agreement calmed the immediate dispute, it also unwittingly exposed a far more fateful gap: swathes of Taiwan in fact lay beyond the effective control of any sovereign state. That a foreign consul could bypass the Qing and conclude a treaty with a chief on his own authority was itself a testament to the emptiness of the imperial frontier. From this Le Gendre drew his own conclusion, keeping his first-hand knowledge firmly in mind. A few years later, when he entered the service of Japan, it was precisely his understanding of the realities of southern Taiwan that allowed him to advise its 1874 expedition against the same region.

Thus the wreck of a single ship set in motion a chain of interlocking events. Beginning with an ordinary shipwreck, it unfolded, stage by stage, to draw both a rising Japan and a reluctant Qing ever deeper into the fate of Taiwan. At the moment the Rover foundered on the reefs of the southern cape, no one could have foreseen that the tragedy would become the prelude to decades in which foreign powers eyed the island and the Qing was forced at last to confront the question of sovereignty over its 'aboriginal territory,' quietly rewriting the place of Taiwan on the modern chessboard of East Asia.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.sinoFrenchWar.de:
In 1884 a war fought far away over suzerainty and control of Vietnam suddenly washed up on Taiwan's shores. As relations between the Qing and France broke down over the Vietnamese question, the fighting spread along China's southeastern coast, and Taiwan — an isolated island guarding the maritime approaches to Fujian — became overnight a frontline in a contest between great powers. For the island's inhabitants it was a disaster that fell from the sky without warning, and they called the whole ordeal the 'Western barbarians' revolt.'

The first blow fell on the north. Admiral Courbet, commander of the French Far Eastern squadron, sought a bargaining chip against the Qing and turned his guns on the port of Keelung and its surrounding coalfields. Keelung's coal was an indispensable fuel for steamships and warships, and its strategic value was immense. In August 1884, under cover of naval gunfire, French troops stormed ashore and seized the town, and for a time gunsmoke hung over the mountains and shore of northern Taiwan while fear gripped the population.

The true turning point came at Tamsui, today's Danshui. On 8 October 1884 the French attempted an amphibious landing at the mouth of the Tamsui River, only to meet fierce resistance from Qing forces under General Sun Kai-hua, fighting alongside local militia. Exploiting familiar terrain and shore defences, the defenders threw the French back into the sea — a rare and celebrated victory on Taiwan's front in the war, remembered as the Great Triumph of Tamsui and passed down through generations of Tamsui residents.

Frustrated on land, the French changed tactics and declared a blockade of the entire island. Their fleet cut off Taiwan's shipping and supply lines, choking off imports and battering the local economy, effectively marooning the whole island in the open sea. The French then sailed south and occupied the poorly defended Pescadores, seizing the archipelago that commands the Taiwan Strait, and for a time the campaign settled into stalemate.

Overseeing the island's defence was Liu Ming-chuan, who had been rushed to Taiwan by the court as imperial commissioner for military affairs. Based in the north, he marshalled limited troops and resources to contend with the French along the Keelung–Tamsui line. In the south, the Taiwan intendant Liu Ao organised the defence of the Tainan region on his own, shoring up the walled city and its harbours. Yet the friction and rivalry over authority between Liu Ming-chuan and Liu Ao had already begun to surface during the war, and that rift would bring bitter consequences.

The war finally ended in 1885 with a wider peace between China and France. As the treaty was signed, the siege and blockade were lifted, and French forces withdrew from Keelung and the Pescadores, bringing to a close the conflict that had swept over northern Taiwan and its outlying islands. For the shaken islanders life could return to its ordinary rhythms, though the scars the war had left on the land and in memory did not fade easily.

Brief though it was, the war taught the Qing court a hard lesson about Taiwan's strategic value. Long dismissed as a peripheral island on the empire's edge, it had now proven to be a linchpin of the entire southeastern coastal defence. Within months of the war's end the court resolved to separate Taiwan from Fujian and elevate it to a full province, appointing Liu Ming-chuan as its first governor. The guns of the Western barbarians' revolt had, unexpectedly, pushed open the door to a new era for Taiwan.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.taiwanAsProvince:
In 1885, in the wake of the Sino-French War — during which French forces blockaded and bombarded Keelung and briefly occupied northern Taiwan — the Qing court recognized the island's strategic importance and elevated it from a prefecture of Fujian to a full province. Liu Mingchuan, the military commander who had successfully defended Taiwan against the French, was appointed as its first governor.

Liu launched the most ambitious modernization program in Taiwan's history to that point. He oversaw the construction of Taiwan's first railway line, connecting Keelung to Taipei and later extending toward Hsinchu. He installed telegraph lines linking the island to the mainland via undersea cables, established a modern postal system, and introduced electric street lighting to Taipei — making it one of the earliest electrified cities in East Asia. He conducted a comprehensive land survey to reform taxation, expanded camphor and tea production to boost revenue, and attempted to extend government authority into indigenous territories. These reforms, though visionary, generated fierce resistance from entrenched local interests and strained the provincial treasury.

Liu's successor, Shao Youlian, scaled back many of these initiatives, citing unsustainable costs. The railway remained incomplete, the land survey unfinished, and modernization stalled. Less than a decade later, China's humiliating defeat in the First Sino-Japanese War led to the Treaty of Shimonoseki (1895), which ceded Taiwan and the Penghu Islands to Japan in perpetuity — ending two centuries of Qing rule and opening a radically different chapter in the island's history.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.wushaOpensKavala:
Beyond the mountains of Taiwan's northeast lay a fertile expanse cradled between the Snow Mountains and the Pacific — the Kavalan plain, today's Yilan. For most of the Qing era this plain lay outside the empire's borders, and Han settlers were expressly forbidden to cross into it. It was the ancestral home of the Kavalan people, who lived by rice farming, fishing, hunting, and trade among the villages scattered across the lowland. Yet on the western coast, only a mountain range away, Han settlement had already saturated the available land, and this rich but unclaimed valley became, in the eyes of adventurers, the most tempting prize of the age.

Wu Sha was one such frontier trader. A man from Zhangzhou who had crossed to Taiwan in his youth, he had spent years dealing with the Kavalan villages around Tamsui and Sandiao, exchanging cloth, salt, and iron tools for mountain goods and deer hides. Those years of contact left him familiar with the roads and the people of the plain, aware of the land's promise, and keenly conscious of the dangers of seizing it. He gathered landless settlers from among the Zhangzhou, Quanzhou, and Hakka communities, stockpiled grain and arms, and waited for his moment.

In 1796 Wu Sha led a band of settlers over the steep pass into the plain and built a walled camp at the northernmost point, Toucheng, the first permanent Han foothold on the Kavalan lowland. The earthen wall was at once a settlement and a fortress. The Kavalan, watching their homeland invaded, resisted fiercely, and the first years of the venture were marked by constant conflict and bloodshed on both sides. Several times the camp stood on the brink of collapse, and the future of the enterprise hung in doubt.

Then the situation turned in a way no one had foreseen. When a smallpox epidemic swept through the Indigenous villages, claiming countless lives, Wu Sha used his knowledge of variolation and healing to treat the stricken. That hand extended in a moment of despair won him a measure of trust that neither weapons nor walls could ever have secured. The strained hostility eased, and the settlers gained a firmer footing on the plain, pushing their frontier inland inch by inch.

Wu Sha died in 1798, only two years after he had entered the plain, with the great work barely begun. But his nephews and kinsmen took up the unfinished task, following the path he had opened and pressing steadily southward. The settlers organized themselves into cooperative pioneering groups under the jieshou system, opening a chain of settlements — Toucheng, Erwei, Sanwei, Siwei, Wuwei — as paddy fields and irrigation channels spread across the plain and villages rose one after another.

Within a single generation the face of the Kavalan plain had been utterly rewritten. Han settlements stretched from north to south, rice harvests were abundant, and the once-forbidden land beyond the pale had become a presence the empire could no longer ignore. The Qing court at last reversed its policy, formally annexing the region during the Jiaqing reign and establishing Kavalan Sub-prefecture to govern it — dispatching officials, surveying fields, and levying taxes, drawing the frontier into the administrative order of the empire.

The opening of the Kavalan plain was the last great chapter in the history of Han pioneer settlement in Qing Taiwan. The western plains had long been fully claimed, and this northeastern valley became the final destination of the settlement wave, marking the close of a pioneering age. It is a story of enterprise, cooperation, and endurance, of migrants rebuilding their lives on unfamiliar and dangerous ground. Yet, as always on the frontier, the achievement was shadowed by the deep dispossession of those who were there first. The Kavalan people lost the plain they had guarded for generations; their numbers dwindled and they were driven to migrate elsewhere — a cost that remains, to this day, an inescapable part of this history.
Wu Sha Opens the Kavalan Plain
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.zhuYiguiRebellio:
In the early eighteenth century, southern Taiwan was a land filled with violence, resentment, and despair. Countless “Luohanjiao” — lone migrant men who had survived the deadly crossing of the Black Ditch — discovered that the island was not the golden frontier promised in rumors back home. Instead, they found themselves trapped beneath the ruthless exploitation of the Qing imperial bureaucracy.

At the time, Taiwan was not a province of its own but administered as part of Fujian under the Taiwan Prefecture headquartered in Tainan. Most officials arrived with a deeply cynical mindset: serve a few years, squeeze out as much wealth as possible, then return home rich. By 1721, during the sixtieth year of the Kangxi reign, the greed of Prefect Wang Zhen and his son Wang Jie had reached extraordinary levels. Under endless fabricated pretexts, they imposed crushing taxes and extortion upon ordinary people. Farmers entering the mountains to gather firewood were forced to pay a “firewood tax.” Fishermen casting nets into the sea paid a “net tax.” Even peasants attempting to reclaim wasteland risked arrest, public whipping, and enormous ransom payments. Within a short period, hundreds of innocent civilians were thrown into prison. Across southern Taiwan, public anger built like a barrel packed with gunpowder, waiting only for a spark.

That spark was lit in Neimen, Kaohsiung — then known as Luohanmen. Isolated among rugged mountain terrain, Luohanmen had become a refuge for wandering migrants, fugitives, and dispossessed men hiding from the authorities. Among them was a twenty-six-year-old immigrant from Zhangzhou named Zhu Yigui.

Zhu Yigui was originally a poor migrant from Fujian. Alone in Taiwan, he survived by raising ducks in the hills of Neimen. Yet he was far from ordinary. Generous by nature and fiercely loyal to his friends, he loved gathering with fellow drifters and outcasts. More remarkably, he seemed to possess an instinctive talent for leadership. His duck flocks were astonishingly disciplined: with a single wave of a bamboo rod, thousands of ducks would march forward in orderly formations like a trained army. The Luohanjiao of the mountains often gathered at Zhu’s duck farm, drinking cheap liquor while listening to him curse the corrupt government. Over time, they came to admire him completely, giving him the nickname “Duck King.”

As Wang Zhen’s oppression pushed the people toward desperation, several leaders from smuggling networks and Tiandihui secret societies — including Huang Dian and Li Yong — secretly visited Zhu’s duck farm one night. Over drinks, the men debated what could be done. Finally, someone slammed the table in rage and shouted, “We’ll die either way. If we stay, the officials will bleed us dry. We might as well rebel!”

Another man suddenly looked at Zhu and exclaimed, “Your surname is Zhu — the imperial surname of the Ming dynasty! Zheng Chenggong fought the Qing under the banner of restoring the Ming, and many people in Taiwan still long for the old dynasty. If you claim to be a descendant of the Ming imperial family, supporters will flock to your cause!”

Looking at the desperate hope in the eyes of the men around him, Zhu’s own outlaw spirit ignited. He agreed immediately. Several ducks were slaughtered on the spot, and the men swore a blood oath together inside the duck farm, formally raising the banner of rebellion.

This improvised “army of Luohanjiao,” armed with duck-herding poles, hoes, and broadswords, unleashed astonishing fighting power. These men had spent years battling the brutal wilderness of frontier Taiwan. They were hardened, physically strong, and utterly fearless. Once the call to rebellion spread, local leaders such as Lin Shuangwen and Du Junying rallied to the cause. Among them, the Hakka leader Du Junying, active around the Gaoping River region — then called the Lower Tamsui River — commanded especially formidable forces.

For survival, Hokkien and Hakka migrants temporarily set aside their ethnic rivalries and formed a united army. Like a bursting flood, they surged northward toward the political heart of Qing Taiwan: Tainan Prefecture.

The Qing troops stationed in Tainan had long grown soft in Taiwan’s relatively peaceful environment. Corrupt, undisciplined, and unused to real combat, they routinely bullied civilians but collapsed almost instantly when confronted by Zhu Yigui’s desperate rebel army. As the rebels approached the city gates, Prefect Wang Zhen, Commander Feng Long, and other senior civil and military officials panicked completely. In terror, they gathered their gold and valuables overnight, abandoned the city’s population, and fled with their families aboard ships bound for Penghu.

Zhu Yigui’s forces entered Tainan with almost no meaningful resistance. Within days, they had seized the island’s highest political and economic center.

It was one of the most surreal scenes in the history of Chinese migration: only days earlier, these men had been homeless drifters, duck farmers, and social outcasts despised by society. Now they had become masters of an entire city — even an entire island.

Escorted by cheering followers, Zhu Yigui entered the prefectural hall dressed in a yellow Ming-style imperial robe borrowed from an opera troupe. There, he formally proclaimed himself king under the title “Zhongxing King,” meaning “King of Restoration.” Declaring the Ming dynasty the legitimate orthodoxy, he established a new reign era named Yonghe, abolished many Qing taxes, and lavishly rewarded the Luohanjiao brothers who had fought beside him with titles of generals and ministers.

For a brief moment, Tainan erupted in celebration. Lanterns filled the streets while former drifters drank wildly in triumph, as though the entire social order had been overturned in a single stroke.

But the intoxication of revolution faded quickly.

The regime formed by these marginalized men possessed a fatal weakness: it lacked political vision and internal discipline. After capturing Tainan, sudden access to power and wealth poisoned the movement almost immediately. Zhu Yigui’s Fujian faction and Du Junying’s Hakka faction soon descended into bitter conflict over rank, rewards, and long-standing ethnic tensions. Furious over perceived inequality, Du Junying withdrew his Hakka forces entirely. At the very moment unity was most essential, the alliance shattered, leaving dangerous gaps in Tainan’s defenses.

Meanwhile, news of Tainan’s fall reached Beijing. The Kangxi Emperor was enraged, viewing the rebellion as a humiliating insult to imperial authority. The Qing court immediately mobilized a massive military response. Senior commanders including Man Bao, Lan Tingzhen, and Shi Shibiao — the son of Shi Lang — were dispatched with more than ten thousand elite Manchu and Han troops supported by heavy artillery.

Lan Tingzhen proved especially cunning and skilled in psychological warfare. After landing at Luermen, he quickly recognized the fatal divisions between the Hokkien and Hakka rebels and exploited them through a strategy of division, negotiation, and suppression. Against the disciplined firepower and organization of the Qing military machine, the fractured rebel army stood little chance.

Under fierce Qing counterattacks, Tainan rapidly fell once again. Zhu Yigui retreated with the remnants of his forces into the southern mountains he knew so well, hoping to wage a final guerrilla resistance. But the tide had already turned. Qing forces hunted him relentlessly, offering large rewards for his capture.

Eventually, somewhere in the wilderness near the modern border between Kaohsiung and Pingtung, Zhu Yigui was betrayed by former followers. Captured in his sleep, bound in chains, he was taken prisoner.

In 1722, Zhu Yigui and his closest commanders were escorted to Beijing. During interrogation, the former “Duck King,” though bloodied and shackled, reportedly stood proudly before Qing officials without fear. He was ultimately sentenced to one of the empire’s cruelest punishments: death by lingchi, or “death by a thousand cuts.”

Thus ended the brief but extraordinary life of Zhu Yigui.
