Although the rebellion lasted barely more than two months, the fact that a duck farmer leading an army of wandering migrants could force Qing officials to flee Taiwan and establish a short-lived kingdom left a deep mark on Taiwan’s collective memory. To this day, Zhu Yigui remains a powerful symbol of the lower classes rising against overwhelming authority.
Volumes.volume.imperialFrontier.zhuqianCity.desc:
The Han Chinese settlement of Taiwan's western plains proceeded roughly from south to north, and the town of Zhudian — known in the Qing records as Zhudian, today as Hsinchu, meaning 'New Bamboo' — was the crucial hinge point where the frontier of northern Taiwan tilted from wilderness into settled agricultural society. The name traces back to the dense bamboo groves that the Taokas indigenous people had long used as natural boundaries around their villages.

Wang Shijie, born in 1661, was among the earliest and most consequential of the Zhudian settlers. He arrived from southern Taiwan at the head of a group of tenant farmers and embarked on an ambitious program of land clearing and irrigation that, over more than a decade, converted the scrubland and bamboo thickets of the Zhudian plain into productive paddy fields. His approach was more contractual than coercive — he negotiated land-use agreements with local Taokas communities, exchanging cloth and iron implements for rights to cultivate specific tracts, establishing a pattern of transactional land acquisition that would characterize Han-indigenous interaction across northern Taiwan for generations.

By the early nineteenth century, Zhudian had become the largest commercial center north of Tainan. Lin Pinhou built a fortune in the salt trade before diversifying into rice milling and landholding, managing the difficult transition from merchant to recognized gentry by making large donations to military funds during periods of unrest. In 1826 he directed the construction of Zhudian's first permanent brick city walls, transforming a prosperous town of wooden buildings into a fortified urban center — a physical statement that this community intended to endure.

Zheng Chonghe occupied a different position in this society: a locally-educated man of letters who served as an informal mediator in community disputes, helping maintain social cohesion during periods when inter-ethnic tensions threatened to tip into open violence. His son Zheng Yongxi would go on to become Taiwan's first native-born imperial examination graduate — a milestone that gave the Zhudian gentry its first direct connection to the scholar-official class that governed the empire.
Among the cultural achievements of Qing-era Taiwan, the literary tradition that flourished in Zhudian — today's Hsinchu — occupies a distinctive position. While most of the island's western plains were still in the early phases of agricultural colonization, Zhudian developed alongside its commercial growth a scholarly gentry culture organized around classical Chinese poetry and the cultivation of Confucian literary values. This was not a transplanted mainland culture maintained by officials on temporary posting; it was a locally rooted intellectual tradition created by people who had been born on the island and thought of Taiwan as their home.

Zheng Yongxi was the central symbol of this achievement. In 1823 he passed the imperial examination at the jinshi level — the highest degree in the Qing educational system — becoming the first person born and raised in Taiwan to achieve this distinction. He was given the sobriquet 'the Pioneer Jinshi of Taiwan,' a title that captured the historical significance of his accomplishment for a community long regarded by the mainland establishment as culturally peripheral. After returning to Taiwan, Zheng devoted himself to local affairs, serving as a mediator between Hokkien and Hakka communities whose competition periodically erupted into large-scale ethnic violence. His reputation for impartiality made him one of the few figures capable of being heard by both sides.

Lin Zhanmei built his cultural legacy through a different medium. Inheriting a substantial commercial fortune, he chose not to pursue examination success but instead created the most celebrated private garden in Qing-era northern Taiwan — the Qianzhen Garden — in the heart of Zhudian. The garden became a gathering place for poets and scholars from across the island, hosted regular poetry competitions, and published collections of verse that transformed Zhudian from a commercial town with scholarly pretensions into a genuine cultural center.

Shi Shijie was the last of this tradition. He passed the jinshi examination in 1894, just one year before the Treaty of Shimonoseki transferred Taiwan to Japan, making him the last imperial examination graduate to emerge from the island under Chinese rule. When Japanese administration began, Shi refused to serve the new government and eventually returned to mainland China, where he spent the rest of his life writing poetry about exile and memory. His verse was the final expression of the Zhudian literary tradition — an elegiac summing-up of everything the classical education system had meant to the Taiwanese gentry, written from the vantage point of someone who had watched it end.
Volumes.volume.lightAndShadow.cairoToTaipeiTreat:
In November 1943, the leaders of China, the United States, and Great Britain reached a consensus at the Cairo Conference, declaring that "all territories Japan has stolen from the Chinese, such as Manchuria, Formosa, and the Pescadores, shall be restored to the Republic of China." Although not a formal treaty, this declaration became the political foundation for post-war territorial rearrangement in East Asia.

After Japan announced its surrender on August 15, 1945, Supreme Allied Commander MacArthur issued General Order No. 1, designating Chiang Kai-shek to accept the surrender of Japanese forces in Taiwan on behalf of the Allies. On October 25 of the same year, Chen Yi presided over the surrender ceremony at Taipei Public Hall, marking the beginning of ROC rule over Taiwan. However, whether this "acceptance of surrender" constituted a transfer of sovereignty or merely military occupation remains contested to this day.

This volume focuses on key diplomatic documents and international conference records from 1943 to 1945, revealing how Taiwan's post-war fate was determined amid great power politics. From the Cairo Declaration and the Potsdam Proclamation to the MacArthur Memorandum, each document shaped the future trajectory of millions of Taiwanese people.
Volumes.volume.lightAndShadow.chiangDiary.descri:
Chiang Kai-shek's diary is an invaluable primary source for studying post-war Taiwan history. In these private notes, we glimpse the national leader's true thoughts on Taiwan affairs — from his expectations for Taiwan's "retrocession," to his dissatisfaction with Chen Yi's governance, to his reflections and responses following the February 28 Incident.

The Chiang revealed in the diaries alternates between empathy for the Taiwanese people and the cold calculations of an authoritarian ruler. These diary entries provide a unique window into the inner world of the decision-maker, revealing the logic of power behind historical tragedy.

This volume curates key Taiwan-related entries from Chiang Kai-shek's diary, accompanied by historical context, to reconstruct this critical period that determined Taiwan's fate.
Volumes.volume.lightAndShadow.chiangDiary.title: Chiang Kai-shek's Diary
Volumes.volume.lightAndShadow.constitutionConven:
At the end of 1946, the Republic of China convened the Constitutional Convention in Nanjing, with Taiwan sending representatives to participate in national-level constitutional deliberations for the first time. These Taiwan representatives — many of them Japanese-educated intellectuals — entered the assembly with expectations for democratic institutions, only to discover vast gaps in language and political culture between themselves and mainland delegates.

The marginalization of Taiwan's representatives during the constitutional process reflected deeper structural issues: although Taiwan had nominally "returned" to the ROC, its actual position within the political system remained ambiguous. The drafting of the ROC Constitution would profoundly influence Taiwan's future political development.

This volume documents the role and predicaments of Taiwan's delegates at the Constitutional Convention, as well as the historical significance of this constitution for Taiwan.
Volumes.volume.lightAndShadow.deJapanization.des:
After taking over Taiwan, the Nationalist government immediately launched comprehensive "de-Japanization" and "re-Sinicization" policies. Japanese was banned in public spaces, Japanese-style place names were replaced with Chinese ones, and school instruction switched from Japanese to Chinese. Social organizations, legal systems, and administrative practices formed during the Japanese era were completely overhauled.

However, this rapid cultural transformation caused severe social ruptures. Taiwanese intellectuals educated in Japanese suddenly lost their linguistic tools, becoming effectively "illiterate" under the new regime. The cultural chasm between native Taiwanese and mainlanders deepened steadily, becoming a significant root cause of future social conflicts.

This volume examines the policies and impacts of this cultural transition period, exploring the deep contradictions in language policy, educational reform, and cultural identity.
Volumes.volume.lightAndShadow.dilemmaOfElites.de:
In the early post-war period, native Taiwanese elites faced an agonizing choice: cooperate with the new regime to secure space for reform, or resist unjust rule? Many intellectuals, local gentry, and professionals who had been active during the Japanese era initially chose to collaborate with the Nationalist government, hoping to improve governance through institutional channels.

However, as Chen Yi's administration increasingly deviated from the public will, the space for cooperation gradually vanished. Some elites turned to criticizing the government, while others were forced into silence. This struggle between collaboration and resistance was not merely an individual moral dilemma but reflected the collective anxiety of Taiwanese society amid regime change.

This volume traces the life trajectories of several native Taiwanese elites to present this history full of contradictions and struggles.
Volumes.volume.lightAndShadow.economicCrisis.des:
In the early days of the takeover, Taiwan experienced severe economic turmoil. The Nationalist government shipped massive quantities of Taiwan's resources to mainland China to support the civil war, causing skyrocketing prices and shortages of daily necessities on the island. Chen Yi's government implemented a command economy that monopolized major industries, and the monopoly bureau system provoked intense public resentment.

Hyperinflation wiped out Taiwanese savings overnight. Between 1946 and 1947, the price of rice surged dozens of times over, making it difficult for ordinary families to maintain basic living standards. Meanwhile, mainland officials and merchants arriving in Taiwan were accused of corruption and profiteering, further exacerbating ethnic tensions.

This volume uses economic data, folk accounts, and official documents to reconstruct how this economic collapse became a critical catalyst for the February 28 Incident.
Volumes.volume.lightAndShadow.eliteDiaries.descr:
Beyond official archives and the ruler's diary, the private diaries of native Taiwanese elites offer another perspective for understanding this history. These diaries record intellectuals' daily observations, emotional fluctuations, and political reflections during the regime transition.

Through these first-person narratives, we see the other side of history — not the grand narrative of international politics, but the micro-experiences of individuals amid upheaval. Each diary entry is a microcosm of an era, reflecting the complexity and gravity of that historical period.

This volume compiles significant excerpts from the diaries of several Taiwanese elites, presenting their inner journeys between hope and despair.
Volumes.volume.lightAndShadow.eliteDiaries.title: Voices from Elite Diaries
Volumes.volume.lightAndShadow.februaryIncident.d:
On the evening of February 27, 1947, Monopoly Bureau agents seized contraband cigarettes from a widow outside the Tianma Teahouse in Taipei's Dadaocheng district, striking her with a pistol butt and, in the ensuing chaos, firing into the crowd and killing a bystander. More than a year of accumulated grievances — runaway inflation, food shortages, official corruption, and the exclusion of native Taiwanese from power — found their outlet that night. The next day, February 28, crowds marched on the Governor-General's Office to petition, only to be raked with gunfire from guards above. Word spread across the island by radio and by mouth, and within days, from Keelung to Pingtung, local committees formed and took over public order. A full-scale uprising against postwar rule had begun.

The revolt moved quickly from the streets to the negotiating table. Gentry and elected representatives formed the "February 28 Incident Settlement Committee" to seek reform through institutional means. Wang Tian-teng, a Taipei city councillor serving as the committee's propaganda chief, broadcast to the island by radio and led the drafting of the Thirty-Two Demands, calling for broad Taiwanese autonomy, the disarming of troops, and the local appointment of officials — the first systematic blueprint for self-government in postwar Taiwan. Governor Chen Yi outwardly accepted talks and promised reform while secretly cabling Nanjing for troops, buying time. The negotiation was a deception from the start.

In some regions the resistance escalated into armed struggle. In Taichung, Hsieh Hsueh-hung rallied students and youth into the "27 Brigade," briefly controlling the city before retreating to fight on in the mountains around Puli and ultimately disbanding, while she herself fled into exile. In the south, Kaohsiung Fortress Commander Peng Meng-chi refused to negotiate and on March 6 ordered his troops to shell and strafe the city from Shoushan, attacking the city hall, railway station, and First Senior High School and leaving hundreds to over a thousand dead or wounded — among the earliest and bloodiest military crackdowns on the island. Peng, later dubbed the "Butcher of Kaohsiung," was rewarded with steady promotion.

On March 8, the 21st Division, dispatched by Chiang Kai-shek from mainland China, landed at Keelung and Kaohsiung and launched an island-wide "pacification" and "village purge." The true catastrophe arrived now: soldiers and secret police hunted down names on their lists, and native elites were seized, disappeared, and executed without trial. Lin Mao-sheng, dean of the College of Liberal Arts at National Taiwan University, was led from his home on March 11 and never seen again; the financier Chen Hsin and the negotiator Wang Tian-teng were killed around the same day; the Tainan lawyer Tang Te-chang, shielding a list of names and taking responsibility upon himself, was paraded through the streets and shot at Taisho Park (today renamed in his memory); the Chiayi painter Chen Cheng-po, serving as a peace envoy in his capacity as a city councillor, was bound and publicly executed before Chiayi Station on March 25. An entire modern-educated leadership class, poised to carry Taiwan's future, was all but torn out by the roots within weeks.

The dead are estimated at ten to twenty thousand; the exact figure remains unknowable. Afterward, surviving families were forced into silence, and "228" became a taboo unspeakable for four decades, redressed, commemorated, and investigated only after martial law was lifted — a reckoning traced in the Transitional Justice volume. This volume returns to that spring of 1947, recording how a cigarette raid ignited an island-wide uprising, how the Settlement Committee's attempt at reform dissolved once reinforcements landed, and how a generation of Taiwanese elites fell amid the gunfire of the purge. Their names — Lin Mao-sheng, Chen Hsin, Wang Tian-teng, Tang Te-chang, Chen Cheng-po — are the starting point for understanding why postwar Taiwan fell silent for so long, and why it ultimately fought so hard for democracy and transitional justice.
Volumes.volume.lightAndShadow.overseasTaiwaneseR:
During the Japanese colonial era, large numbers of Taiwanese were mobilized or voluntarily traveled throughout the Japanese Empire. After the war ended, Taiwanese scattered across mainland China, Southeast Asia, and Japan proper faced the question of repatriation. Some returned to the "motherland" filled with anticipation, only to find their homeland utterly transformed.

Ong Iok-tek — a linguist from Tainan and pioneer of the Taiwan independence movement — chose to remain in Japan after the war, becoming a key figure in the overseas Taiwan independence movement. Su Ni-uo — a Taiwanese intellectual residing in mainland China — witnessed the upheaval of the Chinese Civil War and eventually returned to Taiwan only to face the White Terror.

This volume presents the diaspora experiences and identity struggles of overseas Taiwanese in the aftermath of empire through these personal stories.
Volumes.volume.lightAndShadow.parliamentarySyste:
In the early post-war period, the Nationalist government established local self-governance and political participation systems in Taiwan. In 1946, Taiwan held its first-ever provincial assembly elections, giving Taiwanese their first opportunity to participate in politics through the ballot. However, this system was constrained from the outset: the Provincial Assembly had only an advisory function, with actual decision-making power remaining in the hands of the Chief Executive's office.

Language barriers placed many Taiwanese assemblymen at a disadvantage in the chamber, and Chen Yi's government imposed various restrictions on native Taiwanese political participation, rendering "democracy" a mere decoration in name only. This pattern of "granting form while limiting substance" became a significant factor in native Taiwanese disillusionment with the new regime.

This volume explores the germination of post-war Taiwan's democratic institutions and their structural contradictions.
Volumes.volume.lightAndShadow.postWarOccupationA:
In October 1945, the Nationalist government held a surrender ceremony in Taipei, formally ending Japan's fifty-year colonial rule over Taiwan. However, the joy of "retrocession" was quickly overshadowed by numerous problems during the takeover. Chen Yi's civil-military unified administration, the uneven quality of incoming officials, administrative barriers caused by language differences, and the wholesale transformation of Taiwan's existing institutions rapidly intensified social tensions.

During this period, the United States played a critical role as observer. American military liaison groups stationed in Taiwan closely documented the chaos of the takeover process and repeatedly reported Chen Yi's governance failures to Washington. These reports later became essential archives for understanding Taiwan's political situation in the early post-war period.

This volume includes rare historical photographs of the surrender ceremony, American military observation reports, and the historic scene of Ando Rikichi signing the instrument of surrender, presenting the complex historical turning point from colony to motherland's embrace, from hope to disillusionment.
Volumes.volume.lightAndShadow.shibuyaIncidentAnd:
In the early post-war period, tens of thousands of Taiwanese residing in Japan faced an unprecedented identity crisis. They were no longer Japanese nationals in legal terms, yet the ROC's nationality determination process remained unclear. The 1946 "Shibuya Incident" — a street clash between Taiwanese and Japanese police — became emblematic of this dilemma, drawing international attention to the legal status of Taiwanese people.

In January 1946, the Nationalist government issued an order collectively "restoring" ROC nationality to all Taiwanese. However, GHQ (General Headquarters of the Allied Powers) and some international legal scholars challenged this move, arguing that until a formal peace treaty was signed, Taiwan's sovereignty remained undetermined, rendering the nationality change legally unfounded.

This volume explores the identity issues of post-war Taiwanese caught between international legal frameworks, featuring rare documents including overseas Chinese nationality certificates from Myanmar and the nationality restoration order.
Volumes.volume.lightAndShadow.twentySevenBrigade:
The gunfire of February 28, 1947, spread outward from Taipei, and the fury raced south along the trunk railway; within two days it had reached Taichung. On March 2, residents and students poured into the streets, and the city council convened an emergency citizens' assembly. Onto the platform stepped a woman of forty-six — Hsieh Hsueh-hung. Born into a poor family in Changhua and sold as a child bride, she had taught herself to read and made her way to Shanghai and to the Communist University of the Toilers of the East in Moscow. In 1928 she had helped found the Taiwanese Communist Party, and she had endured repeated imprisonment under the Japanese colonial authorities. In that moment, no one else on the island understood better how to forge a scattered crowd into a force.

At her call, the resistance in Taichung rose swiftly from petition to takeover. On March 3, the crowds occupied the city hall, the police station, and the radio station, collecting weapons and keeping order — for a time the streets were calmer than in ordinary days. Hsieh understood that an angry crowd alone could not hold out for long. She convened a mass meeting at the Taichung Theater, established a "People's Assembly" and an operational headquarters, and set about organizing a local self-governing body that might replace the discredited regime — for this was never mere rioting, but an earnest attempt at self-rule: she argued that Taiwanese should govern Taiwan themselves, that arms were only the means to force concessions, and that the true aim was the remaking of the system. In an age when women were all but excluded from every public decision, that a poor-born woman twice imprisoned should become the highest decision-maker of a city's uprising was itself something unheard of. She organized the incoming youth, demobilized veterans, and students from every school, assigning them to supply, medical care, and sentry duty, so that within a few short days the chaotic streets ran in good order. On March 6 the force was formally named the "27 Brigade," after the February 27 cigarette-seizure incident that had ignited the uprising. Chung I-jen, a former officer in the Japanese army, served as its commander, while Hsieh presided as its spiritual leader and highest decision-maker. Its core came from the students of Taichung Normal School and the Taichung School of Agriculture, joined by aboriginal youth from Puli and a company of Taiwanese men who had fought as Japanese soldiers in the South Seas and only lately returned home. Most were no more than eighteen or nineteen, holding rifles received from the police depots and armories, and for a few short days — the first and only time — they felt as though the island were truly in their own hands.

But the deception at the negotiating table was soon laid bare. On March 8, the 21st Division, dispatched by Chiang Kai-shek from the mainland, landed at Keelung and split southward, strafing with machine guns and arresting at will, drowning one city after another in blood. Facing a well-armed regular army that vastly outnumbered them, the 27 Brigade knew it could not hold the city, and made a decisive choice: to abandon Taichung and withdraw to the mountain town of Puli, sparing the citizenry the ruin of street fighting while leaning on the mountains to preserve its strength and fight on. On March 16, this student-led force fought, near the Wuniulan suspension bridge on the outskirts of Puli, the last and fiercest engagement of the entire February 28 period — the hour-by-hour course of that day in the valley is told in a separate volume of this book. After a daylong battle, its ammunition and relief exhausted, its leaders resolved that night to disband, letting the young fighters scatter and vanish into anonymity. A force that had once shaken the authorities dissolved quietly into the mountains.

Only after the brigade disbanded did the true catastrophe descend. Soldiers and secret police launched an island-wide village purge, going door to door to hunt down by name all who had joined the resistance, preferring to kill the innocent rather than let a suspect slip away. Most members of the 27 Brigade were pursued; Chung I-jen was captured, sentenced to death, and then reprieved to a long imprisonment, spending seventeen years behind bars, while countless nameless student soldiers simply disappeared — some shot where they stood, some sunk in the irrigation canals, some fleeing far away never to look back — becoming a void their families could never speak aloud. That fear did not dissolve when the gunfire ceased; it seeped instead into the daily life of the decades that followed, as people learned not to speak of politics, not to ask about the past, and to bury memory deep. After the disbanding, Hsieh Hsueh-hung made her way through Hong Kong and fled to mainland China, where she founded the Taiwan Democratic Self-Government League and went on striving for Taiwan's future — only to be branded a rightist in the Anti-Rightist Campaign and the Cultural Revolution that followed, denounced and her home ransacked. She died in Beijing in 1970, in bleak circumstances: a woman who had fought the Japanese colonizers in her youth and the Nationalist government in her middle years, only to be humiliated in the end by the very regime she had turned to — caught between two powers, and failed by both.

The 27 Brigade existed for barely two weeks, yet it left an indelible mark on history. It was the most organized and the most resolute armed force of the entire February 28 period, and — rare in modern Taiwanese history — an army built and led by the hand of a woman. While the Settlement Committee in Taipei still sought reform through institutional channels at the negotiating table, hoping to exchange peace for political promises, Taichung had already proven through action that the people of this island were willing to pay the heaviest price for self-rule and dignity. This volume returns to that brief, searing spring of March 1947, recording how Hsieh Hsueh-hung and the 27 Brigade rose up in desperation and took their final bow among the mountains. Their defeat — together with those young faces that never came home — is one of the starting points for understanding why postwar Taiwan fell silent for so long, and why it never gave up its search for freedom.
Volumes.volume.lightAndShadow.usPerspectives.des:
The United States played a subtle yet critical role in post-war Taiwan history. As the principal victor of the Pacific War, the U.S. wielded significant influence over Taiwan's disposition, yet its policies wavered between strategic interests and democratic values.

Reports by American diplomats and military observers stationed in Taiwan meticulously documented the various forms of chaos following the Nationalist takeover. These reports directly criticized Chen Yi's government for corruption, administrative incompetence, and boiling public discontent. However, as the Cold War framework gradually took shape on the international stage, the United States ultimately chose to support the Nationalist government, viewing Taiwan as an important chess piece in its anti-communist strategy.

This volume compiles American diplomatic archives, military reports, and intelligence assessments to reexamine post-war Taiwan's historical turning points from across the Pacific.
Volumes.volume.lightAndShadow.wuniulanBattle.des:
By March 14, 1947, the sky over Taichung had already changed. The 21st Division, which had landed at Keelung on March 8, was driving south, and wherever its machine guns and bayonets reached, blood ran in the streets. The 27 Brigade, which had held the city for barely ten days, could no longer stand against a regular army on the open plain. Hsieh Hsueh-hung and the officers of the operational headquarters made a decision that was heavy yet clear-eyed: to abandon Taichung and withdraw to the mountain town of Puli. This was no rout but a planned redeployment — to draw the fighting away from the crowded city, to spare its innocent residents the ruin of street combat, and, leaning on the barrier of the Central Mountain Range, to preserve the last strength of this young force. That night, trucks and marching fighters wound their way east along the mountain roads, their headlamps forming a thin thread of fire in the darkness, carrying rifles and ammunition — and the last desperate gamble of an entire generation of the island's youth.

Reaching Puli, the brigade set its command post in the Butoku-den and deployed along the contours of the Ailan plateau. Ailan was a red-earth tableland rising above the valley, and its only external link was the Wuniulan suspension bridge spanning the Mei River — narrow, flimsy, wide enough for only a few men at a time. For a force short of ammunition and thin in numbers, such terrain was a godsend of a defensive line: hold the bridgehead and the high ground at the plateau's edge, and an advancing army could not rush across all at once, but had to be fed up the narrow path in small batches. In command of this line was Huang Chin-tao, barely past twenty. Once conscripted as a Taiwanese soldier in the Japanese army, he had seen a real battlefield in the jungles of the South Seas, and among these student soldiers — most of them not yet twenty — he was one of the few who truly understood how to fight. He split his men into groups to hold the heights and thickets on both sides of the bridge, telling them to keep calm, to let the enemy come close before firing, to save every round for the moment that mattered most.

At dawn on March 16, government troops advanced on Puli in several columns, and the vanguard set foot on the Wuniulan bridge. Huang held his fire until most of the enemy had crowded onto the span, jammed together on the narrow deck with no room to advance or retreat — and only then gave the order. The rifles on the high ground cracked as one; the column on the bridge dissolved into chaos, men and animals tumbling into the ravine, the vanguard shattered, and for a time the whole assault ground to a halt. These boys, averaging under twenty and yesterday still at their school desks, had, with the terrain and an unbending will, actually held back a well-armed regular division. All morning the gunfire echoed through the valley; again and again the troops pressed forward, and again and again they were pinned down on the far side of the bridge. It was the finest and most tragic engagement of organized Taiwanese armed resistance in the entire February 28 period — for a few short hours, the island seemed truly to be in their own hands.

But courage in the end could not fill the gulf of strength. By afternoon the troops turned to mortars and flanking maneuvers, finding gaps to slip in behind the plateau; the defenders' rounds ran out one by one, their supplies long since severed, relief nowhere in sight. Huang Chin-tao watched his comrades fall one after another and his magazines empty one after another, and knew this line could no longer be held. As the light faded and the gunfire thinned, the final order came from headquarters: disband. It was the only decision Hsieh Hsueh-hung and the officers could make in that hopeless place — better to let these boys, who had scarcely begun to live, scatter into the night and vanish under new names than to die for nothing; and better, too, than to see the people of Puli who had sheltered them punished later for harboring "rebels." That night the fighters shed their mud- and blood-stained clothes, hid their weapons in the mountain gullies, and slipped away in twos and threes into the dark hill paths. A force that had once shaken the authorities took its quiet final bow among the peaks.

The fighting was over, but the long ordeal had only begun. The purge lists soon reached Puli; most who had fought at Wuniulan were hunted down — some seized on the spot, others hiding under false names for years, yet few escaping prison in the end. Huang Chin-tao was eventually captured and sentenced to a heavy term, spending more than twenty years behind bars, much of it worn away among the reefs and sea winds of Green Island; only in his later years, released at last, did he devote the rest of his life to testimony and oral history, becoming one of the few living witnesses to preserve a first-hand memory of the Battle of Wuniulan, until his death in 2014. And Hsieh Hsueh-hung, who had orchestrated it all, after the disbanding made her way through Hong Kong into exile on the mainland, only to end her life humiliated in the political storms of a foreign land. This volume does not recount the whole arc of the uprising; it draws the lens close to that single daylight in the valley on March 16, 1947 — recording how a band of boys, before one suspension bridge, with their last rounds and a courage utterly out of proportion, wrote for postwar Taiwan the most sorrowful and most unyielding page of its armed resistance.
Volumes.volume.newFormosa.capeNo7FilmRevival.des:
In the summer of 2008, a domestic film set against the backdrop of Hengchun in Pingtung — Cape No. 7 — opened quietly, yet through word of mouth it ignited a wave of moviegoing that swept across Taiwan, ultimately setting a box-office record for a local film in Taiwanese cinema history and coming to be seen as the pivotal starting point of Taiwan's domestic-film revival.

For more than two decades before this, Taiwanese cinema had languished; though there was no shortage of artistic works acclaimed at international festivals, local commercial productions had almost lost the audience's gaze under the squeeze of Hollywood blockbusters, it was rare to see a story that belonged to Taiwan itself on the screen, and many had grown habitually wary of the very words 'domestic film.'

It was precisely in such a trough that director Wei Te-sheng poured in all his effort, even going into debt, and with a work saturated in the scent of the land, rekindled audiences' passion for walking into theaters to watch domestic films. The story of Cape No. 7 interweaves two threads spanning sixty years: one is the seven love letters a Japanese teacher wrote to his Taiwanese sweetheart but never managed to deliver as the Japanese withdrew from Taiwan after the war, their lines brimming with tender affection amid the upheavals of the age; the other is how Aga, a disheartened young band member who failed in Taipei and returned home to contemporary Hengchun, rediscovers himself and the direction of his life amid the town's human warmth and the preparation for a seaside concert.

Set against the sunlight, sea breeze, and small-town daily life of the Hengchun peninsula, the film weaves together Hokkien, Mandarin, Japanese, and even Indigenous languages into the authentic, pluralistic voice of Taiwanese society.

Its vivid, laughing-through-tears small characters — the hot-tempered yet warm-hearted town representative, the Indigenous policeman selling millet wine, and old Mao, the instrument-repairing postman who plays the moon lute — let audiences see in them the shadows of themselves and the people around them, and feel that most sincere human warmth belonging to Taiwan's countryside.

The line 'Stay, or I will go with you,' and the songs running through the film that were sung everywhere for a time, became the shared memory of an entire generation. The success of Cape No. 7 was no accidental box-office miracle; it proved that as long as a story belonging to this land is told with heart, Taiwanese audiences are willing to support their own cinema with action and with the passion of returning to theaters again and again.

Spurred by it, domestic films regained the confidence of investors and the attention of audiences, and the whole industry seemed to wake from a long slumber; in the years that followed, one work after another themed on Taiwan's history, land, and ordinary life appeared in succession — from Indigenous epics to urban youth, from historical wounds to family routine — and Taiwanese cinema welcomed a long-absent pluralistic flourishing, leading more young creators to believe that filming a moving story on this island was a dream worth striving for.

Wei Te-sheng himself, taking this as his starting point, threw himself into far grander historical works, continuing to excavate through images the forgotten memories of Taiwan's land. Cape No. 7 was like a love letter sixty years overdue, reopened in the sea breeze of Hengchun, and like a gentle yet resolute summons, awakening the long-dormant vitality of Taiwanese cinema and teaching this island once more to tell its own stories on the silver screen, with confidence and with feeling.
Volumes.volume.newFormosa.crossStraitRelations.d:
Entering the twenty-first century, the Taiwan Strait once again became one of the most closely watched flashpoints in world politics. The relative equilibrium of the late 1990s — a tacit framework built upon the 1992 talks and Lee Teng-hui's cautious pragmatism — gave way under the weight of three interlocking shifts: Taiwan's consolidating democratic identity, the People's Republic of China's accelerating military and economic power, and the gradual erosion of the post-Cold War status quo in the Indo-Pacific.

Chen Shui-bian's presidency from 2000 to 2008 opened the era on a note of confrontation. Beijing refused to engage with the DPP government, while Chen's constitutional referenda and rhetorical moves toward Taiwan-centered identity met with fierce warnings from across the strait. The Anti-Secession Law of March 2005 codified the People's Republic's standing threat of force against any move toward formal independence, triggering the largest street protest Taipei had seen in years. Ma Ying-jeou's two terms after 2008 brought a dramatic thaw: direct flights, tourism, the 2010 Economic Cooperation Framework Agreement, and a historic meeting with Xi Jinping in Singapore in 2015. Yet the same rapprochement sparked the 2014 Sunflower Movement, in which students occupied the Legislative Yuan for twenty-four days in protest against a services trade pact many feared would bind Taiwan too tightly to an authoritarian neighbor.

The Tsai Ing-wen era from 2016 saw relations freeze anew. Beijing suspended official dialogue, intensified diplomatic isolation campaigns, and — from 2020 onward — launched near-daily air and naval incursions into Taiwan's ADIZ. The August 2022 visit of U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi triggered the largest live-fire exercises around the island in the history of the People's Liberation Army, encircling Taiwan from multiple directions and demonstrating a capability for blockade. Meanwhile, global semiconductor dependence on TSMC, the war in Ukraine, and U.S.–China strategic rivalry elevated the strait from a regional dispute to a matter of planetary consequence.

This volume traces the turning points of cross-strait relations since 2000. Through legislation, treaties, protest manifestos, and defense white papers, it examines how successive Taiwanese governments — and an ever more self-aware electorate — have navigated between economic interdependence, existential threat, and the enduring question of what kind of future the island is willing to accept.
Volumes.volume.newFormosa.firstPartyTurnover.des:
By the late 1990s, Taiwan's political landscape stood at an unprecedented crossroads. More than half a century of uninterrupted Kuomintang rule had weathered the lifting of martial law in 1987, the full re-election of the legislature, and the first direct presidential election in 1996. Yet the island's democratic transition remained incomplete so long as no opposition party had ever assumed the highest office. Internal fissures within the KMT, disillusionment with "black gold" politics, and the maturing organizational strength of the Democratic Progressive Party converged to set the stage for a pivotal contest.

On 18 March 2000, in a three-way race between Chen Shui-bian of the DPP, independent James Soong, and the KMT's Lien Chan, Chen prevailed with 39.3 percent of the vote. When he was sworn in on 20 May, fifty-five years of KMT rule in Taiwan formally came to an end and, for the first time in any ethnically Chinese polity, executive power passed peacefully between rival parties through the ballot box. The international press hailed the transition as a milestone of democratic consolidation; voters on the island, however, soon confronted its hard realities — a divided government in which the KMT retained a legislative majority, unresolved tensions over national identity and cross-strait relations, and a Beijing that refused to congratulate the new president.

The Chen presidency opened an era of contested sovereignty, bitter partisan gridlock, and recurring constitutional referenda. Yet the institutional lesson of 2000 endured: Taiwan's democracy could survive the rotation of power. The second turnover in 2008 returned the KMT under Ma Ying-jeou to office, and the third in 2016 brought Tsai Ing-wen and the DPP back. Each handover reinforced the same quiet norm — that sovereignty rests with the voters, and that elections, not force or faction, decide who governs.

This volume revisits the first party turnover and the turbulent decades that followed. Through inauguration speeches, contested ballots, cabinet records, and contemporary reportage, it traces how Taiwan's young democracy matured from the exhilaration of 2000 into a settled, if often fractious, system in which the peaceful transfer of power has become ordinary.
Volumes.volume.newFormosa.highSpeedRailOpening.d:
On January 5, 2007, the Taiwan High Speed Rail officially entered service. From that day, streamlined orange-and-white trains raced along the western corridor, compressing what had been a journey of several hours between north and south into roughly ninety minutes, thoroughly rewriting the Taiwanese imagination of distance and time, and turning the 'one-day living circle' from a slogan into daily reality.

Before the high-speed rail opened, travel between Taiwan's north and south relied either on conventional railways that stopped all along the way or on frequently congested freeways, often consuming the better part of a day; and when this steel artery of a new era ran through from north to south, the space-time map of western Taiwan was refolded in an instant. Stretching about 345 kilometers, the line runs from Taipei in the north to Zuoying in Kaohsiung in the south, stringing together the most densely populated and industrially concentrated urban belt of western Taiwan.

The project was then one of Taiwan's largest public infrastructure undertakings and one of the rare high-speed railways in the world built through a build-operate-transfer (BOT) model, its construction passing through countless technical, financial, and institutional challenges. It introduced the core systems of Japan's Shinkansen, combined them with European signaling and engineering experience, and built across Taiwan's cramped, geologically complex, and earthquake-prone land a steel dragon that crossed rivers, bored through tunnels, and rode elevated above the plains, its viaduct piers stretching like a spine running hundreds of kilometers, holding up the whole island's dream of swift movement.

The Taichung station at Wuri sits precisely at the midpoint of the western corridor, becoming a vital hub linking central Taiwan and symbolizing how this railway stitched scattered cities into one. What the high-speed rail brought was far more than a gain in speed. It allowed people living in Kaohsiung to travel to Taipei and back in a single day for business, meetings, or visiting relatives, returning home with ease; it gave students in the south and the job market in the north, travelers from the north and the customs of the south, an unprecedented exchange in the span of a morning's departure and an evening's return.

Many families once estranged by distance could now reunite more often through a single rail ticket; the psychological distance between cities shrank dramatically; the maps of commuting, study, tourism, and commerce were reshaped, and the western corridor gradually merged into a living community breathing as one. The high-speed rail also profoundly altered Taiwan's urban-rural relations and regional development.

The specially designated zones around new stations spurred surrounding development and transformation, and once relatively remote areas were seen anew through the convenience of a single stop; local tourism, industry, and population flows all sought new possibilities under the pull of this high-speed axis, and the fates of the cities along the line were thereby bound tightly together.

To be sure, the high-speed rail also faced financial challenges and operational controversies, reminding people of the complex trade-offs and long-term responsibilities behind large public works. Yet it is undeniable that the high-speed rail has become an indispensable artery of modern Taiwanese life, deeply embedded in the daily routines and life trajectories of countless people.

When people board in the south in the morning light, stroll the streets of the north by afternoon, and return to the family dinner table by evening, the two ends of this island have, through the binding of a single steel rail, become within each other's reach. In the moment the high-speed rail opened, Taiwan truly entered the age of the one-day living circle, and the pulse of the whole island drew closer together.
Volumes.volume.newFormosa.identityAndCulture.des:
"Are you Taiwanese, Chinese, or both?" This deceptively plain survey question, first posed systematically by National Chengchi University's Election Study Center in 1992, has become one of the most telling barometers of a society in quiet revolution. At the outset, fewer than twenty percent of respondents answered "Taiwanese only." Three decades later, that figure exceeds sixty percent, while exclusively Chinese identification has collapsed to near single digits. No amount of policy, propaganda, or protest could have produced the shift alone; it is the cumulative work of democratic elections, a free press, generational turnover, cross-strait estrangement, and an expanding civic imagination.

The transformation has been carried not only in opinion polls but in language, curriculum, and public memory. The 1990s and 2000s saw sweeping reforms to history and civics textbooks, relocating Taiwan — rather than a mythologized greater China — to the center of the national story. The Council of Indigenous Peoples was elevated to cabinet rank, sixteen indigenous nations were formally recognized, and the Hakka Affairs Council was established to revive a language once suppressed under Mandarin monolingualism. The rise of the Hokkien-language revival, native-land literature, New Wave cinema, and a vibrant independent music scene in Taiyu and Hakka gave the Taiwan-centered identity not just a political form but an everyday cultural texture.

This reorientation was never uncontested. Older generations raised on Nationalist narratives felt displaced; some argued that the new identity risked flattening the island's own internal diversity — among waishengren, benshengren, Hakka, indigenous peoples, and the growing community of new immigrants from Southeast Asia. The legalization of same-sex marriage in 2019, the first in Asia, crystallized the emergent self-image: Taiwan as a plural, rights-based, democratic society defined less by ancestry than by shared commitments. Yet debates over Mandarin's status, the legacy of Japanese colonization, and the place of Chinese culture in Taiwanese life continue to animate dinner tables, classrooms, and legislative chambers alike.

This volume maps the long arc of Taiwanese identity formation — from colonial memory and postwar suppression to democratic self-assertion and global cultural confidence. Through survey data, textbook revisions, language policies, film and literature, it shows how an island that was for centuries named by others has come, at last, to name itself.
Entering the twenty-first century, Taiwanese society gradually awoke to a profound crisis: the mother tongues passed down for generations on this island — Taiwanese (Taiwanese Hokkien), Hakka, and the languages of the various Indigenous peoples — were rapidly being lost, and many of the younger generation could no longer fluently speak the language of their grandparents; some Indigenous languages even faced the endangered plight of having only a handful of elders left who could speak them.

This awakening and rescue concerning language is one of the most profound and moving pages in the construction of modern Taiwan's cultural subjectivity, and its historical depth can be traced all the way back to the scars left by past language policy. In the authoritarian era, the single-language policy promoting 'Mandarin' suppressed local languages in schools and public spaces; children could even be made to wear a placard reading 'I spoke a dialect' and be fined or punished for speaking their mother tongue at school, and so several generations drifted, unknowingly, ever further from their own native languages, which were for a time even stigmatized as symbols of the vulgar and backward — a linguistic rupture that became an unspeakable hidden grief between generations in many families.

After the lifting of martial law and democratization, as local consciousness rose, the call to rescue the mother tongues grew ever stronger, and people came to recognize anew that every mother tongue is an irreplaceable cultural asset. Beginning in the 2000s, local-language education gradually entered the classrooms of national education, and native-language classes became the starting point for many schoolchildren to reconnect with their mother tongue; public television successively launched dedicated channels and stations in Taiwanese, Hakka, and Indigenous languages, letting the mother tongues flow anew through drama, news, song, and children's programs in everyday life.

Academia and civil society poured in great effort, organizing writing systems, compiling dictionaries, promoting certification exams, and cultivating teachers, and through literature, popular music, drama, film, and online creation, making local languages once again living languages bearing emotion and identity, and leading more and more young people to take pride in speaking their mother tongue and singing songs in it. This wave of revival met a milestone moment in 2019 — the National Languages Development Act formally took effect.

This law stipulated that the natural languages used by all of Taiwan's inherent ethnic groups, along with Taiwan Sign Language, are all national languages, equal in status without distinction by the size of their speaking populations; the state should safeguard the transmission, revival, and development of every national language, and ensure it gains its due space and respect in education, broadcasting, public services, and formal occasions. This meant that Taiwan finally, at the level of law, formally recognized the plurality of its own languages and solemnly took up the responsibility of guarding every mother tongue. The revival of local languages was never merely a question of linguistic survival.

A language carries a people's way of seeing the world, the wisdom accumulated over generations, and the emotion and memory embedded in its very sounds; once a language disappears, what passes away with it is an entire people's unique spiritual world. When a child once again learns to greet grandma and grandpa in the mother tongue, when long-absent folk songs are sung anew in schools and on stages, when the languages of different peoples can all be heard equally and confidently on this island, Taiwan, amid the polyphony of its languages, more profoundly affirms its own face as a pluralistic and inclusive society.

This intergenerational mother-tongue movement continues, quietly and resolutely, to this day, in every classroom, every household, and every conversation.
Volumes.volume.newFormosa.palaceMuseumSouthernBr:
On December 28, 2015, the Southern Branch of the National Palace Museum officially opened for trial operation in Taibao City, Chiayi County, bringing the Palace Museum's collection — long concentrated at Waishuangxi in Taipei — systematically into Taiwan's south for the first time. Positioned as a 'Museum of Asian Art and Culture,' this branch was not merely a newly built exhibition hall, but carried a profound contemporary ideal — cultural equity, and a southern perspective that repositioned Taiwan.

For a long time, Taiwan's cultural resources had been highly concentrated in the north; major museums, performance venues, and large arts events mostly gathered in the Taipei metropolis, and residents of the south and east wishing to behold the Palace Museum's national treasures often had to spend the better part of a day traveling far north — the gap in cultural access between city and countryside became a real, long-neglected issue.

The establishment of the Southern Branch was precisely meant to break this imbalance in the distribution of cultural resources, so that residents of central, southern, and eastern Taiwan, as well as students from surrounding townships who had rarely had the chance to encounter world-class collections, could appreciate precious artifacts close to home and enjoy an equal right of access to culture and an equal right to imagine the world.

Unlike the Taipei branch's focus on the imperial court collections of successive Chinese dynasties, the Southern Branch deliberately cast its gaze toward a broader Asia. Centered on Asian textiles, tea culture, Buddhist art, ceramics, and other cross-cultural exchanges, it presents, through artifacts from across Asia, the pluralistic face of Taiwan as a link in the Asian maritime network, reminding people that Taiwan's cultural coordinates should not look up only to a single Central Plain, but should be reunderstood and resituated within the context of all of Asia and even the maritime world.

This is the deep meaning of the 'southern perspective' — setting out from the land of the south, unfolding toward Asia, toward the ocean, toward the world, allowing Taiwan to recognize anew its place in the world with a broader vision. In architecture, the Southern Branch was designed by a local team, with flowing curved volumes echoing the brush intentions of thick ink, flying white, and wash in calligraphy, set off by the artificial lake, greenery, landscape bridge, and expansive garden landscaping surrounding the grounds, creating a cultural park fusing the humanistic and the natural, open for the public to approach and rest, amid the open expanse of the Chianan Plain.

Although the road to opening was not without obstacles — site selection, construction progress, and the selection and interpretation of exhibits all sparked discussion and scrutiny from various quarters — the significance of the Southern Branch settling on this agricultural plain in Taibao, Chiayi, cannot be overlooked.

It symbolizes Taiwanese society's awareness of cultural equity, symbolizes the state's resources beginning to be willing to tilt toward long-marginalized localities, and symbolizes a turn in values willing to listen to the south, to confront the urban-rural divide, and to redistribute cultural voice.

As national treasures and Asian art slowly unfold under the warm sunlight of southern Taiwan, and children can gaze up at the treasures of the world on the very land where they grew up, the Southern Branch quietly tells of a simple yet profound conviction: culture should not belong only to a certain city, a certain class, or a certain people, but should, like sunlight, fall equally upon every corner of this island.
Volumes.volume.newFormosa.sameSexMarriageLegaliz:
On May 17, 2019, Taiwan's Legislative Yuan passed on its third reading the Enforcement Act of Judicial Yuan Interpretation No. 748, allowing two people of the same sex to establish a permanent union in marriage by law, and Taiwan thereby became the first country in Asia to legalize same-sex marriage.

On the very afternoon of the vote, tens of thousands of people who had waited long gathered on Qingdao East Road outside the legislature, braving a torrential downpour, eyes fixed on the live broadcast on their phones and the big screens; in the moment the clauses passed, the crowd in the rain erupted in earth-shaking cheers and tears, strangers embraced and wept, and rainbow flags flew amid the curtain of rain.

On May 24, the day the law took effect, countless same-sex couples completed their marriage registrations at household registration offices across Taiwan, finally able to become each other's legal family in name and in truth — the end of a long road traveled over decades, soaked with countless tears and struggle.

Taiwan's LGBTQ movement can be traced to around the lifting of martial law, from the early minority voices that emerged with difficulty at society's margins, sometimes forced to hide their names, to the annual Pride march held on Taipei's streets that grew to be the largest in Asia, drawing participants from many countries to join in; generation after generation of activists, scholars, lawyers, physicians, and countless ordinary LGBTQ people and their loved ones continued to fight for the right to be treated equally and to be seen as they truly are, amid stigma, misunderstanding, and at times fierce opposition.

The turning point came in 2017, when the Grand Justices of the Judicial Yuan rendered Interpretation No. 748, holding that the Civil Code's failure to protect the freedom of marriage and equal rights of two people of the same sex was unconstitutional, and requiring the relevant authorities to complete amendments within two years, setting a constitutional-level milestone on the road to equality.

Yet the road to equality remained rugged; the results of several referendums in 2018 reflected society's deep tug-of-war and divergence among traditional values, religious conviction, and marriage equality, and once plunged countless LGBTQ people and their families into despondency. Under the multiple tensions of public opinion, constitutional interpretation, and politics, lawmakers ultimately responded to the Grand Justices' requirement within the framework of the constitutional interpretation, with a special act that genuinely protected the right to same-sex marriage while also seeking to accommodate the pluralistic voices and feelings of society. The significance of legalizing same-sex marriage far exceeds the letter of the law itself.

It established that, regardless of sex, every person enjoys the equal right to love, to unite, and to form a family; it allowed many couples long hidden — some who had not even dared to come out to their closest kin — to finally clasp each other's hands openly and make their lifelong vows before the witness and blessing of loved ones.

For society as a whole, it was a profound lesson in empathy, inclusion, and respect for difference, reminding people that true democracy lies not only in the will of the majority but also in the solemn protection of the rights of the minority. By taking this step as the first in Asia, Taiwan showed the world how a society that had passed through authoritarianism and walked toward democracy could, after fierce debate and the reconciling of differing positions, still choose to protect the basic human rights and dignity of every person through institutions.

The rain and tears woven together on Ketagalan Boulevard and Qingdao East Road that night washed away long-standing stigma and repression, and for the first time truly wrote the words 'love makes no distinction' into the law and collective memory of this island, warming those who came after for a long time to come.
Volumes.volume.newFormosa.sarsHepingHospital.des:
In the spring of 2003, an unprecedented new coronavirus slipped quietly into Taiwan from abroad, and in April Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) erupted into a massive nosocomial outbreak inside Taipei Municipal Heping Hospital, becoming one of the gravest tests in Taiwan's postwar public-health history. That year, SARS spread across many parts of Asia, a disease transmitted by droplets at close range and carrying a fatality rate not to be taken lightly, plunging the whole of society into unprecedented panic.

Heping Hospital stood in the old Wanhua district, a long-established municipal institution serving grassroots medical needs; when unexplained high-fever cases began appearing, the virus had already spread silently through a tangled web of contact among laundry workers, cleaners, and patients, and the hospital's early reporting and isolation failed to halt the outbreak in time, letting the chain of infection burn unnoticed through the entire compound. On April 24, after repeated wrangling between central and local authorities, the Taipei City Government announced the immediate, total sealing of Heping Hospital, ordering all medical staff, employees, and inpatients to return and be collectively quarantined within its walls.

With a single command, more than a thousand people were locked inside with no preparation; panic, anger, and helplessness filled every corridor. Some climbed over walls trying to flee, some hung white banners from windows protesting that 'the hospital had become a prison,' while family members anxiously inquired through the iron gates, and the gaze of the entire city focused on that sealed hospital door.

The hasty lockdown decision also sparked fierce debate over how to weigh procedure, human rights, and epidemic prevention against one another — a case still repeatedly examined in public health and administrative ethics to this day. Yet amid the chaos and fear, more numerous were the figures who quietly held their posts — nurses, resident doctors, cleaning aunties, and volunteers — who, despite severe shortages of protective equipment and limited knowledge of the virus, remained on the front line of the wards, caring for stricken colleagues and patients alike.

There were also medical workers who had already gone off duty but, under the lockdown order, chose to return to the compound to share the ordeal with their colleagues; their choices reflected the deepest professional conscience of healers. During the lockdown, dozens at Heping were infected and several medical workers and staff died, including a head nurse and a physician who fell ill caring for patients; their names were later carved on a memorial, becoming an indelible scar and a mark of honor for the city.

The SARS storm subsided that summer as the climate changed and prevention networks were gradually built. Taiwan paid a bitter price, but tempered profound lessons from it. In the aftermath, the government comprehensively overhauled its communicable-disease control system, establishing a dedicated Centers for Disease Control, building fever-screening and reporting networks, strengthening hospital infection control and negative-pressure isolation wards, advancing amendments to the Communicable Disease Control Act along with legal frameworks for large-scale quarantine, and at the same time building a command architecture for cross-agency coordination and real-time disclosure of information.

These institutional accumulations, won at bitter cost, became, seventeen years later when facing the global COVID-19 pandemic, a crucial foundation that allowed Taiwan to deploy ahead of the curve and respond with relative steadiness, as many of the lessons learned in the Heping Hospital incident were transformed into concrete shields safeguarding the health of the whole people.

The sealing of Heping Hospital is a collective memory woven from fear, sacrifice, and institutional reflection. It reminds us how precious the courage of medical workers is before an invisible virus, and how a society's institutional preparedness, transparency of information, prudence of decision, and mutual trust in the face of crisis often determine the line between life and death.

The walls of that old Wanhua hospital, which once divided inside from outside, life from death, in that spring, have now become one of the most profound lessons in Taiwan's public-health history, quietly recounting those days when an entire people held its breath and supported one another.
Volumes.volume.newFormosa.sunflowerMovement.desc:
On the night of March 18, 2014, a group of students and citizens climbed over the walls, broke through the police lines, and stormed into the legislative chamber on Jinan Road in Taipei, launching an occupation that would last twenty-four days. This movement, later known as the Sunflower Student Movement, was one of the largest and most far-reaching civic movements in Taiwan since the lifting of martial law, and the first time the younger generation intervened so directly and resolutely in the decision of a major national policy.

The fuse of the event was the Cross-Strait Service Trade Agreement then being pushed by those in power. Many feared that this agreement, which involved opening up a wide range of service industries, would, without adequate deliberation or transparency, profoundly impact Taiwan's economic autonomy, industrial ecology, job market, and even democratic procedures. When the agreement was declared 'review complete' in a legislative committee in a mere few dozen seconds, without article-by-article review, and prepared to be sent to the floor for record, long pent-up doubts and discontent erupted instantly; students and citizens resolved to express their protest by occupying the chamber in an unprecedented way, demanding the agreement be withdrawn and a monitoring mechanism for cross-strait agreements be established, defending through action the democratic procedures they cherished.

During the occupation, an unprecedented scene took shape inside and outside the chamber: within, students built barricades from the chamber's desks and chairs, taking shifts to keep watch through the night, organizing supplies, and speaking to the public, while live-streaming every move inside the chamber to the world over the internet, making this movement a highly transparent historical scene voiced by citizens themselves; outside, Jinan Road and Qingdao East Road were packed with supportive crowds, as volunteers in supplies, medicine, law, and media spontaneously built a dense support network, and street lectures, social movement groups, and arts workers all threw themselves in, transforming the protest site into an open civic classroom.

Countless strangers, in those days, sat shoulder to shoulder on the ground out of shared concern, listening to speeches, passing along lunchboxes, and looking after one another, guarding together a faith in the future through the chill spring nights. The movement, named for the sunflower — from the sunflowers supporters sent into the chamber — symbolized a yearning for sunlight, transparency, and hope. On March 30, hundreds of thousands clad in black surged onto Ketagalan Boulevard, voicing their demands through a peaceful and vast assembly that became an unforgettable page in the history of Taiwan's street movements and showed the world the mature, self-disciplined power of Taiwan's civil society.

Although there was a tense episode in which protesters rushed into the Executive Yuan and were forcibly cleared, the movement on the whole maintained a high spirit of nonviolence. After more than twenty days of standoff and negotiation, once the speaker of the legislature promised to establish a monitoring mechanism for cross-strait agreements and the service trade pact was effectively shelved, the occupiers announced their withdrawal on April 10, carefully cleaning the chamber before they left, leaving behind the image of those who 'occupied, and also protected.' The Sunflower Movement profoundly changed Taiwan's political landscape.

It made 'civic oversight,' 'procedural justice,' and 'information transparency' a broad social consensus, gave rise to a new generation attentive to public affairs, and prompted many young people to enter politics, social movements, media, and public participation, injecting new vitality into Taiwan's democracy. This youth-centered movement proved to the whole society that democracy is not merely voting once every few years, but the collective practice of every citizen who refuses to be silent at the critical moment and is willing to take to the streets in person and guard it with their own hands.

The wall of the legislature was climbed over that spring night, and the civic consciousness and passion for participation it opened up continue to grow and blossom on this island to this day.
Volumes.volume.newFormosa.taipei101Completion.de:
On December 31, 2004, as the New Year's bells rang out over Taipei's Xinyi district, a skyscraper reaching 508 meters officially opened — Taipei 101, in that moment the tallest building in the world, lifting Taiwan's skyline onto the international stage. Before its completion, the Xinyi Planning District was still a rising new urban area, and the tower's springing up from the ground was like planting in this city a flag facing the world, symbolizing how Taiwan, after its economic takeoff and democratic transition, yearned to converse with the world in a wholly new posture.

Designed under architect C. Y. Lee, this colossal tower was no mere contest of stacking steel and glass to reach for height, but a structure that deliberately wove Taiwanese cultural codes into modern engineering. Rising in segments of eight floors per unit, its form echoed the auspicious meaning of bamboo joints 'rising ever higher,' its silhouette like a stalk of upright, vigorous bamboo, symbolizing an endless, upward-striving spirit; its shaft was adorned with motifs of ruyi scepters, ancient coins, and auspicious clouds, with giant circular ancient-coin forms hung upon the tower, blending Eastern traditional imagery into a world-class supertall building and making this modern landmark at once a colossal sculpture laden with cultural meaning. In engineering terms, Taipei 101 was also a bold response to Taiwan's own geographic fate.

Sitting on the Pacific Ring of Fire and repeatedly battered by powerful typhoons, to erect a supertall tower on such land was to confront the shaking of earth and sky head-on. To this end, the engineering team drove enormous piles deep into the foundation to reach bedrock, and installed in the tower's upper levels a giant tuned mass damper weighing 660 tons — that golden sphere suspended high in the air, affectionately nicknamed the 'big steel ball,' which sways during strong winds and earthquakes to counteract movement, and was later opened for close-up viewing by visitors, becoming a rare engineering marvel that the public can witness firsthand and letting the world see with its own eyes how Taiwanese engineers tamed the forces of nature with their ingenuity.

Moreover, the high-speed elevators within once set the world record for the fastest, carrying visitors from the ground to the observation deck in mere tens of seconds to overlook the magnificent vista of the entire Taipei Basin. At its opening, Taipei 101 drew global attention with the title of 'world's tallest building,' and its annual New Year's fireworks swiftly became one of Taiwan's most iconic urban images, brilliant flames cascading down the tower's flank, ranked alongside New York and Sydney in New Year coverage worldwide and becoming a major focus as the globe welcomed the new year.

Though the record for the world's tallest was later surpassed by Dubai's Burj Khalifa, Taipei 101's place in the hearts of the Taiwanese has never wavered. It is not merely an office and shopping tower, but a symbol of an era's confidence: after bidding farewell to authoritarianism and walking toward democracy, Taiwan declared to the world, through a building fusing traditional imagery with cutting-edge technology, that it was capable of standing at the summit. Each year-end, as brilliant fireworks cascade down the tower's flank, the Xinyi night sky lights up, and countless Taiwanese in that moment gaze up at the same tower and make the same wish, sharing the same hope for the future amid the countdown to the new year.

Taipei 101 has long transcended the realm of architecture to become this island's spiritual landmark facing the new century and the world, standing quietly at the heart of the city, witnessing the turning of the years and the growth of Taiwan, year after year.
Volumes.volume.newFormosa.transitionalJustice.de:
When martial law was lifted in 1987 and the ban on new political parties and newspapers followed, Taiwan inherited a forty-year backlog of unacknowledged political violence. The February 28 Incident of 1947, in which an uprising against post-war Kuomintang rule was crushed with an estimated ten to twenty thousand dead, had been an unspeakable subject for two generations. Tens of thousands more had been executed, imprisoned, or blacklisted under the White Terror of the 1950s, 60s, and 70s, their files sealed and their families silenced. Democratization without reckoning, many argued, would be democratization in name only.

The first steps came haltingly. In 1995 President Lee Teng-hui formally apologized on behalf of the state for February 28; monuments were raised, a memorial day designated, and modest compensation offered to victims' families. Through the 1990s and 2000s, a patchwork of rehabilitation statutes returned confiscated property, expunged wrongful convictions, and permitted survivors to speak their names in public for the first time. Yet the underlying apparatus of authoritarian memory — the ill-gotten assets of the Kuomintang, the ubiquitous statues of Chiang Kai-shek, the classified security files, the unidentified perpetrators — remained largely untouched.

The passage of the Act on Promoting Transitional Justice in 2017 and the inauguration of the Transitional Justice Commission in 2018 formally institutionalized the work. The Commission was mandated to open political archives, remove authoritarian symbols from public space, restore the reputations of the wrongfully convicted, and recover improperly obtained party assets. Its brief tenure — concluded in 2022 — produced tens of thousands of rehabilitation decisions, a sweeping review of the Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall, and fierce political backlash. Critics from the pan-Blue camp accused it of partisan persecution; survivors and scholars argued its powers were, if anything, too circumscribed to reach those most responsible.

This volume traces Taiwan's long and unfinished reckoning with its authoritarian past. Through compensation decrees, commission reports, memorial inscriptions, and oral histories of the bereaved, it documents how a democracy once built atop silenced graves has slowly, painfully learned to name its dead, question its heroes, and weigh what justice can still mean decades after the fact.
Volumes.volume.seaAndFortress.deerTradeEra.descr:
If a modern person could travel back to seventeenth-century Taiwan, the most astonishing sight would not be Fort Zeelandia, nor the Dutch merchants, nor even the Indigenous villages scattered across the plains.

It would be the deer.

Endless deer.

From present-day Tainan stretching all the way to the plains of Changhua, the western half of Taiwan was once covered in vast grasslands. Before the morning mist fully lifted, thousands upon thousands of Formosan sika deer would emerge from the fields. They ran, grazed, and drank in herds so large they seemed like a moving brown sea flowing across the land.

To the Siraya people of the time, deer were part of everyday life.

Their meat provided food.

Their antlers became tools.

Their hides were used for trade.

When hunting season arrived, warriors would enter the grasslands armed with spears and bows. They knew the migration routes of the herds. They knew where to set traps. For centuries, this rhythm had remained unchanged.

Until the Dutch arrived.

After the Dutch East India Company established Fort Zeelandia in 1624, they quickly discovered an unexpected opportunity.

The Japanese were willing to pay silver for deer hides.

And not just a little.

In the early Edo period, deer leather was in high demand. Samurai used it in armor and weapon fittings. Craftsmen used it to polish blades. Wealthy merchants treated it as a valuable luxury good. As demand surged, Dutch traders realized something remarkable: the deer roaming Taiwan’s plains were not just wildlife.

They were mobile wealth.

And so, a hunting boom began.

The Dutch transformed deer hide production into a fully commercialized industry.

They exchanged iron tools, textiles, and imported goods for deer skins. Indigenous communities increasingly joined the trade network. Hunting was no longer just about survival—it became an economic activity tied to global demand.

More hunters entered the plains.

Fewer deer remained.

At the height of the trade, more than one hundred thousand deer hides were exported from Fort Zeelandia each year.

Warehouses filled with dried skins.

Workers packed shipments day and night.

Ships departed Taiwan one after another.

The hides were sent to Nagasaki in Japan, exchanged for vast quantities of silver. That silver then flowed into Chinese markets, purchasing silk, porcelain, and tea. In this way, a single deer hide connected Taiwan, Japan, China, and Europe—forming a trade network that spanned the entire East Asian world.

Fort Zeelandia prospered.

The Dutch East India Company’s ledgers recorded rising profits year after year.

And Taiwan, for the first time, was fully integrated into a global economic system.

But prosperity often carries its own shadow.

Deer are not infinite.

As hunting intensified, the once-teeming herds of the plains began to shrink. Hunters who once encountered hundreds of deer in a single day now had to travel for hours to find even a trace.

By the mid-seventeenth century, the warning signs were unmistakable.

Deer populations collapsed.

Hunting grounds expanded deeper inland.

Conflicts broke out between villages competing for diminishing resources.

Yet few were willing to stop.

The profits were too great.

Almost everyone believed the grasslands would never run out of deer.

They were wrong.

When Koxinga arrived in Taiwan in 1661, the great herds had already begun to vanish from the western plains. Soon after, waves of Han settlers transformed the landscape. Forests were cleared. Grasslands became farmland. The ecological foundation that had sustained the deer collapsed entirely.
