The animals that once defined the economy of a colonial era slowly disappeared from Taiwan’s western plains.

Today, walking across the Chianan Plain, one sees rice fields, highways, and cities.

Few remember that four centuries ago, this same land was a vast natural pasture filled with wildlife.

The deer that once moved like living tides across the morning mist did more than feed Indigenous communities. They fueled a global trade empire, enriched the Dutch East India Company, and placed Taiwan at the center of East Asian commerce.

In that era, the most valuable resource on the island was not gold.

Not silver.

But a herd of deer running freely across an open land.
Volumes.volume.seaAndFortress.deerTradeEra.title: The Deer That Built an Empire
Volumes.volume.seaAndFortress.dutchArrival.descr:
In the late summer of 1624, several colossal armed merchantmen flying the red, white, and blue tricolor of the Dutch East India Company (VOC) glided gracefully into the shallow, windswept waters of Tayouan, off the southwestern coast of Taiwan. For two grueling years, these fair-haired, flintlock-bearing Western adventurers had been locked in a tense military standoff with the forces of the Ming Dynasty—the precursor to the Qing—from a fortress they had erected on the Penghu Islands. Ultimately, under the crushing tactical pressure and diplomatic orchestration of the massive Ming armies, a tacit trade-off was struck: the Dutch would demolish their citadel on Penghu and retreat to this uncharted, wild island marked on European charts as "Formosa." When the Dutch Governor, Martinus Sonck, first stepped onto this humid, sun-drenched sandbar, his sharp merchant instincts instantly recognized its monumental value. This island was not merely home to tens of thousands of roaming deer; it choked the very throats of the vital sea lanes connecting China, Japan, and the Philippines. The wild winds of the Age of Sail had just struck this beautiful, millennium-slumbering island with unrelenting force.

This historic landing completely altered the trajectory of the island's destiny, raising the curtain on Taiwan's integration into the global arena. Prior to this moment, though Taiwan had occasionally flickered across the nautical charts of Chinese coastal pirates and Japanese smugglers, it had never been regarded as a strategic stronghold by any Western superpower. The arrival of the Dutch marked the very first time in history that Western imperialism extended its governing tentacles directly onto Formosan soil. The moment Governor Sonck, along with his trade factors and soldiers, set foot on the sandbar of Tayouan, they knew they were embarking on an unprecedented maritime venture. They stood face-to-face with unpredictable monsoons, an untamed frontier, and infinite hidden commercial opportunities and geopolitical risks. In this single moment, this beautiful island officially said farewell to its thousand-year isolation and tranquility.

The choice of the Dutch to land and establish a base at Tayouan was the product of a meticulously calculated international trade strategy, driven by the massive global expansion ambitions of the seventeenth-century Dutch "Sea Beggars." At the time, the ultimate objective of the VOC in the Far East was to completely shatter the trade monopolies held by Portugal and Spain, gaining direct access to the vast markets of Ming China and the Tokugawa Shogunate of Japan. However, because the Ming government enforced a strict maritime embargo and harbored immense hostility toward these mysterious "Red-Haired Barbarians," they repeatedly refused formal trade with the Dutch. After bilateral diplomatic negotiations fractured and erupted into open warfare on Penghu, the Dutch desperately needed a buffer port outside the Chinese mainland—one that could evade direct strikes from the Ming navy while luring Chinese smuggling junks out to trade. The natural inner sea and sandbar geography of Taiwan's Tayouan became the absolute perfect historical choice.

From a geographical perspective, the island functioned like a vital central gear nestled within the East Asian seas. To the north, it sailed straight to Nagasaki; to the west, just across the Taiwan Strait, lay the resource-rich coasts of Fujian and Guangdong; to the south, it connected directly to Spanish-controlled Manila, and ultimately stretched to the VOC’s Far Eastern headquarters in Batavia (modern-day Jakarta). The inner sea of Tayouan was deep enough to anchor massive Dutch galleons, while the outer sandbars formed natural breakwaters capable of deflecting fierce summer typhoons. This singular geographical advantage convinced the Dutch that if they could drive a permanent nail into this specific soil, they could weave the isolated strands of Chinese silk and porcelain, Japanese silver, and the VOC’s own Southeast Asian spice networks into a single, golden maritime route of endless, astronomical profit.

As vessel after vessel packed with timber, bricks, cannons, and provisions dropped anchor along the coastline, the waters of Tayouan grew increasingly frantic, and the tricolor flags whipped loudly in the Anping sea breeze. With crowds of Western sailors and merchants rushing across the sandbar, the essence of Western civilization, the logic of mercantilism, and early capitalist institutions were violently injected into the land. This was far more than the mere arrival of foreign ships; it was a head-on collision between the Eastern world and the maritime civilization of the Age of Sail. The currents of the era, driven by an inescapable destiny, dragged this beautiful island from the edge of time into the cruel vortex of global geopolitics and maritime trade. Standing on the shore and gazing into the unknown frontier, Governor Sonck knew that the prelude of history had begun, and this island would never be quiet again.
Volumes.volume.seaAndFortress.dutchArrival.title: The Dutch Arrival
Volumes.volume.seaAndFortress.farmerUprising.des:
In the 1650s, Taiwan entered a period of unprecedented population growth.

After the Dutch established their presence on the island, waves of Han migrants began crossing the Taiwan Strait from Zhangzhou and Quanzhou in Fujian. They cleared forests, reclaimed land, and built irrigation systems, gradually transforming the once wild plains of southern Taiwan into fertile agricultural fields.

The Dutch were pleased.

These settlers required no salaries.

Only land.

And the opportunity to farm it.

For the Dutch East India Company, this was an ideal arrangement. The company could collect revenue from every layer of economic life. Taiwan became, in practice, a colony run like a commercial enterprise.

Taxes.

More taxes.

Farmers paid taxes.

Fishermen paid taxes.

Merchants paid taxes.

Even activities like distilling alcohol or slaughtering livestock required licenses.

To the Dutch, Taiwan was an efficiently managed corporate colony.

To the Han settlers, it was something entirely different.

It was a homeland earned through risk, migration, and survival across a dangerous sea.

From the beginning, these two visions of the island were fundamentally incompatible.

As time passed, tension accumulated.

Farmers complained about excessive taxation.

Merchants resented monopolistic controls.

And migrants who had risked their lives crossing the Blackwater Strait refused to remain permanent tenants in someone else’s land.

Out of this growing discontent, a figure named Guo Huaiyi began to emerge.

Guo Huaiyi was a Fujianese settler and a respected local leader.

He understood that anger among the Han population had already reached a critical threshold.

All that was missing was a trigger.

In the autumn of 1652, that trigger arrived.

A severe crop failure struck the Tainan plains.

Harvests collapsed.

Food became scarce.

Yet the Dutch administration did not reduce taxation. On the contrary, colonial officials continued to collect levies at full scale.

For many, it felt as if survival itself was becoming impossible.

At that point, rebellion began to feel less like an option—and more like inevitability.

A secret uprising started to take shape.

Guo Huaiyi coordinated with local leaders across the region, recruiting farmers, craftsmen, and migrants. Contemporary accounts suggest that thousands joined the conspiracy.

Some sharpened farm tools.

Others forged spears.

Others stockpiled grain in secret.

All of them waited for a single coordinated moment.

The plan was simple.

Strike Dutch positions simultaneously.

Overwhelm their defenses.

Kill the colonial officials.

And drive the Dutch from Taiwan.

But in history, rebellions are often defeated before they begin—not by armies, but by information.

Someone talked.

News of the uprising reached Dutch authorities before the planned attack.

The colonial government immediately went on alert.

Muskets were issued to soldiers.

Fortifications were reinforced.

Indigenous allied groups were mobilized.

When Guo Huaiyi and his followers finally launched their attack, they did not encounter an unprepared colony.

They faced disciplined firing lines already in position.

The uprising quickly turned into a massacre.

Although the rebels were numerous, most were farmers with little military training.

Their weapons were hoes, sickles, and bamboo spears.

Opposing them were Dutch soldiers armed with firearms, training, and coordinated command structures.

Even more decisively, Indigenous allied forces fought alongside the Dutch.

Gunfire erupted.

Smoke filled the air.

Wave after wave of attackers collapsed across the fields.

According to Dutch records, thousands of rebels were killed within days.

The plains were transformed into a battlefield of devastation.

Guo Huaiyi himself was eventually hunted down.

Some accounts say he died in battle.

Others claim he was killed during his escape.

Whatever the truth, he vanished from the historical record after the uprising collapsed.

In the aftermath, the Dutch carried out sweeping reprisals.

Executions were carried out publicly.

Villages were placed under surveillance.

Colonial control became even more rigid.

On the surface, the rebellion had failed completely.

But the Dutch authorities understood something more disturbing beneath the surface.

The Han population in Taiwan had grown large enough to pose a structural threat.

What had once been a sparsely populated colony controlled by fortresses and cannons was becoming a densely settled migrant society.

And with it came not only labor—but its own social order, ambitions, and power.

Nine years later, in 1661, when Koxinga appeared off the coast of Luerhmen with tens of thousands of troops, many Han settlers chose to support the invading force rather than the Dutch administration.

The Dutch soon realized that the Guo Huaiyi Rebellion had not been an isolated outbreak of violence.

It had been a warning.

A signal that the colonial order was already entering its final stage.

The storm that would ultimately reshape Taiwan was not beginning.

It was already on its way.
Volumes.volume.seaAndFortress.fortZeelandia.desc:
Following the landing of the Dutch on the Tayouan sandbar in the late summer of 1624, they were confronted with nothing but endless dunes and a pristine lagoon, entirely devoid of readymade fortifications. To establish a permanent foothold in this newly carved overseas outpost and to protect their rapidly expanding commercial wealth, the Dutch East India Company (VOC) immediately embarked on a monumental construction project that would span several decades. Selecting the highest vantage point on the sandbar, they utilized bricks imported from Batavia and red sandstone quarried from Chikan, bonding them together with a heavy compound of tropical glutinous rice juice, sugar water, and crushed oyster-shell lime to erect an impregnable European-style fortress: Fort Zeelandia. Designed entirely in accordance with the most advanced Baroque military architecture of seventeenth-century Europe, the citadel featured projecting star-shaped bastions to eliminate blind spots for defensive artillery fire. It was not merely a military shield against foreign invasion, but the supreme center of executive power for Dutch colonial administration and global commerce on Formosa.

The structural layout of Fort Zeelandia was divided into an upper inner court and a sprawling outer court. The towering inner fortress housed the Governor’s grand residence, high-ranking staff quarters, and the high-security armory where bullion, cash reserves, and confidential company archives were stored, with deep subterranean cisterns dug beneath to withstand the grueling trials of a prolonged siege. The outer court extended down to the flat expanse of the sandbar, containing the offices of the trade factors, massive transit warehouses for global commerce, and damp underground dungeons for criminals and dissidents. Looking down from the battlements of this massive brick edifice, a highly organized and heavily bureaucratized colonial apparatus functioned with clinical efficiency. The supreme governing authority on the island was the Council of Tayouan, presided over by the ruling colonial Governor and comprised of senior merchants, military commanders, and the resident Calvinist minister. This council concentrated legislative, judicial, executive, and military powers into a single chamber, where all colonial policies, declarations of war, and complex fiscal regulations were finalized and stamped.

In their day-to-day colonial administration, the Dutch implemented an incredibly shrewd and institutionalized strategy of mercantilism. Facing an acute shortage of European soldiers during the early decades of their rule, the Council developed sophisticated mechanisms to control a burgeoning population of Han Chinese immigrants and fragmented indigenous tribes scattered across the plains. For the native populations, they introduced the Landdag (District Diets) in 1635, dividing the pacified territories into distinct administrative zones. Every spring, the Governor would depart Fort Zeelandia in grand royal state to convene the tribal elders. At these summits, the village chiefs were required to swear solemn oaths of fealty to the Dutch state and symbolically offer native plants as tokens of absolute submission. In return, the authorities bestowed upon them formal velvet robes and silver-headed rattan canes engraved with the VOC emblem, legitimizing their hereditary jurisdiction within their respective clans. This indirect system of rule, blending theatrical benevolence with the raw threat of violence, successfully incorporated fractured tribes into the Dutch imperial order at a negligible administrative cost.

Conversely, toward the waves of Han Chinese immigrants who crossed the strait in search of a livelihood, the Council of Tayouan maintained an iron fist of legal containment and fiscal exploitation. The Dutch viewed the Han population strictly as an economic labor force, harnessing their sweat to clear the raw frontier for the mass cultivation of sugarcane and rice bound for global markets. To extract maximum commercial value, the officials inside Fort Zeelandia engineered an extraordinarily oppressive and intricate taxation network. Han pioneers were not only burdened with a mandatory poll tax (Capitation), but were forced to purchase monopolized licenses and pay exorbitant duties for the right to fish, hunt deer, brew alcohol, or slaughter livestock. Terrified of a coordinated Han insurrection, the authorities enforced strict night curfews and collective punishment laws within the crowded Chinese quarters, while pointing the heavy cannons atop Fort Zeelandia's walls directly at the vulnerable thatched villages on the plains. This highly volatile colonial model, built entirely upon financial extraction and military intimidation, generated astronomical dividends for the VOC, but it simultaneously planted the explosive seeds of racial hatred and eventual rebellion deep within the soil.

During the thirty-eight years that Fort Zeelandia stood dominant upon the Tayouan sandbar, it functioned as the Far Eastern heart of a vast maritime empire, pumping the lifeblood of capital and power through the region day and night. Every gubernatorial edict issued and every fiscal law stamped within its stone halls fundamentally reshaped the social fabric of the island forever. Through this monolithic fortress, the Dutch forcibly grafted Western bureaucracy, legalism, and global capitalism onto the historical trajectory of Taiwan with uncompromising precision. Today, as one gazes upon the surviving, weathered red-brick walls of the Anping Old Fort, the history of colonial administration bound to this architecture stands as a haunting testament to how a seventeenth-century maritime superpower utilized a single structure to build East Asia's very first modern colonial order on the edge of the known world.
Volumes.volume.seaAndFortress.hamadaIncident.des:
In the early seventeenth century, Taiwan was not yet the Chinese island that would later be ruled by Koxinga. Along its southern coast flew the flag of the Dutch East India Company. In 1624, the Dutch constructed Fort Zeelandia on the sandy peninsula of Anping, bringing Taiwan into their rapidly expanding trade network across East Asia.

From that moment onward, the island became a crucial crossroads linking China, Japan, Southeast Asia, and Europe. Merchant ships crowded its harbors. Silver, silk, deer hides, and sugar flowed through its ports in staggering quantities. To outside observers, Taiwan appeared to be a flourishing colonial outpost.

Yet beneath this prosperity, a conflict was quietly taking shape—one that would shake the balance of power across East Asia.

At the same time, Japan was entering the early years of the Edo period. Following the unification of the country under Tokugawa Ieyasu, the economy began to recover rapidly, and overseas trade became increasingly important. Many merchants received official "red-seal permits" from the shogunate, allowing them to conduct foreign commerce legally throughout Asia.

Among them was a wealthy merchant from Nagasaki named Hamada Yahee.

Hamada was no ordinary trader. For years, he had sailed the waters of East Asia with his own fleet and armed crew. He was part merchant, part maritime warlord. Traveling regularly between Japan, Taiwan, and Southeast Asia, he amassed a fortune through the silk trade. In Nagasaki, he was known for his audacity and determination. People often said that although he possessed the instincts of a merchant, he carried the temper of a samurai.

Unfortunately for the Dutch, they chose exactly the wrong man to provoke.

In 1627, seeking to increase revenue, Dutch authorities in Taiwan began tightening their control over Japanese merchants. Taxes were raised. Ships were detained. Cargoes were confiscated. To merchants accustomed to relatively free trade, these measures felt less like regulation and more like outright extortion.

Hamada repeatedly protested to the Dutch governor, but his complaints were ignored. Relations between the two sides deteriorated rapidly.

Then, one night in 1628, Hamada made a decision so reckless that it still sounds unbelievable today.

He decided to kidnap the Dutch governor.

Even by modern standards, the plan bordered on insanity. The Dutch East India Company was one of the most powerful commercial empires on earth, with influence stretching across Asia and Africa. Fort Zeelandia was the strongest military fortress in Taiwan. Yet Hamada believed that continuing to endure humiliation was worse than striking back.

Gathering dozens of armed followers, he approached the Dutch under the pretense of negotiation. As the meeting began, Japanese swordsmen suddenly drew their blades.

Chaos erupted.

Dutch soldiers were caught completely off guard. Steel flashed through the air. Amid the confusion, Hamada successfully seized Governor Pieter Nuyts and forced him aboard his ship.

When news of the incident spread, shock rippled through the colonial administration.

A group of Japanese merchants had penetrated the very heart of Dutch authority in Taiwan and abducted one of its highest-ranking officials. This was not merely a security breach—it was a direct humiliation of Dutch colonial power.

Alarm bells rang throughout Fort Zeelandia. Soldiers were mobilized. Company officials were furious. Retribution seemed inevitable.

But events soon took an unexpected turn.

Rather than killing his captive, Hamada sailed directly back to Japan with Pieter Nuyts as a hostage.

Upon arriving in Nagasaki, he immediately presented his case before the Tokugawa shogunate, accusing the Dutch of abusing and exploiting Japanese merchants in Taiwan. Dutch officials assumed the shogunate would arrest Hamada as a criminal and swiftly release the hostage.

Instead, the opposite happened.

The Tokugawa government had already grown wary of the expanding influence of the Dutch in East Asian waters. When Hamada arrived with a living witness and extensive testimony, shogunate officials reacted with outrage. They concluded that Dutch authorities had indeed mistreated Japanese traders and refused to release Nuyts immediately.

Suddenly, the balance of power shifted.

The mighty Dutch East India Company found itself forced into the uncomfortable position of negotiating from weakness. Envoys were dispatched to Japan. Years of diplomatic discussions followed. Dutch representatives struggled to explain their actions and repair relations with the shogunate.

Meanwhile, Pieter Nuyts remained under effective house arrest, becoming perhaps the most unfortunate pawn in a geopolitical struggle stretching across the seas of East Asia.

Eventually, under sustained pressure from the shogunate, the Dutch East India Company agreed to significant concessions. Nuyts was finally released, but his political career never recovered. Once one of the most powerful men in colonial Taiwan, he returned home disgraced and was severely punished by his own company.

Hamada Yahee, meanwhile, entered Japanese legend.

At a time when European powers were beginning to dominate Asia with cannon fire and global trade networks, most local rulers and merchants had little choice but to accommodate Dutch demands. Yet Hamada accomplished something almost unimaginable. With a handful of ships and armed retainers, he marched into the center of a colonial government and carried off its highest official.

The incident dealt a serious blow to Dutch prestige in East Asia and reminded the Tokugawa shogunate of its own influence in regional trade.

More importantly, it revealed a pattern that would repeat itself again and again throughout history.

Taiwan may have appeared to be only a small island in the seas of East Asia. Yet whenever the interests of great powers converged upon its shores, it became one of the first places where storms began to form.

And just over three decades after the Hamada Yahee Incident, another maritime leader would arrive from the coast of China with tens of thousands of soldiers, forever changing Taiwan's destiny.

His name was Koxinga.
Volumes.volume.seaAndFortress.heTingbinMap.descr:
In history, some people build dynasties with their own hands.

Some lead armies across continents to conquer land.

And some change the fate of entire islands with nothing more than a map.

He Tingbin was one of the latter.

In the mid-seventeenth century, Taiwan appeared outwardly stable.

Fort Zeelandia rose above the coastline, its walls bearing the flag of the Dutch East India Company. Merchant ships from China, Japan, and Southeast Asia entered and left its harbor in a constant rhythm. Deer hides, sugar, and silk flowed outward into the global trading system.

But behind this prosperity, the Dutch relied heavily on the Han population.

Agriculture, commerce, translation, logistics—almost every essential function of the colony depended on migrants from the Fujian coast.

He Tingbin was one of the most successful among them.

He spoke both Chinese and Dutch, understood the machinery of colonial administration, and knew the geography of Taiwan’s ports and waterways better than most Europeans. Through skill and adaptation, he rose into a trusted position within the colonial system.

For a time, his future seemed secure.

But a sudden rupture changed everything.

The exact cause is still debated.

Some say it was a dispute over commercial interests.

Some say it was suspicion and political infighting within the Dutch administration.

Others believe mistrust had been growing for years beneath the surface.

Whatever the cause, the outcome was the same.

He Tingbin lost trust in the Dutch.

And the Dutch lost trust in him.

In the end, the man who once served the colonial administration made a decisive turn.

He chose to defect to Koxinga.

At that time, Koxinga was facing his greatest crisis.

The Qing armies were advancing relentlessly.

Coastal strongholds were falling one after another.

Resistance forces in Fujian and Guangdong were collapsing.

Although Koxinga still commanded a powerful naval fleet, his strategic position was deteriorating rapidly.

He needed a new base.

A place from which he could continue his struggle to restore the Ming.

And then He Tingbin appeared.

According to historical accounts, he arrived in Xiamen carrying something far more valuable than gold.

A map of Taiwan.

But the true value was not the map itself.

It was what the map revealed.

He Tingbin explained that Dutch control of Taiwan depended on a small number of key forts and ports. But this defensive system had one critical vulnerability.

Luerhmen.

The Dutch believed the shallow waters and shifting channels of Luerhmen were impassable for large fleets. As a result, they had left the area lightly defended.

But He Tingbin knew otherwise.

Having spent years trading along Taiwan’s coast, he understood the tides, depths, and seasonal changes of the waterways. Under the right conditions, he argued, a large naval force could pass through Luerhmen and emerge directly behind Dutch defenses.

Straight into the heart of their weakest point.

The information changed everything.

For years, Koxinga had searched for a viable foothold across the sea.

Now, a path suddenly opened before him.

In the spring of 1661, hundreds of warships departed from Kinmen and Xiamen.

Tens of thousands of soldiers boarded the fleet.

Sails filled the horizon like a moving storm across the sea.

It was one of the largest amphibious expeditions in East Asian history.

When the fleet reached Taiwan’s offshore waters, events unfolded exactly as He Tingbin had described.

Koxinga’s forces successfully navigated the Luerhmen passage.

They emerged behind Dutch defensive lines.

When news reached Fort Zeelandia, many Dutch officials refused to believe it at first.

An enemy fleet had appeared where it should not have been possible.

What followed is well known.

Provintia fell.

Fort Zeelandia was besieged.

After nine months of siege and resistance, Governor Frederick Coyett finally surrendered.

Dutch rule over Taiwan—lasting thirty-eight years—came to an end.

And the Kingdom of Tungning was born.

Later generations debated the reasons for Koxinga’s victory.

Some emphasized his military brilliance.

Some praised the discipline of his troops.

Some attributed it to the broader tide of history.

But none of these explanations can fully exclude the role of He Tingbin.

Because before the armies crossed the sea, before the siege began, before the cannons fired, it was a man from within the colonial system who revealed its most fragile point.

Empires do not always fall when walls break.

Sometimes they fall when someone who once believed in the system decides to walk away from it.

And the map he carried away with him did not merely show a coastline.

It opened the door to a new dynasty.
Volumes.volume.seaAndFortress.heTingbinMap.title: A Map That Changed a Dynasty
Volumes.volume.seaAndFortress.indigenousEncounte:
Before the colossus of the Age of Sail crashed through Formosa's pristine coastlines, this emerald island had already thrived for millennia as a sprawling, vibrant, and entirely self-contained ancient cosmos. From the majestic heights of the Central Mountain Range to the expansive western plains and the jagged, sun-drenched reefs of the Pacific coast, countless Austronesian tribes called this island home. These original masters of the land, categorized by later historians as the Plain Tribes and Mountain Tribes, were by no means the isolated, primitive savages depicted in the early logs of Western colonizers. Instead, they had engineered highly complex, sophisticated social structures and spiritual worldviews perfectly calibrated to harmonious coexistence with the natural world. In their cosmic understanding, every mountain, river, and ancient forest was shielded by omnipresent animistic deities and ancestral spirits (Utux or Anito). Moving to the rhythmic cadences of seasonal monsoons and oceanic tides, they wove an extraordinary, unwritten tapestry of human civilization through song, tattoo, and sacred ritual.

The political architecture of this Formosan Austronesian world was guided by an incredibly wise localized governance system, defined primarily by elder councils and matrilineal kinship structures. Across the plains of southern and central Taiwan, in powerful Plain Tribe communities like Sinkan and Mattauw, familial authority and the inheritance of property were held exclusively by women, with men entering the bride's household through matrilocal marriage. Conversely, public administration and territorial defense outside the household were orchestrated by a highly disciplined age-grade organization (Age Organization) for males. Young boys were gathered and raised in the Kuwa (the communal youth longhouses), where they endured brutal endurance run training, hunting mastery, and martial conditioning. When the elder council—the collective governing mind of the village—sounded the alarm, these fleet-footed young warriors, capable of outrunning the swiftest deer through the tall grass, wielded their iron spears and bows to defend the community's ancestral hunting territories to their last breath.

Beyond the sovereign independence of individual villages, the fertile central plains of the island nurtured a fascinating, rare cross-tribal confederation known to history as the Kingdom of Middag (大肚王國). Championed by a coalition of over ten distinct Plain Tribes, including the Papora, the Babuza, and the Pazeh, the supreme ruler of this realm—King Middag—was not merely a hereditary political sovereign, but the absolute high priest of the confederation's collective soul. Unlike Western monarchs or imperial Chinese emperors, King Middag possessed no standing army of suppression or sweeping bureaucracy. His authority flowed purely from his role as an impartial arbiter of territorial disputes among clans, and his spiritual charisma in conducting sacred rainmaking and ancestral rites. At its zenith, even the formidable Han maritime smugglers and pirates operating along the Lukang and Dadu River basins routinely paid tribute to King Middag to secure safe passage and trading rights, showcasing the sophisticated diplomacy and regional integration achieved by the indigenous peoples long before foreign empires arrived.

Yet, the arrival of the global Age of Sail shattered this ancient indigenous universe with sudden, violent irreversibility. As the heavy artillery of the Dutch East India Company rose over the southern sandbars of Tayouan, the calculated logic of global mercantilism aggressively penetrated the everyday rhythm of the villages. Discovering an almost infinite population of Formosan sika deer roaming the interior, the VOC initiated a frantic, predatory "deer hide trade." Utilizing cheap cotton cloth, glass beads, and raw iron implements, Western merchants induced the tribes to abandon their sustainable, traditional rhythms of seasonal hunting in favor of relentless commercial slaughter. Within a few short decades, hundreds of thousands of deer skins were loaded annually onto massive European galleons bound for Nagasaki and Amsterdam. The harmonious ecosystem of the forests was comprehensively devastated, and the original masters of the island were insidiously downgraded from the sovereign owners of the soil to mere "labor harvesters" at the absolute bottom of a global capitalist supply chain.

What followed was a profound, systematic cleansing of the indigenous soul and identity. Armed with European scriptures, Calvinist missionaries marched into the sacred communal longhouses, denouncing the tribal Inibs (female shamans) and ancient ancestral worship as demonic heresies, forcing communities to demolish their ancestral shrines in favor of the Christian God. Under the dual terrors of military intimidation and rampant European smallpox, ancient tribes one by one lowered their battle lances and submitted to the humiliating rituals of the Landdag (District Diets), receiving symbolic silver-headed canes from the Dutch Governor as a token of absolute fealty. Pinioned between advanced firearms, lethal foreign pathogens, and the religious crucifix, the social fabric of the indigenous world fractured into complete collapse. Today, when we recount the epic maritime histories of this era, we must never silence the memories of the island's first masters, who bled, lost their ancestral lands, and saw their gods erased in the clamor of empire. Their deep tragedy remains the unforgettable, solemn undertone of Taiwan's history.
Volumes.volume.seaAndFortress.koxingaSiege.descr:
On the pale morning of April 30, 1661, as the heavy mists over the Tayouan sea slowly dissolved in the dawn light, the Dutch garrison standing watch upon the battlements of Fort Zeelandia witnessed the most breathtaking and terrifying spectacle of their lives. Across the distant horizon, the turbulent waves of the Taiwan Strait churned beneath hundreds of massive Chinese warships. Their bows were carved into ferocious dragon heads, and their rigging fluttered with the crimson banners of the "Prince of Yanping." It was an elite vanguard of twenty-five thousand ironclad warriors, commanded by the legendary warlord Zheng Koxinga. Facing near-total defeat on the mainland by the advancing armies of the Qing Dynasty, Koxinga had turned his calculated gaze across the strait to this beautiful island, which had been governed by the Dutch East India Company (VOC) for thirty-eight years. This was far more than a routine campaign for territory; it was a titanic, nine-month clash between two entirely different maritime civilizations, military structures, and geopolitical ambitions, known to history as the Siege of Fort Zeelandia.

From its very inception, this epic siege manifested a high-stakes chess match of tactical maneuvers. Although the Dutch Governor of Taiwan, Frederick Coyett, had warned the distant headquarters in Batavia for over a year of a potential assault by Koxinga, the European garrison inside the forts was caught completely unprepared when the thunderous roar of artillery erupted across the plains. Utilizing local Han Chinese guides, Koxinga’s fleet exploited a spring tide to precisely navigate the shallow, treacherous Luermen channels—a waterway the Dutch had deemed utterly impassable for heavy warships. Landing swiftly, the Ming loyalist forces severed the vital communications and supply lines between the coastal stronghold of Fort Zeelandia and the inland redoubt of Fort Provintia. Within days, starved of water, the Dutch garrison at Provintia capitulated. Control of the entire island shifted in a heartbeat, leaving Fort Zeelandia isolated on its lonely sandbar, like a battered ship in a raging ocean, desperately resisting the overwhelming tides of the Han army.

Confronting the towering, masterfully engineered brick bastions of Fort Zeelandia—designed with the latest Renaissance star-fort architecture—Koxinga’s forces encountered an unprecedented wall of fierce, calculated resistance. In the opening phase of the siege, the Ming loyalist army launched a devastating, full-scale frontal assault, attempting to breach the stone curtains through sheer mass of infantry waves. However, the Dutch brilliantly exploited the overlapping fields of fire created by their star-shaped bastions, pushing their advanced European artillery and matchlock muskets to their absolute lethal limits. Though the Han warriors fought with fanatical bravery under heavy armor, they were cut down in rows within the interlocking crossfire, staining the sandbars beneath the fortress a deep crimson. This catastrophic failure forced Koxinga to a sobering realization: this Western citadel was nothing like the earthen city walls of mainland China, and direct assaults would yield only pointless butchery. Pivoting his strategy, the Prince ordered the construction of miles of siege trenches and deployed his fleet to lock down the harbor, resolving to conquer the heretics through the slow, agonizing crucible of starvation.

The ensuing nine-month standoff devolved into a grueling war of attrition that pushed the psychological and physical endurance of both armies to their absolute limits. Within the stone walls of the fortress, provisions dwindled to nothing, and virulent outbreaks of smallpox and scurvy swept through the humid, suffocating quarters. Every single day, European soldiers perished in delirium and high fevers, leaving Governor Coyett to pen heart-wrenching indictments of hunger and death in his official logs. Outside the walls, Koxinga’s forces faced an equally desperate crisis of starvation, forcing his troops to disperse across the island in a frantic bid to cultivate wild lands, which triggered bloody, localized skirmishes with hostile indigenous tribes. Just as both sides teetered on the precipice of total collapse, a long-awaited relief fleet from Batavia finally arrived in August. A dramatic naval showdown erupted in the Anping waters, where Koxinga’s nimble junk navy, utilizing superior numbers and devastating fireship tactics, incinerated the Dutch flagships, permanently shattering Coyett’s grand dream of imperial rescue.

The hand of destiny turned irrevocably in January 1662. A Germanic mercenary sergeant named Radis, deeply embittered by his treatment inside the Dutch ranks, defected to the Ming loyalist camp under the cover of night. He revealed a fatal vulnerability to Koxinga: the isolated Utrecht Redoubt, perched upon a hilltop overlooking the rear of the fortress, was the definitive key to the entire complex; its capture would allow artillery to rain down directly into the inner court of Fort Zeelandia. Seizing this intelligence, Koxinga consolidated his heaviest artillery and unleashed a relentless, apocalyptic two-day bombardment upon the small ridge. When the Utrecht Redoubt dissolved into a heap of smoking rubble and the crimson banners of the Ming were hoisted over its ruins, the inner chambers of Fort Zeelandia lay completely exposed to Chinese fire. Recognizing that all hope had evaporated, Governor Coyett signed an honorable instrument of surrender on February 1, 1662. The Dutch surrendered the fortress and its vast treasures, departing by ship with the remnants of their pride. The conclusion of this legendary siege not only terminated thirty-eight years of Dutch colonial rule on Formosa, but violently thrust Taiwan into a brand-new era of Chinese governance, forever frozen in the annals of history as one of the most magnificent chapters of Asia’s maritime past.
Volumes.volume.seaAndFortress.koxingaSiege.title: The Siege of Fort Zeelandia
Volumes.volume.seaAndFortress.mattauWar.descript:
In the early seventeenth century, the southwestern plains of Taiwan were not a unified land ruled by any single state.

Before the arrival of the Dutch, this region was a mosaic of dozens of Indigenous communities. From present-day Tainan stretching northward toward the plains of Chiayi, the land was scattered with independent settlements of the Siraya people. Each village had its own leader, its own hunting grounds, its own alliances—and its own enemies.

There were no emperors, no royal courts, no central authority.

For these communities, land belonged to the ancestors, forests belonged to hunters, and any outsider who wished to enter this world had to first earn permission through negotiation, alliance, or force.

In 1624, after the Dutch East India Company established Fort Zeelandia in Anping, they quickly discovered a fundamental problem.

Despite their cannons, their fortifications, and their European military discipline, the world beyond the walls of the fortress did not belong to them. Dutch patrols were frequently attacked after leaving Anping. Soldiers and missionaries who ventured into the interior often disappeared without a trace.

To the Europeans, Fort Zeelandia was not the center of power—it was an isolated island surrounded by an unfamiliar and hostile land.

Among all the Indigenous villages, none troubled the Dutch more than Madou She.

Madou She, located in what is now Madou District in Tainan, was one of the most powerful Siraya settlements of the time. It was populous, agriculturally rich, and strategically positioned along key routes across the plains. Its warriors were known for their strength, and smaller villages in the region often fell under its influence.

For the Dutch, controlling Madou She was not just a military objective—it was the key to controlling the entire southwestern plain.

The conflict finally erupted in 1629.

That year, a Dutch armed patrol of more than sixty men departed from Fort Zeelandia on a routine mission. As they moved through the area near modern-day Wushantou, they were ambushed by Madou She warriors and their allied villages.

Arrows rained from the forest. Spears and blades struck from every direction. The Dutch column, unable to form ranks or mount an effective defense, collapsed into chaos almost immediately.

Within hours, the entire patrol was annihilated.

More than sixty Dutch soldiers were wiped out.

The defeat sent shockwaves through Fort Zeelandia.

Since their arrival in Taiwan, the Dutch had never suffered such a catastrophic loss. For the Dutch East India Company, this was not merely a battlefield failure—it was a direct challenge to colonial authority itself. If they failed to respond, every village on the plains would see them as vulnerable.

A war of retaliation began.

For six years, the Dutch prepared their response with increasing intensity.

The governor authorized a campaign of calculated brutality. The Dutch forged alliances with rival Indigenous villages, exploiting long-standing local tensions to fracture resistance from within. Firearms, artillery, and mercenary forces were brought into the interior in greater numbers than ever before.

What had begun as punishment evolved into a plan to permanently reshape the balance of power on the island.

In the winter of 1635, the decisive campaign began.

Hundreds of Dutch soldiers, supported by thousands of allied Indigenous warriors, advanced across the plains toward Madou She. The force moved like a storm gathering strength across the landscape.

When they arrived, the first volleys of gunfire broke the silence.

The Siraya warriors had never encountered such concentrated firepower. The thunder of muskets shattered the air. Smoke swallowed the village. Arrows and spears—once dominant tools of war—became ineffective against disciplined volleys of bullets.

Many warriors fell before they even reached the enemy lines.

What followed was not a battle, but a collapse.

Dutch troops advanced into the settlement, burning homes and destroying granaries. Any resistance was met with immediate execution. Flames consumed house after house. Screams mixed with gunfire as the village was reduced to ash and ruin.

By the time the fighting ended, Madou She had been destroyed.

The southwestern plains fell into silence.

One by one, surrounding villages sent emissaries to Fort Zeelandia. They brought deer hides, agricultural goods, and offerings of submission. Fear had become the dominant language of the region.

The Dutch used this moment to construct a new order.

Villages were required to pay tribute, submit disputes to Dutch judgment, and allow missionaries to enter Indigenous territories. In 1636, the Dutch convened the first major “regional assembly,” where dozens of Indigenous leaders gathered under colonial supervision to swear allegiance.

For the Dutch East India Company, this marked a turning point. They were no longer merely coastal traders—they had become rulers of a territorial colony.

But this order was never built on consent.

It was built on memory.

On burned houses. On shattered bodies. On the smoking ruins of Madou She.

Fear, not legitimacy, held the system together.

Years later, Dutch officials would look back on 1635 as a defining moment in their colonial expansion. It was the year they believed Taiwan’s western plains had finally been brought under control.

Yet they did not see what lay beneath that control.

Because any order built on force carries within it the certainty of its own undoing.

Twenty-six years later, when Koxinga appeared off the coast of Luerhmen with tens of thousands of soldiers, many of the villages that had once submitted to the Dutch did not choose to defend them.

The empire that once seemed unshakable collapsed with surprising speed.

And the fire that once consumed Madou She became the first great omen of Taiwan’s colonial age—an age defined not by permanence, but by the repeated rise and fall of powers that believed they had finally conquered the island.
Volumes.volume.seaAndFortress.mattauWar.title: The Madou She War
Volumes.volume.seaAndFortress.sinckanScript.desc:
In the early seventeenth century, the plains of Taiwan had no written language.

At least, not in the sense understood by the outside world.

For the Siraya people who lived there, language was alive—but it lived only in speech. They had stories, myths, and histories of their own. Elders gathered around night fires to recount how their ancestors survived great floods. Hunters passed down knowledge of forests and rivers to the young. Ritual specialists remembered the songs and prayers of every ceremony.

But all of it existed only in memory.

When the speaker died, part of history vanished with them.

In the 1630s, the Dutch arrived from a distant continent on the other side of the world.

For the Dutch East India Company, religion was never the primary mission. Trade and governance came first. Yet colonial officials soon discovered that ruling dozens of Indigenous communities required more than weapons and ships. They needed communication. They needed law. They needed contracts that could be understood beyond spoken negotiation.

And so, missionaries were sent to Sinckan village.

Sinckan—located in the heart of what is now the Tainan plains—was one of the most important Siraya settlements of the time. Its population was large, and its relationship with the Dutch was relatively cooperative. It became the center of early missionary activity.

At first, communication between the two worlds resembled an extended guessing game.

The missionaries pointed toward the sky and asked what it was called.

The Siraya responded.

They pointed at rivers, trees, birds, and the sun.

Day after day. Year after year.

Slowly, almost imperceptibly, something unprecedented began to take shape.

It was as if a writing system was being born from nothing.

The missionaries discovered that the Latin alphabet could be adapted to represent most of the sounds of the Siraya language. From this realization came dictionaries, catechisms, and teaching materials. Children were brought into mission schools, sitting on rough wooden benches, learning for the first time how to place their spoken language onto paper.

It was an extraordinary scene.

European letters—shaped by centuries of Old World history—were now being used to capture the voice of Taiwan’s Indigenous language.

At the time, few could have realized what was happening.

But this became the first large-scale written record of a native language in Taiwan’s history.

Soon, a small group of literate Siraya speakers emerged in Sinckan.

They learned to write their names on paper, to record transactions, and to read religious texts written in their own language. For many, it felt like a form of magic. What had once existed only in oral tradition could now survive across time, preserved in ink.

The Dutch were satisfied.

Literacy made governance easier. Written language created intermediaries between colonial authority and Indigenous society. It made administration more stable, more predictable, more controllable.

But history is rarely so obedient.

In 1662, Koxinga captured Fort Zeelandia and expelled the Dutch from Taiwan. Missionaries left the island. Churches fell silent. Schools disappeared. By all logic, the Sinckan script should have vanished alongside colonial rule.

It did not.

For more than a century after the Dutch departure, Siraya communities continued to use this writing system.

They wrote contracts in Sinckan script.

They recorded land transactions.

They documented debts and repayments.

They managed family inheritances.

In documents unreadable to Qing officials, they inscribed their language line by line, preserving a legal and cultural world of their own.

Even into the nineteenth century, such manuscripts continued to appear.

When historians later examined these faded pages, they found something astonishing.

The Dutch empire had long vanished from the island—but the writing system it introduced remained alive.

The alphabet no longer belonged to its creators.

It had become something else entirely.

It had become Siraya writing.

Today, we call it the Sinckan Manuscripts.

It is not only the earliest extensively preserved writing system of Taiwan’s Indigenous languages—it is also one of the most unusual survivals in the island’s history.

A group of European missionaries created a tool to translate an oral world into text.

And in the end, it was the very people once subjected to colonial rule who preserved it, expanded it, and carried it forward long after the empire that introduced it had disappeared.

Empires fade. Fortresses collapse. Governments change.

But sometimes, a page filled with borrowed letters outlives every power that ever tried to control it.
Volumes.volume.seaAndFortress.spanishNorthernTai:
In the pale dawn of 1626, as the Pacific monsoons swept across the northeastern cape of Formosa, several towering Spanish galleons flying the red-and-yellow imperial banners glided into the magnificent natural harbor known today as Keelung. Under the direct decrees of the Governor-General in Manila, these Catholic adventurers crossed the treacherous Luzon Strait to launch a forceful military landing on the island of Jilong (modern-day Heping Island). In the eyes of the Spaniards, this was far more than a routine voyage of discovery; it was a desperate, high-stakes geopolitical gambit engineered by Manila to counter the rapidly expanding global trade monopoly of the Dutch East India Company in southern Taiwan. The Spanish pioneers immediately constructed a massive redoubt of stone and heavy timber—Fort San Salvador—before extending their governing tentacles westward to Tamsui to erect Fort San Domingo. The cold steel and religious fervor of the Age of Sail had violently shattered the millennium-long slumber of northern Taiwan.

The strategic impetus behind this grand Spanish expedition northward was rooted in one of the most intense, blood-soaked rivalries of the colonial era. On the global oceans of the seventeenth century, the Protestant Dutch "Sea Beggars" were systematically cannibalizing the vast East Asian commercial networks that Spain and Portugal had painstakingly cultivated for over a century. When the Dutch firmly secured Fort Zeelandia at Tayouan in 1624, the golden maritime highway connecting Spanish Manila to Nagasaki, as well as the lucrative smuggling routes for Chinese silk along the Fujian coast, became directly exposed to the devastating cannon fire of VOC warships. Manila understood profoundly that if the red-haired heretics were permitted to hold exclusive dominion over Formosa, the commercial lifeblood of Spain's Far Eastern empire would be completely severed. Thus, Spain resolved to plant a formidable military and economic counter-bastion in northern Taiwan, intending to aggressively restructure their maritime empire.

In stark contrast to the highly bureaucratized and heavily institutionalized mercantile apparatus of the Dutch in the south, Spanish rule in northern Taiwan manifested a unique dual-track administrative model driven by a combination of military fortresses and evangelical fervor—the strategy of the cross and the musket. At the executive and military level, the successive Spanish governors dispatched to the north were tasked with the singular mission of defending Fort San Salvador while projecting martial intimidation over surrounding indigenous villages. However, because the central treasury in Manila was perennially bankrupt and consumed by relentless localized rebellions across Southeast Asia, the actual allocation of military provisions, bullion, and European soldiers to northern Taiwan remained severely restricted. Devoid of immense commercial capital or an expansive army, this isolated outpost suffered from crippling administrative stagnation, forcing the authorities to rely heavily on a different kind of power to sustain their grip on the frontier.

This spiritual vanguard was comprised of Catholic friars from the Dominican Order who landed alongside the garrison, driven by a passionate zeal for religious martyrdom. Clad in their distinctive black-and-white robes, these missionaries braved rampant tropical fevers, a hostile wilderness, and the fierce initial animosity of native tribes to venture deep into the plains of Keelung, Tamsui, and even into the hidden expanses of the Taipei Basin. The Dominicans demonstrated an extraordinary capacity for cultural adaptation, learning local dialects and compiling what became the world's very first comparative dictionaries between Spanish and Formosan indigenous languages, such as Basay. By erecting chapels and administering holy baptism across fragmented clans, these friars transformed themselves into the primary diplomatic bridge between the Spanish Crown and the indigenous populace. On countless occasions, a lone missionary wielding a crucifix and commanding the absolute trust of a village proved far more effective at pacifying the frontier than the cold, silent cannons lining the stone battlements of Fort San Salvador.

Yet, this ambitious colonial expansion directed from Manila was ultimately denied a permanent chapter in the history of the island. When the Tokugawa Shogunate of Japan enforced its draconian Sakoku (closed-country) edicts, completely outlawing the Catholic faith, Spain’s grand dream of utilizing northern Taiwan to force open the gates of Japanese commerce vanished overnight. Concurrently, Chinese merchant junks failed to arrive in Keelung in the anticipated volumes, saddleing both Fort San Salvador and Fort San Domingo with devastating annual fiscal deficits. By 1638, an emotionally and financially drained Governor-General in Manila resolved to execute a severe strategic contraction, ordering the deliberate demolition of Fort San Domingo in Tamsui and recalling the vast majority of Keelung's elite garrison and artillery back to the Philippines. This fatal order effectively crippled the northern defensive lines, reducing Spanish presence to a historical nadir.

Upon learning that the Spanish bastions had been left hollow and exposed, the Council of Tayouan in southern Taiwan moved without hesitation. In the sweltering midsummer of 1642, the Dutch Governor dispatched a powerful expeditionary fleet packed with frontline warships and hundreds of battle-hardened European soldiers to assault the north. A fierce, thunderous artillery duel erupted across the beaches and ridges of Heping Island. Though the remnants of the Spanish garrison inside Fort San Salvador fought with desperate bravery, they found themselves trapped in a hopeless material vacuum—starved of reinforcements, depleted of ammunition, and completely outgunned by superior Dutch weaponry. Left with no alternative, the garrison lowered the red-and-yellow imperial flag and opened the city gates in absolute capitulation. Spain's brief sixteen-year tenure in northern Taiwan reached its sudden, tragic end, vanishing into the ocean winds and the drifting smoke of Keelung.
Volumes.volume.silentIsland.coldWarAndUSAid.desc:
After the Korean War erupted in June 1950, the United States reversed the Truman administration's earlier position of strategic abandonment and reincorporated Taiwan into its Asia-Pacific anti-communist defense line. Within days, President Truman ordered the Seventh Fleet to neutralize the Taiwan Strait, simultaneously protecting the Chiang Kai-shek regime from a PLA invasion it could not have repelled and restraining KMT counter-attacks against the mainland. The 1954 Sino-American Mutual Defense Treaty institutionalized this commitment, stationing U.S. advisors, signals-intelligence facilities, and fighter squadrons on Taiwanese soil, and the massive American aid that accompanied it poured into Taiwan, stabilizing the embattled KMT regime and laying the foundation for Taiwan's economic development.

From 1951 to 1965, total U.S. economic assistance to Taiwan exceeded 1.5 billion dollars — roughly a hundred dollars per Taiwanese per year at a time when per-capita income hovered near 200 dollars. Aid arrived as wheat and cotton under Public Law 480, as rolled steel for infrastructure, as grants to rebuild the Taiwan Power Company, as scholarships that sent engineers to MIT and Purdue, and as counterpart-fund budgets that bankrolled everything from the Cross-Island Highway to agricultural extension stations. By the early 1960s, U.S. aid had underwritten more than a third of Taiwan's investment in industrial expansion and virtually all of its foreign-exchange reserves, allowing the regime to delay painful fiscal reforms while still funding its oversized military.

However, American aid was not a gift without strings. The U.S. deeply intervened in Taiwan's domestic and military decision-making — insisting on currency reform, land reform, the creation of a technocratic economic planning apparatus under K.Y. Yin and K.T. Li, and restraint from adventurism against the mainland — while packaging the Chiang Kai-shek regime as "Free China" to grant it legitimacy in the international community and a permanent UN Security Council seat that, increasingly, fewer states recognized as representative. The ROC's expulsion from the United Nations in October 1971, in favor of the PRC, and the U.S. establishment of diplomatic relations with Beijing on January 1, 1979 — these two diplomatic earthquakes fundamentally transformed Taiwan's international position, severing its formal standing with most of the world and throwing its domestic legitimacy into a crisis that accelerated both repression and reform.

This volume traces Taiwan's strategic role within the Cold War framework, from the economic impact of U.S. aid shipments unloaded at Keelung harbor to the Seventh Fleet's patrols of the strait, from "Free China" propaganda to the midnight UN vote that stripped Taipei of its seat, and from the difficult transition into diplomatic isolation — the unsigned Taiwan Relations Act, the severed embassies, the improvised substitute institutions — that paradoxically gave Taiwan the space, finally, to redefine itself on its own terms.
Volumes.volume.silentIsland.crossProvincialDemoc:
Amid the intensifying Cold War confrontation between the United States and the Soviet Union during the 1950s, Chiang Kai-shek’s regime, isolated in Taiwan after retreating from mainland China, upheld the slogan of “retaking the mainland” as the unquestionable supreme national policy. Yet as political realities gradually shifted by the end of the decade, a group of far-sighted intellectuals within Taiwan began attempting to challenge the one-party authoritarian system imposed under martial law. The 1960 “Lei Chen and Free China Magazine Case” became not only one of the most shocking political purges of Taiwan’s authoritarian era, but also the first tragic attempt in postwar Taiwanese history to forge a cross-ethnic democratic alliance between mainlander and native Taiwanese elites within the existing political framework.

At the center of this historical drama stood Lei Chen, a native of Zhejiang Province in China and once a trusted mainlander adviser within Chiang Kai-shek’s inner circle. Following the implementation of constitutional government under the Republic of China, Lei had served as a Minister without Portfolio in the Executive Yuan. After the Nationalist government relocated to Taiwan in 1949, Lei — with the support of liberal scholars such as Hu Shih and Hang Li-wu — founded the biweekly magazine Free China. Initially, the publication was intended to promote anti-communism, liberal democracy, and support for the Nationalist government.

However, as Chiang Kai-shek steadily consolidated authoritarian rule in Taiwan and imposed indefinite martial law, Lei Chen and the editorial circle surrounding Free China — including figures such as Yin Hai-kuang and Tai Tu-heng — underwent a profound intellectual transformation. They came to believe that without genuine constitutional democracy and institutional checks on power, anti-communism itself would merely become a justification for dictatorship. Gradually, Free China evolved into one of the few remaining platforms openly criticizing political abuses and advocating freedom of speech, judicial independence, and constitutional governance. When Chiang Kai-shek sought a controversial third presidential term through constitutional manipulation, the magazine published editorials sharply condemning the move.

What alarmed the Chiang regime even more was that Lei Chen sought to transform intellectual criticism into organized political action. Around 1960, Lei recognized that any democratic movement led solely by mainlander intellectuals would remain politically rootless unless it formed alliances with Taiwan’s native local elites. He therefore joined forces with influential Taiwanese political figures such as Kao Yu-shu, Lee Wan-chu, Kuo Yu-hsin, and Wu San-lien in an effort to establish a genuine opposition party capable of challenging Kuomintang rule: the “China Democratic Party.”

This alliance marked a historic breakthrough in postwar Taiwan’s deeply divided political landscape. Mainlander intellectual elites contributed constitutional arguments, legal theory, and national-level discourse, while native Taiwanese local leaders brought extensive grassroots electoral support. To the ruling one-party state, such a cross-ethnic and cross-class democratic coalition represented nothing less than a direct threat to political control itself. Inevitably, it drew the full attention of Taiwan’s intelligence apparatus and secret police.

On September 4, 1960, just days before the planned announcement of the China Democratic Party’s establishment, the authoritarian state moved decisively. Agents of the Taiwan Garrison Command raided Lei Chen’s residence in Taipei as well as the offices of Free China magazine. Lei Chen, editor Fu Cheng, manager Ma Chih-su, and several associates were arrested on the spot.

To destroy the nascent opposition movement completely, the authorities immediately banned Free China magazine and initiated sweeping military prosecutions under charges such as “sedition” and “failure to report communist activities.” During the subsequent secret military tribunal, despite widespread international concern and extensive rescue efforts by Hu Shih in the United States, the outcome had already been determined. Chiang Kai-shek personally ordered that “Lei Chen’s sentence must not be less than ten years.” The military court ultimately sentenced Lei Chen to ten years in prison, while Fu Cheng, Ma Chih-su, and others received severe punishments and political reeducation sentences.

The brutal suppression of the Lei Chen case effectively crushed Taiwan’s first postwar cross-ethnic opposition movement before it could fully emerge. Following Lei’s imprisonment, fear spread rapidly among Taiwan’s local political elites. Under the suffocating atmosphere created by the secret police state, the China Democratic Party collapsed before its formal founding, delaying Taiwan’s democratization process by nearly a quarter century.

Throughout his decade-long imprisonment, Lei Chen endured both psychological and physical torment, yet he consistently refused to surrender his principles. While incarcerated, he wrote a massive memoir reportedly totaling several million words, though prison authorities later confiscated and destroyed the manuscript. By the time he was released in 1970, he was already an elderly man with white hair, yet his commitment to constitutional reform and democratic governance remained unbroken.

Viewed through the broader sweep of history, the 1960 Lei Chen case was far more than a simple prosecution over published writings. It was a calculated and devastating assault by the authoritarian state against the possibility of cross-ethnic democratic cooperation. Today, the former detention facilities of the Taiwan Garrison Command have been transformed into Taiwan’s National Human Rights Museum, while the once-banned issues of Free China now survive as historical archives. Yet the ideals that Lei Chen and his allies ignited in the darkness of authoritarian rule — the pursuit of cross-ethnic political cooperation and genuine party politics — did not disappear with their suppression.

Two decades later, those same ideals directly inspired the Tangwai movement during the Kaohsiung Incident era, ultimately becoming one of the intellectual foundations that enabled Taiwan to abolish party bans and evolve into a pluralistic democratic society.

This painful chapter of history continues to remind later generations that the political freedoms, party alternation, and rule of law enjoyed in Taiwan today were not achieved without sacrifice. They were built upon the shared struggles of countless mainlander and native Taiwanese predecessors who, during decades of authoritarian darkness, risked their freedom together in order to secure a more democratic future for generations yet to come.
Volumes.volume.silentIsland.culturalControl.desc:
During the martial law era, cultural production in Taiwan was subject to tight state control exercised through an interlocking grid of institutions: the Taiwan Garrison Command's publication review boards, the Government Information Office's licensing of newspapers, the Ministry of Education's textbook committees, and the Chinese Cultural Renaissance Movement's directives on "healthy" literature and film. Publication censorship, book banning that eventually indexed over three thousand titles — including Lu Xun, Shen Congwen, Ba Jin, and any author suspected of "remaining on the mainland" — and press restrictions that capped the number of licensed newspapers at thirty-one from 1951 to 1988, curtailed the free circulation of speech and ideas to a degree comparable to contemporary Soviet bloc societies.

The Mandarin-only policy, enforced through fines on students who spoke Taiwanese in school corridors, through compulsory "Mandarin speaking" badges of shame hung around their necks, and through the gradual reduction of Taiwanese-language broadcasting to a single daily half-hour timeslot by the mid-1970s, suppressed the public use of Taiwanese, Hakka, and indigenous languages, creating deep cultural ruptures that would take generations to repair and whose consequences for inter-generational language transmission remain visible today in the declining fluency of younger Hakka and indigenous speakers.

Yet beneath this heavy-handed control, undercurrents surged in literature and the arts. The Nativist Literature Movement of the mid-1970s — driven by Chen Ying-chen, Wang Tuo, Yang Ching-chu, and Huang Chun-ming — challenged the official anti-communist literary line with local language and rural themes, depicting the daily lives of small-town merchants, fishermen, and factory workers in ways that implicitly indicted developmental inequalities. Modernist writers including Pai Hsien-yung, Wang Wen-hsing, and Chen Jo-hsi used metaphor, stream of consciousness, and symbolism to obliquely critique the authoritarian system, while cinema directors experimented within the censorship boundaries that would eventually loosen into the New Taiwan Cinema of Hou Hsiao-hsien and Edward Yang. The founding of the Free China Journal by Lei Chen and its forced closure in 1960 — when Lei was jailed for attempting to organize a new party with Taiwanese opposition figures — became an iconic episode in intellectuals' confrontation with authoritarianism, its last issue passing from hand to hand in mimeographed form long after the print run was confiscated.

This volume traces the mechanisms of cultural control during the martial law era alongside the undercurrent of literary and artistic resistance, presenting the voices that were never truly silenced during the age of silence — and reconstructing, through banned-book registers, newspaper suspension orders, private correspondence, and the coded language writers deployed to outfox the censors, the ways a generation of Taiwanese cultural producers kept imagination alive under conditions explicitly designed to extinguish it.
Volumes.volume.silentIsland.economicTransformati:
The land reforms of the 1950s — the 37.5％ rent reduction of 1949 that capped tenant rent at 37.5 percent of the annual main-crop yield, the release of public land originally seized from the Japanese sugar industry to cultivating tenants, and the Land-to-the-Tiller program of 1953 that compulsorily purchased landlord holdings in exchange for government bonds and shares in state enterprises — were among the most profoundly impactful socioeconomic policies in post-war Taiwan. Executed with U.S. technical advice and underwritten by the political reality that the KMT leadership had no local constituency among Taiwan's landowning class, these reforms dismantled the landlord system dating from the Japanese era, redirected agricultural surplus capital toward industrialization, and simultaneously weakened the economic and political power of the native Taiwanese landlord class in a way the regime could never have achieved on the mainland.

From the 1960s onward, under the technocratic leadership of K.Y. Yin, K.T. Li, and Sun Yun-suan, Taiwan shifted to an export-oriented industrialization strategy with currency devaluation, export-processing legislation, and aggressive pursuit of Japanese and American investment. The establishment of export processing zones at Kaohsiung (1966), Nantze (1969), and Taichung (1971) — the first of their kind in the developing world — concentrated bonded manufacturing in compact zones with streamlined customs clearance, drawing electronics assembly, garment production, and light-industrial subcontracting to Taiwan on a scale that absorbed the surplus labor released by mechanized agriculture. The flourishing of small and medium enterprises rooted in family networks, the densification of subcontracting chains, and an abundant, disciplined labor force willing to work extended shifts collectively drove the world-renowned "Taiwan Economic Miracle" in which per-capita income grew tenfold between 1960 and 1985.

By the 1970s, the Ten Major Construction Projects — including the North-South Freeway, Taichung Harbor, the Suao-Hualien Highway, the North-Link Railway, Taoyuan International Airport, China Steel, the CPC Petrochemical Complex, the Chiang Kai-shek International Airport, and the nuclear power program — further modernized Taiwan's infrastructure and signaled a shift to heavy industry and strategic autarky as the island confronted the 1973 oil shock and diplomatic isolation simultaneously. Yet the miracle had its shadows: long workdays, industrial accidents, environmental degradation, and the invisible costs borne by the young women recruited from farming villages into assembly-line dormitories on three-year contracts.

This volume examines this period of rapid economic growth, exploring the policy logic behind it, its social costs, and the complex relationship between economic development and political authoritarianism — a relationship that gave the regime the revenue base for its security apparatus while creating the urban middle class that would ultimately demand democratic reform.
Volumes.volume.silentIsland.indigenousElitePurge:
Beneath the shadow of Cold War confrontation and martial law in the mid-twentieth century, Taiwan’s authoritarian government launched sweeping campaigns to consolidate control over the island’s mountainous regions, natural resources, and indigenous communities. Determined to eliminate all potential local autonomy movements and prevent any perceived communist infiltration, the regime carried out systematic political purges across every level of society.

Among these crackdowns, the “Kao Yi-sheng and Tang Shou-jen Case” — also known as the “Alishan Indigenous Rebellion Case” — which unfolded between 1952 and 1954, stands as one of the most tragic and consequential chapters in modern Indigenous Taiwanese history. The case not only nearly annihilated the first generation of postwar Indigenous intellectuals and political leaders, but also violently extinguished the early seeds of Indigenous self-governance movements, forcing Taiwan’s mountain communities back under the suffocating surveillance of the party-state.

At the center of this historical tragedy stood Kao Yi-sheng, known in the Tsou language as Uongu Yatauyungana — a visionary Indigenous leader whose intellect and international outlook were extraordinary for his era.

Educated under Japanese colonial rule, Kao received elite modern training and graduated from Tainan Normal School. He was fluent in Russian, Japanese, Mandarin Chinese, and Tsou, and possessed remarkable literary and musical talent, composing several Tsou songs that remain cultural classics today.

After the war, the Nationalist government appointed Kao as the first township chief of Wufeng Township — today’s Alishan Township in Chiayi County. Kao understood clearly that if Taiwan’s Indigenous peoples were to survive the arrival of a new regime with dignity intact, they would need both economic independence and political autonomy.

To that end, he promoted the ambitious “New Highland Reclamation Project,” encouraging Indigenous communities to collectively relocate and cultivate lowland agricultural land. He also fought to ensure that revenues from Alishan forestry operations would remain within local communities to fund schools, healthcare, and infrastructure in Indigenous regions.

Standing beside Kao Yi-sheng was another prominent Tsou intellectual and former wartime officer: Tang Shou-jen, known in Tsou as Yabpasu Uyonguana.

Tang had graduated from Japanese military academies during the colonial era and served overseas during the Second World War, earning widespread respect for his military ability and leadership. After returning to Taiwan, he became deeply troubled by the poverty and political marginalization facing Indigenous communities under the new regime.

Together, Kao and Tang advocated an unprecedented idea for their time: “mountain autonomy.”

They envisioned a broad Indigenous alliance transcending tribal boundaries, one that would demand recognition of Indigenous land ownership over ancestral territories while pursuing genuine local self-government. Their political philosophy blended traditional Indigenous identity with modern ideas of citizenship, human rights, and democratic autonomy.

But within the rigid logic of Taiwan’s one-party authoritarian state, such ideas were viewed as dangerously subversive. Calls for Indigenous self-governance appeared to the regime as a challenge to centralized authority itself, drawing increasing suspicion from intelligence agencies and secret police.

As Cold War tensions intensified in the early 1950s, Chiang Kai-shek’s government expanded nationwide crackdowns against all organizations deemed politically unreliable. Around 1952, intelligence agencies intensified efforts to dismantle underground communist networks linked to the Taiwan Provincial Working Committee of the Chinese Communist Party.

During these investigations, authorities discovered that Tang Shou-jen had participated in local resistance activities during the February 28 Incident and had maintained contact with certain underground activists afterward. Although both Kao Yi-sheng and Tang Shou-jen later surrendered voluntarily and handed over weapons in hopes of protecting their communities from collective punishment, the state had already identified these Indigenous leaders — charismatic, armed, and respected among their people — as dangerous obstacles that had to be eliminated.

On September 10, 1952, the purge began.

Under the pretext of convening a “Mountain Security Conference,” intelligence agents lured Kao Yi-sheng, Tang Shou-jen, and several Indigenous local leaders down from the mountains to Chiayi. The moment they entered the meeting site, armed security agents emerged from hiding, forced them to the ground, and placed them in handcuffs.

Simultaneously, sweeping arrests spread throughout the Alishan region. Nearly all major Indigenous intellectuals and political figures of the postwar generation were detained, including Wang Ching-shan, Fang Yi-chung, the Atayal leader Lin Jui-chang, and Kao Tse-chao.

The arrested leaders were transferred to the notorious underground prisons of the Taiwan Garrison Command, where they endured endless interrogation and torture.

To legitimize the purge, the authorities accused them not only of conspiring to overthrow the government but also fabricated charges of embezzlement and theft of mountain development resources. The regime sought not merely to destroy them physically, but also to ruin their moral reputations within Indigenous society itself.

During more than a year of secret imprisonment and military trials, Kao Yi-sheng wrote dozens of letters to his wife and children from prison. Written partly in Japanese and partly in Tsou, these farewell letters contained no bitterness or hatred. Instead, they were filled with longing for the mountains of Alishan and concern for how his family would survive in poverty after his death.

In one letter, he wrote:

“One day my injustice will be understood. You must live on bravely, and bloom again in spring like the cherry blossoms of Alishan.”

But the dictatorship offered no path to survival.

At dawn on April 17, 1954, following military sentences personally approved by Chiang Kai-shek, Kao Yi-sheng, Tang Shou-jen, Lin Jui-chang, Wang Ching-shan, Fang Yi-chung, and Kao Tse-chao were executed by firing squad at the Ankeng execution grounds in Taipei.

Before the execution, the six men reportedly exchanged silent glances and stood upright with dignity as they faced the rifles.
