With the crack of gunfire echoing across the desolate morning field, an entire generation of Indigenous political, literary, military, and intellectual leadership was extinguished in a single moment. Their deaths marked the destruction of Taiwan’s first postwar Indigenous autonomy movement.

The terror unleashed by the arrests and executions quickly spread throughout Alishan and Indigenous communities across Taiwan.

Families of the accused were branded as relatives of “communist rebels.” Their property was confiscated, and many were forced into decades of poverty, surveillance, and social isolation. Fear spread through mountain villages where discussions of politics, Indigenous rights, or even cultural identity became dangerous taboos.

More devastating still, the state used the purge to expand direct control over Indigenous territories. Traditional land rights were stripped away, while assimilation campaigns such as the “National Language Movement” and “Life Improvement Campaigns” aggressively suppressed Indigenous languages, customs, and identity. For nearly three decades, Taiwan’s Indigenous communities endured a profound period of collective silence and cultural rupture.

Viewed through the broader lens of history, the Kao Yi-sheng and Tang Shou-jen Case was far more than a political miscarriage of justice. It represented a devastating assault by the authoritarian state against Indigenous identity, autonomy, and self-determination under the geopolitical pressures of the Cold War.

Today, the Ankeng execution grounds have disappeared into history, while the convictions against the six Indigenous leaders have finally been overturned and formally rehabilitated. Their historical significance has gradually been restored within Taiwan’s collective memory.

And when modern Taiwan listens once again to Song of Spring — the haunting melody Kao Yi-sheng composed while imprisoned — its sorrowful echoes still seem to drift through the valleys of Yushan and Alishan.

The song reminds later generations that Taiwan’s democracy and diversity were not built solely through the struggles of Han political elites. They were also forged through the blood, suffering, and sacrifice of Indigenous peoples who, in the darkest years of authoritarian rule, fought to defend the dignity of their lands, cultures, and right to self-governance.
Volumes.volume.silentIsland.institutionalIndepen:
In the early autumn of 1964, the nights in Taipei felt suffocatingly still, as if even the wind had vanished beneath the weight of fear. Taiwan at the time lay buried beneath the iron curtain of martial law. Across the island, walls and alleyways were plastered with grim anti-espionage slogans, while newspapers and radio stations endlessly broadcast the regime’s political mythology of “retaking the mainland.” It was an era in which even private conversations about politics could invite imprisonment — or worse, the destruction of one’s entire family.

Yet inside a modest faculty residence at National Taiwan University, one solitary lamp remained lit deep into the night. Beneath the rhythmic clatter of a typewriter, sounding almost like coded transmissions, three intellectuals sat gathered around a table, quietly attempting to shatter the suffocating silence of their age.

They were men with every prospect of prestige and comfort within the system itself: Peng Ming-min, then only forty-one years old, a Paris-trained Doctor of Law and the youngest chair in the history of NTU’s Department of Political Science; his gifted student Hsieh Tsung-min, then serving as a magazine editor; and Wei Ting-chao, a young research assistant at Academia Sinica’s Institute of Modern History.

Together, these teacher and students were risking the single gravest political crime imaginable under the regime — sedition and conspiracy against the state, punishable by death — as they secretly drafted a document titled A Declaration of Formosan Self-Salvation. Through reason and conscience, they sought to expose the political falsehoods that the party-state had maintained for fifteen years.

The intellectual roots of what would later become known as the Peng Ming-min Case emerged from the trio’s sober understanding of international reality. Since the Nationalist government’s retreat to Taiwan in 1949, the slogan of “recovering the mainland” had been treated as untouchable state doctrine. Yet Peng Ming-min, deeply familiar with the world of diplomacy and international law, understood that changing geopolitical realities had already rendered the dream politically impossible.

Night after night, the three men debated Taiwan’s future. Eventually they arrived at a radical conclusion for their time: Taiwan’s destiny could no longer be tied to the fantasy of reconquering China, nor could it remain trapped between the competing authoritarianisms of the Chinese Communist Party and the Kuomintang. Taiwan, they believed, had only one path left — self-salvation.

Drafted initially by Hsieh Tsung-min, revised by Wei Ting-chao, and finalized by Peng Ming-min, the declaration opened with words that struck like thunder:

“A powerful self-salvation movement is unfolding in Taiwan among people unwilling to submit to Communist rule and unwilling to be destroyed by Chiang Kai-shek.”

Unlike many overseas Taiwanese independence movements of the time, which often emphasized ethnic divisions between mainlanders and native Taiwanese, the declaration deliberately framed its arguments around civic nationalism, constitutionalism, human rights, and the rule of law. It asserted that “one China and one Taiwan” had already become an undeniable political reality, and it called upon all Taiwanese — regardless of provincial background — to unite in overthrowing the illegitimate regime, drafting a new constitution, and entering the United Nations under a new national identity.

Politically, the document was decades ahead of its era.

But within a Taipei saturated by informants and secret police, the plan to print ten thousand copies and distribute them by mail to influential figures across Taiwan was an almost impossible undertaking.

In mid-September 1964, Wei Ting-chao and Hsieh Tsung-min cautiously delivered the manuscript to a small printing shop in Taipei, taking elaborate steps to avoid surveillance. Fate, however, dealt the young intellectuals a devastating blow. As the printing workers watched the lead type emerge from the machines, phrases such as “overthrow the illegal regime” immediately filled them with terror. Fearing for their own safety, they secretly reported the matter to the Taiwan Garrison Command.

On September 20, 1964, the state struck with overwhelming force.

Security agents stormed the printing factory and confiscated all ten thousand copies of the declaration before a single one could be distributed. Hsieh Tsung-min and Wei Ting-chao were seized violently in the streets by plainclothes operatives, while that same night heavily armed agents surrounded the NTU faculty residences and forcibly arrested the soft-spoken Professor Peng Ming-min.

The three men were thrown into the notorious underground prisons of the Taiwan Garrison Command, where they endured endless interrogations, sleep deprivation, and brutal torture. The younger Hsieh and Wei suffered the harshest physical abuse, including electric shocks and forced water torture. During one interrogation, secret police agents beat out several of Wei Ting-chao’s front teeth, yet he continued trying to shoulder responsibility alone in order to protect the others.

As for Peng Ming-min — already an internationally respected legal scholar — intelligence officials alternated between threats and promises, pressuring him to sign confessions and statements of repentance. Yet before the military tribunal, Peng stood proudly and dismantled the charges with calm legal reasoning, insisting that democratization was the only path capable of saving Taiwan.

In April 1965, military prosecutors convicted the three men of preparing to overthrow the government. Hsieh Tsung-min received a ten-year prison sentence, while Peng Ming-min and Wei Ting-chao were each sentenced to eight years.

At first glance, the self-salvation movement appeared to have been crushed completely beneath the iron machinery of the authoritarian state. Yet Peng Ming-min’s arrest rapidly attracted international attention. American academics from numerous leading universities signed petitions demanding his release, while Amnesty International and foreign observers pressured Chiang Kai-shek’s government intensely. Concerned about preserving diplomatic legitimacy and continued American support, the regime took the extraordinary step of issuing a presidential pardon later that same year, releasing Peng from prison in November 1965.

But leaving prison did not mean freedom.

After his release, Peng was stripped of his academic position and placed under relentless surveillance. Dozens of plainclothes agents monitored his daily movements, effectively confining him under permanent house arrest.

His two students were far less fortunate. Though eventually released after reduced sentences, both would later be falsely implicated once again by security authorities following Peng Ming-min’s successful escape from Taiwan, leading to a second round of political imprisonment.

Living under suffocating surveillance, Peng eventually realized that remaining in Taiwan would almost certainly lead to his quiet disappearance at the hands of the regime. With the secret assistance of Japanese friends and foreign missionaries, plans were set in motion for a daring escape.

On January 2, 1970, taking advantage of slightly relaxed security during the New Year holiday, Peng disguised himself and used a forged Japanese passport to evade the intelligence services and board a flight bound for Japan. He later reached Sweden, where he obtained political asylum. The dramatic escape stunned Taiwan’s entire security establishment.

Though Peng Ming-min would remain in exile abroad for twenty-three years, the Declaration of Formosan Self-Salvation — never successfully distributed inside Taiwan in 1964 — nevertheless found wings of its own. Overseas Taiwanese students translated the document into English, and portions of it eventually reached international audiences through publications such as The New York Times, becoming one of the key texts through which the world came to understand Taiwan’s suppressed political aspirations.

Within Taiwan itself, the declaration’s ideas continued to flow underground like hidden magma beneath the island’s authoritarian surface. In the decades that followed, they nourished the rise of the Tangwai movement and became one of the indispensable intellectual foundations of Taiwan’s democratization.

Time has long since transformed the former underground prisons into today’s National Human Rights Museum, and the guilty verdicts against the three men have all been formally overturned. Yet when modern Taiwanese society looks back upon that grim autumn night in 1964, the sound of that late-night typewriter still seems to echo across history.

It reminds future generations that Taiwan’s democracy was never granted by those in power. It was illuminated instead by people like Peng Ming-min, Hsieh Tsung-min, and Wei Ting-chao — individuals willing to abandon comfort, status, and safety in order to sacrifice themselves for ideals larger than their own lives, leaving behind a beacon of courage and conscience for generations to come.
Volumes.volume.silentIsland.intellectualDisillus:
At the historical crossroads of the mid-twentieth century — as the Second World War had only just ended and the iron curtain of the Cold War rapidly descended across the globe — Taiwanese society experienced a devastating emotional rupture, moving from the euphoria of liberation from Japanese colonial rule to the profound disillusionment of the February 28 Incident. The “Chung Hao-tung and The Enlightenment Newspaper Case” of 1949–1950 became not only one of the earliest and most representative political purges of Taiwan’s White Terror era after the imposition of martial law, but also a tragic requiem for an entire generation of passionate intellectuals whose idealism led them toward destruction and martyrdom amid the chaos of a divided world.

At the center of this historical tragedy stood Chung Hao-tung — born Chung Ho-ming — principal of Keelung Senior High School and a man who had only recently returned to Taiwan from the anti-Japanese battlefronts of China. Witnessing the corruption of the postwar Nationalist government and the economic collapse unfolding across the island, Chung fell into profound despair. In that darkness, he gradually turned toward socialism, hoping to use words and ideas to illuminate a path of salvation for Taiwan.

Chung Hao-tung was born into a prominent Hakka family in Gaoshu, Pingtung, and was the half-brother of renowned Taiwanese writer Chung Li-ho. During the Japanese colonial era, he had already developed strong anti-colonial and nationalist convictions. As a young man, determined to resist Japanese imperialism, he and his wife Chiang Pi-yu — the adopted daughter of Taiwanese anti-Japanese pioneer Chiang Wei-shui — risked their lives by secretly crossing into mainland China to join the war against Japan.

Yet when Chung returned to Taiwan after the war and assumed leadership of Taiwan Provincial Keelung Senior High School, the reality that greeted him was one of devastation: rampant corruption, social collapse, and ultimately the 1947 February 28 Incident, which shattered much of Taiwan’s educated elite. The brutality of the massacre completely destroyed Chung’s remaining faith in the Nationalist government.

Like many progressive intellectuals of his generation, Chung underwent a profound ideological transformation amid the agony of realizing that reform within the system had become impossible. Eventually, he joined the Taiwan Provincial Working Committee of the Chinese Communist Party, believing that only revolutionary social transformation could overthrow the dictatorship unfolding before him.

In the summer of 1949, just before the full machinery of the White Terror descended upon Taiwan, Chung Hao-tung gathered a circle of progressive mainlander and Taiwanese teachers within Keelung Senior High School. In secret meetings held inside the principal’s residence and hidden mountain retreats, they began publishing an underground newspaper titled The Enlightenment.

Though modest in size and crudely printed, the paper carried essays analyzing international affairs, criticizing social injustice, and promoting socialist ideals. Beneath the tightening steel grip of martial law, the publication sought to awaken political consciousness among Taiwan’s younger generation.

To Chung Hao-tung, The Enlightenment was not an instrument of treason, but rather the final expression of intellectual conscience — an attempt to save ordinary people through truth and ideas.

Yet within a Taipei consumed by surveillance, informants, and political paranoia, these idealistic scholars failed to realize that the authoritarian state had already woven a vast invisible net around them.

The cruel turning point arrived in August 1949.

While investigating a separate student case involving alleged leftist sympathies at National Taiwan University, agents of the Bureau of Investigation unexpectedly discovered several copies of The Enlightenment. The underground publication, which directly challenged the foundations of authoritarian rule, immediately alarmed the highest levels of Chiang Kai-shek’s regime. Intelligence agencies were ordered to solve the case at all costs.

Following the trail of the newspaper, secret police eventually traced the network back to Keelung Senior High School.

Late one night in mid-August 1949, heavily armed security forces and intelligence agents surrounded the school campus and the principal’s residence. Chung Hao-tung, who had been revising manuscripts beneath a desk lamp, was arrested on the spot. What followed was a sweeping crackdown throughout the school. Teachers, students, and sympathizers were all rounded up. Overnight, a campus once known for its atmosphere of intellectual openness became a landscape of terror, false accusations, and political fear.

Chung was subsequently transferred to the infamous interrogation chambers of the Taiwan Garrison Command, where he endured nearly a year of psychological torment and relentless interrogation.

Because of Chung’s prestige within educational and intellectual circles, the authorities initially refrained from employing the most visibly brutal physical torture. Instead, intelligence officers attempted to persuade him into cooperation. They promised that if he signed a confession and identified other underground networks, he could regain his freedom and even continue serving as school principal.

But the scholar refused to betray his conscience.

Far from begging for mercy, Chung openly acknowledged his socialist beliefs before his interrogators. He insisted that pursuing a society free from exploitation and grounded in justice was the unavoidable historical responsibility of intellectuals. He steadfastly refused to betray his comrades or students.

When his wife Chiang Pi-yu was later interrogated by security agents, she reportedly declared proudly:

“For our ideals, we are willing to die.”

Such unwavering conviction shocked even the veteran interrogators accustomed to seeing prisoners collapse in fear.

Yet within the unforgiving ideological climate of the early Cold War, the authoritarian state had no room for idealists.

At dawn on October 14, 1950, following a secret military tribunal and final sentencing, Chung Hao-tung was condemned to death.

As he was escorted toward the Machangding execution grounds in Taipei, witnesses recalled that he remained calm and composed. Before leaving his cell, he nodded farewell one by one to his fellow prisoners. Then, as he walked down the prison corridor, he began singing The Wagon Song — a progressive song he had loved since his anti-Japanese days.

The solemn melody echoed hauntingly through the dark prison halls.

Moments later, a single gunshot rang out across the barren execution field of Machangding, ending the life of a thirty-five-year-old educator, intellectual, and idealist at the height of his maturity.

The execution of Chung Hao-tung and the destruction of the Keelung Senior High School network marked the bloody beginning of Taiwan’s full-scale White Terror in the 1950s. In the years that followed, the Nationalist government carried out devastating purges throughout schools, universities, cultural institutions, and intellectual circles across the island. Countless young people who dared to dream of social justice or criticize the regime were swallowed by the machinery of repression.

Viewed through the broader currents of history, the Chung Hao-tung and The Enlightenment case was far more than a simple espionage investigation. It represented the collective tragedy of a generation of Taiwanese intellectuals trapped between the geopolitical fractures of the twentieth century, desperately searching for a path forward for their homeland, only to descend into ideological disillusionment and historical catastrophe.

Today, the former execution grounds at Machangding have been transformed into the green expanses of Taipei’s Youth Park, while the convictions against Chung Hao-tung and many other White Terror victims have since been formally overturned.

Yet when contemporary Taiwan looks back upon this long-buried chapter of history, the melody of The Wagon Song still seems to echo faintly across time.

It reminds later generations that the freedoms of thought and expression enjoyed today were not freely given. They were purchased through the suffering and sacrifice of countless individuals who, driven by ideals that may have seemed naïve or impossible, nevertheless paid the ultimate price in pursuit of a more just world.
Volumes.volume.silentIsland.kinmenArtilleryBattl:
At 6:30 in the evening on August 23, 1958, the artillery emplacements along the Fujian coast opened fire simultaneously. Within two hours, more than fifty-seven thousand shells fell on the Kinmen archipelago — an area of less than 150 square kilometers — a density that led contemporary observers to describe it as the heaviest concentration of shellfire per unit of ground since the Second World War. The opening salvo struck Cuigu, the valley housing the Kinmen Defense Command, killing three deputy commanders — Chi Hsing-wen, Chao Chia-hsiang, and Chang Chieh — where they stood, and wounding Defense Minister Yu Ta-wei, who happened to be inspecting the front. Over the forty-four days that followed, what became known as the 823 Artillery Battle, or the Second Taiwan Strait Crisis, poured close to 470,000 shells onto the island.

Beijing's objective was never Kinmen alone. Blockading Liaoluo Bay, severing the supply line, and forcing a Nationalist withdrawal from the offshore islands were tactical aims. The deeper purpose was to probe the boundaries of the 1954 Sino-American Mutual Defense Treaty, which explicitly covered Taiwan and the Penghu Islands but remained deliberately vague about the islands hugging the mainland coast. What Beijing wanted to learn was precisely how far Washington would go for a few outcrops of granite.

The answer proved harder than expected. The U.S. Seventh Fleet escorted resupply convoys to the three-mile limit, allowing Nationalist landing craft to run the final stretch and unload directly onto the beaches of Liaoluo Bay under fire. On September 18, eight-inch self-propelled howitzers arrived on Kinmen, giving the defenders counter-battery reach and weight for the first time. Sidewinder air-to-air missiles arrived in the same period, and in late September Nationalist fighters used them to inflict lopsided losses in the air battles over the strait. By October 6, Peng Dehuai issued his "Message to Compatriots in Taiwan," announcing a seven-day suspension of the bombardment. What followed settled into something close to ritual: shelling on odd-numbered days, silence on even ones, with most of the shells packed not with explosive but with propaganda leaflets. This strange metronome ran for two full decades, stopping only on January 1, 1979 — the day the United States established diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China.

For Taiwan, however, the true price of the battle was written into the Dulles–Chiang joint communiqué of October 23 that same year. Secretary of State John Foster Dulles flew to Taipei and secured a public declaration from the Republic of China government that the recovery of the mainland would be pursued "principally through the implementation of Dr. Sun Yat-sen's Three Principles of the People, and not by the use of force." With that sentence, the possibility of an armed return to the mainland was formally surrendered in an international document. The slogan of recovery continued to be shouted daily, but it had been quietly demoted from a military plan to a domestic political necessity.

For the people of Kinmen, the years after the shelling were a different kind of long. The entire island was militarized under the Wartime Administration system: curfews, blackout regulations, compulsory civil defense units, permits required to enter or leave. Tunnels were cut inch by inch into the granite, and air-raid shelters spread beneath every village. On Taiwan proper, meanwhile, the reality of shellfire at the front became the most powerful argument martial law ever had. When shells were genuinely falling, the "Period of Mobilization for the Suppression of Communist Rebellion" ceased to be a legal abstraction, and any questioning of the party-state could be recast as destabilizing the rear.

Today Kinmen's tunnels are tourist attractions, and its shell casings are forged into kitchen knives that visitors carry back to the main island as souvenirs. But the valley at Cuigu, where three generals died in the first minute, and the twenty-year rhythm of odd days and even days, still testify to something particular about this island: here the Cold War was not an abstraction of geopolitics but the daily texture of an entire generation's life.
Volumes.volume.silentIsland.lukuIncident.descrip:
At one of the harshest moments of Cold War confrontation in the 1950s — while the smoke of the Chinese Civil War had not yet fully cleared — Taiwan’s authoritarian government launched the largest anti-communist purge of the martial law era in an effort to eradicate underground armed networks affiliated with the Chinese Communist Party. The “Luku Incident” of late 1952 became not only the largest military suppression campaign and mass arrest operation of Taiwan’s White Terror period, but also one of the bloodiest political tragedies to devastate ordinary rural communities, destroying countless farming and mining families who had little understanding of the ideological conflict consuming the island around them.

What began as a military operation against an underground communist base soon transformed into a sweeping political catastrophe that engulfed the mountainous regions of Taipei County — present-day New Taipei City — dragging an isolated and largely illiterate mountain village into the abyss of torture, wrongful imprisonment, and collective terror.

The origins of the tragedy lay in the post-February 28 expansion of the Taiwan Provincial Working Committee of the Chinese Communist Party. Following the 1947 uprising and massacre, underground communist networks gradually spread throughout Taiwan. Led by figures such as Tsai Hsiao-chien, the organization sought to coordinate with the broader strategy of “liberating Taiwan” promoted by the Chinese Communist Party on the mainland.

In the rugged mountains between Shiding, Xizhi, and Ruifang, organizers established a secret guerrilla base known as the “Taiwan People’s Armed Defense Force.” Hidden among tea plantations and mining settlements deep within the hills of Luku, the network attempted to recruit impoverished farmers, coal miners, and progressive intellectuals in preparation for a future communist invasion of Taiwan, hoping to create a local resistance force capable of cooperating with the People’s Liberation Army.

Yet the underground movement began collapsing rapidly after 1950, when Tsai Hsiao-chien himself was arrested and defected to the authorities. Over the next two years, intelligence agencies painstakingly traced surviving underground networks throughout Taiwan. Eventually, their attention focused upon Luku — one of the final remaining strongholds of the provincial communist organization.

Late on the night of December 28, 1952, beneath the freezing winds of the Taipei mountains, the government launched a massive operation code-named the “Luku Project.”

The Taiwan Garrison Command and Bureau of Investigation mobilized more than ten thousand personnel, including infantry divisions, military police, and intelligence agents. The entire mountain region surrounding Luku was sealed off under full military lockdown. Checkpoints were established along every mountain road, enforcing a strict “entry permitted, exit forbidden” policy while troops advanced inward through systematic search operations.

Against the overwhelming force of a modern army, the several dozen underground guerrilla members hiding within the mountains quickly collapsed under combat and pursuit. Some leaders escaped temporarily into exile, while others — including Chen Pen-chiang — were captured. Within only a few days, the armed base that the regime had portrayed as a grave threat to national survival was completely destroyed.

But the collapse of the guerrilla network did not satisfy the state’s fury.

What followed instead was an extraordinarily brutal expansion of repression against the civilian population.

Before military forces withdrew, intelligence agencies converted the local Luku Guanyin Temple into a temporary interrogation prison and detention camp. Hundreds of local villagers — farmers, miners, laborers, and even children barely in their teens — were rounded up indiscriminately simply for being suspected of carrying supplies, delivering food, or maintaining personal contact with underground members.

Many of these villagers were completely illiterate and possessed little understanding of communism itself.

Yet inside the darkened temple halls, they encountered unimaginable brutality.

Under relentless interrogation, Bureau of Investigation agents subjected detainees to electric shocks, water torture, suspension beatings, and savage physical abuse that left limbs permanently broken. Day and night, the sacred Buddhist halls became scenes of terror and agony. Unable to endure the torture, many villagers eventually pressed bloody fingerprints onto confessions and accusation lists already prepared in advance by the secret police.

The military tribunals that followed revealed the full extremity of authoritarian justice under Cold War paranoia.

More than two hundred people were ultimately prosecuted and sentenced in what became the largest armed suppression case of Taiwan’s White Terror era. Among them, thirty-five individuals — including local villagers and progressive intellectuals — were condemned to death and executed at Taipei’s Machangding execution grounds. Nearly one hundred others received life imprisonment or prison terms exceeding ten years. Some villagers, permanently disabled or mentally broken by torture, disappeared silently within prison walls.

The consequences for Luku itself were catastrophic.

After the purge, the once peaceful mountain village — formerly filled with tea harvests and miners’ songs — was left devastated. Many adult men had been executed or imprisoned. Fields fell abandoned. Women and children who survived were branded as “families of communist spies,” their property confiscated and their lives subjected to decades of surveillance, poverty, humiliation, and social isolation.

Viewed through the broader lens of history, the 1952 Luku Incident was not merely a successful counterinsurgency operation or anti-espionage campaign. It became one of the defining examples of how state violence during Taiwan’s White Terror inflicted collective trauma upon the island’s grassroots communities.

Through torture, mass arrests, and arbitrary military trials, the authoritarian state demonstrated to the entire population that martial law permitted no challenge to its authority.

Today, Luku Guanyin Temple has long since returned to religious tranquility, and memorial monuments now stand within the mountain region commemorating the victims. Among them is a steel sculpture symbolizing shattered bones and the distortion of history itself — a silent witness to the suffering endured there decades ago.

In recent years, many of the original convictions connected to the Luku Incident have been formally overturned following investigations by Taiwan’s government and Control Yuan.

Yet when modern Taiwanese society looks back upon the catastrophe that unfolded in those mountain villages more than seventy years ago, the scars of history remain painfully visible.

The tragedy serves as a solemn reminder that the rule of law and human rights now cherished in Taiwan were not achieved without sacrifice. Behind them lie the suffering, blood, and broken lives of countless ordinary people like the villagers of Luku — individuals crushed by the machinery of authoritarianism and the tragedies of their time, often without fully understanding why they had been condemned at all.
Volumes.volume.silentIsland.lukuIncident.title: The Luku Incident
Volumes.volume.silentIsland.martialLawGovernance:
During the martial law era, Taiwan's party-state-military trinity permeated every corner of society. The KMT controlled economic lifelines through party-owned enterprises such as Central Investment Holding, Central Trading and Development, the Broadcasting Corporation of China, and Central Motion Picture — conglomerates whose revenues funded party operations, patronage networks, and cadre training, and whose existence blurred every line between public policy and party interest. It monitored social dynamics through overlapping intelligence agencies that reported back to Chiang Ching-kuo in the 1950s and 1960s, and instilled party-state ideology through a centralized education system in which every classroom displayed the Generalissimo's portrait, every textbook framed Taiwan as a province of China, and every schoolchild recited the KMT-authored "National Anthem" before morning assembly.

The "perpetual parliament" — occupied indefinitely by representatives elected on the mainland in 1947 and frozen in place by a Council of Grand Justices' interpretation that suspended re-elections so long as the mainland was "unrecovered" — symbolized the hollowing out of democratic institutions. By the 1980s, many of these elderly legislators attended sessions in wheelchairs or sent proxies; some had been dead for years but remained on the roster while the party arranged their seats. The perpetual parliament was not a clerical oversight but a deliberate constitutional architecture that kept national-level representation permanently out of Taiwanese voters' reach.

Although local elections — for mayors, county magistrates, provincial assembly members, and township representatives — continued to be held, under strict party discipline, mobilized voter organizing via the Nationalist-affiliated farmers' associations and fishers' associations, and a dense patronage system that traded party nominations for loyalty and budget allocations, election outcomes were almost entirely controlled by the party machine. The Taiwan Provincial Assembly became one of the few forums where native Taiwanese elites — the so-called "five dragons and one phoenix" of the early assemblies — could publicly question the government, but its formal powers were narrow and its influence was extremely limited; even skilled legislators such as Kuo Yu-hsin or Li Wan-chu were ultimately contained within a system that could always override them.

This volume dissects the operational mechanisms of the martial law regime — from the Taiwan Garrison Command's seditious-publication review boards, overlapping intelligence organizations, and party-owned economic systems, to the Ministry of Education's ideological oversight and the KMT's rolling census of youth through its Salvation Corps youth-leadership program — revealing how authoritarian rule penetrated the very fabric of Taiwanese society, and how its institutional legacies continue to surface in debates over party assets, constitutional revision, and civic education well into the democratic era.
Volumes.volume.silentIsland.militaryInternalPurg:
In the turbulent historical crossroads of the 1950s Cold War escalation, after the Nationalist government retreated to Taiwan, Chiang Kai-shek’s regime moved swiftly to establish absolute personal authoritarian control over the island. Beyond the large-scale suppression of civilian dissent, the purge also turned inward toward the military itself. The 1955 “Sun Li-jen Coup Plot Case” — also known as the “Kuo Ting-liang Rebellion Case” — became not only the largest and highest-level military purge during Taiwan’s authoritarian era, but also a historical turning point in which the party-state dismantled potential American influence within Taiwan’s armed forces and transformed the military into a fully politicized instrument of personal and party rule.

At the center of this historical tragedy stood General Sun Li-jen, one of the most celebrated Chinese commanders of the Second World War. A graduate of the Virginia Military Institute in the United States, Sun earned international acclaim for leading Chinese Expeditionary Forces to major victories against Japan in the Burma Campaign, winning deep respect from Allied commanders and American political leaders alike. After the war, he became Commander-in-Chief of the Army and Commander of Taiwan Defense Command, where he established the Army Training Command in Fengshan and personally trained what became the most modernized elite force in postwar Taiwan.

Yet Sun Li-jen had also been deeply influenced by Western democratic ideals regarding civil-military relations. He firmly advocated for the “nationalization of the military,” insisting that the armed forces should serve the state rather than any political party or individual ruler. He strongly opposed Chiang Kai-shek and Chiang Ching-kuo’s efforts to impose the Political Warfare system and party apparatus throughout the military. His unwavering commitment to military professionalism — combined with his immense prestige in American eyes, which in some respects exceeded even Chiang Kai-shek’s — increasingly made the Chiang father and son view him as a dangerous political threat during a fragile period of consolidating power.

Following the signing of the Sino-American Mutual Defense Treaty in 1954, Chiang Kai-shek secured stronger backing from Washington and stabilized his rule over Taiwan. Rumors within diplomatic circles that the United States had once quietly considered replacing Chiang with Sun Li-jen gradually faded away. For Chiang Kai-shek, the moment had arrived to eliminate the powerful army commander who refused to submit fully to party control.

In May 1955, under the direction of Chiang Ching-kuo, Taiwan’s intelligence agencies launched a sweeping crackdown. They first arrested Major Kuo Ting-liang, one of Sun Li-jen’s closest subordinates, before expanding the purge to more than three hundred officers who had either been promoted by Sun or trained through the Fengshan military academy system. Secret police employed brutal torture methods to force Kuo into signing fabricated confessions alleging plans to launch an armed coup during a military parade in Pingtung, while accusing General Sun of serving as the hidden mastermind behind the so-called rebellion.

In August 1955, Chiang Kai-shek formally removed Sun Li-jen from his post as Senior Military Adviser to the Presidential Office. A secret “Nine-Man Investigation Committee” organized by the Ministry of National Defense then conducted a closed military tribunal. Although the regime ultimately refrained from executing Sun — partly out of concern for American reaction and Sun’s international reputation — he was placed under indefinite house arrest at his residence on Xiangshang Road in Taichung.

That confinement lasted for thirty-three years.

Only after Chiang Ching-kuo’s death in 1988 and Taiwan’s subsequent democratization was Sun finally released. By then, the once-renowned anti-Japanese war hero was already eighty-eight years old. Meanwhile, the more than three hundred implicated officers were subjected to unjust trials, severe prison sentences, or dismissal from service, effectively destroying an entire generation of Taiwanese military elites trained in modern American-style military doctrine.

Viewed through the broader lens of history, the 1955 Sun Li-jen case was far more than a simple miscarriage of military justice. It represented the decisive consolidation of authoritarian dictatorship within Taiwan. Through this purge, the Chiang regime eradicated the last liberal faction within the military that opposed party indoctrination and political warfare control, successfully transforming the national armed forces into a private instrument of the Chiang family and the Kuomintang state.

Thereafter, ideological control within the military intensified dramatically. Political indoctrination programs such as the Juguang political education system, alongside an extensive party supervision network, came to dominate military promotions, thought, and loyalty. Taiwan subsequently entered more than three decades in which intelligence agencies and political warfare officers exercised overwhelming control over the armed forces.

Today, the former residence of General Sun Li-jen in Taichung — now preserved as a memorial hall — still contains the roses personally planted by the general himself. In 2011, Taiwan’s Control Yuan formally exonerated Sun Li-jen and the officers implicated in the case after extensive historical investigation.

As contemporary Taiwanese society revisits this military tragedy, long obscured for half a century, the scars left by the purge continue to serve as a solemn historical warning. The story reminds later generations that the principles of military neutrality and constitutional democracy were not achieved without sacrifice. Behind them lie the blood, suffering, and shattered lives of men like Sun Li-jen and his subordinates — individuals who refused to surrender military honor and professional integrity before the machinery of personal dictatorship.
Volumes.volume.silentIsland.nineYearCompulsoryEd:
On June 27, 1967, at a memorial assembly in the Presidential Office, Chiang Kai-shek directed that compulsory education be extended from six years to nine. The instruction moved through the system with unusual speed: legislation was completed before the end of the year, the Statute for the Implementation of Nine-Year National Education was promulgated in January 1968, and the new system took effect at the start of the autumn term that same year. From announcement to operation took less than fifteen months.

At the heart of the reform was the abolition of the junior high school entrance examination. Until then, primary school graduates had to pass a fiercely competitive exam to continue, with pass rates hovering around fifty percent — which is to say that for nearly half of all children, education ended at the age of twelve. The new system converted junior middle schools into "national middle schools" and assigned every primary graduate a place without examination. The gate that had stood at age twelve was simply removed.

The administrative cost was staggering. Several hundred new middle schools had to be founded within a single year, thousands of classrooms built, and tens of thousands of teachers hired. The pace was such that many buildings were still unfinished shells when term began, and teaching posts were filled in bulk through short training courses and substitute appointments. The financing was improvised to match: entertainment taxes were raised, land tax surcharges increased, a dedicated education levy introduced, and the formula for distributing local education funds rewritten. It was a reform pushed through under simultaneous institutional and fiscal strain.

The effects, however, ran deep. Middle school enrollment rose from roughly half to over ninety percent within a decade, literacy climbed sharply, and the cohort that completed nine years of basic schooling entered the labor market precisely during the 1970s — the generation on the export processing zone assembly lines who could read a work instruction and learn a new machine. Discussions of Taiwan's economic takeoff return endlessly to institutions, American aid, and exchange rate policy; the broadening of education is often passed over, though it may be the least substitutable factor of them all.

The shadows are equally clear. Examination pressure did not disappear; it moved from age twelve to age fifteen, with the senior high entrance examination becoming the new bottleneck. Ability-based streaming was institutionalized within middle schools, and the so-called "cattle-herding classes" turned the decision of which children to give up on into an administrative procedure. Expanded compulsory schooling was also an expanded ideological channel: the curriculum intensified Chinese history and geography, the Three Principles of the People, and military training, portraits of the head of state hung in every classroom, and speaking a mother tongue still drew a penalty. Nine-year education kept more children in school, and it kept more children inside the party-state's story of itself.

This makes it one of the hardest policies of the authoritarian era to summarize in a single sentence. The same regime, in the same years, was both the perpetrator of the White Terror and the architect of universal basic education; and the schooling it built with its own hands eventually produced the generation that took to the streets in the 1980s to demand that it hand over power. Nine-year compulsory education is among the very few authoritarian-era policies that no one proposed reversing after democratization. History rarely sorts credit and blame into columns this cleanly — which is exactly why this case deserves to be remembered whole.
On August 25, 1968, Taipei Municipal Baseball Stadium was packed. On one side stood the Red Leaf Elementary School team from Yanping Township in Taitung County — a dozen or so Bunun children from a mountain village that did not yet have running water. On the other stood a visiting Kansai all-star youth team from Japan. The final score was seven to nothing.

The newspapers reported it as a victory over the world champions. Strictly speaking, it was not: the Kansai side was one of several Japanese schoolboy selections, not the winner of the Little League World Series. But in the Taiwan of 1968 nobody examined that detail too closely, and nobody wanted to. What the press circulated instead was a different set of images: bats whittled from bamboo, balls made of stones wrapped in cloth, boys batting barefoot on a gravel riverbed because there were no shoes. A team of indigenous children, poor to the point of absurdity, had beaten a side from the former colonial metropole. The story might have been designed for the emotional needs of the moment.

Red Leaf's victory ignited a national obsession that would last more than a decade. The following year the Golden Dragons traveled to Williamsport, Pennsylvania, and brought home the Little League World Series title. Through the 1970s Taiwanese teams won repeatedly at the Little League, Senior League, and Big League levels, several times taking all three in a single year. The games were played in the American daytime, which meant the small hours in Taiwan; an entire generation's childhood memory is of being shaken awake, gathered around a black-and-white television set, and then firecrackers going off across the whole village afterward.

The fever was never only about sport. Its timeline overlaps almost exactly with the darkest decade in Taiwan's diplomatic history: expulsion from the United Nations in 1971, the severing of relations with Japan in 1972, the American announcement of derecognition in 1978. As the state was struck from one international register after another, the flag of the Republic of China was raised in the stands at Williamsport and the national anthem played. The government understood exactly what that footage was worth. It promoted the slogan of "dignity and self-reliance" relentlessly, and cast these teenage players as vessels of national honor. Baseball became compensation — the one arena still available for winning in a decade when winning was impossible everywhere else.

The other half of the story took far longer to be told in full. Late in the same year as the famous victory, investigators found that several Red Leaf players had competed under other children's school registrations and were over the age limit; the coach and the principal were convicted. Most of these boys came from desperately poor Bunun communities, and when the brief moment of heroism passed, no institution caught them. Few continued in school or in the sport. They spent their adult lives in manual labor and poverty, and a striking number of them died young. That seven-to-nothing afternoon turned out to be the brightest and the shortest stretch of light in their lives.

Seen from today, Red Leaf is a monument to two things at once. It records how a suppressed society found an outlet in a ball game, and it records how skillfully the state converted the talent of a group of mountain children into the political language it needed — and how completely it declined to look back once it was done.
Red Leaf and the Baseball Fever
Volumes.volume.silentIsland.taiyuanIncident.desc:
February 8, 1970 — the third day of the Lunar New Year. Inside Taiyuan Reformatory Prison in Donghe Township, Taitung County, several hundred of Taiwan's political prisoners were being held, most of them young men serving heavy sentences handed down in the 1950s and 1960s for sedition or advocacy of Taiwanese independence. On that day, five of them — Cheng Chin-ho, Chan Tien-tseng, Hsieh Tung-jung, Chen Liang, and Chiang Ping-hsing — launched the only organized armed action ever attempted inside a prison in postwar Taiwan.

On paper the plan was complete: seize the guards' weapons, take control of the prison, then occupy the nearby radio station, broadcast across the island, declare Taiwanese independence, and call on mountain communities and Taiwanese conscripts in the armed forces to rise in support. They had spent months building the network, winning the acquiescence or active help of several Taiwanese guards. On the day itself, the five killed the guard sergeant Lung Jun-nien in the struggle — but the armory was never opened. Without weapons, every subsequent step lost its foundation.

The five fled into the Coastal Mountain Range. They had hoped to make contact with Amis communities and find shelter, but a large-scale military and police sweep of the mountains captured all of them within ten days. On May 30 of the same year, they were executed by firing squad at an execution ground on the outskirts of Taipei. A sixth man, Cheng Cheng-cheng, was judged to have been taken along under duress and escaped the death penalty, receiving a fixed prison term instead.

By military standards, the Taiyuan Incident did not succeed for a single minute. Yet it altered what followed on several levels. For the authorities, the action demonstrated that concentrating hundreds of political prisoners on the main island — where guards and inmates belonged to the same linguistic community — was an unacceptable risk. In 1972 the Ministry of National Defense built the Oasis Villa reformatory on Green Island and transferred political prisoners from across Taiwan to the offshore facility. The Taiyuan Incident is the direct reason Green Island became a synonym for political imprisonment.

In intellectual history, Taiyuan forms a pair with the 1964 Declaration of Formosan Self-Salvation written by Peng Ming-min and his students. The same proposition, argued two ways: one side chose text and persuasion within the system, the other chose weapons and the willingness to be destroyed. Both failed within days, and both remained unspeakable in public for decades afterward. And in that single year of 1970, Taiwan had Taiyuan at home and, in April, the attempted assassination of Chiang Ching-kuo by Peter Huang and Cheng Tzu-tsai on a New York street abroad — actors half a world apart reaching the same conclusion in the same year: that waiting would not bring change.

The site of Taiyuan Prison remains a correctional facility today, the mountains and coastline unchanged. Green Island has become a human rights memorial park, the names of the victims carved into its walls. The names of these five men were sealed in classified files for decades. Their action woke no one at the time, because no one was permitted to know it had happened. Only later did history fill the gap: that in an era when even private conversation could be fatal, there were still people who judged a single chance at a radio broadcast worth their lives.
Volumes.volume.silentIsland.whiteTerror.descript:
On May 20, 1949, the Taiwan Provincial Government declared martial law, initiating thirty-eight years of authoritarian rule that would bracket the island's post-war history and define the political reflexes of three generations. Within weeks of the declaration, the Taiwan Garrison Command assumed sweeping jurisdiction over civilians through military courts; a month later, the enactment of the "Statute for the Punishment of Sedition" and the "Statute for the Detection and Eradication of Communist Spies" provided the legal scaffolding that would justify four decades of extrajudicial detention, summary trial, and capital punishment, all under the legal framework of the "Period of National Mobilization for Suppression of Communist Rebellion."

Under this framework, the KMT government launched massive political purges targeting dissidents, leftist intellectuals, trade unionists, literary circles, returned overseas students, and even entire village associations caught up in manufactured "organizational cases," all under the pretext of "preventing communist infiltration." The intelligence architecture that carried out these purges was deliberately multi-headed and competitive: the Taiwan Garrison Command, the Investigation Bureau of the Ministry of Justice, the Political Warfare Department of the Military, and Chiang Ching-kuo's personal network in the Intelligence Bureau frequently investigated each other's informants and duplicated each other's files, producing a culture of mutual denunciation in which a careless letter, a classroom discussion, or a study group reading Lu Xun could escalate into a sedition indictment.

Beginning in the early 1950s, thousands of Taiwanese were arrested, tried, imprisoned, and even executed on charges of "espionage" and "sedition." Political prisons at Green Island, Jingmei, and Taiyuan became the most painful witnesses of this era. The Green Island concentration camp at its peak housed over two thousand political prisoners in stone barracks ringed by barbed wire; the Ma-chang-ting execution ground at Liuzhangli received truckloads of prisoners in the dawn hours of June 1950 during the single largest execution wave of the era. Many trials lacked due process, defense counsel was restricted or token, confessions were often extracted through torture, and verdicts were frequently returned within twenty-four hours of arraignment.

This volume presents how the White Terror systematically destroyed an entire generation of Taiwanese intellectuals and social activists through testimonies of political victims, military tribunal verdicts, the chilling rehabilitation certificates issued decades later by the Transitional Justice Commission, and recently declassified intelligence agency documents — and how its shadow, long after martial law itself was lifted, continued to shape family silences, career choices, and the structural asymmetries of Taiwan's democratic society.
Volumes.volume.silentIsland.whiteTerror.title: The White Terror
Volumes.volume.silentIsland.withdrawalFromUnited:
Late in the evening of October 25, 1971, the United Nations General Assembly voted on Resolution 2758, tabled by Albania and others. Beforehand, the United States had introduced an "important question" motion requiring a two-thirds majority to expel the Republic of China; it was defeated fifty-five to fifty-nine. Once that line broke, the outcome was settled. Foreign Minister Chow Shu-kai rose before the formal vote was completed to announce that the Republic of China was withdrawing from the United Nations, and the delegation walked out. The resolution passed seventy-six to thirty-five, recognizing the People's Republic of China as the sole legitimate representative of China at the UN.

When the news reached Taipei, Chiang Kai-shek issued a message to the nation containing the phrase that would define the decade: remain dignified and self-reliant, unshaken in the face of change, careful in counsel and decisive in action. The words were printed on textbooks, posters, and matchboxes, and became the official emotional register of the 1970s.

The dominoes fell quickly. In February 1972 Nixon visited Beijing and signed the Shanghai Communiqué. That September, Prime Minister Tanaka Kakuei established relations with the People's Republic and severed them with the Republic of China. Japan's reversal cut especially deep: it was among Taiwan's most important trading partners, and for many Taiwanese it was an inseparable part of their own life histories. The number of states maintaining diplomatic relations fell from more than sixty in 1970 to little over twenty by 1979.

The heaviest blow arrived in the pre-dawn hours of December 16, 1978, when Ambassador Leonard Unger woke Chiang Ching-kuo to inform him that President Carter would announce the establishment of relations with the People's Republic effective January 1, 1979, the severing of relations with the Republic of China, the termination of the Mutual Defense Treaty, and the withdrawal of American forces from Taiwan. The government suspended the supplementary national legislative elections then underway — a decision whose consequences far exceeded what anyone intended. The dangwai opposition, already mobilized and campaigning in the expectation of enlarging its foothold, abruptly lost the only legal arena it had, and its energy had nowhere to go but the street. Barely a year separated that suspension from the Kaohsiung Incident of December 1979.

In April 1979 the U.S. Congress passed the Taiwan Relations Act, preserving substantive relations and defensive arms sales through domestic legislation. The act would become the load-bearing pillar of the relationship for decades — but at the time it did little to soften the shock of having been set down by an ally.

Paradoxically, this sequence of diplomatic defeats loosened the most solid ideological foundation the regime possessed at home. Once the international community no longer accepted that Taipei represented all of China, the doctrine of legitimate succession lost its external support, and people began to ask: if we are not China, then what are we. The Diaoyutai protest movement of 1971 and the Nativist Literature debate of 1977 were both forms of that question being asked aloud. Chiang Ching-kuo read the same signal and began a policy of localization, drawing Taiwanese figures such as Lin Yang-kang and Lee Teng-hui into the core of the system — a personnel adjustment made to secure the regime that turned out to be the opening move in its transformation.

The decade in which the state was struck from the world's registers was also the decade in which its society first thought seriously about who it was.
Losing the Seat: The UN and the Diplomatic Dominoes
Volumes.volume.silentIsland.zhongliIncident.desc:
On November 19, 1977, Taiwan held local elections for five categories of public office. The race for Taoyuan county magistrate was unusually tense. Hsu Hsin-liang, a provincial assemblyman from the Kuomintang, had run without the party's nomination and been expelled for it; his opponent was the party's endorsed candidate, Ou Hsien-yu. It was a direct confrontation between a dangwai challenger and the ruling party — and everyone understood that what happened at the counting table often mattered more than what happened at the ballot box.

That morning, a disturbance broke out at polling station 213 at Zhongli Elementary School. A dentist named Chiu Yi-pin accused the supervising officer, school principal Fanchiang Hsin-lin, of spoiling a ballot with an ink-stained thumb while assisting an elderly illiterate couple, thereby invalidating it. Police escorted Fanchiang to the Zhongli precinct station, but the crowd read this as protection rather than investigation. Hundreds became thousands, and eventually more than ten thousand people surrounded the station.

After dark the situation broke down. Police vehicles were overturned and burned, the station itself was set alight, and police opened fire, killing a National Central University student, Chiang Wen-kuo, and a teenager, Chang Chih-ping. What was genuinely extraordinary, however, was what did not happen next. The army was not deployed. There were no mass arrests, no midnight raids of the kind martial law had accustomed people to expect. With an election in progress and international attention on the island, the authorities chose restraint. When the count was done, Hsu Hsin-liang had won the magistracy by roughly 220,000 votes to 130,000.

The weight of that day in postwar Taiwanese history lies not in the casualty figures but in a psychological threshold. Since the February 28 Incident and the White Terror, Taiwanese society had internalized an iron rule: to take to the street was to die. At Zhongli, tens of thousands of people tested that rule in person and found that, under at least some conditions, it did not hold. Once fear has been empirically checked, it never returns to its former height.

In the same election, dangwai candidates coordinated across county lines for the first time in an organized way, winning four magistracies and twenty-one provincial assembly seats and demonstrating an island-wide capacity for mobilization. Over the next two years that energy advanced along two tracks: the organizational structure built around Formosa Magazine, and the street. On December 10, 1979, the two converged in Kaohsiung. Many historians therefore read Zhongli as the rehearsal for the Kaohsiung Incident — not merely the step before it in time, but the first step in the same logic of action.

Hsu Hsin-liang himself did not walk the whole road. In 1979 he was suspended from office for supporting the Bridgehead demonstration on behalf of Yu Teng-fa and his son, and he spent more than a decade in exile. But the afternoon that began with a single spoiled ballot ultimately changed how an entire island understood the requirement that votes be counted in the open. The Taiwanese habit of standing outside a counting station watching each ballot held up to the light and to the cameras is not self-evident common sense. It was bought in the winter of 1977, in Zhongli, with two lives.
Volumes.volume.soundOfFormosa.campusFolk.campusF:
Beginning in the mid-1970s, a generation of college students, singer-songwriters, and campus musicians asked a deceptively simple question — "Why don't we sing our own songs?" — and set in motion a movement that would reshape the soundscape of Taiwan for the next two decades. Responding to a music market dominated by translated Japanese hits and licensed Western pop, figures such as Yang Hsien, Li Shuang-tse, Hu Teh-fu, and Lee Chien-fu began performing original Mandarin-language compositions in university auditoriums, folk cafés, and the living rooms of Taipei, blending acoustic guitar idioms drawn from American folk revival with Chinese lyrical sensibilities and a distinctly local student ethos.

The movement's cultural impact extended far beyond its campus origins. Independent labels such as New Formosa Records and Rock Records emerged to record and distribute this new music, professionalizing what had begun as an amateur movement and laying the commercial infrastructure that would support Taiwan's rise as the production capital of Mandarin-language pop. The Golden Melody Awards, established in 1990, institutionalized quality standards and critical recognition. Folk singers crossed over into mainstream pop — Jonathan Lee became one of Asia's most influential producers, while Teresa Teng's recordings conquered markets from Tokyo to Southeast Asia. By the mid-1980s, campus folk had evolved into a sophisticated Mandopop industry centered in Taipei, and the question 'Why don't we sing our own songs?' had been answered with a catalog that defined Chinese-language popular music for a generation.
Volumes.volume.soundOfFormosa.contemporary.conte:
From the lifting of martial law in 1987 onward, Taiwan's music industry entered a period of radical reopening. The New Taiwanese Song movement — led by Lin Chiang, whose 1990 debut 'Marching Forward' became an anthem of post-authoritarian exuberance, Chen Ming-chang, Chu Yueh-hsin, and later Wu Bai and Bobby Chen — brought Taiwanese-Hokkien back onto the main stage of popular music, no longer as a minor "local" idiom but as a vehicle for urban working-class feeling, political reflection, and rock'n'roll swagger. In parallel, the indigenous voices of Panai, Suming, and Matzka, and the Hakka songwriting of Lin Sheng-hsiang, staked out space for languages and communities long excluded from the mainstream.

The 1990s and 2000s marked a golden age for Mandopop under Rock Records, Magicstone, and the generation of Jay Chou, Stefanie Sun, and David Tao — artists who made Taipei the unrivaled center of Chinese-language popular music worldwide. Simultaneously, an indie ecosystem took root: venues like The Wall and Revolver hosted a flourishing underground scene, while festivals such as Spring Scream in Kenting and the Megaport Festival in Kaohsiung became annual pilgrimages for independent music fans. Today, younger artists such as Enno Cheng, 9m88, Sunset Rollercoaster, and No Party for Cao Dong navigate a multilingual ecosystem — Taiwanese-Hokkien, Mandarin, Hakka, indigenous languages, English — negotiating what it means to make music from Taiwan in a globalized streaming era where genre boundaries dissolve and audiences span the Pacific.
Volumes.volume.soundOfFormosa.hokkien.gramophone:
In the mid-1920s, the gramophone and the shellac record arrived in Taiwan along the commercial arteries of the Japanese empire. In the shop windows of trading firms in Taipei's Sakaechō and Dadaocheng, and along the wharves of Keelung, the phonograph gradually became a fashionable fixture in middle-class homes. The earliest locally recorded products were mostly excerpts of gezaixi, beiguan, and nanguan, produced to serve the existing market for traditional opera; yet the gramophone also carried into Taiwan the shidaiqu of Shanghai, the ryūkōka of Japan, and the rhythms of Western jazz, preparing the soil for a wholly new genre of "popular song" aimed at urban listeners.

In 1932, Shanghai Lianhua Film Company's silent picture Peach Blossoms Weeping Blood premiered at Taipei's Eiraku-za. To promote the film, the distributor commissioned lyrics from Zhan Tianma and a melody from Wang Yunfeng, and had the singer Chunchun (Liu Ching-hsiang) record a title song to be played through the streets as advertisement. Intended merely as an advertising tool, the song unexpectedly swept across Taiwan, posting astonishing record sales and demonstrating for the first time that a popular song "sung in Taiwanese-Hokkien and released on disc" could stand as an independent commercial product. Columbia Records (コロムビア) swiftly established a dedicated recording division in Taipei and signed lyricists and composers such as Lee Lin-chiu, Teng Yu-hsien, Chen Chun-yu, and Chou Tien-wang, along with singers including Chunchun, Ai-ai, and Lin Shih-hao — building Taiwan's first systematically integrated pop-music industry.

The years 1933 to 1936 were Columbia's golden quartet. Bāng Chhun-hong (Longing for the Spring Breeze) — composed by Teng Yu-hsien with lyrics by Lee Lin-chiu — wrapped colonial youth's longing for self-determined lives in the delicate feelings of a young woman's first love; Hō-iā-hoe (Rainy Night Flower) — with lyrics by Chou Tien-wang and music by Teng Yu-hsien — used a flower battered by wind and rain as a metaphor for the women at the bottom of society whom fate had crushed. Moon Night Sorrow, Four Seasons Red, and Riverside Spring Dream each captured, in turn, urban romance, festive life, and the nostalgia of displacement. These songs circulated through record shops, cafés, taverns, and radio stations, weaving together a shared aural memory for the urban middle class of mid-period Japanese-ruled Taiwan.

This volume chronicles the twelve critical years in which Taiwanese-Hokkien popular song was born from nothing: from the material conditions of the recording industry and the first hit song catalyzed by film advertising, to the complete lyricist-composer-singer-recording-distribution system built by Columbia. It shows how an entirely new form of mass art emerged in the interstices of colonial rule and, within only a few years, accumulated a songbook rich enough to be sung across generations. These songs would later face the successive fates of being banned, rewritten, banned again, and revived; but the musical vocabulary they established in the mid-1930s has permanently rewritten the way Taiwanese people hear their own voices.
Volumes.volume.soundOfFormosa.hokkien.wartimeVar:
In July 1937 the Marco Polo Bridge Incident broke out, pulling Japan into all-out war and sweeping colonial Taiwan into the same orbit of total mobilization. The Government-General launched the Kōminka campaign, abolishing the Chinese-language columns of newspapers, scrapping Chinese-language classes in the public schools, restricting gezaixi and glove-puppet theatre performances, and subjecting the record market to strict censorship. Releases of Taiwanese-Hokkien songs by Columbia, Victor, and Taihei collapsed; many pre-war works were placed on the list of banned songs for being "decadent" or "defeatist," and within only two years the nascent Taiwanese-Hokkien pop industry had nearly come to a standstill.

The demands of war, however, unexpectedly allowed some Taiwanese-Hokkien songs to survive in transfigured form. In 1938, Hō-iā-hoe, composed by Teng Yu-hsien, was given new Japanese lyrics by the songwriter Kurihara Hakuya and reworked into the martial song Homare no Gumpu (The Glorious Conscript Laborer), which was used to encourage Taiwanese youth to enlist; Bāng Chhun-hong was rewritten as Daichi wa Maneku (The Land Beckons) as a propaganda song for colonial settlement; Moon Night Sorrow was reshaped into The Conscript's Wife. The melodies of the original songs were thus preserved in the air, but the emotions they carried were completely replaced — a young woman's private longings became a loyal lament for a husband sent off to war. This predicament, in which "the tune survived while the lyrics were colonized," became the shared, voiceless condition of Taiwanese cultural workers in wartime.

Even as official release channels were blocked, underground listening life did not entirely die out. Old records were replayed endlessly in private homes; taverns and cafés played pre-war standards at low volume late at night; some lyricists turned to gezaixi discs, radio dramas, or children's singing games to avoid censorship. Teng Yu-hsien himself left the record industry in 1940 to take a post as a training officer at Hsinchu's Chiung-lin Public School, and died of illness in 1944 at the age of only thirty-eight. Lee Lin-chiu and Chou Tien-wang struggled on through the rationing and air raids of the late war years, hiding a batch of unreleased works in their desk drawers to await the light of the post-war world.

This volume records the dormancy and transfiguration of Taiwanese-Hokkien popular song during the war years: from the systematic suppression of the culture industry by Kōminka policies, to the strange fate of hit songs being rewritten as military anthems, to the figures of lyricists and composers who kept the spark of creation alive in silence. Although these eight years appear on the surface to be an "interruption" in the history of Taiwanese-Hokkien pop, they were in fact a period of enforced underground resilience — so that when the war ended in 1945 and the bans were loosened, the melodies that had been rewritten would resurface laden with even more complex emotions, becoming one of the keys by which the next generation would understand where it came from.
Volumes.volume.soundOfFormosa.postwarRevival.pos:
After 1945, Taiwan's music industry rebuilt itself amid political upheaval and a radically shifting linguistic landscape. The Nationalist government's cultural policies favored Mandarin as the national language, and state-controlled radio stations increasingly promoted Mandarin-language songs as the soundtrack of the 're-Sinicized' nation. Yet beneath this official current, Taiwanese-Hokkien music found ways to survive and even flourish — not through confrontation, but through quiet adaptation.

The cover song became the era's defining musical form. Japanese-era melodies — many of them already beloved across the island — were given new Taiwanese-Hokkien lyrics and released on shellac records, then later on vinyl, by small labels in Taipei and Kaohsiung catering to working-class audiences. This practice was partly pragmatic (reusing proven melodies reduced production costs) and partly subversive (keeping Taiwanese-language music alive under a regime that increasingly marginalized it). Singers such as Wen Hsia, who sold millions of records and starred in over a hundred Taiwanese-language films, and Hung I-feng, whose 'Longing for the Spring Breeze' became an unofficial anthem of nostalgia, defined a postwar Hokkien sound that blended Japanese enka's sentimental vocal style with local narratives of migration, factory labor, and homesickness.

By the 1960s, however, the Nationalist government's restrictions on Taiwanese-language broadcasting — limiting Hokkien and Hakka programming to a small fraction of airtime — began to squeeze the commercial viability of Taiwanese pop. The quiet revival that had sustained itself through dancehalls, night markets, and the portable transistor radio was slowly pushed to the margins, setting the stage for the Mandarin-dominated campus folk movement that would follow.
Volumes.volume.tungningDynasty.battleOfPenghu168:
In the sweltering midsummer of 1683, the winds over the Taiwan Strait violently shifted. This was the ultimate showdown that would decide the fate of Taiwan, a clash filled with profound irony—a duel between former brothers-in-arms. Standing atop the flagship of a massive 200-ship fleet was Admiral Shi Lang, entrusted by the Kangxi Emperor with the supreme command of the Qing navy.

Ready to defend the island’s final outer line of defense was Liu Guoxuan, the premier military commander of the Kingdom of Tungning. Decades earlier, these two men had fought side-by-side under the very same banner of Zheng Koxinga. However, Shi Lang had later crossed Koxinga, a rift that resulted in the brutal execution of his father and brother on the mainland. This blood feud burned within Shi Lang for thirty years. After decades of waiting in the shadows, he had finally returned to the black waters of the strait with the ironclad vessels of the Qing Empire, and the only man standing between him and his vengeance was his old comrade, Liu Guoxuan.

On July 10, 1683, these two master tacticians collided in the waters surrounding the Penghu archipelago. The battle raged fiercely around the main islands of Penghu, Cat Islet, Straw Islet, and the vital harbor of Magong. Knowing that the fall of Penghu meant the defenseless ruin of Taiwan, Liu Guoxuan had lined the islands with miles of fortified artillery batteries, adopting a strategy of fierce, entrenched defense.

Shi Lang, relying on his brilliant naval instincts, drove his flagship directly into the heart of the Zheng defenses. In the opening skirmishes, Liu Guoxuan utilized his intimate knowledge of the treacherous local currents to lure the Qing fleet into deadly whirlpools, nearly blinding Shi Lang in his right eye and inflicting heavy casualties. Yet, Shi Lang possessed a terrifying willpower; wrapped in bandages, he stayed on deck, calmly observing the unique tides and wind patterns of Penghu, waiting for the perfect moment to strike back.

The hand of destiny turned on the morning of July 16. A sudden, powerful southern breeze swept across the ocean, favoring the Qing fleet. Shi Lang seized this heavenly opportunity instantly, ordering a relentless, all-out assault. The Qing warships tore downwind, unleashing hundreds of advanced western cannons simultaneously.

For hours, the inner sea of Penghu roared with thunderous explosions, as smoke and fire transformed the azure water into a raging inferno. Wooden warships were blasted to splinters under the dense artillery barrages. Though Liu Guoxuan commanded desperately from his flagship, his fleet was overwhelmed by the shifting winds and the crushing firepower of the Qing navy. The elite maritime forces of the Zheng regime, meticulously trained over two decades, were utterly decimated, leaving the sea stained crimson.

Seeing that all was lost, Liu Guoxuan broke through the enemy lines under the cover of night, escaping back to the Anping headquarters in Tainan with only a handful of surviving vessels. The Battle of Penghu, one of the largest naval engagements of its era, ended in a decisive triumph for Shi Lang. The loss of Penghu completely stripped the Kingdom of Tungning of its strongest shield, leaving Tainan entirely exposed to the Qing blade.

This ultimate confrontation between former comrades not only allowed Shi Lang to avenge his family after thirty years, but it also sounded the death knell for the regime. Upon returning to Taiwan, a defeated Liu Guoxuan knew there was no hope for a reversal, and he ultimately persuaded the twelve-year-old puppet king to surrender, bringing a fiery end to the saga of Taiwan's first Han regime.
Volumes.volume.tungningDynasty.britishTaiwanComm:
In the summer of 1670, a majestic vessel named The Experiment, flying the flag of the English East India Company, glided gracefully into Anping Harbor in Tainan. At that moment, Taiwan was suffocating under the harsh maritime embargo of the Qing Empire’s "Great Clearance" policy, which had severed almost all supplies and trade revenues from the Chinese mainland.

Inside the Anping Royal Palace, the sovereign of Eastern Ning, Zheng Jing, knew his regime had reached a perilous crossroads. When he learned that these fair-haired, strangely attired European merchants had arrived with a desire for trade, he recognized that this was far more than a simple merchant deal.

It was a golden, desperate opportunity to shatter the Qing blockade and thrust his kingdom onto the global stage. Assisted by his brilliant adviser Chen Yonghua, Zheng Jing received the English representatives with a grand royal ceremony, launching a secret web of international diplomacy and maritime commerce in Tainan.

The negotiations unfolded in an atmosphere thick with calculated political maneuvering and sharp diplomatic wit. The English East India Company was desperate to establish a new base in East Asia, hoping to use Taiwan as a vital stepping stone to break into the lucrative Japanese and Chinese markets, which were then heavily monopolized by the Dutch and Spanish. Zheng Jing’s demands, however, were far more immediate and visceral—he needed the strategic materials to fuel his war against the Qing.

The two parties ultimately signed a formal commercial treaty, and the Zheng regime allocated a large villa in Anping to serve as the very first Western trading post in Taiwanese history: the English East India Company’s Anping Factory.

In this historic accord, the English were granted extraordinary trading privileges, including the freedom to travel and conduct business throughout the island. In return, the English agreed that every vessel arriving in Taiwan must carry a specified quota of gunpowder, muskets, cannons, and raw iron, which the Zheng government would purchase entirely at premium prices.

This English factory in Anping rapidly transformed into a bizarre, vibrant crossroads of East and West at the height of the Age of Sail. Every morning, the docks of Anping Harbor choked with oxcarts laden with native Taiwanese sugar, deer hides, and local crafts harvested from the mid-southern military settlements, all bound for the English warehouses.
