At night, under the heavy shroud of darkness, the English merchantmen quietly unloaded crates of advanced Western weaponry and ammunition, transferring them directly into the royal armories.

Cloaked by the unique international status of the English ships, the Zheng maritime fleets were able to bypass the Qing naval blockades, re-establishing lucrative smuggling networks with Chinese merchants in Nagasaki, Manila, and across Southeast Asia. Taiwan, once a desperate and isolated rebel island, transformed almost overnight into an indispensable and thriving hub along the global maritime trade routes.

This transnational pact stands as the very first formal commercial treaty signed between Taiwan and a Western superpower, showcasing the sophisticated maritime diplomacy of the Zheng regime.

Although this global partnership dissolved thirteen years later when the Qing Empire conquered the island and the Anping Factory fell into ruin, the treaty proved that as early as the seventeenth century, Taiwan possessed a distinct maritime DNA, capable of leveraging its strategic geography to play the dangerous game of geopolitics.

Today, when we discuss Taiwan's role in global trade and international diplomacy, we find its earliest roots in that autumn twilight over 350 years ago, when a young king stood on the ramparts of Anping Castle and signed a piece of parchment that connected his island to the wider world.
Volumes.volume.tungningDynasty.chenYonghuasBluep:
In the year 1665, in the Ningnan Quarter of Tainan, the tropical sun pierced through the vibrant canopy of flamboyant trees, casting its warm glow upon the crimson walls of a newly constructed palace. This was the very first Confucian Temple in the history of Taiwan, destined to become the island’s highest institution of learning.

Standing at the opening ceremony, quietly observing the fruit of his labor, was a middle-aged scholar known to all as the "Prime Minister of Eastern Ning"—Chen Yonghua. He was the most trusted adviser to the young king, Zheng Jing.

At this moment, Taiwan was a fragile, turbulent frontier, still reeling from the sudden death of Koxinga and a bloody war of succession. Indigenous tribes in the central plains were restless, while across the strait, the Qing Empire maintained a suffocating economic embargo.

Facing an isolated island that many deemed a hopeless wasteland, Chen Yonghua chose not to echo the frantic military cries of his fellow generals. Instead, he presented a visionary blueprint to his king, encapsulated in a single, enduring philosophy: "Ten years to nurture the people; ten years to educate them."

To survive on an isolated island starved of resources, Chen Yonghua knew he had to first solve the desperate crises of food and manpower. To this end, he aggressively implemented the Tuntian (military settlement) system, dispatching tens of thousands of Han soldiers across the landscape to clear the wilderness. He decreed that whenever soldiers were not actively fighting, they must work the fields, achieving a state of "soldiers among farmers, and farmers in the military."

Under his masterful orchestration, military camps transformed into self-sustaining villages—a tactical settlement pattern that permanently shaped the geography of Taiwan, leaving its mark on modern city names like Xinying, Zuoying, Liuying, and Qianzhen. To shatter the Qing economic blockade, Chen Yonghua also acted as the chief economic architect of the kingdom.

He learned and refined sugar-refining techniques from the indigenous tribes, turning local sugarcane into a highly lucrative global commodity, while introducing the advanced "filtered-brine sun-drying method" to establish Taiwan's very first salt pans in Tainan. This single innovation ended the island's reliance on inferior smuggled salt from the mainland, ensuring the populace had access to clean, locally produced salt.

Yet, in the heart of Chen Yonghua, merely filling the bellies of the people was never enough. He understood profoundly that a regime relying solely on swords and silver was no better than a pirate crew; to give this island a true, enduring soul, it had to be injected with the cultural essence of civilization. In 1665, he fought through fierce opposition from military generals who slammed the project as a "waste of public funds," and successfully built the Tainan Confucian Temple—revered through the ages as the "First Academy of Taiwan."

Chen Yonghua did not just construct a building; he personally designed the island's very first system of public education and civil service examinations. He decreed that regardless of whether a child was the son of a high official or a penniless farmer, anyone who passed the tiered academic evaluations could enter the royal academy for advanced studies and earn the right to serve in government.

This meritocratic system reignited hope among the thousands of exiled Han scholars who had fled the mainland, and it drew countless literati to risk their lives crossing the dangerous Taiwan Strait. Confucian philosophy and classical education, from that moment on, took deep and permanent root in the soil of the island.

Chen Yonghua spent his entire life working himself to the bone for the state, a devotion so legendary that centuries later, the martial arts novelist Louis Cha transformed him into "Chen Jinnan," the mythical grandmaster of the anti-Qing secret society, the Heaven and Earth Society.

Yet, in the unvarnished truth of history, he possessed no gravity-defying martial arts; he was a slender, soft-spoken scholar who used institutions, education, and industry to build a centenary foundation for Taiwan. Though his twilight years were marred by the political betrayals of the ruthless courtier Feng Xifan, leading to his sorrowful death in Tainan, the blueprint he left behind permanently altered the destiny of the island.

He transformed Taiwan from a volatile pirate enclave and military outpost into a sophisticated, lawful Han society rich in education and global commerce. Today, when we walk beneath the weathered red walls of the Tainan Confucian Temple, or ride the high speed rail through the bustling cities that still bear the names of his ancient military camps, we are walking upon a landscape shaped by the sheer foresight and enduring warmth of the Prime Minister of Eastern Ning.
Volumes.volume.tungningDynasty.coupOfEasternNing:
In the deep twilight of an autumn day in 1681, inside the secluded inner chambers of the Anping Royal Palace in Tainan, a white-haired, grief-stricken matriarch wept softly, leaning on her maidservants for support. She was Lady Dong, the Grand Dowager consort of the founding king, Koxinga.

For the past twenty years, the eyes of the world had been fixed on the battlefield, watching her husband and son command fleets across the roiling seas, while completely overlooking this "Iron Lady" who silently held the regime together from behind the curtain.

Lady Dong’s life was an epic of relentless compromise against fate, family tragedy, and political intrigue. She had stood by Koxinga through the grueling hardships of founding a new nation, only to witness him sink into madness on his deathbed, where he brutally ordered her own execution alongside their son over a devastating family scandal. In that era of tempestuous storms, she survived purely on iron will, emerging after her husband's death as the most powerful and respected political mediator within the regime.

Yet, most of the political tears shed by this Iron Lady were wept for her own unyielding, troubled descendants. When her son, Zheng Jing, succeeded to the throne, he managed to govern Taiwan beautifully with the counsel of the "Eastern Ning Prime Minister" Chen Yonghua, but in his later years, he fell into utter despair after the catastrophic failure of his mainland military campaign during the Revolt of the Three Feudatories.

Upon retreating back to Taiwan, Zheng Jing drowned his sorrows in alcohol and indulgence, dying suddenly in 1681 at the age of thirty-nine. Staring at the coffin of her prematurely taken son, Lady Dong felt her heart break into pieces. But fate granted the old grandmother no time for grief; the sudden vacuum of power immediately ignited a bloody storm within the palace walls.

Following Zheng Jing’s death, the throne rightfully belonged to his eldest son, Zheng Kezang—a young man who had been meticulously groomed for leadership and was widely respected for his unyielding integrity and righteousness. However, his rise provoked fierce opposition from corrupt courtiers and royal relatives who despised his strict discipline.

Seizing the moment, the powerful courtier Feng Xifan, desperate to install his own twelve-year-old grandson Zheng Keshuang onto the throne, allied with ambitious members of the royal clan to trigger a palace coup known as the "Coup of Eastern Ning." They flooded Lady Dong’s ears with malicious slander, falsely claiming that Zheng Kezang was not of royal blood at all, but rather a merchant’s orphan adopted by Zheng Jing years ago in Xiamen.

Exhausted and emotionally hollowed out by back-to-back family deaths and palace conspiracies, the aging matriarch finally buckled under the united pressure of the courtiers and her own kin. In a haze of confusion and helplessness, she quietly sanctioned the decree to depose Zheng Kezang. She could never have foreseen that this single decision would condemn her most treasured grandson to death—that very night, Zheng Kezang was brutally strangled to death within the palace gates by Feng Xifan's men.

The brutal murder of her cherished grandson and the absolute tyranny of the courtiers became the final, deepest blade thrust into Lady Dong’s heart. In the wake of the coup, as she watched her twelve-year-old, puppet grandson Zheng Keshuang thrust onto the throne, surrounded by the arrogant clamor of Feng Xifan and his faction, the Iron Lady who had witnessed three generations of dynastic change finally saw the tragic destiny of the kingdom. Consumed by endless regret, isolation, and self-reproach, her health collapsed rapidly.

Within just a few short months of the coup, she passed away in bitterness inside her bedchambers at the Anping Palace. With a lifetime of tears and stoic endurance, she had borne witness to both the glorious rise and the fratricidal collapse of the Zheng family in Taiwan. Her departure officially stripped the Kingdom of Tungning of its very last pillar of internal stability, accelerating its final slide toward total surrender just two years later.
Volumes.volume.tungningDynasty.fallOfTungning.de:
The Kingdom of Tungning did not so much collapse as unravel from within. When Zheng Jing died of illness in March 1681, he was barely forty and the failed Fujian campaigns of the previous decade had drained both his treasury and his political capital. The succession was immediately contested. A palace faction led by the general Feng Xifan murdered Zheng Jing's designated heir, the competent and popular Zheng Kezang, within days of the king's death, and installed Kezang's twelve-year-old half-brother Zheng Keshuang on the throne. The coup fractured the court: loyalist officers defected, Chen Yonghua's reform apparatus went into eclipse, and intelligence of the disarray traveled quickly across the strait.

The Qing court had waited two decades for such an opening. The Kangxi Emperor, having suppressed the Revolt of the Three Feudatories in 1681, now turned his full attention to the offshore kingdom that had embarrassed his father and grandfather. In an audacious bureaucratic decision, he entrusted the invasion to Shi Lang — a former Zheng lieutenant who had defected to the Qing after Koxinga executed his father and brother. Shi Lang knew the Zheng fleet from the inside, and he had been campaigning in Beijing for twenty years for a chance to return. Appointed Admiral of Fujian in 1681, he spent two years rebuilding a fleet of three hundred warships and training coastal crews in the waters around Tongshan.

The hammer fell in the summer of 1683. On the sixteenth day of the sixth lunar month, Shi Lang's armada engaged Liu Guoxuan, the kingdom's finest admiral, in the waters off Penghu. The battle lasted seven days. Superior Qing numbers, tighter signal discipline, and the exploitation of seasonal wind conditions that Shi Lang himself had charted as a youth proved decisive. Liu's fleet was shattered; some two hundred Tungning ships were destroyed or captured, thousands of sailors perished. With Penghu lost, Taiwan lay open. On the twelfth day of the seventh month, Zheng Keshuang submitted a formal memorial of surrender. He shaved his head in the Qing fashion, dispatched his royal seal, and consented to relocation to Beijing, where he was granted a nominal Chinese title and quietly retired from history. Twenty-one years of Zheng rule, and twenty-two of Han-Chinese sovereignty on the island, came to an end.

This volume reconstructs the fall of Tungning through the documents of its ending: the murdered heir's court rolls, Feng Xifan's coup correspondence, Shi Lang's battle memorials to the Kangxi Emperor, Liu Guoxuan's defeat dispatch, and Zheng Keshuang's surrender memorial. It traces how the first Han-Chinese polity on Taiwan, founded in haste by a father and refined in substance by a son, was undone in a single summer — clearing the way for Taiwan's incorporation into the Qing Empire and more than two centuries of imperial frontier rule.
Volumes.volume.tungningDynasty.hanSettlement.des:
Under Koxinga and Zheng Jing, Taiwan absorbed what was, for its time, a demographic flood. The 25,000 soldiers who crossed with Koxinga in 1661 did not leave; over the following two decades tens of thousands more Fujianese — some driven from the mainland by Qing coastal clearance policies, others drawn by the promise of land — made the eight-hour crossing from Xiamen or Quanzhou in shallow-draft junks. By the time the kingdom fell in 1683, the Han population of Taiwan had grown perhaps tenfold over what the Dutch had counted, and the island's ethnic map had been permanently redrawn.

The tuntian military colonies were the forward edge of this settlement. Regimental units, disbanded or semi-retired after campaigns, took up the plow on lands allocated by Chengtian Prefecture, giving rise to the grid of "ying" (encampment) and "zhen" (garrison) place-names that still anchors the geography of southern Taiwan. Behind them came civilian pioneers: lineage-based settlement from Zhangzhou and Quanzhou, Hakka households pushing inland from the foothills, merchants setting up shophouses along the Tamsui, Lukang, and Kaohsiung coasts. Land was opened through the ken-ho (patent) system, in which approved headmen received rights to recruit tenants and develop tracts in exchange for tax obligations — a structure that would shape Taiwan's rural society for the next two centuries.

The consequences for the island's indigenous peoples were profound and asymmetrical. The lowland Siraya, Makatao, Hoanya, and Pazeh nations — the so-called "Pingpu" or plains aborigines — found themselves increasingly displaced from the same alluvial soils now prized by Han cultivators. Relations were a tangled fabric of trade, intermarriage, conversion, and conflict. The Zheng administration taxed indigenous communities through the existing "village assessor" system it inherited from the Dutch, but tightened levies and extended corvée demands. Some villages negotiated accommodation by leasing land to Han tenants; others retreated into the hills, eastward toward territory still held by highland nations whose sovereignty no outside regime had yet challenged.

This volume traces the settlement transformation that turned Taiwan's demographic map upside down in a single generation. Through land-patent documents, military-colony registers, village tribute rolls, and the terse marginalia of indigenous tribute records, it reconstructs how, beneath the surface of formal proclamations, a new Han-majority society was quietly taking root across the southwestern plains — and what that rooting meant for the peoples who had lived there for centuries before.
Volumes.volume.tungningDynasty.koxingaKingdom.de:
In May 1661, following the successful landing of Zheng Koxinga’s twenty-five thousand elite troops at the Luermen channels, this emerald island—governed by the Dutch for thirty-eight years—witnessed the dawn of its very first Han Chinese regime. At this historical crossroads, though Fort Zeelandia remained locked in a fierce defense under the Dutch Governor, Frederick Coyett, the Prince of Yanping could not wait to commence his grand nation-building project upon the coastal plains. He decreed that the captured Fort Provintia in Chikan be transformed into the "Chengtian Prefecture," serving as the supreme imperial capital of the Ming Dynasty’s overseas orthodoxy, while establishing Tianxing and Wannian counties to the north and south. In a grand proclamation, Koxinga formally christened the island "Dongdu" (The Eastern Capital of the Ming). This was never meant to be a mere temporary refuge; it was a sovereign kingdom carved out of the wilderness by a desperate warlord whose mainland dreams had fractured, a final, sacred sanctuary for a fallen empire.

This newly born island kingdom was immediately confronted with a lethal, terrifying challenge that threatened its survival: an acute, total shortage of grain. Sustaining over twenty thousand soldiers accustomed to mainland diets, alongside thousands of Han civilian refugees who had crossed the dangerous strait, required an astronomical volume of food. To prevent his grand army from disintegrating into mutiny and starvation before Fort Zeelandia could be taken, Koxinga stood inside his temporary palace at Chengtian and authorized the Tuntian (military settlement) system—a strategy that permanently reshaped the geography of Taiwan. He decreed a policy of turning soldiers into farmers, keeping only a core vanguard to maintain the siege while dispersing the remaining military divisions across the northern and southern plains. Officers and foot soldiers dropped their iron spears to seize wooden plows, clearing the wild, overgrown frontier to turn native hunting grounds into fertile fields. Modern Taiwanese city names like Xinying, Liuying, and Zuoying stand today as historical ironclad proof of where Koxinga's grand army once pitched their agricultural camps.

Yet, behind the grand blueprints drawn by the Prince, dark, turbulent currents were swirling across the humid island realm. The aggressive expansion of the military settlements and the forced confiscation of lands inevitably violated the ancestral hunting territories of the indigenous tribes. Across the plains, native clans began launching bloody, localized retaliations against the encroaching Han military camps. Concurrently, across the strait, the Qing court reacted to Koxinga's capture of Taiwan with absolute fury, ruthlessly upgrading the "Great Clearance" policy into a total maritime blockade designed to starve the island kingdom into submission. Trapped between a domestic grain crisis and racial friction on the frontier, and assaulted by the strict economic embargo from abroad, Koxinga sat in his temporary hall, working through the night to review grim dispatches detailing failed harvests and the rapid death of his soldiers to tropical fevers.

By early 1662, after nine grueling months of siege, the Dutch finally signed the instrument of surrender, officially bringing Fort Zeelandia into the domain of the Zheng Kingdom. This was the absolute zenith of Koxinga’s career; he had comprehensively driven out the Western colonizers to become the undisputed "King of Taiwan." Moving his supreme command into the massive brick fortress, he renamed it "Anping." Standing atop this citadel, which had taken a Western superpower decades to construct, the Prince watched the crimson banners of the Ming Dynasty whip in the sea breeze, yet his heart harbored none of the joy of a founding monarch. The exhausting decades of maritime warfare, the mental torment of the grain crisis, and the shattering news that the Qing had executed his father Zheng Zhilong and desecrated his ancestral tombs were beginning to erode his sanity. This island kingdom, whose foundations had been laid with such immense blood and sweat, was about to enter a dark, terrifying tempest driven by the fading mind of its king.
Volumes.volume.tungningDynasty.koxingasFuryAndMa:
In the early days of 1662, the air over Anping was thick with the acrid stench of gunpowder and the heavy, salty tang of the sea breeze. This massive brick fortress, once known to the Dutch as "Zeelandia," now flew the vibrant crimson banners of the Ming Dynasty’s Prince of Yanping.

After a grueling nine-month siege, the thirty-nine-year-old warlord Koxinga (Zheng Chenggong) had finally forced the Dutch Governor, Frederick Coyett, to sign the instrument of surrender. Standing atop this fortress, which had taken the Dutch East India Company thirty years to build, Koxinga watched the enemy’s merchant ships carry the remnants of their defeated garrison away from Anping Harbor. To the outside world, this was the absolute zenith of his career—he had carved out a sovereign sanctuary for the Han people across the sea with his bare hands, rising from the son of a pirate king to become a legendary founding hero.

Yet, when we step into the final one hundred and twenty days of this great man’s life, we find not the grand triumph of a founding monarch, but a harrowing psychological tragedy woven from profound rage, paranoia, betrayal, and madness. During these final months, Fort Zeelandia was not a cornerstone for a new empire, but a psychological cage that slowly consumed its master. Koxinga’s descent into madness did not ignite from nothing; fate dealt him a succession of devastating blows across those short months. 

Just as the echoes of victory over the Dutch began to fade, the first catastrophic news arrived from across the strait. To permanently sever Koxinga’s supply lines, the Qing court had enforced the ruthless "Great Clearance" policy, forcing coastal residents to move miles inland and banning all maritime activity. Worse still, the Qing took bloody vengeance on his family.

A secret dispatch from Beijing revealed that his father, Zheng Zhilong—the legendary maritime tycoon who had surrendered to the Qing—had been publicly executed, and his brothers slaughtered. To shatter the Zheng family’s imperial ambitions, Qing troops had even desecrated the ancestral tombs in Fujian, scattering the bones of his mother and ancestors into the wind. In a Confucian society that viewed filial piety as the ultimate virtue, the execution of his father and the desecration of his ancestral tombs were weights too heavy to bear.

Koxinga collapsed to the floor of his bedchamber, coughing up blood. His anti-Qing crusade had always been torn by the agonizing conflict of choosing loyalty over filial piety; now, his father was dead because of him, and his ancestors disgraced. Deep guilt and rage warped his mind, twisting into a profound, suffocating paranoia toward everyone around him.

If the cruelty of the Qing court was a devastating external blow, the betrayal from his home base in Xiamen was a fatal blade plunged directly into his chest. While he was still reeling from the loss of his father, a messenger arrived from Xiamen carrying a letter from his eldest son and heir, Zheng Jing, announcing the birth of a newborn grandson. However, a subsequent secret report unmasked a scandalous truth: the infant was not born to Zheng Jing’s legitimate wife, but was the product of an illicit affair between the prince and his younger brother’s wet nurse, Zhaoniang.

The wife’s grandfather, a high-ranking official named Tang Xianyue, wrote a scathing letter to Koxinga across the sea, demanding justice for his granddaughter's public humiliation: "If you cannot rule your own house with righteousness, how can you rule a nation? You hold massive armies abroad while your heir commits incest at home.

How can you command the respect of the people?" This letter ignited the volcanic wrath pent up inside Koxinga's chest. For a man who defined his entire rebellion on the orthodox moral laws of Confucianism—a warlord who executed his own generals for the slightest moral failure—this was an intolerable stain. In the grand council hall of Fort Zeelandia, a psychologically shattered Koxinga flipped the tables, drew his sword, and issued a terrifying, desperate decree: he ordered his cousin, Zheng Tai, to sail to Xiamen and immediately execute his heir Zheng Jing, his own wife Lady Dong, the wet nurse, and the newborn infant to wash away the family shame in blood.

Koxinga could never have anticipated that this manic command would push him into absolute isolation. In Xiamen, the veteran generals stared at the decree in shock. Executing a nursemaid was easy, but executing the Prince's wife and heir would destroy the very foundations of the regime. Declaring that the King had gone mad in Taiwan, the generals chose collective mutiny; they killed the nursemaid but placed Lady Dong and Zheng Jing under armed protection. When news of this insubordination reached Taiwan, Koxinga realized he was utterly alone.

Fort Zeelandia had become a true prison. To the north lay the iron blockade of the Qing Empire; to the west, his own generals in Xiamen refused his commands; beneath his feet, the newly conquered island simmered with native unrest. Koxinga locked himself in the highest tower of the fortress, refusing to see any officials.

Witnesses described the late-stage warlord pacing frantically along the corridors, his eyes bloodshot and predatory. He began issuing death sentences daily—executing officials for minor agricultural delays and soldiers for trivial infractions. In his final four months, more of his own men died from his paranoid fury than had fallen during the entire nine-month war against the Dutch. He began to hallucinate in the sweltering heat of the tropical nights, claiming he could hear his executed father calling to him from across the waves, or seeing the ghosts of his slain generals demanding his life.
By early May 1662, Koxinga's body finally collapsed under the relentless burning of his mind.

He contracted a severe tropical fever that ravaged his immune system, but he refused to take to his bed. Instead, he sat upright in a wooden chair like a wounded wolf, his hand clenched tight around the hilt of his royal sword. On May 8, when General Ma Xin entered the chamber, he witnessed one of the most tragic sights in history. The grand commander who had once terrified the Dutch East India Company and broken the sleep of Qing emperors was disheveled, his robes torn. His fingernails were caked with dried blood—in his final paroxysms of anxiety and mental torment, he had used his own hands to claw his face and forehead into a bloodied, unrecognizable ruin.

Staring out the window at the vast waves of Anping Harbor, he knew the strait he had crossed so many times had become an impassable gulf, and his dream of reclaiming China had vanished. Summoning his absolute last reserves of strength, Koxinga stood up, pressed the imperial codes of the Ming Dynasty’s founding emperor to his face, and unleashed a final, thunderous roar that shook the stone walls of the fortress: "How can I face my emperors in the world below? Oh Heaven! Oh Heaven! Why have you driven me to such an extreme?"

With those final words, he sprayed a fountain of blood across the pages, and his tall, imposing frame crashed heavily onto the wooden floors of Fort Zeelandia.

He was only thirty-nine years old.

Koxinga’s death bears the profound weight of a Shakespearean tragedy. He was an undisputed hero, but he was also a fragile human being driven to madness by the shifting tides of an era, a pathological moral perfectionism, and an unquenchable thirst for vengeance. His rage was born from the unstoppable collapse of the dynasty he loved; his madness, from the unraveling of his own family.

Today, when we stand beneath the weathered brick walls of Fort Zeelandia in Tainan, enjoying the warm southern sun, it is hard to fathom the sheer agony of the soul that was once imprisoned here. Koxinga died in a tempest of fury and madness, but the island he left behind did not vanish with him. Instead, from the moment he fell, this former pirate outpost was permanently injected with Han civilization, classical education, and an uncompromising spirit of rebellion.

The King died in madness, but the true history of Taiwan was born in that blood-stained hall of Fort Zeelandia.
Volumes.volume.tungningDynasty.mingDynastyLoyali:
In the sweltering midsummer of 1683, a suffocating aura of despair hung over the city of Tainan. Ominous news had traveled across the black waters of the strait—the main naval forces of the Zheng regime had been utterly obliterated at the Battle of Penghu, and the twelve-year-old puppet king, Zheng Keshuang, along with his ministers, had already resolved to tender their submission to the Qing Empire.

The history of this island as the final bastion of Ming loyalism was rushing toward its end. Inside the Ningjing Royal Palace in Tainan, an elder stood quietly, dressed in the grand crimson ceremonial robes of a Ming prince. He was Zhu Shugui, Prince of Ningjing, a ninth-generation descendant of the Ming Dynasty’s founding emperor, Zhu Yuanhang.

Exiled overseas for over twenty years, his royal blood had borne witness to the collapse of his empire. Now, facing an inescapable defeat, a final, unyielding flame of dignity ignited within his heart—give me liberty, or give me death.

When Zhu Shugui gathered his five concubines—Lady Yuan, Lady Wang, and his attendants Xiujie, Meijie, and Hejie—to break the news of his impending martyrdom, he braced himself for a scene of agonizing weeping and sorrowful farewells. Yet, these five women, ordinary in origin but extraordinary in spirit, merely exchanged a quiet glance before bowing gracefully to the prince.

With profound serenity, they spoke in unison: "Since Your Highness has resolved to die for the Ming Dynasty, we will absolutely not live to suffer dishonor. We wish to precede you into the afterlife and hold your horse's reins on the road to the Yellow Springs."

Stepping into the grand hall of the palace dressed in immaculate traditional Han garments, the five women took their own lives one by one, hanging themselves from the wooden rafters in a fierce, poetic declaration of loyalty to their love and their fallen dynasty. Stifling his immense grief, the prince personally arranged their remains and buried them together at Kuandou Hill, just outside the city walls.

The following morning, the gates of the Ningjing Royal Palace were thrown wide open. Zhu Shugui laid out a grand feast, summoning the civil officials, military officers, and local tenant farmers who had followed him for years. He brought out every single land deed and property title registered in his name and set them ablaze before the astonished crowd, announcing to the farmers: "From this day forth, these lands belong entirely to you. When the Qing forces arrive, live peacefully as law-abiding citizens."

With everything settled, he walked into his private chambers, lifted his brush, and inscribed his final poem upon the wall, a verse that would be passed down through centuries: “Since the rebel armies captured the capital in 1644, we have held onto the Ming realm for thirty-nine years. Today, all is lost. How can I live in disgrace?

Let them shave my head and change my garments, for I would have no face to meet my ancestors in the world below!” Finishing his writing, he unbuckled his jade belt, placed his royal crown upon his head, and hanged himself, drawing a noble, heartbreaking curtain over the blood and tears of the exiled Ming royalty.

The tragic farewell of the Prince of Ningjing and his five concubines remains one of the most poignant pages in Taiwanese history. This tragedy was not merely the end of a royal house, but the final stand of Han dynastic pride on the island.

Following the Qing takeover, Admiral Shi Lang, deeply moved by their uncompromising loyalty, ordered the Ningjing Royal Palace to be converted into the Grand Matsu Temple to preserve the historic architecture. Meanwhile, the burial site of the five courageous women became revered as the "Temple of the Five Concubines," where incense still burns to this very day.

Located amidst the shaded greenery of modern Tainan, this ancient shrine holds no overbearing divine majesty; instead, it softly whispers to every passerby of a Ming prince and five women who, in a desperate bid to preserve their freedom against mandatory submission, demonstrated a level of dignity and resolve that shook their era to its core.
Volumes.volume.tungningDynasty.twilightOfTheBoyK:
In the golden autumn of September 1683, a suffocating silence fell over the sunset-drenched city of Tainan. The bustling ports of Erhulmen and Anping, once the vibrant crown jewels of the Age of Sail, were no longer filled with merchant vessels. Instead, the horizon was choked with the dense, looming fleet of the Qing Empire, their banners rippling ominously in the sea breeze.

Inside the grand hall of the Chengtian Royal Palace, twelve-year-old Zheng Keshuang sat motionless on a hollow wooden throne. He wore the ceremonial dragon robes of the Ming Dynasty—robes that were far too heavy and wide for his slender, youthful frame. Since the catastrophic defeat at the Battle of Penghu, and following the successive deaths of his matriarch grandmother, Lady Dong, and the brilliant minister Chen Yonghua, this overseas bastion of Ming loyalism had run entirely out of time and options.

On this fateful evening, the fierce rhetoric of resisting the Qing and restoring the Ming had vanished. In its place echoed only the helpless sighs of corrupt courtiers and the low, muffled weeping of civil officials.

On the night before he was scheduled to shave his head, change his attire, and formally surrender his kingdom, the boy-king walked into the Zheng Family Ancestral Shrine for the very last time.

Inside, the eternal incense burned low, cast in a dim glow that cradled the wooden ancestral tablets of his grandfather, Koxinga, and his father, Zheng Jing. Looking up at those names—names that had once struck terror into the hearts of Qing emperors—the young Keshuang and the royal clan members kneeling behind him finally broke.

They wept bitterly in the flickering candlelight. They wept for the king's own helpless youth, for the treacherous manipulation of the court factions, and above all, for the tragic reality that this haven of Han civilization, carved out of the wilderness by their ancestors, could not escape the cruel destiny of conquest.

As the sacrificial joss paper turned to ash in the burning braziers, the legitimate royal lineage of the Prince of Yanping, which had reigned over Taiwan for twenty-one years, reached its heartbreaking end.

The next morning, the final curtain fell upon Taiwan’s first Han Chinese regime at the Baoning Temple. Shi Lang, the victorious Admiral of the Qing navy, marched into the royal palace with a heavy, disciplined stride, flanked by his top commanders.

Under the watchful, tearful eyes of the court and the local populace, the twelve-year-old Zheng Keshuang, aided by his attendants, raised his trembling hands to untie the Ming scholar’s cap from his head.

Before the crowd, a Qing military barber took a razor and shaved the front of the boy's head, braiding the remaining hair into the mandatory Manchu queue. He stripped off the silken Han garments that symbolized the orthodox Ming lineage and put on the official robes of the Qing court.

The boy-king then knelt before Admiral Shi Lang, raising the written Instrument of Surrender and the gold royal seal of the Prince of Yanping high above his head. At that exact moment, cries of anguish erupted throughout Tainan. To the scraping hiss of razors against skin, the gears of history turned ruthlessly, burying the twenty-one-year maritime saga of the Kingdom of Tungning into the dust of the past.
The fall of the Zheng regime marked a violent turning point in Taiwanese history.

Following his capitulation, Zheng Keshuang, along with the scheming courtier Feng Xifan and other members of the royal clan, were immediately escorted under armed guard to Beijing. To prevent the Han population in Taiwan from ever rising in rebellion under the Zheng name again, the Kangxi Emperor spared the twelve-year-old boy's life.

Instead, he placed him under house arrest in the capital, granting him the empty, hollow title of "Duke of the Han Banners," leaving him to live out the remainder of his days in poverty and constant paranoia. In 1684, the Qing Empire officially incorporated Taiwan into its imperial domain, establishing the Taiwan Prefecture.

Today, when you walk into the ancient Zheng Successor Ancestral Shrine in downtown Tainan and gaze upon the statue enshrined in the main hall, the swirling incense still whispers to every visitor of the sheer helplessness and sorrow of that twelve-year-old boy who untied his crown and surrendered his kingdom in the autumn twilight of 1683.
The Twilight of the Boy King
Volumes.volume.tungningDynasty.vanishingPlainTri:
In the 1660s, the landscape of central Taiwan offered a stark contrast to the highly sinicized, scholarly atmosphere taking root in Tainan. This was a wild, untamed frontier nourished by the currents of the Dadu and Zhuoshui rivers.

Across these vast plains and rolling hills flourished a powerful, multi-ethnic confederation of over ten indigenous Plain Tribes—including the Papora, the Babuza, and the Hoanya—which later historians would call the Kingdom of Middag. Their supreme ruler, revered as King Middag (Kamachat Aslamie), governed an ancestral homeland that had never been touched by the hand of any imperial Chinese dynasty.

However, as the Ming-Zheng regime aggressively pushed its "military settlement system" northward to sustain its anti-Qing campaigns, thousands of Han soldiers armed with steel blades and matchlock guns began encroaching upon the frontier. These Han settlers, desperate for grain and territory to survive, were placed on a violent, inevitable collision course with native warriors sworn to defend their ancestral hunting grounds.

The spark of conflict erupted into an absolute inferno at the Shalu Community (modern-day Shalu District, Taichung City). Desperate to alleviate a severe grain crisis racking his military camps, Zheng Jing imposed forced labor and heavy agricultural taxes upon the tribes of the Kingdom of Middag—a demand that, to an indigenous society reliant on hunting and shifting cultivation, amounted to total cultural annihilation. 

Pushed beyond the brink of endurance, the Plain Tribe warriors of the Shalu community rose in open rebellion, launching fierce guerrilla raids against the Han agricultural outposts. Upon hearing news of the uprising in the central plains, Zheng Jing ordered a ruthless military pacification. He dispatched Liu Guoxuan and Feng Xifan—the regime’s premier commanders, renowned for their cold, calculated efficiency—to march north with a heavily armed elite force. It was a deeply unequal war of technology and tactics; despite the native warriors' flawless mastery of the terrain and unmatched bravery, their defenses were rapidly obliterated under the crushing volleys of Han musketry and ironclad cavalry.

Upon breaching the defenses of the Shalu Community, the Ming-Zheng army enacted a devastating strategy of total extermination. To permanently shatter any residual spirit of indigenous resistance across central Taiwan, Liu Guoxuan ordered the complete annihilation of the settlement. Soldiers torched the thatched-roof villages, and whether they encountered armed Papora warriors or defenseless women, children, and the elderly, all were ruthlessly cut down in a tempest of fire and blade.

According to historical records, this brutal "Shalu Incident" reduced a thriving tribal community of hundreds down to a mere handful of traumatized survivors, effectively wiping the settlement from the face of Taiwan's history. Horrified by the sheer cruelty of the Shalu massacre, King Middag and the remaining confederated tribes bowed to the Ming-Zheng regime in grief and terror, reluctantly accepting the humiliating terms of imperial taxation and forced labor.

The tragedy of the vanishing Plain Tribe warriors remains a profound and solemn elegy in the history of Taiwan. While this merciless military conquest allowed the Ming-Zheng regime to successfully expand its dominion into central Taiwan and open fertile plains for Han agriculture, it dealt a fatal blow to the vitality of the Kingdom of Middag, causing the ancient confederation to fracture and collapse over the ensuing decades.

The proud warriors who once ran free across the central plains, their skin etched with tribal tattoos and their ears adorned with traditional discs, were gradually silenced and erased from the margins of written history. Today, as coastal trains rumble through the high-rises of modern Shalu, it is hard to imagine that over three centuries ago, an ancient kingdom bled its last drop of life upon this very soil—and that the wheel of Taiwanese history moved forward heavily, rolling over the bones of these forgotten warriors.
Zheng Jing inherited the Kingdom of Tungning in the summer of 1662 amid circumstances that should have ended it. He was in Xiamen when word of his father's death arrived, and a faction in Taiwan had already proclaimed his uncle Zheng Xi regent. It took a brief but resolute expedition across the strait to reassert the succession before Zheng Jing could finally turn to the work of governing an island still raw from conquest. What followed was a near-two-decade reign (1662–1681) that, quietly and without the father's mythic stature, became the true founding era of an organized Taiwanese polity.

At the center of the reform program stood Chen Yonghua, a Fujianese scholar-official whose quiet competence reshaped the kingdom. On his advice, Zheng Jing built Taiwan's first Confucian temple at Tainan in 1665, paired it with the Mingluntang academy, and instituted civil examinations for local appointment — laying the institutional scaffolding for Han literate culture on the island for the first time. Military colonies were expanded deeper into the Chianan plain; salt flats, sugar mills, and refined drainage works multiplied the tax base. Chen's careful supervision of granaries and grain reserves enabled the kingdom to weather famines that would have broken a less-organized state.

Beyond land reform, Zheng Jing leveraged his inherited Zheng-family merchant network into one of the most formidable maritime commercial operations of seventeenth-century East Asia. Tungning fleets called regularly at Nagasaki and Manila, and through intermediaries reached Batavia, Siam, and the Ryukyus. English East India Company factors established a trading lodge at Anping in 1672, exchanging woolens and firearms for deerskin, sugar, and Japanese silver. This was no isolated "bandit kingdom" as Qing propaganda styled it, but a genuine maritime polity with its own revenues, standing army, and diplomatic correspondence. Zheng Jing himself twice led invasions of the Fujian coast during the Revolt of the Three Feudatories (1674–1680), at one point holding Zhangzhou, Quanzhou, and Xiamen before being forced to withdraw.

This volume examines the reforms that transformed Koxinga's hasty conquest into a durable state. Through Confucian-temple inscriptions, examination rolls, trade ledgers with English and Japanese merchants, and the administrative archives of Chen Yonghua's chancellery, it documents how a twenty-year island regime organized itself as a kingdom, educated a generation of scholar-officials, and imagined a sovereign Han-Chinese future independent of continental dynasty.
Volumes.volume.tungningDynasty.zhengJingsEastern:
In the early summer of 1662, as the founding king, Zheng Koxinga, drew his last breath amidst frantic, agonizing cries inside Fort Zeelandia, the political climate across both sides of the Taiwan Strait plummeted to absolute freezing point. The sudden demise of the warlord did not merely leave behind an unsolidified overseas regime; it unleashed a devastating moral deadlock born from his own final, draconian decree of "honor-killing" his own family.

At this critical juncture, the civil officials and military generals marooned in Anping were thrust into an unprecedented crisis of legitimacy. In their eyes, the eldest son, Zheng Jing—who remained behind to guard Xiamen—was not only a sinner carrying the permanent moral stain of an illicit affair with his brother's nursemaid, but a condemned man whom the late king had explicitly ordered to be executed. To preserve the survival of the regime and protect their own interests, powerful generals in Taiwan, including Huang Zhao and Xiao Gongchen, swiftly joined forces.

They thrust Koxinga’s younger brother, Zheng Xi, into power as the "Acting Governor." This declaration, masked as a move to stabilize the state, was in truth a meticulously calculated coup d’état, violently fracturing the fledgling regime into two warring factions: Taiwan and Xiamen.

Stranded across the sea in Xiamen, the young Zheng Jing found himself backed into an absolute dead end. His father’s sudden death had stripped him of both his greatest shield and his most terrifying oppressor, while the news of the mutiny in Taiwan pinned him to the wall. If he chose compromise, he would permanently forfeit his birthright and face eventual liquidation by the faction in Taiwan; if he chose to fight, he would bear the heavy infamy of inciting a bloody civil war, leading an army to attack the very sanctuary his father had died to conquer.

Yet, the blood of pirates and ruthless warlords coursed through Zheng Jing's veins, and in this hour of peril, he displayed a calculated decisiveness and ferocity far beyond his twenty years. Backed by the unwavering support of the elder statesman Chen Yonghua and the brilliant admiral Zhou Quanbin, Zheng Jing held a massive rally in Xiamen, swearing allegiance to the orthodox Ming lineage and officially claiming his succession as the Prince of Yanping.

He understood profoundly that political legitimacy is never granted through moral charity—it is seized through raw, uncompromising power. To reclaim his empire, he mobilized every elite warship in Xiamen’s naval fleet, embarking on a do-and-die "Eastern Conquest" across the perilous black waters of the strait.

It was a fateful, bloody crusade across the treacherous Taiwan Strait. In the deep autumn of 1662, Zheng Jing’s armada successfully punched through the roiling surf, forcing a landing at Luermen. By then, the plains of Anping and Chengtian Prefecture were heavily fortified by the defensive lines of Huang Zhao and Zheng Xi. The two sides clashed in a brutal war of attrition across the Tainan plains and along the muddy coastlines—comrades who had stood shoulder-to-shoulder just months prior to drive out the Dutch were now slaughtering one another for the crown.

At the height of the engagement, the Taiwanese faction utilized superior positioning to push Zheng Jing's lines to the brink of collapse. Refusing to retreat, Zheng Jing personally landed on the shores to command the front, while his elite commander, Zhou Quanbin, led a fierce suicide squad to carve a path of blood through Chikan. As twilight fell, a sudden, blinding fog rolled in and swallowed the battlefield. In the chaotic, misty crossfire, the rebel commander Huang Zhao was struck by a stray bullet and killed instantly.

The sudden death of their general broke the morale of the Taiwanese garrison, causing lines of soldiers to drop their weapons in mass surrender. Zheng Jing’s forces swept through the defenses, capturing Fort Zeelandia and dragging his uncle, Zheng Xi, out of the royal palace in chains, bringing a swift and absolute end to this bitter family war.

Standing inside the grand, shadow-filled halls of Fort Zeelandia—the very fortress where his father had spent his final, maddening days—the twenty-year-old prince unleashed an iron-fisted political purge. He ordered the immediate public execution of the coup's ringleaders, including Xiao Gongchen, to strike absolute terror into the hearts of any remaining dissidents.

Yet, when dealing with the figurehead of the rebellion, his uncle Zheng Xi, Zheng Jing demonstrated a surprisingly mature, calculating political tact. Instead of executing him, he spared his life but stripped him of all political influence, placing him under permanent house arrest and sending him back to the Chinese mainland under armed guard. Soon after, Zheng Jing officially renamed the island realm "Eastern Ning" (Tungning) and proclaimed himself its sovereign ruler. 

This Taiwanese version of the "Xuanwu Gate Incident," though drenched in the blood of fratricide and political betrayal, effectively prevented the realm from fracturing into self-destructive warlord states at its very inception. Zheng Jing had consolidated his reign with absolute ruthlessness, and under the brilliant guidance of Chen Yonghua, he prepared to transform Taiwan from a volatile military base into a sophisticated, independent maritime kingdom.
Volumes.volume.tungningDynasty.zhengJingsWestwar:
In the winter of 1673, a political storm of cataclysmic proportions erupted across the half-shattered domain of the Qing Empire. Wu Sangui, the Prince of West-Pacification in Yunnan, Shang Zhixin in Guangdong, and Geng Jingzhong, the Prince of South-Pacification in Fujian, rose in open rebellion against the young Kangxi Emperor over his aggressive policies to dismantle their fiefdoms, a conflict known to history as the "Revolt of the Three Feudatories."

When this earth-shattering news crossed the strait to the Royal Palace in Tainan, the long-dormant court erupted into a frenzy of anticipation.

For the Eastern Ning sovereign Zheng Jing and his ministers—who had been penned up on their island bastion for over a decade—this was undoubtedly a heaven-sent, once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to launch a final, grand counter-offensive to reclaim their lost mainland empire. In the spring of 1674, Zheng Jing rallied his forces in Tainan and launched a massive westward campaign, mobilizing nearly all of Taiwan’s elite naval assets and grain supplies to cross the black waters of the strait, vowing to finish the sacred work of his grandfather and father.

Initially, the returning armies of the Zheng regime unleashed a display of unstoppable military might along the southeastern coast of China. Zheng Jing successfully landed his forces in Fujian, swiftly recapturing Xiamen, Quanzhou, and Zhangzhou—the historic strongholds of his family—while pushing the front lines deep into the territory of Chaozhou in Guangdong. As war engulfed the south, the Qing defensive lines along the coast buckled, and local citizens, hearing rumors that "the army of King Koxinga has returned," rose up in droves to join the rebellion.

Yet, this counter-offensive, which had seemed so assured of victory, began to quietly disintegrate as the allies fell prey to mutual suspicion and greed. Geng Jingzhong of Fujian, though fighting under the same anti-Qing banner, soon found himself deadlocked with Zheng Jing over the partitioning of land, military rations, and supreme command. Instead of uniting their forces to march north, the two factions turned their weapons upon each other in a series of bitter fratricidal skirmishes.

This internal fracturing granted the Qing court a critical moment to breathe; the Kangxi Emperor swiftly deployed a massive army of Manchu and Han troops, utilizing a brilliant strategy of divide-and-conquer to deal a fatal blow to the campaign.

When an overwhelmed Geng Jingzhong capitulated to the advancing Qing forces, the Zheng army found themselves entirely isolated along the mainland coast. The Qing navy and land forces launched a ferocious counter-offensive, forcing Zheng Jing to retreat into his stronghold at Xiamen, where the war devolved into a brutal war of attrition.

By 1680, after years of relentless combat, the troops and strategic resources accumulated over twenty years in Taiwan were utterly exhausted. Following a catastrophic defeat in a final, massive naval engagement, Zheng Jing saw that the tide had turned irrevocably.

To prevent the complete annihilation of his remaining forces, he ordered the abandonment of Xiamen. Amidst the smoke of burning fortifications and the weeping of his exhausted soldiers, Zheng Jing boarded his ship and sailed away. This grand campaign, which had lasted six years and drained the blood and wealth of Taiwan, ended in absolute ruin, forcing the battered remnants of the army back across the strait.

The failure of the westward campaign during the Revolt of the Three Feudatories sealed the twilight fate of the Kingdom of Tungning. The war had stripped the regime of its last foothold on the mainland and hollowed out Taiwan's economic foundations, leaving the island's populace impoverished and rife with discontent.

Upon returning to his palace in Tainan, Zheng Jing suffered a devastating psychological collapse; he became profoundly despondent, withdrawing entirely from state affairs and drowning his sorrows in alcohol. The dream of reclaiming the mainland had vanished forever like a mirage.

From that moment on, Taiwan was no longer a dynamic frontline base poised for an offensive strike, but a vulnerable, isolated stronghold awaiting the ultimate, inevitable judgment of the Qing Empire.
Volumes.volume.underTheRisingSun.armedResistance:
The early decades of Japanese rule were marked by persistent armed resistance, revealing the depth of opposition to colonial authority across both Han and indigenous communities. In the first years after annexation, guerrilla fighters known as 'righteous bandits' (義匪) waged a sustained insurgency across the countryside, prompting the colonial government to launch massive 'bandit suppression' campaigns that killed thousands.

The most significant uprisings punctuated the colonial period like recurring tremors. The Beipu Incident of 1907 saw Hakka and indigenous Saisiyat fighters briefly seize a Japanese police station in Hsinchu. The Tapani Incident of 1915, led by Yu Qingfang under the banner of a syncretic religious movement, was the last major Han armed revolt — its suppression resulted in nearly 900 death sentences, later commuted under public pressure. The Wushe Incident of 1930 sent shockwaves through the empire: Seediq warriors led by Chief Mona Rudao attacked a Japanese sports day gathering, killing over 130 settlers and officials. The colonial government's retribution was devastating — deploying aircraft, poison gas, and allied indigenous groups in a campaign that nearly annihilated the Seediq communities involved.

This volume traces the arc of armed resistance from the guerrilla campaigns of the 1890s through the watershed Wushe Incident, examining how each uprising reshaped colonial policy — from military suppression toward increasingly sophisticated systems of surveillance, co-optation, and assimilation — and how the memory of resistance became foundational to Taiwanese identity.
Volumes.volume.underTheRisingSun.awakeningTaiwan:
In the Taiwan of the 1920s, as the armed resistance and outlaw legends of the dark night fell silent one after another under Japanese police pressure, a different revolution erupted — one without bloodshed, without weapons, yet striking far deeper at the heart of imperial rule. This "revolution of identity" exploded into the streets of Dadaocheng and the scent of tea. It was a golden age of global ideological currents, in which the Taiwanese subjective consciousness finally opened its eyes after a long dark night. Taiwan had stepped out of the wild disorder of the Qing era, only to fall into institutional discrimination as "second-class subjects" under the Government-General.

The storm-center of this spiritual awakening was led by two historical giants of radically different character and origin who came together for a shared ideal. One was Lin Hsien-tang, master of the "Wufeng Lin family," scholarly and grave in bearing — Taiwan's most prestigious magnate, the embodiment of the warmth and stability of the traditional Taiwanese gentry. The other was Chiang Wei-shui, a fiery young doctor from Yilan who had opened the "Da-an Hospital" in Dadaocheng. His eyes burned, his words cut, and through his veins ran the rebellious revolutionary blood of the grassroots.

When the two met in Taipei, they sensed sharply that against a Japanese empire armed with modern aircraft and cannon, mere physical violence was useless sacrifice. If the Taiwanese were ever to rise, the only true battlefield was not in the mountains and forests, but in the mind. The Qing officials who had fled in shame in 1895 had left the Taiwanese no dignity. This time, the Taiwanese would reclaim sovereignty through their own knowledge. On 17 October 1921, Lin Hsien-tang and Chiang Wei-shui called together a thousand impassioned intellectuals and young students from across the island and formally founded the "Taiwan Cultural Association" in Dadaocheng, Taipei.

For this cultural enlightenment movement, Chiang Wei-shui composed a famous medical diagnosis that history would never forget — the "Clinical Lecture." In this peculiar piece of writing, Chiang treated "Taiwan" as his patient, diagnosing the island with acute "intellectual malnutrition." The only prescription he wrote was not drugs or a scalpel, but "education, newspapers, libraries, cultural lectures, and reading societies." He cried out that only by lifting the level of Taiwanese knowledge could the island's soul finally stand on its own feet.

The climax of this struggle was the miracle that quickly followed: "cultural lectures" and "reading societies" lit up like stars across Taiwan's horizon.

The young students of the Cultural Association walked the towns and villages of western Taiwan on foot through blazing sun and bitter wind. At temple gateways, beneath great trees, on grain-drying yards — wherever sunset arrived, they would drag a few benches over, hang a single oil lamp, and call out loudly to the Taiwanese farmers and laborers who had bled and sweated in the fields all their lives. Standing on benches, they spoke in the most down-to-earth Hokkien and Hakka, explaining with fierce passion to the illiterate poor what world human rights were, what freedom and equality meant, and why the Taiwanese should never accept being second-class slaves on their own soil.

This sweeping spiritual baptism touched every raw nerve of the Government-General's authoritarian system. The Tokkō (Special Higher Police) began trailing every lecture as if by shadow. In black uniforms with police sabers at the hip, they sat sullenly in the front row with notebooks in hand. Whenever a speaker reached an impassioned passage and mentioned "freedom" or "the rights of the Taiwanese," the Japanese officers would leap to their feet, shouting in shrill, severe Japanese: "Surveillance! Unstable! Stop!"

But this did not frighten the impassioned Taiwanese — instead it gave rise to scenes of dark, witty humor. Each time the police shouted "Stop!," the crowd, far from dispersing, erupted in thunderous applause and laughter. The speaker would smile faintly, deftly switch to a near-synonymous tongue-twister of a topic, and keep dancing along the legal tightrope just out of the officers' grasp.

Meanwhile, from the rear, Lin Hsien-tang used his vast wealth and prestige to launch the more-than-a-decade-long "Petition Movement for the Establishment of a Taiwanese Parliament." A group of Taiwanese intellectuals donned Western suits and top hats, carried petitions bearing the signatures of tens of thousands of their countrymen, and again and again crossed the sea to the Imperial Diet in Tokyo, openly pressing on the colonial motherland the democratic demand that "the affairs of Taiwanese must be governed by Taiwanese themselves." It was a brilliant era in which Taiwanese pushed the legal system of the Japanese Empire into a corner with pens and words, displaying immense moral spine.

The whirlwind reached its peak around 1927. Though the Taiwan Cultural Association soon faded amid a bitter left-right ideological split, Chiang Wei-shui did not stop. He founded the first legal political party in Taiwanese history — the "Taiwan People's Party" — and threw his support behind the "Taiwan Federation of Labor Friends," pushing the cultural enlightenment movement into concrete class struggle.

Sadly, the revolutionary who had burned his life away never saw the island's final outcome. In 1931, at the age of only forty, Chiang Wei-shui died of typhoid fever at his Da-an Hospital. On the day of his funeral, the tea houses of Dadaocheng closed, the shops shuttered, and tens of thousands of tear-streaked Taiwanese walked into the streets unprompted to escort his coffin. The "Mass Funeral," as history would call it, was Taiwan's deepest tribute to its spiritual teacher.

The 1920s cultural whirlwind led by Lin Hsien-tang and Chiang Wei-shui was the most beautiful and proudest chapter of spiritual awakening in Taiwan's Japanese era. Through fourteen years of peaceful struggle and cultural baptism, they uprooted the ancestral feuds that had drained Qing-era Taiwan of its strength, forging a "Taiwanese identity" that crossed class and ethnic lines.

It was the ancestors gathered at temple gates to hear lectures and bent over world maps in reading societies who, with passion and pens, poured into Taiwan the soul of modern democracy, liberty, and selfhood. This spark of spirit, though it sank underground in the dark years of the Second Sino-Japanese War and the Kominka campaign, never went out. In the end, it became the most original and unshakable century-long foundation on which modern Taiwan made its way to a free and democratic society.
Volumes.volume.underTheRisingSun.chiananIrrigati:
In 1920s southern Taiwan, while the gunfire of the "indigenous pacification policy" still echoed faintly through the depths of the Central Mountain Range and the literati of Taipei's Dadaocheng still cried out for liberty and equality, a vast yet lifeless wasteland stretched across the horizon of southern Taiwan. That was the Chianan Plain — fully 150,000 hectares of it.

In that era, this was no golden granary of rolling rice waves but a wasteland of weeds and cracked earth, "fields that depend on the sky" that had drained the tears of countless farmers. Without any proper irrigation system, the plain was held hostage year-round by extreme drought, by floods triggered by torrential rain, and by severe salinization seeping in from the coast. In winter, a furious northeast monsoon swept the surface, lifting clouds of yellow dust; salt crystals bloomed white on the dried mud like a thick layer of snow, allowing nothing to grow. Farmers here could only stand barefoot on earth as hard as iron beneath a burning sun, looking helplessly to the heavens, living in hunger and cold and depending entirely on the sky for survival.

The fate of this land turned completely in 1920. That year, a thirty-four-year-old Japanese civil engineer with curly hair, a firm gaze, and burning passion arrived in Guantian, Tainan, with his surveying instruments. His name was Yoichi Hatta.

A graduate of Tokyo Imperial University, Hatta was a brilliant engineering prodigy. Standing on the undulating hills of Guantian, gazing at the lifeless white expanse before him, he ignited an almost insane vision: on this wasteland that the Qing Empire had been unable to tame in two centuries of rule, he would build the largest super-hydraulic engineering work in all of Asia at the time, a miracle even by the standards of world hydraulic history — the Wushantou Reservoir and the Chianan Canal.

The scale of the project was suffocating. Hatta planned a massive dam across the Guantian Creek standing fifty-six meters high and more than a thousand meters long. To draw the abundant waters of the Zengwen River beyond Guantian into the reservoir, he boldly decided to cut a diversion tunnel more than three thousand meters long straight through the belly of the Wushan Mountain. At the same time, he would lay a labyrinth of channels with a total length of sixteen thousand kilometers — enough to wrap half the globe — to carry clean water to every corner of the Chianan Plain.

This was no detached design drawn up at an office desk. It was a decade-long pilgrimage of blood and tears.

Construction formally began in 1920. Hatta moved his entire family — his wife Toyoki and their young children — into the worker dormitories at the Wushantou construction site. He shared every hardship with thousands of Han Taiwanese laborers, indigenous youths, and Japanese technicians. In an age without modern excavators or advanced ventilation, the cutting of the mountain and the building of the dam were done entirely by hand, by laborers with pickaxes, iron shovels, and dynamite, hacking inch by inch through hard rock and clinging mud.

The most brutal and moving battlefield of the entire project was the excavation of the Wushan Mountain diversion tunnel. Sunless and lightless, with subterranean temperatures soaring past forty degrees Celsius, the air there hung thick with toxic gases and volatile natural gas ready to ignite. The fires of the 1895 Yiwei War had long died out, yet in this pitch-black tunnel another battle against fate was only just beginning.

In the early winter of 1922, a thunderous gas explosion erupted deep within the tunnel. Fire instantly consumed the shaft, mudslides surged in, and more than fifty Taiwanese and Japanese laborers lost their lives in an instant. As the charred bodies were carried out one by one, lamentations shook the entire Wushantou site, and countless laborers, in terror, packed their belongings and fled into the night. The project ground to a complete and despairing halt.

At this critical moment — hearts shaken, even the Government-General preparing to abandon the bottomless project — Yoichi Hatta revealed a moral spine that transcended nationality and class. Choking back grief at the loss of his comrades, he stood himself in the construction yard and cried out to all the laborers: "On this site there are no Japanese and no Taiwanese! There are only brothers sweating together, struggling together for this land!" He then funded a "Martyrs' Monument" by the reservoir, carving into a single stone the names of every Taiwanese and Japanese laborer killed or felled by illness — without distinction of rank or nationality. He personally visited the family of every fallen Taiwanese worker, delivering compensation and pledging to care for their well-being for the rest of their lives.

Hatta's sincerity and selflessness completely won the hearts of the Taiwanese laborers. They wiped away their tears, picked up their iron shovels again, and walked back into the black hole that could collapse at any moment.

To meet the project's harshest challenges, Hatta produced a series of miracles in world hydraulic history. Rejecting the concrete-dam techniques then in vogue in Europe and America, he adapted to local conditions and adopted the radically forward-looking "Semi-hydraulic Fill" method. Mixing silt, clay, and gravel, he used water's buoyancy and natural gravity to allow the dam body to compact itself naturally — building a "living reservoir" fused with the natural landscape. To this day, despite decades of powerful earthquakes and storms, the Wushantou Reservoir remains intact.

The climax of history arrived on 10 April 1930 (Showa 5).

On that day, after ten full years of labor, more than fifty million yen of astronomical investment, and the sacrifice of one hundred and thirty-four lives, the Chianan Canal was formally completed and the water was at last turned on.

Yoichi Hatta and his countless mud-caked, emaciated Taiwanese laborers stood silently before the great outlet of the Wushantou Reservoir. As the floodgate rose to the heavy scrape of its steel cables, a clear and torrential current — like a long ribbon of white silk, like a water dragon that had slept for a thousand years — burst out roaring, surging through the lattice of channels toward the parched Chianan Plain.

In distant fields, thousands of Taiwanese farmers at work heard the rush of water from afar. When the cool clear water flowed into their cracked rice paddies and washed away the white salt crust on the soil, every farmer, every woman, every child — heedless of the mud on their bodies — rushed wildly into the channels. They scooped the water with their hands and drank in great mouthfuls, splashed it on their faces, looked at the rising green of their fields, and burst into cheering and weeping that rang up to the sky.

That night, all of southern Taiwan blazed with lights. Farmers held operatic celebrations at temple gates as if it were the new year.

Through the sweat of Hatta and his laborers, the Chianan Plain rewrote its fate overnight. The dry, drought-stricken "fields of the sky" became a golden granary of three-year crop rotations and annual abundance. Rice and sugarcane yields in Taiwan multiplied many times over, finally uprooting the existential cancer of chronic water shortage that had plagued southern Taiwan for two centuries of Qing rule and that had so often sparked ethnic feuds.

Tragically, the engineering master who had given his life to the soil of Taiwan met his end in the Pacific War. In 1942, Hatta was ordered to the Philippines for a hydraulic survey of cotton cultivation. The merchant ship "Taiyo Maru" carrying him was torpedoed by an American submarine near the Goto Islands. Hatta perished at the age of fifty-six. His wife Toyoki, refusing after Japan's defeat in 1945 to leave the land that had bound her so deeply to her husband, walked one rain-lashed night to the outlet of the Wushantou Reservoir and threw herself into the water, following him in death.

Yoichi Hatta's story is the most border-transcending and the most constructive chapter of Taiwan's Japanese era. While imperial politicians were busy plundering and imperial armies were busy killing across the battlefields of East Asia, Hatta poured ten years of his youth, his exquisite technical genius, and his immense love for his workers into carving from the earth a wellspring of life that still pulses to this day.

Today, when you drive past Guantian, Tainan, and see the still waters of the Wushantou Reservoir resting like a single emerald coral among the mountains, in the shade of the trees beside the reservoir you can still find Yoichi Hatta's bronze statue. He is not arrayed in dignified imperial uniform or a Western suit; instead he wears working clothes, his curly hair still on his head, one hand running through that hair, sitting cross-legged on the ground in deep concentration, gazing quietly at the plain of abundance that he and his pioneers irrigated with their blood and sweat. That tenderness toward the land has become, in Taiwan's historical memory, the most indelible legend in the long annals of this island.
Volumes.volume.underTheRisingSun.erlinIncident.d:
Under Japanese colonial rule, Taiwan's sugar industry was built into one of the empire's most important economic pillars — yet that sweet wealth rested on the sweat and humiliation of the cane farmers. Through the system of designated "raw-material collection zones," the Government-General carved every stretch of cane field into the territory of a single assigned sugar company, so that the cane a farmer grew could be sold only to the one mill within his zone. As a result, when the cane would be harvested and weighed, how it would be graded, and what price each hundred catties would fetch were all decided by the company alone. The farmers had no room to bargain and no way to check whether the scales — held entirely in the company's hands — were honest. Day after day of toil brought them suppressed prices and weights that had plainly been tampered with. Small wonder that a bitter, wry saying passed from mouth to mouth: "the smartest man in the world can't beat the sugar company's scales." That single refrain captured an entire generation of growers' resignation and resentment toward this structural exploitation.

As the 1920s arrived, stirred by currents of thought sweeping the world and by the awakening of intellectuals, that silent resignation began to loosen. In Erhlin, in Changhua, a man who was both a physician and a social activist stepped forward — Li Ying-chang. While healing the sick, he also walked out among the field ridges to teach the farmers of his district what rights and fairness meant. Under his rallying call, in the summer of 1925 the cane farmers of Erhlin gathered together and formed the first cane growers' union in Taiwan's history. The union's demands were not radical, but they struck at the heart of the matter: the farmers asked that prices be agreed before the cane was harvested, that they be allowed to send representatives to witness the weighing, and that they have a say in and knowledge of the grading standards. For farmers who had long been at the company's mercy, this was the first collective voice they had ever raised — an attempt to wrest back some measure of their fate from beneath those opaque scales.

The union's adversary was the powerful Lin Pen-yuan Sugar Company, which had no intention of giving ground. When the cane-harvesting season came that October, the company disregarded the farmers' calls to agree prices and negotiate first, and simply sent its men into the fields to seize the harvest. In that moment, the grievances accumulated over years found their outlet.

On 22 October 1925, the farmers of the Erhlin area came face to face with the police who had been sent to guard the harvest, and the taut situation escalated at last into physical conflict. To the colonial authorities, that farmers should dare to stand collectively against both company and police was a provocation that could not be tolerated. In the aftermath, the authorities launched mass arrests: scores of participants were detained and imprisoned, among them the union's core leaders, and dozens more were formally prosecuted and brought before the colonial courts. Li Ying-chang and many of the farmers' leaders thus paid the price in prison and in trial.

The Erhlin Incident was the first large-scale, organised farmers' protest since the beginning of Japanese rule over Taiwan. Unlike the scattered armed resistance of the past, it was a modern social movement built around a union and framed as a struggle for economic rights. Although the protest was outwardly suppressed under the authorities' crackdown — its leaders behind bars and the union's activities set back for a time — the flame it had lit reached far beyond the bounds of this small sugar town.

The example set by the Erhlin cane growers' union let farmers across the island, suffering the same exploitation, see the power of solidarity. Inspired by it, in less than a year an organisation emerged that crossed regional lines and linked farmers throughout Taiwan: in 1926, Chien Chi, Chao Kang and others drove the founding of the Taiwan Farmers' Union, gathering a struggle once confined to a single town into a tide of rural protest that swept the whole island. From a quarrel over the scales in one corner of Erhlin to farmers across Taiwan rising for their land, their tenancy, and their dignity, the thread of resistance was drawn taut and continuous.

Looking back, the meaning of the Erhlin Incident has long since outgrown the cane and the scales themselves. It made Taiwan's farmers realise for the first time that, in the face of structural injustice, only by organising and raising a collective voice could they hope to move a balance that had always tilted toward the company. Those nameless farmers who were detained and prosecuted wrote, with their imprisonment and their sacrifice, a crucial opening chapter to the sweeping social movements of the colonial era.
Volumes.volume.underTheRisingSun.kanoBaseball.de:
In 1930s Taiwan, while the wastelands of the south, irrigated by Hatta Yoichi's Chianan Canal, broke into endless waves of golden rice, another miracle — a storm of sweat, tears, and black-earth youth — exploded onto the red-clay baseball diamond of Chiayi. It was a colonial era of rigid class lines and high ethnic walls. On the baseball map of the Empire of Japan, Taiwanese teams had long been regarded as "second-tier ragtag outfits," and no one ever believed that boys from this southern island could one day step onto Japanese baseball's supreme sanctum — Koshien.

Taiwan's baseball world at the time was split by an invisible but stark line. Teams of Japanese were known for "defense and tactics." Han Chinese teams (Hokkien and Hakka) were known for "hitting." And the physically gifted indigenous Taiwanese teams — chiefly Amis and Seediq players — had unmatched "speed and explosiveness." In daily life these three ethnic groups were full of estrangement; on the diamond, they played their own games and refused to yield to one another.

But this seemingly unbreakable prejudice met in 1929 a man who would shatter all the rules. He was a stern-faced, eagle-eyed legendary Japanese coach named Kondo Hyotaro. Invited to become head coach of the baseball team at the "Chiayi Agriculture and Forestry Institute" (KANO for short, from the Japanese reading), Kondo on his first day looked at the sun-darkened, threadbare boys assembled before him and made a decision then considered pure fantasy. He would break the ethnic barriers and weld Japanese, Han, and indigenous players into one unprecedented "cocktail" team.

Kondo's training was, in the most literal sense, an iron-blooded discipline. On Chiayi's red clay scorched by sun, Kondo gripped his wooden bat and tirelessly hammered out drive after drive. He howled at the boys who rolled in mud and dust. He ordered them every dawn to run laps through the streets of Chiayi while shouting at the top of their lungs a slogan that every townsperson found laughable at the time: "Koshien! Koshien!"

Against townspeople's mockery and their own bodies' limits, these boys from different peoples — through year upon year of tears and sweat — fell into a strange chemistry. The indigenous players set aside their wariness of the Han; the Han players took on Japanese discipline. They shared the same bowl of white rice in the dorm and clapped one another on shoulders raw with bruises. Kondo Hyotaro watched these boys' eyes harden into the gaze of wolves and smiled faintly, because he knew the team had earned the iron-blooded creed that would burn through an era: "Do not think of winning. Think of not losing."

The climax of history thundered into 1931 in the height of summer.

This once-unknown "ragtag outfit" that had not won a single match seized the all-Taiwan selection tournament in a stunning upset, claiming the single ticket that would take a team from Taiwan to Osaka. When the four English letters KANO appeared on the giant scoreboard at Koshien Stadium in Japan, tens of thousands of arrogant Japanese spectators and reporters cast doubtful and disdainful glances.
