They sneered that this was a "wild children's team" from a barbaric southern island.

But when the umpire shouted the start of the game, the cocktail team unleashed a fearsome force that left Japan breathless. The indigenous power hitter Hirano Yasuro (Amis, Han name Luo Baonong) swung his bat and sent a baseball flying into the Koshien night sky. The shortstop Uematsu Koichi (Tsou) launched himself across the black clay in a flying dive to glove a sure base hit. And the core of the team, the ace pitcher Wu Mingjie (Hakka), used his astonishingly fast and ferocious fastball to shut down inning after inning the lineups of Japan's traditional baseball powers.

KANO cut through opponent after opponent and, like a dark horse, miraculously slashed its way into the final championship game.

But fate delivered its cruelest blow at the moment of greatest glory. After several consecutive complete-game performances at the highest intensity, the skin of ace pitcher Wu Mingjie's pitching fingers split open from prolonged friction against the baseball's seams. Blood streamed from his fingers mixed with sand. On the diamond in the final against Japan's Chukyo Commercial School, every pitch he threw came with searing pain. His velocity crashed, his control collapsed, and he gave up walk after walk.

The Japanese crowd in the stands began to jeer. In the dugout, Kondo Hyotaro's face turned iron-gray; he was preparing to relieve his exhausted ace. But at that very moment, the indigenous and Han teammates on the field rushed forward together and surrounded Wu Mingjie, his face streaked with tears and blood.

"Mingjie, throw it. Let them swing!" His teammates wiped the dripping blood from his hands with the black earth and pounded on his chest in frenzy: "We are behind you! We will get every ball! Because we are KANO!"

In that moment, they crossed ancestral lines, crossed ethnic groups, crossed the great gulf between colonizer and colonized. Wu Mingjie clenched his teeth, his eyes blazing with one last savage fury. He climbed back onto the mound, willed himself through his broken knuckles, and with the last of his strength hurled that blood-soaked baseball at home plate again and again. Behind him, his teammates ran like madmen across the black earth of Koshien, dove, and threw their bodies in front of every batted ball.

Though KANO finally took only second place — undone by the gap in strength and by injury — the moment the final out was recorded and the game ended, the entire Koshien stadium fell into a deathly silence. Then, slowly, tens of thousands of once-arrogant Japanese spectators rose to their feet. They did not cheer for the champions. Instead they poured wave upon wave of applause and tears toward these Taiwanese boys who knelt on the mound, weeping as they scooped Koshien's black earth into their hands to take home as a keepsake.

A famous Japanese writer and editor — pen trembling in his hand — set down on that day's newspaper a verdict that has echoed through Asian baseball history ever since: "KANO under heaven!"

KANO's battle on the black earth was the most impassioned and most warm-hearted final curtain of Taiwan's Japanese era. The sweat and blood they spilled on Koshien melted clean away the colony's towering ethnic walls. By their actions they proved to everyone that on this island — whether you were Han, indigenous, or Japanese — if you held one shared goal and stood shoulder to shoulder on the same red clay, you could create miracles that moved the world.

That "never give up" spirit of KANO drove itself deep into the genes of the Taiwanese people, becoming, for the decades that followed and for modern Taiwan to this day, the most rebellious and most resilient spiritual origin of every appearance on baseball's international stages.
The Taiwan of the early 1920s stood in an unusual political season. In the wake of the First World War, the ideals of national self-determination and constitutional politics swept across the globe and quietly crossed the strait as well. A generation of Taiwanese intellectuals, schooled in the new learning, was no longer content to live under the Governor-General's unchecked rule. Instead they sought, within the seams of the system, to win a measure of voice for the island's six million people. The stage they chose was not the street with its blades and guns, but the assembly hall and the petition — a struggle waged in the language of law.

Out of this current the parliament petition movement took shape. Its advocates argued that since Taiwan had been folded into the empire, it deserved an elected assembly, chosen by Taiwanese and empowered to deliberate the island's budget and laws, rather than leaving legislative and executive authority wholly in the Governor-General's hands. To give the cause a formal and lasting body, in February 1923 activists in the petition movement founded the League for the Establishment of a Taiwan Parliament, a formal political organization to press their demands. They hoped that lawful association would gather scattered petitioning into an organized civic movement with a charter and a purpose.

The colonial authorities, however, were deeply alarmed by this openly constituted political body. In the eyes of the Governor-General's Office, a standing organization led by Taiwanese and publicly challenging the structure of rule was far more threatening than any single petition. The authorities first refused to register the League in Taiwan; unwilling to be turned away, the activists moved to Tokyo and re-founded the League in the imperial capital, seeking to exploit the relatively looser space for association in the metropole so that the organization might survive. This maneuvering between Taiwan and Tokyo revealed both the movement's resilience and the coming of a head-on collision.

The collision finally broke in deep winter. In the early hours of 16 December 1923, while the island still slept in darkness, the Governor-General's Office launched a coordinated, island-wide sweep, arresting and searching dozens of movement leaders under the Public Order Police Law, seizing documents and interrogating those involved. It was a carefully staged operation meant to intimidate — the authorities wanted everyone to understand that crossing the line of political association would carry a price. The episode took its name, the Chih-ching Incident, from that very Public Order Police Law that served as its legal basis.

Among those hauled in were Chiang Wei-shui and Tsai Pei-huo, the movement's two best-known figures. The former was an activist who wielded a physician's pen to diagnose the ailments of "the island of Taiwan"; the latter a tireless organizer who moved for years between cultural work and petitioning. Together with the other detainees, they formed the backbone of the Taiwanese national movement of the day. What the government intended as a warning — a single sweep to smother the movement's heat — instead produced the opposite effect. The arrests did not silence the cause; they built for it a stage unlike any before.

The public trials of 1924 and 1925 became a national sensation. The courtroom, meant by the authorities as a place to convict, was turned by the defendants into a lectern. Before packed galleries and a rapt press, they set out, point by point, the legitimacy of a Taiwanese assembly and argued openly for the political rights of the Taiwanese people. The twists of the proceedings only heightened the drama: the defendants were first acquitted, and then, after the prosecution appealed, the verdict was reversed on appeal, and several defendants received short prison terms. The sentences were light, yet the process held the whole island's gaze.

The moral victory the trials handed the movement, however, was far larger than the sentences themselves. Day after day the newspapers carried the words spoken in court, delivering the defendants' arguments into countless Taiwanese homes; a trial meant to suppress became instead a pulpit from which political ideas were preached across the island. The composed, unbowed bearing of the accused let many who had watched coolly from the sidelines feel, for the first time, that "Taiwanese too have the right to speak" was no empty phrase.

The Chih-ching Incident thus became the first great political trial in Taiwanese history, a moment when the language of law and rights was spoken aloud in a colonial court. It shifted the form of resistance from force toward reason and public opinion, and it steeled a whole generation of activists — the names that walked out of that courtroom would carry the nerve and experience the trial had earned them into the cultural and political struggles still to come.
Volumes.volume.underTheRisingSun.kominka.descrip:
In 1937, gunfire at the Marco Polo Bridge crossed the Yellow Sea and bore down upon this island. As freighters continued to load Taiwan's rice, sugar, and camphor for the Japanese home islands, and as the canals of the Jianan Plain went on watering a land already colonized for thirty years, atop the newly consecrated grounds of the Taiwan Grand Shrine at Yuanshan in Taipei, a ritual bell rang out through the morning mist, again and again. In that very same hour, inside a century-old temple on the island's western coast, the wooden body of Guanyin was kicked to the earth by the boots of the military police, and fire spread across the mud — this was the "Temple Rectification Movement." Shrine and flame together carved the deepest fissure in Taiwan's colonial history: the Kōminka Movement, a vast imperial project that sought, in less than a decade, to rewrite the soul of an entire generation of Taiwanese.

The architect of this transformation of the soul was the seventeenth Governor-General of Taiwan, Kobayashi Seizō (1877–1962), who took office in 1936. A cold-eyed admiral from Hiroshima, he declared in his inaugural address the "Three Principles" that would shake the entire island: kōminka (imperialization), industrialization, and the doctrine of the "southern advance base." Taiwan was to become the empire's steel platform for expansion into Southeast Asia — and the first prerequisite was that its inhabitants must first be turned into "Japanese." The National Language Movement rolled out across the island; Chinese instruction vanished from the public schools; the Chinese-language columns of newspapers were abolished that same year; shop signs, family door couplets, and ancestral tablets were all ordered, decree by decree, to be replaced. In 1940 he launched the "Name-Changing Movement": Taiwanese who adopted Japanese surnames would receive preferential access to rations, employment, and schooling. It was a noose disguised as a favor — soft to the touch, iron in its grip.

In 1940, Hasegawa Kiyoshi (1883–1970) took over the Government-General and pushed the movement still deeper into wartime totalization. He established the Kōmin Hōkōkai — the Imperial Subjects Public Service Association — weaving every neighborhood, ward, township, school, factory, and women's association on the island into one dense net of mobilization. Patriotism, Public Service, Decisive Battle — three words now covered every school assembly and every radio broadcast. Kōminka was no longer merely a cultural remaking; it had become the machinery through which an entire generation of the island's young would be prepared to be pushed into the fires of war.

The first face pushed onto the propaganda stage was that of an Atayal girl named Sayun (1921–1938). In the autumn of 1938, carrying the luggage of her departing Japanese teacher Tabei Masaki — who had been called up for military service — she stepped onto a wooden bridge in the Nan'ao mountains in the middle of a typhoon, slipped, and fell into the ravine below. Her body was never recovered. The Government-General sensed at once the political weight this mountain accident could carry. Hasegawa Kiyoshi himself presented the inscribed "Bell of the Patriotic Maiden Sayun." The full literary machine of empire then went into motion: the film Sayun's Bell, starring Li Xianglan, opened across Taiwan; the theme song poured from every radio, day and night; textbooks turned her into a model of virtue; the memorial bell was hung at the entrance of the Nan'ao public school. A seventeen-year-old indigenous girl was thus sculpted into the most perfect face of Kōminka.

Li Xianglan (1920–2014) herself was the most exquisite product of that same machine. Her real name was Yamaguchi Yoshiko; she was Japanese by birth, yet her fluent Mandarin, Japanese, and Manchu carried her between Man'ei and Tōhō, singing "When Will You Return?" and "Fragrance of the Night" — the silver-screen voice of the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere. Her songs drifted from Shanghai back into the radios of Taipei, and made an entire generation of youth half-believe that the culture of empire could be soft, luminous, even tender.

As for Suniyuwu (1919–1979), an Amis youth renamed Nakamura Teruo, he was drafted into the Takasago Volunteer Unit and sent to the South Seas. In the jungles of Morotai he fought out the war's final battle — never learning that Japan had surrendered. He hid alone beneath the coconut palms for a full twenty-nine years, until Indonesian troops discovered him in 1974. When he was brought back to Taiwan, he had been renamed once more — this time as Lee Kuang-hui. Three names in a single lifetime: the record of a man christened, in turn, by three regimes.

Yet not every Taiwanese would accept that new name. Lin Hsien-tang (1881–1956) of Wufeng — the soul of the Taiwan Parliament Petition Movement — refused, to the very end, to change his surname, refused to appear at Shinto worship, refused to hang the Rising Sun flag at his gate. With the almost-silent bearing of a gentleman, he inscribed "non-cooperation" into a long, patient form of resistance. The far more radical Wang Min-chuan (1889–1942), leftist leader of the Taiwan Cultural Association, had already been swept up in the 1923 political prosecutions and the crackdowns that followed; at the height of the Kōminka years he died of illness inside the Taichung Prison, never living to see the movement's end. Chen Cheng-po (1895–1947), meanwhile, kept guard over his colors on canvas — the temple courtyards of Chiayi, the red brick of Chihkan Tower, the yellow dusk of Tamsui — the landscape being taken away inch by inch by shrines and the national language, he sealed into oil paint, one brushstroke at a time.

In August 1945, Emperor Hirohito's "Jewel Voice Broadcast" reached Taiwan through the crackle of the radio. The shrine bells fell silent; the Rising Sun vanished from the streets overnight. Those who had changed their names walked back to the household registry to change them again, one stroke at a time — but they could not erase the Japanese lullabies in their memory, nor the school assemblies, nor the afternoons of youth spent lifting wooden rifles on the training ground. The Kōminka Movement had ended, but the wound it left lay not upon the body — it was carved into the seams of the soul of an entire generation. They would spend their lives searching, between two languages, two names, and two ancestral tablets, for the answer that truly belonged to themselves. This volume looks back upon that: a state-imposed remaking of the soul, and its deepest scar — a place where even hatred has been folded into silence.
Volumes.volume.underTheRisingSun.kominka.title: Kōminka Movement
Volumes.volume.underTheRisingSun.modernInfrastru:
Japanese colonial rule brought systematic modernization to Taiwan on a scale unprecedented in the island's history. The colonial government constructed a north-south railway trunk line completed in 1908, expanded modern harbors at Keelung and Kaohsiung, built a comprehensive network of roads, and established a public health system that dramatically reduced mortality from malaria, plague, and cholera through quarantine stations, water treatment, and mandatory vaccination campaigns.

The agricultural transformation was equally far-reaching. The Chianan Irrigation Project — an engineering marvel designed by Hatta Yoichi and completed in 1930 — converted the barren Jianan Plain into Taiwan's most productive rice and sugar-growing region by channeling water from the mountains through an extensive canal system. Scientific agriculture, improved seed varieties, and chemical fertilizers boosted crop yields to levels that made Taiwan a crucial food supplier for the Japanese homeland. Sugar refineries operated by zaibatsu corporations like Mitsui and Mitsubishi became the backbone of the colonial economy.

Yet this modernization was fundamentally extractive. Taiwan's resources — rice, sugar, camphor, timber — flowed overwhelmingly to Japan. Taiwanese students were segregated into a separate and inferior education track. Employment in government and major corporations was reserved for Japanese nationals. Political participation was nonexistent until the limited local elections of the 1930s. The contradiction between modern infrastructure and colonial inequality would become a defining tension of the era — one that shaped how later generations remembered and debated the legacy of Japanese rule.
Volumes.volume.underTheRisingSun.newLiteratureMo:
The Taiwan of the 1920s was living through a double awakening, political and cultural. As the parliament petitions and the lectures of the Cultural Association stirred the island's political consciousness, a parallel revolution quietly caught fire on the page. Inspired at once by China's May Fourth vernacular movement and by modern Japanese literature, a younger generation of Taiwanese intellectuals began to ask in earnest: in what language, and for whom, should literature be written?

For generations the Taiwanese literary world had been dominated by the old literati, men steeped in ornate classical Chinese and the trading of composed verses. Their themes rarely strayed beyond wind, flowers, snow and moon, remote from the real lives of the toiling majority. Such a literature could neither carry the ideas of a new age nor shed light on the suffering at the base of colonial society.

In 1924 the young writer Chang Wo-chun, then living in Beijing, threw a bombshell. In a series of fiercely worded essays — "A Letter to Taiwan's Youth," "The Wretched State of Taiwanese Letters" — he denounced the stagnation of the old literature and called for renewal through the vernacular. The "old-versus-new literature debate" that followed, with its sharp exchanges, sounded the first gong for the arrival of a new writing.

The man who gave the ideal flesh and blood was the Changhua physician Lai He. In a plain vernacular full of sympathy he wrote of cane farmers exploited by the sugar companies, commoners bullied by officials, and voiceless women; stories such as A Steelyard, The Festival and Trouble distilled the everyday injustices of colonial life into unforgettable art. Lai He not only wrote himself but, as editor of the literary pages of the Taiwan Minpao, opened those pages to a whole generation and mentored younger writers, earning the lasting title "father of Taiwanese new literature."

As the movement deepened, a debate arrived over the very language of writing. Around 1930 Huang Shih-hui and others argued for a written Taiwanese vernacular that could depict the native soil and speak for the toiling masses, igniting the "nativist literature and written-Taiwanese debate." It pushed the relationship of literature to the land and the common people to the centre of everyone's thought, and deepened the consciousness of why, and for whom, one wrote.

Into the 1930s the venues for publication flourished. The magazine Nan-yin appeared, and Taiwanese students in Tokyo formed an arts research society and issued Formosa, kindling the flame of new literature on the island and in Tokyo at once. In 1934 writers from across the island gathered to found the Taiwan Literary Federation and publish Taiwan Literature, and the movement swelled into a mighty current.

It was in that same year that Yang Kui's story The Newspaper Carrier was selected by Tokyo's Literary Review, a milestone as the first work by a Taiwanese writer to break into Japan's central literary press. Yang Kui later founded New Taiwan Literature, giving the leftist and realist voices a fresh stage. At the same time Lu Heruo with The Oxcart, Lung Ying-tsung with The Small Town with Papaya Trees, and Chang Wen-huan with his nativist writing together carried Taiwanese new literature to an artistic peak.

Beyond fiction, new poetry and criticism flourished too. The Salt Belt poets led by Wu Hsin-jung wrote plain verse steeped in the smell of the land, amid the salt pans and farming villages of the south; and Wang Pai-yuan, in his Japanese-language poetry collection The Thorny Road, gave voice to the anguish and searching of the colonial intellectual. These diverse voices meant new literature was no longer the stage of novelists alone but the shared spiritual map of a whole generation.

The movement nurtured a whole generation of gifted writers who, with their individual pens, together portrayed the face and inner voice of colonial Taiwan, proving that the island's own people, language and land were every bit as worthy of first-rate literature. Yet the wheel of the age soon rolled over them: when war with China broke out in 1937 and the Governor-General pushed the assimilation campaign and abolished the Chinese-language sections of newspapers, harsh wartime censorship forced many writers to lay down their pens or fall silent. Though interrupted by the fires of war, the New Literature Movement had already given the island its first modern literary voice — a precious inheritance that later generations would go on rediscovering, carrying forward and honouring long after the war.
Volumes.volume.underTheRisingSun.opiumWar.descri:
In early twentieth-century Taiwan, while "the Greatest Thief Under Heaven," Liao Tianding, leapt across rooftops in the dark and challenged the Government-General with raw force, another struggle — bloodless, yet even more breathtaking — was quietly opening in laboratories and hospital wards, waged by a scholarly young man in gold-rimmed glasses. The enemy of this war was not the proud Japanese police, but a white demon that had gnawed at Taiwan's social structure since two centuries of Qing rule had begun, leaving over a hundred thousand families ruined: opium.

The soul of this opium war was Du Cong-ming, born in 1893 in Sanzhi, New Taipei. He would become Taiwan's first doctor of medicine — a medical giant who combined brilliance with deep human compassion. The Government-General faced a uniquely difficult mess in Taiwan: more than a hundred thousand registered opium users were officially recorded on the island. These addicts had drowned for years in opium smoke, losing all productivity and becoming the heaviest burden on the lowest rungs of society.

At first the Japanese government had no answer. A harsh outright ban could trigger mass riots from over a hundred thousand addicts and dealers in agonizing withdrawal; passive tolerance, as in the early Qing years, would leave Taiwan's economy and society barred from modernity forever. With the Government-General caught between these poles, even considering mass internment, Du Cong-ming stepped forward, founded the "Renewal Hospital" (Gengsheng-yuan) in Taipei, and formally declared war on opium.

Du Cong-ming was a true scientist and a compassionate physician. In an age that treated drug users as criminals or social refuse, he issued a historically foresighted diagnosis. He declared openly: "Opium smokers are not criminals; they are patients. And since they are patients, we should heal them with science and medicine."

The climax of this war erupted inside the isolation wards of the Renewal Hospital.

There Du faced patients whose addictions to powerful morphine and opium reached deep into the bone. When these men were brought into the Renewal Hospital and cut off from their drugs, the wards became a living hell. Crushing withdrawal sent patients writhing on the floor, beating their heads against walls in hysterics, even biting their own skin in frenzy. The wails went on through the night.

Japanese officials and the police watched in horror, many demanding handcuffs and whips to subdue the frenzied addicts. Du calmly placed himself across the ward's door. He knew that forced "cold turkey" complete withdrawal would simply kill them. Drawing on his deep knowledge of pharmacology, he devised what would become his world-famous "Gradual Withdrawal Method" — a reduction-based detoxification protocol.

Du Cong-ming worked sleeplessly in his laboratory, extracting compounds from plants and precisely formulating replacement medications that could ease the agony without producing strong new addiction. In nights lit by flickering flame, Du personally led his nurses and orderlies into the ward thick with sweat and cries. Half-kneeling beside beds stained with mud and waste, he gently soothed the delirious patients and injected the medications into their veins with his own hand.

A miracle followed. Patients who minutes earlier had thrashed like beasts saw their fever and convulsions subside within minutes of injection and at last fell into deep sleep. Du Cong-ming monitored the data with rigorous scientific discipline, reducing dosage drop by drop, day by day, paired with psychological counseling and nutritional therapy. Within a few short weeks of treatment, the gaunt, hollow-eyed addicts miraculously regained their wits and walked back through the wooden doors of the Renewal Hospital — restored as upright men in society.

The results of this opium war were stunning. Within a few years, the Renewal Hospital cured tens of thousands of severe addicts across Taiwan completely of their opium and morphine dependence. Through precise injections and selfless love, Du pulled this group of "wandering ghosts abandoned by their age" back from the brink of death and madness. It was not merely a medical victory; it was a pivotal miracle in which science rescued the demographic structure of Taiwanese society.

After Japan's defeat in 1945, Du Cong-ming carried his love of this land forward. He took over the College of Medicine at National Taiwan University, and later in life moved south to Kaohsiung, where he founded Taiwan's first private medical college — Kaohsiung Medical College, today Kaohsiung Medical University — training generation after generation of frontline physicians serving the island.

Du Cong-ming's story was the most rational and most humanitarian chapter of Taiwan's Japanese era. While Liao Tianding cut sparks of rebellion through the night with his dagger, Du, in Taipei's laboratories and wards, with a stethoscope and limitless compassion, completed a far larger, far deeper "redemption of souls."

He did more than excise the white tumor from the body of his society — with the modern scientific spirit, he laid the firmest, most unshakable century-long foundation for Taiwan's public health and modern medicine.
Volumes.volume.underTheRisingSun.opiumWar.title: The Opium War
Volumes.volume.underTheRisingSun.orphanOfAsia.de:
In 1943, as the fires of the Pacific War swept across the South Seas and censorship on Taiwan reached its height, in the corner of a Taipei newspaper office a Taiwanese reporter past the age of forty spent his days writing copy that glorified the "holy war." By night, however, he returned to his rented room and, by the dim glow of a lamp, secretly filled sheet after sheet with a novel he knew could never be published. He understood that if the patrolling military police ever uncovered the manuscript, prison — or something worse — awaited him. This man was Wu Zhuoliu, and the manuscript he hid in drawers and in the gap above the ceiling would later be hailed as an immortal classic of Taiwanese literature: Orphan of Asia. The word "orphan" was the annotation he wrote for the inner life of an entire generation of Taiwanese.

Wu Zhuoliu, born Wu Chien-tien in 1900 in a Hakka village in Xinpu, Hsinchu, was steeped from childhood in classical Chinese learning and poetry. After graduating from the Governor-General's National Language School, he returned home to teach at public elementary schools, a calling he pursued for nearly two decades. From the lectern he saw with his own eyes how Taiwanese teachers, however diligent, were always paid and promoted below their Japanese colleagues, and he witnessed the arrogance and contempt with which Japanese inspectors treated both Taiwanese children and their teachers. In 1940, a clash sparked by an inspector's discrimination became the final straw: he resigned from his secure post and turned his back on half a lifetime of teaching.

After leaving teaching, Wu crossed the sea to Nanjing in China to work as a reporter for the Continental Daily News. He had carried with him an image of the "motherland," imagining he might find there a sense of belonging as a Han Chinese; yet the realities of wartime China, and the suspicion with which locals regarded "Taiwanese" as neither Japanese nor purely Chinese, gave him a taste of yet another kind of rejection. He soon returned to Taiwan and made his living in journalism. The experience showed him plainly: in Japanese eyes the Taiwanese were second-class colonial subjects; in Chinese eyes they were outsiders stamped with the mark of Japan. Acknowledged by neither, belonging to neither — this was the most painful core of the "orphan of Asia."

Orphan of Asia lays this condition of belonging nowhere bare through the life of its protagonist, Hu Tai-ming. A Taiwanese youth with a modern education, Hu studies in Japan, where he is dismissed as a "slave of the Qing"; he travels with high hopes to mainland China, only to be guarded against as a Japanese spy; and back in Taiwan he is ground down by colonial discrimination and the crush of war until his mind gives way. Hu's tragedy is not death but the impossibility of finding any land, any community, willing to say to him without reservation, "You are one of us." Through this character Wu gave voice to the silent cry of a whole generation struggling in the cracks between empires.

When Japan surrendered in 1945, Wu, like many Taiwanese, briefly brimmed with hope at the return to the "motherland." But the chaos of the takeover that followed, the bloody suppression of the February 28 Incident, and the long White Terror that came after quickly shattered that hope. He poured his firsthand witness and his disillusionment into the autobiographical works The Fig Tree (無花果) and Taiwan Lianqiao (臺灣連翹) — both banned for a time after publication for candidly touching on the February 28 Incident and other political taboos, and not fully released until around the lifting of martial law. A different flag had been raised, yet the orphan remained an orphan: this was the heaviest question Wu bequeathed to post-war Taiwan.

Though he tasted the margins under both regimes across his life, Wu did not choose silence. In 1964 he single-handedly founded the magazine Taiwan Literature (臺灣文藝), holding open a space for the long-suppressed nativist writing of the post-war years; and in 1969 he donated his personal savings to establish the Wu Zhuoliu Literary Award, encouraging writing centered on Taiwan itself and nurturing generation after generation of younger authors. He died in Taiwan in 1976 at the age of seventy-six. Today he is widely regarded as a pioneer of Taiwanese nativist literature, and Orphan of Asia has transcended the novel itself to become the most representative emblem of the identity dilemma of colonial Taiwan — a reminder to every generation that knowing who you are remains this island's deepest, and most necessary, question.
Volumes.volume.underTheRisingSun.seediqBale.desc:
After the fires of the Yiwei War died out in 1895, the Rising Sun flag was planted across the plains and harbors of Taiwan. Yet deep in the Central Mountain Range — those forests forever wreathed in mist, revered by the Seediq as the sacred domain of their ancestral spirits — the empire's rule could never truly conquer the human heart. Thirty-five years later, a rage of blood and tears, long suppressed, would erupt upon the hunting grounds of Wushe.

More than a thousand meters above sea level in Nantou, Wushe was the Government-General's proudest showcase of its "indigenous pacification policy." Here stood a post office, a police station, a clinic, even the Wushe Public School for indigenous children. But beneath this veneer of song and prosperity, the six Tgdaya tribes of the Seediq who had lived here for generations endured unimaginable oppression. The Japanese police ruled the mountains like petty emperors: they forced the warriors to haul heavy timber to build dormitories and Shinto shrines without pay, banned the traditional facial tattoo and the hunt, and even courted and then abandoned the women of the tribes through "political marriages." To a people whose entire faith rested on the Rainbow Bridge and the dignity of the hunting ground, bodily exhaustion could be endured — but the trampling of the soul had left no room for retreat.

This rage finally crystallized into a storm of vengeance in the heart of Mona Rudao (c. 1882–1930), chief of the Mahebo tribe. Powerfully built and eagle-eyed, he had in his youth been a legendary hunter whose name struck terror into his enemies, and he had once been taken by the Japanese government to tour the home islands, where he saw with his own eyes the empire's suffocating aircraft, cannons, and warships. He understood, better than anyone, that to resist Japan was to hurl an egg against a stone.

What lit the powder keg was an ordinary tribal wedding feast. Mona Rudao's eldest son, Tado Mona (1901–1930), clashed physically with a Japanese constable named Yoshimura while offering a toast; the police threatened severe punishment, plunging the whole family into fear of reprisal. Looking upon the young warriors seething around him, Mona Rudao knew this would be a war destined to annihilate his people. Yet he understood something greater: that if they did not resist, the Seediq soul would forever be reduced to a faceless slave, unable in death to cross the Rainbow Bridge to the land of the ancestors. So in the depths of the midnight forest he swore a blood pact uniting the six tribes around Wushe, resolved to launch one final "hunt" against the Empire of Japan in the season of harvest.

At dawn on October 27, 1930, the Wushe Public School was holding its annual joint athletic meet. As the whole assembly stood at attention singing the Kimigayo, a bone-chilling war cry suddenly erupted from the surrounding slopes. Mona Rudao led over three hundred warriors armed with hunting blades and matchlocks, sweeping down from the forest like black lightning; Tado Mona was the spearhead of the fighting, leading his people to cut the telephone lines and storm the police outposts. In under two hours, thirty-five years of accumulated grievance became the flash of blades across the schoolyard, and one hundred thirty-four Japanese lay dead. News of this "Wushe Incident" shook Taipei and reached all the way to the cabinet in Tokyo.

And yet, not every Seediq could raise the blade with an untroubled heart. In that blood-red dawn of the uprising, two model figures deliberately cultivated by colonial assimilation were torn apart by the deepest crisis of identity. Hanaoka Ichiro (born Dakis Nomin, 1908–1930) and Hanaoka Jiro (born Dakis Nawi, 1908–1930) were both Seediq youths from the Paran tribe, educated in Japanese schools and serving as policemen. They shared the surname "Hanaoka" yet were of no blood relation — a pair of model brothers the Government-General paraded to boast of its "pacification" success. When the uprising broke out, they could neither betray the people who had raised them nor turn against the system they served; in the end they hanged themselves alongside their families in the mountains, in the Japanese manner. Ichiro left behind a note bearing the words "we had no choice" — the most sorrowful distillation of a soul forcibly severed by civilization.

Reeling from shock and humiliation, the Government-General unleashed one of the most lopsided sieges in Taiwan's history. Taiwan Army Commander Kamada Yahiko (1879–1948) was ordered to direct the suppression, mobilizing over three thousand troops and police equipped with mountain artillery and machine guns, and even deploying aircraft, bearing down in a black tide upon the primeval forests of Wushe. Against Seediq guerrillas who knew the terrain and struck like ghosts, the Japanese army was held back and suffered heavy losses. Deadlocked, Kamada gave the order to deploy blister-agent gas bombs in violation of international norms, dropping them by aircraft into the valleys where the tribespeople hid. As the yellow-green gas seeped through the sacred forest, the trees withered and countless women and children died in agony.

In the final hour, with ammunition and hope alike exhausted, the Seediq wrote one of the most uncompromising epics of dignity in human history. So as not to burden the husbands and sons at the front, and so as not to fall into enemy hands to be defiled, the women of the tribes took their children and hanged themselves together beneath the towering great trees. Tado Mona led the remnants in a retreat to the cliffs and rock caves of Mahebo, fighting to the last before taking his own life. And Mona Rudao, unwilling to let his corpse become a trophy for the Japanese to parade, walked alone into a lightless natural cave deep in the mountains and shot himself late that year; his remains dried into a mummy, not to be found by hunters until four years later.

The catastrophe did not end there. The following year, the Japanese induced rival tribes to launch the "Second Wushe Incident," all but exterminating the six insurgent tribes — of more than twelve hundred people, only some two hundred elderly, women, and children remained. Mona Rudao's daughter, Mahung Mona (1908–1973), survived this annihilation of her family and her people, yet carried the crushing grief of losing her father, her brothers, and most of her kin. Forcibly resettled with the survivors at Kawanakajima (today's Qingliu in Nantou) under close watch, she lived on through the war's end as a survivor, preserving her lived memory in oral testimony — becoming a vital witness for later generations seeking the truth of the Wushe Incident.

"A true person must walk across the Rainbow Bridge." This is Gaya, the ancestral law of the Seediq — and it is the very weight carried in the phrase Seediq Bale, the "true person." This lament from the depths of the mist, though forcibly erased by the empire's iron and gas, laid bare the utter bankruptcy of Japan's "pacification policy." The fatal final hunt of Mona Rudao and his son, the impossible dilemma of the Hanaoka brothers, and the surviving memory of Mahung Mona together drove, into the very ground of Taiwan's history, an iron pillar of a soul that longs for freedom and dignity — and can never be tamed.
Volumes.volume.underTheRisingSun.sunMoonLakeHydr:
To remake Taiwan from a farming colony into an industrial base that could produce for the empire, the colonial state craved one thing above all: cheap, abundant electric power. Casting its eye across the island, it found the answer in the ceaseless mountain streams deep in the central ranges. And so a plan took shape, audacious almost to the point of fantasy — to tame the waters of the mountains and channel them into Sun Moon Lake.

The conception was ingenious. A dam would be raised at Wujie on the upper Zhuoshui River, and the water led through a tunnel bored across the ridges into Sun Moon Lake, raising and enlarging that highland lake into a vast natural reservoir; the stored water would then rush down a steep drop of more than three hundred metres to strike the generators of a power station far below. It was a gamble against terrain and river, on a scale unprecedented in the East Asia of its day.

In 1919 the Taiwan Power Company was founded and the great project broke ground. But the ideal soon collided with a wall of reality. Costs climbed relentlessly, funds ran dry, and, compounded by the economic slump after the First World War and the heavy blow that the Great Kanto Earthquake dealt to Japan's home finances, the works stalled for most of the 1920s. Half-finished tunnels and buildings were left to decay, standing as a monument to overreach and, for a time, an object of public ridicule.

The turning point came with a sweeping financial reorganisation. Under the forceful leadership of the Taiwan Power Company's president, Matsuki Kan'ichiro, the company raised huge sums by restructuring and taking on foreign loans, bringing the long-abandoned wreck back to life. Work resumed in the early 1930s, and thousands of labourers again poured into the deep mountains to bore tunnels, build dams and string transmission lines across treacherous, slippery terrain — and no small number lost their lives to injury, illness and accident along the way.

In 1934 the first Sun Moon Lake power station was at last completed and brought online, with an installed capacity of a hundred thousand kilowatts, making it at a stroke one of the largest hydroelectric plants in East Asia. A steady flood of cheap power was sent across the whole island, transforming the very constitution of Taiwan's economy — industry that had once depended on imported fuel or small thermal plants now had powerful and reliable energy to drive it.

Cheap power acted like a magnet, drawing power-hungry heavy industry to settle on the island one after another. Japanese aluminium interests built smelters at Kaohsiung and Hualien, and chemical, metal and munitions-related industries rose through the late 1930s, so that for the first time Taiwan saw modern industrial clusters of real scale. The Sun Moon Lake project thus became the hidden but powerful engine beneath Taiwan's wartime industrialisation.

What this power station set in motion, moreover, was not only an industrial map. To carry the electricity, an island-wide high-voltage grid gradually took shape, and electric light began to reach more towns and villages, quietly changing the daily lives of ordinary people. A vast undertaking born purely for industry and war ended up, almost incidentally, lighting the whole island.

The completion of the project was loudly proclaimed by the colonial government as a great achievement of its rule, and the dam and halls of the Sun Moon Lake station became a symbol of Taiwanese "progress" on postcards and in propaganda photographs. Yet behind this image of modernity lay the toil, and sometimes the deaths, of countless labourers in the deep mountains, and the Indigenous people and villages long settled in the highlands who were forced to move as the dam and the rising waters changed their lives. The price of progress was borne, as so often, in silence by those least heard.

The significance of this power station thus reached far beyond every unit of electricity it generated. It was the crucial hinge on which colonial Taiwan turned toward an industrial society, and the first foundation stone of the vast electrical grid the island would inherit. After the war the system was taken over by the Taiwan Power Company and went on undergirding the island's economic take-off. Beneath the shimmering surface of Sun Moon Lake lies a chapter of modernisation written at immense cost, and by sheer engineering will.
Volumes.volume.underTheRisingSun.taitenArtExhibi:
In 1927 the history of art in Taiwan turned a new page. That year the colonial education authorities founded the Taiwan Fine Arts Exhibition — the Taiten — giving the island for the first time a grand and public stage on which painters could compete for recognition before every eye. Held annually and later continued as the Governor-General's exhibition, the Futen, it ran until 1943 and became the beating heart of Taiwan's first true art world.

The very first Taiten dropped a bombshell. In the Eastern-painting section, prized for its meticulous brushwork, three unknown young Taiwanese — Chen Chin, Lin Yu-shan and Kuo Hsueh-hu — were all selected, while many long-established Japanese painters were passed over. Amid the public uproar the press dubbed the three startling newcomers "the three youths of the Taiten," a name written into the island's art history ever since.

Among the three, Chen Chin shone especially bright. She was the only woman, born into a well-to-do Hsinchu family, who travelled to the Women's Fine Arts School in Tokyo to master the refined, meticulous gouache technique of Eastern painting. Her portraits of elegant women and Buddhist figures were repeatedly selected for the Taiten and Japan's Imperial Exhibition, and she became the first professional female painter Taiwan had ever known, breaking open a door in a field long closed to women. Kuo Hsueh-hu's Near Yuanshan and Lin Yu-shan's Lotus Pond, too, became classics of Taiwanese gouache through their rich colour and close observation.

The Taiten was divided into Eastern-painting and Western-painting sections, each with its own strengths. On the Western side, Chen Cheng-po, Liao Chi-chun, Li Mei-shu, Li Shih-chiao and Yen Shui-long studied in Tokyo and returned to render Taiwan's streets, landscapes and people in oils; Chen Cheng-po in particular entered Japan's Imperial Exhibition with works such as Outside Chiayi Street, coming to represent the Taiwanese oil painters who made their name in the central art world.

Behind the Taiten's stage stood a group of important guides. The watercolourist Ishikawa Kinichiro taught for years in Taiwan, and through his gentle style and ardent teaching nurtured a generation of Western-style painters such as Chen Cheng-po; while Japanese painters resident on the island — Shiotsuki Toho, Gobara Koto, Kinoshita Seigai — deeply shaped the exhibition's taste and direction as judges and creators.

It was on this stage, too, that "Taiwan" first became the true subject of the canvas. Painters no longer merely copied the ancients or chased exotic effects but turned their eyes to the ground beneath their feet — the fierce southern sun, the water buffalo in the paddies, the bustle of the temple courtyard, women in traditional dress. This conscious pursuit of "local colour" meant the land and life of Taiwan were, for the first time, seriously seen and recorded in the form of art.

The Taiten's success also stirred energy beyond officialdom. In 1934 a group of Taiwanese and Japanese painters resident on the island founded the Tai-yang Art Association and held the Tai-yang Exhibition, standing as a counterpart to the official Taiten and making the island's artistic life richer and more diverse. It is worth noting that Taiwanese had begun their ascent even earlier — the sculptor Huang Tu-shui was selected for Japan's Imperial Exhibition as early as 1920, lighting a lamp for the painters who followed.

In these works one can clearly see how Taiwanese painters felt their way toward a path of their own, between the academic training of Japan and their own feeling for the native soil. Chen Chin rendered women playing instruments with a gentle brush, Kuo Hsueh-hu filled his canvases with the milling crowds of temple fairs, and Lin Yu-shan's beasts, birds and flowers brimmed with life — inheriting the deep traditions of East Asian painting while holding the light and mood that belonged to this island alone, so that "Taiwanese art" was no longer a vague notion but a concrete and moving presence.

The years of the Taiten and Futen proved that Taiwan could bring forth art of the first rank. They trained technique and opened a stage for exhibition, but they also quietly nourished a cultural confidence and sense of identity — a belief that Taiwan was worth painting, and worth being seen. The tradition these painters laid down, and the bright, tender island under their brushes, still shape to this day how Taiwan looks upon and imagines itself.
Volumes.volume.underTheRisingSun.taiwanParliamen:
In the early 1920s, a group of Taiwanese students living in Tokyo began, under the lamplight of a foreign city, to rethink their own destiny and that of their island. Japan was then in the high tide of Taisho democracy; the vocabulary of parliamentary politics, liberty, and human rights circulated through the streets and campuses of the imperial capital. Taiwan itself, however, remained bound by a colonial system in which the Governor-General held legislative, executive, and judicial power in a single hand. It was within this gap that these young men formed the New People's Society in 1920 — a core group to gather like-minded comrades and search for a way forward, and the seed of a political movement that would last more than a decade.

Out of the Society's debates a clear line of thought gradually emerged. Rather than talk idly of outright independence, or submit to complete assimilation, they would seek political rights for Taiwanese within Japan's own constitutional framework. Their concrete aim was to demand an elected parliament for Taiwan, one holding the power to legislate and to approve the colony's budget. It was a shrewd and cautious middle path — acknowledging the reality of the colonial framework while prying open, within that framework, a space of self-rule for the island's people. Another current of opinion on the island called instead for assimilation, for Taiwanese to be granted the same treatment as Japanese in the home islands. But the petitioners understood that complete assimilation would in the end erase Taiwan's own face, and that only self-rule centered on a parliament could allow Taiwanese to take part, as subjects in their own right, in the political decisions that governed their lives. This insistence on subjecthood gave the movement, beneath its moderate surface, a far-reaching and clear-eyed political ambition.

The movement's acknowledged leader was Lin Hsien-tang, the gentleman of Wufeng. Born of a distinguished family and long esteemed, he became, through his measured and steady bearing, the figure around whom the various factions gathered. Beside him, Chiang Wei-shui labored with fierce energy to organize and connect, while Tsai Pei-huo advanced the cause through his pen and his gift for organization. The three men complemented one another, forming the campaign's most important driving force, and behind them stood countless doctors, lawyers, teachers, landlords, and young students.

In 1921 the first Petition for the Establishment of a Taiwan Parliament, carrying 178 signatures, was formally submitted to the Imperial Diet. Over the following fourteen years the petitioners crossed the sea to Tokyo fifteen times in all, again and again placing the Taiwanese demand at the center of imperial politics. The number of signatories climbed with each round, repeatedly gathering thousands of names, far surpassing the original scale — a sign that this was no longer the lonely cry of a small elite but a steadily spreading island consensus.

Each petition journey to Tokyo was itself a public event. The delegations' departures and returns, the speeches and gatherings along the way, resounded across the island through newspapers and word of mouth. Crowds seeing the petitioners off at the wharf, cheers before the railway stations — these became concrete scenes in which the island's people expressed a shared identity. For Taiwanese long excluded from politics, these actions were like open lessons in civic life, teaching people to understand their own condition in the language of rights, representation, and the rule of law. To sign a petition was no longer merely to write one's name, but to make a public political declaration; to join a farewell rally was to acknowledge oneself a part of this island's fate. In this back-and-forth, round after round, the long-dormant political consciousness of an entire generation was slowly awakened.

Yet the colonial authorities never granted the parliament. Faced with this steady, peaceful pressure, the Governor-General's Office alternated between conciliation and suppression, but yielded not an inch. As the 1930s arrived, militarism rose within Japan, the pace of outward expansion quickened, and the political space on the island tightened accordingly. Squeezed between mounting pressure and the gathering shadow of war, the movement was quietly wound down at last in 1934.

The Taiwan Parliament Petition Movement never won a true parliament, yet it was the longest and most sustained peaceful campaign of the entire colonial era. Across those fourteen years, in the gentlest and most tenacious of ways, it proved that Taiwanese could express a collective will with discipline and strategy. The seeds it sowed — of rights, of representation, of the imagination of self-rule — sank deep into the island's soil, becoming the spiritual bedrock to which every later Taiwanese political and social movement would return, and from which it would draw nourishment.
Volumes.volume.underTheRisingSun.taiwanPeoplesPa:
In the early 1920s, driven by the newspaper Taiwan Minpao and by lecture meetings held across the island, Taiwanese society experienced an unprecedented awakening. Islanders who had once known only taxes and corvée began to speak openly of assemblies, local self-government, and basic civil rights. At the forefront of this current stood a generation of newly educated intellectuals, physicians, and young landowners, gathered beneath the banner of the Taiwan Cultural Association, founded in 1921 with cultural enlightenment as its mission. Through reading rooms, summer schools, and touring lectures, the sparks of awakening were scattered into towns and villages across the island.

Yet there was more than one road to awakening. By the mid-1920s, as socialist and labour-movement ideas circulating across the world reached the island, fissures opened within the Cultural Association. Those who favoured moderate reform and the pursuit of legal political space drifted ever further from the leftist youth, who inclined toward class struggle and placed workers and farmers at the centre. In 1927 that rift could no longer be bridged; the Cultural Association that had once led the island's awakening split apart, its leadership passing to the left, and the moderates were forced to seek another path.

Out of that rupture, on 10 July 1927, Chiang Wei-shui and his allies gathered in Taichung and founded the Taiwanese People's Party. It was the first legally sanctioned political party ever organised by Taiwanese, and under the severe apparatus of colonial rule the mere granting of permission to associate was itself a hard-won breakthrough — a milestone in the island's political history. From that point, Taiwanese political demands were no longer scattered petitions but a lasting force with a clear platform, standing organs, and an organisational backbone.

At its founding the party raised the banner of local self-government and civil liberties, demanding wider political participation for Taiwanese, the reform of an unjust colonial system, and room for speech, assembly, and association. But under Chiang's leadership its centre of gravity leaned increasingly toward the plight of workers and farmers. He believed that unless the lives of the labouring masses could be improved, self-government and civil rights would remain the empty talk of a propertied few. This orientation gradually carried the party from a purely political association toward a mass party bound tightly to social movements.

In 1928 the party helped establish the Taiwan General Federation of Labour, linking scattered unions and labour groups into a single body and throwing its weight behind strikes and rural disputes. This was an important step in the organisation of the Taiwanese labour movement, and it sank the party's roots deep into grassroots society. Its members moved among factories, cane fields, and wharves, carrying the language of politics into the daily lives of ordinary working people; labour disputes and peasant protests now had an organisation to lean on — something the colonial authorities watched with growing wariness.

The party did not shrink from embarrassing the colonial regime. Its most celebrated action concerned the Governor-General's opium licensing policy: when the authorities reopened licences for opium smoking, public opinion was outraged, and the party cabled international bodies to lodge a protest, carrying Taiwan's grievances to eyes beyond the island. This appeal to the international arena, an open challenge to the colonial order, displayed the maturity and nerve of the Taiwanese political movement and let observers at home and abroad glimpse the contradictions of colonial rule — but it also sharply raised the tension between the party and the Governor-General's Office.

That combativeness sealed its fate. As the party's line grew sharper and drew ever closer to workers and farmers, and its ties to the labour movement deepened, the colonial authorities at last ceased to tolerate it. On 18 February 1931, in the very midst of a party gathering, the authorities declared the Taiwanese People's Party an illegal organisation and ordered it dissolved on the spot. The first legal party Taiwanese had built with such care came to an abrupt end, less than four years after its founding, and with it closed the island's brief experiment in legal party politics.

The heavy blow of the ban, compounded by years of tireless labour for the movement, had long eroded Chiang Wei-shui's health. Only months after the party's dissolution, the physician later honoured as a leader of the Taiwanese national movement died of typhoid fever, leaving countless ideals unfinished. Yet in its short life the People's Party had already proved one thing: that Taiwanese could build and run a modern political organisation of their own, and could fuse political, social, and labour movements into a single force. That lesson outlived the decree of prohibition, and it became one of the wellsprings from which later Taiwanese would draw in their continuing pursuit of self-government and democracy.
Volumes.volume.underTheRisingSun.takasagoVolunte:
When the Pacific War spread in 1942 into the dense jungles of the Philippines, New Guinea and the islands of the South Seas, the Japanese army — trained for temperate warfare — suddenly faced an enemy it could not overcome: not the Allies, but the tropical rainforest itself. Humidity, disease and trackless undergrowth paralysed supply lines and felled soldiers by the score. It was then that the army turned to an unlikely source of manpower — the Indigenous peoples of Taiwan's high mountains. Having lived for generations among steep ridges and deep forest, their skill at moving, hunting, finding paths and surviving in the wild was unmatched by any regular unit.

And so, from 1942 onward, wave after wave of recruitment began. Thousands of young Indigenous men were formed into the Takasago Volunteers and shipped across the sea to the front lines of the Philippines, New Guinea and the South Seas. The word "volunteer" implied free choice, yet behind that "voluntary" enlistment lay the accumulated pressure of decades of colonial rule. For years the Government-General had pursued its policies of "governing the savages" and imperial assimilation, teaching village youths to take pride in loyalty to the Emperor. In the atmosphere of total wartime mobilisation, enlistment was cast both as a path to prove one's loyalty and earn dignity and status, and as a social and administrative expectation that was hard to refuse. For many young men the line between "willing" and "compelled" was, in truth, deeply blurred.

Once they reached the battlefield, they were handed the hardest and most dangerous work. They cut roads and dug trenches, and through mud and rainforest that no truck or horse could cross they carried heavy ammunition, rations and the wounded on their own shoulders. When the fighting grew desperate, they too were pushed to the firing line, charging forward and grappling with Allied troops at close quarters. Their endurance, sense of direction and survival skills in the jungle were praised again and again by Japanese commanders, who believed that without these men much of the supply could never have reached the front at all.

Yet praise did not buy safety. Casualties in the South Seas were appalling: beyond the hail of gunfire, still more men fell to malaria, dysentery, hunger and the encirclements of the Allied counteroffensive. Many of those sent overseas never returned to the villages of their birth; and those who by fortune survived and made their way home were met by a world that had utterly changed beneath their feet.

When the war ended and a defeated Japan withdrew, Taiwan passed into the hands of the Republic of China. The Takasago men who had served the Emperor lost, overnight, both the object of their loyalty and the identity that came with it. The new authorities did not regard them as soldiers of merit, and there was no vanished empire left to which they could turn for redress. The blood they had shed, the burdens they had carried, and the comrades whose bones lay in foreign soil were swiftly forgotten amid the postwar changing of regimes, as if none of it had ever been.

The most haunting epilogue of this history belonged to a soldier who hid for years in the jungle of Morotai. Not knowing the war was long over, he survived alone in the dense forest until he was found in 1974. When at last he emerged, he discovered that the Japan he had served and the Taiwan he had left were both gone; even the language, home and kin he had known had changed beyond recognition across nearly three decades. Alone, he bore for an entire unit the loneliness of being left behind by his age.

The story of the Takasago Volunteers embodies the cruelest paradox of the colonial experience. They were conscripted by an empire that had conquered their grandparents only a generation before, sent to distant foreign jungles to kill and to die for that empire. With their lives they proved their courage and their loyalty, and in return they earned a double forgetting: a nation that had never truly counted them as its own left, in the end, no place for them. Today, as this buried history is opened again, the young Indigenous men who sleep forever in the South Seas remind us that beneath the grand narratives of empire there is always a group of people who were the most silent — and the least deserving to be forgotten.
The high mountains of Taiwan were the homeland of Indigenous peoples who for centuries had bowed to no lowland power. To a colonial state hungry for the resources of the forests and determined to complete its rule over the whole island, these cloud-wreathed ranges were the last and hardest frontier to conquer. In 1910 Governor-General Sakuma Samata launched a Five-Year Plan to Subjugate the Aborigines of unprecedented scale, resolved to bring the highlands into the fold by force.

At the heart of the plan was the relentless advance of the guard-line deep into the mountains. This guard-line was a cordon woven from stationed guards, watch-blockhouses, electrified wire, mines and artillery. The colonisers deployed it in tier upon tier along the ridgelines, a vast net drawn slowly tighter to sever the communities' contact and their lines of retreat and force them to surrender their arms.

Behind it all, driving the will of the state, lay the immense value of the camphor locked in those forests. Taiwan's camphor output then led the world, an indispensable raw material for making celluloid and smokeless powder; whoever controlled the camphor-clad highlands commanded a fortune great enough to move world markets. "Pacification" was never merely about "civilising" — it was a seizure of resources and land.

The plan's climax was the 1914 campaign against the Truku people of the eastern mountains, the largest military operation in the entire history of colonial pacification. Undaunted by his age, the seventy-year-old Sakuma personally took the field and directed the campaign, commanding a combined force of army and police numbering more than twenty thousand that converged on the depths of the gorges from several directions, from Hehuanshan and the inner Taroko country.

The Truku were a people renowned for their valour and their consummate skill at mountain warfare. Against this vastly better-armed modern host, their warriors, numbering only a few thousand, resisted stubbornly amid the deep gorges and dense forest, relying on an intimate knowledge of the terrain. They knew every rock face, every hunting trail, every pass fit for ambush, and made the Japanese pay a real price in the steep and difficult mountains, dragging the campaign out for months.

Yet under the merciless grinding of machine guns and mountain artillery, this desperately unequal resistance could not, in the end, be sustained. The Truku strongholds were broken one by one, and the people were forced to lay down their arms and submit to the coloniser's rituals of "surrender." After the war the authorities went further, carrying out "collective relocation," forcibly moving many highland communities to the foothills or the plains for easier surveillance and control — severing forever the traditional hunting grounds and the dwelling places of the ancestral spirits.

The war left its own deep mark on the old governor. Gravely injured while directing the fighting in the mountains, Sakuma stepped down the following year and died in 1915 — he had spent almost the last years of his life on the conquest of these ranges, binding his name forever to this blood-stained chapter of history.

The Taroko campaign was, in fact, no isolated event but the climax of the Five-Year Plan. Before it, the colonisers had already launched a string of campaigns against the Atayal and the Daxi groups of the north, pressing forward with the guard-line and breaking community after community with artillery; the victory at Taroko set a blood-red full stop to this five-year conquest of the highlands.

From then on the Governor-General was able to plant police stations and "savage children's schools" across the vast mountains, embedding the power of the police and the education of assimilation deep among the communities. The people who had once ranged freely over their hunting grounds now lived under close surveillance, and even the guns and ammunition on which their hunting depended were registered, controlled and tightly restricted, their traditional way of life shaken to its roots.

The Taroko War brought the highlands firmly under colonial administration and opened the way for the large-scale timber extraction, camphor monopoly and resource plunder to come. Yet the "submission" won by force was only a thin calm laid over the embers. The deep resentment sown by Sakuma's iron-fisted rule did not die with the fighting; sixteen years later, not far away at Wushe, it would erupt once more, with a roar, in a form more terrible still.
Volumes.volume.underTheRisingSun.treatyOfShimono:
On April 17, 1895, the Treaty of Shimonoseki ended the First Sino-Japanese War and ceded Taiwan and the Penghu Islands to Japan in perpetuity. The decision was made without any consultation of Taiwan's inhabitants — their fate was sealed in a conference room in the Japanese port city of Shimonoseki, where Qing envoy Li Hongzhang and Japanese Prime Minister Itō Hirobumi negotiated the terms of China's surrender. For the Qing court, Taiwan was a disposable bargaining chip; for the two million people living on the island, it was a catastrophe.

The news ignited desperate resistance. Local elites, led by Tang Jingsong — the Qing-appointed governor — hastily proclaimed the 'Republic of Formosa' (臺灣民主國) on May 25, 1895, in an attempt to invoke international sympathy and deter Japanese annexation. It was Asia's first republic in name, but it lacked meaningful military capacity or foreign support. When the Japanese army landed at Keelung on May 29, Tang Jingsong fled to the mainland within days, and the republic's capital at Taipei fell without a fight. Resistance continued in the south under Liu Yongfu and local militia, but by October the Japanese had secured the entire island through a campaign that cost thousands of lives on both sides.

This volume examines the diplomatic negotiations that severed Taiwan from the Qing empire, the brief and tragic experiment of the Republic of Formosa, and the military campaign that marked the beginning of Japan's fifty-year colonial rule — a period that would fundamentally transform every aspect of Taiwanese society, from language and law to infrastructure and identity.
Volumes.volume.underTheRisingSun.wartimeMobiliza:
When full-scale war with China broke out in 1937, Taiwan's fate was utterly rewritten. No longer merely the colonial agricultural base of the Japanese empire, it was pushed forward as a frontline springboard for the 'southward advance' into Southeast Asia. Beginning with the last military Governor-General, Kobayashi Seizo, who proclaimed the threefold line of 'imperialization, industrialization, and use as a southward base,' the whole island was progressively remade into an indispensable part of the empire's war machine. The eighteenth Governor-General, Hasegawa Kiyoshi, who succeeded him in 1940, was the key figure who drove this line to its extreme. A Japanese navy admiral by background, he governed Taiwan in the crucial years when the Pacific War broke out in full, and in 1941 he founded the Kominhokokai (Imperial Subjects Public Service Association), enrolling the whole island's population from the top down in a service organization that mobilized manpower, materiel, and spiritual energy in support of the front. Compared with his predecessor he took a somewhat more conciliatory cultural stance, courting the Taiwanese gentry under the slogan of 'Japan and Taiwan as one' in an effort to win their full commitment to the war.

The human cost of mobilization was staggering. Beginning as 'military laborers' (軍伕) tasked with construction and logistics, Taiwanese men were progressively drawn deeper into the war. From 1942, the colonial government introduced a volunteer-soldier system for Taiwanese, recruiting army and then navy volunteers — later turned into outright conscription — and sending Taiwanese youth to the battlefields of the South Seas. Over 200,000 Taiwanese served in the Japanese military across the Pacific theater, from the jungles of Burma and New Guinea to the Philippines and Hainan Island, and more than 30,000 never returned. Thousands of indigenous youth were enrolled as 'Takasago Volunteers' (高砂義勇隊), prized for their jungle survival skills and deployed in some of the war's most brutal campaigns. The Amis man Suniuo from Taitung — known by the Japanese name Nakamura Teruo and the postwar Chinese name Li Kuang-hui — embodied this most symbolic tragedy: sent with the Takasago Volunteers to the Indonesian island of Morotai in 1943, he became separated from his unit when the war ended and survived alone in the jungle for nearly thirty years, only to be discovered in 1974, stunning the world and standing as an epitome of the Taiwanese soldiers who were mobilized and then forgotten.

The war also penetrated the realms of spirit and culture. The Imperial Subjects Public Service Association drove wartime mobilization into every household and village: people were required to worship at Shinto shrines, to revere the Emperor's official portrait, and to set up a 'kamidana' household altar; schools enforced the everyday use of the 'national language' (Japanese), encouraged people to adopt Japanese surnames, and rewarded model 'national-language families.' Students were organized into 'student soldiers' and labor service corps, boy workers were recruited to travel to Japan's military factories to build aircraft, and women were enrolled in the 'Patriotic Women's Association' to sew uniforms, donate gold ornaments, and see departing soldiers off to the front. Amid this layered penetration, the war was no longer merely a distant battlefield but the whole of daily life. In 1938, the Atayal girl Sayun of Yilan slipped and drowned while helping to escort her departing Japanese teacher to the front; what had been a simple mountain accident was embellished by the Governor-General's Office into a moving legend of a 'patriotic maiden' devoting herself to the nation, honored during Hasegawa Kiyoshi's tenure with the presentation of the 'Bell of Sayun' and turned into a representative case of wartime mobilization propaganda. In 1943, Li Xianglan (whose real name was Yamaguchi Yoshiko), a film superstar famous across China, Japan, and Manchukuo, starred in the state-policy film The Bell of Sayun, adapted from Sayun's story; with her sweet image and singing she carried this mythologized tale across the whole of East Asia, making film and stars too a part of the empire's propaganda machine.

The burden of the wartime economy likewise fell on Taiwanese shoulders. An agriculture once centered on the export of cane sugar and rice was forcibly redirected toward military production; sugar mills, salt fields, and mines were absorbed into a controlled economy, with goods, labor, and capital all marshaled by the Governor-General's Office. Under the slogan of 'increase production to repay the nation,' the rationing system grew ever harsher, and people queued for rice, sugar, cloth, and fuel as the shadows of the black market and hunger gradually settled over the island. The war also left women with wounds that are hard to speak of — some Taiwanese women were sent overseas through deception or coercion to serve as 'comfort women' for the Japanese military, a history long buried in silence and only bravely uncovered by survivors decades after the war. For many Taiwanese families, wartime mobilization meant fathers and brothers who never came home, youth that was conscripted away, and homes reduced to ashes in air raids.

On the home front, Taiwan's factories were converted to produce munitions, aircraft parts, and fuel. Its airfields launched bombing sorties against Allied positions. Food rationing grew severe as agricultural output was requisitioned for the military. In 1944–1945, Allied bombing raids devastated Taipei, Taichung, Kaohsiung, and other major cities, destroying infrastructure that had taken decades to build. When Emperor Hirohito announced Japan's surrender on August 15, 1945, Taiwan entered an uncertain interregnum — its people exhausted by war, its cities in ruins, and its future about to be decided by powers that understood little of the island's complex colonial experience.

What wartime mobilization left behind was a collective memory full of contradiction and trauma. Hasegawa Kiyoshi won cooperation through conciliation, Sayun was molded into a patriotic maiden, Li Xianglan lent her songs to the empire's propaganda, and Suniuo walked alone through nearly thirty years in the jungle — one and the same era, yet refracting the utterly different fates of the ruler, the propaganda machine, and the mobilized. After the war, these Taiwanese soldiers of the Japanese army, conscripted laborers, and wounded women were often forgotten amid the change of regimes, their sacrifices neither acknowledged by the old empire nor easily tolerated by the newly arriving power. Wartime mobilization was not merely a single page in Taiwan's being swept into the Pacific War; it laid bare, more profoundly, the helplessness of a colony under the empire's war regime, and the countless individual stories that were jostled by the tides of history yet long kept silent.
Volumes.volume.underTheRisingSun.worldsGreatestT:
In the early twentieth century in northern Taiwan, while the Imperial Japanese Government-General forged the island into an iron-bound police state through the strict baojia system and the omnipresent "branch-station" Japanese police, in the damp midnight of Taipei's Dadaocheng a dark figure was moving — gliding across the red-brick roofs of Baroque-style mansions, leaping rooftops in the night sky like a swallow.

It was an age in which the people of Taiwan kept silent under the heavy hand of the Japanese police. Yet among the tea houses, wine pavilions, and merchant mansions of Dadaocheng, one name circulated — a name that made the elite Japanese police gnash their teeth even as the city's poor Han laborers and Luohanjiao quietly cheered it on. That name was Liao Tianding.

Liao Tianding, the story's protagonist, was born in 1883 to a poor farming family in Qingshui, Taichung. As a youth he came alone to bustling Dadaocheng to make his living, drifting through the rough-and-tumble streets of Bangka (Wanhua) and Dihua Street. Dadaocheng was then thick with merchant wealth from the "tea gold" trade, but the wealth was all in the hands of Japanese officials, merchants, and a few pro-Japanese Han compradors. The laboring Taiwanese at the bottom could only sweat and bleed under the harsh sun while enduring open discrimination. Under such extreme class and colonial oppression, the nimble, rebellious Liao Tianding resolved to declare war on the system in his own way.

Liao Tianding's legend was a dark nocturnal aesthetic. He was not tall, but his legs were powerfully built, and he had mastered hand-to-hand combat and the art of running across rooftops. His most famous weapons were a razor-sharp dagger and a sash several meters long that he wore tightly wrapped around his waist. In action, he could throw the sash over a high wall or onto the balcony of a mansion, push off with his legs, and vault as if spring-loaded onto roofs several meters high.

He chose his targets carefully: pro-Japanese Han merchants, corrupt officials, and the residences of Japanese officials. He worked with astonishing speed, slipping in during the gaps in Japanese patrols, prying open safes, sweeping up foreign silver and jewels, then vanishing into the night. What humiliated the Japanese police most was that Liao did not rob simply for his own gain — late at night after each haul, he would toss heavy silver dollars into the broken thatched huts of Dadaocheng's poor or hand them out to the starving coolies on the wharves.

On one occasion he was bold enough to slip into the official residence of the Japanese chief of police, silently making off with the chief's ceremonial sword and official seal, and leaving on the desk a slip of paper that read defiantly: "The Great Thief Liao Tianding." This act of "tilling the soil on the head of Jupiter" — provoking the most powerful — left the Government-General mortified. They immediately issued the island's highest-priority arrest warrant, dispatched hundreds of officers and informers, and vowed to tear Liao Tianding to pieces.

Yet what followed on the streets of Taipei was a modern game of cat and mouse. Liao was a master of disguise. One day he might pass an officer as a shoulder-pole peddler; another day he sat in Dadaocheng's most elegant restaurant, the Jiangshanlou, dressed in a Western suit, sipping wine and watching the Japanese police search the streets for him outside.
